{'title': 'How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform', 'doi': '10.1186/s40461-025-00202-7', 'year': 2025, 'venue': 'Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training', 'url': 'http://dx.doi.org/10.1186/s40461-025-00202-7', 'source_db': 'eric_search', 'populations': ['Graduate / Doctoral'], 'user_types': ['Student', 'Educator'], 'study_design': 'Quasi-Experimental Design (QED)', 'extended_summary': 'This paper investigates whether an analytical AI feedback system can improve lesson planning in vocational teacher education. {'title': 'Advancing Education through Tutoring Systems: A Systematic Literature Review', 'doi': None, 'year': 2025, 'venue': 'arXiv', 'url': 'http://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09748v1', 'source_db': 'arxiv_search', 'populations': ['Elementary (PreK-5th)', 'Middle School (6th-8th)', 'High School (9th-12th)', 'Undergraduate'], 'user_types': ['Student'], 'study_design': 'Meta-Analysis / Systematic Review', 'extended_summary': 'This paper addresses how tutoring systems have evolved from early computer-assisted instruction to modern AI-driven Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) and Robot Tutoring Systems (RTS), and what that evolution means for learning, engagement, and ethics in education. The study uses a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review of 86 representative studies selected from an initial pool of 340 records spanning 1972 to 2024. The population context is broad rather than tied to a single sample, because this is a review of prior studies across educational settings. The main conclusions are that tutoring systems show strong promise for improving learning outcomes, personalization, and student engagement, but different forms have different strengths. {'title': 'Studying the effect of AI Code Generators on Supporting Novice Learners in Introductory Programming', 'doi': '10.1145/3544548.3580919', 'year': 2023, 'venue': 'Proceedings of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems', 'url': 'https://doi.org/10.1145/3544548.3580919', 'source_db': 'openalex_search', 'populations': ['Elementary (PreK-5th)', 'Middle School (6th-8th)', 'High School (9th-12th)'], 'user_types': ['Student', 'Educator'], 'study_design': 'Quasi-Experimental Design (QED)', 'extended_summary': 'This paper examines whether AI code generators such as OpenAI Codex help or hinder novice learners who are first learning introductory text-based programming. paper_profiles.title: Identifying the characteristics of effective teacher professional development: a critical review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper critically examines the evidence base behind the widely cited claim that effective teacher professional development (PD) shares a standard set of characteristics: it is sustained, collaborative, teacher-endorsed, subject-specific, externally supported, and practice-based. The authors ask whether the consensus is actually warranted by the underlying studies and whether the way prior reviews have been conducted has led to overconfident conclusions.

The paper is not an intervention study itself; instead, it reviews previous PD reviews, meta-reviews, and primary studies that were cited as evidence for the consensus view. The authors trace the literature backwards from policy documents and review articles, then inspect the original studies underpinning those reviews, focusing especially on studies using pupil achievement as the main outcome. Their illustrative example of a more defensible approach is instructional coaching, which they describe as an observation-feedback-practice cycle led by an expert mentor.

The main conclusion is that the consensus view is not well supported by the evidence as synthesized in prior reviews. The authors argue that many reviews used weak inclusion criteria, included studies that could not establish baseline equivalence or causal impact, and then made invalid inferences from recurring features in successful interventions to claims about causal ingredients. They propose instead combining rigorous causal evidence on whole interventions with independent evidence on mechanisms. In the case of instructional coaching, they argue that repeated practice in the classroom, plus feedback and review, is a more plausible active ingredient than generic claims such as collaboration or duration alone.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a critical methodological review and theory paper, not an empirical evaluation of an intervention. It synthesizes and critiques prior literature rather than reporting a primary study with a causal design or quantitative outcome analysis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has substantial influence on policy and research framing around professional development, especially the critique of consensus features and the proposed evidence-of-mechanism approach. However, it does not itself estimate an intervention effect on student or teacher outcomes, so its empirical impact is indirect and unclear.

paper_profiles.title: The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines how teachers support students’ self-regulated learning (SRL) in classroom practice. The paper asks two broad questions: how teachers attempt to promote SRL, and what is known from classroom observation studies about the relationship between those practices and student outcomes. The authors distinguish between direct promotion of SRL through explicit strategy instruction and indirect promotion through learning environments that require students to regulate their own learning.

The paper does not test a new intervention. Instead, it synthesizes 17 classroom observation studies published between 1990 and 2019, drawing on research conducted in primary and secondary school settings across several countries. The reviewed studies involve teachers and students in subjects such as mathematics, writing, physics, and mixed subject areas. The authors use this evidence to build a framework contrasting explicit strategy instruction, implicit strategy instruction, and indirect activation of SRL through constructivist and autonomy-supportive learning environments.

The main conclusion is that teachers in typical classrooms spend relatively little time on explicit metacognitive strategy instruction, although some classrooms do provide learning environments that indirectly encourage SRL. The review argues that effective support for SRL requires explicit teaching of strategies, including explanations of what to do, when, why, and how, alongside opportunities for reflection and practice. It also concludes that classroom observation should be complemented with teacher and student self-report when studying SRL practice, because observations capture overt behavior but not teachers’ intentions or students’ internal regulation processes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed conceptual/systematic review of classroom observation studies, but it is not a meta-analysis or a primary causal study. Its evidence base is observational and heterogeneous, so it meets only limited credibility criteria for causal inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear relevance for K-12 instructional practice and baseline coaching design, but it does not estimate a causal effect of a specific intervention. Its impact is therefore conceptual and moderate rather than demonstrably large or directly measurable.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual review of 17 classroom-observation studies on teachers’ support for self-regulated learning (SRL), not an intervention effect study. Across the reviewed studies, teachers typically provided very little explicit strategy instruction; for example, suggestions for strategy use were reported in only 2.28% of observation intervals in one study (Moely et al., 1992), and explicit strategy teaching was rare overall. The review argues that explicit instruction, metacognitive reflection, and supportive learning environments are the key baseline/non-AI mechanisms for improving students’ metacognition and SRL.
finding.measure: Classroom observation ratings of direct/indirect SRL support; teacher/student ratings; student self-reported strategy use and achievement where reported in the reviewed studies
finding.study_size: n=541 teachers; n=2318 students across 17 studies reviewed

finding.finding_summary: The review summarizes evidence that when teachers explicitly address metacognitive strategies, students’ strategy use and sometimes performance improve, but the paper itself does not report a new pooled effect size. In the included studies, explicit instruction was associated with better performance in one study (Kistner et al., 2010), while another study found no difference in mathematics progress despite more regular and explicit strategy promotion, though students’ metacognitive strategy use increased over time (Depaepe et al., 2010).
finding.measure: Observed direct strategy instruction; student performance in mathematics; student metacognitive strategy use

paper_profiles.title: Scaling up successfully: Lessons from Kenya’s Tusome national literacy program
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how Kenya’s Tusome national early grade literacy program was implemented at scale and whether the education system had the capacity to support the program’s instructional changes. The authors frame the study around a systems-oriented question: whether Tusome strengthened three core functions of an education system—setting expectations, monitoring progress/accountability, and providing differentiated support to schools and teachers.

Tusome built on prior pilot work, especially the PRIMR initiative, and was designed to deliver structured literacy instruction through teachers’ guides, student books, teacher training, and ongoing coaching. The program was implemented nationally in Kenyan public primary schools and low-cost private APBET schools, with curriculum support officers (CSOs) or instructional coaches visiting classrooms, observing lessons, and providing feedback. The paper draws on program documents, training materials, dashboard data, internal monitoring information, and an external evaluation of learning outcomes.

The authors conclude that Tusome succeeded in clarifying benchmark expectations, increasing classroom visits and feedback, and creating functional monitoring systems through government structures. Basic instructional inputs were widely available, and student learning gains were large on both Kiswahili and English assessments. However, the program did not fully use classroom observation data to target support to the teachers and schools that needed it most. Overall, the paper argues that coherent, structured pedagogy plus frequent coaching and monitoring can support large-scale instructional reform, but differentiated intervention based on data remained underdeveloped.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed implementation/scale-up case study using program documents, monitoring data, and an external evaluation, but it is not itself a randomized or quasi-experimental impact study. The paper’s methodology is primarily descriptive and qualitative with some secondary quantitative reporting, so it meets limited credibility criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported learning gains are large for K-12 interventions, with effect sizes ranging from 0.63 to 1.04 SD on early grade reading outcomes and substantial benchmark increases. The intervention also shows strong system-level improvements in monitoring, accountability, and instructional support at national scale.

finding.finding_summary: This paper evaluates Kenya’s national Tusome literacy scale-up and finds that the program strengthened system capacity for setting expectations, monitoring performance, and delivering instructional support through government structures. The study reports large gains in learning outcomes as well: external evaluation results showed average effect sizes of 0.63 SD in Class 1 and 0.76 SD in Class 2 for Kiswahili, and 0.67 SD in Class 1 and 1.04 SD in Class 2 for English, alongside improved benchmark attainment from 34% to 65% in English and 37% to 66% in Kiswahili for Class 2 students.
finding.measure: System capacity indicators (expectations, monitoring, support), classroom visit counts, dashboard/accountability use, and external evaluation reading outcomes/benchmark attainment
finding.study_size: national_scale; external evaluation sample size not_reported
finding.effect_size: 0.63 SD (Kiswahili Class 1 avg), 0.76 SD (Kiswahili Class 2 avg), 0.67 SD (English Class 1 avg), 1.04 SD (English Class 2 avg)

finding.finding_summary: Tusome produced large and statistically significant improvements in early grade reading outcomes in both Kiswahili and English. In Kiswahili, all six subtasks improved with average effect sizes of 0.63 SD (Class 1) and 0.76 SD (Class 2); in English, all eight subtasks improved with average effect sizes of 0.67 SD (Class 1) and 1.04 SD (Class 2).
finding.measure: EGRA-style reading subtasks: letter sounds, syllable fluency, invented/nonword decoding, oral reading fluency, reading comprehension, listening comprehension, phoneme segmentation, vocabulary
finding.study_size: national_scale; external evaluation sample size not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Does combined cognitive training and physical activity training enhance cognitive abilities more than either alone? A four-condition randomized controlled trial among healthy older adults
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether combining cognitive training with physical activity produces greater cognitive benefits than either intervention alone in healthy older adults. It also examines whether the gains from cognitive training are distinct from, or additive to, those from mild aerobic exercise. The study is positioned as a replication and extension of earlier work on single-domain and combined interventions for cognitive aging.

The intervention used a four-arm randomized controlled design in a retirement community: cognitive training, mild physical activity training, combined cognitive-plus-physical training, and a book-reading/discussion control condition. The cognitive intervention was a computerized, individually adapted CogniFit program delivered in 48 forty-minute sessions over 16 weeks. The physical activity intervention used a group-based senior exercise video with warm-up, cardiovascular, strength, and flexibility components delivered three times per week for 16 weeks. The combined group completed both interventions, and the control group read and discussed a book about active living. Participants were healthy volunteers living at Lakeview retirement community in Lenexa, Kansas, United States, and the study was implemented with support from the community, volunteers, and external partners.

Results showed that participants who received cognitive training, either alone or combined with physical activity, improved on several cognitive outcomes including hand-eye coordination, global visual memory, speed of information processing, visual scanning, and naming. The physical activity-only group did not show comparable cognitive gains. The authors conclude that the observed improvements in the combined condition were driven primarily by cognitive training rather than by mild aerobic activity. They also report substantial attrition before and during training, and note that social support and guided implementation likely contributed to adherence.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled trial with a clear multi-arm design, baseline comparability checks, and repeated-measures analyses, which supports relatively strong causal inference. However, there are notable concerns including substantial attrition, no long-term follow-up, and a non-equivalent active control limited to book reading/discussion rather than a fully matched attention control.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The cognitive training produced medium-to-large improvements on several cognitive outcomes, which is meaningful, but the study is in healthy older adults rather than K-12 learners or teachers. The relevance to the requested K-12 baseline question is therefore indirect and the practical impact is modest for the target education context.

interventions.use_case: Computerized personalized cognitive training delivered through the CogniFit platform with adaptive task selection, practice on memory/attention/visual-spatial exercises, and immediate item-level feedback for older adults.

finding.finding_summary: In a 4-group randomized controlled trial (total recruited n=180; completers n=122), participants who received cognitive training improved on multiple cognitive abilities relative to groups that did not receive cognitive training. The paper reports significant gains in hand-eye coordination, global visual memory, speed of information processing, visual scanning, and naming, with medium-to-large effects (Cohen's d=0.6 to 0.8) and no comparable gains in the physical-activity-only or book-reading control groups.
finding.measure: Computerized neuropsychological evaluation of cognitive abilities (e.g., hand-eye coordination, global visual memory, speed of information processing, visual scanning, naming)

finding.finding_summary: Adherence was reasonably high after baseline testing, with 122/180 completers overall (67.8%), but the combined training group had the highest non-completion rate (39.6%) compared with the cognitive training group (26.7%) and the control group (31.0%). The authors attribute adherence to community and instructor support, and note that health problems and time constraints were the most common barriers.
finding.measure: Study adherence / completion rates and reasons for dropout

paper_profiles.title: Prevention of Mental Health Disorders Using Internet- and Mobile-Based Interventions: A Narrative Review and Recommendations for Future Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This narrative review examines whether Internet- and mobile-based interventions (IMIs) can prevent the onset of mental health disorders, and what research gaps remain. The paper is motivated by the limited reach of traditional face-to-face prevention programs, especially given shortages of clinicians and barriers such as travel, time, and stigma. It asks whether scalable digital preventive interventions can reduce first onset or relapse of disorders, particularly in populations without a full mental disorder at baseline.

The paper synthesizes randomized trials of IMIs across several prevention types: indicated prevention for subthreshold depression and anxiety symptoms, selective prevention for eating disorders and depression risk factors, universal prevention in adolescents, and relapse prevention after prior depressive episodes. The interventions were mostly Internet-delivered cognitive behavioral or mindfulness-based programs, sometimes with guided self-help, asynchronous coach feedback, or occasional mobile reminders. The reviewed studies included adults, young adults, adolescents, and one school-based sample, with contexts such as workers, epilepsy patients, students, and previously hospitalized adults.

The review concludes that evidence is still limited, but there is the most consistent support for indicated prevention of depression. Evidence for anxiety prevention is not positive, and eating-disorder prevention appears promising only in very high-risk subgroups. The authors argue that the field needs larger and more rigorous trials, better diagnostic assessment at baseline and follow-up, stronger attention to human support formats, and more work on mobile features, prediction algorithms, and dissemination strategies. They also emphasize that many studies used small samples, self-report outcomes, or lacked long-term follow-up, limiting confidence in the findings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review and recommendations paper, not an empirical K-12 intervention study. It summarizes prior studies but does not itself report a primary causal design or original outcome data in education settings.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct educational intervention impact estimate to map to the K-12 framework. Its value here is conceptual only, helping define baselines and support models rather than demonstrating measured impact.

paper_profiles.title: Readiness to Implement School-Based Social-Emotional Learning Interventions: Using Research on Factors Related to Implementation to Maximize Quality
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is the introduction to a special issue on readiness to implement school-based social-emotional learning (SEL) interventions. It asks how researchers and practitioners should think about implementation readiness: what factors present before an intervention starts are likely to predict later implementation quality, and how schools can build capacity before adopting evidence-based interventions (EBIs).

Rather than evaluating a single intervention outcome, the paper synthesizes implementation science concepts and uses SEL as the focal domain. It reviews multi-level influences on implementation across school, classroom, and teacher levels, and argues that readiness is a multi-dimensional construct combining motivation, general capacity, and intervention-specific capacity. The paper highlights that implementation success depends not only on whether an intervention is evidence-based, but also on whether the school and its staff are prepared to carry it out with fidelity.

The context is school-based SEL programming, especially preschool and elementary settings, with examples drawn from K-12 school systems and teacher preparation. The authors describe existing capacity-building initiatives such as schoolwide SEL planning supports, leadership-focused professional learning, and preservice teacher preparation as potential ways to increase readiness. Their main conclusion is that future studies should measure readiness before intervention delivery and use those measures to tailor implementation supports, allocate resources strategically, and improve fidelity and sustainability.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual introduction to a special issue on readiness for SEL implementation, not an empirical evaluation of an intervention. It does not present a study design, sample, or causal evidence of outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct measured impact estimates. It is useful for framing implementation readiness and baseline counterfactuals, but it does not report outcome effects.

paper_profiles.title: Telehealth and Autism Prior to and in the Age of COVID-19: A Systematic and Critical Review of the Last Decade
paper_profiles.venue: Clinical Child and Family Psychology Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the evidence base for telehealth use in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) assessment and intervention over the prior decade, with added emphasis on developments accelerated by COVID-19. The review was motivated by the growing need for remote service delivery and by the limited synthesis available on telehealth applications for children and adolescents with ASD and their families.

The authors conducted a systematic search across multiple databases using PRISMA procedures, screened 472 records, and retained 55 studies after quality review. The included studies covered a range of telehealth-supported services, including diagnostic assessment, speech and language assessment, functional assessment, preference assessments, parent training, applied behavior analysis, functional communication training, and cognitive-behavioral interventions. Telehealth was delivered primarily via video conferencing, with some studies using web platforms or apps, and participants included children with ASD, parents, teachers/staff, and other interventionists.

Across studies, telehealth was generally found to be feasible, acceptable, and often comparable to in-person delivery, with many studies reporting improved fidelity, reduced problem behavior, or gains in communication and other child outcomes. The review concludes that telehealth is a promising service modality for ASD, while noting the need for continued research on feasibility, efficacy, and the digital divide that may limit access for some families.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic and critical review, but it is not a meta-analysis and does not present a single pooled estimate or a controlled primary study. Its conclusions depend on heterogeneous underlying studies with varying designs and quality.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests telehealth can improve access and service delivery for ASD, but the paper itself reports no pooled medium/large effect size. The impact is therefore important but evidence is qualitative and heterogeneous rather than directly quantified.

finding.finding_summary: This systematic and critical review synthesized 55 telehealth studies in ASD and concluded that telehealth services were generally equivalent or better than face-to-face delivery across assessment and intervention contexts. The paper emphasizes implementation feasibility, access, and acceptability rather than a single effect estimate; it also notes the digital divide as an important limiting factor.
finding.measure: Systematic review of telehealth assessment/intervention outcomes, feasibility, acceptability, fidelity, and diagnostic agreement across 55 studies

paper_profiles.title: Not quite eye to A.I.: student and teacher perspectives on the use of generative artificial intelligence in the writing process
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how undergraduate students and teachers perceive the appropriate use of generative AI (GenAI), specifically ChatGPT, across stages of the writing process. The authors focus on a practical and policy-oriented question: when is it acceptable for a person to use GenAI to brainstorm, outline, write, revise, provide feedback, or evaluate writing, and how do students and teachers differ in those judgments?

The study used a cross-sectional questionnaire design with 226 participants: 158 students and 68 teachers. Students were recruited from a public research university in the United States, while teachers were recruited through purposive and snowball sampling from multiple institutions worldwide; most teachers were teaching adult/university-level English as a new language or modern languages. Participants rated example ChatGPT prompts and outputs that represented different levels of use or misuse, including use as a model, use with disclosure, and use without disclosure. The questionnaire also included survey items about attitudes toward AI, familiarity with AI, and whether participants’ institutions had AI policies or training.

Results showed broad agreement that GenAI is more acceptable when used as support for brainstorming, outlining, or modeling ideas, and less acceptable when it is used to fully complete writing assignments or when AI-generated text is submitted without disclosure. Teachers and students were generally aligned, but students tended to be somewhat more permissive about undisclosed use, while teachers were somewhat more accepting of GenAI as a model for feedback and evaluation. The authors conclude that GenAI needs clear policies, transparency requirements, and teacher professional development, since both groups reported high concern but low institutional preparedness, little AI training, and limited policy guidance.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed cross-sectional questionnaire study using descriptive statistics, Mann–Whitney U tests, and factor analysis, but it is not an experimental or causal design. Evidence quality is therefore correlational and perceptual rather than intervention-based.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study does not report achievement or behavioral effect sizes from an implemented intervention, only acceptability and preparedness perceptions. Any educational impact is therefore indirect and unclear, though the policy implications are relevant.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a generative AI chatbot to support or perform writing-process tasks such as brainstorming, outlining, drafting, revising, giving feedback, and evaluating student writing.

finding.finding_summary: This study did not measure writing performance gains; instead, it assessed educators’ and students’ perceptions of acceptable GenAI use in the writing process (n=226; students n=158, teachers n=68). Both groups viewed GenAI as more acceptable for brainstorming/outlining and less acceptable for drafting or revising full essays, especially without disclosure. Significant between-group differences appeared on several items, e.g. teachers were more negative about GenAI-written essays with disclosure and without disclosure, while students were more accepting of some uses.
finding.measure: Likert-scale acceptability ratings for GenAI use across brainstorming, outlining, writing, revising, feedback, and evaluation tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper found a strong perceived lack of preparedness at the institutional level for GenAI in writing education. About 94.1% of teachers reported their institution had no AI policy and 95.6% reported no AI training; around 89.7% had not educated students about appropriate AI use. The authors conclude that explicit policies, training, and disclosure guidelines are urgently needed.
finding.measure: Yes/no survey items on institutional AI policy, AI training, and teacher education of students about AI use

paper_profiles.title: The use of ChatGPT in the digital era: Perspectives on chatbot implementation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how educators and students perceive the use of ChatGPT in education during the digital era. Rather than testing an instructional intervention with measured learning outcomes, the study asks what participants think ChatGPT can do in educational settings, what concerns they have, and how it might fit into day-to-day academic support.

The study used a qualitative design with in-depth interviews and content analysis. It sampled 25 participants from higher education institutions in Krabi, Thailand: ten educators and 15 students. Participants were selected purposively and had current experience with ChatGPT. The interview protocol focused on perceived impacts on learning, workload reduction, accuracy of chatbot responses, the possible loss of human interaction, privacy and security, and how ChatGPT might be improved or balanced with human support.

Findings were generally positive. Educators and students saw ChatGPT as useful for answering routine questions, giving immediate feedback, generating ideas, summarising texts, and supporting independent learning. Educators especially valued its potential to reduce workload and free time for more complex teaching tasks. At the same time, participants raised concerns about inaccurate or incomplete responses, bias in training data, reduced personal interaction, and data privacy risks. The paper concludes that ChatGPT can be a helpful educational resource if used alongside human guidance, critical evaluation, and stronger privacy protections.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative interview study with purposive sampling and content analysis, so it provides contextual insight but limited causal credibility. It is peer-reviewed, but it does not test an intervention experimentally or with a comparison group.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports perceived benefits such as workload reduction and immediate feedback, but provides no quantitative impact estimates or demonstrated outcomes. Its overall impact is therefore suggestive and unclear rather than measurable.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a conversational educational assistant for students and educators to answer routine questions, provide immediate feedback, generate ideas, and support academic tasks in higher education.

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that ChatGPT reduced educator workload by answering routine student questions and freeing time for higher-order tasks such as lesson planning and individualized support. This was based on qualitative interviews with n=25 participants (10 educators, 15 students) in higher education in Krabi, Thailand; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived educator workload reduction and task efficiency from qualitative interviews

finding.finding_summary: Educators and students described ChatGPT as increasing confidence, engagement, and motivation because it provided immediate answers and support outside classroom hours. At the same time, participants worried about reduced personal interaction, which could weaken rapport and belonging in the classroom; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived engagement, motivation, confidence, and sense of personal connection from interviews

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT may improve educational practice through faster feedback and support, but also raises institutional concerns about accuracy, privacy, and data security. These are qualitative findings from interviews and discussion rather than a quantitative policy evaluation; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceptions of institutional benefits and risks, including privacy, accuracy, and governance concerns

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models, especially ChatGPT-style systems, for education. Rather than reporting an empirical intervention study, it synthesizes early applications and argues for ways these models might support learning and teaching while also introducing risks related to bias, privacy, integrity, and overreliance. The paper is framed as an early conceptual response to the rapid uptake of large language models in educational settings.

On the learner side, the paper discusses uses such as generating quizzes, summaries, explanations, practice problems, language support, conversational tutoring, and assistance for students with disabilities. On the teacher side, it highlights possible uses in lesson planning, personalized feedback, assessment support, content generation, professional development, and semi-automated grading. The authors emphasize that these applications depend on careful prompting, domain adaptation, and human oversight, but the paper does not evaluate a specific deployed system.

The context is broad rather than tied to one population or institution: the paper addresses primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional learning settings, with a focus on both students and teachers. The main conclusion is that large language models could become powerful educational tools if they are integrated responsibly, with attention to critical thinking, fact-checking, curriculum alignment, fairness, transparency, and governance. The paper proposes mitigation strategies such as human review, training for educators, ethical data practices, and monitoring for bias and misuse.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper and literature-informed conceptual review, not an empirical study with a clear experimental or quasi-experimental design. It provides useful synthesis and recommendations, but does not meet causal evidence standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper plausibly discusses high-level impacts on teaching, learning, and institutional practice, but it reports no original effect sizes or outcome estimates. Its practical implications are broad but still speculative rather than demonstrated empirically.

interventions.use_case: position paper discussing ChatGPT/GPT-3 and related large language models as educational assistants for tutoring-like dialogue, personalized practice, lesson planning, and teacher support
AI-generated feedback on student writing and answers, including semi-automated grading, highlighting strengths/weaknesses, and adaptive feedback for revision
grammar/style correction, summarization, translation, outlining, and language-learning support for students and teachers
generation of quizzes, practice problems, prompts, and instructional materials for classroom and self-directed learning
using AI-based evaluation of student work to identify areas where students are struggling and inform targeted instruction

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by automating or semi-automating lesson planning, quiz generation, grading, and feedback creation. It does not report a new experiment, but cites prior studies as evidence that grading effort can be reduced by up to 85% with NLP-based feedback systems and that automated quiz/question generation can save manual design time.
finding.measure: teacher workload, grading effort, and time savings from automated content/feedback generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests LLMs may support critical thinking, problem-solving, and collaboration through prompts, debate structure, and curated feedback, but also warns that overreliance may weaken these skills. This is a conceptual synthesis rather than a controlled study, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and related 21st-century skills

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can improve reading and writing support through grammar correction, style suggestions, summaries, outlines, and personalized feedback. It synthesizes prior work on automated quiz generation, code explanations, and writing support, but does not present a new empirical test with effect sizes.
finding.measure: reading comprehension, writing quality, grammar/style improvement, and text understanding

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes LLMs as useful for language learning through translation, conversation practice, vocabulary support, pronunciation practice, and grammar explanations. Evidence is discussed from prior conversational-AI studies, but the paper itself does not report a direct experimental estimate.
finding.measure: language-learning performance, conversation practice, pronunciation support, and vocabulary learning

finding.finding_summary: The position paper emphasizes that LLMs can generate and explain content across domains such as mathematics, physics, chemistry, medical education, and programming. It cites examples like quiz generation, code explanations, and medical exam performance, but provides no new quantitative synthesis.
finding.measure: subject-matter learning across STEM and professional domains

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests LLMs may increase engagement, curiosity, and participation, especially through pedagogical agents and interactive prompts. These claims are based on cited examples and recommendations rather than direct evaluation in the paper, so no effect size is available.
finding.measure: engagement, curiosity, and participation

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is the institutional need for governance, privacy, bias mitigation, human oversight, curriculum integration, and fair access. The authors frame LLM adoption as beneficial if responsibly managed, but they also stress risks related to copyright, privacy, cost, and inequality; no quantitative effect size is reported.
finding.measure: policy, governance, privacy/security, fairness, curriculum integration, and access conditions

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the impact of ChatGPT: conversational AI in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the broad question of how ChatGPT affects education, including its benefits, challenges, ethical risks, safeguards, and implications for teachers and learners. Rather than testing a specific intervention in a classroom, it synthesizes prior literature to understand how conversational AI is being discussed and evaluated in educational contexts.

The study is a systematic literature review following Kitchenham and Charters’ SLR approach and PRISMA reporting guidance. It searched multiple databases, screened approximately 729 publications, and included 70 peer-reviewed sources published between 2022 and 2023. The review focused on educational uses of ChatGPT as a conversational AI tool, with particular attention to student engagement, learning outcomes, ethical considerations, and the changing role of educators. The review also extracted themes, advantages, limitations, and recommendations from the literature.

The population is not a single empirical sample but the broader set of ChatGPT users in education discussed across the reviewed studies, especially students and teachers in educational settings. The paper concludes that ChatGPT can support personalized learning, prompt feedback, engagement, and easier access to information, while also raising concerns about bias, accuracy, privacy, transparency, and overreliance. It argues that responsible deployment requires human supervision, user education, clear guidelines, monitoring, and ethical safeguards, and that educators’ roles shift toward facilitation, guidance, and oversight rather than direct content delivery.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic literature review with PRISMA-oriented procedures and stated quality assessment rules, but it does not present primary empirical data or a quantitative meta-analysis. Evidence strength is therefore limited to secondary synthesis and narrative aggregation of prior studies.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports generally positive implications for engagement, critical thinking, and efficiency, but without pooled effect sizes or direct causal estimates. Its impact claims are plausible but remain modest and unclear at the quantitative level.

interventions.use_case: Systematic literature review of ChatGPT as a conversational AI tool in education, including student-facing tutoring, prompt-based interaction, feedback, and educator support/monitoring workflows.

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes prior studies suggesting ChatGPT can improve student engagement through personalized responses, prompt feedback, and immediate access to information. It does not report a pooled effect size, but repeatedly characterizes engagement as improved across the 70 reviewed papers (n=70 papers reviewed, not student participants).
finding.measure: Student engagement, participation, and interactive learning experience as reported across reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT use is associated with improved critical thinking, inquiry, and questioning skills, largely through personalized dialogue and follow-up questioning. This is a narrative synthesis rather than a quantitative estimate, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, inquiry, and questioning skills as described in reviewed literature

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that ChatGPT improves efficiency by giving quick answers, rapid access to information, and supporting drafting, summarizing, and literature-review tasks. No quantitative effect size is provided, but the synthesis consistently frames the tool as saving time for both students and educators.
finding.measure: Task efficiency, rapid information access, and writing support

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that ChatGPT requires institutional safeguards such as human supervision, privacy protection, user education, transparency, and clear guidelines. It also suggests the technology shifts educators from content delivery toward facilitation and monitoring, implying organizational and policy changes rather than a direct measured effect.
finding.measure: Ethical safeguards, governance practices, and educator-role changes synthesized from reviewed studies

paper_profiles.title: Integrating Generative AI in University Teaching and Learning: A Model for Balanced Guidelines
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how generative AI should be integrated into university teaching and learning in a way that is ethical, balanced, and adaptable to local contexts. Rather than testing a specific AI product, the author proposes a policy-oriented model for institutions and instructors, grounded in Chan’s AI Ecological Education Policy Framework and informed by feedback from students and faculty. The goal is to create practical guidelines for responsible AI use in course development, implementation, assessment, and student engagement.

The study developed a six-part guideline document covering rationale, institutional position, key terms, teacher guidelines, student guidelines, and guideposts. The teacher-facing sections emphasize using AI to support course design and implementation while setting clear boundaries for acceptable use, managing authorship, and protecting academic integrity. The student-facing sections are organized around the “6Cs” — consulting, citing, checking, correcting, confessing, and controlling — to encourage responsible use and disclosure of AI assistance.

The paper draws on qualitative feedback from 118 students and 14 academics at a teacher education institution in the Philippines, including undergraduate and graduate students and faculty colleagues. Participants discussed AI’s benefits, risks, and the clarity and practicality of the proposed policy. The main conclusion is that universities should adopt flexible, context-sensitive AI guidelines supported by stakeholder consultation, AI literacy, ethical oversight, curricular adaptation, and institutional readiness rather than outright prohibition.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative design-thinking/policy-development study with thematic analysis of stakeholder feedback, not a controlled impact evaluation. It provides useful implementation evidence, but credibility for causal claims is limited because there is no comparison group, randomization, or quantitative outcome testing.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful institutional and workflow benefits from balanced AI guidance, but it reports perceptions rather than measured impacts. Because no effect sizes or direct outcome changes are demonstrated, the impact is plausible but unclear.

interventions.use_case: Use of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Copilot, and Gemini as teacher- and student-facing assistants for course development, learning support, and academic work, with an emphasis on balanced institutional guidelines rather than a tested tutoring intervention.
Use of tools like Grammarly, QuillBot, and Turnitin for grammar checking, writing support, and academic integrity checks in teacher and student workflows.

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes and refines a balanced, context-sensitive generative AI guideline for higher education using feedback from 118 students and 14 academics plus 14 teachers in a focus group. Participants generally endorsed the need for explicit AI policies, ethical boundaries, and institutional readiness, suggesting the guideline could support governance, curriculum integration, and implementation planning, but no quantitative effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative feedback on proposed AI policy/guidelines; thematic analysis of open-ended responses and focus group discussion
finding.study_size: n=132 students/academics in feedback plus n=14 teachers in FGD (total reported relevant participants n=146)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and students reported that generative AI and related tools can streamline academic tasks such as drafting reports, checking grammar, curating materials, and simplifying work processes. The paper does not provide experimental effect sizes, but the qualitative findings consistently frame AI as improving productivity and reducing routine workload.
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of task simplification, assistance, and productivity in academic workflows

finding.finding_summary: Participants saw potential support for planning and decision-making, but also raised concerns about intellectual laziness, dependence, reduced critical thinking, and threats to authentic learning. The evidence is qualitative and does not report effect sizes; overall, AI was viewed as helpful for some cognitive support tasks while simultaneously posing risks to critical thinking and originality.
finding.measure: Qualitative perceptions of critical thinking, dependence, authenticity, and responsible AI use

finding.finding_summary: Students expressed enthusiasm, willingness to adopt AI, and a desire to use it responsibly, while teachers emphasized cautious adoption and ethical boundaries. The study suggests AI can increase engagement and openness to innovation, but it also generates anxiety around misuse and academic dishonesty; no quantitative measures were reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative perceptions of enthusiasm, engagement, responsible use, and concern about misuse

paper_profiles.title: A systematic literature review of empirical research on ChatGPT in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the early empirical evidence on how ChatGPT has been used in education and what initial effects, opportunities, and concerns have been reported. The authors note that ChatGPT rapidly entered educational settings, but that there was no systematic synthesis focused specifically on empirical studies, so they set out to review how students and teachers had begun using it and what findings those studies reported.

The intervention/approach studied is not a single classroom program, but the use of ChatGPT as an AI-supported tool across educational tasks such as answering questions, giving feedback, generating lesson plans, creating quizzes, supporting writing, translating and paraphrasing text, and aiding self-directed or personalized learning. The review followed PRISMA and included 14 empirical studies published up to April 10, 2023. The populations represented were mainly higher-education students and teachers, plus one elementary-school teacher study; the reviewed studies came from multiple countries and used qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods designs.

The review concludes that ChatGPT can support learning and teaching by acting as a virtual assistant, improving writing and language tasks, helping with concept understanding, and increasing teacher productivity. At the same time, the paper emphasizes risks such as inaccurate outputs, overreliance, reduced creativity or collaboration, and threats to academic integrity. The authors argue that effective use requires structured training, clear rules and regulations, and broader policy and research attention to responsible integration in education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review of 14 empirical studies, but it synthesizes mostly small, heterogeneous, and largely qualitative or quasi-experimental studies rather than a single well-controlled causal design. The review itself is peer-reviewed and methodologically transparent, yet the underlying evidence base has limited credibility for strong causal inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests meaningful but mostly unquantified benefits for learning support and teacher productivity, with some negative concerns around overuse and integrity. Because no pooled effect sizes are reported and the primary evidence is heterogeneous, the overall impact appears modest and somewhat unclear rather than clearly large.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a virtual intelligent assistant, on-demand question answerer, lesson-planning aid, writing coach, and personalized learning support tool for students and teachers across educational contexts.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed empirical studies (n=14 studies total; writing/language use reported in multiple studies), ChatGPT generally supported writing and language tasks such as idea generation, essay writing, summarizing, paraphrasing, translation, and grammar checking. However, the review also notes that overuse could reduce innovative capacity and collaborative learning competencies, suggesting benefits for literacy tasks but possible harms when reliance is excessive.
finding.measure: Writing tasks, language-use tasks, participant perceptions, and reported writing/language performance or proficiency outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that ChatGPT helped students in mathematics education understand concepts, follow structured learning plans, and improve problem-solving performance. Specific studies found improved efficiency and learning experiences in solving mathematics problems, but the review does not provide a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Mathematics problem-solving performance, understanding of problem-solving processes, and participant reports

finding.finding_summary: Some reviewed studies suggest ChatGPT can support discipline-specific reasoning, such as critical thinking, hazard recognition, and problem analysis in journalism and construction education. These findings indicate potential gains in reasoning-related academic tasks, though the evidence is heterogeneous and not summarized with effect sizes.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, reasoning, and hazard recognition outcomes in applied disciplinary contexts

finding.finding_summary: The review indicates that ChatGPT supported understanding of concepts, homework completion, structured learning plans, and task clarification across several non-math domains, including computer engineering, construction education, journalism, English education, early education, and social sciences. These studies generally report improved learning support and subject-specific task completion, but no standardized pooled effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Concept understanding, homework/task completion, subject-specific learning support, and participant perceptions

finding.finding_summary: The review reports positive effects on engagement and motivation in some studies, with ChatGPT supporting more interactive and personalized learning experiences. At the same time, it notes concerns that overuse may reduce motivation to attend class and weaken collaborative learning, so the overall pattern is mixed.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, collaborative learning tendencies, and learner perceptions

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was associated with gains in critical thinking, reasoning, problem-solving, and independent learning in several studies, especially when used for guided exploration and step-by-step support. However, the review also highlights that overuse may weaken innovative capacities and collaborative competencies, yielding a mixed overall picture.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, reasoning, problem-solving, innovation, collaboration, and self-directed learning indicators

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that ChatGPT improved productivity and efficiency by helping them create lesson plans, generate quizzes, provide resources, preplan activities, and answer questions more quickly. The review also describes reduced workload and time savings, but does not provide quantitative effect sizes.
finding.measure: Teacher productivity, workload, time savings, and task efficiency; also student task efficiency in some studies

finding.finding_summary: The review emphasizes the need for structured training, clear rules and regulations, and ongoing policymaker/stakeholder dialogue to ensure responsible ChatGPT use. It also notes concerns about academic integrity, plagiarism, hallucinations, and the need to redesign assessment practices, but these are synthesized recommendations rather than direct causal estimates.
finding.measure: Policy and governance recommendations, academic integrity concerns, and assessment redesign implications

paper_profiles.title: Examining Korean EFL College Students’ Experiences and Perceptions of Using ChatGPT as a Writing Revision Tool
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of English Teaching through Movies and Media
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how Korean EFL college students experienced and perceived ChatGPT when using it to revise English paragraphs in a general English course focused on academic writing. The paper asks whether students found ChatGPT helpful for revision, what challenges they encountered, and what roles they expected teachers to play when AI tools are used in writing instruction.

The intervention/approach was a classroom-based writing revision activity in which students wrote paragraphs during class and then, as homework, used generative AI chatbots—primarily ChatGPT—to proofread and revise their original texts. Students were not given fixed prompts; instead, they were shown example prompts such as asking the AI to proofread or revise a paragraph. They then completed a survey with Likert-scale and open-ended questions about satisfaction, perceived usefulness, feedback quality, difficulties, and teacher roles. The analysis combined descriptive statistics and thematic analysis.

The participants were 71 Korean university students in a mandatory general English course at a metropolitan four-year university in South Korea. Most were first-year undergraduates and self-identified as English beginners or low-intermediate learners. The findings show generally positive perceptions: students valued ChatGPT’s convenience, immediate feedback, and error correction in vocabulary, grammar, and coherence. However, they also reported problems such as lack of explanations for corrections, overly advanced vocabulary, misaligned responses, uncertainty about learning effectiveness, and a sense that AI revisions sometimes erased their authorship.

Overall, students did not view ChatGPT as a full replacement for teachers. They expected instructors to clarify and verify AI feedback, teach effective prompting, supervise ethical use, and provide emotional encouragement. The paper concludes that ChatGPT can support writing revision as a supplementary tool, but effective integration requires human oversight, guidance on prompt design, and balanced use of AI and teacher feedback.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative/survey study with descriptive statistics and thematic analysis, but it is not experimental and relies on self-report data from one course cohort. It provides useful implementation evidence, but causal inference is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceptions and practical benefits, but no objective learning gains or effect sizes were measured. The impact is therefore suggestive and modest/unclear rather than demonstrated at scale.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a writing revision chatbot for Korean EFL college students to proofread and revise paragraphs, generate feedback on grammar, vocabulary, clarity, coherence, and organization, and provide alternative rewritten versions.
Generative AI writing support for EFL paragraph revision, including proofreading, vocabulary replacement, coherence editing, and content enrichment in academic writing assignments.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported generally positive experiences using ChatGPT for paragraph revision in a general English academic writing course (n=71). Satisfaction with receiving feedback and revising with ChatGPT was high (M=4.13/5, SD=0.79), and students rated its help for vocabulary, grammar, clarity, coherence, and organization positively (e.g., vocabulary/expression M=4.23, grammar M=4.17).
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of satisfaction, helpfulness, and perceived improvement in writing quality; thematic responses about revision benefits

finding.finding_summary: Students expressed strong willingness to continue using ChatGPT for future paragraph editing (M=4.21/5, SD=0.91) and described the tool as convenient, fast, and reassuring. Qualitative comments also noted increased confidence and satisfaction, though some students worried about frustration, anxiety, and diminished authorship.
finding.measure: Future-use intention, satisfaction, and thematic comments on convenience/confidence

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests some metacognitive support from ChatGPT because students used it to identify errors and compare revisions, but many also reported uncertainty about learning effectiveness and difficulty critically evaluating AI feedback. The authors highlight that students often needed teacher guidance to interpret outputs, which limits claims of independent skill development.
finding.measure: Survey responses and open-ended reflections on understanding feedback and evaluating revisions

finding.finding_summary: Students strongly valued the time-saving and always-available nature of ChatGPT for revision, describing it as easy, fast, and hassle-free. Qualitative responses emphasized instant replies and no restrictions of time or place, indicating improved efficiency in obtaining writing feedback.
finding.measure: Survey Likert items and thematic comments on convenience, instant reply, and access

finding.finding_summary: Students did not believe generative AI could fully replace human instructors for feedback (M=2.35/5, SD=1.10), and most preferred either a combination of ChatGPT and instructors or instructors only. They expected teachers to clarify AI feedback, verify accuracy, teach prompt use and ethical practices, and provide emotional support, implying a blended human-AI instructional model rather than replacement.
finding.measure: Survey item on replacement of instructor feedback; choice between ChatGPT and instructor feedback; thematic analysis of anticipated teacher roles

paper_profiles.title: Potential of ChatGPT as a digital language learning assistant: EFL teachers’ and students’ perceptions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines EFL teachers’ and students’ perceptions of ChatGPT as a digital language learning assistant, addressing a gap in the literature on how generative AI is understood and potentially used in everyday language education. The study focuses on whether ChatGPT is seen as useful for language acquisition, motivation, authentic resource access, autonomy, and feedback, while also documenting concerns about accuracy, reliability, and suitability across different learners.

The paper uses a cross-sectional survey design with 80 EFL teachers and 46 EFL students in East Java, Indonesia. Participants were recruited through convenience sampling from educational institutions, and both groups completed a 14-item questionnaire developed for the study and reviewed by experts in technology-enhanced language learning. Data were collected online over one week and analyzed descriptively using frequencies, percentages, means, and standard deviations.

Findings suggest that both teachers and students generally view ChatGPT positively for language learning support, especially for real-time feedback, increased engagement, autonomous practice, and access to authentic language resources. At the same time, respondents raised concerns about language accuracy, technical limitations, the need for teacher guidance, and the importance of clear guidelines and training. The study concludes that ChatGPT has promise as a language learning assistant, but effective integration depends on pedagogical support, curricular alignment, and structured use rather than unmediated adoption.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed cross-sectional survey study with convenience sampling and self-report measures, so it provides descriptive evidence but cannot support causal claims. The design is correlational/attitudinal rather than experimental, and the paper reports perceptions instead of observed outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests generally positive perceived impact, but it does not report measurable achievement gains or effect sizes. The evidence is therefore useful for implementation insights but the real-world impact on learning remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a digital language learning assistant for EFL learners and teachers, providing conversational practice, immediate feedback, personalized support, and access to authentic language resources.

finding.finding_summary: EFL teachers and students perceived ChatGPT as beneficial for language acquisition and proficiency. Among teachers (n=80), 63.7% agreed or strongly agreed that ChatGPT can benefit language acquisition and proficiency (mean=4.08, SD=0.839); among students (n=46), 93.4% agreed or strongly agreed that it can benefit English proficiency, with strong consensus (SD=0.620).
finding.measure: Perceptions of ChatGPT’s effect on language acquisition and English proficiency (Likert-scale survey items)

finding.finding_summary: Respondents believed ChatGPT could improve engagement and motivation in language learning. Teachers (n=80) reported 56.3% agreement and a mean of 4.13 (SD=0.862), while students (n=46) reported 93.4% agreement/strong agreement with very high consensus (SD=0.620).
finding.measure: Perceptions of engagement and motivation in language learning activities (Likert-scale survey items)

finding.finding_summary: Participants viewed ChatGPT as facilitating access to authentic language resources and knowledge. Teachers (n=80) showed moderate agreement (36.2% agree, 23.8% strongly agree; mean=3.69, SD=1.038), and students (n=46) also largely agreed that ChatGPT improves access to authentic resources (47.8% agree, 26.1% strongly agree; SD=0.855).
finding.measure: Perceived access to authentic language resources and knowledge (Likert-scale survey items)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and students perceived ChatGPT as supporting autonomous learning and self-directed practice. Teachers reported 76.3% agreement/strong agreement (mean not explicitly provided in text for this item), and students reported 93.5% agreement/strong agreement, indicating strong perceived support for independent practice and self-direction.
finding.measure: Perceptions of autonomous learning and self-directed language practice (Likert-scale survey items)

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that ChatGPT may improve planning and instructional support through personalized feedback, timely constructive feedback, and clearer workflows, but this is based on perceptions rather than observed productivity outcomes. Teachers and students strongly agreed that proper training, clear guidelines, and timely feedback would improve effectiveness, suggesting perceived gains in implementation efficiency rather than measured workload reduction.
finding.measure: Perceptions of support, guidance, clear guidelines, and timely feedback for effective use (Likert-scale survey items)

paper_profiles.title: A Systematic Review of ChatGPT for English as a Foreign Language Writing: Opportunities, Challenges, and Recommendations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how ChatGPT is being used in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing and what opportunities, challenges, and recommendations emerge from the existing literature. Rather than reporting a new classroom intervention, it systematically reviews 20 of the most relevant empirical studies on ChatGPT and EFL writing published in 2023–2024, following PRISMA guidelines. The review draws on studies of learner perceptions, writing improvement, automated feedback, automated essay scoring, and teacher feedback support.

Across the reviewed literature, ChatGPT is portrayed as a tool that can support multiple stages of writing, including brainstorming, outlining, drafting, revising, proofreading, summarizing, and reflective comparison of AI output with human knowledge. The paper emphasizes that ChatGPT can provide instant feedback, generate prompts, and sometimes approximate human scoring or error detection, but it is weaker on deep structure, pragmatics, and context-sensitive judgment. Several studies also suggest that ChatGPT may improve learner motivation, self-efficacy, and teacher self-efficacy when integrated into instruction.

The paper focuses on EFL learners and teachers in a range of international contexts, especially studies from East Asia, and argues for a balanced, supervised, and collaborative approach to AI integration. The author concludes that ChatGPT should complement rather than replace human instruction, with teacher oversight, critical engagement, and AI literacy practices built into writing curricula. The recommendations stress ethical use, collaboration between teachers and learners, and deliberate alignment between ChatGPT use and writing pedagogy.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review, but it synthesizes heterogeneous primary studies rather than presenting a single well-controlled causal design. The evidence base includes a mix of experimental, correlational, and descriptive studies, so credibility is informative but not high enough for blue/green on the review alone.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reviewed studies suggest meaningful promise for writing improvement and motivation, but the paper does not report pooled effect sizes and repeatedly notes limitations and context dependence. Overall impact appears promising but still modest/unclear at the review level rather than definitively large.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of ChatGPT use in EFL writing for brainstorming, drafting, editing, proofreading, feedback generation, register awareness, and writing assessment support.
ChatGPT used as an automated writing evaluation and feedback tool to identify errors, provide corrective feedback, and compare with human teacher feedback.
ChatGPT used as a conversational writing assistant/mentor that answers questions, supports prompt-based writing tasks, and scaffolds planning and revision.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, ChatGPT generally improved EFL writing quality, especially organization, coherence, grammar, vocabulary, clarity, and cohesion. Evidence included significant gains in writing skills in several intervention studies (e.g., Song & Song, 2023; Yan, 2023; Ghafouri et al., 2024), but the review also noted limitations in detecting deep-structure and pragmatic errors and uneven effectiveness across registers.
finding.measure: EFL academic writing performance, writing skill ratings, error detection, coherence/clarity, register knowledge, automated essay scoring, revised essay scores
finding.study_size: various studies reviewed; not_reported for aggregate synthesis

finding.finding_summary: The review reports improved writing motivation, self-efficacy, engagement, and behavioral intention to use ChatGPT among EFL learners. For example, studies summarized in the review found significant gains in motivation and self-efficacy after AI-assisted instruction, and positive attitudes toward continued use.
finding.measure: Motivation surveys, self-efficacy scales, attitudes, behavioral intention, engagement reports
finding.study_size: various studies reviewed; not_reported for aggregate synthesis

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was framed as supporting critical thinking and collaborative writing, but the review also warned that over-reliance could weaken critical thinking and independent writing development. Students were reported to engage in collaborative writing and reflective comparison tasks, yet the paper emphasized the need for corroboration, critical evaluation, and human oversight.
finding.measure: Collaborative writing tendency, reflective comparison tasks, critical engagement with AI output, reported dependence/over-reliance concerns
finding.study_size: various studies reviewed; not_reported for aggregate synthesis

finding.finding_summary: The review consistently describes ChatGPT as improving writing efficiency through rapid feedback, automated drafting support, brainstorming, summarization, and scalable scoring. It was repeatedly characterized as reducing teacher workload and speeding up editing/proofreading, although the paper does not report a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Feedback turnaround, writing efficiency, teacher workload, scalability of assessment, automated workflow support
finding.study_size: various studies reviewed; not_reported for aggregate synthesis

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT may reshape writing curricula, teacher roles, and AI literacy practices, but it also highlights governance concerns such as academic integrity, privacy, and unequal access. Recommendations emphasize curriculum integration, teacher-student communities of practice, and supervised implementation rather than unfettered adoption.
finding.measure: Curriculum recommendations, academic integrity concerns, privacy/ethics considerations, institutional guidance

paper_profiles.title: Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how university students perceive generative AI technologies, especially ChatGPT, in higher education. It focuses on students’ familiarity with GenAI, their willingness to use it, their perceptions of its benefits, and the concerns they associate with its use. The study is motivated by the rapid growth of GenAI and the need for evidence to inform how such tools might be responsibly integrated into teaching and learning.

The authors used an online survey with both closed-ended and open-ended items. Data came from 399 undergraduate and postgraduate students across six universities in Hong Kong and covered students from multiple disciplines. The questionnaire examined knowledge of GenAI, willingness to use it, and concerns about accuracy, privacy, ethics, skill development, career prospects, and educational value. Responses were analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and thematic analysis of open-ended responses.

The findings suggest that students generally understand both the potential and the limitations of GenAI and are broadly positive about using it for learning, writing, brainstorming, research, and administrative support. Students especially valued personalized feedback, immediate help, and 24/7 availability. At the same time, they raised concerns about inaccurate output, transparency, privacy, plagiarism, over-reliance, weakened critical thinking and creativity, job displacement, and the lack of institutional policy guidance. The paper concludes that educators and policymakers should improve AI literacy, provide ethical guidance and safeguards, and develop clear institutional policies to support responsible and effective GenAI integration in higher education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed cross-sectional survey with open-ended responses, so it provides useful descriptive evidence but no causal estimate. It mainly captures student perceptions rather than measured learning effects, which limits credibility for impact claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests potentially meaningful benefits for writing support, research assistance, and efficiency, but these are self-reported perceptions rather than demonstrated learning gains. Because no effect sizes or outcome improvements were measured, the practical impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: student-facing generative AI/ChatGPT used for personalized learning support, immediate question answering, brainstorming, writing feedback, literature search, and research assistance in higher education
genAI used to provide personalized and immediate feedback and suggestions on assignments and writing, including grammar, paraphrasing, and polishing text
generative AI used as a writing assistant for brainstorming, drafting support, paraphrasing, and language polishing for academic writing

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test an intervention effect, but it reports that 399 Hong Kong university students generally favored institutional integration of GenAI and wanted policies, guidelines, and safeguards to support responsible use. Students emphasized the need for implementation strategies, governance, privacy protection, and curriculum adaptation to make GenAI acceptable in higher education.
finding.measure: Survey responses and open-ended thematic analysis about policy, governance, and institutional integration of GenAI

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived GenAI as useful for writing support, including idea generation, feedback, grammar correction, paraphrasing, polishing articles, and citation help. This was based on survey means and qualitative responses from the full sample (n=399), but no learning outcome effect size was estimated because the study measured perceptions rather than performance.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness for writing, brainstorming, grammar, paraphrasing, and assignment feedback

finding.finding_summary: Participants also viewed GenAI as beneficial for research and analysis tasks, such as literature searching, summarizing readings, information retrieval, and generating hypotheses from data. The paper reports descriptive survey findings and thematic examples from n=399 students, indicating a broadly positive perception of GenAI for academic research workflows.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness for research, literature searching, summarization, and initial data analysis

finding.finding_summary: Students saw GenAI as helpful for supporting deeper thinking and creativity when used as a prompt or feedback tool, but they also worried that over-reliance could reduce critical thinking and creativity. The study is qualitative/correlational and reports perceptions rather than outcomes, so no effect size is available.
finding.measure: Perceived impact on critical thinking, creativity, and decision-making

finding.finding_summary: Students believed GenAI could save time and reduce workload by handling repetitive tasks, providing immediate support 24/7, and helping with administrative or routine academic work. The paper reports positive perceptions in a survey of 399 students, but does not evaluate actual time savings or productivity gains.
finding.measure: Perceived time-saving, immediacy, and workload reduction

paper_profiles.title: AI to the rescue: Exploring the potential of ChatGPT as a teacher ally for workload relief and burnout prevention
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can help reduce teacher workload and prevent burnout by supporting lesson planning and content development. The authors focus on non-teaching tasks that are especially time-consuming for teachers, arguing that these duties contribute substantially to stress and burnout.
