paper_profiles.title: Exploring LLM-Generated Feedback for Economics Essays: How Teaching Assistants Evaluate and Envision Its Use
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether LLM-generated feedback can serve as useful suggestions for human instructors when grading knowledge-intensive student writing, and how such feedback should be presented to support human review. Rather than testing student learning outcomes, the study focuses on teaching assistants’ experiences comparing AI-generated feedback with their own handwritten comments on economics essays.

The authors developed an LLM-based feedback pipeline for short essay responses in an introductory college economics course. The system decomposed feedback generation into modular steps: identifying relevant evidence in the essay, judging whether a rubric criterion was met, and generating a feedback comment. The feedback was visualized as in-text comments in a Word document, alongside highlighted sentences and, in some cases, retrieved historic instructor feedback. GPT-4o was used to generate the AI feedback.

The study was conducted in Fall 2024 in one university ECON101 course with 5 teaching assistants over 20 one-hour think-aloud sessions across four writing assignments. TAs first graded essays as usual, then reviewed AI feedback on the same essays and discussed whether they would use it in practice. The findings suggest that AI feedback was often more detailed, more rubric-aligned, and more likely to include praise, explanations, and guiding questions than human comments. TAs felt it could speed reading and comment writing, improve consistency, and act as a useful second opinion.

At the same time, participants noted important limitations: the system could be overly rigid, miss broader conceptual misunderstandings, and fail when rubrics were underspecified. The paper concludes that AI feedback is best treated as a supplementary tool rather than a replacement for human judgment, and that explicit rubrics, sentence highlights, and intermediate outputs are important design features for useful human-AI collaboration.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, IRB-approved think-aloud study with 5 TAs and no randomized comparison or quantitative outcome estimation. It provides credible exploratory evidence about usability and perceived value, but not causal evidence of learning or productivity effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports promising but subjective benefits such as faster grading and better feedback quality, without measured effect sizes or student outcomes. Impact appears modest and unclear at the population level because the evidence is based on a small, specialized sample and qualitative judgments.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated rubric-based feedback on college economics essays, presented as in-text comments with highlighted evidence and suggested revisions for teaching assistants to review and potentially reuse

finding.finding_summary: In think-aloud sessions with 5 teaching assistants over 20 one-hour sessions across 4 writing assignments, participants consistently reported that AI-generated feedback and sentence highlights would expedite grading and feedback writing. They described the system as saving time in reading, locating evidence, constructing comments, and standardizing decisions, but these were perceptions rather than measured productivity gains; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: TA perceptions of grading speed, time saved reading and writing feedback, and workflow efficiency from think-aloud interviews

finding.finding_summary: The AI feedback was perceived as more detailed, personalized, and aligned with rubric criteria than human/instructor historical feedback, often including praise, explanations, and guiding questions that TAs valued. However, participants also noted that rubric-driven feedback could be too rigid, overly fragmented, or miss broader writing quality and deeper conceptual issues, so the perceived quality advantages were conditional rather than uniform.
finding.measure: TA evaluations of feedback quality, specificity, personalization, and rubric alignment for economics essay comments

paper_profiles.title: Feedback Capacity and a Variant of the Kalman Filter with ARMA Gaussian Noises: Explicit Bounds and Feedback Coding Design
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a control and information-theoretic problem: how to characterize the feedback capacity of additive colored Gaussian noise channels when the noise follows a finite-order ARMA process. The authors aim to derive explicit lower bounds on feedback capacity and to provide feedback coding schemes that can achieve those bounds.

The central approach is to connect the feedback-channel problem to a variant of the Kalman filter. By reformulating an ARMA-noise channel as an equivalent Kalman filtering system, the paper derives structural conditions under which the closed-loop system yields a lower bound on feedback capacity. The analysis is developed for general finite-order ARMA measurement noise, with special attention to first-order ARMA and second-order MA cases.

The paper does not study a human or educational population; it is a mathematical/theoretical contribution in communication theory. Its main conclusions are that the proposed bounds are consistent with and, in some special cases, tight relative to prior results in the literature. The authors also derive recursive coding schemes based on the Kalman-filter interpretation, and they note that the framework may be extended in future work to obtain tighter bounds or broader structural insights.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a theoretical/control-theory paper on feedback capacity in Gaussian communication channels, not an empirical study of educational technology or teacher coaching. It contains no study design, participants, or educational intervention evaluation relevant to the retrieval topic.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no measured educational impact, effect size, or practical intervention outcome related to teacher planning, feedback quality, or instructional coaching. The paper does not provide evidence of positive or negative impact on the requested education outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Feedback generation of quantum Fock states by discrete QND measures
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a control-theoretic problem in quantum physics: how to use feedback from quantum non-demolition (QND) measurements to drive a microwave cavity toward a desired photon-number (Fock) state. The authors focus on the mathematical design and proof of convergence for a closed-loop feedback scheme, rather than on human learning or educational intervention.

The proposed approach combines a discrete-time quantum filter, which estimates the cavity state from atom detector clicks, with a Lyapunov-based control law that injects coherent microwave pulses to increase the probability of a target Fock state. The system is modeled as a truncated finite-dimensional quantum Markov process representing atom-cavity interactions in a superconducting microwave cavity setup.

The paper proves almost sure convergence to the target Fock state under ideal measurement and model assumptions, and also shows robustness properties under certain detection imperfections through simulations. It further proves a contraction property for the associated quantum filter, suggesting that the estimator forgets its initial condition over time. The work is theoretical and physics-oriented, with no educational population, instructional setting, or teacher-coaching component.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a theoretical/control-systems paper about quantum feedback for photon-number states, not an education study. It does not evaluate any educational intervention, learner population, or instructional outcome.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no demonstrated educational impact relevant to teacher planning, coaching, or instructional feedback. The content is unrelated to the requested education/AI intervention topic.

paper_profiles.title: AGN Feedback: Does it work?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback is strong enough to influence galaxy and cluster evolution in the ways often assumed by theoretical models. Rather than studying education or human learning, it examines astrophysical outflows from AGNs and evaluates whether their mass and energy output can plausibly regulate cooling flows, black hole growth, and other large-scale processes.

The paper focuses on AGN outflows, especially warm absorbers observed with Chandra and XMM-Newton, and discusses how difficult it is to infer mass and energy outflow rates because the location and geometry of the absorbing gas are uncertain. It highlights a novel measurement approach applied to NGC 4051, where time-resolved spectroscopy was used to infer absorber density and distance, enabling estimates of mass and ენერგy outflow rates.

The authors conclude that in NGC 4051 the outflow rates are 4 to 5 orders of magnitude below what would be needed for efficient feedback. They also compare outflow and escape velocities across a sample of AGNs and find that outflow velocity is generally below escape velocity, suggesting that in most Seyfert galaxies the feedback may be too weak to play the strong regulatory role often attributed to it.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a domain paper about AGN astrophysics, not an education study, and it does not evaluate any educational technology or AI intervention. There is no relevant empirical methodology for the requested education taxonomy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational impact is studied or reported. The paper has no measurable effect on teacher planning, feedback, or learner outcomes in an education context.

paper_profiles.title: Regularity and stability of feedback relaxed controls
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies the theory of feedback control for continuous-time stochastic exit-time control problems with finite action sets. The core question is how to construct feedback policies that are not only optimal for a given model, but also stable and robust when the underlying system parameters are perturbed. The motivation comes in part from reinforcement learning, where adding an exploration reward is often used heuristically to improve robustness, but where theoretical justification for stability has been limited.

The authors introduce a relaxed-control regularization framework in which the controller chooses a probability distribution over actions rather than a single action. They define a corresponding Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation with an exploration reward term and prove existence, uniqueness, and regularity of classical solutions under Hölder assumptions. They also show that the induced feedback control is Hölder continuous and Lipschitz stable with respect to perturbations in the model coefficients, unlike the original maximizer-based feedback control, which can be discontinuous and unstable.

The paper further proves a first-order sensitivity equation for the value function and the relaxed feedback policy, and analyzes how the pre-computed policy performs when applied to a perturbed system. It also studies the limit as exploration vanishes, showing monotone convergence back to the original control problem and, for certain smoothing functions, an exact regularization property that recovers the pure exploitation strategy without sending the exploration parameter to zero. The work is entirely theoretical and is not an empirical study of teachers, students, or educational settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical mathematics/control paper on relaxed stochastic control and PDE regularity, not an empirical study of educational technology or teacher coaching. It contains no experimental, observational, or implementation methodology relevant to the retrieval topic.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There are no measured educational outcomes, no teacher-planning intervention, and no effect estimates. The paper has no direct impact evidence for instructional coaching or lesson-plan feedback in education.

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Plan by Updating Natural Language
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of using large language models (LLMs) to solve complex tasks that require more than direct step-by-step prompting. The authors argue that, for difficult reasoning tasks, an LLM needs a reusable natural-language task plan that contains general step-by-step solutions and behavioral instructions, rather than only an ad hoc answer or a single task instruction. Their central question is how to automatically learn such a task plan from error feedback instead of relying on expensive human-written plans.

They propose a method called Learning to Plan, which iteratively identifies wrong samples under the current plan, prompts the LLM to generate candidate plan updates from those errors, compresses and validates those candidates, and then appends the best update to the evolving plan. At test time, the learned plan is inserted into the prompt to guide inference. The paper evaluates this approach on eight reasoning datasets spanning five reasoning types, including mathematical, causal, logical, symbolic, and combinatorial reasoning tasks, using ChatGPT and also testing transfer to GPT-4 and open-source models such as Vicuna.

The main conclusion is that iteratively learning a natural-language plan from errors improves LLM performance relative to zero-shot CoT, few-shot CoT, a self-plan baseline, Automatic Prompt Engineer, and kNN selection. The authors also report that plans learned by one LLM can transfer to another LLM, and that the method can improve open-source models as well. Because this is an NLP/LLM reasoning paper rather than a study of teachers or classrooms, it does not provide evidence on instructional coaching or lesson-planning support for educators.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed experimental NLP paper, but it is not a K-12 educational study and does not use an educational RCT/QED design. The evidence is quantitative and comparative across baselines, yet relevance and credibility for the requested teacher-coaching question are indirect.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows large gains on reasoning benchmarks in LLM performance, but these are not direct educational or teacher-planning outcomes. For the requested use case, the impact on teacher planning quality and feedback usefulness is unclear and only indirectly inferable.

interventions.use_case: learning-to-plan prompting method that uses ChatGPT/GPT-4/Vicuna to iteratively generate, update, compress, and transfer natural-language task plans for reasoning tasks

finding.finding_summary: Across 10 AMPS math tasks, ChatGPT + Learning-to-Plan improved zero-shot CoT average performance from 48.3 to 66.6 and few-shot CoT from 64.0 to 73.9. On the Math dataset, average performance increased from 27.4 to 29.8 in zero-shot and from 30.6 to 31.3 in few-shot settings. The paper reports task-level gains but does not provide effect sizes or confidence intervals.
finding.measure: Task accuracy / percentage correct on math reasoning datasets (AMPS and Math)
finding.study_size: AMPS n=3,765 total across 10 tasks; Math n=5,312 total across 7 tasks

finding.finding_summary: The method improved performance on non-mathematical reasoning tasks that still require structured reasoning, including causal judgment, counterfactual reasoning, logical reasoning, date understanding, last-letter concatenation, and SayCan-style action sequencing. In zero-shot CoT, the average across these six tasks rose from 54.0 to 66.0, and in few-shot CoT from 63.5 to 67.1. The paper frames these as reasoning outcomes rather than domain knowledge gains; no standardized effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Task accuracy / percentage correct on reasoning benchmarks (causal, counterfactual, logical, symbolic, combinatorial reasoning)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention is explicitly designed to improve planning and stepwise reasoning by learning general natural-language task plans from error feedback, which is a metacognitive/durable skill proxy rather than a content-learning outcome. Evidence is indirect but strong within the paper: performance gains on reasoning tasks are attributed to better task planning and plan transfer across models (e.g., ChatGPT-learned plans improving GPT-4). No effect size is reported beyond task accuracies.
finding.measure: Reasoning-task accuracy as a proxy for planning / metacognitive strategy quality

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that iterative plan learning and compression reduce the need for human-authored task plans and improve the usefulness of generated plans, but it does not evaluate teacher workload or planning time in an educational setting. Operationally, the method adds algorithmic efficiency via plan selection/compression, yet it also requires extra inference and validation steps; no direct timing or cost results are reported. Because this is not measured in teachers or classrooms, the evidence is indirect.
finding.measure: Algorithmic plan-update/selection process efficiency; no direct teacher workload measure

paper_profiles.title: An Achievable Rate Region for the Broadcast Channel with Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a communication-theoretic problem, not an education intervention: it studies how feedback can enlarge the achievable rate region of a two-receiver discrete memoryless broadcast channel. The authors ask whether a transmitter can send private and common messages more efficiently when it receives generalized feedback from the receivers, including noiseless, partial, or noisy feedback.

The proposed approach combines Marton coding, block-Markov superposition coding, and joint source-channel coding. In the first phase, fresh information is sent using a Marton-style broadcast strategy; when receivers cannot fully decode, they retain lists of candidate codewords. In the next block, the transmitter sends correlated resolution information to help each receiver disambiguate its list. The key technical contribution is a single-letter achievable rate region for broadcast channels with generalized feedback, with an additional simplified region used for the AWGN case.

The paper analyzes general discrete memoryless broadcast channels and then applies the results to a stochastically degraded AWGN broadcast channel with noisy feedback from only one receiver. It shows that feedback can strictly improve achievable rates relative to the no-feedback capacity region, even when the feedback is noisy. The paper also compares its region with prior results by Bhaskaran, Ozarow-Leung, and Shayevitz-Wigger, and demonstrates that some known examples are recoverable through the new region.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a theoretical information theory/coding paper on broadcast channels with feedback, not an empirical study of educational technology or instructional coaching. It contains no study design, participants, or educational outcomes relevant to the requested topic.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention, teacher outcome, or learner outcome is evaluated, so there is no evidence of impact on education practice or performance.

paper_profiles.title: Using Large Language Models to Provide Explanatory Feedback to Human Tutors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how large language models (LLMs) might support automatic explanatory feedback in online tutor-training lessons. The central problem is that novice tutors need timely, specific feedback on their responses to constructed-response questions, but manually providing such feedback at scale is difficult. The authors focus on whether machine learning can identify effective versus ineffective praise and then use those predictions to generate feedback that explains why a tutor response is appropriate or not.

The proposed approach combines binary classification with named entity recognition (NER). First, the authors annotate tutor responses from an online lesson on giving effective praise and train BERT-based classifiers to detect effort-based and outcome-based praise. Second, they use NER to highlight the relevant parts of tutor responses so they can be inserted into template-based explanatory feedback. The study uses 65 volunteer tutors and 129 tutor responses from the “Giving Effective Praise” lesson, an online scenario-based tutor-training context.

Results suggest that BERT can identify effort-based praise reasonably well, but performs much more weakly on outcome-based praise. The NER approach also shows limited performance, though it can sometimes correctly identify relevant praise spans and support feedback generation. The paper concludes that LLM-facilitated classification and NER are promising for automated tutor feedback, but that the current approach is constrained by small and imbalanced data and would benefit from more annotation, better evaluation metrics, and improved models before practical deployment.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a workshop/work-in-progress paper with a small annotated dataset and model-development focus, not a controlled impact study. It reports algorithmic performance metrics rather than a rigorous evaluation of educational outcomes or comparative effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful automation for tutor feedback, but it does not demonstrate measurable impact on tutor performance or student outcomes. Any practical effect is therefore modest and still uncertain.

interventions.use_case: BERT/LLM-assisted automatic classification and named-entity recognition to provide real-time explanatory feedback to novice tutors composing responses in an online lesson on giving effective praise.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the proposed LLM/BERT-based feedback system can support tutors’ learning by identifying effective praise components and highlighting relevant text spans for explanatory feedback. In the authors’ framing, this is intended to improve tutor reasoning about praise quality and help novice tutors revise responses more effectively, but no causal learner-outcome evaluation was conducted.
finding.measure: Model performance for classifying praise types and tagging named entities used to generate explanatory feedback
finding.std_deviation: Classification SD for Effort F1=0.046; Outcome F1=0.235; NER SD=0.039

finding.finding_summary: The system is presented as a way to deliver timely, specific, and scalable corrective/explanatory feedback to tutors, reducing reliance on human feedback generation. However, the paper does not report direct measurements of planning speed, workload reduction, or uptake of feedback in authentic use; the evidence is limited to automated classification and NER performance.
finding.measure: Automated classification accuracy/F1 and NER F1 as proxies for feedback automation capability
finding.std_deviation: Outcome classification SD=0.235; Effort classification SD=0.046; NER SD=0.039

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models, especially ChatGPT/GPT-3-class systems, for education. Rather than testing a specific intervention empirically, it asks how these models could support learning and teaching and what risks arise when they are integrated into educational practice.

The paper discusses a broad range of educational uses, including generating learning materials, supporting writing and research, providing conversational tutoring, giving feedback, assisting lesson planning, and helping with assessment and professional development. It considers use across education levels and contexts, from elementary school through university and professional training, and it explicitly distinguishes learner-facing and teacher-facing applications.

The main conclusion is that large language models have substantial promise for education, but their use must be cautious, human-supervised, and ethically governed. The paper highlights major concerns such as bias, copyright and plagiarism, overreliance by learners and teachers, difficulty distinguishing AI-generated from human-written text, privacy and security risks, lack of adaptability, and access inequities. It recommends transparency, fact-checking, professional training, and ongoing human oversight as key mitigation strategies.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed position paper and literature overview, not an empirical study. It does not present a controlled design, causal identification, or original outcome data, so it does not meet evidence criteria for efficacy estimation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper identifies potentially broad educational and institutional implications of generative AI, but the evidence is largely conceptual and cited qualitatively rather than measured directly. Reported impacts are plausible but not quantified in this paper, so impact is unclear at the paper level.

interventions.use_case: position paper on large language models/ChatGPT as educational assistants for tutoring, question answering, feedback, lesson planning, and dialogue-based learning support
LLM-based automated feedback on student writing and other student work, including adaptive feedback, grading support, and evaluation of student answers
LLM-supported writing, grammar/style correction, summarization, translation, and language-learning assistance for students and teachers

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by automating or semi-automating tasks such as lesson-plan creation, quiz/question generation, grading support, and feedback drafting. Reported benefits are qualitative rather than effect-size based; for example, the paper cites one study where grading effort in large courses could be reduced by up to 85% with NLP-based feedback systems, but this position paper itself does not report a new empirical estimate.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, and time spent generating instructional materials/feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that LLMs may support critical thinking, problem-solving, and inquiry when used as a scaffold, but also warns that overreliance could weaken those same skills by making answers too effortless. No new quantitative effect is reported; the claim is conceptual and based on cited examples plus theoretical risk analysis.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, inquiry, and fact-checking behaviors

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that conversational AI and other LLM applications may improve engagement, participation, and curiosity, especially in dialogue-based or curiosity-prompting uses. These benefits are described qualitatively, with cited prior work noting increased curiosity expression, but the position paper itself does not provide a new controlled estimate.
finding.measure: Engagement, participation, curiosity, and willingness to communicate

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can support reading and writing through grammar correction, style suggestions, summaries, outlines, and text explanations. It presents these as potential benefits across school levels, but does not report a new literacy outcome study or effect size.
finding.measure: Writing quality, reading comprehension support, grammar/style improvement, summarization assistance

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes LLMs as useful for subject-specific learning across mathematics, physics, computing, medicine, and professional training, mainly by generating explanations, practice problems, and domain-specific text. These claims are illustrative and synthesis-oriented rather than a direct empirical evaluation in this paper.
finding.measure: Subject-specific learning support and domain-task completion

finding.finding_summary: A central contribution of the paper is a risk-and-governance analysis of LLM use in education, highlighting privacy, bias, copyright, fairness, sustainability, and the need for human oversight. It argues that responsible deployment requires institutional policies, monitoring, fact-checking, and regulatory compliance, but it does not test these policies empirically.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, privacy/security, bias mitigation, and responsible deployment considerations

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the potential of artificial intelligence tools in educational measurement and assessment
paper_profiles.venue: EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence, especially large language models such as ChatGPT and related NLP-based systems, can be used across the educational measurement and assessment process. Rather than evaluating a specific intervention experimentally, the article offers a conceptual review of AI applications in test purpose specification, blueprint development, item generation, test instructions, item selection, administration, scoring, interpretation, appraisal, and reporting.

The paper is framed around classroom assessment and broader educational measurement, with examples drawn from a variety of AI tools used by teachers, assessment specialists, and institutions. It discusses how AI may support personalized feedback, automate grading, identify learning difficulties, and improve efficiency in assessment workflows. The authors also emphasize that teachers remain essential for design, interpretation, feedback, and ethical oversight.

A major focus of the paper is the limitations and risks of AI in assessment. The authors highlight concerns including bias, lack of transparency, privacy issues, limited human interaction, limited scope for higher-order or affective/psychomotor skills, inadequate training, technical difficulties, and possible overreliance on AI. They argue that AI can improve assessment practices only if it is implemented with human oversight, stakeholder involvement, and ethical safeguards.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review/opinion-style article rather than a primary empirical study, RCT, or meta-analysis. It discusses potential applications and risks of AI in assessment but reports no original data or comparative effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for assessment efficiency and institutional decision-making, but these are conceptual rather than measured. Impact is therefore unclear/modest in evidence terms, with no demonstrated effect sizes.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual review of large language models such as ChatGPT/Bard for classroom assessment tasks, including test purpose specification, blueprinting, item generation, instructions, item assembly, administration support, scoring, interpretation, analysis, and reporting.
AI-generated feedback on student written responses and assessment results, including automated essay scoring, grammar/syntax feedback, and interpretive feedback for test performance.
Using AI/learning analytics to analyze student attendance, engagement, and performance data to flag at-risk learners and support targeted intervention.
Broader AI-enabled assessment and computer-based testing platforms used to administer online assessments, monitor progress, and deliver immediate feedback.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools can automate multiple assessment tasks—item generation, scoring, reporting, and administration—thereby saving teacher time and reducing workload. No original effect size or sample size is reported because this is a review article; the claim is conceptual rather than empirical.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, speed/efficiency of assessment tasks

finding.finding_summary: The article states that automated grading and scoring systems can provide immediate feedback and reduce the burden of marking essays and other assignments. This is presented as a general benefit of AI-powered feedback systems, but the paper does not report empirical estimates such as d or n.
finding.measure: Grading speed, scoring efficiency, feedback turnaround time

finding.finding_summary: The review emphasizes that AI could improve assessment accuracy, consistency, and data-driven decision-making, but it also highlights major risks including bias, privacy concerns, lack of transparency, inadequate training, and unequal access. Because no empirical comparison is reported, the overall effect at the institutional level is best characterized as mixed and contingent on governance and implementation.
finding.measure: Assessment system quality, fairness, transparency, privacy, institutional adoption

paper_profiles.title: The impact of ChatGPT on foreign language teaching and learning: Opportunities in education and research
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Educational Technology and Innovation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual discussion of ChatGPT’s implications for foreign language education. It addresses widespread concern about generative AI in schooling, especially cheating, weak writing, and threats to assessment validity, while also arguing that the technology can create new opportunities for teaching, learning, and research.

The paper does not report an empirical intervention. Instead, it explains how ChatGPT works, clarifies common misconceptions, and discusses potential uses such as authentic language interaction, instant writing feedback, personalized tutoring, lesson-plan generation, and support for flipped and formative assessment practices. It is framed around second/foreign language teaching contexts, with examples and references relevant to higher education and Macao, but no participant sample is studied.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT should not simply be banned; educators should understand its limitations and adapt teaching and assessment accordingly. The author emphasizes both benefits and risks, including inaccurate or fabricated outputs, shallow responses, and ethical concerns about copyright and professionalism. The paper also calls for future research on how ChatGPT affects learners at different proficiency levels and on how teachers use it in practice.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/opinion article and literature-informed commentary, not an empirical study with a defined design, sample, or causal identification strategy. It provides useful framing but no direct evidence meeting K-12 research credibility criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for potentially meaningful effects on language learning, teacher workload, and assessment policy, but it reports no measured effect sizes or outcome data. Because the claims are plausible yet untested here, the impact is best treated as unclear/modest rather than established.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT as a conversational AI for language learning, personal tutoring, generating discussion topics, and providing instant writing feedback in foreign language education

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can support writing development by pinpointing language and organizational issues, suggesting corrections, and generating writing ideas for EFL/SL learners. No empirical effect size is reported because this is a conceptual/review-style article rather than an intervention study.
finding.measure: None reported; conceptual discussion of writing support, correction, and feedback capabilities

finding.finding_summary: The article claims ChatGPT can enable authentic conversations in the target language and provide conversational practice that may help speaking and related language use. It does not report quantitative learner outcomes or any sample size.
finding.measure: None reported; conceptual discussion of authentic conversation and oral language practice

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests ChatGPT may improve learner motivation, confidence, and engagement through personalized interaction, but it also notes anxiety, apprehension, and ethical concerns among teachers and institutions. These are discussed as anticipated effects rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher and learner perceptions, motivation/confidence/engagement discussed conceptually

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that ChatGPT can reduce teacher workload by marking student writing, generating tasks and lesson plans, and giving instant feedback. No empirical evaluation is provided, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: None reported; conceptual discussion of workload reduction and instant feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes institutional risks and governance issues, including cheating, plagiarism, assessment validity, ethics, copyright, and the need for new ground rules and assessment redesign. It does not provide empirical estimates, but argues that campuses and teachers must adapt policies and practices to manage these risks.
finding.measure: Policy, assessment validity, ethics, and institutional responses discussed conceptually

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the impact of ChatGPT: conversational AI in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what the educational benefits, challenges, ethical issues, and teacher-related implications are of using ChatGPT in education. It is a systematic literature review that synthesizes research published between 2022 and 2023, with particular attention to student engagement and learning outcomes, safeguards for responsible use, and how ChatGPT changes educators’ roles.

The study does not implement a single classroom intervention; instead, it reviews 70 published studies identified through a systematic search and PRISMA-style screening. The population represented in the reviewed literature includes students and teachers in educational settings, spanning general educational contexts rather than one specific grade or institution. The paper treats ChatGPT as a conversational AI tool used for personalized assistance, prompt feedback, tutoring-like support, and support for teaching and writing tasks.

The review concludes that ChatGPT can improve engagement, provide personalized responses, increase access to information, and support differentiated learning. At the same time, it identifies important risks, including bias in AI outputs, inaccurate or misleading responses, overreliance on AI, privacy and data-protection concerns, and the need for human supervision and critical evaluation. The authors argue that responsible deployment requires clear guidelines, teacher oversight, user education, and regular monitoring, and they emphasize that educators’ roles shift from content delivery toward facilitation, guidance, and monitoring student use.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic literature review with a defined search strategy and quality appraisal, but it synthesizes heterogeneous studies rather than presenting a controlled causal evaluation. The evidence is peer-reviewed and methodologically structured, yet it remains secondary qualitative evidence rather than a meta-analysis or RCT.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for engagement, learning, and efficiency, but it does not report pooled effect sizes or direct causal estimates. Because the evidence is largely narrative and mixed with important risks and limitations, the overall impact is best treated as promising but unclear.

interventions.use_case: Systematic literature review of ChatGPT as a conversational AI tool in educational settings, including student support, tutoring-like interactions, and teacher-facing educational use cases.

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that ChatGPT is associated with improved learning experiences and learning outcomes across the included education literature, mainly through personalized responses, prompt feedback, and easier access to information. No pooled effect size or primary-study effect sizes were reported in this review; the paper synthesizes 70 sources rather than estimating an aggregate causal effect.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of reported learning outcomes and learning experience effects across reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that ChatGPT tends to increase student engagement by providing personalized interactions, rapid responses, and interactive learning experiences. These benefits are described qualitatively across the 70 reviewed articles, with no pooled effect size or standardized engagement measure reported.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of student engagement and participation reports

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can support critical thinking and inquiry by prompting students to ask questions, evaluate responses, and compare information. This is a qualitative synthesis only; the review does not report effect sizes or primary-study statistics for critical thinking outcomes.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of critical thinking and questioning skill effects

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that ChatGPT can save time and increase efficiency through immediate answers, quick access to information, and support for drafting, summarizing, and literature review tasks. These are synthesis claims from included studies rather than measured effect estimates; no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of teacher/researcher productivity and response-time advantages

finding.finding_summary: The review emphasizes major institutional risks and safeguards around ChatGPT adoption, including bias, inaccuracy, privacy/data protection, transparency, human supervision, and the need for clear guidelines and monitoring. It also notes role shifts for teachers toward facilitation and guidance, but these conclusions are qualitative and not tied to effect sizes or a single empirical study.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of ethical, governance, and implementation issues

paper_profiles.title: AI and Chat GPT in Language Teaching: Enhancing EFL Classroom Support and Transforming Assessment Techniques
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Higher Education Pedagogies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses how artificial intelligence, especially ChatGPT-like systems, can support English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teaching and assessment. It focuses on three main areas: personalized language learning, real-time language practice, and assistance with lesson planning. The paper also examines how AI changes examination techniques through adaptive testing, automated grading, feedback, and test security, while noting ethical issues such as privacy, equity, bias, and responsible use.

The article is primarily a conceptual and position-oriented essay rather than an empirical study. It draws on examples such as Duolingo, ChatGPT use in EFL classrooms, ExamSoft, Rosetta Stone, AI writing assistants, and AI-enabled virtual reality to illustrate potential applications in language education. The intended context is EFL instruction, including classroom learning, assessment settings, and university language departments.

The paper concludes that AI can enhance instruction and assessment by making learning more personalized, feedback more immediate, and testing more efficient and secure. However, it argues that AI should complement rather than replace teachers. It emphasizes that educators remain essential for interpreting AI outputs, ensuring fairness, addressing limitations in AI-generated content, and maintaining human interaction, ethical safeguards, and equitable access.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative/essay-style article with no original experimental design, no comparison groups, and no quantitative analysis. It is useful for conceptual mapping of claims and risks, but it does not provide rigorous empirical evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no measurable effect sizes and no original outcomes; its claims are qualitative and illustrative. As a result, observed impact cannot be established from the article itself.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-style conversational AI used in EFL classrooms for real-time language practice, student questioning, and teacher support.
AI-driven language learning and writing support tools such as Duolingo, Rosetta Stone, Grammarly, and similar EFL applications that adapt practice and provide grammar/pronunciation feedback.
Automated grading and feedback for student responses, including short-answer and written EFL assignments, with grammar/spelling/coherence suggestions.
AI-powered adaptive language learning platforms that tailor lessons and practice to learner performance and proficiency, such as Duolingo and Rosetta Stone.
AI-supported instructional assistance for lesson planning, material generation, and classroom practice activities in EFL instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI and ChatGPT improve EFL speaking/practice opportunities by enabling real-time conversational practice, immediate responses, and feedback on pronunciation, grammar, and vocabulary. No original experimental effect size is reported; the paper cites case examples and prior studies to support claims of improved proficiency and confidence.
finding.measure: Language practice quality, pronunciation/grammar/vocabulary feedback, learner proficiency and confidence (descriptive/case-based)

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents AI writing assistants and automated feedback as improving written English by detecting grammar and spelling errors, suggesting revisions, and evaluating clarity/coherence. It cites a case study at New York University reporting 'substantial improvements' in written English proficiency, but no numeric effect size or sample size is provided in the paper text.
finding.measure: Written English proficiency, grammar/spelling accuracy, clarity/coherence of writing

finding.finding_summary: Automated grading and feedback are described as speeding evaluation of written assignments and providing immediate corrective input. The paper states that NLP/ML systems can identify grammar and spelling errors and evaluate coherence, but it reports no original quantitative estimate.
finding.measure: Automated writing feedback and grading of written/short-answer work

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims AI-supported practice and adaptive assessment can boost student confidence and reduce anxiety, especially in low-pressure chatbot and adaptive testing contexts. These are narrative claims rather than measured outcomes, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Student confidence, test anxiety, engagement/motivation (descriptive)

finding.finding_summary: Adaptive testing is described as reducing test anxiety by matching question difficulty to ability and fostering a sense of accomplishment. The paper offers no empirical estimate, only a conceptual rationale for improved affective outcomes during assessment.
finding.measure: Test anxiety and confidence during adaptive testing

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly argues that AI reduces teacher workload by generating lesson plans, answering common questions, automating grading, and streamlining exam proctoring. Benefits are described qualitatively for tools like ChatGPT, Duolingo, and ExamSoft; no quantitative workload reduction is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading efficiency, lesson-planning efficiency, proctoring efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes institutional benefits such as improved test security, consistency in grading, and broader access to personalized language support, but it also highlights risks involving privacy, equity, algorithmic bias, and overreliance on AI. No empirical institutional effect sizes are reported; the evidence is mainly conceptual and case-based.
finding.measure: Test security, equity/access, privacy/data security, bias, institutional adoption and governance

paper_profiles.title: Unveiling Gender Bias in Large Language Models: Using Teacher’s Evaluation in Higher Education As an Example
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models generate gender-biased teacher evaluations in higher education. The central question is not about improving teaching through AI coaching, but about whether GPT-4 reproduces stereotypes when asked to write short student-style evaluations of instructors. The study is motivated by concerns that LLM-generated evaluative text may reflect and amplify societal bias, which could matter in settings where AI is used for performance reviews or instructional feedback.

The approach uses GPT-4 to generate 360 teacher evaluations from prompts that vary only by instructor gender and subject area. Two fictitious instructor names were used, and six university subjects were selected: Computer Science, Engineering, Economics, Foreign Languages, Psychology, and Education. The analysis combines several text-based methods: Odds Ratio analysis to find gender-associated adjectives, WEAT to test associations between words and gendered concepts, sentiment analysis to compare emotional tone, and contextual close reading of selected terms in Engineering.

The findings indicate consistent gendered patterns in the model’s outputs. Female instructors were more often described with communal, supportive, and approachable language, while male instructors were more often linked to entertainment- and agentic-style descriptors and to intellectual praise in some contexts. Sentiment scores were slightly more positive for female instructors overall, but contextual analysis showed that female instructors could still receive subtly negative or limiting framing. The paper concludes that LLM-generated teacher evaluations reflect and may reinforce gender stereotypes, and that quantitative scores alone may miss context-dependent bias.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/observational computational analysis of LLM outputs, not an intervention study or randomized evaluation. The methodology is systematic and multi-method, but it does not meet strong causal evidence criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful institutional risk from biased AI-generated teacher evaluations, but it does not estimate downstream real-world effect sizes on educator outcomes. The impact is therefore important but indirect and unclear in magnitude.

interventions.use_case: Analyzing GPT-4-generated teacher evaluations in higher education for gender bias, using prompt-based generation of short student-perspective reviews across six university subjects.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that GPT-4-generated teacher evaluations reproduce gender stereotypes, with communal/supportive language used more often for female instructors and entertainment/agentic language used more often for male instructors. Across 360 generated evaluations (30 prompts × 12 prompt configurations), sentiment analysis also showed a statistically significant difference favoring female teachers overall (t=2.392, p=0.0378), but contextual analysis revealed negative or limiting uses of language for women that sentiment scores alone obscured.
finding.measure: Odds Ratio analysis of adjective use, WEAT association tests, TextBlob sentiment scores, and contextual qualitative analysis of generated teacher evaluations

paper_profiles.title: Physics task development of prospective physics teachers using ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT 3.5 can support prospective physics teachers in developing high-quality assessment tasks, and how its use compares with a traditional textbook. The authors focus on the broader question of whether large language models can help teachers create classroom assessment items, while also identifying potential shortcomings such as weak task specificity, missing context, or misleading output.

In a randomized controlled trial, 26 prospective physics teachers at Ludwig-Maximilians-University Munich were assigned either to use ChatGPT 3.5 or to use a high school physics textbook as support for creating four conceptual physics tasks. The tasks targeted Newtonian mechanics content for 10th-grade German high school students, and the study assessed task quality using categories such as specificity, clarity, correctness, context, and difficulty. The intervention group also completed usability and perceived usefulness ratings for ChatGPT.

The results showed that ChatGPT-supported and textbook-supported participants produced similarly correct tasks and tasks of comparable overall quality and difficulty for the target grade level. However, textbook-supported tasks were clearer and more often embedded in meaningful context. Both groups struggled with task specificity, meaning important information was often missing for students to solve the tasks. Participants generally found ChatGPT easy to use, but rated its output quality only neutrally and reported difficulties with the generated tasks. The study concludes that ChatGPT can support assessment task development, but users still need strong subject knowledge and prompt design skills, and some limitations of AI-generated tasks cannot be solved without explicit user intervention.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled trial with expert-rated outcomes and a clearly described comparison condition, which gives it relatively strong credibility. However, the sample is small (n=26), the setting is narrow (prospective physics teachers at one university), and outcomes are task-quality ratings rather than student learning, so there are notable concerns about generalizability.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows a moderate-to-large positive effect for some usability and task-quality dimensions, but the main academic effects are mixed and one large effect favors the textbook over ChatGPT on context. Overall impact on the broader education population is therefore modest and uneven, with important limitations around specificity and output quality.

interventions.use_case: Using ChatGPT 3.5 to support prospective physics teachers in generating and revising 10th-grade kinematics assessment tasks, including prompt-based task creation and iterative adaptation.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized controlled trial with n=26 prospective physics teachers, tasks created with ChatGPT 3.5 were comparable to textbook-based tasks on correctness and adequate difficulty, but worse on clarity and context. There was no significant difference in correctness or task specificity, while textbook-supported tasks scored higher in clarity (p=0.04, d=0.38) and context (p=6×10^-5, d=1.04).
finding.measure: Expert ratings of physics assessment task quality: specificity, clarity, correctness, misleadingness, difficulty, context, relevance to target concept, overall quality
finding.effect_size: d=0.38 (clarity), d=1.04 (context); no significant difference for correctness/specificity/difficulty

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined task-development/problem-posing skill in prospective physics teachers. Participants in both groups struggled with task specificity, and many ChatGPT-generated tasks were used with little modification (75% of tasks in the ChatGPT group were used as provided), suggesting limited improvement in problem-posing quality and some reliance on the tool rather than deeper task refinement.
finding.measure: Expert coding of participant-generated and adapted assessment tasks; number and type of task modifications

finding.finding_summary: Participants rated ChatGPT’s usability positively (mean 4.1/5) but judged its perceived usefulness as neutral (mean 3.24/5) and output quality as below neutral (mean 2.76/5). Response time was not seen as a major barrier (mean 2.09/5 on the reverse-coded item), indicating the system was easy to use but not consistently productive for high-quality physics task creation.
finding.measure: System Usability Scale (SUS) and Technology Acceptance Model 2 items on perceived usefulness, response time burden, and output quality

paper_profiles.title: Implicit Grading Bias in Large Language Models: How Writing Style Affects Automated Assessment Across Math, Programming, and Essay Tasks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models used as automated graders exhibit implicit bias when scoring student work, even when they are explicitly instructed to ignore writing style and judge only content correctness. The central question is whether stylistic differences in otherwise equivalent responses can systematically affect grades, and whether this varies by subject area and perturbation type.

The authors construct a controlled synthetic dataset of 180 student responses across three subjects: Mathematics, Programming, and Essay/Writing. Each response is derived from a correct base answer and then perturbed in one of three ways: grammar errors, informal language, or non-native phrasing. Two open-source LLMs, LLaMA 3.3 70B and Qwen 2.5 72B, are used as graders with a standardized prompt that explicitly tells them not to penalize style-related features. The study compares model scores against human-assigned ground-truth scores and analyzes score penalties, significance, effect sizes, and agreement with human ratings.

Results show a strong subject-dependent pattern. Essay/Writing tasks exhibit statistically significant bias across all perturbation types for both models, with informal language penalized most heavily. Mathematics and Programming show little to no bias, with only one statistically significant non-native phrasing effect in Mathematics for Qwen. The paper concludes that prompt-based debiasing is insufficient for high-stakes educational grading and recommends perturbation-based bias audits, restricting LLM grading to more objective assessment types, and using style-aware fine-tuning plus human oversight for subjective evaluation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a controlled experimental audit study, but it is a preprint under review rather than a peer-reviewed RCT or QED, and it uses synthetic responses rather than authentic classroom data. It provides strong internal control and clear statistical testing, but credibility is limited by external validity and study design constraints.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The observed penalties are medium to very large in essay grading and therefore could meaningfully affect high-stakes student outcomes if deployed. The impact is important for priority populations such as non-native English speakers, but the evidence comes from an experimental audit rather than a real-world deployment study.

interventions.use_case: LLM-based automated grading of student responses across math, programming, and essay tasks, with the model scoring answers and generating brief justifications; the paper evaluates grading bias in this assessment workflow rather than feedback generation per se.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds strong negative bias in essay/writing assessment: both LLaMA 3.3 70B and Qwen 2.5 72B penalized informal language, grammar errors, and non-native phrasing despite explicit instructions not to do so. In Essay/Writing tasks, all six conditions were statistically significant with very large effects (Cohen’s d ranging from 0.64 to 4.25); the largest penalty was LLaMA’s informal-language effect (∆=1.90 points on a 10-point scale, d=4.25), and both models showed weak overall agreement with human scores (LLaMA r=0.315, MAE=0.922; Qwen r=0.339, MAE=0.856).
finding.measure: LLM grading scores on essay/writing responses; score penalties relative to base answers; correlation/MAE versus human ground-truth scores
finding.study_size: n=180 perturbed responses plus 60 base responses; 480 total evaluations

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics grading showed minimal bias overall, with most perturbation conditions failing to reach statistical significance. The only notable exception was Qwen’s non-native phrasing condition in math (∆=0.40, d=0.59, p=.017), while LLaMA’s math conditions were essentially zero bias in some cases (e.g., grammar ∆=0.00, d=0.00, p=1.00).
finding.measure: LLM grading score penalties for perturbed math responses; human-LLM agreement metrics
finding.study_size: n=60 math base responses and 120 perturbed math evaluations across two models

finding.finding_summary: Programming responses were graded with very little style-related bias, with most conditions non-significant and penalties near zero. Human-LLM agreement was strongest here relative to other subjects (r≈0.48 for both models), indicating that the models handled objective coding tasks more consistently than subjective writing tasks.
finding.measure: LLM grading scores on programming tasks; correlation with human ground-truth scores
finding.study_size: n=60 programming base responses and 120 perturbed programming evaluations across two models

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that prompt-level anti-bias instructions do not reliably prevent biased automated grading, creating a serious governance and fairness risk for institutional adoption. Bias was subject-dependent and systematic across models, with essay/writing tasks most vulnerable; the authors recommend mandatory bias auditing, restricting automated grading to objective tasks, and maintaining human oversight for subjective assessments.
finding.measure: Observed grading bias across subjects and perturbation types; significance rates and effect sizes across conditions
finding.study_size: n=2 LLMs, 3 subjects, 3 perturbation types, 18 experimental conditions
finding.effect_size: d=0.64 to d=4.25 in essay/writing conditions; overall bias indices 0.472 (LLaMA) and 0.350 (Qwen)

paper_profiles.title: AI, Expert or Peer? Examining the Impact of Perceived Feedback Source on Pre-Service Teachers Feedback Perception and Uptake
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether pre-service teachers evaluate and use feedback differently depending on whether they believe it comes from an LLM, an expert, or a peer. The paper is motivated by concerns that even high-quality AI-generated feedback may be underused if recipients distrust it or misjudge its source. The authors focus on perceived source, source-recognition accuracy, and feedback quality as drivers of feedback perception and actual uptake.

In a randomized experiment, 273 bachelor’s students in a German teacher education program received one of 30 written feedback messages on a mathematics learning goal, with feedback actually generated by an LLM, an expert, or a peer. Participants identified the presumed source, rated the feedback on fairness, usefulness, acceptance, willingness to improve, and affect, and then revised the learning goal to show feedback uptake. The study also coded objective feedback quality and tested whether recognition accuracy moderated source effects.

Results showed that perceived source strongly influenced cognitive feedback perceptions: LLM feedback was rated more positively when it was mistakenly believed to come from an expert, reflecting an expertise heuristic. However, perceived source and recognition accuracy did not predict behavioral uptake once feedback quality was controlled. Instead, objective feedback quality was the only significant predictor of implementation. The authors conclude that source labels and AI-related biases shape how pre-service teachers feel about feedback, but actual use depends mainly on message quality.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized experiment with 273 pre-service teachers and controlled comparison conditions, giving it relatively strong internal validity. However, it is a single-site study with some analytic and measurement limitations (e.g., restricted uptake variance, varying feedback quality across providers, and no individual-difference measures), so it does not fully meet the highest rigor tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows clear but mostly indirect effects: source labels changed perceptions, while actual behavioral uptake was driven by feedback quality rather than AI source. The practical implications are meaningful for teacher education, but the observed behavioral impact of the AI intervention itself is limited and context-specific.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated written feedback on a mathematics lesson-plan learning goal, compared against expert- and peer-written feedback; participants judged source, perceived quality, and revised the learning goal based on the feedback.
ChatGPT-4 was used to generate the feedback messages, but the intervention studied was AI-generated feedback rather than interactive tutoring.

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers revised a mathematics learning goal after receiving feedback on a right-triangle/Pythagorean theorem lesson objective. LLM feedback produced the highest absolute and relative uptake (52%) compared with expert feedback (45%) and peer feedback (42%), but regression showed that source and recognition accuracy did not predict uptake once feedback quality was controlled; only feedback quality did (b=1.27, SE=0.50, z=2.52, p=.012, R²=.078, n=161 in the uptake model).
finding.measure: Feedback uptake/correction rate on a mathematics learning goal revision task

finding.finding_summary: The study directly measured feedback perception dimensions relevant to metacognition and judgment, including fairness, usefulness, acceptance, and willingness to improve. LLM feedback was rated most favorably when misattributed to an expert; for example, fairness and usefulness showed significant source-recognition interactions (fairness b=1.21, SE=0.59, p=.042; usefulness b=1.76, SE=0.67, p=.009; n=227), but these perception effects did not translate into higher uptake once quality was accounted for.
finding.measure: Feedback perception questionnaire (fairness, usefulness, acceptance, willingness to improve)
finding.effect_size: b=1.21; b=1.76; adjusted R² up to .171

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint examines how pre-service elementary science teachers in South Korea envisioned and planned the use of ChatGPT in science lessons. The paper asks how ChatGPT can be integrated into science lesson planning, how well pre-service teachers can align it with curriculum and pedagogy, and what benefits and concerns they perceive when using generative AI in science teaching and learning.

The intervention/context was a short instructional sequence in a university science education course. Twenty-nine pre-service elementary teachers first received four 2-hour sessions introducing ChatGPT, discussing potential uses, reviewing science teaching methods (for example POE, learning cycle, analogy generation, and cooperative learning), and learning how to write lesson plans. They then created lesson plans for a typical 45-minute elementary science class that had to incorporate ChatGPT, and they attached simulated chat interactions. Researchers evaluated the plans with a modified TPACK-based rubric and analyzed open-ended survey responses and chat examples.

The sample covered multiple elementary science content areas, including biology, chemistry, earth science, physics, and environmental science, but all participants were pre-service elementary teachers at one Korean university. The study found that participants saw ChatGPT as useful for questioning, individualized support, formative feedback, and helping structure activities such as role-play or cooperative learning. Overall lesson-plan quality was relatively high, but teachers were less skilled at selecting appropriate ChatGPT functions than at linking ChatGPT to curriculum goals or instructional strategies. Reported concerns centered on inaccurate or biased responses, the risk of student overdependence, and the need to verify ChatGPT outputs. The authors conclude that generative AI may support science learning and lesson design, but teachers need digital literacy, critical evaluation skills, and stronger professional development to avoid misuse and overreliance.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/descriptive preprint study of 29 pre-service teachers' lesson plans and survey responses, with no experimental manipulation or student outcome comparison. It provides useful exploratory evidence but does not meet stronger causal or quantitative design standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports perceived benefits and risks rather than measured learner effects, so impact is unclear. Any practical impact appears modest and context-specific, mainly informing future teacher use of ChatGPT rather than demonstrating realized gains.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used by pre-service elementary science teachers to support lesson planning, student questioning, role-play scripting, individualized learning support, and formative feedback within science lesson plans.

finding.finding_summary: Across 29 pre-service teachers' lesson plans, ChatGPT was most often envisioned to support science learning through questioning, prediction/explanation, inquiry, and formative assessment. However, the paper also identified inappropriate uses that could undermine scientific reasoning, including reliance on non-existent YouTube links, use for visually dependent tasks, and using ChatGPT to design experiments in ways that might weaken practical inquiry skills.
finding.measure: Modified TPACK-based lesson-plan rubric plus qualitative analysis of lesson plans and survey responses
finding.std_deviation: SD=.91 overall TIAR score; SD=.99 instructional strategies & ChatGPT; SD=.93 ChatGPT function selection

finding.finding_summary: Participants anticipated ChatGPT would increase motivation, interest, and self-directed learning by enabling instant, context-aware, individualized support. These claims were based on 29 lesson plans and open-ended survey responses, but no student outcome data were collected.
finding.measure: Pre-service teacher perceptions of motivation, interest, and self-directed learning potential

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers expected ChatGPT to support critical thinking, collaboration, and digital literacy, especially through consecutive questioning and structured group discussion. At the same time, they worried about overdependence, misconceptions, and reduced practical inquiry if students relied on ChatGPT too heavily.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of lesson plans and survey responses on critical thinking, collaboration, digital literacy, and dependence concerns

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was viewed as helping teachers and students save time by generating role-play scripts, summarizing long scenarios, and providing rapid follow-up responses during planning and instruction. The paper does not report a measured efficiency gain, but the perceived efficiency benefit was a recurring theme in the qualitative data from 29 participants.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness for planning efficiency, summarization, and quick feedback

paper_profiles.title: What Users Value and Critique: Large-Scale Analysis of User Feedback on AI-Powered Mobile Apps
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines what users praise and criticize about AI-powered features in mobile apps, with an emphasis on understanding common concerns, co-occurring praise and complaints, and differences across app categories. The authors argue that user reviews are an underused but valuable source for evaluating AI features “in the wild,” especially given the scale and variability of feedback across modern app stores.

The study analyzes 2.2 million cleaned Google Play reviews from 292 AI-driven apps across 14 categories, identifying 894K reviews that explicitly reference AI features. The approach combines large language models for AI-related review classification and aspect-sentiment extraction with k-means clustering to organize more than 1.1 million aspect-sentiment pairs into 18 positive and 15 negative user topics. The analysis is not an educational intervention; it is a large-scale review-mining study of app feedback.

Across categories, users most often value productivity, intelligent assistance, personalization, and helpful answers, while negative feedback concentrates on scanner/OCR failures, pricing and access barriers, language limitations, and other technical issues. The paper also finds that praise and criticism frequently co-occur within the same review, especially for core features such as chat, voice, math, and answer quality. The main conclusion is that AI-powered apps should prioritize reliability, clearer pricing, and better language support, while also addressing category-specific pain points; however, the paper does not study teacher coaching, lesson-plan feedback, or educational effectiveness.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a large-scale observational/qualitative text-mining study of app-store reviews, not a randomized or quasi-experimental evaluation of an educational intervention. It is well-documented and uses validation steps, but it does not meet causal evidence criteria for educational effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has important descriptive value for understanding user-reported strengths, failure modes, and category differences in AI mobile apps, including education-related apps. However, it does not estimate causal effects on learning or teacher outcomes, so the practical impact on education remains indirect and uncertain.

interventions.use_case: large-scale analysis of AI-powered mobile apps and their user reviews, including education-category apps with AI features such as math solvers, scanning, language support, and personalized assistance

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test learning outcomes; it analyzes 894K AI-related reviews from 292 mobile apps and finds that users value AI for productivity, intelligent assistance, and personalized help, but also criticize failures, pricing barriers, and language limitations. The most frequent positive themes were AI Assistant (6,949 aspects; 48,999 reviews), ScanToSolve (6,260; 30,680), and Smart & Personalized (5,988; 49,682), while leading negative themes included Scanner Issues (13,208; 62,598), Access & Pricing (12,526; 31,927), and AI understanding limitations (9,932; 29,450).
finding.measure: User review aspect-sentiment analysis and topic clustering of AI-related feedback in mobile apps

finding.finding_summary: In education apps, math-related AI features were a prominent use case and source of both praise and criticism. Positive feedback highlighted math solvers and scan-to-solve tools, while negative feedback emphasized Math Issues and scanner/OCR failures; the paper reports 6,080 negative aspect mentions for Math Issues and 19,426 positive mentions for Mathsolver, but no experimental effect size because this is review mining rather than an intervention study.
finding.measure: User review mentions of math solver quality, scan-to-solve performance, and incorrect math solutions
finding.study_size: n=154,350 education-app reviews among 894K AI-related reviews

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies writing and language-support features as both valued and criticized, especially in education and communication-related apps. Positive themes include AI Writing (4,634 aspects; 28,429 reviews) and Language Support (2,432 aspects; 34,715 reviews), while negative themes include Language Limitations (5,123 aspects; 37,549 reviews) and answer-quality issues that affect comprehension and text assistance.
finding.measure: User review themes related to AI writing support, grammar/editing help, and multilingual functionality

paper_profiles.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence-Guided User Studies: An Application for Air Taxi Services
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative AI can support early-stage user studies by rapidly creating virtual experimental scenarios, reducing the cost, time, and safety burdens of conventional prototyping. The authors frame the problem in human-computer interaction and transportation design: real-world user testing of emerging technologies such as air taxis is difficult because physical prototypes are immature, expensive to build, and may raise safety concerns during early iteration.

The proposed approach uses OpenAI GPT-4 to generate prompts, pain points, user needs, design requirements, mockups, and storyboard content for an air-taxi journey. AI image and video generators (Midjourney and Runway) were then used to visualize these materials into a virtual experimental scenario. The resulting air-taxi journey was presented to 72 adult participants in an online questionnaire, and their pre/post attitudes toward taking air taxis and their satisfaction with the experience were measured using Likert-scale items.

The study found that viewing the AI-generated journey significantly improved participants’ willingness to take an air taxi and that overall satisfaction was moderate to high. Effects varied by subgroup: education level significantly influenced attitude change, and gender significantly influenced satisfaction, with females reporting lower satisfaction than males. Age and employment status did not show significant differences. The authors conclude that generative AI can help design virtual user-study scenarios for early-stage technology development, but the method should be refined to better simulate real participant responses and to account for demographic differences in attitudes and satisfaction.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical user study with pre/post measures and subgroup analyses, but it is not an educational intervention study and lacks randomization/control conditions relevant to K-12 evidence standards. The design is closer to an HCI mixed-methods evaluation than a rigorous causal study in education.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows a moderate positive attitudinal shift in a non-educational setting, but the effect is on user acceptance of air taxis rather than learning outcomes. There is no direct educational impact, so the relevance to the requested education-focused taxonomy is limited.

interventions.use_case: LLM-guided user-study design for an air-taxi journey, including prompt-based generation of pain points, user needs, design requirements, mockups, and storyboards, then visualized with AI image/video generators for evaluation.

GPT-4 used as a generative assistant to produce design-thinking outputs (empathize, define, ideate, prototype) and simulate participant responses; not tutoring students, but a conversational AI used to support iterative design and evaluation.
