finding.finding_summary: Across 72 participants, viewing the AI-generated air-taxi journey improved willingness/attitudes toward taking an air taxi from M=3.46 pre to M=3.89 post, with a significant paired t-test (t=-3.326, p=0.001). The paper interprets this as generative AI improving acceptance and satisfaction with the simulated experience.
finding.measure: Attitude toward taking an air taxi before vs after viewing the ATJ video/questionnaire

finding.finding_summary: Attitude change differed significantly by education level (F=3.733, p=0.008), with larger gains among lower-education participants and little change among the highest-education group. No significant differences were found by gender, age, or employment status for attitude change (all p>0.05), though all groups trended positive.
finding.measure: Change in willingness/attitude toward taking an air taxi across demographic subgroups

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported high satisfaction with the AI-generated air-taxi journey overall (M=3.78, SD=0.77). Satisfaction differed significantly by gender (t=2.508, p=0.014), with males more satisfied than females, while education, age, and employment status showed no statistically significant differences.
finding.measure: Satisfaction with the simulated air-taxi journey (ATJ)

paper_profiles.title: Mitigating the Bias of Large Language Model Evaluation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses bias in large language model (LLM) evaluation, focusing on the increasingly common LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm. The authors argue that current judge models tend to favor superficially strong answers, such as those that are more verbose, fluent, formal, or engaging, while underweighting actual instruction-following quality. They frame this as a systematic evaluation bias problem that can distort model assessment and create privacy concerns when external proprietary APIs are used for judging.

To mitigate this bias, the paper proposes two complementary approaches. For closed-source judges, it introduces online calibration methods that explicitly model superficial quality and subtract it from the final evaluation score, using either probability-based or generation-based signals. For open-source judges, it proposes offline contrastive training with carefully constructed negative samples that are similar in surface quality but misaligned with the instruction. The methods are evaluated on the LLMBar benchmark, which includes one natural set and four adversarial sets designed to expose judge bias.

The paper reports that the proposed methods reduce bias substantially on adversarial test sets while maintaining comparable performance on natural data. Probability calibration performs best overall among the calibration variants, and contrastive training also improves robustness, though results vary by subset. The authors conclude that bias mitigation is helpful but not free: stronger debiasing can reduce accuracy because superficial quality is also correlated with human preference. The work is methodological and does not study teachers, students, schools, or classroom interventions.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a computational NLP benchmark study with systematic experiments, but it is not an education study and does not use a randomized or field-based design relevant to K-12 intervention evidence. The methodology is empirical, yet it is best characterized as a technical evaluation rather than causal evidence in an educational setting.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows meaningful gains in benchmark accuracy and bias reduction for LLM judging, but the work is about evaluator calibration rather than direct educational outcomes. Its impact for education is therefore indirect and unclear, with no demonstrated effect on learners or teachers.

interventions.use_case: mitigating bias in LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation systems for comparing model outputs, using calibration for closed-source judges and contrastive training for open-source judges

finding.finding_summary: The proposed bias-mitigation methods improved the reliability of LLM-based evaluation while keeping comparable performance on natural data. On LLMBar, probability calibration and contrastive training raised accuracy on adversarial sets substantially (e.g., Text-davinci-003 logprobs from 48.88 average to 67.02; Vicuna-7B from 39.74 to 54.82 or 57.20 depending on contrastive variant), with only small or no degradation on the natural set.
finding.measure: LLM evaluator accuracy on LLMBar Natural and adversarial test sets

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that bias mitigation can reduce systematic evaluator bias, including verbosity/formality/self-enhancement tendencies, and notes privacy concerns with external API-based judging as a motivation for local mitigation. Results suggest that calibration/contrastive training can improve fairness and reduce over-reliance on superficial quality, but with a tradeoff: too much mitigation can lower accuracy, indicating unresolved governance and reliability risks.
finding.measure: Bias on adversarial benchmark sets; discussion of privacy and fairness risks in LLM evaluation

paper_profiles.title: Impact of Criterion-Based Reflection on Prospective Physics Teachers’ Perceptions of ChatGPT-Generated Content
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory study examines whether engaging prospective physics teachers in criterion-based reflection changes how they perceive ChatGPT-generated content. The paper asks whether structured evaluation can shift judgments of answer quality and helpfulness, and whether students become more aware of limitations in AI-generated didactic materials. It also explores how participants interpret ChatGPT’s functionality and how their prior experiences shape these judgments.

The intervention was a criterion-based evaluation approach built around four criteria: clarity, correctness, appropriateness, and precision. Thirty-nine German prospective physics teachers completed pre- and post-questionnaires with 5-point ratings and open-ended responses, and they discussed ChatGPT outputs in group sessions. They evaluated ChatGPT 3.5 responses to didactical tasks such as creating context-oriented teaching sequences in acoustics for grade 10 and developing teaching-learning sequences on energy and power for grade 7.

The results show that critical reflection made students more aware of ChatGPT’s weaknesses and slightly reduced ratings of both answer quality and helpfulness. Students identified problems including vague terminology, incorrect or incomplete content, poor fit to grade level and prior knowledge, and weak logical structure. However, some students still overestimated ChatGPT because of confirmation bias linked to prior positive experiences. The paper concludes that criterion-based evaluation can support media literacy and critical thinking in teacher education, while also showing that students may misunderstand how ChatGPT works and may need explicit instruction about its capabilities and limitations.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small exploratory qualitative/pre-post study without a control group, randomization, or inferential effect estimates. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically transparent, but it offers limited causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention appears to modestly improve critical reflection and awareness of limitations in a priority population of prospective teachers, but the observed pre/post shifts are small and not statistically significant. The impact is therefore promising but unclear for broader educational outcomes.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT3.5 used by prospective physics teachers to generate didactical content for lesson planning, including context-oriented teaching sequences in acoustics and teaching-learning sequences on energy and power, then evaluated with criterion-based reflection.

finding.finding_summary: Criterion-based reflection improved prospective physics teachers’ critical evaluation and awareness of ChatGPT’s limitations. Across 39 participants (n=39), mean ratings of answer quality decreased from 3.16 (SD=0.76) pre to 2.66 (SD=0.85) post, and helpfulness decreased from 3.31 (SD=0.95) to 3.08 (SD=1.05), indicating more critical judgment after structured evaluation.
finding.measure: Pre/post 5-point ratings of ChatGPT answer quality and helpfulness; qualitative reflection on didactical criteria (clarity, correctness, appropriateness, precision)
finding.std_deviation: Quality pre SD=.76, post SD=.85; Helpfulness pre SD=.95, post SD=1.05

finding.finding_summary: The intervention changed students’ perceptions of ChatGPT in both positive and negative directions, with some students becoming more skeptical while others retained or increased positive views due to prior favorable experiences. The paper reports three perspective groups: extreme negative, extreme positive, and balanced, but does not provide inferential effect sizes or statistical tests beyond noting the pre/post changes were not statistically significant.
finding.measure: Pre/post self-ratings of perceived helpfulness and quality; thematic analysis of group discussions

finding.finding_summary: The study found that students could identify didactical shortcomings in ChatGPT-generated physics lesson material, especially for learning goals and teaching-learning sequences. All 39 students recognized the difficulty with non-operational verbs in learning goals, and most criticized missing clarity, correctness, appropriateness, and precision in a grade-7 energy and power task.
finding.measure: Qualitative evaluation of ChatGPT-generated didactical tasks in physics education

paper_profiles.title: HIVE: Harnessing Human Feedback for Instructional Visual Editing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of improving instructional image editing so that generated edits better match human intentions and preferences. The authors argue that existing instruction-based editing systems can misinterpret instructions, over-edit images, or produce results that do not align well with what users want. To address this, they propose HIVE (Harnessing Human Feedback for Instructional Visual Editing), a framework that adds human preference learning to diffusion-based image editing.

HIVE is a three-stage approach. First, the authors perform instructional supervised fine-tuning using a large dataset of image-instruction-edit triplets, including newly collected training data and data derived from InstructPix2Pix. Second, they collect human rankings of multiple edited outputs for the same image-instruction pair and train a reward model to predict human preference. Third, they fine-tune the diffusion model using the learned rewards, either by weighting examples according to reward or by conditioning on reward labels.

The study uses synthetic evaluation data and a self-collected 1,000-example user-study dataset of real images and human-written instructions, with crowdsourced annotators on Amazon Mechanical Turk. The results show that incorporating human feedback improves alignment with instructions and preserves irrelevant parts of images better than the baseline model trained without feedback. The authors also report that the reward-conditioning variant performs slightly better in stability, and that cycle-consistency augmentation improves performance.

The paper concludes that human feedback is valuable for instruction-following image editing, but it also notes several limitations and risks: some instructions are still hard to understand, counting and spatial reasoning remain failure cases, object grounding can be wrong, and the model may inherit bias or harmful content from foundation models. The authors also mention that cases where all candidate outputs are similarly wrong are not helped much by preference learning, and that some edited outputs can become unstructured.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a technical generative-model paper, not an education study, and it does not evaluate student or teacher outcomes, school settings, or instructional practice. The paper reports model-training procedures, benchmark comparisons, and user preference studies for image editing quality, but no educational intervention evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no demonstrated impact on education outcomes or teacher coaching. Any gains are within the domain of image-editing model preference and alignment, so the education-relevant impact is not assessable from this paper.

interventions.use_case: human-feedback-guided diffusion model fine-tuning for instructional visual editing (image editing from text instructions)

paper_profiles.title: Personalisation within bounds: A risk taxonomy and policy framework for the alignment of large language models with personalised feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how large language models (LLMs) should be personalised to individual users, and what risks and benefits arise when models learn from user-specific feedback. Rather than presenting an empirical evaluation, the authors argue that existing alignment methods such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) are a form of implicit personalisation, often shaped by a narrow set of crowdworkers and design choices made by technology providers.

The paper proposes a taxonomy of benefits and risks associated with personalised LLMs at both the individual and societal levels. It frames possible benefits as improved efficiency, utility, autonomy, empathy, inclusion, diversity, participation, and labour productivity. It also identifies risks including extra user effort, addiction and over-reliance, bias reinforcement, essentialist profiling, anthropomorphism, privacy intrusion, access disparities, polarisation, malicious use, labour displacement, and environmental harms.

The context is broad and not tied to a specific educational intervention, school level, or country. The authors discuss potential use cases across domains such as education, healthcare, law, and finance, but the paper itself is a policy and conceptual framework rather than a study of teachers, students, or classrooms. The main conclusion is that personalisation should be allowed only within clear bounds, with governance constraints at national, provider, and end-user levels to reduce unsafe or socially harmful model behaviours.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/framework paper rather than an empirical study. It synthesizes prior literature to propose a risk taxonomy and governance framework, but does not report a primary experimental or observational design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has potentially high conceptual relevance for governing generative AI coaching and feedback systems, especially around safety, privacy, bias, and overreliance. However, it reports no direct measured educational impact, so the empirical impact on outcomes is unclear.

interventions.use_case: A policy-and-risk analysis of personalized large language models as user-adaptive conversational assistants, including tailored feedback, dialogue, and information support across contexts such as education, healthcare, and general-purpose assistance.

paper_profiles.title: CLIMB: A Benchmark of Clinical Bias in Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces CLIMB, a benchmark for systematically evaluating clinical bias in large language models (LLMs). The authors argue that existing evaluations are limited because they often cover only a narrow set of diagnoses, do not separate intrinsic from extrinsic bias, and do not adequately account for clinical setting-specific attributes such as sex, ethnicity, and insurance type.

CLIMB studies bias in two ways. First, it measures intrinsic bias using a modified implicit-association-style method, where diagnoses are paired with demographic proxies (names) and the model’s next-token probabilities are used to quantify association disparities across multiple demographic groups. Second, it measures extrinsic bias by counterfactually changing demographic information in clinical notes from CLIBENCH/MIMIC-IV-style cases and observing changes in diagnostic recall. The evaluation focuses on open-source Mistral and LLaMA family models, including medically adapted variants.

The benchmark is built around a clinical diagnosis task in a real-world hospital/EHR context, with analyses by sex-neutral and sex-specific diagnoses and by ethnicity and insurance. The main conclusion is that almost all evaluated models exhibit clinically meaningful bias, including demographic association disparities and performance shifts under counterfactual perturbations. The paper also finds that medically adapted models are not necessarily less biased and can sometimes be worse than their base counterparts. The authors conclude that more robust bias evaluation and mitigation methods are needed for clinical LLM deployment.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark/method paper evaluating bias in LLMs for clinical diagnosis rather than an intervention study with learner outcomes. It uses a systematic experimental setup and reports quantitative comparisons, but it is not an RCT or QED in an education setting.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct educational impact and does not test instructional improvement effects. Its impact is methodological, highlighting bias and safety risks in clinical LLM use, which is relevant to AI evaluation but not evidence of outcome gains.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models, especially ChatGPT-style systems, for education. Rather than reporting a single empirical intervention, it synthesizes plausible use cases and concerns for both learning and teaching. The paper asks how large language models might support content generation, personalized feedback, tutoring, assessment, and professional development, while also identifying the ethical, pedagogical, legal, and technical risks that accompany their use.

The paper is not an intervention study with participants. It discusses educational applications across multiple contexts and user groups, including elementary, secondary, tertiary, and professional learning, with a particular emphasis on students and teachers. Examples include automated quiz generation, explanation of code, language learning support, adaptive feedback, lesson planning, and semi-automated grading.

Its main conclusion is that large language models could become powerful educational tools, but only if they are integrated carefully and responsibly. The authors stress the need for human oversight, critical thinking, fact checking, bias mitigation, privacy protections, sustainability considerations, and educator training. They argue that these systems are promising but still brittle, can produce biased or inaccurate output, may encourage overreliance, and require clear governance and pedagogical framing to avoid harm.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper and narrative review, not an empirical evaluation. It synthesizes opportunities and risks but does not report a new study design, sample, or causal identification strategy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for potentially broad institutional and pedagogical impact, but because it is non-empirical and reports no measured effects, the impact is best characterized as unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Position paper on large language models/ChatGPT as educational assistants for tutoring, question answering, personalized practice, teacher support, lesson planning, and feedback generation.
Uses LLMs to generate feedback on student writing and answers, including assessment support, adaptive feedback, and semi-automated grading.
Uses LLMs for writing support, grammar/style correction, summarization, translation, and language-learning assistance for students and teachers.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by automating or accelerating lesson planning, feedback generation, grading support, and content creation. Reported examples include grading-effort reductions of up to 85% in prior NLP feedback work cited by the paper, but this position paper itself does not present new empirical estimates.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, and time saved in lesson planning/feedback tasks (reported in cited prior studies rather than new data)

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests LLM-supported conversational agents may improve student engagement, curiosity, participation, and willingness to communicate, and may help reduce language-learning anxiety. These claims are framed as opportunities and literature-backed possibilities rather than results from a single new experiment in this article.
finding.measure: Engagement, curiosity expression, participation, and language-learning anxiety (reported from cited studies and conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: A central theme is that LLMs may support critical thinking, problem-solving, and creativity when used as a supplement, but may also undermine these skills if learners or teachers over-rely on generated answers. The paper provides conceptual risk analysis rather than a controlled estimate, and repeatedly emphasizes the need for human oversight and fact-checking.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and fact-checking capacity (conceptual synthesis; no new quantitative measure)

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s strongest focus is on governance, safety, ethics, and institutional readiness for LLM adoption in education. It identifies major risks including bias, privacy/security, copyright/plagiarism, sustainability, cost, and difficulty distinguishing machine-generated from human-generated text, while recommending human oversight, transparency, and policy safeguards.
finding.measure: Policy/governance risks and mitigation requirements (bias, privacy, copyright, sustainability, integrity, and access)

paper_profiles.title: Distributed agency in second language learning and teaching through generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a theoretical and position-oriented discussion of how generative AI is reshaping second language learning and teaching. It asks how agency is distributed among learners, teachers, and AI systems, and argues that AI should be understood not simply as a tool but as an active participant in language-learning ecologies.

The article surveys current and emerging uses of generative AI such as ChatGPT for language practice, corrective feedback, lesson-plan creation, writing support, assessment, and immersive learning. It emphasizes critical AI literacy, describing why learners and teachers need to understand both the capabilities and limitations of large language models. The paper also discusses ethical concerns, bias, inaccuracies, pragmatic limitations, and unequal access, especially for less privileged users.

The context is broadly instructed second language education rather than a single empirical site or intervention. The author draws on ecological theories, sociomaterialism, and relational pedagogy to frame AI-human interaction as shared and distributed agency. The main conclusion is that AI can support learning and teaching, but only when used critically, ethically, and with awareness of sociocultural limitations, power relations, and the need to preserve human agency and multilingual, context-sensitive language use.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/emerging-technologies column rather than an empirical study. It synthesizes prior work and offers theory, examples, and cautions, but does not present a defined study design, comparison, or original outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No original effect estimates or outcome data are reported, so there is no measurable impact to classify. The paper is useful as a theoretical overview of benefits and risks, but not as evidence of effectiveness.

interventions.use_case: generative AI chatbots and custom GPT-style tools used for second-language practice, conversational interaction, prompt-based feedback, and teacher-created AI-assisted language learning materials
AI-assisted writing support for L2 learners, including grammar checking, style improvement, translation, brainstorming, drafting, revision, and customized prompt-based writing feedback
AI-generated corrective feedback and rubric-based feedback on student writing, including individual text analysis and suggestion of revisions

paper_profiles.title: A pedagogical design for self-regulated learning in academic writing using text-based generative artificial intelligence tools: 6-P pedagogy of plan, prompt, preview, produce, peer-review, portfolio-tracking
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of how students and teachers should use text-based generative AI tools, such as ChatGPT, for academic writing without undermining academic integrity, critical thinking, or self-regulation. The authors argue that generative AI can be useful in education, but only if learners are taught to use it as a tool rather than a substitute for thinking and writing.

To respond to this problem, the paper proposes a six-phase pedagogical framework called 6-P pedagogy: plan, prompt, preview, produce, peer-review, and portfolio-tracking. The design is grounded in Zimmerman’s self-regulated learning model and the authoring cycle. It emphasizes that students should first plan their writing, then prompt the AI, critically preview and verify AI output, produce their own coherent text, use peer review to refine it, and finally reflect through portfolio-tracking.

The intended population is university students, with an implementation context described at a university in Hong Kong that adopted the framework for General Education and all undergraduates. The paper is theoretical rather than empirical: it does not report outcome data from a controlled intervention, but instead lays out a conceptual model, its rationale, and implications for teachers, institutions, and future research. The main conclusion is that generative AI literacy, self-regulation, and critical thinking are essential for safe and effective academic use of generative AI, and that the 6-P framework offers a structured way to support these goals.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual framework paper with no empirical study design, no comparison group, and no outcome data. It is useful for theory-building but does not provide evaluative evidence on intervention effectiveness or heterogeneity.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper proposes a potentially important classroom framework for generative AI-supported writing, but it reports no observed effect sizes or validated outcomes. Its impact is therefore speculative and unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: A six-phase pedagogical framework (6-P: plan, prompt, preview, produce, peer-review, portfolio-tracking) for student use of text-based generative AI tools such as ChatGPT in academic writing.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper rather than an empirical evaluation, so it does not report measured effects on writing quality or literacy outcomes. The authors propose a 6-P pedagogy for academic writing with generative AI and explicitly state that the framework has not yet been validated in a real-world setting.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: No empirical outcome data are reported, but the paper’s central intended outcomes are critical thinking and self-regulation while using text-based generative AI for writing. The authors argue the 6-P model is designed to develop these durable skills, yet they note that validation evidence is still lacking.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test institutional policy effects, but it proposes that schools and universities adopt guidelines, teacher development, recording of AI interactions, and generative AI literacy supports. These are presented as implications and future directions rather than measured impacts.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT in foreign language lesson plan creation: Trends, variability, and historical biases
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how well ChatGPT can generate foreign language lesson plans and how much the quality of those plans changes when prompts become more specific. The authors focus on a practical teacher workflow problem: whether zero-shot prompting can produce lesson plans aligned with common language-teaching criteria and licensure expectations, and whether added prompt detail improves the result reliably.

The intervention studied is not a classroom implementation but a prompt-engineering experiment using ChatGPT-4.0. The authors created five increasingly specific prompts for a 45-minute high school Spanish lesson on a Costa Rican restaurant, then ran each prompt 10 times in separate chats to assess output variability. They scored 50 generated lesson plans against a rubric based on best practices and edTPA-aligned criteria, using quantitative analyses of score trends, word counts, dissimilarity, and clustering.

The study was conducted in the context of foreign language teacher preparation in the United States, specifically around UNCC’s teacher-licensure-oriented lesson-plan template. The main conclusion is that ChatGPT often produced usable lesson plans, but more detailed prompts did not consistently improve quality. Adding a checklist of required criteria helped most, yet outputs remained highly variable even with identical prompts. The authors also found that many outputs reflected outdated pedagogical practices and biases, especially toward scripted, audio-lingual-style instruction and weak attention to culture. They argue that teachers should critically review and revise AI-generated plans rather than use them unedited.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical study with a clear method, but it is a descriptive/analytic evaluation of AI-generated lesson plans rather than a causal intervention study with human participants. It provides useful evidence on variability and bias, but not on learner outcomes or a randomized design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical benefits for teacher workload and AI literacy, but the demonstrated impact is indirect and modest, based on generated text quality rather than measured educational outcomes. No effect sizes on learner or teacher outcomes were reported.

interventions.use_case: Using ChatGPT v4 with zero-shot prompting to generate foreign-language teacher lesson plans, then probing how prompt specificity and repeated chats affect output quality, variability, and bias in the generated plans.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that ChatGPT could streamline lesson-plan creation for foreign language teachers, but quality was inconsistent. Across 50 generated lesson plans (5 prompts x 10 iterations), mean rubric scores ranged from 19.6/25 to 21.6/25, and outputs sometimes omitted multiple required components despite added specificity.
finding.measure: Lesson-plan rubric scores and word count of ChatGPT-generated lesson plans

finding.finding_summary: A central finding was that users need to critically evaluate and revise AI-generated lesson plans because outputs were non-deterministic and sometimes reflected outdated pedagogical practices. The paper did not measure teacher learning directly, but it argued that AI literacy, metatechnolinguistic competence, and prompt refinement are necessary to safely use the tool.
finding.measure: Rubric alignment, presence/absence of required lesson components, and qualitative analysis of prompt/output variability and bias

paper_profiles.title: The Theory and Practice of Online Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book is a revised second edition of a broader volume on online learning and distance education, not an empirical study of a specific intervention. The text surveys theory, infrastructure, course design, delivery, quality assurance, and student support in online learning, and frames online learning as a complex and rapidly evolving field shaped by changes in technology, pedagogy, and institutional practice.

The opening chapter discussed in the excerpt argues that effective online learning depends on instructional design grounded in learning theory rather than on technology alone. It reviews behaviorist, cognitivist, constructivist, and connectivist perspectives, and suggests that online materials should be designed to support motivation, interaction, feedback, contextual learning, and individual differences.

Across the book, the intended context is higher education and distance education, especially at Athabasca University and similar institutions. The chapter summaries emphasize issues such as online course development, quality control, student support, mobile learning, and social software. Because the text is theoretical and descriptive rather than evaluative, it does not report an intervention effect, a participant sample, or comparative findings by teacher experience, subject area, grade level, or school context.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a book chapter introducing and synthesizing theory and design principles for online learning, not an empirical study of a specific intervention. It contains no original research design, sample, or effect estimation relevant to intervention effectiveness or heterogeneity.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No measurable intervention impact is reported. The chapter is conceptual and descriptive, so there is no evidence of effects, subgroup differences, or safety risks specific to generative AI-supported teacher coaching or lesson-plan feedback.

paper_profiles.title: Confronting the Challenges of Participatory Culture: Media Education for the 21st Century
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report argues that participatory digital culture has changed the skills young people need to fully participate in social, civic, creative, and economic life. It identifies three core problems that make adult guidance and media education necessary: unequal access to meaningful opportunities for participation (the participation gap), difficulty recognizing how media shape perception and meaning (the transparency problem), and the lack of ethical preparation for public participation online (the ethics challenge).

Rather than studying a specific classroom intervention, the paper proposes a framework for media literacy and participatory culture. It describes forms of participation such as affiliations, expressions, collaborative problem solving, and circulations, and it outlines a set of new media literacies including play, performance, simulation, appropriation, multitasking, collective intelligence, judgment, transmedia navigation, networking, and negotiation. The report emphasizes that these skills emerge through social and cultural practices, not just access to technology.

The context is primarily U.S. youth, especially teens, school-aged children, and informal learners in online communities, after-school settings, and classrooms. The paper concludes that schools, after-school programs, and parents all have roles in fostering these competencies, and that media education should address access, critical reflection, and ethical participation together rather than treating technology use as sufficient on its own.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a book-length conceptual and policy report, not an empirical study with a defined intervention, comparison group, or original quantitative design. It synthesizes prior literature and provides expert argumentation, but does not meet criteria for experimental or quasi-experimental evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The report has substantial conceptual influence on media literacy and participatory culture discourse, but it does not estimate a measurable intervention effect. Its likely educational impact is important yet indirect and not empirically quantified in this paper.

finding.finding_summary: This is a policy and theory report arguing that schools and after-school programs should respond to participatory culture, but it does not evaluate an intervention experimentally. It identifies likely risks and inequities in educational use of digital media, including the participation gap, transparency problems, and ethics challenges, based on cited observational studies rather than new effect estimates.
finding.measure: Policy analysis and synthesis of prior studies on participatory culture, media literacy, and youth digital practices

finding.finding_summary: The report argues that participatory media environments can support collaboration, networking, judgment, transmedia navigation, and negotiation, drawing on examples such as fan communities and game-based participation. However, these claims are conceptual and supported by cited prior work rather than direct experimental evidence in this paper, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual synthesis of media literacy skills, collaboration, and participatory learning practices

finding.finding_summary: The report suggests that participatory culture can increase confidence, belonging, and motivation by giving youths meaningful roles in communities where their contributions matter. These claims are grounded in examples and secondary literature, not a direct outcome evaluation, so no effect size or sample size is available.
finding.measure: Self-confidence, sense of belonging, and participation in communities of practice

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emergence of ChatGPT and its implications for higher education, especially assessment, learning, and teaching. The central question is not whether ChatGPT is effective in a controlled educational intervention, but how a powerful generative AI system should be understood in relation to existing educational technology and what opportunities and risks it creates for universities and instructors.

The authors use a desktop analysis approach combining an extensive literature review with hands-on experimentation using ChatGPT. They situate ChatGPT within the broader Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd) literature, particularly student-facing, teacher-facing, and system-facing applications. The paper also discusses ChatGPT’s functionality, strengths, and limitations, including its performance on explanatory, essay-writing, and Chinese-language tasks.

The relevant population context is higher education, with discussion focused on university students, teachers, and institutions rather than a specific sample. The paper argues that ChatGPT can support idea generation, conceptual explanation, and some writing assistance, but it is weak at higher-order critical and analytical tasks, may produce generic or inaccurate text, can fabricate references, and is limited by its knowledge cutoff and bias/safety problems. The authors conclude that higher education should adapt assessment and teaching practices rather than simply banning the tool.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed conceptual/review article with exploratory self-testing and literature synthesis, not a controlled empirical evaluation. It provides useful analysis of risks and opportunities, but does not meet experimental or quasi-experimental credibility criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially important implications for writing, assessment, and institutional policy, but it reports no quantified impacts and no causal evidence. The practical implications are substantial, yet the measured impact is unclear and mostly speculative.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT as a general-purpose generative AI chatbot for higher-education student support, drafting, question answering, brainstorming, and teacher-facing feedback/assessment discussions
ChatGPT-like text generation used for drafting and revising academic writing, including essay generation, plagiarism evasion, and feedback-style language support
AI writing support and language generation for essay drafting, paraphrasing, Chinese composition generation, and writing assistance analogous to Grammarly/Wordtune and ChatGPT-based writing help

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT could quickly generate essay-like text, but the resulting writing was often generic, descriptive, and weak on evidence, citations, and depth. In one example, a 2000-word essay prompt produced only about 500 words and five references, with the authors noting the output was usable mainly for 'leisure reading' rather than academic writing. No controlled effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Quality of generated essay writing, coherence, depth, citation use, and language quality in author prompts

finding.finding_summary: When prompted to write a Chinese composition, ChatGPT produced text that was grammatically poor, illogical in parts, and appeared to be directly translated from English. The authors judged Chinese to be a weak language for the system, aligning with cited evidence that performance is much better on high-resource European languages than on Chinese or Romanian. No numeric effect estimate was reported.
finding.measure: Quality and grammaticality of generated Chinese composition

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can support idea generation, experimentation, collaboration, and problem-solving, but is weak at higher-order thinking tasks such as critical and analytical writing. In the authors’ own prompt tests, the model handled conceptual explanations well yet produced shallow analysis when asked for an academic essay requiring evaluation and evidence. No controlled effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Author-assessed support for critical thinking, analysis, and problem solving in prompted outputs

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly notes that ChatGPT can produce responses within roughly 60-120 seconds, suggesting time-saving potential for drafting, brainstorming, and quick explanation. However, this efficiency is tempered by failures such as network errors, character limits, and the need for human checking because outputs may be generic or inaccurate. No controlled effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Observed response time, ease of use, and workflow efficiency in exploratory prompts

finding.finding_summary: The article frames ChatGPT as a major challenge for assessment policy, plagiarism detection, and institutional governance in higher education. It reports that anti-plagiarism software used in the authors’ testing did not detect ChatGPT-generated work, but also notes that Turnitin was reportedly enhancing detection capabilities; the paper is qualitative and policy-oriented rather than experimental.
finding.measure: Assessment integrity, plagiarism-detection reliability, and institutional policy implications

paper_profiles.title: What if the devil is my guardian angel: ChatGPT as a case study of using chatbots in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines concerns about using ChatGPT in education, especially among early adopters, and asks what risks and cautions should accompany adoption of generative AI chatbots in teaching and learning. Rather than testing a formal instructional intervention, the authors use ChatGPT as a case study to explore public discourse, stakeholder perceptions, and hands-on use in educational scenarios.

The study uses a three-stage qualitative design: social network analysis of tweets about ChatGPT and education, content analysis of 19 publicly recruited interviews with users who had experience using ChatGPT in educational contexts, and user-experience testing by three experienced educators across ten educational scenarios. The participants included educators, students, developers, and AI freelancers; the educational use cases ranged across teaching, instructional design, essay writing, quiz generation, and information retrieval. The paper does not focus on a specific grade band or school system, but rather on higher education and adult educational users interacting with ChatGPT online.

The authors conclude that ChatGPT is perceived as promising and potentially transformative for education, but that its use requires caution because it can produce inaccurate or generic responses, contradictory outputs, misleading privacy claims, dishonest or manipulative behavior, and content that may encourage cheating, plagiarism, laziness, or reduced critical thinking. The paper also highlights heterogeneity in outputs: the same prompt can yield different answers of different quality across users. No evidence is provided that effects differ by teacher experience, subject area, grade level, or school context in a controlled way; instead, these are presented as concerns and open research questions for future work.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative instrumental case study with social network analysis, interview content analysis, and scenario-based user testing. It is peer-reviewed and systematic, but it does not provide experimental or causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially important educational and institutional implications, but the evidence is exploratory and qualitative rather than measured impact. Its conclusions about benefits and risks are plausible but not quantified with effect sizes.

interventions.use_case: Qualitative case study of ChatGPT as an educational chatbot used for teacher/learner support, lesson planning, quiz generation, answering questions, and conversational assistance in education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds both potential benefits and risks for durable skills. Participants said ChatGPT can support learning, prompt understanding, and help with instructional design, but they also warned it may reduce students’ critical thinking and encourage dependence on easy answers. No quantitative effect size was reported; evidence came from 19 interviews, 2330 tweets, and 3 educators’ scenario tests.
finding.measure: qualitative perceptions of critical thinking, dependence, and learning support; scenario-based observations
finding.study_size: n=19 interviews; 2330 tweets; 3 educators in scenario testing

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was viewed as useful for reducing teacher workload by generating lesson materials, quizzes, outlines, and immediate feedback. However, the paper also showed that outputs can be generic, inconsistent, inaccurate, or differently structured for the same prompt, which can increase teacher effort to verify and revise them. No quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: perceived usefulness for lesson planning, quiz creation, feedback, and teacher workload reduction

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues ChatGPT may shift educational practice, assessment, policy, and school governance, but also introduces institutional risks such as cheating, privacy leakage, misinformation, bias, and manipulation. It highlights concerns about bans, the need for new teaching philosophies, and the need for responsible-use guidelines and regulation. No quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: policy and governance concerns; institutional responses; cheating/privacy/fairness risks
finding.study_size: n=19 interviews; 2330 tweets; 3 educators scenario testing

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can function as a scalable teacher coach by automatically scoring classroom instruction and generating useful feedback. The authors focus on three tasks: scoring transcript segments using classroom observation rubrics, identifying highlights and missed opportunities in teaching practice, and generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

The study evaluates zero-shot ChatGPT on elementary mathematics classroom transcripts from the NCTE dataset. The transcripts come from 317 U.S. teachers across four school districts and are linked to expert ratings from two established observation systems: CLASS and MQI. For the qualitative tasks, two experienced math teachers, one with decades of coaching experience and one with six years of teaching experience in Title I public schools, rated model outputs for relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty.

Overall, the paper finds that ChatGPT has promise but is not yet reliable as a teacher coach. Its numerical scores correlate poorly with human ratings, and its qualitative feedback is often not insightful, especially for MQI-related technical aspects of mathematics instruction. For suggestions, the model frequently repeats what the teacher is already doing rather than offering novel advice. The authors conclude that generative AI could complement human coaching in the future, but current systems need better grounding, more conservative inference, and human-in-the-loop design.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical evaluation with a clear methodology, but it is qualitative/correlational rather than an RCT or QED. It also uses a small human-evaluation sample (2 teachers) and a limited set of transcripts, which constrains internal and external validity.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows limited or negative performance on key coaching-quality metrics, with low correlations and high redundancy/unfaithfulness, so demonstrated impact is unclear rather than strong. Any benefit is mainly potential and theoretical, not evidenced as a modest or large effect on teacher or student outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Zero-shot use of ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) as an automated teacher coach to score classroom transcript segments, identify highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and generate actionable suggestions for eliciting more student mathematical reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT performed poorly as a scorer of elementary math instruction transcript segments. Across 100 sampled segments, Spearman correlations with expert ratings were low or near zero for CLASS and MQI items (e.g., CLPC 0.00/0.04/-0.06; CLBM 0.35/0.23/0.07; EXPL 0.02/0.12/-0.11; SMQR 0.17/0.17/0.06 across DA/DA+/RA prompts), and adding rubric descriptions or reasoning did not improve performance. The model also struggled to identify insightful or relevant math-instruction examples, with MQI examples rated worse than CLASS examples (e.g., relevance No=55%, insightfulness No=71%).
finding.measure: Spearman correlation between model-predicted and human scores on CLASS/MQI rubric items; human ratings of relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness for feedback examples
finding.study_size: n=100 transcript segments for scoring; n=216 CLASS examples and n=288 MQI examples for highlight/missed-opportunity evaluation; n=36 suggestions
finding.effect_size: Spearman rho values reported; no Cohen's d/g

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests potential efficiency benefits from scalable automated coaching, but the realized output quality was limited. ChatGPT generated many actionable suggestions for teachers, yet 82% of suggestions were redundant and repeated something the teacher already did, and 20-30% of highlight/missed-opportunity responses were judged unfaithful, indicating substantial risk if used to reduce coach workload without human review.
finding.measure: Human teacher ratings of actionability, novelty, relevance, and faithfulness of model-generated feedback/suggestions
finding.study_size: n=36 suggestions; n=216 CLASS examples; n=288 MQI examples

paper_profiles.title: To what extent is ChatGPT useful for language teacher lesson plan creation?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how useful ChatGPT is for creating foreign language lesson plans and whether the quality of its outputs changes when prompts become more specific. The authors focus on three issues: how prompt specificity affects lesson-plan structure and content, how consistent ChatGPT is when given the same prompt multiple times, and what strengths or weaknesses appear across outputs regardless of prompt type.

The intervention/approach studied was zero-shot prompting of ChatGPT 4.0. The authors created five prompts that progressively added more specificity for a 45-minute high school Spanish lesson on Costa Rican restaurant language, then ran each prompt 10 times in separate chats, producing 50 lesson plans. Outputs were scored against a 25-item rubric aligned with ACTFL guidelines and the edTPA-based lesson-plan template used in a foreign language teacher preparation program at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte.

The study context was preservice foreign language teacher training in the United States, with outputs designed for a high school Level I Spanish classroom. Results showed that ChatGPT often produced generally high-quality lesson plans, but greater prompt specificity did not produce a simple linear improvement. Adding a lesson-plan template sometimes reduced scores, while adding an explicit checklist of required criteria produced the best average performance. The authors also found substantial variability: the same prompt could yield much better or worse plans across repeated trials. Weaknesses included inconsistent integration of ACTFL standards, weak treatment of cultural comparison, and occasional reversion to outdated or teacher-centered pedagogical practices.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT can be a useful aid for lesson planning, but only when teachers critically evaluate and revise its outputs. The authors emphasize that generative AI may reproduce historically biased or outdated instructional approaches, so AI literacy should include careful checking for quality, coherence, and alignment with modern language-teaching practice.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical study, but it is a small-sample descriptive/analytic prompt experiment rather than a causal educational trial. It provides useful evidence about model behavior and output quality, but does not meet higher-rigor causal standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical utility for teacher lesson-plan drafting, but the estimated impact is modest and indirect, with no student learning outcome data and no effect size on educational achievement. Its main contribution is workflow efficiency and risk identification rather than demonstrated large-scale educational impact.

interventions.use_case: Using ChatGPT-4.0 via zero-shot prompting to generate foreign language teacher lesson plans and assess how prompt specificity affects lesson-plan quality and variability.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was generally useful for producing language-teacher lesson plans, suggesting potential to reduce teacher workload in instructional design. Across 50 generated lesson plans (5 prompts x 10 iterations), mean rubric scores ranged from 19.6/25 to 21.6/25, with the highest mean under the most detailed prompt (P.5).
finding.measure: Rubric-based lesson-plan quality score; word count; presence/absence of 25 lesson-plan criteria

finding.finding_summary: Prompt specificity sometimes improved alignment with target criteria, but the relationship was not linear and outputs remained highly variable. ANOVA found a marginal overall difference across prompt groups (F=2.668, p=0.0442), while pairwise tests were not significant after correction; PERMANOVA also indicated multivariate differences between prompt groups (F=3.1556, p=0.001).
finding.measure: Prompt-output alignment to lesson-plan rubric; Jaccard distance/NMDS/PERMANOVA/ANOSIM on binary criteria scores

finding.finding_summary: The generated lesson plans were often high quality for foreign-language lesson planning, but several important pedagogical elements were inconsistently included. Some criteria, such as meaningful context and proficiency-appropriate activities, appeared in nearly all outputs, while cultural connections and standards integration were often missing or only present in about half of outputs even under the most detailed prompt.
finding.measure: Presence/absence of foreign-language lesson-plan components aligned to edTPA/ACTFL criteria

paper_profiles.title: LessonPlanner: Assisting Novice Teachers to Prepare Pedagogy-Driven Lesson Plans with Large Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: UIST ’24 (The 37th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge novice teachers face when preparing lesson plans and selecting effective instructional strategies and materials. The authors investigate whether large language models (LLMs) can support lesson-plan creation in a pedagogy-driven way rather than through unstructured prompting or generic chat use.

They first conduct a formative study with six novice teachers and teaching assistants to identify needs and concerns. Based on those findings, they build LessonPlanner, a web-based system powered by GPT-4 that structures lesson planning around Bloom’s Taxonomy and Gagne’s Nine Events of Instruction. The system helps users generate lesson goals, lesson-plan outlines, section-specific materials, instructional suggestions, and slide guidance, while allowing iterative editing and regeneration.

The evaluation combines a within-subjects user study with 12 university students acting as teachers and expert interviews with six teachers across university, elementary, and high-school contexts. The study found that LessonPlanner improved the quality of lesson plans and reduced workload compared with a ChatGPT baseline. Participants valued the organized outline and generated ideas, but the authors also report concerns about accuracy, the need for subject-specific judgment, and the cognitive burden of prompting.

Overall, the paper concludes that LLMs can be useful for assisting lesson-plan preparation when carefully constrained by pedagogical structure and interactive controls, but they should be treated as supportive tools rather than autonomous teaching experts.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed HCI user study with a within-subjects comparison and follow-up expert interviews, but it is small and not a randomized field trial in authentic classroom deployment. Evidence is useful and moderately rigorous, but credibility/relevance constraints remain substantial.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports a positive but small-scale productivity benefit for novice teachers rather than a measured learning outcome, and it does not report effect sizes in the excerpt. The practical impact is promising but still unclear in magnitude and generalizability.

interventions.use_case: An interactive lesson-planning assistant built on GPT-4 that generates lesson goals, lesson outlines, pedagogical activities, teaching materials, and feedback for teachers using Gagne’s Nine Events and Bloom’s Taxonomy.

finding.finding_summary: In a within-subjects study with n=12 university students preparing lesson plans, LessonPlanner significantly improved the quality of outcome lesson plans and eased workload compared with a ChatGPT web-app baseline, but the paper does not report the exact test statistics or effect size in the excerpt provided. Questionnaire and interview data also indicated reduced mental burden during lesson preparation and better support for organizing the planning process.
finding.measure: Lesson plan quality ratings by an expert teacher; NASA-TLX workload ratings; SUS; trust questionnaire

paper_profiles.title: Understanding Teacher Revisions of Large Language Model-Generated Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers revise feedback generated by large language models before it is delivered to students. The authors focus on a key but under-studied question in AI-supported education: not only whether LLMs can generate plausible formative feedback, but how teachers actually interact with, edit, and mediate that feedback in practice.

The study analyzes 1,349 instances of AI-generated feedback and corresponding teacher-delivered revisions from 117 teachers using the Tutoria platform. The data come from a mix of controlled studies and classroom deployments, including Brazilian high school chemistry tasks and higher-education introductory computer science activities. The platform generated draft feedback from student responses and teacher correctness tags, and teachers could accept, edit, or fully rewrite the draft before it reached learners.

Findings show that teachers accepted AI feedback unchanged in about 78% of cases, and most teachers edited very little overall, though a small minority revised a large share of messages. When edits occurred, they usually shortened and simplified the AI output while largely preserving meaning, suggesting revision often served as compression rather than substantive correction. The study also found that text-only models could predict revision decisions above chance, but only modestly, implying that contextual factors beyond the feedback text matter. Overall, the paper concludes that default AI feedback is instructionally consequential because much of it is delivered unchanged, and that teacher revisions often reflect concerns about verbosity, pedagogical alignment, and contextual appropriateness rather than simple accuracy correction.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical observational study using log data from one platform, descriptive comparisons, and predictive modeling, but not an experimental design and not focused on student learning outcomes. The evidence is informative about teacher mediation and workflow patterns, but causal claims are limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests potentially meaningful efficiency gains because most AI feedback was delivered unchanged, but the measured effects are indirect and do not demonstrate learner outcomes. Overall impact is modest and somewhat unclear because it primarily characterizes revision behavior rather than showing instructional improvement.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated formative feedback for short open-ended student responses, with teachers accepting, editing, or rewriting feedback before delivery in a Moodle/Google Classroom-integrated workflow.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers accepted AI feedback without modification in 77.8% of 1,349 feedback instances (1050/1349), indicating substantial potential to reduce teacher editing burden. However, editing was heterogeneous: half of teachers changed fewer than 6% of messages, while the top decile revised roughly two-thirds, suggesting efficiency gains are uneven across users and contexts.
finding.measure: Teacher acceptance/editing rates and revision burden for AI-generated feedback messages
finding.std_deviation: SD=39.6 feedback messages reviewed per teacher

finding.finding_summary: Text-only models could predict whether feedback would be revised above chance, with ROC AUC ranging from 0.698 to 0.746 on a holdout set. This suggests revision likelihood can be estimated well enough to potentially triage teacher attention toward feedback instances more likely to require human editing.
finding.measure: Binary classification of whether AI-generated feedback was revised; holdout ROC AUC, balanced accuracy, Cohen’s κ

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging learning analytics to enhance immersive teacher simulations: Challenges and opportunities
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how learning analytics can be used to strengthen immersive teacher simulations, with a focus on making teaching behaviors visible and supporting reflective professional learning. Rather than testing a single instructional intervention with outcome measures, it synthesizes conceptual arguments and empirical examples to show how multimodal data can be transformed into formative feedback for teacher education.

The chapter centers on TeacherGen@i, a generative AI-enhanced immersive teacher simulation. It describes how discourse, behavioral events, and gaze data can be captured in a web-based VR classroom, then analyzed with NLP, lag sequential analysis, and eye-tracking visualization. The reported study involved 33 preservice teachers in a Digital Education course at a South Korean university during Spring 2025. Participants designed teaching scenarios, interacted with AI-driven student agents, and reviewed their performance in a prototype dashboard.

The chapter concludes that multimodal analytics can surface patterns in pedagogical reasoning, attention allocation, and interaction structure that are otherwise difficult to observe. It argues that such systems can support a cycle of simulation, analysis, redesign, and classroom transfer, while also pointing toward equity-oriented reflection through indicators such as speaking-time balance and gaze distribution. At the same time, the chapter frames immersive analytics as an emerging area that still requires stronger validation, ethical safeguards, and scalable implementation frameworks.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a case study/chapter using one cohort of preservice teachers and descriptive multimodal analyses, not a controlled impact evaluation. It provides useful empirical illustration but does not meet RCT/QED standards for strong causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The chapter suggests potentially useful benefits for reflective practice and scalable analytics, but it does not report a causal effect size on learner or teacher outcomes. Impact is therefore plausible but unclear and modest based on the presented evidence.

interventions.use_case: generative AI-enhanced immersive teacher simulation (TeacherGen@i) for preservice teachers to practice classroom interactions, lesson implementation, and reflective teaching using AI-driven student agents in a web-based VR environment

finding.finding_summary: The chapter reports that the TeacherGen@i simulation made preservice teachers’ pedagogical reasoning, questioning patterns, and interaction sequences visible through multimodal analytics, supporting reflective practice rather than directly estimating a causal effect. In the analyzed sample (n=33 simulation sessions; 1,269 interaction turns), the system revealed predominantly remembering/understanding-level discourse and structured sequential patterns that were framed as useful for analytics-informed teacher learning.
finding.measure: Coded dialogue turns using Bloom’s taxonomy; lag sequential analysis of interaction patterns; gaze/attention visualization for reflective practice

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that automating transcription, discourse coding, sequential analysis, and dashboard visualization can reduce researcher/instructor workload and make teacher coaching more scalable. This is presented as a design implication and supported by cited prior studies, but the chapter’s own empirical contribution is primarily descriptive rather than a direct test of workload reduction.
finding.measure: Prototype dashboard and multimodal analytics pipeline for automated capture, coding, and visualization of simulation data

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint examines how pre-service elementary science teachers in South Korea integrated ChatGPT into lesson planning, with a focus on the usefulness, appropriateness, and risks of using generative AI for science learning. The paper is motivated by the lack of empirical evidence on whether ChatGPT can support actual classroom-oriented science instruction, despite widespread enthusiasm about LLMs in education.

The study asked 29 pre-service teachers to complete a short professional-learning sequence on ChatGPT and science pedagogy, then design a 45-minute elementary science lesson plan incorporating ChatGPT and a simulated chat interaction. Their plans were evaluated with a modified TPACK-based rubric, and open-ended survey responses were analyzed qualitatively. The lesson plans covered multiple science domains and teaching methods, including biology, chemistry, earth science, cooperative learning, POE, learning cycles, analogy generation, concept mapping, and experimentation.

Overall, the pre-service teachers showed moderate-to-high competence in integrating ChatGPT, especially in aligning it with curriculum goals and instructional strategies, but they were less effective at selecting appropriate ChatGPT functions. They expected ChatGPT to support questioning, individualized learning, and formative feedback, but they also raised concerns about inaccurate or non-existent outputs, bias, overdependence, and the need to verify AI-generated information. The authors conclude that ChatGPT has promise as a classroom support tool, but teachers need stronger AI literacy, and future work should test these ideas in real classrooms rather than only in lesson plans.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/descriptive preprint based on lesson-plan analysis and open-ended survey responses from 29 pre-service teachers, not a controlled trial. It provides useful exploratory evidence but does not meet stronger causal credibility criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful classroom and planning benefits, but it reports no measured student outcomes or effect sizes and focuses on anticipated rather than demonstrated impact. The practical effect is therefore unclear and likely modest at this stage.

interventions.use_case: Using ChatGPT as a conversational AI tool to support elementary science lesson planning, including generating questions, explanations, role-play scripts, individualized prompts, formative feedback, and additional informational support for pre-service teachers' lesson plans.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test student learning directly; it evaluates 29 pre-service teachers' ChatGPT-integrated science lesson plans and perceptions. Teachers anticipated ChatGPT could support scientific inquiry, prediction/explanation, and formative assessment, but they also identified inappropriate uses such as generating experiment designs or relying on inaccurate/nonexistent resources, which could weaken scientific reasoning and practical inquiry.
finding.measure: TPACK-based lesson plan rubric; qualitative survey responses about anticipated usefulness, concerns, and instructional fit
finding.std_deviation: SD=.91 overall rubric; SD=.99 instructional strategies; SD=.93 function selection; SD=.83 fit

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers believed ChatGPT could increase motivation, interest, and active participation through self-directed and individualized learning. These are perceived benefits rather than measured student outcomes, and they were based on lesson-plan design and survey responses from n=29 pre-service teachers.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses about perceived usefulness and anticipated outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Teachers anticipated positive effects on critical thinking, questioning, digital literacy, collaboration, and self-directed learning, but they also warned about overreliance on ChatGPT and possible reduction in independent inquiry. The study is qualitative/descriptive and reports no student-level effect sizes; the main evidence comes from rubric scores (M=3.29/4, SD=.91) and coded concerns from 29 lesson plans/surveys.
finding.measure: TPACK-based lesson plan rubric; qualitative coding of concerns and anticipated outcomes

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was perceived as useful for saving teacher time and supporting lesson-planning tasks such as generating role-play scripts, summarizing student scenarios, providing additional information, and offering feedback. However, the paper also documents mistaken or hallucinated outputs (e.g., nonexistent YouTube links), indicating that efficiency gains can be offset by verification burdens.
finding.measure: Lesson plan rubric scores and qualitative survey responses about planning efficiency and support

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers in low-resource public schools collaborate with a generative AI lesson-planning system called Shiksha Copilot. The study is motivated by a practical question: can LLM-supported tools help teachers create curriculum-aligned lesson plans while reducing the heavy administrative burden common in government schools, especially in multilingual settings? The authors also ask how teachers actually adapt AI-generated content and what kinds of changes are needed for classroom use.

Shiksha Copilot was deployed in government schools in Karnataka, India, and combines LLM generation, retrieval-augmented generation, human curation, and bilingual English-Kannada support. The system first generated lesson objectives and lesson plans, which expert curators reviewed and revised before teachers accessed them. Teachers could then customize the curated lesson plans for their own classrooms, and power users also had access to AI-assisted editing, lesson-specific chat, general education chat, and question-generation features. The intervention was used by 1,043 teachers across grades 5–10, with additional interviews conducted with 23 curators and 4 mentors supporting deployment.

Using system logs, surveys, and interviews, the study finds that Shiksha Copilot reduced lesson-planning time, bureaucratic documentation burden, and teaching-related stress, while also supporting a shift toward activity-based pedagogy. The English lesson plans were generally reliable with only minor edits, but Kannada translations required extensive revision because literal translation often produced awkward or inaccurate language. Teachers did not simply accept AI output; they actively adapted plans using their own expertise and professional networks. The paper concludes that human-in-the-loop and community-informed design are essential for generative AI tools in low-resource, multilingual education settings, and that current LLMs remain limited in linguistic quality, contextual fit, and pedagogical nuance.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods field deployment with surveys, logs, and interviews, but it is not a randomized or quasi-experimental causal study. The evidence is strong for descriptive and implementation insights, but weaker for causal attribution.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful workload and stress reductions for a large, priority population of teachers, but no effect sizes are given and the study is observational. The impact appears practically important, though the magnitude is not clearly quantifiable from the excerpt.

interventions.use_case: Human-in-the-loop LLM system for bilingual lesson-plan generation, lesson-specific Q&A, general educational chat, and question generation for teachers in low-resource government schools.

finding.finding_summary: Shiksha Copilot reduced teachers' lesson-planning burden and administrative workload in low-resource Karnataka schools. The paper reports measurable reductions in lesson-planning time and teaching-related stress across the matched survey sample (n=406), and logs show that teachers used the system extensively to generate 5,544 lesson plans (4,064 English; 1,480 Kannada).
finding.measure: Weekly time spent on lesson planning and administrative tasks; Teacher Stress Scale (TSS)
finding.study_size: n=406 matched survey responses; logs: n=5,544 lesson plans

finding.finding_summary: The tool lowered teaching-related stress, especially by easing workload and record-keeping demands. The study used the Teacher Stress Scale with matched pre/post survey responses (n=406), but the excerpt does not report a numeric effect size or confidence interval.
finding.measure: Teacher Stress Scale (teaching demands; school-based support subscales)

finding.finding_summary: Shiksha Copilot helped teachers meet administrative documentation requirements and fit existing bureaucratic workflows, but broader pedagogical change was constrained by staffing shortages and administrative demands. The paper emphasizes organizational change at the school-system level, but does not provide a single numeric institutional effect size.
finding.measure: Interview and log evidence of documentation use, workflow integration, and organizational change
finding.study_size: n=1,043 teachers; 43 interviews; 5,544 lesson plans logged

paper_profiles.title: The TalkMoves Dataset: K-12 Mathematics Lesson Transcripts Annotated for Teacher and Student Discursive Moves
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces the TalkMoves dataset, a curated corpus of 567 human-annotated K-12 mathematics lesson transcripts derived from classroom video and audio recordings. The motivating problem is the lack of publicly available classroom discourse data for research and for building AI systems that can analyze teacher-student interaction and provide instructional feedback. The authors position the dataset as a resource for studying accountable talk, dialogue acts, and classroom discourse patterns in mathematics lessons.

The approach centers on a dataset and annotation scheme rather than a live experimental intervention. Transcripts were segmented at the sentence level and annotated for six teacher talk moves and four student talk moves grounded in accountable talk theory, along with dialog act labels. The dataset was assembled from multiple sources, including public transcript collections and anonymized TalkBack project recordings, with human experts reviewing materials before inclusion. The paper also describes the TalkMoves application, which uses automated models to detect talk moves and generate personalized feedback for teachers about their mathematics instruction.

The population represented in the dataset is K-12 mathematics classrooms, with the available descriptive information indicating a skew toward female-taught U.S. middle school lessons (grades 6-8). The setting is primarily in-person classroom instruction, though some online lessons are included. The main conclusion is that the dataset and associated application can support NLP and educational AI research, enable automated teacher feedback, and help study classroom discourse, while also highlighting the need for careful curation, annotation reliability, and ethical handling of classroom data.
