paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a dataset/system description paper with some benchmarking, not a causal evaluation of educational outcomes. It is peer-reviewed research with clear methodology, but it provides descriptive and model-performance evidence rather than direct effectiveness evidence in classrooms.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potential educational value and reports moderate model performance, but it does not demonstrate measurable student- or teacher-level impact. Any downstream instructional benefit remains unverified in this paper.

interventions.use_case: automated, immediate feedback to K-12 mathematics teachers on classroom discourse and accountable talk moves using transcript/video analysis

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents a dataset and NLP pipeline intended to scale up feedback that is otherwise sporadic, time-consuming, and expensive to obtain from trained classroom observers. It does not report a causal outcome study of teacher workload reduction, but it explicitly frames the TalkMoves application as improving the efficiency of providing timely, detailed discourse feedback to teachers.
finding.measure: Availability of automated feedback workflow; descriptive system capability rather than a measured workload outcome

finding.finding_summary: The dataset and application are built specifically around K-12 mathematics lessons and accountable talk moves intended to support rigorous mathematical discussion. The paper reports benchmark model performance for talk-move detection on a held-out test set, with teacher-model macro-F1 up to 76.32 (RoBERTa-base) and student-model macro-F1 up to 73.12 (BERT-base), but it does not directly measure student math achievement.
finding.measure: Talk-move classification performance on test set (macro-F1, MCC) for teacher and student utterances

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers think about integrating artificial intelligence education into existing non-computing subjects, and what supports they need to do so. The authors argue that AI should not be confined to computer science classes and that teachers need scaffolding to make AI instruction accessible across core curriculum areas. The central question is how to co-design AI curriculum with teachers in ways that reflect classroom realities and teacher values.

The study used a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 participants who were primarily K-12 teachers, along with some educational directors. Participants learned basic AI concepts and tools, completed pre-work based on their own curriculum, and then worked in small groups with researchers to design integrated lesson plans. The groups produced draft curricula embedding AI into social studies, ESL, and literacy for students with learning disabilities, with integration points including data use, student reflection, and ethics discussions.

The paper concludes that teachers value evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration when designing AI lessons, and that they can meaningfully connect AI to core subjects through subject-related datasets, reflection activities, and ethics/scaffolding. It also notes that teachers are interested in teaching AI ethics but may feel apprehensive without structured support. The work emphasizes that co-design can help create more accessible AI curricula for non-CS classrooms, but the authors caution that findings come from a small, non-generalizable workshop context.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small qualitative co-design study with 15 participants, based on workshop observations, artifacts, and pre/post questionnaires. It is peer-reviewed but does not use a controlled design or inferential impact evaluation, so credibility is limited to exploratory evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports modest positive changes in teacher self-reported readiness and produces implementable curriculum drafts, but it does not measure student outcomes or demonstrate sustained classroom impact. The likely impact is promising but unclear and limited to a small, specialized sample.

interventions.use_case: remote teacher co-design workshop for integrated AI curriculum development, using AI learning tools and lesson-plan brainstorming rather than evaluating a student-facing tutor or feedback system

finding.finding_summary: The workshop increased teachers’ self-reported familiarity with AI from an average of 4.8/7 to 5.8/7, and confidence in integrating AI into their curriculum to 5.6/7 after the co-design sessions. Qualitatively, teachers reported greater understanding of how to connect AI to non-CS subjects and how to scaffold ethics, reflection, and data discussions.
finding.measure: pre/post self-report familiarity with AI; self-reported confidence in integrating AI into curriculum; thematic analysis of workshop discussions and curriculum drafts
finding.std_deviation: AI familiarity pre-workshop SD not reported; age SD=11.6

finding.finding_summary: Teachers valued concrete tools, frameworks, and scaffolds to make AI integration feasible, and the workshop produced first-draft implementable curricula in three subject areas. The paper suggests that co-design, exemplar lesson plans, and tool guidance can reduce the burden of designing AI-integrated lessons, though no formal workload metric was reported.
finding.measure: completion of draft integrated curricula; qualitative reports of logistical needs and supports

paper_profiles.title: Introducing General Relativity in high school: a guide for teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to introduce General Relativity and related gravity concepts in high school through a teacher professional-development approach based on the rubber sheet analogy (RSA). The authors are motivated by the need to make modern physics accessible in secondary education and by the recognized strengths and weaknesses of the RSA as an instructional model.

The intervention began with iterative testing of the RSA with varied audiences, then high school students, and finally high school teachers. In the student phase, the authors worked with about 400 Italian students across 14 classes and mixed groups, using questionnaires before, immediately after, and four months after the activity to assess understanding and retention. In the teacher phase, about 25 teachers from the Rome area participated in professional development sessions where they experienced the RSA and discussed how to adapt it for classroom use.

The paper reports that the RSA helped students visualize, understand, and remember Newtonian gravity and some GR topics such as Kepler’s laws, gravitational lensing, and black holes. Teachers responded positively and expressed interest in using the activity themselves. The authors also developed a manual with step-by-step guidance, materials, and suggestions for addressing misconceptions, and they conclude that the approach can support autonomous classroom implementation of modern physics topics.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/descriptive professional-development paper with questionnaire feedback and observational evidence, not a controlled trial. It provides useful implementation detail but limited methodological rigor for causal inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are positive and relevant to a priority population (high school science teachers and students), but the evidence is modest and largely self-reported. No standardized effect sizes are reported, and the study does not test generalizable impacts across contexts in a controlled way.

interventions.use_case: hands-on educational simulation using a physical rubber-sheet spacetime model (lycra sheet, marbles, weights) to teach general relativity and Newtonian gravity to high school teachers and students

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the rubber-sheet analogy helped students and teachers visualize, understand, and remember gravity-related physics concepts better than a traditional treatment. In the student questionnaires (about 200 students; 154 responses analyzed), the authors report that only 3% selected a downward-force misconception item after instruction, suggesting improved conceptual understanding, though no standardized effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Questionnaires on understanding of gravity concepts; post-activity misconception item selection; qualitative teacher feedback
finding.study_size: n=154 questionnaire responses (about 200 students exposed); teachers n=25

finding.finding_summary: The activity was described as engaging, entertaining, and curiosity-provoking for both students and teachers, increasing willingness to ask questions and interact. Teachers and public participants responded positively to the interactive format, but the paper provides no numerical engagement effect size.
finding.measure: Participant reactions, engagement, and willingness to interact/question, reported from observations and questionnaires

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the manual and teacher-training approach make it easier for teachers to autonomously run the gravity activity in classrooms. Readers rated the book as clear and complete (e.g., 68% gave 5/5 for interest; 72% gave 5/5 for clarity/completeness), but the study does not report formal efficiency outcomes or workload measurements.
finding.measure: Teacher-readiness, perceived clarity/completeness, feasibility ratings in questionnaire
finding.study_size: n=22 questionnaire responses to the manual

paper_profiles.title: AI-Generated Rubric Interfaces: K–12 Teachers’ Perceptions and Practices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines K–12 teachers’ perceptions and experiences with AI-supported rubric generation and AI-assisted feedback for block-based programming assignments. The authors focus on a practical classroom problem: rubric creation is time-consuming and cognitively demanding, especially when teachers need clear performance-level distinctions, grade-appropriate language, and alignment with instructional goals. The study asks whether generative AI can help teachers create rubrics more efficiently while still preserving teacher judgment and instructional control.

The intervention was a professional development workshop in which teachers used MagicSchool.ai to generate rubrics from assignment descriptions, grade-level information, and standards, then used the generated rubrics to evaluate a sample Snap! programming task. Teachers also experimented with an AI chatbot to provide rubric-based feedback on the same work. Data came from pre- and post-workshop surveys, open-ended responses, exit tickets, and thematic analysis of discussion data. The sample included 25 middle- and high-school teachers, many of whom taught computer science or block-based programming, and the workshop took place in North Carolina in a summer PD setting.

Findings show that teachers generally viewed AI-generated rubrics as useful starting drafts that improved structure, clarified vague criteria, and saved time, but they consistently emphasized the need for substantial teacher oversight. Reported weaknesses included generic or grade-misaligned language, occasional mismatch with learning objectives, and difficulty editing criteria. Teachers also raised ethical and practical concerns about fairness, equity, accuracy, privacy, transparency, workflow barriers, and the risk of overreliance on AI. Overall, the paper concludes that AI rubric tools are most promising when they support teacher-directed customization rather than replacing teacher judgment, and that adoption depends on editability, alignment, and classroom fit.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative + descriptive survey study of a small professional-development sample (n=25), with thematic analysis and Likert item summaries rather than a controlled impact design. It provides credible evidence about teacher perceptions, risks, and adoption conditions, but not causal effects on student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests moderate practical relevance for teacher workflow and adoption, but it does not report measurable student learning gains or quantified implementation effects. Impact is therefore promising but unclear at the population level.

interventions.use_case: AI-supported rubric generation and rubric-based feedback for K–12 block-based programming assignments, using MagicSchool.ai to draft/edit rubrics and a chatbot to generate feedback from those rubrics

finding.finding_summary: Teachers generally viewed AI-generated rubrics as time-saving starting drafts that reduced the effort of creating rubrics from scratch. In the post-survey, they rated the tool positively on usefulness and flexibility (e.g., rubric helps students understand evaluation, M=4.12; assignment-goal alignment, M=4.0), but editing was a clear bottleneck: adding/removing/revising criteria received the lowest usability score (M=2.75, SD=1.23) among the measured items.
finding.measure: Pre/post surveys and open-ended workshop reflections about rubric creation time, editability, and usability

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI-generated rubrics were generally clear and reasonably aligned with assignment goals, but they were not always well matched to instructional priorities or grade level. Survey ratings were positive for criteria clarity (M=3.94, SD=0.93) and performance-level differentiation (M=4.13, SD=0.96), while grade-level language appropriateness was lower and more mixed (M=3.5, SD=1.211), indicating that the outputs needed teacher refinement for classroom fit.
finding.measure: Survey ratings of rubric clarity, performance-level differentiation, grade-level language appropriateness, assignment alignment, and focus-area fit

finding.finding_summary: Hands-on exposure appeared to increase teachers’ openness and confidence toward using AI rubric tools in future practice, though adoption remained conditional on teacher control and workflow fit. Teachers commonly said they would consider using the tool because it improved clarity and reduced workload, but they wanted continued oversight to avoid overdependence and preserve professional judgment.
finding.measure: Post-workshop intention-to-adopt responses and open-ended reflections

finding.finding_summary: Teachers raised institutional and governance concerns about fairness, equity, transparency, privacy, and school/district restrictions on AI use, suggesting adoption depends on policy and implementation context. They also reported workflow barriers such as incomplete LMS integration and school blocking AI tools, while still expressing interest in classroom adoption if those constraints were addressed.
finding.measure: Open-ended discussion themes on fairness, privacy, transparency, workflow barriers, and school policy constraints

paper_profiles.title: Teacher-student relationship and teaching styles in primary education. A model of analysis.
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Professional Capital and Community
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students perceive the relationship with their teachers in primary education and how those perceptions are associated with two teaching styles: directive and participative. The authors address a gap in the literature by studying the interaction between teaching style and teacher-student relationship from the student’s point of view, rather than relying on teacher reports or direct classroom observation.

The study uses a structural equation model built from existing questionnaire data from the 2018/2019 Diagnostic Assessment in the Canary Islands, Spain. The sample includes 21,126 sixth-grade primary students from 623 schools. The authors construct latent variables for directive teaching style, participative teaching style, emotional relationship, and educational relationship from student questionnaire items, and then test whether the relationships between these constructs differ by student characteristics such as gender, quarter of birth, and parents’ educational level.

The main findings are that participative teaching style is more strongly associated with positive perceived teacher-student relationships than directive teaching style. Directive style is more tied to the educational relationship, while participative style is more tied to the emotional relationship. The study also finds heterogeneity in student perceptions: girls report more participative teaching and more positive emotional and educational relationships than boys, while students from lower parental educational backgrounds tend to perceive directive teaching more clearly and, in some cases, report stronger educational relationships. The paper concludes that student feedback is useful for understanding classroom practice, but interpretation must account for differences in student background.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational study using structural equation modeling and mean-comparison tests on census data, not an experimental design. It provides moderate methodological rigor for association testing, but it cannot establish causal effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports statistically significant but non-causal associations and no intervention effect sizes in the K-12 sense. Its practical impact is mainly conceptual and measurement-focused, with potential usefulness for policy and school diagnostics rather than demonstrated outcome gains.

finding.finding_summary: Using census data from 21,126 sixth-grade students in the Canary Islands, the study found that perceived teaching style is strongly associated with students’ perceptions of teacher-student relationship. Participative teaching style correlated more with both emotional and educational relationship than directive style (all coefficients significant at 1%), but these are correlational SEM results rather than causal effects.
finding.measure: Structural equation model of student questionnaire latent constructs: directive teaching style, participative teaching style, emotional relationship, educational relationship

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main contribution is a replicable measurement model for student feedback on teaching styles and teacher-student relationship, with potential use in periodic diagnostic assessments and cross-context educational policy analysis. It argues the model could support context-specific policy proposals, but this is proposed utility rather than observed institutional impact.
finding.measure: Proposed SEM-based model for diagnostic assessment / student feedback use

paper_profiles.title: Discussion Tracker: Supporting Teacher Learning about Students’ Collaborative Argumentation in High School Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of helping K-12 teachers learn to facilitate collaborative argumentation in classroom discussions, a skill that many teachers find difficult to develop. The authors present Discussion Tracker (DT), a classroom discussion analytics system that uses NLP to automatically code student talk along three dimensions: argument moves, specificity, and collaboration. DT then generates visualizations and feedback such as annotated transcripts, collaboration maps, strengths/weaknesses summaries, and planning support for the next discussion.

The system was evaluated in high school English Language Arts classrooms. Eighteen teachers from four schools each led a discussion on a literary text; their discussions were recorded, transcribed, manually annotated, and then used to evaluate DT. Teachers used DT after a brief demo and completed surveys plus 45-minute cognitive interviews while reviewing their students’ discussions. The NLP classifiers were also tested against human annotations from the collected corpus.

The study found that teachers perceived DT as useful for reflecting on student discussion and for identifying strengths and weaknesses in facilitation, with generally high usability ratings. The automated classifiers achieved moderate to substantial agreement with human labels for argument moves and specificity, but collaboration prediction was weaker for some classes, especially agree and challenge/probe. The paper concludes that discussion analytics can support teacher learning, while noting the need for further model improvement, more data collection, automated transcription/segmentation, and interface refinement.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small classroom deployment with usability evaluation and model benchmark results, not a randomized or quasi-experimental impact study. The evidence is qualitative/survey-based with classifier validation, so it meets only limited credibility criteria for outcome impact claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports high teacher-perceived usefulness but does not measure student learning gains or provide causal impact estimates. Any impact is therefore modest and unclear, with no effect size meeting a medium/large threshold.

interventions.use_case: classroom discussion analytics system (Discussion Tracker) using NLP classifiers to code teacher-recorded high school discussion transcripts for argument moves, specificity, and collaboration, then generate visual analytics and planning support for teacher reflection

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that Discussion Tracker was very helpful for learning to facilitate collaborative argumentation in high school literature discussions. On the usability survey (n=18 teachers), nine of 13 items had a mean of 4.5/5 or higher, including strong ratings for the annotated transcript (mean=4.89), pie charts (mean=4.78), and overall helpfulness for teaching literature discussions (mean=4.72).
finding.measure: Teacher usability/perceived usefulness survey ratings; Likert-scale items on support for collaborative argumentation facilitation

finding.finding_summary: The system was perceived as helping teachers recognize student strengths and weaknesses and giving them more insight than they usually get from reflecting on discussion, suggesting workflow support for analysis and planning. Teachers also rated the goal-setting and instructional resources favorably, though ease of use was slightly lower than other features (mean=4.11).
finding.measure: Teacher survey ratings of system usefulness for recognizing strengths/weaknesses, gaining insight, and supporting goal-setting/planning

paper_profiles.title: Active Teacher Selection for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a core limitation in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF): most systems assume feedback comes from a single human teacher, even though real feedback often comes from multiple teachers with different levels of expertise, rationality, and cost. The authors argue that this assumption can make reward learning less accurate and potentially less safe or reliable.

To study this, they introduce the Hidden Utility Bandit (HUB) framework, which models learning from multiple teachers whose feedback quality and cost differ. They also propose Active Teacher Selection (ATS), an algorithm that decides both when to query teachers and which teacher to query, using a POMDP formulation solved with POMCPOW and custom rollouts. The paper presents theoretical derivations, query-complexity bounds, and simulations, rather than a human-subject educational intervention.

The empirical evaluation uses two non-education domains: a paper-recommendation task and a COVID-19 vaccine-testing proof of concept. In both settings, ATS outperforms baseline methods by learning more accurate hidden utilities while using teacher queries more efficiently. The main conclusion is that explicitly modeling teacher heterogeneity and actively choosing teachers can improve reward learning robustness, accuracy, and efficiency. The paper does not study teachers, students, schools, or classroom implementation in an education context.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/computational methods paper with simulation and proof-of-concept applications, not a study of an educational intervention or a causal evaluation in schools. It does not provide an empirical design relevant to K-12 evidence criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct educational outcome or student impact is measured. The paper proposes infrastructure for safer multi-teacher reward learning and demonstrates algorithmic performance in non-educational domains, so educational impact is indirect and unquantified.

interventions.use_case: Framework and algorithm for active teacher selection in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), modeling multiple teachers with different rationality/expertise/costs and choosing when and which teacher to query.

paper_profiles.title: AI-Based Feedback in Counselling Competence Training of Prospective Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-based feedback can support the training of prospective teachers’ counselling competence, especially in teacher-parent conversations. The authors focus on the challenge that traditional feedback for such conversations is subjective and hard to measure reliably, particularly for paraverbal and nonverbal communication features. They ask whether AI can provide objective, actionable feedback and how students perceive such feedback in a teacher-education setting.

The intervention is an iterative four-day block seminar at the University of Augsburg that combines communication theory, peer role-play, a recorded simulated teacher-parent counselling session, expert feedback, and AI-based feedback. The AI pipeline uses transcription and multimodal feature extraction tools to analyse verbal, paraverbal, and nonverbal behaviour, including conversational phases, communication techniques, pitch, loudness, gaze, smiling, and facial emotion cues. Students receive collective and individual feedback through tables, parallel coordinate plots, radar charts, and playback in the NOVA system, and qualitative interviews are used to capture their perceptions.

The population consists of 29 prospective elementary-school teachers in Germany, mostly undergraduate students in primary school pedagogy. The study finds modest predictive capability of nonverbal and paraverbal features for expert ratings, strong inter-rater agreement for the verbal annotation task relative to typical early-stage work, and generally positive student reactions to the AI feedback. Students especially valued the combination of raw numeric summaries and video playback, but they also wanted clearer interpretation and prioritisation of the data. The authors conclude that AI-supported feedback is promising for teacher education, while noting that verbal annotation guidelines need to be strengthened and that more data are needed for better generalisability.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/user-study and correlational paper with a small sample (n=29), not a controlled intervention trial. Evidence is suggestive but limited by the absence of randomized comparison, pre-post learning outcomes, and reliance on subjective perceptions plus model agreement analyses.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported benefits are promising but modest and largely indirect: students perceived the feedback positively, and transcription efficiency improved, but no robust learning effect size was demonstrated. The impact is therefore unclear-to-modest for the broader population of prospective teachers.

interventions.use_case: AI-based multimodal feedback for prospective teachers practicing simulated teacher-parent counselling, using transcript, audio, facial expression, gaze, and voice features to provide collective and individual coaching feedback.

Multimodal behavior analysis and visualization toolkit (NOVA/DISCOVER) used to extract and display paraverbal and nonverbal features for feedback, annotation, and reflective playback during teacher training.

finding.finding_summary: Prospective teachers (n=29) reported that AI-based feedback was helpful for improving counselling competence and self-reflection in simulated teacher-parent conversations. The study did not report a causal pre-post learning gain, but students preferred the combined playback-plus-data feedback and said it helped them identify areas to work on; inter-rater agreement for the verbal annotation task was 66.9% for conversational phases and 72.4% for communication techniques.
finding.measure: Qualitative interview perceptions of AI feedback; expert ratings of simulated counselling; annotation agreement for conversational phases and communication techniques

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that integrating WhisperX reduced interview transcription time by two-thirds, indicating substantial workflow efficiency gains in the feedback and reflection process. The system also automated extraction and visualization of multimodal features, reducing manual effort in analysis, although some downstream errors remained because of incomplete sentences and VAD segmentation issues.
finding.measure: Transcription time reduction; automated feature extraction/analysis workflow

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the effectiveness of ChatGPT-based feedback compared with teacher feedback and self-feedback: Evidence from Chinese to English translation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether ChatGPT-based feedback can improve translation performance as effectively as teacher feedback (TF) and self-feedback (SF), and whether the effects differ across overall translation quality and specific linguistic dimensions. The authors frame ChatGPT as a potentially useful automated feedback tool, but note concerns that AI feedback may be generic, inconsistent, or unable to capture nuanced syntactic and cultural issues in translation.

The intervention compared three feedback conditions on Chinese-to-English translation revisions: ChatGPT-generated feedback, teacher feedback, and self-feedback. Participants were 45 advanced Chinese MTI students at a top university in China. Each student completed revisions under all three conditions, with two-week intervals between tasks. Outcomes were assessed objectively using BLEU scores and Coh-Metrix indicators for lexicon, syntax, and cohesion.

Results showed that teacher feedback produced the best overall translation quality, while self-feedback also outperformed ChatGPT on BLEU. ChatGPT was stronger for lexical gains, including longer word choices, more specific verbs, and better referential cohesion, but teacher and self-feedback were better for syntactic improvement, especially verb phrase density and passive voice use. The study concludes that ChatGPT is best used as a supplement rather than a replacement for human feedback, particularly in translation contexts requiring cultural and syntactic sensitivity.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical comparative study with experimental revisions and statistical analyses (CFA, SEM, ANOVA), but it is a small single-site study without random assignment or broad generalizability. It provides useful causal-inference-relevant evidence, but credibility is limited by sample size, task specificity, and repeated-measures design details.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows a mixed, modest effect: ChatGPT improved some lexical outcomes but did not improve overall translation quality and was weaker than teacher feedback on syntax and BLEU. The practical impact appears limited and context-specific to advanced translation students.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-generated feedback on student Chinese-to-English translation drafts, used as an automated feedback source compared against teacher feedback and self-feedback.
AI-generated translation feedback for revising student work, focusing on lexical, syntactic, and cohesion-related suggestions rather than full tutoring.

finding.finding_summary: In this comparative study of 45 advanced MTI students (135 revised texts), ChatGPT-based feedback improved some writing/translation subskills but underperformed human teacher feedback on overall translation quality. BLEU scores were highest for teacher feedback (0.501), followed by self-feedback (0.485), with ChatGPT lowest (0.472), while ChatGPT produced higher lexical scores and referential cohesion but weaker syntactic gains.
finding.measure: BLEU score for overall translation quality; Coh-Metrix linguistic indicators (lexicon, syntax, cohesion)

finding.finding_summary: Teacher feedback outperformed ChatGPT-based feedback on overall translation quality, with mean BLEU scores of 0.501 vs. 0.472, a difference of 0.029 (larger than the paper’s cited 0.02 threshold for meaningful improvement). Teacher feedback also produced stronger syntax-related outcomes, including denser verb phrases and more agentless passive voice.
finding.measure: BLEU score; Coh-Metrix syntax indicators (DRVP, DRPVAL, SYNSTRUTt)
finding.effect_size: ΔBLEU = 0.029; other effects reported as significant with p-values, not standardized effect sizes

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT-based feedback improved lexical performance relative to teacher feedback and self-feedback. It yielded the highest mean lexicon score (0.135) and significantly higher word length (5.664) and more specific verbs (WRDHYPv = 1.814) than TF and SF, with ANOVA results showing strong differences (e.g., F(2,132)=16.181 for word length, p<.001, ηp2=.197).
finding.measure: Coh-Metrix lexicon indicators: word length (DESWLlt) and verb hypernymy (WRDHYPv)
finding.effect_size: ηp2=.197 for word length; ηp2=.157 for verb hypernymy; other pairwise coefficients reported but not standardized effect sizes
finding.std_deviation: TF mean/SF mean/ChatGPT mean reported: DESWLlt 5.193/5.371/5.664; WRDHYPv 1.557/1.507/1.814

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT-based feedback was less effective than teacher feedback for syntax development. Teacher feedback produced higher syntax scores than ChatGPT, and pairwise tests showed TF outperformed ChatGPT on syntactic indicators such as verb phrase density and agentless passive voice (e.g., DRVP and DRPVAL), suggesting weaker grammar-structuring guidance from ChatGPT.
finding.measure: Coh-Metrix syntax indicators: verb phrase density (DRVP), agentless passive voice (DRPVAL), sentence similarity (SYNSTRUTt)
finding.effect_size: ηp2=.046 for overall syntax ANOVA; additional pairwise coefficients reported, not standardized effect sizes
finding.std_deviation: TF mean/SF mean/ChatGPT mean reported: DRVP 171.49/149.719/137.35; DRPVAL 13.274/9.594/5.627

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging Peer, Self, and Teacher Assessments for Generative AI-Enhanced Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teacher, peer, and self-assessments compare within a generative AI-supported feedback system for higher education. The authors focus on whether these human evaluative sources align with one another, whether they relate similarly to the teacher’s independently assigned overall grade, and whether systematic scoring biases are present. The motivation is to improve the design of generative AI feedback tools so they do not simply average inputs, but instead account for differences in evaluator reliability, strictness, and perspective.

The study is situated in an engineering education context at Universidad Autónoma de Madrid and uses the AICoFe collaborative feedback system. Forty-six undergraduate students in a final-year telecommunication engineering course gave individual oral presentations in a face-to-face classroom setting. Each presentation was assessed by the teacher and two randomly assigned peers using a shared 15-item rubric, and students also completed self-assessments while reviewing video recordings of their presentations. The teacher additionally assigned a separate global grade. The paper reports agreement statistics, correlations, and paired comparisons across the three assessment sources.

Results show moderate to substantial agreement overall, with peers and peer-self comparisons performing somewhat better than teacher-self comparisons. Teacher rubric scores were most strongly aligned with the teacher’s overall grade, while peer and self scores were somewhat less aligned but still significantly correlated. The analysis also found mild systematic bias: peers and students tended to score slightly higher than the teacher, and the teacher’s rubric scores were stricter than her holistic grade. The authors conclude that generative AI feedback systems should incorporate weighted evaluator inputs, bias detection, and context-aware reasoning rather than treating all assessment sources as equally reliable.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a correlational/observational analysis of 46 evaluation sets within a course-based implementation, with agreement, correlation, and paired comparisons rather than an experimental impact study. It is peer-reviewed scholarly work with clear methodology, but it does not establish causal effects of the GenAI feedback intervention.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful alignment and modest bias patterns, but no direct learner-outcome effect size or demonstrated performance gain from the GenAI system. Its practical impact is promising mainly as a design and validation study for feedback systems rather than evidence of medium or large educational gains.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI-enhanced collaborative feedback in the AICoFe system, combining teacher, peer, and self-assessments of engineering students' oral presentations to generate personalized rubric-based feedback with weighted aggregation and bias detection.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates a GenAI-supported feedback system for oral presentation performance in higher education, using rubric-based scores on 46 presentation evaluation sets (n=46). The system is associated with moderate-to-substantial agreement across evaluators and strong alignment between rubric scores and the teacher's overall grade, suggesting the feedback process can support assessment of speaking/presentation performance; however, the study does not report an intervention effect size on learner performance outcomes.
finding.measure: Oral presentation rubric scores, inter-rater agreement, and correlation with teacher's overall grade

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on evaluative judgment, reflection, and self-assessment calibration in the context of GenAI-supported feedback for oral presentations (n=46). Results show moderate alignment between self-assessments and teacher ratings (teacher vs self r=0.59; weighted kappa=0.22; AC2=0.58), but also systematic leniency in self-ratings (+0.36 vs teacher rubric, p=0.037), indicating partial support for metacognitive skill development alongside calibration bias.
finding.measure: Self-assessment alignment, agreement coefficients, paired mean differences, and correlations

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI-supported collaborative feedback can improve scalability and reduce teacher burden in large higher-education classes, although it does not directly measure workload reduction. The proposed AICoFe/GePeTo design is intended to combine human assessments with automated aggregation and context-aware feedback generation to make feedback more efficient and timely.
finding.measure: System design for feedback aggregation and human oversight; no direct efficiency outcome measured

paper_profiles.title: AI to the rescue: Exploring the potential of ChatGPT as a teacher ally for workload relief and burnout prevention
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can serve as a teacher assistant to reduce workload and help prevent burnout. The authors frame teacher burnout as being strongly linked to heavy non-teaching demands, especially lesson planning and content development, and ask how ChatGPT might streamline these tasks and improve planning efficiency.

The intervention/approach studied is not a classroom deployment with students, but a structured set of prompt-based tests of ChatGPT. The researchers created lesson-planning prompts for English, science, and math at secondary levels (ages 12–15 and 16–18), then iteratively refined the prompts when the first outputs did not fully align with the 5Es instructional model. They also asked ChatGPT to revise lesson plans, generate real-life examples, differentiate for learner levels, and produce formative assessments and other supporting materials. The study emphasizes a human-in-the-loop workflow in which teachers evaluate, correct, and further prompt the model rather than accepting the first response.

The context is the United Arab Emirates, where AI adoption in education is a policy priority. The paper concludes that ChatGPT can produce useful lesson-plan drafts and content recommendations when prompts are specific, curriculum-linked, and followed by teacher review. It argues that the main mechanism of benefit is workload reduction through faster drafting and idea generation, which can free teachers to focus on instruction and student support. However, the authors stress that outputs are not reliably high quality on the first attempt, so effective use depends on careful prompt design, alignment to pedagogical frameworks such as the 5Es, and teacher oversight to avoid oversimplification and preserve educational quality.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed exploratory qualitative study using prompt-based testing and rubric-based review, not a controlled experiment. It offers a clear methodology but has limited credibility for causal inference because there is no comparison group, no student outcomes, and no quantitative effect estimate.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful workload savings for teachers, but the impact is inferred qualitatively rather than measured, and no effect size is reported. The likely impact is therefore modest and unclear rather than established at scale.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-facing use of ChatGPT to generate, revise, and adapt K-12 lesson plans and instructional materials for math, science, and English, including 5Es-aligned planning, differentiation, formative assessment prompts, and real-world examples.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that ChatGPT can reduce teacher workload by speeding up lesson planning and content development, which were identified as major contributors to burnout. Across prompt iterations, ChatGPT generated usable lesson plans for Grade 8 math, Grade 10 chemistry, and Grade 7 creative writing, and the authors concluded that detailed prompting plus human review can make outputs sufficiently high quality to save planning time. No quantitative effect size was reported; evidence is based on qualitative evaluation of generated plans against the 5Es framework.
finding.measure: Qualitative evaluation of ChatGPT-generated lesson plans and teaching materials against the 5Es instructional model; teacher workload reduction inferred from planning utility

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT may support teacher decision-making, planning quality, and reflective revision through an iterative prompt-feedback loop. In practice, the tool improved after human oversight and more explicit prompts, suggesting a mechanism of assisted planning rather than autonomous generation. No quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative assessment of iterative prompt refinement, rubric alignment, and human oversight in lesson-plan generation

finding.finding_summary: The authors frame ChatGPT as potentially supporting UAE education reform and AI integration goals by helping reduce teacher burnout and improve instructional planning capacity. The paper argues that institutional training, ethical guardrails, and prompt-design workshops are needed for effective adoption, but it does not test policy outcomes empirically. No quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Policy and practice implications derived from literature review and exploratory testing

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the potential benefits, risks, and educational applications of large language models (LLMs), with ChatGPT used as the central example. The paper asks how LLMs may support learning and teaching across educational levels, while also identifying the technical, pedagogical, ethical, and governance challenges that must be addressed before these systems can be used responsibly in schools and other educational settings.

The paper does not evaluate a specific intervention or report an empirical study. Instead, it reviews emerging uses of LLMs for generating educational content, tutoring, feedback, assessment, lesson planning, and professional development. For teachers, it highlights possible workflows such as inputting a source corpus to generate a syllabus, lesson ideas, questions, quizzes, summaries, feedback on student writing, and support for differentiated instruction. It also discusses expected mechanisms for improvement, including saving teacher time, supporting personalization, generating prompts and practice materials, and helping teachers provide more targeted feedback and assessment.

The context is broad K-12, higher education, and professional learning rather than one specific population or site. The paper argues that LLMs may improve planning and decision-making when used as complementary tools under continuous human oversight, with guardrails for bias, copyright, privacy, verification, and sustainability. Its main conclusion is that LLMs are promising educational technologies, but responsible use requires teacher expertise, critical thinking, fact-checking, curriculum alignment, and institutional governance rather than unsupervised adoption.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper with no original empirical study design, no control group, and no quantitative evaluation of an intervention in K-12 settings. Its claims are conceptual and literature-synthesizing rather than evidentiary in the RCT/QED sense.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for potentially important educational and operational benefits, especially for teacher planning and feedback, but it does not present measured effects from a real implementation. Any impact is therefore plausible but unquantified in this paper.

interventions.use_case: Position-paper discussion of ChatGPT/large language models as teacher- and student-facing conversational assistants for education, including lesson planning, personalized feedback, question generation, explanations, and tutoring-like support.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can save teachers time by semi-automating lesson planning, personalized material creation, feedback on student work, and assessment support. Reported examples in the literature include grading effort reductions of up to 85% for textual student answers with high precision (Bernius et al. [39]), though this position paper itself does not present a new experiment.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / grading effort; quality of generated feedback and assessment support

finding.finding_summary: The paper expects LLM-supported workflows to improve critical thinking, problem-solving, and collaboration when used to generate prompts, discussion structures, and targeted questions. At the same time, it warns that overreliance may weaken these same skills if learners or teachers treat model outputs as answers rather than as a support tool.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and fact-checking practices

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes LLMs as useful for writing support, including syntax correction, style improvement, summaries, outlines, and feedback on essays and other written assignments. It frames these affordances as likely to improve writing quality and revision efficiency, but provides no new quantitative evaluation in this paper.
finding.measure: Writing quality, grammar/style improvement, summarization, outlining, text feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that educational adoption of LLMs depends on governance, privacy, fairness, copyright compliance, human oversight, and teacher training. It argues these safeguards are necessary to prevent bias, misuse, integrity problems, and inequitable access, but again reports no direct intervention outcome data.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, privacy/security, fairness, access, and institutional readiness

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how AI should be integrated into education in ways that improve learning while avoiding overreliance, plagiarism, hallucinations, and other risks. Rather than evaluating a specific classroom intervention with outcome measures, it presents a conceptual discussion grounded in the author’s teaching experience at Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich, Switzerland, together with informal discussions with students and staff and a narrative literature review.

The paper argues that effective educational use of AI rests on three core competencies: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. It describes a university-level policy response (“AI guidelines”) that allows generative AI use in academic work, but requires transparency about which model was used, how it was used, how outputs were critically evaluated, and where in the manuscript AI contributed. The author also provides practical examples of classroom uses such as student AI experiments, AI-generated case studies, AI-supported curriculum design, gamification, and immersive technologies.

The population and context are primarily higher-education students and educators at a Swiss university of applied sciences, though the author notes the ideas may also be useful for children and K-12 settings. The main conclusion is that banning or fully unrestricted use of AI are both problematic; instead, institutions should build a culture of responsible AI use through guidelines, workshops, ongoing staff support, explicit curriculum integration, and instruction in prompting and critical evaluation. The paper emphasizes that AI is most useful when treated as a sparring partner that can generate ideas and suggestions, but whose outputs must be checked against evidence and not copied verbatim.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual discussion and narrative literature review rather than an empirical evaluation of a specific AI intervention in K-12. It does not report a controlled study, quantitative outcomes, or a reproducible methodology for impact estimation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper proposes general guidance, workflows, and institutional recommendations for AI literacy and prompt engineering, but it does not measure learner or teacher outcomes. As a result, there is no demonstrated impact size to classify beyond theoretical or practical suggestions.

paper_profiles.title: The role of ChatGPT in higher education: Benefits, challenges, and future research directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper examines the potential benefits and challenges of ChatGPT in higher education, using constructivist theory as its conceptual lens. Rather than evaluating a specific intervention with participants, the paper asks what roles ChatGPT could play in teaching, learning, assessment, research support, and administration, and what risks it may introduce in these contexts.

The paper focuses on higher education users, including students, academics/educators, and administrative staff, and discusses how ChatGPT might be integrated through APIs, learning management systems, and feedback workflows. It argues that ChatGPT could support adaptive learning, individualized feedback, research and writing assistance, automated administrative support, and innovative assessment design, especially when used to scaffold prior knowledge, provide immediate responses, and extend learners’ active engagement with content.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT may improve learning and decision-making when used responsibly and alongside human oversight, but it also raises concerns about academic integrity, bias, hallucinations, inequitable access, and the erosion of authentic assessment and graduate skill development. The authors recommend training, ethical-use policies, new assessment strategies, and explicit attention to AI literacy, while emphasizing that ChatGPT should complement rather than replace human instruction and collaboration.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective/theoretical paper with no original empirical design, no comparison group, and no measured outcomes. It is peer-reviewed, but the evidence base is conceptual rather than observational or experimental.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for potentially meaningful institutional and instructional changes, but it does not provide empirical effect estimates. Any impact is therefore plausible but unquantified, yielding unclear to modest expected impact rather than demonstrated gains.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a conversational AI for adaptive learning, individualized feedback, research/writing support, administrative support, and generating lesson plans, assessments, and curriculum-related outputs in higher education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can support writing tasks by generating drafts, assisting with language translation, and helping non-English-speaking authors overcome language barriers. No quantitative study was conducted, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Writing support, text generation, and language translation assistance

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents ChatGPT as potentially supporting critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and metacognition through scaffolded prompts, critique of generated outputs, and authentic assessment design. At the same time, it warns that superficial use may undermine critical thinking and collaboration; no empirical effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual claims about critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and metacognition

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims ChatGPT can reduce grading burden, automate feedback elements, summarize student emails, generate response templates, and provide administrative support. These are presented as expected efficiency gains rather than empirically estimated effects; no sample size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher/administrator workload, feedback time, and administrative efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses heavily on institutional issues including academic integrity policies, equitable access, AI literacy, copyright concerns, and assessment redesign. It argues institutions must build guardrails and new assessment strategies, but provides no empirical evaluation, sample size, or effect size.
finding.measure: Academic integrity policy, equity/access, assessment design, and institutional governance

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT and large language models in academia: opportunities and challenges
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial examines the rapid emergence of ChatGPT and other large language models (LLMs) and asks how they may be used responsibly in academia. Rather than reporting an empirical intervention study, the paper synthesizes opportunities and concerns around LLMs for academic writing, education, programming, and grant-related work, with attention to plagiarism, hallucination, bias, accessibility, and computational cost.

For education, the authors argue that LLMs can support students as interactive study guides, content generators, and sources of immediate feedback, and can support educators in lesson planning, assessment, evaluation, and course design. The paper discusses how students or educators might use prompts, iterative prompting, fact-checking, and editing to improve outputs, while warning that outputs must be scrutinized because models can confidently fabricate information or reflect training-data bias. The discussion is general and spans K-12, higher education, and research settings, not a single implemented classroom program.

The paper concludes that LLMs should be embraced as academic tools but only with careful safeguards: users should document usage, verify factual accuracy, check for plagiarism, and remain aware of bias and limitations. It frames human oversight as essential, with the human prompt engineer responsible for validating and adopting any generated content before sharing it.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an editorial/opinion piece with no original empirical study, no comparison condition, and no systematic evaluation of outcomes. It is peer-reviewed and informative, but it does not meet criteria for causal or quantitative evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper describes potentially meaningful uses of LLMs for teacher planning, writing, and education governance, but provides no measured effect sizes or demonstrated implementation impact. Its practical relevance is moderate, yet the actual impact remains unverified.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-facing and student-facing use of ChatGPT/LLMs as conversational assistants for lesson planning, education support, immediate feedback, content generation, and instructional design; the paper discusses educators using the tool to facilitate course development, lesson planning, assessment, and evaluation, rather than evaluating a classroom implementation.

Using ChatGPT/LLMs as a writing and editing aid for drafting, revising, summarizing, translating, and polishing academic text; the paper emphasizes prompt-based editing of human-authored text, grammar/tone/readability improvement, and help overcoming writer’s block.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can increase efficiency for academic work and educator workflows, especially by speeding up drafting, editing, idea generation, and lesson/course planning. This is a conceptual/editorial claim rather than a measured effect, so no sample size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Perceived efficiency gains in academic writing, lesson planning, assessment creation, and coding support

finding.finding_summary: The editorial states that ChatGPT/LLMs may support writing quality through grammar correction, clarity, tone, readability, summarization, and editing, particularly for non-native English speakers. These benefits are described qualitatively and illustratively, without experimental comparison or quantified writing outcomes.
finding.measure: Writing/editing quality, grammar, clarity, tone, readability, and drafting support

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that constructive use of ChatGPT can support student critical thinking and metacognition when learners act as prompt engineers, fact checkers, and editors rather than submitting raw output. It also proposes process-oriented assignments such as submitting chat transcripts, comparing drafts with tracked changes, and identifying model errors to reinforce these skills.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, fact-checking, editing, and process-oriented learning behaviors

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that LLMs could improve educational and academic workflows, but it also emphasizes major institutional concerns including plagiarism policy, bias, accuracy, access inequity, and the need for disclosure rules and guardrails. No empirical institutional outcome is measured; the discussion is normative and policy-oriented.
finding.measure: Policy and governance considerations for responsible educational use of LLMs

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a review article that surveys the emerging literature on artificial intelligence in education, with a particular focus on chatbots and ChatGPT. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it asks how these tools may transform teaching and learning, what benefits they may provide, and what ethical and practical concerns accompany their adoption.

The article synthesizes prior work on AI technologies such as intelligent tutoring systems, automated grading, learning analytics, adaptive learning systems, and chatbots. It discusses how these tools can support personalized learning, instant feedback, language learning, student engagement, and teacher productivity. For teachers, the paper highlights potential uses such as automated assessment, progress monitoring, feedback generation, and reducing repetitive administrative work so that more time can be spent on lesson planning and student support.

The context is K-12 and higher education broadly, but the paper does not report a primary empirical sample or a specific implementation site. Its main conclusion is that ChatGPT and related AI tools have strong potential to enhance instruction and feedback processes, yet effective use depends on pedagogical alignment, teacher preparation, privacy protections, transparency, and safeguards against bias, inaccuracy, and over-reliance. The authors argue that responsible integration into curricula and policy is necessary for these tools to benefit education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed narrative review/conceptual article rather than an empirical study. It synthesizes prior literature on ChatGPT and AI in education but reports no original data, design, or causal evaluation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for potentially meaningful educational impact, especially for teacher support and feedback, but does not provide direct evidence of effect sizes or measured outcomes. Its practical implications are plausible but remain speculative in this article.

interventions.use_case: Review and conceptual discussion of ChatGPT as a generative conversational AI for education, including teacher support, student Q&A, feedback, and instructional assistance.
Discussion of AI systems that provide instant feedback on student work, including writing and code feedback, automated grading, and assignment evaluation.
Overview of AI systems that monitor student data to predict performance, identify disengagement risk, and support early warning/retention decisions.

paper_profiles.title: The Potential of AI Chatbots in Enhancing Lesson Planning in K-12 Education - Insights from Practicum-Experienced Teaching Graduate Students
paper_profiles.venue: Master of Arts thesis, Ontario Institute for Studies in Education, University of Toronto
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This thesis examines how K-12 preservice teachers use generative AI chatbots to support lesson planning during practicum teaching, and what benefits, challenges, and ethical concerns they perceive. The central question is whether tools such as ChatGPT and education-focused systems like Magic School AI, Eduaide.AI, and Education Copilot can function as useful instructional supports for teacher candidates entering the profession.

The study used a mixed-methods design combining an anonymous online survey and semi-structured interviews. Survey participants were teacher candidates in an Ontario teacher-education program who had practicum experience in K-12 settings; four volunteers also completed interviews. The paper describes common workflows in which participants used AI to generate lesson ideas, classroom discussion prompts, feedback on student work, homework help, rubrics, teaching slides, and activity ideas, sometimes expanding core concepts into curriculum-aligned lessons.

Findings suggest that AI chatbots were widely adopted and were generally perceived as time-saving tools that improved lesson efficiency and, in some cases, the perceived quality of instruction. At the same time, participants raised concerns about over-reliance, poor output quality, privacy, intellectual theft, bias, and the need for human judgment when aligning outputs to curriculum standards. The thesis concludes that generative AI may support planning and decision-making through scaffolding and idea generation, but that its use in teacher education requires ethical oversight, professional development, and clear guardrails.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods thesis using an anonymous survey and four semi-structured interviews, which provides useful descriptive evidence but not experimental causal identification. The study is credible as qualitative/correlational evidence, but it has a modest response rate and relies on self-report.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests modest practical benefits for teacher planning efficiency and perceived lesson quality, but it does not estimate learning gains or institutional outcomes with effect sizes. Impact is therefore plausible but unclear, and best characterized as modest/indirect.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-facing generative AI chatbots used by practicum-experienced K-12 preservice teachers to generate lesson-plan content ideas, classroom discussion questions, activity ideas, rubrics, handouts, slides, homework support, and feedback on student work during practicum lesson planning.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that 78% of survey respondents (n=103 valid responses) used AI chatbots for lesson planning during practicum, and participants consistently reported that the tools improved planning efficiency. Teacher candidates described using ChatGPT and similar tools to quickly generate lesson ideas, activities, rubrics, and teaching materials, reducing preparation time and supporting more efficient lesson development.
finding.measure: Survey reports of AI chatbot use for lesson planning and self-reported efficiency/benefit perceptions; interview themes on planning workflow

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports broad concerns and enabling conditions around AI adoption in K-12 practicum settings rather than a direct institutional effect estimate. Participants noted the need for careful integration, oversight, privacy protection, and curriculum alignment, while also raising concerns about over-reliance, intellectual theft, and inequitable access.
finding.measure: Survey and interview responses on ethical concerns, privacy, curriculum alignment, and student/teacher use norms

paper_profiles.title: Integrating CALL Systems with Chatbots as Conversational Partners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a longstanding limitation of computer-assisted language learning (CALL): while CALL systems can present lessons, exercises, and immediate feedback for vocabulary, grammar, pronunciation, and writing, they are weaker at supporting authentic conversational practice. The author argues that conversation is an essential component of language learning and reviews how dialogue systems and chatbots can fill this gap.

The paper is primarily a conceptual and review-based article. It surveys the evolution of CALL, its common exercise types, and limitations identified in prior work, then discusses integrating conversational agents into CALL environments. It also reviews several related systems and trials, including language-learning chatbots, embodied conversational agents, and dialog-based tutoring systems such as Web-CALL, STyLE, AutoTutor, and others. These examples are used to motivate the claim that chatbots can serve as conversational partners, provide practice opportunities, and increase learner engagement.

The population context is broad rather than a single empirical sample: the paper discusses language learners generally, with examples including adult non-native English speakers, university and college students, school learners in a Taiwan pronunciation study, and learners of Afrikaans, Swedish, Italian, Maori, and English. The main conclusion is that integrating CALL with chatbots or conversational agents can improve language-learning outcomes and learner experience, especially for conversational practice, though the paper also notes technical limitations such as limited domain coverage and weak linguistic understanding in current chatbot implementations.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review / conceptual paper with selective reports of prior experiments rather than a new controlled study. It cites some empirical evaluations, but the methodology is not systematic and effect sizes/confidence intervals are largely absent.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful effects on language practice and learner enjoyment, but the evidence is mostly qualitative or from small, heterogeneous prior studies. Reported outcomes are promising yet unclear in magnitude for the broader K-12 or teacher-preparation populations.

interventions.use_case: web-based computer-assisted language learning (CALL) with exercises, hints, immediate feedback, and online self-study materials for foreign language learning
chatbots and conversational agents used as conversational partners for practicing spoken/written language in CALL environments
embodied conversational agents and virtual language teachers used to provide guided language practice and feedback

finding.finding_summary: Across the studies reviewed, integrating chatbots/conversational agents into CALL was reported to improve language practice outcomes, especially pronunciation and conversational skills. For example, Ville evaluation with n=402 showed pronunciation improved more than writing and listening, and GeCALL with n=52 reported pronunciation gains; the paper also reports that Web-CALL outperformed a traditional class on comprehension and word order, though exact effect sizes were not reported.
finding.measure: pronunciation, comprehension, word order, conversational practice, language-learning test outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that chatbots as conversational partners improve opportunities for language production and interaction, with users reporting that they enjoyed chatting and found it useful for practicing a language. In the Afrikaans chatbot trial, users were positive about the experience despite many nonsensical responses, indicating perceived usefulness for language practice even when system quality was limited.
finding.measure: user feedback, conversational practice experience, language-use engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that learners enjoyed chatbot-supported CALL and felt more relaxed chatting with a bot than with a real human partner. In the Web-CALL evaluation, 87% of students enjoyed the class, 86% studied positively, and 85% felt free to study at their own pace, suggesting improved motivation and affective comfort.
finding.measure: student questionnaire responses on enjoyment, positive study attitudes, and self-paced learning comfort

finding.finding_summary: Chatbots were described as reducing anxiety and making language practice feel more relaxed and amusing, which the authors frame as beneficial for persistence and willingness to engage. These claims are qualitative and synthesised from prior evaluations rather than a single controlled comparison.
finding.measure: qualitative user reactions, perceived relaxation, enjoyment, willingness to continue chatting

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the impact of artificial intelligence on teaching and learning in higher education
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual and literature-based exploration of how artificial intelligence may affect teaching, learning, and the broader organization of higher education. Rather than evaluating a specific AI product through a controlled study, the authors discuss the rise of AI, machine learning, and “teacherbots” as emerging technologies that could automate or augment tasks such as student support, administrative assistance, basic feedback, and supervision. The paper also situates these developments within wider concerns about technology hype, corporate control, privacy, and the limits of algorithmic systems in complex educational settings.

The paper does not report a participant sample or a school/institution-level intervention. Its context is higher education, with examples drawn from universities and from AI applications such as IBM Watson, Siri, Google DeepMind, and Georgia Tech’s Jill Watson teaching assistant. The discussion is framed around the potential for AI to scale support in large-enrollment online courses and to relieve staff burden, while emphasizing that education remains a human-centered activity that cannot be reduced to automated information delivery.

The main conclusion is cautious: AI can augment teachers and improve support functions, but it is not yet able to replace the full complexity of human teaching. The authors argue for continued skepticism toward AI hype, more research on ethical implications, and a rethinking of teachers’ roles and pedagogies in light of AI’s growth. They also suggest that universities should preserve human judgment, creativity, and critical inquiry while selectively adopting AI tools for predictable and administrative tasks.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual, narrative review/opinion piece about the future role of AI in higher education, not an empirical evaluation of an intervention. It does not present a study design, comparison group, or measured outcomes relevant to the requested K-12 teacher-facing feedback topic.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No quantitative impact is reported and no intervention is tested, so there is no measurable educational effect to classify. The paper is useful only as background discussion of AI possibilities and risks in higher education.

paper_profiles.title: A comprehensive AI policy education framework for university teaching and learning
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for an artificial intelligence education policy for university teaching and learning in the context of rapidly emerging text-generative AI tools such as ChatGPT. The author argues that higher education institutions need clearer guidance on academic integrity, ethical use, privacy, accountability, access, and the pedagogical implications of AI adoption.

The study used a mixed-methods survey design with online questionnaires administered to 457 students and 180 teachers and staff members across Hong Kong universities. Quantitative items measured prior use of generative AI, perceptions of its educational value, concerns about misuse, and views on issues such as time-saving, personalized feedback, and the role of teachers. Open-ended responses were analyzed thematically to identify policy priorities and stakeholder concerns.

Findings suggest that respondents were cautiously optimistic about the educational potential of generative AI, especially for saving time, offering immediate feedback, improving digital competence, and supporting learning. At the same time, they expressed concerns about cheating, over-reliance, unequal access, weak ability to detect AI misuse, and risks to transferable skills. The paper concludes by proposing an AI Ecological Education Policy Framework with pedagogical, governance, and operational dimensions, emphasizing training, ethical guidelines, monitoring, and a balanced human-centered approach to AI integration in higher education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed descriptive survey with qualitative thematic analysis, not an experimental or quasi-experimental comparison of AI coaching versus human feedback. It provides useful stakeholder evidence but does not meet higher causal inference criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports perceptions and policy implications only; it does not estimate observed learning gains or productivity effects. Reported positives are moderate and expectancy-based, so overall impact is unclear to modest.

interventions.use_case: Text generative AI such as ChatGPT used as a university teaching-and-learning support tool, including personalized feedback, guidance for coursework, and AI-assisted support for student learning and teacher planning policy considerations.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is primarily a policy and stakeholder-perception study rather than an intervention efficacy trial. Across 457 students and 180 teachers/staff, respondents endorsed institutional planning for generative AI (students mean=4.5, teachers mean=4.54) and saw value in structured governance, training, and ethical guidelines for university teaching and learning.
finding.measure: Survey ratings on AI policy need, governance, training, and institutional planning; open-ended thematic responses

finding.finding_summary: Participants perceived generative AI as useful for saving time and providing immediate, personalized support, but this was based on self-reported expectations rather than a controlled efficiency experiment. Students rated time savings highly (mean=4.23) and both groups endorsed personalized feedback (students mean=3.75; teachers mean=3.86).
finding.measure: Survey ratings on time saving and personalized/immediate feedback

finding.finding_summary: Respondents believed generative AI could support digital competence and some academic skills, but also worried about over-reliance, reduced critical thinking, and weaker transferable skills. For example, teachers reported concern about over-reliance (mean=4.24), while respondents also endorsed possible gains in digital competence (students mean=3.8; teachers mean=3.83).
finding.measure: Survey ratings and thematic comments on digital competence, critical thinking, teamwork, and transferable skills

paper_profiles.title: The Promises and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence for Teachers: a Systematic Review of Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews empirical research on how teachers use artificial intelligence (AI) applications and machine-learning methods in education. The authors were motivated by the fact that AI is increasingly present in education, but teachers’ perspectives, roles, and needs have been less examined than student-facing applications. Their review asks what kinds of data are collected from teachers, what roles teachers play in AI-based research, what benefits AI offers teachers, what challenges arise, and which AI methods are most commonly used.
