The review searched Web of Science for English-language journal articles published over the previous 20 years and identified 44 empirical studies focused on in-service K-12 teachers and pre-service teachers. The studies covered a range of AI uses, including automated scoring, predictive models of teacher outcomes, classroom monitoring, adaptive feedback, and tools informed by teacher data. Teachers appeared in several roles, such as models for training AI, providers of performance data, sources of student information, and evaluators of assessment systems.

The authors conclude that AI is most often reported as helping teachers with planning, implementation, and assessment by identifying student needs, supporting timely monitoring and feedback, and reducing workload. However, they also identify major challenges, including limited reliability, limited technical capacity, infrastructure constraints, context-specificity, and slow or insufficiently adaptive feedback. They argue that more research is needed on pre-service teachers, multimodal data, and deeper teacher involvement in AI system design.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review, but it does not present a new causal evaluation or pooled effect estimate for the focal comparison. The review synthesizes observational and design studies, so the evidence quality for the specific teacher-facing AI coaching/feedback question remains indirect and correlational/qualitative overall.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical promise for AI in teachers’ planning, monitoring, and assessment, but it reports no effect sizes for lesson quality, feedback usefulness, revision quality, uptake of feedback, or planning speed. Its contribution is mainly conceptual and descriptive rather than demonstrating measurable impact on the requested outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses how artificial intelligence is changing education and argues that effective use of AI in classrooms and academic work depends on three core competencies: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. Rather than testing an intervention experimentally, the article is a conceptual discussion grounded in the author’s teaching experience and informal discussions at a Swiss university, combined with a narrative literature review. The paper focuses on the risks of uncritical AI use, such as hallucinations, overreliance, and ethical misuse, as well as the opportunities for AI to support personalized learning and more interactive teaching.

A central part of the paper is a case study from Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich, where the institution created internal guidelines for student use of generative AI in written work. These guidelines require transparency about which tools were used, how they were used, and how outputs were critically evaluated. The paper also describes broader recommendations for building an “AI culture” in education through workshops, regular updates, budgeted support, and dedicated staff roles.

The article further argues that AI literacy should be taught explicitly through courses covering AI concepts, machine learning, ethics, governance, and hands-on practice. It presents prompt engineering as a pedagogical tool that can improve engagement and help students think critically, and it outlines several prompting methods such as chain-of-thought, role-play prompting, self-consistency, automatic prompt engineering, generated knowledge prompting, and tree-of-thought prompting. Overall, the paper concludes that AI should be treated as a sparring partner rather than a tutor or ghostwriter, and that responsible AI use in education requires transparency, training, and critical evaluation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: The paper is a conceptual discussion with a narrative literature review and an illustrative case study, not a controlled empirical evaluation. It provides no experimental design, comparison group, or quantitative outcome analysis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No impact effect sizes or measured outcomes are reported, so there is no basis for estimating educational impact. The paper offers recommendations and theory rather than demonstrated effects.

interventions.use_case: Use of ChatGPT/GPT-4, Bard, Claude, and similar LLMs as an 'informed conversational partner' for student academic writing, brainstorming, source-finding, and classroom AI experimentation; also discussed as a tool for teacher-created case studies and curricula.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual discussion and case-based institutional reflection rather than an empirical comparison study. The paper argues that simple AI-use guidelines and bans are insufficient; it proposes AI literacy training, prompt-engineering instruction, workshops, and institutional supports to improve responsible AI use, transparency, and critical engagement, but reports no quantitative effect estimates.
finding.measure: Institutional policies, AI guidelines, and proposed implementation practices; no formal outcome measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central claim is that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking should be taught together because they can improve students’ ability to evaluate AI outputs and avoid hallucinations. However, this is asserted on conceptual and literature-review grounds, not tested with experimental outcome data.
finding.measure: Critical thinking / AI literacy / prompt engineering competence; no formal measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that LLMs can help teachers create curricula, generate case studies, and support planning more efficiently, but it also notes that prompting for high-quality outputs may take substantial time and can sometimes be less efficient than doing the task manually. No empirical timing or workload data are reported, so the net effect remains unclear.
finding.measure: Teacher planning efficiency / curriculum development workload; no formal measure reported

paper_profiles.title: Speculative Futures on ChatGPT and Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Collective Reflection from the Educational Landscape
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper explores the promises and pitfalls of ChatGPT and generative AI in education through a speculative methodology rather than empirical testing. The authors aim to examine possible future directions, tensions, and implications of conversational AI by writing and analyzing fictional narratives about educational uses of AI, including both optimistic and critical scenarios.

The intervention or approach studied is not a deployed classroom intervention but a collective speculative exercise. Contributors produced fictional narratives imagining how ChatGPT-like systems might shape learning, teaching, assessment, collaboration, access, and academic integrity. The paper also includes a narrative generated by ChatGPT itself, which the authors use as part of the reflection on human versus AI contributions.

The context is broad educational practice, including K-12 and higher education references, but no primary participant sample was studied. The paper concludes that generative AI has potential benefits such as personalization, accessibility, language support, and efficiency, while also posing risks including bias, privacy concerns, dependence, inequity, and threats to academic integrity and human agency. The authors argue that education should remain human-centered and that AI should be adopted critically, ethically, and with careful attention to context.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a speculative collective reflection using fictional narratives, not an empirical study with a testable design. It is peer-reviewed, but it does not provide causal evidence or measured outcomes relevant to the requested comparison.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper offers broad conceptual influence on how educators think about generative AI, but it reports no measured effect sizes or direct intervention impact. Its practical implications are plausible yet unclear and entirely non-quantitative.

interventions.use_case: Speculative discussion of ChatGPT and similar generative AI as conversational educational support for learners and teachers, including tutoring, lesson-planning assistance, feedback, translation, and AI-mediated academic communication.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can support writing and language development by providing instant feedback, suggestions, and conversation practice, but this is presented as speculative rather than empirically tested. In the fictional narratives, ChatGPT-like tools help students improve writing, translate texts, and refine expression; no quantitative effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Narrative/speculative claims about writing support, translation, and language skill development

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly suggests that conversational AI can improve language skills through dialogue practice, pronunciation support, and real-time translation. Example narratives describe AI helping learners practice oral communication and remove language barriers, but these are fictional scenarios with no measured effect sizes or sample sizes.
finding.measure: Narrative/speculative claims about oral communication, pronunciation, and translation support

finding.finding_summary: The discussion claims generative AI may support creativity, problem-solving, and critical thinking by providing alternative ideas and tailored learning pathways, though it also warns these skills could be undermined by over-reliance. Because the paper is speculative and non-empirical, no effect sizes or quantitative evidence are reported.
finding.measure: Narrative/speculative claims about critical thinking, creativity, and problem-solving

finding.finding_summary: A central claim is that ChatGPT-like tools can save teachers time by drafting lesson plans, grading assignments, summarizing concepts, and generating questions, thereby increasing efficiency. The paper does not provide empirical workload data, effect sizes, or controlled comparisons; these are speculative projected benefits.
finding.measure: Narrative/speculative claims about teacher time-saving, lesson planning, grading, and summarization

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents a mixed institutional picture: AI could improve access, equity, and multilingual participation, but could also intensify privacy risks, bias, inequality, surveillance, and academic integrity concerns. These claims are based on speculative narratives and commentary rather than empirical system-level evaluation.
finding.measure: Narrative/speculative claims about access, equity, privacy, bias, integrity, and institutional change

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT and large language models in academia: opportunities and challenges
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial examines the rapid emergence of ChatGPT and other large language models (LLMs) and discusses their implications for academic work. The paper is not an empirical evaluation of an intervention; instead, it offers a position-oriented review of opportunities and risks, including how LLMs may affect writing, programming, education, peer review, and bias.

With respect to education, the authors argue that LLMs can support students and educators by providing quick answers, generating practice materials, assisting with lesson planning, supporting assessment, and giving immediate feedback. They also note that these tools could function as editing aids for academic writing, especially for non-native English speakers, and could help with coding tasks such as generating, explaining, and debugging code.

The paper's broader context is academia in general, with examples drawn from higher education, grant writing, programming, and teaching. The authors emphasize that LLM outputs can be inaccurate, biased, or fabricated, and that users must verify content carefully. Their main conclusion is that LLMs should be embraced as useful academic tools, but with attention to bias, transparency, and validation of outputs.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed editorial/commentary rather than an empirical evaluation. It does not present a study design, comparison groups, or original outcome data on teacher-facing generative AI coaching or lesson-plan feedback.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No empirical impact is estimated because the paper contains no measured outcomes, sample sizes, or effect sizes. It is useful background discussion but provides no evidence of intervention impact for K-12 teacher planning or feedback.

interventions.use_case: Editorial discussion of ChatGPT and similar large language models as a conversational AI tool for education, including lesson planning, assessment, immediate feedback, and teacher/learner support.

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a review article that surveys the emerging literature on artificial intelligence in education, with particular attention to chatbots and ChatGPT. The authors ask what AI is, how chatbot-based systems work, and what kinds of educational opportunities and risks these tools present. Rather than evaluating a specific intervention, the paper synthesizes conceptual and prior empirical work to explain why generative AI has attracted attention in teaching, learning, assessment, and administration.

The discussion centers on AI-supported and AI-empowered uses of chatbots, including personalized learning, instant feedback, grading support, lesson-planning support, and student assistance. The paper highlights examples such as AI tutoring systems, automated grading, writing support tools, and virtual assistants used in educational contexts, but it does not report a primary study with a defined participant sample or setting. It also emphasizes ethical issues such as bias, privacy, deception, academic integrity, and over-reliance on AI, arguing that teacher preparation and institutional support are important for responsible adoption.

The main conclusion is that AI and generative chatbots have substantial potential to improve educational efficiency, feedback, engagement, and personalization, but these benefits depend on careful implementation and attention to ethical and practical constraints. The authors call for further research and policy development to understand how ChatGPT and related tools can be integrated effectively into education while preserving transparency, fairness, and the role of human educators.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a review/opinion article with no original empirical evaluation of an intervention, comparison group, or measured outcomes. It synthesizes prior literature and discusses potential applications and risks rather than testing effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct impact estimate is reported for teachers or students in this paper. The article is theoretical and descriptive, so there is no measurable intervention effect to classify.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual discussion of ChatGPT as a generative chatbot for education, including its potential to provide teacher support, feedback, and assistance in instructional tasks such as lesson planning and student support.

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how pre-service elementary teachers integrate ChatGPT into science lesson planning and what they believe ChatGPT contributes to science teaching and learning. The authors focus on the practical question of whether a generative AI tool can support lesson design, instructional strategies, and formative feedback in K-12 science education, while also identifying perceived risks such as misinformation and over-dependence.

The intervention/approach was a short instructional sequence in a university science education course: 29 pre-service elementary teachers in Korea received four two-hour sessions introducing ChatGPT, its possible educational uses, science teaching methods, and lesson-plan writing. Participants then created a 45-minute elementary science lesson plan requiring at least one ChatGPT query and attached a simulated chat conversation. Their lesson plans were evaluated with a modified TPACK-based rubric adapted from the Technology Integration Assessment Rubric, and open-ended survey responses were analyzed qualitatively.

The sample consisted of pre-service elementary science teachers at a Korean teachers' university, mostly sophomores, preparing for future classroom teaching. Results suggest that participants saw ChatGPT as broadly applicable across science topics and instructional methods, especially for cooperative learning, Predict-Observe-Explain, learning cycles, analogy generation, and concept mapping. Lesson plans scored relatively high overall, but participants were less effective at choosing appropriate ChatGPT functions than at aligning ChatGPT with goals and instructional strategies. They viewed ChatGPT as useful for questioning, individualized support, and formative assessment, while also expressing concerns about accuracy, bias, and student over-reliance. The authors conclude that ChatGPT has promise for science lesson planning, but that teacher preparation in AI literacy and careful pedagogical design are needed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/descriptive preprint using lesson-plan artifact analysis and open-ended survey responses, not a controlled comparison or randomized design. It provides useful early evidence on intended use and perceived value, but it does not test causal effects of ChatGPT on student or teacher outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports moderately high lesson-plan rubric scores (M = 3.29/4) and strong perceived utility, but no actual effect sizes on learning, feedback quality, or planning speed. Its impact is therefore suggestive rather than demonstrated, with unclear magnitude for K-12 practice.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used by pre-service elementary teachers to design science lesson plans, generate supporting explanations and questions, assist role-play planning, provide adaptive follow-up questions, and suggest formative feedback during lesson-planning activities.

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers expected ChatGPT to support science learning by enabling questioning, exploration, prediction, explanation, and formative assessment within lesson plans, especially in inquiry-oriented methods like POE and the learning cycle. However, this paper did not measure student science achievement; it reported descriptive evidence from 29 pre-service teachers' lesson plans and survey responses, with the lesson plans scoring M = 3.29/4 (SD = .91) on a modified TPACK-based rubric for integrating ChatGPT into science instruction.
finding.measure: Modified TPACK-based lesson-plan rubric; qualitative analysis of lesson plans and survey responses about science learning uses

finding.finding_summary: Participants repeatedly described ChatGPT as supporting critical thinking, self-directed learning, and collaborative planning, but these were anticipated benefits rather than measured learner outcomes. The paper reports that 5/29 participants linked ChatGPT to critical thinking and 9/29 to individualized/self-directed learning, while 11/29 proposed structured classroom strategies to reduce over-dependence on ChatGPT.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses about perceived usefulness and concerns

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers anticipated that ChatGPT could increase motivation and interest through individualized and self-directed learning support. These are perception-based findings from 29 participants; the study did not directly measure student motivation or engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses on anticipated outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests ChatGPT could improve planning efficiency by helping teachers summarize scenario ideas, generate role-play structures, and provide quick feedback during lesson planning. The strongest directly reported quantitative evidence is the lesson-plan quality score of M = 3.29/4 (SD = .91), but no time-on-task or speed metric was collected.
finding.measure: Lesson-plan rubric scores; qualitative comments on planning support and feedback utility

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI as a Learning Buddy and a Teaching Assistant: Preservice Teachers’ Use and Attitudes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how preservice teachers use generative AI (GenAI) across academic learning and instructional preparation tasks, and whether demographic factors predict their attitudes toward and frequency of GenAI use. The study is motivated by growing interest in GenAI in teacher education, especially in under-resourced contexts in the Global South, and by concerns about how future teachers are using these tools for both learning and teaching-related work.

The authors conducted a cross-sectional survey of 167 preservice teachers enrolled in teacher education programs at four institutions in Ghana. They measured how often participants used GenAI as a “learning buddy” for tasks such as finding reading materials, explaining concepts, and generating practical examples, and as a “teaching assistant” for tasks such as finding teaching resources, identifying assessment strategies, developing lesson objectives, and creating lesson plans. The study also assessed attitudes toward GenAI’s learning benefits, teaching benefits, and ethical/accuracy concerns.

Results showed that preservice teachers used GenAI more often for their own academic learning than for instructional planning. Most participants reported positive attitudes toward GenAI, particularly its usefulness for increasing access to materials and improving pedagogical skills, though they also expressed concerns about inaccuracy, cost, and possible academic dishonesty. Age and class level predicted some usage patterns, but age, gender, and class level did not meaningfully predict overall attitudes. The paper concludes that GenAI is already being used by preservice teachers in Ghana, but that teacher education programs need stronger AI literacy and guidance on ethical, responsible use.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed cross-sectional survey with descriptive and regression analyses, so it provides correlational evidence but no causal comparison of GenAI against human feedback or alternative planning supports. It is useful for mapping use patterns and perceptions, but it does not meet RCT/QED criteria for stronger causal inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for preservice teachers’ planning autonomy and perceived usefulness of GenAI, but the evidence is self-reported and descriptive with no effect sizes on performance outcomes. Its impact on the target comparator question is therefore modest and unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: preservice teachers’ use of generative AI/ChatGPT-like tools as a learning buddy for finding reading materials, getting content explanations, and examples, and as a teaching assistant for lesson planning, identifying objectives, assessment strategies, teaching resources, and sample lessons

finding.finding_summary: This cross-sectional survey of 167 preservice teachers in Ghana found that GenAI was used frequently for instructional planning and academic support, especially for finding reading materials (38.11%, n=93), teaching resources (33.33%, n=90), content explanations (25.41%, n=62), and assessment strategies (21.48%, n=58). The study did not test causal effects, but descriptive results indicate that preservice teachers perceived GenAI as helpful for academic and teaching preparation tasks.
finding.measure: Self-reported use frequencies for learning and instructional tasks; item-level attitude ratings about GenAI usefulness

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that GenAI helped them work more autonomously and reduced dependence on peers and instructors for routine preparation tasks. Frequency was substantial for both learning and teaching uses, with 28.14% reporting using GenAI 'very often' for learning and 14.97% 'very often' for teaching, suggesting perceived productivity gains rather than measured time savings.
finding.measure: Self-reported frequency of use and attitude items about dependence on colleagues/instructors and confidence in preparation

finding.finding_summary: The authors report generally positive attitudes toward GenAI’s support for independent learning and pedagogical preparation, but also note concerns about academic dishonesty and reduced critical/creative skill development. Because the study is descriptive, this is an attitudinal finding rather than a measured skill gain; the most relevant items showed agreement that GenAI improves understanding and pedagogical skills (e.g., M=3.98 for understanding complex study areas; M=3.88 for improving pedagogical skills).
finding.measure: Attitude scale items related to autonomous learning, pedagogical confidence, cheating, and critical/creative skill concerns

paper_profiles.title: AI and Chat GPT in Language Teaching: Enhancing EFL Classroom Support and Transforming Assessment Techniques
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Higher Education Pedagogies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses the role of artificial intelligence and Chat GPT in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teaching, focusing on how these tools can support personalized learning, real-time language practice, lesson planning, assessment, and evaluation. Rather than reporting a controlled empirical comparison, it presents a conceptual discussion of how AI can transform language instruction and educational assessment.

The paper argues that AI-powered systems can tailor lessons to learners' needs, provide immediate feedback on grammar, pronunciation, and vocabulary, and help teachers generate lesson plans and learning materials more efficiently. It also describes AI uses in adaptive testing, automated grading, continuous formative assessment, performance analysis, and test security, emphasizing that teachers remain essential for interpretation, judgment, and instructional decision-making.

The context is EFL education, with examples drawn from platforms and tools such as Duolingo, Rosetta Stone, ExamSoft, Grammarly, and university EFL settings. The paper concludes that AI and Chat GPT can enhance language learning and assessment, but their successful use depends on balancing technology with human interaction and addressing ethical issues such as privacy, equity, bias, and access.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative essay/review article rather than an empirical study. It contains no original dataset, comparison design, or statistical analysis of teacher-facing generative AI feedback.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for EFL teaching, writing support, and grading efficiency, but these are descriptive and not quantified. The practical impact is therefore plausible but unclear from the evidence presented.

interventions.use_case: Chat GPT use in EFL classrooms for real-time language practice, answering student questions, and providing conversational support/feedback to learners and teachers
AI-powered language learning platforms such as Duolingo and Rosetta Stone that adapt lessons and practice to learner performance and pacing
AI-driven automated grading and feedback for written responses, including grammar/spelling correction and coherence suggestions
AI writing assistants and pronunciation/grammar feedback tools for EFL writing and language development
AI-enhanced performance analysis and learning analytics to identify students struggling with topics and guide instructional intervention

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI writing assistants and automated feedback systems improve EFL writing quality by identifying grammar and spelling errors, suggesting revisions, and supporting clearer and more coherent written responses. It cites a case study at New York University reporting substantial improvements in students' written English proficiency, but the article does not report a precise effect size or sample size.
finding.measure: Written English proficiency, grammar/style quality, coherence of student writing

finding.finding_summary: Automated grading and feedback on written assignments are described as helping students learn from mistakes and make necessary improvements. The article presents this as a beneficial application of AI in assessment, but provides no original experimental estimates, effect sizes, or sample information.
finding.measure: Quality of written assignment feedback and revision support

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims that Chat GPT-based chatbots and other AI language tools provide immediate feedback on pronunciation, grammar, vocabulary, and comprehension, improving learners' language proficiency and confidence. These claims are presented through descriptive discussion and cited cases rather than a controlled study, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Pronunciation, grammar usage, vocabulary usage, speaking/conversation practice, language proficiency

finding.finding_summary: AI-powered language learning platforms are described as providing adaptive practice and instant pronunciation feedback that support oral language development. The paper cites Duolingo, Rosetta Stone, and AI-powered apps for young learners as examples, but does not present new comparative data or statistics.
finding.measure: Language proficiency, pronunciation feedback, conversational practice

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly argues that AI-generated lesson plans, automated grading, and chatbot support reduce teacher workload and save time in planning and assessment. This is a descriptive claim supported by examples such as Chat GPT assisting teachers and ExamSoft streamlining grading, but no empirical effect size is provided.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, planning time, grading efficiency

finding.finding_summary: AI-enhanced examination software is described as improving grading consistency, speeding up assessment, and increasing test security through automated proctoring. The paper treats these as practical efficiency gains, but offers no quantitative evaluation of time saved or error reduction.
finding.measure: Grading speed, assessment efficiency, test security processes

finding.finding_summary: The article emphasizes ethical concerns including privacy, equity, access, and bias as central consequences of AI adoption in education. It does not test institutional outcomes experimentally, but argues that AI can widen or narrow access depending on implementation and governance.
finding.measure: Privacy, equity/access, algorithmic bias, responsible AI governance

paper_profiles.title: A systematic literature review of empirical research on ChatGPT in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the early empirical literature on ChatGPT in education, asking how students and teachers have initially used the tool and what findings have emerged from those studies. The authors conducted a systematic literature review of 14 empirical studies published up to April 10, 2023, using PRISMA 2020 and Okoli’s review procedures. Their search covered Dimensions.ai, Lens.org, Scopus, Web of Science, and ERIC, and they screened studies for empirical evidence on ChatGPT use in educational contexts.

The reviewed studies covered higher education most often, with one elementary-school study, and involved students, teachers, and mixed teacher-student samples across multiple countries. The review found that students used ChatGPT primarily as a virtual intelligent assistant for immediate feedback, answers, explanations, writing support, language support, and self-directed or personalized learning. Teachers used it to create lesson plans, generate quizzes, obtain resources, and improve productivity. Several studies also suggested potential benefits for reasoning, problem solving, and efficiency, though many were based on small samples and short-term use.

The main conclusions are that ChatGPT shows promise as a support tool for both learning and teaching, but its use raises concerns about accuracy, overreliance, reduced creativity or collaboration, academic integrity, and the need for clear guidance. The review emphasizes that structured training, support, and policies are important for responsible use. It does not provide comparative evidence against human coach feedback, peer feedback, rubrics, or usual planning practice in K-12 lesson-planning settings; instead, it synthesizes early descriptive and evaluative empirical studies of ChatGPT adoption in education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review of 14 empirical studies, but the included studies were mostly qualitative, quasi-experimental, small-sample, and heterogeneous, and the review does not report a meta-analysis or pooled causal estimates. That places it in the lower-confidence evidence tier despite being peer reviewed and methodologically transparent as a review.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests meaningful practical benefits, especially for teacher productivity and student support, but the evidence is not quantified with effect sizes and includes notable concerns about overuse and accuracy. Overall impact is promising but still unclear/modest for the target K-12/teacher-prep question.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used by students and teachers as a conversational AI assistant for answering questions, giving immediate feedback, generating lesson plans, quizzes, learning resources, and supporting self-directed learning and writing tasks in educational settings.

finding.finding_summary: The review found that ChatGPT was widely used to support writing and language tasks, including generating ideas, composing essays, summarizing, paraphrasing, translating, and checking grammar. However, the evidence base was descriptive and not designed to estimate a causal effect size; the review synthesizes 14 empirical studies rather than reporting a pooled effect.
finding.measure: Observed use and reported perceptions of writing support, essay composition, summarization, paraphrasing, translation, and grammar checking

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, ChatGPT was reported to help with critical thinking, reasoning, problem-solving, and some collaborative learning processes, but overuse was also associated with reduced innovative capacity and weaker collaboration competencies. The review specifically notes negative findings in 3 studies (21.4%) regarding overuse and innovative/collaborative skills, but does not provide pooled effect sizes.
finding.measure: Reported changes in critical thinking, reasoning, problem-solving, innovation, and collaborative learning competencies
finding.study_size: n=14 studies reviewed; negative findings in n=3 studies

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and students reported that ChatGPT improved productivity and efficiency by speeding lesson planning, quiz generation, resource creation, and task completion. The review characterizes these as recurring benefits across multiple studies, but it does not report a pooled quantitative effect size or experimental estimate.
finding.measure: Reported productivity, workload, and time-saving perceptions; task completion efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The review indicates that ChatGPT supported learning in subject-specific contexts such as mathematics, journalism, engineering, construction, early education, and social science by helping students understand concepts, solve problems, and complete homework or projects. These findings are synthesized from the included studies and are not accompanied by pooled quantitative effects.
finding.measure: Reported subject-area learning support, concept understanding, homework help, and problem-solving

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities, risks, and educational implications of large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-3 and ChatGPT. Rather than reporting a single empirical study, it synthesizes the state of the field and argues that LLMs can support both learning and teaching activities, while also introducing important concerns around bias, privacy, copyright, overreliance, and the difficulty of distinguishing machine-generated from human-generated text.

On the teaching side, the paper discusses how LLMs may help educators with lesson planning, personalized content creation, assessment support, feedback generation, and professional development. On the learning side, it highlights uses such as generating practice questions, summaries, explanations, writing support, tutoring, and conversational practice across elementary, secondary, tertiary, and professional learning contexts. The paper also surveys examples of existing research using LLMs for quiz generation, code explanations, curiosity prompting, adaptive feedback, and automated assessment.

The paper’s main conclusion is that LLMs have substantial potential to augment education, but only if they are used as complementary tools under active human oversight. The authors recommend careful integration guided by pedagogy, critical thinking, fact checking, fairness, and responsible governance. They argue that further research is needed to establish best practices and to ensure that adoption does not worsen educational inequities or compromise academic integrity.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper and narrative review, not an empirical study. It offers conceptual discussion and cites prior work, but does not present a clear original methodology or comparative evidence meeting causal-inference criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially broad educational relevance of LLMs for teaching workflows, but it provides no direct effect estimates for lesson quality, feedback usefulness, revision quality, uptake, or planning speed. As a result, the practical impact is plausible but empirically unmeasured in this paper.

interventions.use_case: Position paper discussing ChatGPT and related large language models as teacher-facing assistants for lesson planning, generating classroom materials, providing feedback on student work, and supporting personalized instruction.
LLM-based generation of feedback for student writing and other student responses, including highlighting strengths/weaknesses and suggesting improvements for teacher review.
LLM-supported generation of quizzes, exercises, questions, summaries, explanations, and instructional content for classroom use.

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how pre-service elementary science teachers incorporated ChatGPT into lesson planning and what they thought about its usefulness and risks for science teaching and learning. The authors address a gap in empirical evidence about generative AI in education by focusing on a teacher-facing use case: lesson planning rather than student chat use. They ask what kinds of science content and instructional methods can be paired with ChatGPT, how well teachers can plan such integration, and what benefits and concerns they anticipate.

The study involved 29 pre-service elementary teachers enrolled in a science education course at a Korean teachers' university. After four class sessions introducing ChatGPT, its potential uses, science-teaching methods, and lesson-plan writing, participants created a 45-minute elementary science lesson plan that integrated ChatGPT and attached a simulated chat transcript. The researchers evaluated the plans using a modified TPACK-based technology integration rubric and analyzed open-ended survey responses about rationale, anticipated usefulness, and concerns.

Results suggest that the participants envisioned ChatGPT as broadly applicable across science topics and instructional strategies, especially cooperative learning, POE, learning cycles, analogies, and concept mapping. Overall lesson-plan quality was fairly high, but participants were stronger at aligning ChatGPT with instructional strategies than at selecting the most appropriate ChatGPT functions. They saw ChatGPT as useful for questioning, self-directed learning, individualized support, and formative feedback, while also worrying about inaccurate responses and student overdependence. The authors conclude that teacher education should include stronger professional development on AI function selection, critical evaluation of outputs, and structured classroom strategies to prevent misuse or overreliance.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive qualitative/pre-post design using lesson-plan analysis and open-ended survey responses from 29 pre-service teachers, with no control group or causal identification. It provides useful exploratory evidence but does not meet strong credibility criteria for causal inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful applications of ChatGPT for lesson planning and individualized support, but it reports no direct learning gains, no time savings, and no comparative effect sizes. Impact on practice is therefore plausible but still unclear and modest in evidentiary strength.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used by pre-service elementary science teachers to support lesson planning, generate/modify lesson content, suggest instructional strategies, provide follow-up questioning, and simulate feedback within lesson plans.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that pre-service teachers expected ChatGPT to support science learning through questioning, prediction/explanation, formative assessment, and individualized inquiry. In the lesson-plan rubric, science-content alignment and instructional-strategy alignment were relatively high (M=3.44 and M=3.48 on a 4-point scale), suggesting ChatGPT was often planned in ways that could support scientific reasoning, though this was based on planned rather than implemented instruction (n=29).
finding.measure: Modified TPACK-based rubric scores for science lesson plans; qualitative analysis of planned science learning activities and anticipated inquiry support

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers repeatedly anticipated that ChatGPT would foster critical thinking, self-directed learning, and collaborative learning, but they also worried about over-dependence and misinformation. No effect size was reported because the study is descriptive and qualitative, but 5/29 explicitly linked ChatGPT to critical thinking and 13/29 raised dependence concerns.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses about perceived benefits/concerns; lesson-plan analysis of intended instructional uses

finding.finding_summary: Participants viewed ChatGPT as helping them generate lesson ideas, summarize long student scenarios, provide instant answers, and support individualized guidance that a single teacher could not easily provide. The paper does not report a direct speed measure, but the authors argue the tool could make planning and classroom support more efficient; evidence is qualitative/descriptive from n=29 lesson plans and surveys.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness for planning support, summarization, instant response, and individualized assistance

paper_profiles.title: AI, Expert or Peer? Examining the Impact of Perceived Feedback Source on Pre-Service Teachers Feedback Perception and Uptake
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether the perceived source of feedback changes how pre-service teachers judge and use feedback, even when the feedback content itself is held constant. The authors focus on a key question in teacher education and AI-supported feedback: whether LLM-generated feedback is treated differently from feedback thought to come from an expert or a peer, and whether such source perceptions affect both subjective evaluations and actual revision behavior.

The study used a randomized experiment with 273 bachelor’s students in a German teacher-education program. Participants were preparing to teach during a practicum and were shown a mathematics learning goal containing three errors. Each participant received one written feedback message drawn from one of three source conditions: LLM-generated feedback, expert-generated feedback, or peer-generated feedback. The feedback was produced to be comparable across conditions, and participants then guessed the source, rated the feedback on fairness, usefulness, acceptance, willingness to improve, and affect, and finally revised the learning goal to reflect the feedback.

Results showed that source perception strongly shaped feedback judgments. LLM feedback was rated most positively when it was mistakenly believed to come from an expert, suggesting an expertise heuristic and a bias favoring human expert sources. However, these perception effects did not translate into stronger uptake of feedback suggestions. Instead, the main predictor of whether participants implemented suggestions was objective feedback quality, not actual source, perceived source, or recognition accuracy. The authors conclude that teacher education should address source-related biases and AI literacy, while also emphasizing feedback quality as the key driver of behavioral uptake.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized experiment with pre-service teachers and multiple comparison conditions (LLM, expert, peer), which supports internal validity. There are some concerns because feedback quality varied across conditions and the main uptake model had reduced usable n and descriptive rather than causal uptake comparisons, so it falls short of the strongest tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows a modest but meaningful effect on perceptions and a small-to-moderate descriptive advantage for LLM feedback uptake, especially in a teacher-preparation population. However, the behavioral effect on revision was limited by small variance explained (R²=.078) and uptake was driven by feedback quality rather than source, so overall impact is modest rather than large.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated written feedback on a pre-service teacher’s mathematics learning goal and lesson-plan wording, compared against expert and peer feedback; the system used ChatGPT-4 to produce concrete, empathic, activating revision suggestions.

finding.finding_summary: Perceived feedback source strongly shaped judgments about fairness, usefulness, and acceptance, but not actual behavioral uptake. In a randomized experiment with pre-service teachers (N=273; uptake model n=161), LLM feedback was rated more favorably when falsely attributed to an expert (e.g., fairness b=1.21, p=.042; usefulness b=1.76, p=.009), yet source perceptions did not predict revision behavior once feedback quality was controlled.
finding.measure: Feedback perception questionnaire (fairness, usefulness, acceptance, willingness to improve) and feedback uptake/correction rate after revising a learning goal

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests automated feedback can support efficient revision processes in teacher education because LLM feedback achieved the highest relative uptake (52%) versus expert feedback (45%) and peer feedback (42%). However, this was a descriptive comparison rather than a causal efficiency test, and the main inferential result was that higher feedback quality—not source—predicted uptake (b=1.27, p=.012).
finding.measure: Relative feedback uptake / correction rate; number of recognized mistakes and implemented suggestions
finding.effect_size: R²=.078 (uptake model); relative uptake 52% vs 45% vs 42%

finding.finding_summary: The paper focused on revision quality for a mathematics learning goal in teacher-preparation rather than learner achievement on a standardized test. LLM feedback generated the most recognized mistakes (198) and implemented suggestions (103) overall, but actual implementation was explained by feedback quality alone (b=1.27, SE=0.50, z=2.52, p=.012), with no significant effects of source or recognition accuracy.
finding.measure: Revision of a mathematics learning goal; proportion of suggested improvements implemented
finding.effect_size: feedback quality coefficient b=1.27; ANOVA for suggestions implemented η²=.11

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging Peer, Self, and Teacher Assessments for Generative AI-Enhanced Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teacher, peer, and self-assessments align in a generative AI-enhanced feedback environment, with the goal of informing better design for AI-supported feedback systems. The central problem is that feedback in large or scalable learning settings is difficult to provide timely and with enough depth, and current AI systems often treat all human evaluative sources as equally reliable. The authors investigate whether human assessments differ systematically in agreement, bias, and relationship to a teacher’s overall grade.

The study is situated in the AICoFe (AI-based Collaborative Feedback) system and uses a validated rubric to assess oral presentations. The participants were 46 final-year undergraduate engineering students at Universidad Autónoma de Madrid, Spain. Each presentation was evaluated by the teacher and two randomly assigned peers, and students also completed self-assessments after reviewing a video of their performance. The rubric covered content, design, and delivery, and the teacher additionally assigned an independent global grade.

Results showed moderate to substantial agreement across evaluators, with peer ratings aligning reasonably well with teacher judgments and self-assessments showing the weakest alignment. The teacher’s rubric scores correlated most strongly with the teacher’s global grade, while peer and self scores were also significantly correlated but less strongly. The paper concludes that peer and self-assessments are useful but show systematic leniency relative to teacher scoring, and it proposes a refined GenAI feedback design that weights evaluator inputs differently, detects bias, and incorporates self-assessment into AI-generated feedback.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical correlational study with clear methodology, but it is not a randomized or quasi-experimental test of the GenAI feedback system. It primarily analyzes agreement, correlation, and bias among assessors, so causal evidence for the intervention is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report an intervention effect size on learner outcomes; its findings are mainly descriptive and design-oriented. Any practical impact is indirect and unclear, centered on improving future feedback system design rather than demonstrated gains.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI-enhanced collaborative feedback system (AICoFe/GePeTo) that integrates teacher, peer, and self-assessment rubric scores and comments to generate personalized feedback on oral presentations.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies feedback on oral presentation performance in engineering students (n=46), using a 15-item rubric plus teacher overall grades. The main finding is not an improvement intervention effect but that rubric-based assessments from teacher, peers, and self-ratings align moderately to substantially (e.g., peer-teacher r=0.69; self-teacher r=0.59; Kendall's W=0.46-0.51), informing future GenAI feedback design for speaking performance.
finding.measure: Oral presentation rubric scores and teacher overall grades

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines evaluative judgment, metacognition, and self-assessment calibration as part of oral presentation feedback. Self-assessment showed moderate alignment with teacher grading (r=0.59; ρ=0.67) but also a small leniency bias relative to teacher rubric scores (+0.36, p=0.037), suggesting partial but imperfect calibration.
finding.measure: Self-assessment rubric scores, agreement/correlation with teacher ratings, and paired mean differences

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI-enhanced feedback could improve scalability and reduce workload, but it does not experimentally measure time savings or teacher efficiency. Evidence is indirect: the system is positioned as a way to generate personalized feedback from aggregated human assessments, while the empirical study focuses on agreement and bias rather than efficiency outcomes.
finding.measure: Not directly measured; design implication for feedback generation efficiency

paper_profiles.title: AI-Generated Rubric Interfaces: K–12 Teachers’ Perceptions and Practices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K–12 teachers perceive and use AI-supported rubric generation for assessment and feedback in block-based programming contexts. The central question is whether AI tools can help teachers create rubrics more efficiently while still preserving teacher judgment, alignment with learning goals, and fairness. The authors focus on teachers’ experiences with MagicSchool.ai, which generated rubrics and rubric-based feedback for a sample programming activity, and on how those experiences shaped intentions to adopt such tools in future practice.

The study was conducted during summer 2025 professional development workshops with 25 middle- and high-school teachers in North Carolina, USA. Teachers first reflected on their current rubric practices, then created a manual rubric, generated an AI rubric using assignment and standards information, and used the rubric to assess a block-based programming task. They also used a chatbot to produce rubric-based feedback for the same student work. Data came from pre/post surveys, open-ended responses, exit tickets, and thematic analysis of qualitative data.

Findings suggest that teachers saw AI-generated rubrics as strong starting drafts that improved structure, clarified criteria, and saved time. Teachers appreciated the transparency and potential scalability of AI-generated feedback, but also reported important limitations: outputs could be generic, grade-misaligned, or misaligned with instructional priorities, and they often required substantial editing. Overall, teachers were willing to adopt the tools conditionally, especially when they supported easy customization and preserved teacher control over assessment decisions.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative professional-development study with pre/post surveys and thematic analysis, not an experimental design. It provides useful practitioner evidence but lacks causal identification and student outcome measures.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are mainly perceived benefits for teacher workflow and rubric quality, with no direct evidence of student learning gains. Impact on the target population is therefore plausible but modest and unclear.

interventions.use_case: AI-generated rubric creation and rubric-based feedback for K-12 block-based programming assignments, using MagicSchool.ai and a chatbot (Reina) to draft rubrics and provide rubric-based feedback on student work.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers consistently reported that AI-generated rubrics reduced the time and cognitive burden of creating rubrics from scratch. Across the workshop (n=25), participants described the outputs as strong starting drafts that saved time, improved structure, and could scale feedback, though they still required substantial teacher editing.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of time savings, workload reduction, and usability from pre/post surveys and thematic analysis

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests AI-generated rubrics may support clearer evaluation criteria and more detailed feedback, which teachers believed could help students understand expectations and revise work. However, no student outcome data were collected, and teachers also noted concerns about overly harsh scoring, misalignment, and the need for teacher oversight, so evidence for actual improvement in student learning behaviors remains indirect.
finding.measure: Teachers' perceptions of clarity, transparency, and feedback usefulness for student understanding of evaluation expectations

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers in low-resource government schools collaborate with a generative AI lesson-planning system to create, review, and customize lesson plans. The core problem addressed is whether and how LLM-based tools can support teacher planning in multilingual, under-resourced contexts where educators face heavy administrative burdens, limited instructional materials, and substantial time pressure. The authors position the work within the broader challenge of making AI useful for teacher-facing planning tasks without sacrificing curriculum alignment, pedagogical quality, or local relevance.

The intervention, Shiksha Copilot, combines LLM generation, retrieval-augmented generation over state curriculum content, human curator review, and bilingual English-Kannada support. Curators first refined AI-generated learning objectives and lesson plans, then teachers accessed curated plans and customized them for classroom use. The system also included optional AI features such as lesson-specific chat, general educational chat, and question generation. The deployment included 1,043 teachers and 23 curators in government schools across Karnataka, India, with mixed-methods evidence from logs, surveys, and interviews.

The study finds that the system reduced planning time, lowered stress, and eased record-keeping demands while supporting a shift toward more activity-based pedagogy. English lesson plans were generally reliable with relatively few edits, whereas Kannada translations required extensive linguistic and contextual revision. Teachers often adapted plans mentally or using other resources rather than recording every change in the platform, indicating that AI outputs were treated as one resource among many rather than as fixed scripts. Overall, the paper concludes that teacher-AI collaboration can be effective when humans remain central in review and adaptation, but that low-resource multilingual settings require careful curation, contextualization, and organizational support for AI tools to be educationally useful.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods field study with interviews, surveys, and system logs, but it is not a randomized or quasi-experimental comparison study. The evidence is strong descriptively and contextually rich, but causal claims are limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows clear practical benefits in workload reduction and workflow support, but it does not report a numeric intervention effect size for the main outcomes. Impact appears meaningful for a priority low-resource teacher population, though the magnitude is reported qualitatively rather than as a measured effect.

interventions.use_case: Human-in-the-loop generative lesson-planning system for K-12 teachers, where LLMs draft learning objectives, 5E lesson plans, assessment questions, and lesson-specific chat support; curators and teachers then review, edit, translate, and customize plans for English- and Kannada-medium classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that Shiksha Copilot reduced bureaucratic workload and lesson-planning time for teachers in low-resource schools. In surveys and interviews with 1,043 teachers (406 matched pre/post survey responses), teachers reported measurable reductions in time spent on lesson planning and teaching-related stress; log data also showed many teachers used the system to generate plans quickly, with 60.8% (n=622) using it in a single day to create an average of 2.62 lesson plans per session (sd=1.80, range=1-13).
finding.measure: Teacher-reported weekly time spent on lesson planning and administrative tasks; teaching-related stress scale; platform usage logs
finding.study_size: n=406 matched survey responses; n=1,043 deployed teachers; n=622 single-day users

finding.finding_summary: The system improved access to curriculum-aligned, bilingual instructional materials and eased record-keeping demands, supporting a shift in teacher workflows within government schools. The paper argues that the tool helped teachers meet administrative documentation requirements while also supporting classroom teaching, though broader pedagogical change was constrained by staffing shortages and administrative demands.
finding.measure: Teacher interviews, curator logs, teacher surveys on access to instructional resources, and usage patterns
finding.study_size: n=1,043 teachers; n=23 curators; n=43 interviews

paper_profiles.title: LessonPlanner: Assisting Novice Teachers to Prepare Pedagogy-Driven Lesson Plans with Large Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: The 37th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST ’24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of helping novice teachers prepare effective lesson plans, which is time-consuming and difficult when teachers lack experience with instructional strategies and relevant teaching materials. The authors argue that large language models can support lesson planning, but generic chat interfaces such as ChatGPT may produce fragmented, hard-to-organize, or low-confidence outputs that still require substantial prompting skill and iterative refinement.

To address this, the paper introduces LessonPlanner, an interactive web system powered by GPT-4 that structures lesson-plan creation around educational theories, especially Gagne’s Nine Events of Instruction and Bloom’s Taxonomy. The system lets users input course metadata, generate lesson goals and an outline, and then refine each section through preset prompts, sidebar assistance, editable markdown blocks, context-aware querying, and content history. The design was informed by formative interviews and co-design sessions with novice teachers and teaching assistants.

The evaluation combines a within-subjects study with 12 university students acting as novice teachers and expert interviews with 6 teachers across educational levels, including university, primary school, and senior high school. In the comparison against a baseline ChatGPT web interface, LessonPlanner significantly improved the quality of the resulting lesson plans and reduced workload during planning. Expert feedback suggested the system was useful for organizing lesson structure and generating inspiring content, while also highlighting concerns about accuracy and the need for user control and verification.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed HCI user study with a within-subjects comparison plus expert interviews, but it is not an RCT in a K-12 instructional outcome sense and the excerpt does not report full effect statistics. The evidence is useful and moderately credible, but primarily qualitative/UX-oriented rather than high-rigor causal evidence of educational impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive but modestly scoped benefits for lesson-plan quality and planning efficiency in a small sample of prospective teachers, with no reported effect sizes in the excerpt. Impact is promising for teacher planning workflows, but the magnitude and generalizability remain unclear.

interventions.use_case: An interactive lesson-planning assistant powered by GPT-4 that generates lesson goals, outlines, pedagogically structured content, examples, questions, and teaching-material suggestions for novice teachers preparing K-12/university lesson plans.
A baseline ChatGPT web interface using GPT-4 for lesson-plan drafting and refinement, used as the comparison condition against the custom LessonPlanner interface.

finding.finding_summary: In a within-subjects study with 12 university students acting as teachers (n=12), LessonPlanner significantly improved the quality of produced lesson plans and reduced workload during preparation compared with the baseline ChatGPT interface. The paper reports statistically significant gains but does not provide the exact effect size, confidence interval, or standard deviation in the excerpt provided; outcomes were based on expert-rated lesson-plan quality and NASA-TLX-style workload ratings.
finding.measure: Expert-rated lesson plan quality; NASA-TLX-style workload ratings during lesson planning

finding.finding_summary: Expert interviews with 6 teachers (n=6) indicated that LessonPlanner was useful for lesson planning because it provided a well-organized outline, inspiring generated content, and support for refining materials. Teachers reported that it eased the planning process and helped them prepare lesson plans more efficiently, but the evidence is qualitative rather than numeric.
finding.measure: Semi-structured expert interview judgments about usefulness, workload, and planning support

paper_profiles.title: AI-Based Feedback in Counselling Competence Training of Prospective Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-based feedback can support the counselling competence of prospective teachers in simulated teacher-parent conversations. The motivation is that traditional feedback in teacher training is subjective and limited in its ability to measure paraverbal and nonverbal communication features reliably, such as speaking rate, loudness, gaze, and facial expressions.

The intervention was an iterative four-day block seminar for prospective elementary school teachers in Germany. Students first learned theory and practiced communication techniques, then recorded simulated counselling conversations with actors, received instructor feedback and AI-based feedback, and were subsequently interviewed about their experience. The AI system used speech transcription, sentiment analysis, facial-behavior analysis, and gaze/smile detection to generate collective and individual visual feedback through tables, parallel coordinates, radar charts, and interactive NOVA video playback.

The study included 29 students across four seminar offerings at one university. Quantitatively, the extracted paraverbal and nonverbal features showed some predictive relationship with expert ratings of conversation quality, though model performance was modest. Qualitatively, students generally perceived the AI feedback positively, especially when video playback was combined with tabular or visual summaries, but they also wanted clearer interpretation and prioritization of the data. The authors conclude that AI-based feedback has promise for enriching teacher training, especially for objective feedback on communicative behavior, but that larger datasets and more robust verbal annotation are needed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small-sample mixed-methods / correlational study with qualitative interviews and exploratory classification analyses, not a randomized comparison. It provides useful early evidence, but the methodology and outcome measurement do not meet strong causal-evidence standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The findings are promising but modest and mostly indirect, with no measured learning gains and only a small pilot sample (n=29). The strongest concrete impact is workflow efficiency in transcription, but the educational impact on counselling skill development remains preliminary.

interventions.use_case: AI-based multimodal feedback for prospective teachers' simulated teacher-parent counselling sessions, using transcript, audio, and video features to visualize paraverbal and nonverbal communication (e.g., gaze, smile, pitch, loudness) and support self-reflection and improvement.
Simulated teacher-parent conversation role-play used as the practice environment on which AI feedback is delivered and assessed.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students positively perceived the AI-based feedback used after simulated counselling conversations, especially the combined NOVA playback and tabular feedback. In a small qualitative sample of prospective teachers (n=29), the system was seen as objective and actionable for improving communication behavior, and the feedback process reduced transcription time by two-thirds.
finding.measure: Qualitative interview perceptions of AI feedback; transcription time for interview analysis; multimodal communication feature visualizations

finding.finding_summary: The study found significant predictive tendencies between nonverbal/paraverbal features and expert ratings of conversation quality, with best model accuracy of 56.0% (SD=16.0%) under 5-fold stratified cross-validation. This supports the idea that the AI feedback can surface communication behaviors relevant to counselling competence and self-reflection, though the paper does not report learner gains on a direct skill posttest.
finding.measure: 5-fold cross-validated classification accuracy predicting expert ratings from paraverbal and nonverbal features

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that integrating WhisperX into the interview transcription workflow reduced time requirements by two-thirds, indicating a substantial efficiency gain for the qualitative analysis process. It also argues that AI-based feedback can provide objective, actionable insights and support experts in giving feedback more efficiently, although no workload scale was formally administered.
finding.measure: Transcription time / workflow efficiency for interview analysis

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging learning analytics to enhance immersive teacher simulations: Challenges and opportunities
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how learning analytics can be used to enhance immersive teacher simulations, with a particular emphasis on making teachers’ pedagogical discourse, behaviors, and visual attention visible and interpretable. The paper is framed as both a conceptual discussion and an empirical case study, asking how multimodal analytics can support reflective practice and professional learning in generative AI-enhanced virtual classroom environments.

The empirical component centers on TeacherGen@i, a web-based VR simulation used in a Digital Education course at a university in South Korea. Thirty-three preservice teachers participated during Spring 2025. They designed lesson scenarios, taught in the simulation with AI-driven student agents powered by a large language model, and then reviewed their performance through a prototype dashboard. The study collected real-time verbal transcripts, timestamped behavioral logs, and gaze data, and analyzed them using BERT-based Bloom’s taxonomy coding, lag sequential analysis, and gaze visualization.

Findings showed that preservice teachers’ discourse was dominated by lower-order cognitive moves such as remembering and understanding, while sequential analyses revealed structured interaction patterns including scaffolding chains, student-to-student reasoning, and student-initiated feedback loops. Gaze analytics and dashboard visualizations were presented as tools for supporting reflection on attention allocation, interaction equity, and feedback strategies. The chapter concludes that immersive teacher simulations combined with multimodal analytics can transform teaching practice into a traceable and improvable process, though the work is primarily a prototype and design-oriented empirical case rather than a comparative intervention study.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/case-study chapter with descriptive multimodal analyses from a single preservice-teacher cohort, not a controlled comparison of interventions. It provides useful conceptual and analytic evidence but does not meet RCT or strong QED standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The chapter suggests potentially useful impacts on teacher reflection and scalable feedback, but it does not report intervention effect sizes on lesson quality, feedback usefulness, revision quality, uptake, or planning speed. The empirical impact is therefore unclear and modest at best.

interventions.use_case: generative AI-enhanced immersive teacher simulation (TeacherGen@i) for preservice teachers to practice lesson planning, questioning, and classroom interaction with AI-driven student agents
LLM-powered student agents that generate adaptive, unscripted responses during the TeacherGen@i simulation
post-simulation multimodal dashboard providing analytics-based feedback on discourse, gaze, sequencing, and teaching behaviors
learning analytics / multimodal teacher analytics system using NLP, eye-tracking, and lag sequential analysis to visualize pedagogical reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The chapter reports that preservice teachers in TeacherGen@i predominantly used lower-order Remembering and Understanding questions across 33 sessions (1,269 turns), indicating limited higher-order pedagogical reasoning during simulation. At the same time, sequential analyses identified 215 significant behavioral patterns, suggesting the simulation elicited structured scaffolding and dialogic reasoning that could support reflective practice, but no causal effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Bloom’s taxonomy-coded discourse distribution; lag sequential analysis of interaction patterns
finding.study_size: n=33 preservice teachers; 33 simulation sessions; 1,269 interaction turns

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that automated multimodal analytics and dashboarding can reduce the burden of manual observation and make teacher feedback scalable, but this is presented as a design implication rather than a directly tested effect. No quantitative comparison of planning speed, workload, or time savings is reported in the chapter.
finding.measure: reported dashboard/analytics functionality and conceptual discussion of automation and scalability
finding.study_size: n=33 (simulation data only); no workload comparison study

paper_profiles.title: AI as a Teaching Partner: Early Lessons from Classroom Codesign with Secondary Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report examines how generative AI can function as a teaching partner in K-12 classrooms, focusing on how teacher-facing and student-facing AI tools are designed, implemented, and perceived during classroom codesign. The central question is not a head-to-head efficacy comparison with a human coach, but rather how AI-supported features can extend instruction, provide formative feedback, and help teachers manage planning, assessment, and student inquiry while preserving teacher judgment.

The pilot introduced four Colleague AI Classroom features: Teaching Aide for structured student-AI conversations, Assessment and AI Grading for rubric generation and formative feedback, AI Tutor for student self-directed support, and Student Growth Insights for teacher-facing summaries of student thinking. The study ran for seven weeks in spring 2025 with 21 in-service teachers from Washington State districts and one independent school, serving more than 600 students in grades 6-12. Teachers planned AI-integrated lessons, implemented them in live classrooms, and provided surveys, reflections, meetings, and interviews; platform logs were also analyzed.

Findings suggest that AI was most useful when tightly scaffolded by teachers through clear prompts, goals, rubrics, and monitoring. Teachers valued narrative feedback more than numeric scores, used AI outputs as first-pass formative scaffolds, and relied on teacher oversight to maintain trust and contextualize results. Student engagement and learning were strongest when activities were aligned to instructional goals and developmentally appropriate, while implementation was more mixed in subjects requiring precise reasoning or diagram-based work. Overall, the study concludes that generative AI can augment classroom instruction as a collaborative “third agent,” but its effectiveness depends heavily on teacher AI competency, framing, and human oversight.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, formative pilot with surveys, logs, interviews, and teacher reflections, not a controlled impact study. It provides useful implementation evidence, but the paper explicitly notes reliance on self-report and the absence of direct student outcome measures.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The report suggests promising but unquantified benefits for feedback speed, engagement, and some subject-specific learning, with no standardized effect sizes reported. Because the evidence is exploratory and mostly self-reported, impact is modest and unclear rather than demonstrably large.

interventions.use_case: teacher-authored, teacher-supervised student-AI conversations for class discussion, inquiry, seminar prep, and guided independent tutoring via Teaching Aide and AI Tutor
automated rubric generation, AI-assisted grading, and narrative formative feedback on student work with teacher review and final grading authority
Student Growth Insights that aggregates student-AI interaction logs to surface common questions, misconceptions, and growth patterns for teachers to guide reteaching and instructional adjustment

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI grading and Student Growth Insights reduced time spent on feedback and scanning student work. In the assessment module, median AI grading coverage reached 92.2% across 58 assessments, and teachers described the system as a helpful first-pass feedback engine that sped turnaround and reduced burden; SGI was also described as saving hours of scanning and helping with targeted reteaching.
finding.measure: Teacher reports of feedback usefulness, grading coverage in platform logs, and self-reported time saved on scanning/feedback
finding.study_size: n=19 teachers for assessment implementation; 58 assessments across 33 classrooms; 936 student submissions

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that immediate AI feedback and low-pressure AI conversations sometimes increased student confidence, engagement, and willingness to participate, especially for multilingual learners or anxious students. However, engagement was uneven across classes and some students were overwhelmed by long responses or disengaged when teacher framing was weak.
finding.measure: Teacher exit tickets and surveys on engagement, learning, and confidence; reported student participation patterns
