The context is the broader technology industry in the US and EU, with references to ongoing antitrust actions and the emerging EU AI Act. The main conclusion is that current market structures and regulation may reinforce rather than reduce concentration, and that more substantial empirical analysis of product and geographic markets will be needed to assess dominance and competition in generative AI.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/argumentative workshop paper in law and antitrust, not an empirical education study. It provides no experimental, correlational, or qualitative evidence about teacher-facing generative AI coaching or lesson-plan feedback in K-12 settings.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct impact evidence on K-12 teaching, student outcomes, or teacher practice. Its relevance is limited to broad governance and platform-power concerns, not measured educational impact.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is a legal/policy analysis of generative AI market concentration and antitrust issues, not an empirical study of educational outcomes or teacher-facing AI coaching. It does not report intervention effects, sample sizes, or quantitative outcome measures; instead, it argues that current GenAI markets are dominated by a few firms and that regulation may reinforce existing power structures.
finding.measure: Legal/policy analysis of market dominance, vertical integration, and regulatory implications

paper_profiles.title: Foundations of GenIR
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter/paper explains the foundational role of modern generative AI in information access (IA) systems. It argues that generative models differ from traditional AI because they can produce human-like responses and therefore enable two broad IA paradigms: information generation, where models directly create tailored content, and information synthesis, where models combine retrieved or external information into grounded responses. The paper is not an empirical study of educational intervention or teacher coaching; instead, it is a conceptual survey of methods and research directions in generative AI and information retrieval.

The paper reviews model architecture, scaling laws, training stages, prompt optimization, and multimodal applications for generative models, then turns to retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), generative retrieval, and domain-specific modeling. It emphasizes how LLMs can use retrieval to improve reliability, reduce hallucination, and handle external or time-sensitive knowledge, while also discussing limitations of purely generative systems. The discussion includes when to retrieve, what to retrieve, and where to retrieve in composite information tasks.

Overall, the main conclusion is that generative AI is reshaping information access by moving systems from simple result listing toward grounded synthesis and task completion. The paper also highlights unresolved problems such as hallucination, controllability, inference cost, and system design for integrating retrieval with generation. Because it is a theoretical chapter about IR/LLM methods, it does not report K-12 participants, teacher users, intervention effects, or school-based implementation outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/foundational chapter on generative AI and information access, not an empirical study with a K-12 evaluation design. It provides no original experimental or observational evidence on educational outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct impact on K-12 teaching or learning outcomes is measured. The chapter discusses potential applications and technical challenges only, so there is no estimate of educational effect size to classify as positive impact.

interventions.use_case: Foundational survey/chapter on generative AI for information access, including information generation and information synthesis (RAG, generative retrieval, domain-specific LLMs) rather than a K-12 instructional intervention.

paper_profiles.title: Safety Assessment of Chinese Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of evaluating the safety of large language models (LLMs), with a focus on Chinese-language models. The authors argue that existing safety analyses were incomplete and propose a broader benchmark to assess whether LLMs generate insulting, discriminatory, illegal, harmful, privacy-violating, or otherwise unsafe content, including when prompted through adversarial instruction attacks.

The proposed approach is not an educational intervention but a safety assessment framework. The authors manually construct a taxonomy of 14 safety scenarios: 8 typical harmful-content categories and 6 instruction-attack categories. They then collect prompts for each scenario, run them through 15 LLMs, and use an LLM-based evaluator to automatically judge whether each response is safe. They also create and release SAFETYPROMPTS, a large augmented prompt library intended for red-teaming and further safety evaluation.

The study is centered on Chinese LLMs and models trained on Chinese corpora, including ChatGPT, ChatGLM, MiniChat, OpenAI text-davinci variants, and other Chinese dialogue systems. The results show that instruction attacks generally reveal more safety failures than typical harmful-content prompts, and that ChatGPT performs best overall. The paper concludes that more robust safety benchmarks and stronger defenses against instruction attacks are needed for responsible LLM deployment.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed benchmark/assessment paper with a clear methodology, but it is not an educational intervention study and does not use experimental or quasi-experimental K-12 outcome measurement. Evidence is therefore relevant mainly as safety/systems analysis rather than instructional effectiveness evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no demonstrated K-12 learning or teacher-effectiveness impact. Its contribution is diagnostic for LLM safety and benchmark development, not evidence of educational gains or implementation outcomes.

interventions.use_case: benchmarking and red-teaming large language models for safety, including prompt attack resistance and unsafe content generation assessment

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not study K-12 instructional effectiveness; it evaluates safety performance of 15 Chinese and English LLMs on 14 adversarial safety scenarios. The main finding is that instruction attacks expose safety weaknesses across models, with ChatGPT outperforming other models in safety and some Chinese models lagging especially under goal hijacking and other attacks; no teacher- or school-context heterogeneity is examined.
finding.measure: LLM safety scores across 14 scenarios, based on proportion of safe responses judged by an LLM evaluator
finding.study_size: n=15 models; prompt sets include 700-1,070 prompts per typical scenario and 162-561 per attack scenario

paper_profiles.title: Privacy Preserving In-Context-Learning Framework for Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of preserving privacy when using large language models (LLMs) for in-context learning and synthetic text generation. The core concern is that prompts and generated outputs can leak sensitive information from private records, especially when LLMs are used with user data. The authors propose a differentially private (DP) private-prediction framework that can generate synthetic text from private datasets without fine-tuning model weights.

The method operates in two stages. First, it privately generates synthetic examples by running inference on disjoint subsets of private prompts, clipping and averaging token logits, and blending them with logits from a public prompt before sampling the next token. Second, these synthetic generations are reused as few-shot demonstrations for downstream in-context learning. The approach is evaluated on general NLP benchmark tasks, including AGNews, DBPedia, TREC, MIT-G, MIT-D, and a structured JSON generation task, using decoder-only LLMs such as Gemma 1.1 2B IT. The paper also tests privacy empirically with membership inference and PII extraction attacks.

The results show that the proposed approach can improve in-context learning accuracy compared with prior private-generation baselines while providing formal DP guarantees and reduced leakage in attack evaluations. The authors report that model utility varies with privacy budget, number of shots, and model size, illustrating the privacy-utility trade-off. However, the work is a methodological privacy paper rather than a K-12 education study, and it does not investigate teacher-facing coaching, lesson feedback, or school-based instructional use.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a methods paper on privacy-preserving LLM inference and synthetic text generation, not an education intervention study. It reports benchmark utility and privacy attacks, but does not evaluate K-12 teaching or learning outcomes, teacher experience, or classroom context.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct educational impact on K-12 instruction or student outcomes is studied. The reported gains are computational/utility improvements on NLP benchmarks and privacy leakage reduction, so the paper provides no evidence of instructional impact in schools.

interventions.use_case: privacy-preserving in-context learning and synthetic text generation for LLM prompting, including few-shot demonstration generation and token-level decoding; not a teacher-facing tutoring intervention itself

paper_profiles.title: A Review of AI Tools: Definitions, Functions, and Applications for K-12 Education
paper_profiles.venue: AI, Computer Science and Robotics Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review that surveys AI tools and applications relevant to K-12 education. Its central goal is to help teachers and other school stakeholders understand what kinds of AI tools exist, what they do, and what ethical or practical concerns accompany their use. Rather than testing a single intervention, the paper organizes the landscape of AI in education into categories based on function and use case.

The review discusses machine learning, intelligent tutoring systems, automated essay scoring, and natural language processing, then connects these technologies to classroom uses such as personalized instruction, assessment, lesson planning, and early warning systems. It also reviews a set of popular products used in K-12 contexts, including ChatGPT, Chat for Schools, Class Companion, Copilot, Diffit, DreamBox Learning, Eduaide.AI, Khanmigo, Magic Design, MagicSchool, PowerBuddy, and SchoolAI.

The paper’s audience includes K-12 students, teachers, administrators, parents, and school districts, with a strong emphasis on teacher-facing use. The authors conclude that AI can support teaching productivity, differentiation, feedback, and student engagement, but implementation must be cautious because of risks such as inaccurate or outdated information, plagiarism and cheating, data privacy concerns, surveillance, algorithmic bias, equity gaps, and overreliance on AI that could reduce students’ critical thinking or diminish the human role in instruction. They call for careful tool selection, transparency, and further research on long-term and cross-cultural impacts.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review of AI tools and concerns, not an empirical evaluation of an intervention. It does not present a study design, comparison group, or original outcome data, so it does not meet criteria for higher evidence tiers.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that these tools may improve teaching efficiency and personalized support, but it provides no original effect sizes or direct impact estimates. As a review/practitioner overview, the likely impact is plausible but remains unclear empirically.

interventions.use_case: teacher-facing and student-facing generative AI chatbots used for lesson planning, coaching, brainstorming, tutoring, and feedback in K-12 settings (e.g., ChatGPT, Chat for Schools, Khanmigo, MagicSchool, SchoolAI)

paper_profiles.title: Unpacking the Ethics of Using AI in Primary and Secondary Education: A Systematic Literature Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what ethical issues surrounding the use of artificial intelligence in primary and secondary education have been identified in the literature. Rather than evaluating a single AI tool, the authors conduct a systematic literature review to consolidate and synthesize ethical arguments spread across education, AI, and philosophy-related scholarship.

The review followed PRISMA-Ethics guidelines and searched Scopus, Web of Science, Academic Search Complete, and Google Scholar, ultimately including 48 peer-reviewed English-language sources published between 2016 and 2023. The paper takes a broad view of AI in K-12 education, including machine learning systems, large language models, expert systems, and related educational AI tools. The context is primary and secondary schooling, where students are minors and institutional decisions about curriculum and classroom practice often shape how AI is used.

The review identifies 17 ethical themes, with four potential benefits and 13 concerns. Claimed benefits include easing teachers’ workloads, supporting personalization, improving educational outcomes, and enabling some forms of coaching, monitoring, or administrative support. Major concerns include privacy and surveillance, unfairness and bias, low accuracy and unreliability, autonomy harms, technology limitations, negative effects on learning, and adverse impacts on teachers and educational practices. The authors conclude that empirical research and deeper ethical analysis are needed to judge the real-world implications of AI in K-12 education, especially given risks to minors and the possibility that AI systems may be inaccurate, biased, overly intrusive, or pedagogically unsound.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic literature review using PRISMA-Ethics and inductive thematic analysis, but it does not present primary causal evidence or an experimental design. It is best classified as qualitative evidence synthesis, so credibility is limited for estimating effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not measure impact sizes; it summarizes perceived benefits and risks in the literature. Any claimed effects are qualitative and indirect, so overall impact is unclear rather than demonstrably positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: systematic literature review of ethical issues around AI in primary and secondary education, including teacher-facing AI for lesson preparation, assessment, and teacher support

finding.finding_summary: This review synthesizes ethical and institutional concerns and opportunities around AI in K-12 education rather than testing an intervention effect. Across 48 sources, it reports recurring claims that AI may improve access, efficiency, and support for teachers, but also substantial risks related to privacy, bias, surveillance, inequity, autonomy, and teacher displacement. No primary effect size is reported because the paper is a qualitative systematic review of arguments, not an outcome study.
finding.measure: thematic synthesis of ethical issues in 48 sources (2016-2023)

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies a common claim that AI can reduce teacher workload by automating assessment, administration, lesson planning, and reporting, thereby freeing time for instruction. However, it also emphasizes new burdens from ongoing monitoring, maintenance, data stewardship, and staff training, so the net effect on efficiency is uncertain and context dependent.
finding.measure: thematic synthesis of claims about teacher workload, automation, maintenance, and administration

paper_profiles.title: Unpacking the ethics of using AI in primary and secondary education: a systematic literature review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what ethical implications of using artificial intelligence in primary and secondary education have been identified in the literature. Rather than evaluating a single tool or intervention, the authors conduct a systematic literature review of ethical discussions around AI in K-12 education, including machine learning systems, large language models, expert systems, and related educational technologies. The review followed PRISMA-Ethics guidelines and screened literature published between 2016 and 2023, ultimately including 48 peer-reviewed sources.

The paper is situated in the K-12 context, where AI is increasingly used for tasks such as personalization, assessment, tutoring, monitoring, and administrative support. The authors code the literature thematically and organize the findings into seventeen ethical themes, split between four potential benefits and thirteen concerns. Benefits include facilitating teachers’ work, reducing inequalities, improving outcomes, and offering additional forms of support. The concerns cover privacy, unfairness and low accuracy, perpetuating injustice, threats to autonomy, limitations of the technology, negative impacts on learning and teaching, misuse, low transparency, power asymmetries, commercial interests, regulation, and accountability.

The main conclusion is that the literature is dominated by concern about harms, especially privacy violations, bias, inaccuracy, surveillance, and the risk that AI will distort pedagogy or intensify existing inequalities. The authors argue that the current evidence base is not sufficient to settle the debate, and that more empirical research and deeper engagement with ethical theory and philosophy of education are needed to evaluate whether and when AI should be used in primary and secondary schooling.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic literature review, but it is not an empirical effectiveness study and does not use a comparative causal design. It synthesizes ethical arguments and reported concerns rather than measuring intervention effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful institutional and workflow implications for K-12 schools, especially around privacy, governance, and teacher workload, but it provides no quantitative evidence of effect size. Its impact claims are broad and largely theoretical, so overall impact is unclear rather than demonstrably large.

interventions.use_case: systematic review of AI use in primary and secondary education, covering generative AI/LLMs, adaptive systems, predictive analytics, and other AIPSED tools through an ethics lens

finding.finding_summary: This is a systematic review of 48 sources (2016-2023) on the ethical implications of AI in primary and secondary education, so it does not estimate a single effect size. The paper synthesizes both perceived benefits (e.g., facilitating teachers’ jobs, reducing inequalities, improving educational outcomes) and substantial risks (e.g., privacy, unfairness, low transparency, misuse, and power imbalances), concluding that empirical evidence is still too limited to assess net institutional impact.
finding.measure: qualitative thematic synthesis of ethical implications in 48 peer-reviewed sources

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that multiple sources argue AI could automate tedious teaching tasks, reduce assessment and administration burden, and help prepare lesson plans, thereby increasing teacher productivity. At the same time, it highlights risks of teacher deskilling, increased monitoring, ongoing maintenance costs, and the possibility that teachers may be unable to verify AI-generated recommendations before use.
finding.measure: qualitative thematic synthesis of reported benefits and risks to teacher workload/productivity

paper_profiles.title: Multimodal Methods for Analyzing Learning and Training Environments: A Systematic Literature Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic literature review of applied multimodal learning and training analytics (MMLA). It addresses the problem that prior reviews have focused on individual pieces of the multimodal pipeline, but have not synthesized how multimodal data are actually collected, transformed, fused, and analyzed in authentic learning and training environments, especially under real-world constraints such as noise, privacy restrictions, limited sample sizes, and incomplete data.

The review examines empirical studies from 2017–2025, split into pre- and post-ChatGPT corpora, and proposes a unified framework and taxonomy spanning environments, multimodal data, learning analytics methods, and feedback. The review includes learning and training contexts such as classrooms, online courses, simulations, and workplace-style training, with particular attention to modalities including natural language, vision, physiological signals, human-centered evidence, and logs. It also highlights how recent generative AI and LLMs are reshaping analysis and feedback workflows, especially through text-based and multimodal interpretive systems.

The main conclusion is that multimodal integration can produce richer insights into learner and trainee behavior than unimodal approaches, but practical adoption remains constrained by challenges in data synchronization, annotation, ecological validity, privacy, and deployment in real-world settings. The paper does not evaluate a single educational intervention; instead, it synthesizes the methodological landscape and argues that post-LLM systems increasingly shift from sensor-heavy, log-centered approaches toward text-rich, LLM-mediated analysis and feedback.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic literature review, but it does not present primary intervention effects or a quantitative synthesis. It is methodologically rigorous as a review, yet for the requested K-12 intervention-effect framework it provides descriptive, qualitative evidence rather than causal estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has indirect relevance to K-12 generative AI coaching and lesson-plan feedback because it discusses multimodal methods, privacy constraints, and deployment challenges in learning environments, including K-12. However, it reports no measured impacts on teacher outcomes, student learning, or intervention effectiveness, so the impact on the target topic is unclear and likely modest.

paper_profiles.title: AI-Powered Teaching: Literature Review of ChatGPT’s Impact on University Educators
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Interactive Mobile Technologies (iJIM)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how ChatGPT has been used by university educators in higher education and what benefits, concerns, and recommendations have been reported in the literature since ChatGPT’s release. The authors ask which teaching-related functions ChatGPT supports, how educators perceive it, and what risks accompany its use. Their focus is on educator-facing applications rather than student outcomes.

The study is a systematic literature review following PRISMA 2020 procedures. The authors searched Scopus and Google Scholar for English-language open-access journal articles published between November 30, 2022 and November 30, 2024, and retained 16 studies for in-depth analysis. The included studies were mostly case studies, experiments, and exploratory surveys conducted in higher education settings across several countries, with university educators as the main users.

Across the reviewed studies, ChatGPT was reported to support lesson and course planning, creation of teaching materials, development of exercises and assessments, feedback provision, professional development, and ethical guidance. The review concludes that educators generally view ChatGPT positively because it can save time, generate ideas, personalize support, and act as a virtual teaching assistant. At the same time, the paper emphasizes important concerns: inaccurate or inconsistent outputs, dependence on prompt quality, generic or repetitive advice, technical limitations, bias, plagiarism and cheating risks, privacy concerns, overreliance, and the need for human verification and clear institutional guidelines. The authors also note that the evidence base is limited and heterogeneous, so their conclusions are narrative rather than quantitative.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative systematic review of 16 studies, not a meta-analysis, RCT, or rigorously appraised QED. The authors explicitly note the lack of formal risk-of-bias assessment and the heterogeneity of included study types, so the evidence base is descriptive and qualitative rather than high-causal-credibility.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical benefits for teacher productivity and some learner engagement gains, but it provides no pooled effect sizes and no direct K-12 evidence. Reported impacts are plausible and useful, yet remain modest and largely indirect for the requested K-12 teacher-facing GenAI coaching question.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of ChatGPT use by university educators for lesson planning, assessment generation, teaching-material creation, feedback, and instructional support in higher education.

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes 16 open-access studies and concludes that ChatGPT generally saves educators time by helping generate course outlines, lesson plans, assessment items, and teaching materials. The paper does not report a pooled effect size, but repeatedly characterizes the tool as improving workflow efficiency and reducing workload across pedagogical tasks.
finding.measure: Qualitative synthesis of reported educator uses and perceived workload/time savings

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, ChatGPT is described as supporting critical thinking, analysis, interpretation, and self-regulated learning, especially when used for question generation, discussion prompts, and iterative feedback. However, the paper also notes risks of overreliance, reduced critical engagement, and weak skill assessment when educators use AI outputs uncritically.
finding.measure: Reported effects on critical thinking, analytical reasoning, and self-regulation in the reviewed literature

finding.finding_summary: The review highlights institutional implications such as the need for training, ethics guidance, academic integrity policies, and limits on private/sensitive data disclosure when using ChatGPT. It also flags concerns about bias, plagiarism, cheating, privacy, and the need for human oversight, but does not provide quantitative estimates.
finding.measure: Reported policy, ethics, and governance concerns across the reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that educators perceived ChatGPT as increasing student motivation, autonomy, and engagement when used to provide personalized guidance, instant feedback, and interactive tasks. At the same time, it warns that unmoderated use can encourage dependency and overreliance, making the overall pattern mixed in practice.
finding.measure: Reported motivation, autonomy, engagement, and dependency concerns in qualitative/experimental studies

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can function as an automated coach for teachers by generating classroom-observation scores, identifying instructional highlights and missed opportunities, and offering actionable suggestions to elicit more student reasoning. The authors frame this as a potential low-cost complement to expert instructional coaching, which is often scarce and inconsistent across schools and contexts.

The study uses the National Center for Teacher Effectiveness (NCTE) transcript dataset, consisting of 4th- and 5th-grade elementary mathematics lessons from 317 teachers across four U.S. school districts serving largely historically marginalized students. The model evaluated is gpt-3.5-turbo/ChatGPT used in zero-shot prompting, with tasks aligned to two established observation systems: CLASS and MQI. Task A asked ChatGPT to score transcript segments on selected CLASS and MQI items; Tasks B and C asked it to generate qualitative feedback on instructional strengths, missed opportunities, and suggestions for eliciting mathematical reasoning. Two experienced math teachers rated model outputs for relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty.

Results show that ChatGPT’s scores correlate poorly with human ratings, and that adding rubric descriptions or reasoning prompts does not meaningfully improve performance. For qualitative feedback, the model often produces responses that are relevant but frequently not insightful, and it sometimes hallucinates or misinterprets transcript events. For suggestions, the biggest issue is redundancy: most suggestions restate what the teacher already does in the transcript. The paper concludes that ChatGPT is promising as a scalable support tool, but current systems are not yet reliable enough to replace expert coaching and need stronger safeguards against misleading, generic, or redundant feedback.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical study with a clear evaluation design, but it is primarily a small-sample qualitative/observational benchmark rather than a causal effectiveness study. It has limited human raters, a small number of sampled transcript segments, and no experimental evidence of student or teacher outcome improvement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows limited and inconsistent performance for teacher-facing GenAI coaching, with no demonstrated positive impact on instruction or student outcomes. Its practical value is mainly as a diagnostic study highlighting failure modes rather than showing measurable impact.

interventions.use_case: Zero-shot use of ChatGPT/gpt-3.5-turbo as an automated teacher coach to score classroom transcript segments, identify instructional highlights and missed opportunities, and generate actionable suggestions for eliciting student mathematical reasoning in elementary math lessons.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies whether ChatGPT can provide scalable, cost-effective feedback to teachers, but finds substantial limitations in usefulness. Across 100 transcript segments for scoring and 216 CLASS + 288 MQI qualitative examples, the model produces some actionable feedback, yet much of it is non-novel and often only loosely aligned with the transcript; 82% of suggestions repeat what the teacher already does.
finding.measure: Spearman correlation for score prediction; teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty of generated feedback
finding.study_size: Task A n=100 segments; Task B n=504 examples; Task C n=36 suggestions

finding.finding_summary: For mathematical instruction quality scoring, ChatGPT performs poorly against human ratings on MQI items. Spearman correlations are near zero or negative across EXPL, REMED, LANGIMP, and SMQR (e.g., DA: 0.02, 0.05, 0.00, 0.17; RA: -0.11, -0.06, 0.04, 0.06), and teachers rated MQI feedback worse than CLASS feedback, with 55% not relevant and 71% not insightful for MQI examples.
finding.measure: Human-rated MQI transcript scores and qualitative ratings of feedback on math instructional quality
finding.study_size: Task A n=100 segments; Task B n=288 MQI examples; Task C n=36 suggestions
finding.effect_size: Spearman rho = -0.11 to 0.17 across MQI dimensions

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers can be supported to integrate artificial intelligence education into existing core subjects. The authors ask what teachers value and need when designing AI curriculum, and how AI concepts can be embedded into non-computing classrooms in ways that are usable and meaningful for students.

To address this, the researchers ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 educators from different schools and countries. Participants first learned basic AI concepts and explored AI tools, then worked in small groups to co-create lesson plans that integrated AI into social studies, ESL, literacy, physics, and other subjects. The workshop included presentations, discussions, card sorting, an ethics session, and guided curriculum design with researcher support. Teachers also completed pre- and post-workshop questionnaires and produced curriculum drafts.

The study found that teachers prioritized four practical concerns when designing AI lessons: evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration. Across curriculum drafts, they consistently used three main integration points: data, reflection, and ethics. Teachers were especially interested in ethics but needed scaffolding to feel confident teaching it. The paper concludes that integrating AI into core subjects is feasible and may increase access to AI education for non-CS learners, but broader adoption will require stronger curriculum supports and attention to teachers’ classroom contexts.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative co-design workshop study with 15 K-12 teachers, using interviews/discussions, surveys, and thematic coding. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically clear, but it does not test an instructional intervention with learner outcome measures or a comparison design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has practical relevance for designing teacher-facing AI curriculum and highlights implementation considerations, but it reports no measured student or teacher outcome effects and no evidence of scalable impact. Its contributions are design insights and exemplars rather than demonstrated effectiveness.

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging learning analytics to enhance immersive teacher simulations: Challenges and opportunities
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how learning analytics can be used to improve immersive teacher simulations, with a focus on making teachers’ discourse, behavior, and visual attention visible for reflection and feedback. Rather than evaluating a single instructional intervention in a K-12 classroom, the paper develops and illustrates a multimodal analytics approach for generative AI-enhanced simulation environments. It asks how analytics can support teacher learning by revealing cognitive processes, interaction patterns, and attention allocation during simulated teaching.

The intervention context is TeacherGen@i, a web-based VR simulation in which preservice teachers designed lesson scenarios and interacted with AI-driven student agents. The authors analyzed 33 simulation sessions from 33 preservice teachers enrolled in a Digital Education course at a university in South Korea. Data came from speech transcripts, timestamped interaction logs, and gaze tracking, and were processed using BERT-based Bloom’s taxonomy classification, lag sequential analysis, and heatmap-based attention visualization.

The paper concludes that preservice teachers’ talk was dominated by lower-order cognitive moves such as remembering and understanding, while sequential analyses revealed structured scaffolding and response patterns that can be surfaced through analytics dashboards. The chapter argues that multimodal dashboards can support reflective practice, professional vision, and iterative redesign of teaching, while also noting the importance of equity, accessibility, fairness, and privacy safeguards. However, it is primarily a conceptual and case-based demonstration of analytics design rather than a controlled effectiveness study, and it does not test whether outcomes differ by teacher experience, subject area, grade level, or school context in K-12 settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/case-study chapter with descriptive multimodal analyses and no experimental comparison or causal identification. It is peer-reviewed academic work with a clear method, but the evidence base is exploratory rather than rigorously causal.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The chapter provides promising design implications for teacher-facing generative AI feedback, but it does not report measurable learning gains, subgroup effects, or implementation impacts. The practical influence is therefore suggestive and modest rather than demonstrated at scale.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI-enhanced immersive teacher simulation (TeacherGen@i) for preservice teacher practice in a web-based VR classroom, with AI-driven student agents and post-session analytics/dashboard feedback.
Large-language-model-powered student agents that generate adaptive, unscripted classroom responses and personas during teacher simulation interactions.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter reports that the multimodal analytics framework made preservice teachers' pedagogical reasoning, interaction sequencing, and visual attention observable within TeacherGen@i, supporting reflective practice and professional vision. Across 33 sessions (n=33 preservice teachers; 1,269 turns), the system surfaced lower-order questioning patterns and sequential scaffolding/feedback loops that can inform simulation-based improvement, but the paper does not report causal outcome effects or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Coded discourse patterns (Bloom taxonomy), lag sequential analysis of interaction flows, gaze heatmaps/dispersion, dashboard-based reflective interpretation

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that automating transcription, discourse coding, sequential analysis, and gaze visualization can reduce researcher/instructor workload and make teacher feedback more scalable and timely. However, this is primarily a design/positioning claim supported by one case study (n=33) rather than a quantified efficiency evaluation, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Prototype dashboard usability for post-session analysis; automated transcription/coding/visualization pipeline

finding.finding_summary: The chapter suggests that immersive simulation plus analytics may support self-reflection, analytics literacy, and confidence-building for teacher candidates, but it does not directly measure motivation or self-efficacy in this study. Any positive effect is therefore inferential and based on the proposed use of the dashboard for formative reflection rather than on reported survey outcomes.
finding.measure: Reflective practice/self-regulated improvement via dashboard use

paper_profiles.title: AI-Generated Rubric Interfaces: K–12 Teachers’ Perceptions and Practices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K–12 teachers perceive and use AI-supported rubric generation and AI-assisted feedback in the context of block-based programming assessment. The central question is whether AI-generated rubrics can help teachers create clearer, more usable assessment tools while preserving teacher judgment and instructional alignment. The study is motivated by the time-intensive nature of rubric creation and the difficulty teachers face in defining precise performance levels, especially for creative or novel programming tasks.

The intervention was a summer professional development workshop in which 25 middle- and high-school teachers used MagicSchool.ai to generate rubrics, compared those outputs against manually created rubrics, and then used the generated rubrics to assess a sample block-based programming assignment. Teachers also used a chatbot feature to produce rubric-based feedback. Data came from pre- and post-workshop surveys, open-ended responses, exit tickets, and thematic analysis of qualitative discussions. The sample included teachers with varied computer science and block-based programming experience, mostly teaching grades 6–8, with additional high-school participants.

Overall, teachers viewed AI-generated rubrics as useful starting points that improved structure, clarity, and speed, and many said the tools could help communicate expectations to students. However, they also repeatedly emphasized that the rubrics often contained generic, grade-misaligned, or misaligned criteria and required substantial editing. Teachers expressed concerns about fairness, equity, accuracy, privacy, transparency, and the risk of overreliance, particularly for novices who might copy outputs too readily. The paper concludes that teacher-facing AI rubric tools are most promising when they support customization, scaffolding, and strong teacher control rather than fixed automation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/survey-based professional development study with thematic analysis and descriptive Likert results, not a controlled impact evaluation. It provides useful contextual evidence about teacher perceptions and implementation conditions, but internal validity for causal effectiveness is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests a promising but unquantified positive effect on teacher workflow and adoption intentions, with no direct student outcome evidence. Reported effects are primarily perceived benefits and implementation readiness, so the general impact is modest and unclear.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-facing AI-generated rubric creation and rubric-based feedback for K-12 block-based programming assignments, using MagicSchool.ai and a chatbot to draft criteria, performance levels, and feedback comments.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI-generated rubrics saved time and reduced the burden of drafting rubrics from scratch (n=25). Survey ratings were moderately positive for ease of modification (M=3.5/5, SD=1.26) and flexible starting-point use (M=3.56/5, SD=1.31), though direct support for adding/removing/revising criteria was the weakest usability item (M=2.75/5, SD=1.23).
finding.measure: Post-workshop Likert survey on usability/flexibility; thematic analysis of teacher reflections

finding.finding_summary: Teachers viewed the tool as a helpful starting point for assessment design and a way to improve transparency and consistency, but adoption was conditional on teacher oversight, LMS integration, and district policy fit (n=25). Concerns included privacy, fairness, equity, and school restrictions on AI use, indicating institutional barriers alongside perceived value.
finding.measure: Post-workshop survey items on transparency, bias/fairness, confidence, and equitable use; open-ended reflections about adoption constraints

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI-generated rubrics clarified expectations and could help students understand how their work would be evaluated (n=25). The corresponding survey item was rated highly (M=4.12/5, SD=0.95), suggesting support for metacognitive clarity and goal orientation, though the study did not directly measure student learning gains.
finding.measure: Perceived student understanding of evaluation and rubric clarity/alignment survey items

paper_profiles.title: Understanding Teacher Revisions of Large Language Model-Generated Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers revise formative feedback generated by large language models (LLMs) before it is delivered to students. Rather than asking whether the AI feedback is good in isolation, the study focuses on the human-in-the-loop process that determines what learners actually receive. The authors ask which textual properties are associated with revision, whether revision can be predicted from the AI text alone, and how revisions change the pedagogical type of feedback.

The intervention/approach studied is a feedback-generation workflow in the Tutoria platform, where an LLM drafts feedback on short open-ended responses and teachers can accept, edit, or rewrite it. The dataset includes 1,349 AI-generated drafts and corresponding teacher-delivered explanations from 117 teachers. The sample spans multiple educational contexts, including Brazilian high school chemistry classes, a controlled experiment with higher-education instructors in introductory computer science, and extracurricular computer-science contexts. The analysis combines descriptive statistics, predictive modeling, and theory-informed qualitative coding of feedback types.

The main findings are that teachers accepted AI feedback unchanged in about 78% of cases, and when they did revise it, they usually shortened it while keeping the meaning largely intact. Revision behavior varied greatly across teachers: about half never edited any feedback, while a small minority edited most messages. Text-only models could predict revision with above-chance performance, but not strongly, indicating that context beyond the feedback text matters. When teachers revised feedback, they often simplified overly explanatory, high-information responses into more concise corrective forms. The paper concludes that default AI behavior is highly consequential because most feedback is passed through unchanged, and that future systems should better align with teacher preferences while reducing unnecessary editing effort.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quantitative observational study using platform log data and descriptive/predictive analyses, not an experiment or randomized trial. It provides useful evidence about real-world teacher mediation, but causal claims about effectiveness are limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful workflow implications because most AI feedback was accepted unchanged and modeling revision was above chance (AUC up to 0.75), but it does not evaluate student learning or provide an outcome effect size on educational performance. The impact on K-12 practice is therefore plausible but indirect and modest/unclear.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated formative feedback for short open-ended student responses in a teacher-in-the-loop platform, where teachers can accept, edit, or rewrite the feedback before delivery.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers accepted LLM-generated feedback without modification in 77.8% of 1,349 cases (1050/1349), indicating substantial potential workload savings through teacher-in-the-loop feedback generation. However, when revisions occurred, edited feedback was only modestly longer than unedited feedback and was usually shortened rather than extensively rewritten, suggesting the main efficiency benefit comes from reducing the need for heavy editing rather than eliminating it entirely.
finding.measure: Teacher revision/acceptance rate; feedback length (word count); within-teacher editing differences

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether teacher-in-the-loop generative AI can efficiently support personalized K-12 mathematics tasks, and how much teachers’ prompting and design choices affect the quality of the resulting tasks. The authors focus on context personalization: adapting existing mathematics problems so they connect to students’ interests, with particular attention to the tradeoff between teacher control, personalization grain size, realism/depth, and time burden.

The intervention involved 7 middle school mathematics teachers using ChatGPT (GPT-4o) to modify 143 Illustrative Mathematics problems across two units. Teachers first completed a 2-hour training on personalization, bias, readability, and cultural relevance, then worked in short Zoom sessions while their ChatGPT interactions and speech were recorded. The modified problems were assigned in ASSISTments to 521 seventh-grade students in 6 U.S. schools. Student surveys captured interest, closeness to interests, and open-ended feedback, while teacher logs were analyzed quantitatively and qualitatively.

The study found that teachers most often used ChatGPT to add or swap popular-culture references and to improve realism, numerical plausibility, and age appropriateness. Students preferred fine-grained, specific references, but teachers generally operated at a broader grain size because of feasibility constraints. Personalized problem creation took about 4 minutes per problem on average, and this did not clearly become faster over time; in fact, after reflecting on student feedback, teachers used more prompts and spent more time in the second unit, though student ratings improved. The authors conclude that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can support professional learning and help monitor realism and inappropriate content, but it is time-consuming, difficult to scale to highly individualized versions, and still vulnerable to shallow or mismatched personalization.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory mixed-methods observational study with teacher prompting logs, student surveys, and qualitative coding, but no control group or random assignment. It provides useful evidence about implementation and heterogeneity, but causal claims about effectiveness are limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The observed benefits were modest and context-specific: student ratings improved slightly with an estimated 0.24-point gain on a 5-point scale, while teacher efficiency was poor and often worsened with iteration. Overall impact is unclear and not yet scalable as a general K-12 intervention.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-in-the-loop use of ChatGPT (GPT-4o) to personalize middle school mathematics word problems to students' interests, including iterative prompting to improve realism, readability, and contextual relevance.

finding.finding_summary: Student-rated closeness to interests and interestingness improved when teachers used 3-5 prompts to create a problem, suggesting better-aligned personalized math tasks. In mixed-effects models, using 3-5 prompts was associated with about a 0.24-point increase on a 5-point scale for combined student ratings (B=0.240, SE=0.085, t=2.84, p=0.0073) across 52 problems with student ratings available.
finding.measure: Student 1-5 ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to interests
finding.study_size: n=521 students; 52 problems rated for this analysis

finding.finding_summary: Students more often reported that personalized problems were interesting when they contained specific or general popular-culture references they liked, though many responses were neutral or negative. Across 454 responses to interestingness questions, 163 implied the problem was interesting and 243 implied it was not; average ratings were low overall (interestingness M=2.46, SD=1.24; closeness M=2.53, SD=1.28).
finding.measure: Student survey ratings and open-ended feedback on interest/closeness
finding.study_size: n=521 students; 454 interestingness responses; 449 closeness responses
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.24 for interestingness; SD=1.28 for closeness

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-facing GenAI personalization was not especially time efficient: creating 143 problems took 558 prompts and about 4 minutes per problem on average (M=246 seconds, SD=165.7), with no clear evidence of substantial efficiency gains over time. In fact, from Unit 4 to Unit 6 teachers became slower and used more prompts (prompts: B=1.26, SE=0.41, p=0.0025; time: B=70.4 seconds, SE=29.6, p=0.0189).
finding.measure: Time per personalized problem and number of prompts used with ChatGPT

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how an AI-assisted lesson-planning system, Shiksha Copilot, was used by teachers in low-resource public schools to create, curate, and customize curriculum-aligned lesson plans. The authors focus on a practical question relevant to teacher-facing generative AI: how well can LLM-based tools support lesson planning when they are embedded in a human-in-the-loop workflow with expert curation, bilingual support, and curriculum grounding?

Shiksha Copilot was deployed in government schools across Karnataka, India, and targeted teachers in grades 5–10 teaching Science, Mathematics, Social Science, and English in English- and Kannada-medium classrooms. The system first generated lesson-plan drafts using retrieval-augmented generation, after which subject-matter curators reviewed and refined the outputs before teachers adapted them for their own classrooms. The study combines logs, surveys, interviews, and analysis of curated and teacher-modified lesson plans from 1,043 teachers and 23 curators.

The main finding is that the tool reduced lesson-planning time, bureaucratic burden, and stress, while supporting a shift toward more activity-based pedagogy. English lesson plans were generally rated as highly reliable and required relatively little editing, but Kannada outputs needed substantial linguistic revision, showing that effectiveness differed strongly by language medium and subject-specific terminology rather than by teacher experience alone. Teachers used the system flexibly, often supplementing AI-generated plans with their own expertise and peer resources, and the authors argue that human oversight and community-based curation are essential for quality, cultural relevance, and safe deployment in multilingual, low-resource settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods field study with surveys, interviews, and log analysis, but it is not randomized and does not report causal identification or complete inferential statistics for the main workload outcomes. It provides strong descriptive and qualitative evidence, but only moderate causal credibility.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful workload and stress benefits for a large population of priority-context K-12 teachers in low-resource schools, alongside substantial improvements in access to lesson-planning support. The impact appears modest-to-moderate rather than large, since the main quantitative effect sizes for teacher workload outcomes are not reported in the excerpt.

interventions.use_case: Human-in-the-loop generative AI lesson planning and teacher support system for K-12 teachers, using LLMs with retrieval-augmented generation to draft curriculum-aligned lesson plans, generate questions, and answer lesson-specific or general pedagogy queries.

finding.finding_summary: Shiksha Copilot reduced teachers’ bureaucratic workload and lesson planning burden in low-resource K-12 schools. Across survey and log evidence from 1,043 teachers, the paper reports measurable reductions in lesson planning time and teacher stress, with particularly strong take-up for record-keeping and term-long planning tasks. Quantitative effect sizes for the workload reduction are not reported in the excerpt, but the direction is consistently positive across interviews, logs, and surveys.
finding.measure: Weekly time spent on lesson planning and administrative tasks; teacher stress scale; system usage logs
finding.study_size: n=1043 teachers (survey matched n=406; interviews n=22 teachers, plus 23 curators)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported lower teaching-related stress after using the system, indicating a beneficial effect on teacher well-being. The paper used the Teacher Stress Scale (TSS) pre/post with matched survey responses from n=406 teachers, and reports measurable reductions in teaching-related stress, though the excerpt does not provide a numerical effect size or confidence interval.
finding.measure: Teacher Stress Scale (teaching demands and school-based support subscales)

finding.finding_summary: The tool supported lesson planning across four subjects and two languages, but content quality varied substantially by context. English lesson plans were generally high quality and required only minor edits (96.13% of 7,744 English content blocks rated suitable; 4.1% edited overall), while Kannada translations required extensive substantive revision (94.4% of 26 Kannada lesson plans’ content blocks edited), especially in mathematics and for literal translation issues.
finding.measure: Curator ratings and edit rates for lesson-plan content blocks; teacher ratings of LP usability by medium
finding.study_size: English curation n=7,744 content blocks; Kannada curation n=26 lesson plans; teacher ratings reported for LPs by medium
finding.effect_size: Cramer’s V=0.1768 for curator differences; subject-level edit rate range 0.82%–6.16% in English and 88.9%–99.0% edits in Kannada

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Object Relation in Mean Teacher for Cross-Domain Detection
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses unsupervised domain adaptation for object detection under domain shift, where detectors trained on labeled synthetic or source-domain images perform poorly on real target-domain images. The authors focus on whether Mean Teacher, a semi-supervised consistency-based method, can be extended from recognition to cross-domain detection in a way that better handles object localization and relationships among detected regions.

They propose Mean Teacher with Object Relations (MTOR), a Faster R-CNN-based teacher-student framework. For unlabeled target images, the teacher and student process different augmentations of the same image, and training combines three consistency losses: region-level consistency between teacher and student predictions, inter-graph consistency to align relational graphs built from region features, and intra-graph consistency to encourage regions of the same pseudo-class to be more similar within the student graph. The method is evaluated on cross-domain object detection benchmarks involving Cityscapes to Foggy Cityscapes, SIM10k to Cityscapes, and synthetic-to-real transfers on Syn2Real.

The paper reports that MTOR outperforms source-only training and a prior domain adaptation baseline, with improvements attributable to region-level and graph-structured consistencies. The strongest results are obtained when all three losses are used together, suggesting that modeling object relations improves robustness under domain shift. The study is methodological and does not involve K-12 teachers or educational settings; it is a computer vision domain adaptation paper rather than a study of classroom AI coaching or lesson feedback.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed machine vision paper, but it does not study K-12 education, teacher coaching, lesson-plan feedback, or any instructional context. It is therefore methodologically irrelevant to the requested education taxonomy despite having a clear experimental design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational impact is demonstrated, and there are no K-12 outcomes, users, or school contexts in the paper. The work concerns object detection performance only, so educational impact is not applicable.

finding.finding_summary: This paper evaluates mean-teacher-based unsupervised domain adaptation for object detection, not an educational intervention. Across multiple transfer settings, the proposed MTOR improves detection performance over Source-only and DA baselines, including mAP gains of 3.1 points on Cityscapes→Foggy Cityscapes (35.1% vs. 32.0%) and 2.9 points on SIM10k→Cityscapes (46.6 AP on car vs. 41.9).
finding.measure: Mean Average Precision (mAP) / Average Precision (AP) for cross-domain object detection

paper_profiles.title: AI-Based Feedback in Counselling Competence Training of Prospective Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-based feedback can support the development of counselling competence in prospective teachers during training for teacher-parent conversations. The authors focus on whether AI can provide objective feedback on communicative behavior that is hard for human raters to measure reliably, especially in verbal, paraverbal, and nonverbal dimensions.

The intervention is an iterative four-day block seminar in which prospective primary school teachers first learn theory and practice of counselling communication, then conduct recorded simulated teacher-parent conversations. Their performances are evaluated through instructor feedback, AI-based feedback, and post-session interviews. The AI system uses transcription, speech features, and video-derived nonverbal features in NOVA/DISCOVER to generate collective and individual feedback visualizations such as tables, parallel coordinates, radar charts, and interactive video playback.

The study was conducted with 29 prospective teachers in elementary school pedagogy at the University of Augsburg in Germany, across four seminar offerings. The paper reports significant correlations between nonverbal/paraverbal features and expert-rated conversation quality, and students generally perceived the AI feedback positively, especially when video playback was combined with numerical summaries. The authors conclude that AI-based feedback has promise for teacher training, while noting that verbal annotations still need refinement and that larger datasets are needed for stronger generalization.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, early-stage design and user-study paper with a small sample (n=29) and correlational modeling rather than a controlled impact evaluation. It provides useful evidence on feasibility and perceptions, but not strong causal evidence of learning gains.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported impact is promising but modest and largely indirect: students liked the feedback and transcription efficiency improved, yet no validated learning gains or robust effect sizes were demonstrated. The study suggests potential for teacher training support, but the impact on practice remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: AI-based multimodal feedback for prospective teachers’ simulated teacher-parent counseling, using transcription plus audio/video features to generate collective and individual coaching on verbal, paraverbal, and nonverbal communication.
Simulation-based teacher training seminar with recorded role-play conversations, expert ratings, and interactive playback/visualizations in NOVA used as instructional support.

finding.finding_summary: Prospective teachers reported that the AI-based feedback was helpful for reflection and improvement of counseling competence, especially when combining NOVA playback with tabular summaries and radar charts. The study is qualitative and does not report a causal effect size; however, students described the feedback as actionable for improving communication behaviors in simulated teacher-parent conversations (n=29).
finding.measure: Qualitative interview feedback on perceived usefulness and actionability of AI-based counseling feedback; expert-rated counseling helpfulness used as reference in visualizations

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that integrating WhisperX into transcription reduced interview transcription time by two-thirds, indicating a substantial workflow efficiency gain. This is an operational outcome rather than a learner outcome, and no statistical effect size or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: Transcription time required for interview processing

paper_profiles.title: From Teacher to Colleague: How Coding Experience Shapes Developer Perceptions of AI Tools
paper_profiles.venue: GenAICHI: CHI 2025 Workshop on Generative AI and HCI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether developers’ coding experience is related to their awareness of AI tools, their prior experience with such tools, and the roles they assign to AI in their workflow. The authors ask whether more experienced developers are more likely to adopt AI tools and whether experience changes how developers conceptually frame AI systems.

The study analyzes survey data from JetBrains’ State of Developer Ecosystem Report 2024. The relevant analytic sample included 8,073 developers for awareness/experience measures and 3,380 developers who answered the question about AI roles. Participants reported their coding experience in years, how many AI tools they had tried, whether they had heard of AI tools, and which roles best described AI in their workflow. The survey was conducted online and included developers from many countries and regions; the paper focuses on coding professionals rather than educators or students.

Results show that coding experience does not predict AI adoption or AI experience, and its association with AI awareness is statistically significant but negligible. However, coding experience does shape mental models of AI: less experienced developers are more likely to view AI as a teacher, while more experienced developers are more likely to see it as a junior colleague, a content generator, or as having no role at all. The authors conclude that AI tool design should align with users’ expertise and expectations, because adoption is not driven simply by experience level but by how users interpret the tool’s function in their workflow.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional survey analysis with correlational and logistic regression methods, not an experimental or quasi-experimental causal design. It is useful for describing heterogeneity in perceptions by experience level, but it provides limited causal evidence about intervention effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study does not evaluate K-12 teacher-facing AI coaching or lesson-plan feedback, and it reports no direct educational performance impact. Its implications are indirect and mainly about user perceptions and potential alignment of AI tools with expertise levels.

interventions.use_case: Survey study of developers’ perceptions of AI-assisted coding tools, including how they mentally assign roles such as teacher, junior colleague, content generator, advisor, or assistant to AI tools in their workflow.

finding.finding_summary: Coding experience was not associated with AI tool adoption/experience (Spearman r=-0.005, p=0.652 for coding experience vs AI experience; r=0.031, p=0.005 for awareness, negligible). However, it did significantly shape how developers conceptualized AI, with less experienced developers more likely to view AI as a teacher (OR=0.883, 95% CI 0.814-0.958) and more experienced developers more likely to view AI as a junior colleague (OR=1.170, 95% CI 1.053-1.299) or content generator (OR=1.087, 95% CI 1.025-1.152).
finding.measure: Spearman correlations between coding experience, AI awareness, and AI experience; logistic regression on selected AI role labels
finding.study_size: n=8073 for experience/awareness analyses; n=3380 for role analyses
finding.confidence_interval: teacher OR 0.814-0.958; junior colleague OR 1.053-1.299; content generator OR 1.025-1.152

finding.finding_summary: The paper found no meaningful relationship between coding experience and AI tool adoption or prior experience with AI tools for coding. The correlation between coding experience and AI experience was effectively zero (r=-0.005, p=0.652), and the association with AI awareness was statistically significant but negligible (r=0.031, p=0.005), suggesting experience alone did not explain uptake.
finding.measure: Spearman correlations between coding experience, AI awareness, and AI experience

paper_profiles.title: Exploring K-12 Physical Education Teachers’ Perspectives on Opportunities and Challenges of AI Integration Through Ideation Workshops
paper_profiles.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 physical education (PE) teachers think about artificial intelligence (AI) in their teaching context, with a focus on opportunities, constraints, and implementation risks. The authors address a gap in prior AI-in-education work, which has largely centered on STEM and classroom-based instruction rather than PE, where teachers face distinctive challenges such as large open spaces, safety monitoring, heterogeneous student abilities, and limited time for individualized feedback.

The study used participatory ideation workshops with 17 in-service secondary school PE teachers in South Korea. After a short AI literacy introduction, participants discussed classroom challenges, sketched possible AI applications, created storyboards, and role-played future classroom scenarios. The paper is therefore exploratory and design-oriented rather than evaluative: it does not test an AI system, but gathers teachers’ perceptions about what AI could do in PE classes.

Teachers envisioned AI in four roles: operational assistant, personal trainer, group coach, and evaluator. These roles were intended to support class management, personalized feedback, team balancing, and multidimensional assessment. At the same time, participants raised concerns about institutional and infrastructural barriers, varying teacher tech proficiency, misalignment with PE’s educational goals, overreliance on AI, and student data security and autonomy. The paper concludes that AI for PE should remain a supporting tool and should be designed with teacher involvement, clear pedagogical alignment, and strong privacy and usability safeguards.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative ideation/focus-group study with 17 secondary PE teachers. It provides rich contextual evidence about perceived opportunities, concerns, and implementation conditions, but it does not test an intervention or estimate causal effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful uses of AI for a priority population (K-12 PE teachers), but the evidence is exploratory and does not demonstrate measured impact on learning or classroom outcomes. The practical implications are important, yet the impact remains uncertain because no effectiveness data are reported.

interventions.use_case: Participatory design / ideation workshop to elicit K-12 secondary physical education teachers’ envisioned AI supports for class operations, personalized feedback, team formation, and assessment

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI could reduce workload and save time by supporting class operations, attendance/safety monitoring, environment control, and data management. This was not a measured effect on outcomes; rather, it was a qualitative finding from 17 in-service secondary PE teachers in ideation workshops, who consistently described AI as a way to streamline administrative and instructional tasks.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of workload reduction, time savings, and operational support from ideated AI systems

finding.finding_summary: Participants envisioned AI providing motivational and emotional support to students, including a 'Warm Advice AI' that would offer encouraging feedback to reduce anxiety and pressure during PE activities. This finding is qualitative and preference-based rather than an outcome estimate; it indicates teachers saw AI as potentially supporting student confidence and engagement in PE.
finding.measure: Teacher-identified potential for AI to support student motivation, encouragement, and psychological comfort

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed AI could improve collaboration by helping form balanced teams and by supporting group coaching in team sports, but they also worried that overreliance on AI could reduce student autonomy and self-directedness. The study is qualitative with 17 teachers, so this reflects perceived potential and risks rather than measured effects.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of collaboration, balanced team formation, autonomy, and self-directed learning

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified major institutional and infrastructural barriers, including weak school support, limited space, inadequate Wi-Fi, device durability issues, and uneven teacher readiness for AI adoption. They also emphasized privacy, consent, and data security concerns; these are qualitative concerns from 17 secondary PE teachers rather than measured institutional effects.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported institutional support, infrastructure readiness, privacy/security, and implementation feasibility concerns

paper_profiles.title: AI, Expert or Peer? Examining the Impact of Perceived Feedback Source on Pre-Service Teachers Feedback Perception and Uptake
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether pre-service teachers respond differently to feedback depending on whether they believe it comes from an LLM, an expert, or a peer, and whether those perceptions affect both feedback judgments and actual uptake. The paper is motivated by concern that even high-quality AI-generated feedback may be underused if recipients distrust or misattribute its source.

In a randomized experiment, 273 bachelor’s-level teacher-education students at a German university received one of 30 written feedback messages on a mathematics learning goal. The feedback had been generated by an LLM, an expert, or a peer, and participants then had to identify the source, rate the feedback on cognitive, motivational, and affective dimensions, and revise the learning goal accordingly. The study also coded objective feedback quality and measured source-recognition accuracy.

The main finding is that perceived source strongly shaped perceptions but not behavioral uptake. LLM feedback was rated more positively when participants falsely believed it came from an expert, showing an expertise heuristic and a bias favoring human sources in cognitive judgments. However, actual feedback implementation was driven mainly by objective feedback quality, not by perceived source, recognition accuracy, or subjective perceptions. The authors conclude that teacher education should address source-related bias and AI literacy, while also noting that future hybrid systems may combine scalability with human credibility.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized experiment with a clearly described design, multiple comparison conditions, and quantitative analysis, but it is not a classroom RCT and has some construct/setting limitations (pre-service teachers, hypothetical task, limited uptake variance). The study provides credible evidence on perception and uptake under controlled conditions, though external validity to K-12 classroom implementation is constrained.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows small-to-moderate descriptive differences in perceptions and a small uptake model (R²=.078), with the strongest practical signal being that quality matters more than source labels. Because the outcomes are on pre-service teachers’ feedback on a single mathematics lesson-goal task rather than direct K-12 student achievement or teacher practice, the broader educational impact is modest and indirect.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated written feedback on a pre-service teacher's mathematics learning goal/lesson-plan objective, compared with expert and peer feedback; feedback was analyzed for source perception, recognition, quality, and uptake.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized experiment with n=273 pre-service teachers, feedback was applied to a mathematics learning-goal revision task. Behavioral uptake did not depend on perceived source or recognition accuracy; only objective feedback quality predicted implementation (b=1.27, SE=0.50, z=2.52, p=.012, R²=.078; n=161 in the uptake model), while LLM feedback had the highest descriptive relative uptake (52%) versus expert (45%) and peer (42%).
finding.measure: Revision of a mathematics learning goal; correction rate / implemented suggestions from feedback
finding.effect_size: R²=.078; ANOVA effects reported descriptively (LLM relative uptake 52%)

finding.finding_summary: The study primarily examined how feedback source labels affected feedback perception, source recognition, and uptake. Perceived source changed cognitive judgments (fairness, usefulness, acceptance), but not actual implementation behavior; recognition accuracy also did not moderate uptake after controlling for feedback quality.
finding.measure: Feedback perception questionnaire (fairness, usefulness, acceptance, willingness to improve, positive/negative affect) and feedback uptake/correction rate
finding.effect_size: Fairness interaction b=1.21; usefulness interaction b=1.76; uptake model R²=.078

finding.finding_summary: Source cues influenced perceived fairness and usefulness of feedback, but emotional responses were largely unaffected. No significant effects were found for positive affect or negative affect (all ps ≥ .176), and willingness to improve showed only a non-significant trend for LLM feedback when misattributed to a human source (p=.084).
finding.measure: Positive affect, negative affect, and willingness to improve subscales of the Feedback Perception Questionnaire
finding.study_size: n=218 to n=225 depending on model

paper_profiles.title: Implementing feedback in creative systems: a workshop approach
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how feedback can be incorporated into computational creativity systems, with a broader interest in how AI systems can learn from interaction and critique. The authors argue that feedback is fundamental to creativity and learning, but that computational creativity systems have largely not treated feedback as a central design feature.

To tackle this, the paper proposes the Writers Workshop as a computational model for structured critique. In the proposed workflow, an author/system presents work, critics listen and provide feedback, the author asks clarifying questions, critics respond, and the author reflects and potentially updates its internal model or codebase. The paper develops this as a conceptual framework and illustrates it with a dialogue example and a case study in the FloWr flowchart-based creative system, focusing on computer poetry.

The intended context is not K-12 education but AI and computational creativity research. The paper suggests that a workshop-style protocol could support serendipity, constructive critique, and mutual learning among autonomous systems, and it briefly notes that similar ideas might someday be relevant for educational feedback. Its main conclusion is that a structured workshop model is a promising roadmap for feedback-driven AI systems, though the paper is primarily theoretical and implementation-oriented rather than an empirical evaluation of effectiveness.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper proposing a writers-workshop-inspired feedback model for computational creativity systems. It does not evaluate a K-12 educational intervention, does not report an empirical study with student or teacher outcomes, and provides only illustrative examples and a preliminary implementation discussion.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no measured impact on learners, teachers, or schools. The paper’s relevance to K-12 teacher-facing generative AI coaching is indirect and speculative, so no educational effect size or practical impact can be inferred.
