Participants included students, educators, developers, and AI freelancers; the paper discusses education in general rather than a single school level, although it repeatedly references teachers and learners in K-12 and higher education contexts.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT is seen as powerful and potentially transformative, but it should not be adopted uncritically. The authors argue that its use can support teaching, learning, and content generation, yet it also raises substantial concerns about cheating, misinformation, inconsistent answers, privacy risks, emotional limitations, and manipulative behavior. They recommend that education should focus on responsible use, new assessment and teaching approaches, stronger guidelines and policies, and further work on human-chatbot collaboration rather than simple bans.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative instrumental case study with triangulated evidence from tweets, interviews, and educator scenarios, but it does not use an experimental or quasi-experimental design. It provides rich contextual insight, yet credibility for causal claims is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests important institutional and classroom implications, but it does not report measurable learning gains or sizable effects. Its main contribution is identifying risks, opportunities, and implementation issues rather than demonstrating direct impact on K-12 outcomes.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a conversational AI chatbot for education, including learning assistance, instructional design support, answering questions, generating quizzes and learning content, and providing feedback-like interactions for teachers and students.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT can help students generate essays and written responses, but it can also facilitate cheating and produce inaccurate or generic written content. In scenario-based testing, copying an AI-generated paragraph into a detector was flagged as fake, but adding one word reduced the detected fake level to 24%, suggesting weak robustness in written-work detection rather than learning gains.
finding.measure: Qualitative inspection of AI-generated essays, short-answer responses, and output detector classification of copied text
finding.study_size: n=3 educators for scenario testing; broader qualitative inputs from 19 interviewees and 2330 tweets

finding.finding_summary: Participants saw ChatGPT as potentially useful for stimulating understanding and supporting critical thinking, but many also warned that overreliance could reduce students' critical thinking and innovation. The study is qualitative, so no effect size is reported; the evidence is based on interview themes, tweet sentiment, and scenario analysis showing both promise and concern.
finding.measure: Interview themes on educational transformation, ethics, and usefulness; scenario analysis of user interactions

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly finds that ChatGPT can reduce teacher workload by helping prepare teaching materials, outlines, and quizzes, and by providing immediate answers that may support instructional design. At the same time, the authors note that inconsistent output, errors, and the need to verify results can offset efficiency gains.
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of time-saving for lesson planning, resource creation, and quiz generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses heavily on institutional concerns such as cheating, privacy, misinformation, fairness of access, and the need for policy and new teaching philosophies. It argues that schools should not simply ban ChatGPT, but instead develop guidelines, responsible-use policies, and updated assessment practices; no quantitative policy effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Social media discourse, interviews, and scenario-based policy/ethics analysis

paper_profiles.title: Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence: Early experiments with GPT-4
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports a series of exploratory demonstrations of an early, text-only version of GPT-4 intended to probe whether it exhibits broad, general capabilities associated with artificial intelligence. Rather than evaluating the model with standard benchmark-style experiments alone, the authors use human-generated prompts and novel tasks to test performance across language, coding, mathematics, visual reasoning, tool use, theory of mind, and other domains. The central question is whether GPT-4’s capabilities are sufficiently broad, flexible, and strong to be viewed as an early step toward artificial general intelligence (AGI).

The approach is not an educational intervention and does not study teachers, students, or classrooms. Instead, the paper presents qualitative examples of GPT-4 generating poetry, code, diagrams, structured explanations, and responses to interdisciplinary prompts, often comparing outputs to ChatGPT. It also explores limitations such as hallucinations, arithmetic errors, and weak planning, while arguing that GPT-4 shows notable gains in common sense and cross-domain synthesis despite being text-only at the time.

The paper’s main conclusion is that GPT-4 represents a significant leap in model capability and may be reasonably viewed as an early, incomplete AGI-like system. The authors emphasize that the model is still imperfect, non-human-like in important ways, and limited by the autoregressive architecture, but they argue that its breadth and performance signal a major paradigm shift in AI research.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a research demonstration/position paper with qualitative prompt examples, not a controlled educational study. It is not a K-12 intervention evaluation, and it provides no rigorous causal design, validated outcome measures, or student-level evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not test a K-12 educational intervention or report measurable educational impacts in classrooms. Its relevance is conceptual and methodological for GenAI capability, not evidence of impact on learners or schools.

interventions.use_case: Early experimental use of GPT-4 as a general-purpose conversational AI, including teacher-like comparison prompts, dialogue generation, and assisted reasoning across math, coding, writing, and other tasks.

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4 produced fluent, coherent, style-controlled writing tasks such as rhyming proofs, Shakespeare-style dialogue, and Platonic dialogue, often judged superior to ChatGPT in the paper’s side-by-side comparisons. These are demonstration examples rather than controlled educational outcomes; no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Quality of generated writing and teacher-style comparative judgments

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that GPT-4 can solve or reason through mathematical prompts, including a proof-style task on infinitude of primes and other structured math problems. The evidence is anecdotal and illustrative, with no controlled sample, effect size, or confidence interval reported.
finding.measure: Correctness and coherence of mathematical reasoning on prompted tasks

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4 is shown generating and explaining outputs across programming, visual composition, medicine, law, and interdisciplinary tasks, including code generation for graphics and candidate evaluation. The paper argues these outputs indicate broad cross-domain competence, but provides no quantitative educational effect estimate.
finding.measure: Performance on interdisciplinary generation and task-solving prompts

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes GPT-4’s apparent ability to synthesize information, reason, and adapt style across domains, which it interprets as evidence of flexible generalization and some theory-of-mind-like behavior. This is based on qualitative prompting and comparison examples, not a controlled assessment.
finding.measure: Qualitative assessment of reasoning, synthesis, and style adaptation

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4 is shown as potentially useful for coding and productivity tasks, including passing mock technical interviews and generating usable code artifacts. The paper frames this as evidence of substantial efficiency gains, but does not report standardized workload reduction metrics.
finding.measure: Success on coding interviews and code-generation tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues GPT-4 could have wide societal and institutional implications, including misinformation, bias, labor-market effects, and broader shifts in how knowledge work is done. These claims are speculative and conceptual rather than measured outcomes, so no effect size is available.
finding.measure: Discussion of societal, institutional, and labor-market implications

paper_profiles.title: Examining Science Education in ChatGPT: An Exploratory Study of Generative Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory paper examines how ChatGPT responds to questions about science education and what its outputs suggest for teachers and researchers. The study is framed around three questions: how ChatGPT answers science-education prompts, how educators might use it to generate science teaching resources, and how the author experienced using ChatGPT as a research aid.

The approach is a self-study methodology rather than an intervention study with participants. The author entered a series of prompts into ChatGPT in January 2023 and analysed the AI-generated responses against science education literature. Prompts included questions about effective science teaching, pedagogical choices such as chalk-and-talk versus student-centred teaching, responses to students failing in science, and requests to generate a Year 7 science unit, rubric, and quiz on renewable and non-renewable energy sources.

The paper is situated in science education and teacher practice rather than in a specific classroom implementation with students. The author concludes that ChatGPT can generate broadly plausible and often literature-aligned ideas for lesson design, rubrics, and quizzes, and can be useful for editing and brainstorming. However, the paper emphasises that ChatGPT frequently lacks evidentiary grounding, may produce generic or biased content, and should not replace teacher expertise. The main recommendation is that educators use such tools critically, adapt outputs to context, and remain transparent and reflective about AI use.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed exploratory self-study with qualitative analysis of ChatGPT outputs and literature comparison, but it is not a controlled empirical evaluation. The design provides reflective insight rather than strong causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful applications for teachers, but it reports no measured student gains and no effect sizes. Its contribution is primarily conceptual and practical guidance, so impact on K-12 outcomes is currently unclear.

interventions.use_case: Exploratory self-study of ChatGPT as a conversational AI tool for generating science education explanations, lesson ideas, rubrics, quizzes, and as a research/writing assistant for the author.

finding.finding_summary: The paper qualitatively compares ChatGPT outputs with science education literature and finds strong thematic alignment for inquiry-based teaching, real-world connections, and scaffolding, but also notes major weaknesses in evidence grounding and contextual nuance. No controlled student outcome data were reported; the study is an exploratory self-study of ChatGPT responses rather than an intervention test.
finding.measure: Qualitative comparison of ChatGPT-generated science education responses to cited research themes; author reflection on content quality

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was judged potentially useful for prompting critical thinking, helping educators design units and rubrics, and supporting students to evaluate AI-generated content critically. The paper argues that responsible use of generative AI may help develop critical thinking and source evaluation, but this is a conceptual inference rather than an empirical effect estimate.
finding.measure: Qualitative author reflections on critical thinking, source evaluation, and pedagogical design

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT was used to rewrite sentences and improve phrasing, flow, and clarity in the manuscript, and the author found it helpful for editing and overcoming overly long or complicated sentences. No formal writing outcome was measured, and no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Author-reported writing/editing utility during manuscript drafting

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly positions ChatGPT as a time-saving support for generating science unit plans, rubrics, quizzes, and for editing research text. This is presented as a qualitative benefit for teacher and researcher productivity, but the study does not quantify workload reduction or efficiency gains.
finding.measure: Author reflection on productivity in lesson/resource generation and manuscript editing

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks how pre-service elementary teachers can incorporate ChatGPT into science lesson planning, how well they do so, and what benefits and concerns they anticipate. The paper is positioned against a backdrop of rapid enthusiasm for generative AI in education but limited empirical evidence of how such tools are actually used in science teaching and learning.

The intervention/approach was a short professional learning experience on ChatGPT followed by lesson-plan creation. Twenty-nine pre-service elementary science teachers at a Korean teachers' university attended four 2-hour class sessions: introduction to ChatGPT, discussion of possible benefits, review of science teaching methods, and lesson-plan writing. Participants then created a 45-minute elementary science lesson plan that had to incorporate ChatGPT and at least one previously learned teaching strategy, and they also attached simulated ChatGPT conversations. Their plans were evaluated with a modified TPACK-based rubric, and open-ended survey responses were analyzed qualitatively.

Findings suggest that participants imagined a wide range of uses for ChatGPT across elementary science topics and instructional methods, especially cooperative learning, POE, learning cycle, analogy generation, and concept mapping. Overall rubric scores were moderately high, indicating reasonable ability to align ChatGPT with curriculum goals and instructional strategies, but they were weaker at selecting the most appropriate ChatGPT functions for specific lesson purposes. The teachers-in-training saw ChatGPT as useful for questioning, individualized support, formative assessment, and promoting digital literacy, but they also worried about inaccuracy and student over-dependence. The authors conclude that ChatGPT has promise for science education, but more research in authentic classrooms is needed, along with better professional development on AI integration and safeguards against hallucinations and overreliance.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/descriptive preprint analyzing lesson plans and survey responses from a small sample (n=29) with no student outcome comparison, randomization, or causal identification. It offers useful early evidence about teacher perceptions and design quality, but credibility is limited for claims about educational impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no measured student achievement or behavioral effect sizes, only anticipated benefits and concerns. Because observed impact is not demonstrated and outcomes are largely prospective/perceptual, the overall impact evidence is unclear and modest at best.

interventions.use_case: Pre-service elementary science teachers designed lesson plans that integrate ChatGPT into science teaching and learning, including question-answering, role-play support, individualized guidance, formative feedback, and exploratory prompting within classroom activities.

finding.finding_summary: This preprint did not test student learning outcomes directly; instead, it analyzed 29 pre-service elementary teachers' ChatGPT-integrated lesson plans for science education. Teachers envisioned ChatGPT supporting scientific inquiry, prediction/explanation in POE, and concept development, but also noted inappropriate uses such as generating experiments or providing unreliable science information.
finding.measure: TPACK-based lesson plan rubric and qualitative analysis of lesson plans/survey responses

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers expected ChatGPT to increase student motivation, interest, active participation, self-directed learning, and individualized support in science lessons. These were perception-based expectations rather than measured student outcomes, derived from survey responses and lesson-plan analysis across n=29 participants.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses about anticipated usefulness; lesson plan rationale

finding.finding_summary: Participants anticipated that ChatGPT could support critical thinking through consecutive questioning, collaboration via cooperative learning, and self-directed learning; however, they also worried it could reduce students' independence and over-reliance on AI. The paper provides no direct effect size because it is a qualitative/descriptive study of lesson plans and perceptions.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses and lesson plan coding

finding.finding_summary: Teachers viewed ChatGPT as a way to provide rapid information retrieval, concise summarization, feedback, and individualized support that a single teacher cannot easily provide at scale. The study did not measure workload outcomes directly, but the qualitative data suggest perceived efficiency benefits in lesson planning and classroom support.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses and lesson plan examples

paper_profiles.title: Can AI grade your essays? A comparative analysis of large language models and teacher ratings in multidimensional essay scoring
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 15th International Conference on Learning Analytics and Knowledge (LAK ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can serve as reliable alternatives or supports for teacher essay scoring. The central question is how well several LLMs align with real teacher judgments when assessing student writing across multiple predefined criteria, rather than only producing a single holistic score.

The study compares five models — GPT-3.5, GPT-4, o1, LLaMA 3-70B, and Mixtral 8x7B — against ratings from 37 German teachers. The texts were 20 authentic narrative essays written by Year 7 and Year 8 students in two German secondary schools. Teachers rated each essay on ten criteria covering content and language aspects, using a six-point Likert scale; the average teacher score served as ground truth. Each LLM evaluated each essay ten times under a standardized zero-shot prompt, enabling analysis of both reliability across repeated runs and agreement with human ratings.

Results show that the closed-source GPT models, especially o1, were substantially more reliable and more closely aligned with teachers than the open-source models. Alignment was strongest for language-related criteria such as spelling, expression, and use of literal speech, but weaker for content-related criteria such as introduction, main part, and plot logic. The authors conclude that LLMs, particularly o1, may be useful for assisting teachers with essay evaluation, but they still need refinement to better assess deeper content quality and to avoid over-weighting surface linguistic features.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed comparative correlational study in an authentic K-12 setting, but it is not an RCT or QED and relies on a very small corpus of 20 essays. The design is rigorous for model benchmarking, yet it does not establish causal effects on student outcomes or teacher productivity.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The practical impact is promising but indirect: the paper reports strong agreement for one model (o1) and potential workload reduction, but no measured downstream efficiency gains or learning effects. Evidence suggests useful support for teachers, but the overall impact remains modest and context-limited.

interventions.use_case: automated essay scoring of real German K-8 student narratives using large language models to assign multidimensional rubric-based ratings on content and language criteria
general-purpose large language models used in a teacher-like prompting setup to evaluate student writing and generate ratings, though the paper does not study interactive tutoring

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLM-based essay scoring could reduce teacher workload by supporting the evaluation of student essays. The strongest-performing model, o1, achieved Spearman’s r=.74 with teacher judgments on the overall score and ICC=.80 across repeated runs, suggesting potential utility for streamlining assessment, though the study does not measure time saved directly.
finding.measure: agreement with teacher ratings on multidimensional essay scoring; inter-rater reliability across repeated model runs

paper_profiles.title: LessonPlanner: Assisting Novice Teachers to Prepare Pedagogy-Driven Lesson Plans with Large Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: UIST ’24 (The 37th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge novice teachers face when preparing lesson plans: selecting effective teaching strategies, finding suitable materials, and organizing everything into a usable structure. The authors argue that while large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-4 can help generate content, using them through a generic chat interface can be cognitively demanding and can produce fragmented or hard-to-use outputs.

To address this, the paper introduces LessonPlanner, a web-based interactive system that assists teachers in creating pedagogy-driven lesson plans with LLM-generated content. The system is structured around educational theory, especially Bloom’s Taxonomy and Gagne’s Nine Events of Instruction, and includes preset prompts, block-based outlines, editable generated content, and sidebar assistance for refining lesson sections. The design was informed by interviews and co-design sessions with novice teachers and teaching assistants.

The study includes a formative qualitative phase with six novice teachers or teaching assistants, a within-subjects comparison study with 12 university students acting as teachers, and expert interviews with six teachers across elementary, high school, and university contexts. In the comparative study, participants used LessonPlanner versus a ChatGPT baseline to prepare lesson plans for familiar data structures topics. Results suggest that LessonPlanner improved the quality of the resulting lesson plans and reduced workload, while participants also reported concerns about accuracy and trust in LLM outputs. The authors conclude that LLMs can support lesson planning effectively when embedded in structured, theory-informed interfaces rather than general chat tools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed within-subjects usability/evaluation study with qualitative follow-up, but it is not a randomized controlled trial in authentic K-12 classrooms and uses a small, convenience sample of university students and teachers preparing hypothetical lesson plans. The evidence is useful but has clear external-validity and design limitations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests a potentially meaningful productivity gain for novice teachers, but the measured impact is limited to a small lab study without reported effect sizes in the excerpt and without direct K-12 student outcomes. The likely impact is promising but still unclear at population scale.

interventions.use_case: Interactive lesson-planning assistant for novice teachers using GPT-4 to generate lesson goals, pedagogically structured lesson plan outlines, instructional materials, and refinement suggestions based on Gagne’s Nine Events and Bloom’s Taxonomy.
Non-adaptive lesson-planning workflow and editor that structures instructional content into blocks, markdown sections, and preset prompts/buttons for preparing classroom instruction materials.

finding.finding_summary: In a within-subjects study with n=12 novice/near-novice university student teachers, LessonPlanner significantly reduced workload in lesson-plan preparation compared with a baseline ChatGPT web interface. Participants reported lower mental demand and effort on NASA-TLX-style measures and described the system as easier for organizing, refining, and completing lesson plans.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX workload survey; interview reports on preparation workload

finding.finding_summary: LessonPlanner significantly improved the quality of the produced lesson plans versus baseline ChatGPT in the within-subjects study (n=12). A subject-matter expert rated outcomes using a 7-point rubric adapted from the CIPP model, covering alignment to objectives, student skill acquisition, teaching materials, theory-practice balance, strategy quality, and detail; the paper reports a significant advantage for LessonPlanner but does not provide the effect size in the excerpted text.
finding.measure: Expert-rated lesson plan quality rubric adapted from the CIPP model

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 mathematics educators compare lesson plans produced by generative AI systems versus lesson plans created by human curriculum designers. The central question is whether AI-generated lesson plans can match or exceed human-authored plans in pedagogical quality, and if so, in which instructional components and grade bands they perform best.

The study compares three sources of lesson plans: human curriculum designer-created plans, a customized prompt-based GPT-4 model, and a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model trained on K-12 content. Educators evaluated paired lesson plans across four dimensions: warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall quality. The evaluation used a web-based pairwise comparison interface with blinded plan sources, plus written comments explaining choices. The sample included 20 experienced K-12 mathematics educators spanning elementary, middle, and high school levels, with 16 completing the study and producing 529 complete lesson-plan pair evaluations. The study was conducted online over several weeks in March-July 2024.

Results showed that human-authored lesson plans were generally preferred overall, especially for warm-up activities, main instructional tasks, and elementary-grade plans. However, GenAI outputs were competitive in some contexts, particularly cool-down activities and higher grade levels. Customized GPT-4 was often preferred over fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b, while the fine-tuned model showed stronger performance in high school contexts than in elementary settings. Qualitative analysis suggested educators valued human plans for differentiation, student discourse, contextualization, and inclusive supports, whereas AI plans were praised for structure and coherence. The authors conclude that GenAI is best positioned as an assistive planning tool rather than a replacement for human expertise, with human-AI collaboration likely to be the most effective model for lesson planning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed-style comparative user study with mixed methods, but it is not an RCT of student outcomes and relies on subjective educator preference data. Methodological rigor is moderate, yet evidence credibility is limited by the absence of randomized learner outcomes and by imbalances in pair counts across conditions.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study implies potentially meaningful productivity gains and instructional usefulness for GenAI-assisted lesson planning, but it does not report direct implementation effects on student learning or teacher time with effect sizes. Impact is therefore suggestive rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Comparative evaluation of educator preferences for GenAI-generated K-12 math lesson plans, including customized GPT-4 and fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b, versus human curriculum designer-created lesson plans across warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall quality.

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily suggests a potential efficiency benefit of GenAI for lesson planning, rather than measuring teacher time directly. Educators indicated that GenAI lesson plans can serve as an assistive tool and may reduce educator workload, especially for structured lesson components like cool-downs, but no direct workload effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Educator preferences and qualitative comments about lesson-plan usefulness and workload reduction potential
finding.study_size: n=16 educators; 529 lesson-plan pairs; 2,116 total evaluations

finding.finding_summary: Educators' comments emphasized collaboration, student discourse, scaffolding, and adaptability as key qualities in lesson plans. Human-created plans were generally preferred for fostering meaningful discourse and group work, while GenAI was valued for structure and lesson summarization, indicating mixed comparative performance on these pedagogically important durable skills.
finding.measure: Preference judgments and thematic analysis of comments on group work, student discourse, and adaptability

paper_profiles.title: Classroom AI: Large Language Models as Grade-Specific Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that large language models (LLMs) often fail to produce explanations matched to students’ reading and comprehension levels, even when explicitly prompted to do so. The authors focus on a classroom-facing use case: generating open-ended educational answers that are age-appropriate across multiple grade bands, rather than simplifying source text for summarization or paraphrasing tasks.

The proposed intervention is a fine-tuning framework for LLMs that generates grade-specific educational responses for six levels spanning lower elementary through adult education. The method combines synthetic question generation across eight K-12 curriculum fields, prompt-based answer generation at multiple readability targets, and an integrated grading scheme built from seven readability metrics to label training data. The authors then fine-tune grade-specific models and compare them against prompt-based baselines on multiple datasets including ScienceQA, ELI5_Category, Natural Questions, and synthetic question sets.

The evaluation includes automated readability/compatibility metrics, accuracy checks, and human studies with 208 participants, plus a GPT-4o-based survey analysis. Results show that the fine-tuned models substantially improve alignment with intended grade levels while preserving factual accuracy. The paper concludes that grade-specific LLM fine-tuning can support more comprehensible educational assistance, especially for younger learners, and may help address teacher shortages by complementing classroom instruction.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical model-evaluation study, but it is not a classroom trial or causal study of student learning outcomes. The evidence rests on benchmark performance and human judgments of readability/comprehensibility rather than randomized educational impact on K-12 learners.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for educational text accessibility, with a large improvement in grade-level alignment (35.64 percentage points), but it does not measure student learning gains in authentic instruction. Impact on actual K-12 outcomes is therefore plausible but unproven.

interventions.use_case: Fine-tuning large language models to generate grade-specific educational explanations and answers for open-ended student questions across K-12 and adult levels.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds substantially improved grade-level alignment/readability of LLM-generated educational text after finetuning, compared with prompt-based methods. Across four datasets and six grade levels, the authors report an average 35.64 percentage point increase in target-grade success rate, with human raters (n=208) showing strong agreement with model outputs (Kendall’s τ=0.76).
finding.measure: Readability/grade-level alignment metrics (Flesch Reading Ease, FKGL, CLI, Linsear Write, Gunning Fog, Dale-Chall, Spache, and held-out ARI); human judgments of answer comprehensibility
finding.study_size: n=208 human participants; model evaluation on 4 datasets (sample sizes reported in paper, including DSQ n=10,876; DSQ2 n=10,427; DELI n=12,000; DNQ n=24,000)

finding.finding_summary: The finetuned models preserve factual correctness while adapting explanations to grade level, with accuracy on ScienceQA remaining comparable to the base model. The paper reports minimal performance degradation on the multiple-choice accuracy task (DSQ), indicating the grade-specific adaptation does not materially harm content accuracy.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on ScienceQA (DSQ)

paper_profiles.study_country: Republic of Korea, United States, and England

paper_profiles.title: FACET: Teacher-Centred LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems—Towards Personalized Educational Worksheets
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of helping teachers personalize instructional materials for highly heterogeneous classrooms, especially in mathematics education. The authors argue that existing AI personalization systems are often narrowly performance-focused and student-facing, leaving teachers with substantial workload when adapting content to learners’ cognitive and motivational needs.

To address this gap, the paper proposes FACET, a teacher-facing, large language model-based multi-agent framework for generating individualized worksheets. FACET uses three coordinated agents: learner agents that simulate student profiles, a teacher agent that adapts content using didactical principles and Bloom’s taxonomy, and an evaluator agent that provides automated quality feedback. The system was tested with authentic grade 8 mathematics curriculum content from German secondary education.

The study evaluates feasibility through two forms of evidence: repeated internal agent-based assessments across four learner profiles and exploratory feedback from five K-12 in-service teachers. Results suggest that the system produces stable, pedagogically coherent, and suitably differentiated worksheets, with particularly strong ratings for task suitability and clarity. Teacher feedback was generally positive and highlighted the value of adjustable difficulty and motivational support, though the authors note that the evaluation was preliminary and not conducted in authentic classroom use. The paper concludes that multi-agent LLM systems may offer a scalable path toward teacher support for personalized instruction, while calling for richer learner profiles and in-classroom trials in future work.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/feasibility study with small-sample exploratory teacher feedback and internal agent-based evaluations, not a controlled comparative trial. It provides useful preliminary evidence but lacks randomization, authentic classroom outcome measures, and causal identification.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potential practical value for teachers and personalization in mathematics, but it reports no student achievement gains or effect sizes from real classroom deployment. Impact is therefore plausible but currently unclear and modest at best.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-facing multi-agent LLM system (FACET) that simulates learner profiles, adapts grade 8 mathematics worksheet content, and generates personalized tasks, hints, and motivational comments for heterogeneous K-12 classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that FACET generated individualized grade 8 mathematics worksheets with strong alignment to learner profiles and pedagogical criteria. In automated agent-based evaluation over 10 iterations per profile, suitability for learners averaged M=4.78 (SD=0.06) and clarity M=4.76 (SD=0.12), while K-12 teacher ratings also judged the worksheets as suitable and didactically sound (e.g., suitability M=5.05, range=4-6; didactical structure M=4.95, range=3-6).
finding.measure: Worksheet quality ratings for math task suitability, clarity, and didactical structure; teacher and agent evaluations of grade 8 mathematics worksheets
finding.study_size: n=4 learner profiles for agent-based evaluation; n=5 K-12 in-service teachers
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.06 for suitability, SD=0.12 for clarity, SD=0.22 for didactical structure, SD=0.26 for creativity

finding.finding_summary: The system explicitly incorporated motivational dimensions into worksheet generation, and teachers reported that the outputs supported engagement for low-motivation learners. Qualitative feedback noted that narrative elements, everyday-life relevance, and reduced task load could improve motivation and prevent cognitive overload, but these claims are exploratory and not tied to a causal effect estimate.
finding.measure: Teacher qualitative feedback and worksheet ratings related to motivational support and suitability for low/high motivation profiles

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the multi-agent framework reduces prompting overhead and supports scalable teacher-facing personalization by reusing learner profiles and automating quality assurance. However, the reported evidence is feasibility-oriented rather than a measured workload reduction outcome, so no effect size is available.
finding.measure: Feasibility claims and teacher feedback on usability/workflow support

paper_profiles.title: Physics task development of prospective physics teachers using ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT 3.5 can support prospective physics teachers in developing high-quality assessment tasks, and how tasks created with ChatGPT compare with tasks created using a conventional textbook. The authors focus on task quality, the kinds of revisions teacher candidates make to generated tasks, and participants’ perceptions of ChatGPT’s usability, usefulness, and output quality.

In a randomized controlled trial, 26 prospective physics teachers from Ludwig-Maximilians-University Munich were split into two groups. One group used ChatGPT 3.5 to create text-based physics tasks for four Newtonian mechanics concepts for 10th-grade German high school students; the control group used a standard high school physics textbook. Participants first completed prompt-familiarization examples, then created or adapted tasks. The study rated tasks on specificity, clarity, correctness, whether they were misleading, difficulty, contextualization, relevance to the target concept, and overall quality. Participants using ChatGPT also completed usability and usefulness surveys.

The findings show that ChatGPT-generated and textbook-supported tasks were similarly correct and appropriately difficult, but textbook-supported tasks were clearer and more often embedded in meaningful contexts. Both groups struggled with task specificity, suggesting that neither ChatGPT nor the textbook overcame the challenge of supplying enough information for a task to be solvable. Participants rated ChatGPT as easy to use, but its output quality only around neutral and somewhat problematic. The paper concludes that ChatGPT can support physics task development, but teacher prompts and pedagogical judgment remain important, especially for specificity and contextual quality.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled trial with a direct comparison group and blinded expert task ratings, which is strong evidence for this narrow context. There are some concerns about small sample size (n=26), single institution, and limited generalizability beyond prospective physics teachers in one topic area.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests modest benefits for using ChatGPT to support task creation, mainly comparable correctness but weaker context quality versus textbooks. The largest reported difference was moderate-to-large for context quality (d=1.04), but the practical impact is limited to teacher task authoring rather than direct student learning outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Using ChatGPT 3.5 to generate and revise physics assessment tasks for prospective teachers creating 10th-grade kinematics and Newton's laws questions
Using a digital high school physics textbook as a non-AI comparison resource for task creation and adaptation

finding.finding_summary: In an RCT with 26 prospective physics teachers who produced 103 tasks, ChatGPT 3.5 yielded task correctness comparable to textbook-supported task creation, with no significant difference in correctness or adequacy of difficulty. However, textbook-supported tasks were significantly clearer (p=0.04, d=0.38) and more contextualized (p=6×10^-5, d=1.04), while both groups struggled with task specificity.
finding.measure: Expert ratings of generated physics task quality: specificity, clarity, correctness, not misleading, adequate difficulty, context, relevance to target concept, overall quality
finding.study_size: n=26 prospective teachers; 103 tasks total (51 ChatGPT, 52 textbook)
finding.effect_size: d=0.38 and d=1.04 for clarity and context favoring textbook; other comparisons not reported as significant

finding.finding_summary: Compared with textbook-supported task creation, ChatGPT-generated tasks were equally correct and similarly difficult, but were less often embedded in meaningful context. The study reports no significant difference in correctness, specificity, misleading phrasing, or adequate difficulty, suggesting ChatGPT can support basic physics item generation but does not fully address higher-quality item design needs.
finding.measure: Expert ratings of task correctness, specificity, misleading phrasing, adequate difficulty, and context
finding.effect_size: d=0.38 and d=1.04 for clarity and context favoring textbook; other effect sizes not reported

paper_profiles.title: AI, Expert or Peer? Examining the Impact of Perceived Feedback Source on Pre-Service Teachers Feedback Perception and Uptake
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether pre-service teachers’ perceptions of feedback and their willingness to act on it depend on the perceived source of the feedback: an LLM, an expert, or a peer. The paper addresses a gap in feedback research by asking not only whether participants can identify the source of feedback, but also how correct or incorrect source recognition shapes cognitive, emotional, and behavioral responses to the same feedback message.

The intervention was a randomized experiment in which 273 bachelor’s-level teacher education students at a German university received one of 30 written feedback messages on a mathematics learning goal. The messages were produced by three sources: expert, peer, or ChatGPT-4 (LLM). Participants guessed the source, completed a feedback perception questionnaire, and then revised the learning goal to indicate feedback uptake. Objective feedback quality was coded separately and included in the analyses.

Results showed that source perceptions strongly shaped how feedback was evaluated: LLM feedback was judged more positively when it was misattributed to an expert, supporting an expertise heuristic and indicating a bias in favor of human sources. However, perceived source did not meaningfully predict actual uptake. Instead, feedback quality was the only significant predictor of whether suggestions were implemented. The authors conclude that source-related biases affect how feedback is perceived, but not necessarily how it is used, and argue for stronger feedback and AI literacy in teacher education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized experiment with 273 pre-service teachers, but it is not a K-12 student study and the intervention is a single-task feedback manipulation rather than a full classroom implementation. It is methodologically stronger than correlational work, but relevance and ecological generalizability to K-12 direct-comparison settings are limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study found meaningful perceptual effects and a modest association between feedback quality and uptake, but no direct behavioral advantage for perceived source and only small-to-moderate descriptive differences across conditions. Overall impact on learning behavior is unclear and not large enough to justify a green/blue rating.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated written feedback on a mathematics learning goal, compared with expert and peer feedback, to examine how source perceptions affect feedback evaluation and uptake.

finding.finding_summary: The task centered on revising a mathematics learning goal about identifying right-angled triangles and the Pythagorean theorem. While feedback source changed perceptions, actual uptake of corrections was driven by feedback quality, not source; LLM feedback had the highest relative uptake (52%) compared with expert (45%) and peer (42%) conditions, but source did not significantly predict implementation in the regression model.
finding.measure: Revision of a mathematics learning goal; correction rate / implemented suggestions; number of mistakes recognized and suggestions implemented
finding.effect_size: R²=.078 for uptake model; ANOVA on suggestions implemented η²=.11; mistakes recognized η²=.37

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined feedback perception, feedback literacy-related judgments, and the ability to recognize whether feedback came from an LLM, expert, or peer. Recognition accuracy was low overall (LLM 36%, expert 41%, peer 46%), and misidentifying LLM feedback as human increased perceived fairness and usefulness, but these perception effects did not translate into uptake.
finding.measure: Feedback perception questionnaire (fairness, usefulness, acceptance, willingness to improve, affect) and source recognition accuracy
finding.effect_size: Fairness interaction b=1.21, p=.042; usefulness interaction b=1.76, p=.009; source recognition ANOVA η²=.031

paper_profiles.title: Revealing Networks: Understanding Effective Teacher Practices in AI-Supported Classrooms using Transmodal Ordered Network Analysis
paper_profiles.venue: The 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK ’24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how teacher practices in AI-supported classrooms relate to student learning behavior in an AI tutor, and whether adding evidence about teacher actions improves inference of which students are learning quickly or slowly. The authors focus on a methodological problem in learning analytics: tutor log data alone may miss the classroom context that shapes how students use AI tutors, especially teacher monitoring and teacher-student interactions.

To address this, the study combines three data sources from a middle school mathematics classroom: AI tutor logs from the Lynnette equation-solving tutor, timestamped classroom observation notes, and spatial teacher-position data from ultrawide-band sensors. The authors use Transmodal Ordered Network Analysis, a quantitative ethnography approach, to model temporal co-occurrence among in-tutor and out-of-tutor behaviors. Students were grouped by individualized learning rates estimated from tutor data, and teacher visits were also analyzed before and after they occurred.

The study found that including teacher-practice data improved model fit for distinguishing low- and high-learning-rate students. Teacher screen alignment and teacher talking were associated differently with the two groups: students with low learning rates more often requested hints after teacher monitoring or talking, whereas high-learning-rate students more often produced correct attempts. After teacher visits, low-learning-rate students showed more consecutive correct attempts, suggesting that visits were especially helpful for them. Qualitative review of observation notes suggested that low-learning-rate students tended to receive more procedural support before visits, while visits themselves often included more conceptual prompting, which may explain the improved post-visit behavior.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed observational case study using multimodal learning analytics and quantitative ethnography in one authentic classroom. It is methodologically rich but correlational, with no randomized assignment or causal identification, so credibility is limited to associative evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The observed associations are promising and include moderate-to-strong correlations, but they do not demonstrate that the teacher-practice patterns caused learning gains. The paper suggests a potentially useful analytics approach for K-12 math classrooms, but the direct instructional impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: classroom use of the Lynnette AI math tutor for 7th-grade linear equation solving, including stepwise hints, error feedback, and mastery-based practice

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not test a new instructional intervention on achievement directly, but it finds that incorporating teacher-practice variables into models significantly improved inference of students' learning rates in the math tutor. The multimodal model including out-of-tutor teacher practices fit better than the tutor-log-only model (AIC=150.60 vs 158.30; t=12.76, 95% CI [7.06, 9.63], p<.001) in a sample of n=85 7th-grade students.
finding.measure: Model fit and inferred individualized learning rates in the linear-equation-solving ITS

finding.finding_summary: Teacher monitoring and talking were associated with different student behavioral responses depending on prior learning rate. Low-learning-rate students tended to request more hints after teacher screen alignment and talking, whereas high-learning-rate students tended to produce more correct attempts; the paper interprets this partly through disengagement/hint abuse and partly through differential support type.
finding.measure: Temporal co-occurrence of teacher practices with student hint requests, correct attempts, idling, and tutor misuse
finding.effect_size: r=0.55; r=0.60; r=0.53; r=0.45; r=0.36 (reported for several Wilcoxon tests)

finding.finding_summary: The qualitative replay analysis suggests that conceptual teacher support and self-explanation prompts around teacher visits were linked to more desirable problem-solving behavior, especially for slower learners. After visits, low-learning-rate students showed more consecutive correct attempts (pre-visit median score -0.33 vs post-visit -0.08; V=303, r=0.49, p=.022), indicating improved productive persistence/problem-solving behavior.
finding.measure: Pre/post-visit ordered network scores and consecutive correct attempts in the tutor

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation of ChatGPT and Microsoft Bing AI Chat Performances on Physics Exams of Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates how well two large language models, ChatGPT and Microsoft BingChat, answer physics questions taken from Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination materials. The core question is whether these generative AI systems can perform at a level comparable to Vietnamese high school students on authentic exam items, especially across different difficulty levels from knowledge to high application.

The study uses the VNHSGE physics dataset, which contains multiple-choice questions from real Vietnamese national exams from 2019 to 2023. The authors compare the models’ answers with official solutions and with performance patterns from Vietnamese students. They also examine question difficulty, year-by-year performance, and a few illustrative examples of model outputs.

Overall, the paper finds that both ChatGPT and BingChat can answer easier questions reasonably well, but they struggle on more complex application and high-application problems. BingChat is generally more accurate, while ChatGPT is described as more stable or consistent. When compared with Vietnamese student score distributions, both models perform worse than students overall, leading the authors to conclude that current LLMs cannot yet replace human capability in high school physics teaching, though they may still be useful for immediate feedback and individualized support.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical benchmarking study, but it is not a controlled K-12 intervention trial; it evaluates model performance on exam items and compares against student score distributions. The methodology is systematic but observational and non-experimental, so it fits a lower-causal-strength evidence tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows the models can solve some lower-level physics questions, but performance is below Vietnamese students on average and notably weak on higher-order application items. The practical impact for K-12 teaching is therefore promising but limited and not yet robust enough for strong positive classification.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking ChatGPT and Microsoft BingChat on Vietnamese high school physics multiple-choice exam questions (2019-2023) to assess their potential as physics teaching and homework-support chatbots
Using ChatGPT and BingChat to translate and explain physics exam questions, and to provide immediate feedback and individualized learning support in K-12 physics contexts

finding.finding_summary: Across 200 exam questions from five Vietnamese high school physics exams, ChatGPT averaged 61% accuracy and BingChat 66%, both below Vietnamese students’ performance on the same exams (average student score 6.39/10; ChatGPT converted score 6.1; BingChat 6.6). The models handled knowledge and comprehension items reasonably well but struggled with high-application physics questions, indicating limited capability for complex scientific reasoning.
finding.measure: Accuracy on physics multiple-choice exam questions; converted exam scores compared with Vietnamese student score distributions

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was more stable, while BingChat was more accurate on average across years. ChatGPT averaged 61% accuracy versus BingChat’s 66%, but the paper reports that ChatGPT was more consistent across years and question orders, whereas BingChat varied more substantially (e.g., 55% to 72.5% by year).
finding.measure: Year-by-year accuracy and response stability on physics exam questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can support teachers and students by providing immediate feedback, individualized learning experiences, and assistance with lesson preparation and grading-related tasks. This is presented as a potential benefit rather than a directly measured experimental effect.
finding.measure: Proposed support for feedback, personalization, and teacher assistance

paper_profiles.title: The Long-Term Effects of Teachers’ Gender Stereotypes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teachers’ gender stereotypes in grading are associated with students’ educational and labor-market outcomes over the long run. The central question is whether teachers who hold stronger stereotypical beliefs about boys’ and girls’ abilities in math/science versus language/humanities systematically assign different grades to students, and whether exposure to such grading practices has persistent consequences beyond school.

The study uses administrative data from Peru and constructs teacher-level measures of stereotyped assessment by comparing teacher-assigned grades with blindly graded standardized test scores. It also collects survey and Implicit Association Test (IAT) data from teachers to validate that the grading gaps are linked to implicit gender stereotypes. The main sample includes public high school students in grades 7–11 and tracks cohorts from high school into ages 18–23 using linked education and labor-market records.

The findings show that teachers with stronger gender stereotypes give more favorable grades to boys in math/science and to girls in language arts, relative to blind assessments. Students exposed to more stereotyped grading—especially girls—are less likely to graduate from high school, apply to college, and in some cases are less likely to work in the formal sector or earn as much later on. The paper concludes that teachers’ stereotyped evaluations can have durable, self-reinforcing effects on students’ educational choices and early labor-market outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a strong observational econometric study using linked administrative data, teacher survey data, and a quasi-experimental within-school assignment design, but it is not randomized. Credibility is decent, yet causal identification still relies on selection and conditioning assumptions rather than an experimental intervention.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The estimated effects are consequential for affected girls, with some outcomes around or above 0.20 when expressed relative to group means, but the paper studies an indirect social mechanism rather than a scalable instructional intervention. Its main contribution is identifying harmful bias and long-run consequences, not testing a technology with direct implementation impact.

finding.finding_summary: This paper studies how exposure to teachers with more stereotypical grading practices affects students’ educational trajectories in Peru. Girls assigned to a math teacher with one standard deviation more severe stereotyped assessment are 1.3 percentage points less likely to graduate from high school (1.6% of the group mean), and their college application probability falls by 0.7 percentage points (2.2% of the group mean).
finding.measure: High school graduation and college application rates
finding.study_size: n=1.7 million public high school students; teacher stereotype survey subsample n=2,052
finding.std_deviation: 1 SD increase in stereotyped grading measure

finding.finding_summary: The paper also finds that exposure to stereotyped grading in language arts reduces girls’ likelihood of graduating from high school, though the college-enrollment effect is not statistically significant. Exposure to stereotyped grading in science has smaller negative effects on graduation and college application outcomes but no significant employment effects.
finding.measure: High school graduation and college enrollment/application outcomes
finding.study_size: n=1.7 million public high school students

finding.finding_summary: The paper further documents persistent downstream educational and labor-market consequences associated with stereotyped teacher assessments. Female students’ likelihood of formal-sector employment is 1.3 percentage points lower at ages 18–19 after being assigned a math teacher with one standard deviation stronger stereotyped assessments, and monthly earnings fall by USD 2.6 at ages 18–19.
finding.measure: Formal-sector employment and monthly earnings
finding.study_size: n=1.7 million public high school students; labor-market subsample 485,000 workers
finding.std_deviation: 1 SD increase in stereotyped grading measure

finding.finding_summary: Beyond individual student outcomes, the paper shows that teacher stereotypes contribute to widening gender disparities in educational attainment and labor-market outcomes. The author estimates that the early labor-market earnings loss is large enough to widen the gender wage gap by approximately 32%, indicating a broader institutional and distributional effect.
finding.measure: Gender wage gap and labor-market gender disparities
finding.study_size: n=1.7 million public high school students; labor-market linked administrative records

paper_profiles.title: Group-Differentiated Discourse on Generative AI in High School Education: A Case Study of Reddit Communities
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how Reddit communities discuss generative AI in high school education, with a focus on learning impacts, academic integrity, AI detection tools, and emotional framing. Rather than testing an instructional intervention, the study analyzes naturally occurring online discourse to understand how stakeholder position shapes attitudes toward classroom AI. The authors argue that teachers and students talk about the same technologies in systematically different ways because they occupy different roles in the educational system.

The dataset consists of 3,789 English-language Reddit posts and comments collected from five education-related subreddits between December 2022 and December 2024. The authors use keyword-based retrieval, human-validated relevance filtering, and LLM-assisted annotation to label posts for learning-related frames, integrity/enforcement, and emotions. They then compare student, teacher, and mixed communities using chi-square tests and effect sizes.

The main finding is that teachers are more likely to express explicit pedagogical trade-offs, framing AI as both helpful and harmful for learning, while students more often discuss AI in tactical terms related to accusations, grades, and enforcement. Detector-related discourse is associated with higher negative emotion across all groups, with stronger effects for students and mixed communities than for teachers. The paper concludes that AI detectors function as governance mechanisms that create emotional harm and that process-based assessment is a fairer alternative for academic integrity enforcement in AI-mediated classrooms.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/correlational social media study using human-validated LLM annotation and chi-square analysis, not an intervention trial. It provides descriptive evidence about discourse and governance concerns, but no direct causal estimate of an educational treatment effect.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful but context-specific associations in Reddit discourse, especially around detector-related emotional harm, with effect sizes in the modest range. Its implications are important for policy and practice, but the study does not evaluate a classroom intervention or demonstrate direct student learning impact.

interventions.use_case: Reddit discourse analysis of generative AI in high school education, focusing on AI detectors, academic integrity enforcement, and perceived learning impacts rather than direct classroom implementation.

finding.finding_summary: Across 3,789 Reddit posts, the paper finds that stakeholder position strongly shapes governance discourse around generative AI in schools. Teachers more often articulate dual pedagogical trade-offs, while students discuss AI in enforcement and consequence terms; detector-related discourse is associated with higher negative emotion overall (+0.132 risk difference) and even more strongly among students (+0.194).
finding.measure: Topic- and emotion-labeled Reddit posts; chi-square tests of group differences; risk difference for negative emotion in detector-related posts
finding.effect_size: +0.132 risk difference overall; +0.194 student subgroup; Cram�e9r's V up to 0.190

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI as a Learning Buddy and a Teaching Assistant: Preservice Teachers’ Use and Attitudes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how preservice teachers use generative AI (GenAI) in teacher education, what tasks they use it for, how often they use it, and what attitudes they hold toward it. The study is motivated by growing interest in AI in teacher education, alongside concerns about ethical use, accuracy, and unequal access in under-resourced settings.

The authors conceptualize GenAI in two roles: as a “learning buddy” for academic support and as a “teaching assistant” for instructional preparation. Using a cross-sectional survey, they studied 167 preservice teachers enrolled in four teacher education institutions in Ghana. Participants reported on their GenAI use for learning tasks such as finding reading materials, explaining concepts, and generating examples, as well as teaching tasks such as finding resources, identifying assessment strategies, and creating lesson plans.

Results show that GenAI was used more often for personal academic learning than for instructional planning. Preservice teachers generally held positive attitudes toward GenAI, especially regarding its usefulness for reading materials, content understanding, and pedagogical support. However, they also expressed concerns about inaccurate outputs, academic dishonesty, and the cost of internet data. Demographic factors such as age and class level predicted frequency of use, but not overall attitudes. The study concludes that GenAI literacy and ethical guidance should be strengthened in teacher education programs in the Global South, particularly in Ghana.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed cross-sectional survey with descriptive and regression analyses, but it is non-experimental and self-report based. It provides useful correlational evidence, yet does not establish causal effects of GenAI use.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests modest, context-specific benefits for preservice teachers’ academic support and instructional preparation, but no causal impact estimates are reported. Its main contribution is descriptive and institutional, rather than demonstrating medium or large effects.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT-style tools) used by preservice teachers as a learning buddy for finding reading materials, explaining content, generating practical examples, and supporting reflections; also used as a teaching assistant for lesson planning, identifying assessment strategies, identifying lesson objectives, locating sample lessons, and finding teaching resources.

finding.finding_summary: Preservice teachers reported that GenAI supported academic learning tasks, especially finding reading materials (38.11%, n=93) and seeking in-depth content explanations (25.41%, n=62). Survey means were high for access and comprehension items, including getting more reading materials (M=4.02, SD=0.93) and understanding complex areas of study (M=3.98, SD=0.85), indicating perceived academic benefit.
finding.measure: Self-reported use purposes and attitude items on GenAI for learning (Likert-scale survey)

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests GenAI may support autonomous learning and reduce reliance on peers and instructors for routine preparation tasks, with moderate endorsement that it helps students work more independently. However, respondents also expressed concern that GenAI could enable cheating and weaken critical and creative skills (M=3.28, SD=1.31), so the durable-skills implications were positive but qualified.
finding.measure: Self-reported attitudes about autonomy, dependence, cheating, and critical/creative skill development

finding.finding_summary: GenAI was viewed as improving efficiency in both learning and teaching preparation, especially for locating resources and planning lessons. For teaching tasks, 33.33% (n=90) used it to find teaching resources and 21.48% (n=58) to identify assessment strategies; participants also endorsed that GenAI could improve pedagogical skills (M=3.88, SD=0.90).
finding.measure: Self-reported instructional-task use and attitude items about pedagogical skill gains

finding.finding_summary: The study highlights institutional barriers and implications for teacher education policy, including concerns about high internet data costs, limited access, and ethical/accuracy issues. While attitudes toward integration were generally positive, the authors argue for GenAI literacy, ethical guidance, and policy support in teacher education programs in the Global South.
finding.measure: Self-reported barriers and recommendations for teacher education policy and implementation

paper_profiles.title: Teacher Agent: A Knowledge Distillation-Free Framework for Rehearsal-based Video Incremental Learning
paper_profiles.venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a machine learning problem rather than an educational intervention: how to reduce catastrophic forgetting in rehearsal-based video class-incremental learning without relying on a conventional teacher network for knowledge distillation. The authors argue that standard distillation-based rehearsal methods are computationally expensive for video models and can be misled by inaccurate predictions from the previous-stage teacher, especially as tasks accumulate.

To solve this, the paper proposes a knowledge distillation-free framework called Teacher Agent. The approach replaces the previous teacher model with a lightweight teacher generator that produces soft labels, together with a self-correction loss that helps the model review old knowledge. The framework also includes a unified sampler that selects a fixed number of key frames from stored videos, improving memory efficiency while preserving representative content.

The method is evaluated on four video action recognition benchmarks: Kinetics-incremental, Something-Something V1, UCF101, and HMDB51. Results show improved accuracy and reduced forgetting compared with prior rehearsal-based incremental learning methods such as iCaRL, BiC, and vCLIMB TC, while using substantially fewer FLOPs and lower-resolution video inputs. The authors conclude that the proposed teacher-agent strategy can effectively replace distillation in rehearsal-based video incremental learning and may also transfer to image class-incremental learning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed computer vision/machine learning methods paper on incremental video recognition, not an education intervention study. It does not evaluate a K-12 instructional technology or compare against human coaching, peer review, self-review, or usual classroom practice.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no direct educational impact measured in K-12 settings, and no student learning, teacher practice, or institutional outcome evidence is reported. The paper’s improvements are limited to video classification benchmarks and computational efficiency.

paper_profiles.title: Towards Adaptive Feedback with AI: Comparing the Feedback Quality of LLMs and Teachers on Experimentation Protocols
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can generate feedback on students’ science experimentation protocols that is comparable in quality to feedback written by human teachers and science education experts. The authors focus on a core challenge in formative assessment: providing timely, adaptive, and pedagogically useful feedback that helps students understand their mistakes and improve their experimental reasoning.

The intervention/approach is an LLM-based feedback agent built with a zero-shot prompting strategy. The model, GPT-3.5, was prompted to act as a science teacher and generate feedback for specific errors detected in student-written experimentation protocols. The feedback was evaluated using a multidimensional rubric covering Feed Up, Feed Back, Feed Forward, Constructive Tone, Linguistic Clarity, and Technical Terminology. Four expert raters blinded and shuffled the outputs from the LLM, 11 teachers, and 5 science education experts.

The study used authentic student work from 37 German secondary school students in grades 6–8 who completed two science experimentation tasks. The main finding is that the LLM’s overall feedback quality was similar to that of teachers and experts, but it performed worse on the Feed Back dimension, meaning it was less effective at identifying and explaining the specific error in context. The authors conclude that LLMs are promising for scalable classroom feedback, but human expertise remains important for contextual understanding, and a hybrid teacher-plus-AI approach may be best.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small comparative, blinded-rater study with a clear methodology, but it is not an RCT and does not measure downstream student learning outcomes. It provides useful construct-valid evidence on feedback quality, but generalizability is limited by the small sample and single subject context.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The findings suggest potential for comparable feedback quality and some efficiency benefits, but the study does not report medium or large learner outcome gains. Impact is therefore promising but unclear for actual K-12 classroom practice.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated formative feedback on middle school students' experimentation protocols, including detection of protocol errors and generation of Feed Up, Feed Back, and Feed Forward comments in science inquiry

finding.finding_summary: The study found no significant difference in overall feedback quality between the LLM agent and human teachers/experts when evaluated on student experimentation protocols from grades 6-8 (n=40 protocols, 109 errors). Mean overall ratings were similar across groups: LLM 3.784 (SD=1.238), teachers 3.805 (SD=1.266), experts 3.831 (SD=1.287) on a 5-point scale.
finding.measure: Blinded human ratings of feedback quality on six dimensions for feedback written on science experimentation protocols (Feed Up, Feed Back, Feed Forward, Constructive Tone, Linguistic Clarity, Technical Terminology)
finding.std_deviation: LLM SD=1.238; Teacher SD=1.266; Expert SD=1.287

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues the LLM agent can provide immediate, scalable feedback and may reduce educator workload, with generated feedback typically around 50 words and suitable for classroom use. While not tested as a workload intervention in a field trial, the results suggest practical efficiency advantages relative to expert-written feedback, which was substantially longer.
finding.measure: Feedback length and feasibility for classroom use; qualitative discussion of scalability and teacher workload reduction

paper_profiles.title: LitLinker: Supporting the Ideation of Interdisciplinary Contexts with Large Language Models for Teaching Literature in Elementary Schools
paper_profiles.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge elementary school literature teachers face when designing interdisciplinary teaching contexts that connect reading materials with other subjects such as science, art, history, and music. The authors argue that teachers often use a “reverse thinking” process: they start from a promising interdisciplinary context and then search for texts that fit, but this requires substantial time, domain exploration, and judgment about whether the connections are educationally meaningful.

To support this workflow, the paper introduces LitLinker, a large language model-powered interactive system for elementary Chinese language teachers. LitLinker uses multiple LLM agent roles—Context Analyst, Text Analyst, Text Reviewer, and Context Summarizer—to recommend interdisciplinary contexts, analyze relationships between contexts and texts, support questions and edits, and generate structured lesson plans with introductions and classroom activities. The system is grounded in a context pool built from textbooks and educational materials, and its prompts are designed around teacher-derived evaluation criteria.

The paper reports two kinds of empirical evidence. First, a within-subjects study with 16 novice users of literature teaching compared LitLinker against a baseline LLM web application and found that LitLinker produced deeper integration of subjects, lower workload, and higher satisfaction and efficiency. Second, expert interviews with elementary Chinese language teachers supported the usefulness of the system and informed design principles for LLM-based teaching tools. Overall, the paper concludes that LLMs can support teacher ideation more effectively when they are embedded in structured, interactive workflows that match teachers’ practices rather than used as simple chat interfaces.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed CHI paper with a within-subjects comparison and expert interviews, but it is not an RCT in a classroom setting and the main users were novice teacher participants rather than authentic K-12 classroom implementation. The evidence is therefore qualitative/experimental HCI evidence with some concerns about ecological validity for the target setting.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but modest evidence that the tool improves lesson-planning quality and reduces workload, yet it does not report effect sizes in the provided text and does not evaluate student learning outcomes. The impact is therefore suggestive rather than clearly demonstrated at a medium/large level.

interventions.use_case: LLM-powered teacher-facing system (LitLinker) for ideating interdisciplinary contexts, analyzing reading materials, answering teacher questions, and generating lesson plans for elementary literature instruction; compared against a plain LLM web app baseline.

finding.finding_summary: LitLinker improved the quality of interdisciplinary lesson-plan outputs for elementary Chinese literature teaching relative to a baseline LLM web app. The paper reports that the generated plans had deeper integration of different subjects and were judged against literacy-oriented criteria such as content alignment and educational-objective alignment, but does not provide a numeric effect size in the text excerpt provided.
finding.measure: Expert-rated quality of lesson plans for Chinese literature instruction, including content alignment, alignment with educational objectives, and depth of integration

finding.finding_summary: LitLinker reduced teachers’ workload and was judged more efficient than the baseline LLM web app during interdisciplinary lesson planning. The abstract and study description state that it significantly reduced task workload and increased satisfaction/efficiency, but no numeric effect sizes are reported in the excerpt provided.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX workload ratings; perceived efficiency and satisfaction (SUS-adapted items)

paper_profiles.title: New Curriculum, New Chance – Retrieval Augmented Generation for Lesson Planning in Ugandan Secondary Schools. Prototype Quality Evaluation.
