paper_profiles.venue: Ndejje University Second Annual Research Dissemination Symposium 2024
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This working paper examines whether a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system can produce technically high-quality lesson plans for Ugandan secondary schools under the country’s new competency-based curriculum. The authors frame the problem as one of weak or absent teacher lesson planning, especially in rural settings, combined with the increased burden created by curriculum reform and limited teacher time, materials, and training.

To address this, the team developed the NDU Lesson Plan Generator, a prototype built with Cohere LLM, sentence embeddings, and LangChain. The system retrieves content from government-accredited secondary school textbooks and generates lesson plans in the Ugandan government format. The prototype was trained on three Secondary 1 textbooks: History (and Political Education), Mathematics, and ICT. Twenty-four lesson plans were generated and then rated by three independent raters using an adapted Lesson Plan Analysis Protocol (LPAP) designed for East African competence-based curricula.

The paper reports that the generated lesson plans scored highly overall, averaging about 75–80%, which the authors interpret as “very good” technical quality. They conclude that the RAG system can generate lesson plans that meet the technical standards needed for use in Ugandan classrooms and that its outputs compare favorably with human-written lesson plans in related LPAP-based studies. The authors also note an important limitation: the system can hallucinate when the textbook content is insufficient, so human review is still recommended.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a grey-literature working paper/prototype evaluation using a descriptive technical assessment of 24 generated lesson plans with three raters. It is not a controlled comparative trial in authentic classrooms, so causal evidence is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effect is promising but indirect: high LPAP scores and curriculum alignment suggest potential for reduced teacher workload and improved implementation, but there is no measured student learning or real-world adoption effect. The practical impact is therefore plausible but still unclear.

interventions.use_case: Retrieval-augmented generation system for automatically generating curriculum-aligned lesson plans from government-approved textbooks for Ugandan secondary school teachers.

finding.finding_summary: The prototype was designed to reduce teacher workload by automating lesson-plan creation. In the evaluation of 24 generated lesson plans (n=24), the plans achieved an average LPAP score of 75-80%, suggesting the system can produce lesson plans efficiently while meeting technical quality criteria for direct classroom use.
finding.measure: Lesson Plan Analysis Protocol (LPAP) technical quality score; lesson-plan generation quality

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the RAG-based generator could support implementation of Uganda's new competency-based curriculum by producing aligned lesson plans from approved textbooks. This is presented as facilitating faster and more efficient curriculum rollout across secondary schools, though the study only directly evaluates prototype lesson-plan quality rather than downstream policy outcomes.
finding.measure: Alignment of generated lesson plans to new curriculum and government lesson-plan format

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Instructional Quality: Leveraging Computer-Assisted Textual Analysis to Generate In-Depth Insights from Educational Artifacts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how computer-assisted textual analysis, including natural language processing, machine learning, and large language models, can be used to improve instruction by analyzing educational artifacts. Rather than reporting one new intervention trial, it synthesizes prior work and uses Richard Elmore’s Instructional Core Framework to organize the discussion around three domains: teachers, students, and content.

The paper focuses on several AI-supported workflows relevant to education, including automated analysis of classroom discourse for teacher coaching, generative AI for producing rubric-aligned feedback on lesson segments, automated grading of student work, and human-centered machine learning for evaluating and generating high-quality lesson plans and open educational resources. It emphasizes mixed human-AI approaches such as human-coded transcript analysis, zero-shot prompting with ChatGPT for observation rubrics and coaching suggestions, and teacher/instructional-coach involvement in rubric development and model validation.

The context is K-12 education, especially U.S. elementary and middle-grades mathematics, classroom observation, and teacher professional development. The paper’s main conclusion is cautiously optimistic: AI can help scale feedback, support coaching, and improve curriculum/materials analysis, but its value depends on aligning models with pedagogical goals, using high-quality domain-labeled data, and keeping human expertise in the loop. The paper also highlights ethical concerns, data quality, bias, and the need for tighter integration between educational theory and AI methods.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is primarily a conceptual review with illustrative case studies and summaries of prior work, not a new empirical evaluation with a controlled design. It provides useful synthesis and examples, but the methodology is not strong enough for green/blue evidence classification.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful improvements in instructional coaching and lesson-plan review, but it does not report direct impact estimates from a new study. Reported effects are mostly indirect, descriptive, or drawn from cited studies, so overall impact is unclear to modest.

interventions.use_case: computer-assisted textual analysis and generative AI for teacher lesson-plan feedback, classroom observation scoring, and instructional coaching using transcripts and educational artifacts
ChatGPT-style zero-shot prompting to generate rubric-based coaching feedback, highlights/missed opportunities, and actionable suggestions for teachers
AI/ML analysis of lesson-plan and curriculum artifacts to align instructional materials with quality measures and curricular needs

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI/NLP systems can streamline instructional improvement workflows by automating analysis of classroom discourse, scoring observation rubrics, and screening large collections of lesson plans. In the discussed case studies, automation is presented as lowering cost and increasing speed relative to human coding, but the paper is largely a review and does not report a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: process efficiency, scalability of rubric scoring, and reduction in manual coding/feedback workload

finding.finding_summary: For mathematics instruction, the paper summarizes evidence that AI-assisted analysis can identify accountable talk moves, rubric features, and lesson-plan qualities tied to stronger mathematical reasoning and instructional quality. It also reports that fine-tuned GPT-3.5 outperformed BERT in automatic scoring across six assessment tasks, with an average accuracy gain of 9.1%, though this result is described from a cited study rather than newly run in this paper.
finding.measure: rubric-based observation scores, lesson-plan quality ratings, and automated scoring accuracy for math-related assessment tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper links AI-mediated feedback on teacher discourse and lesson planning to improved instructional quality, higher-order questioning, and better opportunities for student reasoning. These benefits are framed as supporting critical thinking and metacognitive engagement rather than as directly measured student outcomes in the paper itself.
finding.measure: higher-order questioning, instructional quality indicators, and opportunities for student reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that AI-supported textual analysis can democratize access to high-quality feedback and expand classroom observation and lesson-plan review at scale across school systems. It presents this as a pathway toward more consistent, scalable instructional coaching and curricular alignment, while also noting ethical and data-quality constraints.
finding.measure: scalability of instructional coaching, observation systems, and curriculum-quality screening at scale

paper_profiles.title: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to scale expert guidance for novice educators in real time, especially in K-12 tutoring settings where high-quality instructional support is costly and difficult to provide at scale. The authors argue that conventional professional development is too expensive, too static, and often misaligned with the immediate needs of tutors working with students during live instruction.

To address this, they introduce Tutor CoPilot, a human-AI tutoring support system that generates expert-like pedagogical suggestions during live tutoring sessions. The system is integrated into a virtual tutoring platform used by tutors to support math instruction, and it draws on conversation context, lesson topic, and selected instructional strategies to produce guidance. Tutors can also edit, regenerate, or switch strategies, making the workflow interactive rather than fully automated.

The study was a randomized controlled trial with 900 tutors and 1,800 K-12 students from Title I schools in a large southern U.S. district, delivered through an in-school virtual tutoring program in mathematics for grades 3-8. Results show that access to Tutor CoPilot improved student mastery on exit tickets by 4 percentage points overall, with larger gains for lower-rated or less-experienced tutors. Analyses of tutoring language suggest that treatment tutors used more high-quality strategies such as prompting student reasoning and asking guiding questions, while tutors reported the system was helpful but sometimes produced guidance that was not well aligned to grade level.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a preregistered randomized controlled trial with a sizable sample and clear causal identification, which supports strong credibility. There are some concerns about generalizability, attrition/compliance, and reliance on proximal outcomes rather than longer-term standardized achievement, so it falls short of blue.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced a modest but meaningful effect on a priority population: a 4 percentage point increase in math exit-ticket mastery, with larger gains for lower-rated tutors. The effect is practical and scalable, but the absence of larger standardized-test gains keeps it in the modest-impact range.

interventions.use_case: human-AI live tutoring support that generates real-time, expert-like pedagogical suggestions for tutors during K-12 math sessions, including hints, guiding questions, worked examples, and strategy selection
real-time instructional guidance/feedback to tutors on how to respond to student misconceptions and improve tutoring moves during live sessions

finding.finding_summary: In a preregistered randomized controlled trial with 900 tutors and 1,800 K-12 students, students whose tutors had access to Tutor CoPilot were 4 percentage points more likely to pass exit tickets in mathematics than control students (62% to 66%, p<0.01). Conditional on attempting the exit ticket, treatment students were also 3 percentage points more likely to pass (p<0.01).
finding.measure: Math exit ticket pass rate (attempted and unconditional pass outcomes)

finding.finding_summary: Effects were larger for less effective tutors. Students of lower-rated tutors in the treatment group were 9 percentage points more likely to pass exit tickets (56% to 65%) and students of lower-experience tutors were 7 percentage points more likely to pass (61% to 68%) relative to control. This suggests Tutor CoPilot narrowed performance gaps by helping weaker tutors achieve outcomes comparable to stronger peers.
finding.measure: Math exit ticket pass rate by tutor quality rating and tutoring experience

finding.finding_summary: Student survey outcomes did not show statistically significant differences between treatment and control. Measures of whether the tutor cared about understanding, cared about how well the student did in math, and student confidence items were mixed in sign but all non-significant.
finding.measure: Student post-session survey responses on tutor care, perceived support, and confidence in learning math

finding.finding_summary: Tutor CoPilot changed tutor discourse toward higher-quality pedagogical strategies. Using NLP classifiers over 550,000+ messages, treatment tutors were more likely to prompt students to explain and ask guiding questions, and less likely to give away answers or solution strategies; some of these shifts were reported at about 2 standard deviations on the z-scored log-odds scale.
finding.measure: Classifier-based counts of high- and low-quality pedagogical strategies in tutor chat

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed and used as a low-cost support tool, with estimated annual cost of about $20 per tutor based on observed usage. The paper argues this is far cheaper than traditional educator professional development and can scale real-time expertise without requiring extensive off-platform training time.
finding.measure: Estimated annual cost per tutor; usage-based cost analysis

paper_profiles.title: Empowering Educators in AI: Insights from Co-Designing an AI Microcredential with and for K-12 Educators
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what professional learning needs K-12 educators anticipate when integrating AI into their classrooms, and how those needs can inform the design of an AI professional development microcredential. Rather than evaluating an instructional intervention with outcome measures, the study focuses on a co-design process that surfaces educator priorities, concerns, and desired features for AI-focused professional learning.

The authors worked with six participants: four middle school teachers and two instructional coaches/facilitators. Across three one-hour co-design sessions, participants completed semi-structured focus groups and a card-sorting activity to rank professional learning statements (e.g., what they can, want to, will, and need to do). The project produced an initial conjecture map for an Introduction to AI microcredential and iterative revisions based on educator feedback. The microcredential was intended for global use by teachers with varying AI experience and was not tied to a specific AI product.

The main findings emphasize that teachers want AI PD that is ethical, practical, unbiased, standards-aligned, and quick to use. Key themes included the need to teach ethical AI integration, the reality that teacher agency is constrained by district and standards requirements, the desire for unfiltered and critical understanding of AI limitations, the importance of modernizing classrooms on teachers’ own terms, and the need for continuous just-in-time learning rather than one-off sessions. The paper also describes example microcredential activities, including bias exploration with Teachable Machine and scenario-based ethics reflection tasks, as design responses to these themes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative co-design study using focus groups, card sorting, inductive coding, and conjecture mapping. It provides useful design evidence, but it does not test intervention efficacy or include a comparison group.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear relevance for AI professional development design in K-12 settings, but it reports no measurable outcome effect sizes or direct impact on student or teacher performance. Its impact is therefore promising but still indirect and mainly formative.

interventions.use_case: Co-design and development of an AI microcredential for K-12 educators, including short asynchronous modules, AI ethics scenarios, bias exploration with Teachable Machine, and reflection activities to support classroom AI integration.

finding.finding_summary: This is a qualitative co-design/design-research paper focused on building a teacher AI microcredential, not a causal impact study. The paper reports that educator input materially reshaped the course design toward short, actionable, standards-aligned, ethics-focused professional learning resources that can be used across school contexts (n=6 co-design participants, plus anecdotal feedback from n=8 elementary educators on one activity).
finding.measure: Co-design session themes, conjecture map revisions, and qualitative feedback from focus groups/card sorting
finding.study_size: n=6 co-design participants; anecdotal feedback from n=8 elementary educators

finding.finding_summary: Educators repeatedly requested quick, easily accessible, asynchronous learning activities and just-in-time resources that would not add to workload. The resulting microcredential was redesigned to include short videos (less than 5 minutes) and short activities estimated to take less than 15 minutes, indicating a practical efficiency-oriented design response rather than measured productivity gains.
finding.measure: Educator preferences for PD format; design requirements translated into module length and activity duration

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes teacher development of AI literacy, critical evaluation of tools, and reflective judgment about ethical and classroom use of AI. It also reports that teachers wanted resources to help them modernize instruction on their own terms and make informed decisions about AI tool selection and standards alignment, but these are qualitative design findings rather than measured learning gains.
finding.measure: Qualitative themes about AI literacy, agency, and reflective practice

paper_profiles.title: Is a Seat at the Table Enough? Engaging Teachers and Students in Dataset Specification for ML in Education
paper_profiles.venue: CSCW'24 / ACM Conference on Computer-Supported Cooperative Work and Social Computing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines a core challenge in education-oriented machine learning: how to involve teachers and students meaningfully in the upstream specification of datasets, rather than only consulting them after data decisions have already been made. The authors argue that fairness, accountability, transparency, privacy, and utility problems in ML for education are rooted partly in weak understanding of educational context and in the lack of structured stakeholder participation during dataset design.

To study this, the authors ran ten virtual co-design workshops with 40 participants across five roles: ML engineers, teachers, students, designers, and legal/ethics professionals. Using four education ML scenarios (student engagement image classification, student drop-out risk prediction, automated essay grading, and a resume-based career recommendation scenario), participants collaboratively defined dataset motivation, composition, collection, evaluation, and continued-use specifications. The sessions were designed around dataset documentation questions, prompts, and examples drawn from datasheets-style frameworks.

The paper finds that teachers and students contributed crucial contextual knowledge that changed how groups defined relevant variables, labels, collection procedures, validation criteria, and downstream use expectations. Participants frequently moved across the data pipeline to anticipate harms, identify bias and reliability threats, and negotiate trade-offs between predictive performance and educational meaning. The authors conclude that simply including stakeholders is not enough; effective participation requires structured support such as shared standards, information scaffolds, continuous iteration, and explicit mechanisms for co-evaluation across technical and non-technical participants.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative study using co-design workshops, grounded theory coding, and thematic analysis. It provides useful evidence about collaborative ML specification practices, but it does not test an intervention with outcome comparisons or causal identification.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially important institutional implications for how schools and ML teams structure human-AI collaboration, but it does not measure student- or teacher-level impact outcomes. The evidence is conceptual and process-oriented rather than demonstrating direct effects on educational performance or efficiency.

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative co-design study found that teachers and students can meaningfully improve ML data specification by contextualizing dataset composition, collection, labeling, validation, and continued-use decisions for education applications. Across 10 workshops with 40 participants, stakeholders surfaced bias, privacy, consent, and representativeness concerns and proposed structured supports such as continuous iteration, shared data-quality standards, and information scaffolds.
finding.measure: Qualitative themes from 10 co-design workshops; stakeholder recommendations and observed collaborative practices

paper_profiles.title: Task automation and instructional planning support with large language models: a systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews research on the use of large language models (LLMs) in education, with a particular focus on teacher-facing uses such as task automation, instructional planning, content generation, and feedback support. The authors ask whether LLMs reduce the time teachers spend generating educational materials and whether they improve the perceived quality and usefulness of those materials, as well as how they support planning-related tasks compared with traditional human-only workflows.

The review covers peer-reviewed literature published between 2023 and 2025 and includes 16 studies: 13 primary empirical studies and 3 secondary syntheses. The evidence base is concentrated in higher-education settings, though the review also includes mixed settings and one study in informal medical education. The included studies used tools such as ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude, LLaMA, and other LLM-based systems for generating explanations, lessons, assessments, feedback, rubrics, summaries, and instructional materials. Across studies, the reviewed workflows often involved human-in-the-loop use: teachers or users prompted the model, then reviewed, edited, and adapted the outputs before use.

The review finds that LLMs are associated with reported time savings, improved clarity, and perceived usefulness of generated resources, especially for drafting and first-pass feedback. However, the evidence is heterogeneous, often self-reported, and frequently based on small, short-term studies with unclear risk of bias. Major constraints include prompt sensitivity, incomplete or non-exhaustive outputs, hallucinations, privacy concerns, and limited integration into learning management systems. The authors conclude that LLMs can support instructional workflows, but effective use requires pedagogical framing, standardized evaluation, and human oversight rather than fully automated substitution.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review with a transparent search and appraisal process, but the included evidence is mostly qualitative, observational, or quasi-experimental, with heterogeneous measures and several unclear risk-of-bias domains. It is useful for mapping the field, but it does not provide a high-credibility causal estimate.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests modest, mostly perceived benefits for teacher productivity and instructional-material generation, but the evidence is not pooled and does not report a consistent effect size. The likely impact is promising yet still unclear because most studies are small, short-term, and concentrated in higher education.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-facing use of large language models such as ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude, and LLaMA to draft lesson materials, generate explanations, create questions/exercises, produce feedback, and support instructional planning and task automation in educational settings.

finding.finding_summary: Across 16 included studies, LLM-supported workflows were associated with reported reductions in time spent generating educational content and producing teacher feedback, along with perceived gains in usefulness and clarity of outputs. The review does not report a pooled effect size because the underlying evidence was heterogeneous and often self-reported; examples included studies with small samples and short-term deployments, and the authors emphasize that magnitude varies by task and context.
finding.measure: Time saved in content generation, automation of planning/feedback tasks, and perceived usefulness/clarity ratings
finding.study_size: n=16 studies (13 primary empirical, 3 secondary syntheses)

finding.finding_summary: The review found that LLMs were widely used to generate educational content such as lesson plans, slides, study guides, quizzes, explanations, and subject-specific materials across higher-education and teacher-training contexts. Effects were described narratively as improved clarity, usefulness, and pedagogical alignment, but the evidence base was heterogeneous and lacked standardized objective achievement measures.
finding.measure: Perceived quality/usefulness of generated instructional materials and educational content outputs
finding.study_size: n=16 studies (most with small samples; median quantitative sample roughly 70 in the primary empirical studies)

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing U.S. K-12 Competitiveness for the Agentic Generative AI Era: A Framework for Integrating AI in U.S. K-12 Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of how U.S. K-12 education systems can systematically integrate artificial intelligence in ways that improve curriculum, teacher preparedness, and national competitiveness. It frames AI integration as a policy, curriculum, and professional development problem, arguing that current implementation is uneven and that educators often feel underprepared to use AI effectively in classrooms.

The paper does not report a primary intervention study. Instead, it proposes a multi-tiered framework for AI-integrated curriculum development, differentiated teacher professional development, and technical architecture for generative AI tools in educational settings. The framework emphasizes AI literacy competencies across grade levels, modular training pathways for educators, security and privacy safeguards, ethical implementation, and alignment with federal and state policy initiatives.

The context is U.S. K-12 schooling, with comparative references to international examples such as Finland, China, and the United Kingdom. The paper synthesizes cited literature, policy documents, and implementation examples to support its framework. Its main conclusion is that structured, human-centered, and well-resourced AI integration can improve student engagement and computational thinking while maintaining ethical guardrails and supporting teacher upskilling.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is primarily a framework and literature-synthesis paper, not an original empirical study. It reports many quantitative claims from cited sources but does not present a clearly specified new design, sample, or identification strategy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for potentially substantial system-level impact, but the evidence is mostly synthesized, indirect, and not tied to a single rigorous effect estimate. The reported gains are promising, yet they are largely literature-based projections and benchmarks rather than directly demonstrated impacts from the paper itself.

interventions.use_case: System-level framework for integrating generative AI into K-12 curriculum, teacher professional development, and district implementation, including human-centered design, governance, and phased rollout guidance.
Generative AI tools for educational settings discussed as supports for lesson planning, teacher upskilling, and potential classroom use, including prompt engineering and human review of AI outputs.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that structured AI integration frameworks can improve school- and system-level readiness for AI adoption, citing international and domestic benchmarks. Reported figures include 80-90% teacher participation in Finland’s Generation AI project versus 30-40% in U.S. programs, and 42% of schools with formal AI literacy programs. These are synthesized from cited literature rather than generated by a new empirical study.
finding.measure: Teacher participation rates, AI literacy program adoption, implementation readiness indicators

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that AI-supported school implementation is associated with improved teacher productivity and reduced administrative burden, including a cited 57% improvement in lesson planning efficiency and a 42% reduction in administrative task time. These figures are presented as literature-based claims supporting the framework rather than results from a single original experiment.
finding.measure: Lesson planning efficiency, administrative task time, teacher work-life balance

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes evidence that structured AI implementation can improve educator confidence and engagement, reporting a 64% increase in educator confidence from professional development and a 19% enhancement in teacher work-life balance metrics in cited case studies. It also notes 25-35% higher student STEM engagement in schools with structured AI curricula.
finding.measure: Educator confidence, teacher work-life balance, student STEM engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims that structured AI curricula are associated with improved computational thinking and problem-solving, including 40-50% gains in computational thinking scores and 47% higher computational thinking with 52% greater problem-solving proficiency in cited longitudinal work. These outcomes are central to the framework’s argument about AI literacy and future-ready skills.
finding.measure: Computational thinking scores, problem-solving proficiency, critical thinking and AI literacy indicators

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that schools implementing structured AI curricula see stronger STEM-related learning outcomes, including 25-35% higher student STEM engagement and 31% higher student engagement in STEM subjects in cited survey data. It also cites a 27% increase in interest in computer science careers, suggesting broader academic and pathway effects beyond a single subject area.
finding.measure: STEM engagement, interest in computer science careers, digital literacy assessment scores

paper_profiles.title: Factors influencing teachers’ adoption of artificial intelligence tools in K-12 education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Applied Resilience and Sustainability
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what factors influence teachers’ adoption of artificial intelligence tools in K-12 education. It is motivated by the uneven uptake of AI-based instructional tools in schools, despite rapid growth in generative AI, intelligent tutoring systems, learning analytics, and other AI-supported teaching applications. The authors frame adoption as shaped by technological, pedagogical, psychological, institutional, and ethical conditions rather than by technical capability alone.

The study is a systematic literature review conducted under PRISMA 2020 guidelines. It synthesized 47 empirical and theoretical studies published between 2019 and 2025 from major databases including Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and PubMed. The review focuses on teachers in K-12 settings, including in-service and pre-service educators, and considers established acceptance models such as TAM, UTAUT, and TPACK, along with newer constructs such as AI literacy, trust, AI readiness, human-AI collaboration, and ethical AI.

The main conclusion is that teachers’ intention to use AI tools is most strongly shaped by perceived usefulness, ease of use, professional development, institutional support, trust, and ethical concerns. The review also emphasizes that successful AI adoption in schools depends on alignment with pedagogy, curriculum, and policy, as well as continuous training and organizational readiness. It highlights emerging AI applications such as lesson planning, automated grading, adaptive learning, chatbots, and smart classroom systems, but argues that adoption is constrained when these tools are not transparent, trustworthy, or well integrated into school workflows.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic literature review using PRISMA 2020, but it is not a primary causal study and does not estimate intervention effects. The evidence base is synthesized narratively from heterogeneous studies, so credibility is moderate rather than high.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper identifies potentially important adoption drivers for AI use in schools, but it does not demonstrate measured student or teacher outcome gains from an intervention. Its impact is therefore informative for implementation and policy, but the empirical effect on practice is unclear.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of AI adoption factors for K-12 teachers across AI-supported teaching tools, including generative AI, intelligent tutoring systems, learning analytics, automated grading, smart classroom systems, and AI-based professional development.

finding.finding_summary: This PRISMA-based systematic literature review synthesizes 47 studies on teacher adoption of AI tools in K-12 settings rather than testing a single intervention effect. The review concludes that adoption is strongly shaped by institutional support, policy alignment, professional development, AI literacy, ethical concerns, and organizational readiness; it does not report a pooled effect size or experimental outcome estimate.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of adoption factors and implementation conditions across 47 reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that teachers are more willing to adopt AI when it reduces workload, especially for lesson planning, grading, feedback, and routine instructional tasks. These benefits are described as increasing perceived usefulness and effort expectancy, but no pooled effect size is reported because the paper is a qualitative synthesis of prior studies.
finding.measure: Reported teacher perceptions of workload reduction, usefulness, and ease of use across reviewed studies

paper_profiles.title: The role of Artificial Intelligence in Transforming Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This thesis examines how artificial intelligence is transforming higher education, with particular attention to pedagogical practice, student equity, and academic integrity. It asks how AI is changing teaching and learning, and what the implications are for fairness and institutional governance across diverse learning environments. The motivation is the rapid spread of generative AI, learning analytics, intelligent tutoring systems, and other AI tools, alongside concerns about bias, privacy, overreliance, and unequal access.

The study uses a case study of a single university, supported by a literature review, stakeholder surveys, qualitative interviews, document analysis, and analysis of academic performance and administrative efficiency metrics before and after AI integration. The context is higher education rather than school settings: participants include students, faculty, and administrators, with attention to disciplinary differences and digital inequality. The thesis also draws on frameworks such as responsible AI principles, the AI Literacy Heptagon, and the AI Assessment Scale to interpret adoption and governance.

The findings suggest that AI-based tutoring systems, early alert tools, learning analytics, and AI-assisted assessment can improve personalization, efficiency, and some outcomes such as dropout rates and response times. However, adoption varies by discipline and demographic group, and concerns remain about algorithmic bias, academic integrity, and uneven access to infrastructure and digital literacy. The thesis concludes that AI can improve learning and operational workflows when implemented with inclusive policy, ethical oversight, infrastructure support, and training, but that benefits must be balanced against equity risks.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods case study thesis with surveys, interviews, document analysis, and system logs, so it provides qualitative and correlational evidence rather than a controlled experiment. The design is informative but does not meet strong causal credibility criteria for blue or green tiers.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports broadly positive institutional and workflow effects, but the evidence is largely descriptive and no effect sizes are provided. The practical impact appears plausible yet modest and unclear in magnitude at the population level.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI chatbots and course assistants used by students for explanations, feedback, idea generation, writing support, and exam preparation in higher education settings.
AI-based learning analytics and early alert tools used to monitor student activity, predict performance, and reduce dropout risk through intervention signals.
Adaptive tutoring systems used for personalized learning support, student modeling, and step-by-step instructional guidance within university courses.
AI-supported formative assessment and feedback workflows that provide automated or semi-automated feedback on student work and learning progress.

finding.finding_summary: The thesis reports that AI integration improved institutional workflows, with reduced response times and improved administrative efficiency after AI adoption. It also suggests AI enhanced personalization and supported policy development, though outcomes varied by discipline and demographic group.
finding.measure: Administrative efficiency metrics, response times, dropout rates, stakeholder perceptions

finding.finding_summary: AI-based tutoring systems and early alert tools were associated with faster processing and more efficient academic support workflows. The paper specifically states that response times fell and that AI reduced administrative burden in the case university, but no numerical effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Response times, system usage logs, administrative processing time

finding.finding_summary: Student users reported favorable experiences with generative AI for explanations, feedback, and idea generation, suggesting improved engagement and perceived usefulness. However, the paper notes concerns about overreliance, academic integrity, and unequal access, so the overall pattern is positive but uneven.
finding.measure: Survey responses on adoption and perceived usefulness; interviews on student experiences

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can support critical thinking through scaffolding, but also warns that overreliance may undermine critical thinking and higher-order reasoning. This outcome is discussed conceptually and qualitatively rather than with a quantified test measure.
finding.measure: Interview themes and literature synthesis on critical thinking and agency

paper_profiles.title: Empowering Educators with AI: A Review of Google's 'Generative AI for Educators' Free Online Course
paper_profiles.venue: Expertnet: Exploration Journal of Technological Education Trends
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the need for practical, accessible AI training for teachers and evaluates Google’s free online course, “Generative AI for Educators.” The author frames the problem as a gap between the growing promise of AI in education and teachers’ limited readiness, confidence, and support for integrating AI into everyday instructional practice. The review is positioned as a response to the need for educator-focused AI literacy rather than only AI tools for students or general technology training.

The paper analyzes the course content using qualitative content analysis of primary course materials, including lesson plans, AI tool demonstrations, assessment strategies, and instructional design elements, alongside secondary literature on AI in education. The course is described as a self-paced, two-hour online program developed by Google with MIT RAISE, intended for teachers with no prior technical experience. It covers generative AI basics, classroom applications such as lesson planning, feedback, and assessments, prompt writing, and responsible AI use.

The review concludes that the course is useful for improving teacher efficiency, confidence, and practical AI literacy, especially because it is accessible, structured, and aligned with real teaching tasks. At the same time, the paper argues that the course would be stronger with deeper content, more interactive learning, more classroom-specific case studies, stronger ethics and bias training, and continued support after completion. Overall, it presents the program as a promising model for scalable teacher AI training, while noting that long-term impact and broader implementation support remain important needs.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative review/content analysis of a commercial training course rather than an empirical comparison study. It reports no original controlled data, no validated outcome measurement, and no causal design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful potential benefits for teacher efficiency and AI readiness, but the evidence is largely descriptive and self-reported, with no quantified effect sizes or rigorous outcome evaluation. The impact is therefore unclear to modest rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Google's Generative AI for Educators course teaches teachers to use Gemini and similar generative AI tools for lesson planning, assessment creation, feedback drafting, prompt writing, and classroom workflow support.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the course improves educator efficiency by automating routine tasks such as lesson planning, grading, feedback drafting, and administrative work. It reports course statistics that 83% of educators expect to save over two hours per week using AI for routine tasks, and notes that participants reported noticeable time savings and greater confidence in applying AI.
finding.measure: Self-reported time savings, educator confidence, course-reported participant feedback

finding.finding_summary: The review frames the course as a scalable professional development model that can broaden AI literacy and support institutional AI adoption across diverse educator backgrounds. It also highlights accessibility, certification, and post-course support as factors that may strengthen longer-term implementation at school and district levels, though no formal institutional outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative review of course design and implementation potential

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence (AI) has been studied in higher education, where the literature is coming from, how AI is conceptualized, and what ethical or practical concerns are reflected in the published research. The authors systematically reviewed peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2007 and November 2018, identifying 146 studies from an initial pool of 2,656 records.

Rather than evaluating a single intervention, the paper synthesizes the higher-education AI literature across four main application areas: profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment and evaluation, and adaptive systems/personalisation. The review also distinguishes between learner-facing, teacher-facing, and system-facing applications, and considers whether studies address academic support services or institutional/administrative services. Most studies were quantitative and came largely from computer science and STEM fields; relatively few were authored from education departments.

The reviewed studies were predominantly situated in undergraduate contexts, with some at the postgraduate level and some unspecified. The paper concludes that AI in higher education has been used mainly for prediction, automated assessment, feedback, and adaptive support, often with promising technical accuracy. However, the authors argue that the field shows very limited pedagogical grounding and very little critical reflection on ethics, privacy, costs, and broader risks, and they call for stronger educational and ethical perspectives in future research.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review, but it is primarily descriptive and synthesizes heterogeneous primary studies rather than reporting a meta-analysis or a single rigorous experimental design. The underlying evidence base includes many quasi-experimental and observational studies, so credibility is moderate rather than high.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests broad but uneven practical relevance for higher education, especially for prediction, assessment, and tutoring support, but it does not provide pooled effect sizes demonstrating clear medium or large impact. Most findings are promising or operational rather than outcome-transformative, so overall impact appears modest/unclear.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of machine-learning-based student profiling, prediction, and early warning applications in higher education, including dropout risk, admission decisions, course scheduling, student engagement, and academic achievement prediction.

Systematic review of classical intelligent tutoring systems that teach course content, diagnose knowledge gaps, provide automated feedback, curate learning materials, and support collaboration in higher education.
Systematic review of AI systems that generate automated grading and feedback on student work, especially essay scoring, writing feedback, and other assessment-related feedback applications.
Systematic review of adaptive systems and personalized learning environments that recommend content, tailor learning paths, and support teachers and students with adaptive course resources.

finding.finding_summary: The review found that AI applications in higher education were increasingly used for institutional and administrative functions such as admissions, course scheduling, retention, and student services. Across 146 reviewed articles, 48 studies (32.8%) addressed institutional/institutional-administrative uses, suggesting substantial uptake and potential organizational value, although the paper does not report pooled effect sizes.
finding.measure: Descriptive coding of AI application areas across reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: The review repeatedly notes that AI systems were designed to reduce workload and improve efficiency through automated grading, feedback, prediction, and teacher support. Examples include high classification accuracy for admission and dropout prediction (e.g., ANN accuracy 81.19% for dropout prediction in one study; 97.17% accuracy for admission classification in another), but the review itself does not synthesize a single effect size.
finding.measure: Classification accuracy, agreement with human raters, and descriptive synthesis of workload-reduction applications
finding.study_size: n=146 reviewed articles; individual primary studies varied

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed studies targeted student engagement, motivation, and retention, generally with positive or promising results, but the review emphasizes that most studies were short-term pilots and that novelty effects were often not controlled. One cited study on dropout prediction reported ANN accuracy of 81.19% (n=25,224 freshmen) for identifying at-risk students, but this is a predictive performance metric rather than a direct student outcome effect.
finding.measure: Engagement prediction, dropout/retention risk modeling, motivation modeling
finding.study_size: n=146 reviewed articles; individual studies varied

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies limited evidence that AI-supported collaboration and feedback tools may support collaboration, self-regulation, and metacognitive processes, but these studies were few and typically small-scale. Reported findings were mostly positive or satisfactory, yet no pooled effect sizes were available and the authors call for more research on these functions.
finding.measure: Collaboration support, self-regulation, process-oriented learning behaviors
finding.study_size: n=146 reviewed articles; relevant subset much smaller

finding.finding_summary: Automated essay scoring and automated writing feedback were widely studied and often showed high agreement with human raters, but feedback quality concerns remained. For example, the review cites a medical essay grading study with 94.6% to 98.2% agreement between computer classification and human raters, while also noting that more detailed feedback could increase student skepticism about grades and that some feedback may not suit beginning language learners.
finding.measure: Essay scoring agreement, writing feedback quality, revisions
finding.study_size: n=146 reviewed articles; cited primary studies varied

paper_profiles.title: Interacting with educational chatbots: A systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the growing use of educational chatbots and the need to systematically synthesize evidence about how they are designed, deployed, and evaluated in education. The authors argue that prior reviews focused mainly on learning outcomes or broad benefits, but did not sufficiently examine interaction style, platform, educational role, design principles, empirical evidence, and limitations.

To answer these questions, the study systematically reviewed 36 papers published between 2011 and 2021. The review covered chatbots used in educational settings across multiple fields, with most studies involving computer science and general education, and smaller numbers in language learning, mathematics, engineering, and other domains. The reviewed systems were mostly web-based, with some mobile and desktop deployments, and the chatbot roles included teaching agents, peer agents, teachable agents, and motivational agents.

The review concludes that educational chatbots are typically chatbot-driven rather than user-driven, often using flow-based or intent-based interaction. Common design principles include personalized learning, experiential learning, social dialog, collaborative learning, affective learning, learning by teaching, and scaffolding. Empirical studies generally report improved learning, engagement, interest, or satisfaction, although the authors also note limitations such as inadequate training data, weak reliance on usability heuristics, and gaps in design and implementation reporting.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review of 36 prior studies with transparent search and screening procedures, but it is not a single causal study and the underlying evidence is heterogeneous in design and measurement. The review synthesizes mostly experiments, questionnaires, and evaluation studies, but does not itself establish a uniform causal estimate.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests generally positive educational effects, but reported impacts are mostly qualitative or statistically significant without standardized effect sizes, and some findings are mixed. Overall impact appears promising but modest/unclear at the meta level for general school settings.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of educational chatbots/conversational agents used as teaching, peer, teachable, and motivational agents across school and higher-ed learning contexts.
Review includes chatbot systems explicitly described as intelligent tutoring systems, including web-based tutoring agents that present questions, feedback, and adaptive learning paths.

finding.finding_summary: Across reviewed studies, educational chatbots generally improved language-learning outcomes and related language practice, with several experiments reporting better learning or feedback quality. The review notes one foreign-language study where interest in communicating with the chatbot declined over an 8-week period, indicating that effects were not uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Language learning outcomes, post-tests, and engagement in foreign-language chatbot studies

finding.finding_summary: The review includes mathematics-oriented chatbots, including a teachable-agent math system, and reports improved learning in the cited experimental evidence. One listed experiment with the teachable agent (n=183) found statistically significant improvement (p < 0.001) on learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Math learning outcomes / post-test performance

finding.finding_summary: Most reviewed chatbot studies reported improved learning outcomes across computer science, general education, and other subjects. Examples include experiments with n=1000 (p=0.01), n=182 (p < 0.001), n=55 (p < 0.05), and n=126 (p=0.65, still reported as improved learning in the review’s summary table), indicating generally favorable academic effects but with some inconsistency across studies.
finding.measure: Learning outcomes, post-tests, quiz performance, and task completion in computer science/general education contexts

finding.finding_summary: The review found that chatbots often improved subjective satisfaction, engagement, motivation, and interest in learning. Several experiments reported statistically significant gains in engagement (e.g., n=56, p < 0.0001) and interest (e.g., n=28, p < 0.001), while one longitudinal study found declining interest over 8 weeks, suggesting mixed effects over time.
finding.measure: Engagement, interest in learning, subjective satisfaction, motivation surveys
finding.study_size: multiple studies; examples include n=56, n=28, n=34, n=122

finding.finding_summary: The review reports benefits for skills such as argumentation, collaboration, and reflective learning, especially in chatbot-supported collaborative and adaptive writing tasks. For example, one study on adaptive tutoring for writing found students produced more convincing texts and better formal argumentation quality, although the review does not provide a standardized effect size.
finding.measure: Argumentation quality, collaboration in group discussion, reflective learning outcomes

paper_profiles.title: 2020 EDUCAUSE Horizon Report | Teaching and Learning Edition
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report examines major trends shaping higher education teaching and learning and identifies emerging technologies and practices likely to influence institutional strategy. Rather than testing a single intervention, it synthesizes expert panel judgments about social, technological, economic, political, and higher-education trends, and it highlights six emerging areas: adaptive learning technologies, AI/machine learning education applications, analytics for student success, elevation of instructional design/learning engineering/UX design, open educational resources, and XR technologies.

The report specifically discusses how artificial intelligence is already being used in higher education for educational services, curriculum design, feedback on student work, virtual teaching assistant functions, translation, accessibility support, and automation of routine cognitive tasks. It also frames these technologies within broader institutional concerns such as equity, privacy, cost, faculty receptiveness, and learning outcomes. The context is postsecondary education, especially colleges and universities, with examples drawn from institutions in the United States and several other countries.

Its main conclusion is that these technologies and practices have meaningful potential, but they are not effective in isolation; success depends on integration with pedagogy, instructional design, and institutional support. The report emphasizes that institutions should focus less on prediction of adoption timelines and more on understanding the likely impacts, risks, and implementation requirements of these tools within changing higher-education environments.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a Horizon Report, a grey-literature landscape and foresight piece rather than an empirical study. It synthesizes examples and expert judgment, but it does not present a formal research design or causal evaluation of interventions.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The report suggests potentially meaningful institutional and instructional impacts of AI and adaptive learning, but it provides no direct effect sizes or experimental outcome evidence. Because the document is descriptive and speculative, the impact on learners is unclear rather than demonstrably positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: Higher-education landscape report discussing AI/machine learning applications for teaching and learning, including AI-enabled feedback on student work, virtual teaching assistants, chatbots, translation tools, voice assistants, and predictive analytics in student support.
Machine-learning model using SIS and admissions data to predict student grade performance and flag academic risk before courses begin.
Adaptive learning technologies and courseware used for personalized, software-delivered instruction and course redesign.

paper_profiles.title: Augmented visual, auditory, haptic, and multimodal feedback in motor learning: A review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a theoretical review of augmented feedback in motor learning, asking how human- or technology-provided feedback can best support learning and performance in motor tasks. It synthesizes prior research on visual, auditory, haptic, and multimodal feedback, with particular attention to when concurrent feedback helps or hinders learning, and how task complexity changes these effects.

The review covers a wide range of motor-learning contexts, including sports, rehabilitation, and laboratory-based movement tasks. Although it mainly discusses studies with healthy adults, it also notes some rehabilitation studies with patients. The paper does not evaluate a single intervention; instead, it compares feedback strategies such as concurrent versus terminal feedback, feedback frequency, self-controlled feedback, bandwidth and fading schedules, and different visualization or sonification designs.

The main conclusion is that feedback effectiveness depends heavily on task complexity, learner skill level, modality, and display design. Concurrent visual feedback often helps early learning in complex tasks but can impair retention in simple tasks if it creates dependency. Auditory and haptic feedback may reduce visual overload and offer useful alternatives, but their mappings must be intuitive. Overall, the paper argues for carefully designed, task-specific, and modality-appropriate feedback systems that support learning without creating overreliance on the external feedback source.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical review, not an empirical study with a defined experimental design, sample, or causal estimation. It is peer-reviewed academic literature, but it does not provide direct evidence for the requested school-based AI lesson-plan feedback or instructional coaching use case.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not test an intervention in the education domain and reports no measurable effect on the target outcomes. Its relevance to the retrieved topic is only indirect and conceptual, so there is no demonstrable impact on teacher feedback workflows.

interventions.use_case: The paper is a theoretical review of augmented feedback modalities in motor learning, including visual, auditory, haptic, and multimodal feedback systems for sports and rehabilitation training; it does not evaluate an education-specific AI tutoring workflow.

paper_profiles.title: Are We There Yet? - A Systematic Literature Review on Chatbots in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how chatbots have been used in education and what research gaps remain. The authors systematically review prior studies on educational chatbots to identify their objectives, pedagogical roles, mentoring functions, adaptation approaches, and application domains. Rather than testing a single chatbot intervention, the paper synthesizes the literature to map the state of the field.

The review screened 3,619 search results from major academic databases and ultimately analyzed 74 publications. The studies covered a range of educational contexts, mostly in schools and higher education, and involved chatbots used for learning support, administrative assistance, and mentoring. Across the reviewed literature, the most common goals were skill improvement, educational efficiency, student motivation, and availability of support. Chatbots were mainly used in three pedagogical roles: learning, assisting, and mentoring.

The authors conclude that educational chatbot research is still developing and is not yet aligned with the breadth of its stated goals. They argue that evaluations are often too narrow, focusing on usability or acceptance rather than educational outcomes. They also find that mentoring and adaptation capabilities are underexplored, with most adaptive systems limited to quiz contexts. The paper identifies three future challenges: aligning evaluation with implementation objectives, exploring chatbots for mentoring students, and leveraging adaptation more fully.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic literature review, which provides structured synthesis but not direct causal evidence. The paper is peer reviewed and methodologically transparent, yet it does not present primary experimental data or a meta-analysis with pooled effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests potentially meaningful educational and operational uses of chatbots, but the impact is mostly descriptive and the underlying empirical evidence is sparse and heterogeneous. No robust effect sizes are reported, so the practical impact remains unclear to modest.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of educational chatbots used as conversational tutors, assistants, and mentors in schools and higher education; synthesizes applications such as language learning, administrative support, and self-regulated learning coaching.

finding.finding_summary: The review finds chatbots are frequently intended to support motivation, self-regulation, and mentoring, but the empirical literature is thin and uneven. Only 11 publications addressed mentoring roles, with most focused on scaffolding self-regulated learning or life skills; the paper argues evidence is insufficient to conclude strong effectiveness.
finding.measure: Mentoring role categories and reported educational objectives across 74 reviewed publications
finding.study_size: n=74 reviewed publications; n=11 mentoring publications

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies mentoring chatbots as targeting metacognitive and learning-skills outcomes, especially self-regulated learning, but notes that these uses remain limited and not yet comparable to human mentoring. It highlights a gap between the intended support for reflection/planning and the small body of empirical work (n=11 mentoring papers) demonstrating such effects.
finding.measure: Mentoring topics and pedagogical roles extracted from reviewed studies
finding.study_size: n=74 reviewed publications; n=11 mentoring publications

finding.finding_summary: A major objective of educational chatbots in the review is improving efficiency through automation and around-the-clock information access. Across the 74 publications, efficiency of education was the second most common objective (25%), with many examples of administrative, campus, course, and library assistance chatbots reducing routine workload and improving service availability.
finding.measure: Categorized implementation objectives and domain distributions across reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: Language learning is the largest learning-chatbot domain in the review, comprising 19 studies and 53% of the learning-chatbot subset. The paper describes these systems as conversation partners used to practice dialogue, vocabulary, and grammar, but does not report a pooled effect size or controlled outcome estimate.
finding.measure: Domain frequency and qualitative synthesis of language-learning chatbot studies
finding.study_size: n=19 language-learning studies within n=74 reviewed publications

paper_profiles.title: Speculative Futures on ChatGPT and Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Collective Reflection from the Educational Landscape
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper explores the promises and pitfalls of ChatGPT and generative AI in education through a speculative methodology rather than empirical testing. The authors use fictional storytelling and collective reflection to imagine positive and negative future scenarios, with the aim of identifying emerging themes, challenging assumptions, and provoking critical discussion about how AI may reshape educational practice.

The approach is not an intervention study but a conceptual exploration written by a globally diverse group of scholars. The narratives discuss possible uses of conversational AI for personalized learning, feedback, assessment, language support, accessibility, collaboration, and administrative efficiency, while also raising concerns about bias, privacy, academic integrity, inequity, over-reliance, and the possible dehumanization of education.

The paper’s conclusions argue that AI should be integrated into education thoughtfully, ethically, and with human educators remaining central. It emphasizes the need for new AI literacies, updated curriculum and assessment practices, and careful attention to equity, ethics, and context before large-scale adoption of generative AI tools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a speculative, collective reflection article using fictional narratives rather than an empirical evaluation. It does not use a clear experimental, correlational, or qualitative study design to test intervention effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has potentially meaningful conceptual influence on how educators think about AI integration, curriculum, and assessment, but it does not provide measured impact estimates. Its practical impact is therefore plausible but currently unclear and not evidence-quantified.

interventions.use_case: Speculative discussion of ChatGPT and similar generative AI chatbots as educational agents for tutoring, feedback, lesson support, translation, and conversational practice in school and higher education settings.
Generative AI used for writing assistance, language improvement, translation, and text production/editing, including helping students draft essays, improve grammar, and communicate across languages.
AI used to provide immediate feedback on student work and learning progress, including automated grading and response suggestions within the speculative narratives.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can support writing and broader literacy development by giving instant feedback, translation, and language-skill support. In the speculative narratives, AI helps with essay writing, editing, and multilingual access, but no empirical effect size is reported because this is a speculative reflection rather than an evaluative study.
finding.measure: Speculative narrative themes about writing, editing, translation, and language-support tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents conversational AI as beneficial for language learning, especially oral practice, pronunciation, and removing language barriers. Examples include AI-mediated English conversation practice and real-time translation, but the paper provides no quantitative language outcome data or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Speculative narrative themes about oral/written language practice, translation, and pronunciation support

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests generative AI may support some durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and access to alternative ideas, but it also warns that over-reliance may weaken creativity and critical thinking. Because the work is speculative and not empirical, no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Speculative narrative themes about critical thinking, creativity, problem-solving, collaboration, and learner agency

finding.finding_summary: A recurring claim is that ChatGPT can save educators time by drafting lesson plans, summarizing content, generating quiz questions, automating grading, and assisting with routine communication. These are presented as anticipated efficiency gains in the speculative narratives, but the paper reports no measured workload reduction or effect size.
finding.measure: Speculative narrative themes about teacher time savings, grading, planning, summarization, and communication support

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI may require curriculum redesign, new assessment practices, AI literacy, and clearer human/AI role definitions, while also raising concerns about equity, privacy, bias, and academic integrity. The overall institutional impact is framed as significant but contingent and context-dependent, with no empirical estimate reported.
finding.measure: Speculative narrative themes about curriculum integration, assessment reform, AI literacy, ethics, equity, and policy

paper_profiles.title: Early Adopters: Navigating AI Integration in Special Education Teacher Preparation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article addresses how generative AI can be integrated into special education teacher preparation in ways that are practical, ethical, and instructionally useful. The authors argue that AI is reshaping teaching and learning, and they position AI as a tool that can support curriculum alignment, assignment design, lesson and case study generation, assessment development, and reflective coaching.

The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it is a practice-based and reflective conceptual piece grounded in the authors’ experiences as faculty and administrators in teacher preparation programs at two universities in the Northeastern United States. The context includes undergraduate and graduate teacher preparation courses serving both special education and general education candidates, with a particular emphasis on pre-service special educators. Examples include using chatbots for prompt engineering, lesson planning, differentiated supports for learners with disabilities and emergent bilinguals, video-based coaching, and AI-supported formative assessment tools.

The authors conclude that AI can enhance efficiency and personalization in teacher preparation, but only when it is used critically and with strong attention to ethics, bias, transparency, and human judgment. They emphasize that AI-generated outputs should be treated as starting points rather than final products, and that faculty expertise remains essential for contextualizing instructional decisions, especially in special education settings. The article also highlights the need for future research on AI’s impact on educator preparation and student learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/practice-oriented article with no clear empirical study design, no comparison group, and no reported quantitative outcomes. It is peer-reviewed, but it is not intervention research and provides primarily descriptive examples and professional recommendations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report measurable impacts or effect sizes on learner or teacher outcomes. Its contribution is conceptual and descriptive rather than evidence of demonstrated impact.

interventions.use_case: generative AI chatbots and LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) used by teacher educators and teacher candidates to draft and refine course outcomes, lesson plans, case studies, prompts, and reflective coaching questions in special education teacher preparation

AI-assisted feedback/coaching tools for teacher reflection and assessment, including video-based coaching (e.g., Vosaic AI Mate) and instructional writing/discussion support (e.g., Packback) that generate time-stamped feedback, prompts, and performance annotations

AI-supported writing and language assistance for drafting rubrics, lesson objectives, assessments, and student writing/discussion scaffolds, including support for prompt engineering and revision of AI-generated text

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that generative AI substantially reduced faculty time spent on curriculum alignment, syllabus/lesson drafting, rubric creation, and feedback generation in special education teacher preparation. No quantitative effect size is reported, but the authors repeatedly describe substantial time savings and offloading of lower-order tasks (e.g., course design, prompt-based revision, video annotation) that allowed more time for higher-level instructional work.
finding.measure: Perceived faculty workload/time savings and efficiency in curriculum design, lesson development, and feedback/coaching

finding.finding_summary: AI-supported tools such as Packback, Vosaic AI Mate, and Otter.ai are presented as ways to scale feedback, annotation, transcription, and assessment analysis. The paper does not report experimental data, but it clearly claims these tools reduce instructor workload and increase efficiency in providing real-time or time-stamped coaching, discourse support, and qualitative data analysis.
finding.measure: Faculty and teacher-candidate workload reduction; speed of annotation, transcription, and feedback generation

finding.finding_summary: The article emphasizes improved prompt engineering, critical evaluation of AI outputs, reflective practice, and pedagogical documentation as key skills developed through AI use. Although no quantitative outcomes are reported, the authors describe teacher candidates becoming more sophisticated at crafting contextualized prompts and using AI to support analysis, reflection, and revision.
finding.measure: Prompt quality, reflective ability, and critical analysis of AI outputs

finding.finding_summary: The paper is primarily a conceptual/practice article arguing that AI adoption can reshape special education teacher preparation, assessment norms, and ethical protocols. The authors highlight institutional needs for transparent AI policies, consent procedures, bias mitigation, and shifts toward pedagogical documentation, but they do not provide outcome data.
finding.measure: Institutional policy, ethical norms, and teacher-preparation practice change

paper_profiles.title: Learning with, rather than through, AI: co-designing science education for critical AI literacy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This opinion paper addresses how generative AI, especially tools like ChatGPT, is changing science education and science communication. The central question is not whether AI should be used in schools, but how teachers can keep students engaged in critical thinking, ethical reasoning, and disciplinary understanding when AI can instantly provide answers, explanations, and writing support.

The paper argues for a shift from learning through AI to learning with AI. It proposes that teachers should treat generative AI as a classroom tool to be used deliberately, with students learning to question outputs, verify claims, and reflect on bias, misinformation, and academic integrity. The author emphasizes teacher agency, human judgment, and participatory pedagogy, where students help co-design norms for ethical AI use.

The context is mainly science education, especially high school classrooms, though the discussion is conceptual rather than based on a new empirical intervention. Examples include using ChatGPT for pre-lesson explanations, critique of AI-generated answers, debate activities, and guided reflection. The conclusion is that AI should augment, not replace, teachers, and that critical AI literacy should become part of science curricula so students can engage responsibly and thoughtfully with AI-rich learning environments.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a 2025 opinion article and not an empirical study. It offers conceptual arguments and cites other work, but it does not present a new research design, sample, or original outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has potentially meaningful influence on practice and policy by framing how teachers should integrate generative AI, but it does not demonstrate measured impact in a study sample. Its practical implications are broad yet remain theoretical rather than evidenced in this article.

interventions.use_case: Discusses ChatGPT and similar generative AI chatbots as classroom knowledge brokers, student explanation tools, and teacher assistants for drafting quizzes, worksheets, lesson plans, and feedback; emphasizes guided, critical use in science education.

finding.finding_summary: This opinion piece argues that generative AI can either undermine or strengthen durable skills depending on how it is used. The article cites prior studies and reports suggesting possible reductions in critical thinking and brain engagement with uncritical ChatGPT use, while advocating structured classroom use to promote metacognition, evidence evaluation, and critical AI literacy; no new effect size is reported in this paper.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognition, and evidence-evaluation skills discussed conceptually; no direct empirical measure in this paper

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can support scientific reasoning when students use ChatGPT to explain concepts, detect errors, and critique AI-generated responses, but can also weaken reasoning if students outsource thinking to the tool. This is an opinion/review piece and does not report a primary empirical effect size or sample for scientific reasoning outcomes.
finding.measure: Scientific reasoning, conceptual understanding, error detection in science tasks; discussed through classroom examples
