finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that teachers who use AI say it saves time on tasks such as preparing worksheets, quizzes, and lesson plans, and that it can improve the quality of adapting materials and providing feedback. The article cites a report in which about 80% of U.S. teachers using AI said it saved time and about 60% said it improved their work quality, but those figures are secondary citations rather than original study results in this paper.
finding.measure: Teacher time savings and perceived quality of planning/adapting materials and feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central contribution is normative and institutional: it argues for ethical AI integration, guided-use policies, and participatory pedagogy in science education. It does not estimate a quantitative institutional effect, but it frames AI literacy and teacher agency as system-level responses to widespread student access to generative AI.
finding.measure: Policy and pedagogical recommendations for school/institutional AI integration

paper_profiles.title: STEM Application in Education: Implication of STEM Computational Paradigm on Employment Prospects
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science, Management and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses the role of STEM education and computational thinking in preparing learners for employment in an increasingly automated digital economy. It frames artificial intelligence, machine learning, cloud computing, and related technologies as part of a broader STEM computational paradigm that is reshaping education, work, and sustainable development. Rather than evaluating a specific classroom intervention, the article surveys and synthesizes prior literature and workforce statistics to argue that STEM competencies are central to employability, innovation, and national development.

A substantial portion of the paper focuses on how ChatGPT and other generative AI tools can support teaching and learning. The authors describe ChatGPT as a writing coach, a tool for generating questions, supporting peer review, scaffolding communication, and helping teachers promote critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, and problem-solving in STEM instruction. The discussion is presented at a conceptual level, with examples of how educators might use generative AI to support lesson activities and student skill development.

The paper is not an empirical study of a defined sample of teachers or students; instead, it is a theoretical and exploratory review drawing on published sources from 2022–2024 and on labor-market data. The main conclusion is that technology, including generative AI, can strengthen STEM education and support sustainable development goals, but successful use requires improved teacher preparation, access to instructional resources, and attention to digital divide and ethical concerns. The article especially emphasizes the importance of preparing teachers to integrate computational thinking and AI-supported pedagogies across subjects.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative, exploratory review/opinion piece rather than a primary empirical study. It does not report a clear evaluation design, comparison group, or original outcome data for the AI intervention discussed.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No measurable intervention effect is reported, so there is no evidence of impact size on learning, teaching, or institutional outcomes. The paper is conceptual and theoretical, not an outcomes study.

interventions.use_case: Descriptive discussion of ChatGPT as a writing coach and classroom support tool for teachers and students, including generating questions, outlines, feedback on drafts, and support for critical thinking, peer review, and communication in STEM learning.

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint examines how pre-service elementary science teachers think about and plan to use ChatGPT in lesson planning for science instruction. The paper addresses a gap in empirical research on generative AI in education by moving beyond visionary claims and analyzing concrete lesson plans produced by future teachers. The central question is how ChatGPT can be integrated into science lessons, what kinds of science content and pedagogical strategies it supports, and what benefits and concerns pre-service teachers associate with its use.

The study involved 29 pre-service elementary teachers from a Korean university. After a short instructional sequence introducing ChatGPT, discussing its educational potential, reviewing science teaching methods, and practicing lesson-plan writing, participants created lesson plans for a 45-minute elementary science class that incorporated ChatGPT. They also answered open-ended survey questions about their design choices, perceived usefulness of ChatGPT, and concerns about its use. The lesson plans were evaluated with a modified TPACK-based rubric focusing on curriculum goals, instructional strategies, function selection, and overall fit.

Results showed that the participants envisioned ChatGPT being used across multiple science domains, especially biology, chemistry, earth science, physics, and environmental science, and across several instructional approaches such as cooperative learning, Predict-Observe-Explain, learning cycle, analogy generation, experimentation, and concept mapping. Overall rubric scores were moderately high, but the teachers were less strong at selecting the most appropriate ChatGPT functions than at aligning ChatGPT with goals and strategies. Qualitatively, participants saw ChatGPT as useful for questioning, individualized support, and formative feedback, but worried about inaccurate output and student over-dependence. They proposed safeguards such as using multiple information sources, teacher mediation, and structured peer interaction. The paper concludes that pre-service teachers can imagine broad pedagogical uses of generative AI, but they need further professional development to use it critically and appropriately in science teaching.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/descriptive study of lesson plans and survey responses from 29 pre-service teachers, with no experimental comparison or student learning outcome measurement. It provides useful exploratory evidence, but methodological rigor is limited for causal claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful applications of ChatGPT for science lesson planning and individualized support, but it does not demonstrate measured gains in student performance. The impact is therefore plausible but unquantified and modest/unclear.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used in pre-service elementary science teachers' lesson planning as a generative AI tool to support questioning, role-play scripting, individualized learning support, and formative feedback in science lessons.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that 29 pre-service elementary science teachers believed ChatGPT could support scientific inquiry, prediction/explanation, concept development, and formative assessment in science lessons. Their lesson plans received a mean TIAR score of 3.29/4 (SD=0.91), with the strongest area being instructional strategies & ChatGPT (M=3.48, SD=0.99) and high scores for curriculum goals & ChatGPT (M=3.44, SD=0.87), suggesting generally strong perceived alignment with science instruction.
finding.measure: Modified TPACK-based Technology Integration Assessment Rubric (TIAR) applied to lesson plans; qualitative analysis of science lesson-plan design and survey responses

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers anticipated ChatGPT would strengthen critical thinking through consecutive questioning, comparison of sources, and structured reflection. The paper also reports that teachers saw value for collaboration and role-based learning (e.g., cooperative learning, role play), but these were design intentions rather than measured student outcomes.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses and lesson-plan content coding

finding.finding_summary: Participants expected ChatGPT to increase motivation, interest, and self-directed learning, but they also expressed concerns that students could become over-dependent on the tool or develop misconceptions from inaccurate responses. The evidence here is based on perceptions and lesson-plan intentions rather than observed student outcomes.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses; thematic coding of perceived benefits and concerns

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers viewed ChatGPT as a way to provide individualized support, summarize lengthy student-generated ideas, and assist with lesson-planning tasks like role-play scripting and feedback. This is an anticipated productivity gain in instructional design and classroom management, not a measured efficiency outcome.
finding.measure: Lesson-plan analysis and survey responses about perceived utility

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can function as a teacher coach by producing automated feedback on classroom instruction. The authors focus on three coaching tasks: scoring transcript segments using classroom observation rubrics, identifying instructional highlights and missed opportunities, and generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

The study evaluates ChatGPT in a zero-shot setting using the NCTE transcript dataset, which contains elementary mathematics classroom transcripts from U.S. schools. The quantitative component compares ChatGPT’s rubric scores against expert human ratings on selected CLASS and MQI observation items. The qualitative component asks experienced math teachers to judge the model’s feedback on relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty.

The findings suggest that ChatGPT can produce responses that are often relevant and sometimes actionable, but it struggles to provide accurate, insightful, and novel coaching. Score predictions correlate weakly with human ratings, and many generated suggestions simply restate what teachers already do in the transcript. The paper concludes that current generative AI may complement, but cannot replace, expert instructional coaching, and that future work should focus on reducing hallucinations and improving feedback quality with educator involvement.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical paper with a clear evaluation protocol, but it is primarily a qualitative/benchmarking study with small human-evaluation samples and no randomized design or causal identification. The evidence is useful for feasibility assessment, but not strong causal evidence of impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows current zero-shot ChatGPT coaching has limited performance and therefore no demonstrated positive educational impact yet. Any practical impact is unclear and likely modest at present, especially since the study measures model quality rather than student or teacher outcomes.

interventions.use_case: zero-shot use of ChatGPT as an automated teacher coach to score classroom transcript segments, identify highlights and missed opportunities, and generate actionable suggestions for eliciting student mathematical reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that ChatGPT is not yet reliable as a teacher-coaching tool for operationalizing classroom observation and feedback. Across CLASS and MQI scoring tasks, correlations with human ratings were low (e.g., CLBM r=0.35, CLPC r=0.00, EXPL r=0.02, SMQR r=0.17 under direct-answer prompting), indicating limited alignment with expert scoring and suggesting substantial current workflow burden if used in practice.
finding.measure: Spearman correlation between ChatGPT-predicted observation scores and human ratings; qualitative ratings of feedback relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty
finding.study_size: n=100 segments for scoring; n=216 CLASS examples and n=288 MQI examples for highlights/missed opportunities; n=36 suggestion examples

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teacher-facing generative AI can help teachers personalize mathematics problems for students’ interests, and whether having the teacher “in-the-loop” is efficient and effective. The central question is how teachers interact with ChatGPT when modifying existing curriculum problems, what kinds of prompting moves they use, and how students respond to the resulting personalized tasks.

The study involved seven middle school mathematics teachers who used GPT-4o/ChatGPT to personalize problems from the Illustrative Mathematics curriculum. Teachers began with a two-hour training on personalization, student interests, bias, readability, and cultural relevance, then worked in short Zoom sessions with researchers while their ChatGPT interactions were logged. They modified 143 problems for 521 seventh-grade students in six U.S. schools, and students provided both closed-ended ratings and open-ended feedback on the assignments.

Findings show that teachers mainly prompted ChatGPT to adjust the broad popular-culture topic or to add/swap specific references, while also spending substantial effort improving realism, numerical plausibility, age fit, and readability. Students generally preferred narrower, more specific cultural references, but they cared less about realism than about whether the reference matched their own interests. Teacher prompting in the “3–5 prompt” range was associated with higher student ratings, yet personalizing a single problem still took about four minutes on average and did not become clearly faster over time. The authors conclude that teacher-in-the-loop personalization supports professional learning and quality control, but it is still time-consuming and tends to produce broader-grained personalization than many students want.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/observational design with descriptive and correlational analyses of teacher prompting and student feedback, not a randomized or quasi-experimental causal design. It is methodologically detailed and empirical, but it provides exploratory evidence rather than high-causality evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful but unclear effects: student interest ratings were modest and teacher efficiency gains were not demonstrated. There is some positive signal for task personalization quality, but the overall impact on learning or efficiency appears limited and mixed.

interventions.use_case: teacher-in-the-loop use of ChatGPT/GPT-4o to personalize existing middle school mathematics problems to students' interests and improve task context personalization
ASSISTments delivery of the personalized math assignments and collection of student ratings/feedback on the tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily studies how generative AI was used to personalize middle school mathematics problems, not student achievement. Across 143 personalized problems given to 521 7th graders, students rated the tasks moderately on interestingness and closeness (overall means 2.46 and 2.53 on a 5-point scale), and ratings improved from Unit 4 to Unit 6 (interestingness 2.27 to 2.56; closeness 2.28 to 2.66; B=0.33, SE=0.095, p=0.0012).
finding.measure: Student 1-5 ratings of task interestingness and closeness to students' interests; math problem personalization quality

finding.finding_summary: Student responses showed that personalized tasks were sometimes interesting when they matched preferred popular culture references, but many students still found them uninteresting or irrelevant. The strongest positive reaction came from finer-grained specific references, while broad-topic personalization often failed to match individual preferences; the paper reports 163 responses implying interest vs 243 implying not interested.
finding.measure: Open-ended student feedback on interest/liking and perceived match to personal interests; 1-5 interest ratings
finding.study_size: n=521 students; 454 responses to interest question

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-facing GenAI personalization was not especially time efficient. Teachers used 558 prompts to create 143 problems, averaging 3.2 prompts per problem and about 246 seconds per problem (SD=165.7), and the authors found no clear evidence that time decreased with experience; in fact, Unit 6 took longer than Unit 4 (286 vs 204 seconds per problem; B=70.4, p=0.0189).
finding.measure: Time per personalized problem; number of prompts per problem; mixed-effects regression on time and prompting

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Scores: Explainable Intelligent Assessment Strengthens Pre-service Teachers’ Assessment Literacy
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '26 (Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that pre-service teachers often struggle to interpret diagnostic assessment outputs and translate them into instructional decisions. The authors argue that traditional assessment tools present opaque scores or technical parameters, which can hinder reflection, self-regulation, and the development of assessment literacy. To address this, they design XIA, an explainable intelligent assessment platform that combines statistical diagnostic information with visualized reasoning, contrastive explanations, and counterfactual explanations.

The paper includes two components of empirical work. First, the authors conducted formative interviews with seven in-service teachers in China to identify the kinds of assessment information teachers value and to derive design requirements for the system. Second, they evaluated XIA in a single-session pre-post controlled study with 21 pre-service teachers, using quantitative tasks, questionnaires, and semi-structured interviews. The participants were teacher candidates rather than practicing teachers, and the substantive evaluation centered on teacher-facing assessment reasoning rather than student learning outcomes.

Findings suggest that teachers wanted item-level and class-level information such as question difficulty, typical error patterns, and whether items exceeded curricular scope, but they also wanted to understand why the system reached its conclusions. The XIA interface appeared to support reflection, assessment awareness, and self-regulation, and was associated with more accurate judgments and fewer assessment errors. Overall, the paper concludes that explanatory scaffolding can bridge assessment theory and classroom practice by helping teachers move from score-based judgments to evidence-based reasoning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/formative design study plus a small pre-post controlled evaluation, not a randomized controlled trial. It provides useful preliminary evidence, but the small sample and mixed methods limit causal strength and generalizability.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports promising but preliminary benefits for a priority population (pre-service teachers), with no quantified medium or large effect size in the text provided. Its likely impact is meaningful for design knowledge, but the empirical impact on outcomes is still unclear.

interventions.use_case: explainable intelligent assessment platform for teacher-facing assessment literacy support, using cognitive diagnostic modeling with contrastive and counterfactual explanations and decision-support dashboards
formative teacher-facing intelligent assessment tooling with visualized diagnostic reasoning and natural-language teaching suggestions

finding.finding_summary: In a single-session pre-post controlled study with 21 pre-service teachers, the XIA explainable assessment platform was associated with improved components of assessment literacy, especially reflection, self-regulation, and assessment awareness. The paper also reports more accurate judgments and smaller assessment errors after exposure to the system, but does not provide a numerical effect size in the text provided.
finding.measure: pre-post assessment literacy tasks, questionnaires, and semi-structured interviews; judgment accuracy and assessment errors

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed to help pre-service teachers interpret assessment data more efficiently by surfacing item-, class-, and knowledge-level cues rather than only raw scores. The paper suggests this reduced search effort and supported faster translation of diagnostic results into instructional decisions, but no quantitative efficiency metric is reported.
finding.measure: teacher interpretation and decision-support usability in the pre-post study and formative design analysis

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary students and teachers perceive a generative AI-powered learning activity for creative mathematical writing. The authors focus on whether GenAI can support students in generating, revising, and enriching math stories while also helping teachers observe students’ understanding, creativity, and misconceptions.

The intervention used a three-step classroom activity called Ask, Represent, and Transform. Students first analyzed story-based math prompts, then represented their thinking visually, and finally used a GenAI system built with GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 to co-create culturally relevant math stories. The study was implemented in six 5th-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools with 79 students and six elementary teachers. Data came from student focus groups, teacher interviews, open-ended surveys, and classroom observations, and were analyzed thematically.

Findings suggest that GenAI-supported mathematical writing can foster creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, interest in learning, curiosity, and ownership. At the same time, both students and teachers identified challenges such as weak critical evaluation of AI output, limited opportunities for independent creation, lack of adaptive pedagogical feedback, reduced social interaction, and accessibility gaps. The paper concludes that GenAI can be educationally valuable in elementary math writing, but only if designers intentionally balance AI support with opportunities for student agency, peer interaction, and teacher guidance.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative thematic analysis of classroom interviews, open-ended survey responses, and observations rather than an experiment. It provides rich descriptive evidence but does not establish causal effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests potentially meaningful benefits for a priority K-12 population, but it reports perceptions rather than measured learning gains and provides no effect sizes. The practical impact is promising but still unclear in magnitude.

interventions.use_case: GenAI-powered classroom tool for creative mathematical writing where 5th-grade students input math goals, characters, settings, and events, and GPT-4 generates story drafts with DALL·E 3 images; students then revise and evaluate the AI-generated stories.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and students reported that the GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing activity helped students understand fraction-based math problems, represent mathematical ideas, and uncover misconceptions. The study is qualitative with 79 5th-grade students and 6 teachers across six classrooms, so no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student and teacher perceptions from semi-structured interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations about mathematical understanding and problem representation

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that working with GenAI made math learning more interesting, sparked curiosity, and increased ownership over learning. Students described the activity as fun and motivating, and teachers observed higher attention and engagement during the math story-writing tasks.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership from interviews, survey responses, and observations

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that GenAI-supported story writing promoted creativity, divergent and convergent thinking, flexible thinking, original creation, and AI literacy/prompt engineering. Students learned to iteratively refine prompts and critically evaluate AI outputs, but the study is qualitative and does not report quantitative effects.
finding.measure: Perceptions of creativity, prompt engineering, critical evaluation of AI output, and flexible problem solving from interviews and observations

finding.finding_summary: Although the main academic focus was mathematics, the activity required students to produce and revise creative written stories, and participants said AI helped them draft, expand, and improve those stories. The paper does not report standardized writing outcomes or effect sizes, but it substantively studies writing-related classroom experiences.
finding.measure: Perceptions of creative writing quality, story drafting, and revision during math-story composition

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Primary Teacher Training through Academic Portfolios in Advanced Mathematics Courses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines a persistent challenge in primary teacher education: the gap between advanced mathematical theory and the practical knowledge future primary teachers need for classroom instruction. The authors ask whether academic portfolios can serve as a purpose-driven assessment method that helps preservice teachers connect abstract mathematics content to teaching practice, while also improving engagement, assessment quality, and anxiety related to mathematics.

The intervention was implemented in two advanced mathematics courses, Algebra and Number Systems I and II, within the primary teacher education program at Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile. The portfolio approach was introduced through a negotiated learning contract between instructors and teacher candidates, structured rubrics, reflective writing, draft-and-feedback cycles, presentations, and discussion tables. The participants were 37 female preservice teachers in their ninth and tenth semesters, all specializing in mathematics education and concurrently completing professional teaching practice.

Using attendance records, grade trends, platform analytics, self-assessments, peer evaluations, and reflective texts, the study reports increased attendance, stronger engagement, improved grades, and more positive perceptions of learning and organization. Participants also reported that portfolios helped them connect course content to teaching, support self-regulated learning, and reduce mathematics anxiety. The paper concludes that academic portfolios may be a useful way to strengthen mathematics teacher preparation, though the authors note that causal claims are limited by the study design and that more rigorous, larger-scale research is needed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-site, mixed-methods, pre/post descriptive study with no control group or random assignment. It provides useful practice-based evidence, but the causal credibility is limited and outcomes rely partly on self-report and observational trends.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported improvements are promising but appear modest and are not supported by causal effect sizes. The study focuses on a small preservice teacher sample in one university setting, so generalizable impact is unclear.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports improved performance in two primary-teacher mathematics courses after introducing academic portfolios. In MAT2920, the average grade increased from 4.43 in the prior semester to 5.89 when portfolios were introduced, and later to 6.44; in MAT2925, grades rose from 5.52 to 5.80 and then 6.44. These are descriptive, uncontrolled semester-to-semester comparisons rather than causal estimates.
finding.measure: Course grades on the Chilean 1.0–7.0 scale in Algebra and Number Systems I and II

finding.finding_summary: Teacher candidates reported better engagement, increased intrinsic motivation, and reduced mathematics anxiety after portfolio implementation. On the end-of-semester survey, 11 of 12 respondents (91.7%) said alternative assessment methods such as portfolios helped mitigate math-anxiety-related feelings, and all participants reported strong time investment and positive alignment between effort and grades.
finding.measure: Self-assessment survey responses on motivation, engagement, and mathematics anxiety
finding.study_size: n=12 survey respondents for anxiety item; n=37 participants overall

finding.finding_summary: The portfolio process was associated with stronger self-regulation, time organization, reflection, and peer-evaluation skills. In self-reports, 100% of respondents said portfolios improved time organization and 85.7% reported gains in self-study; peer review and reflective paragraphs were used to support metacognitive engagement and critical assessment of classmates' work.
finding.measure: Self-assessment surveys, peer evaluation surveys, and reflective portfolio paragraphs
finding.study_size: n=37 overall; n=12 survey respondents for some items; n=7 peer-evaluation subgroup

paper_profiles.title: Moroccan pre-service elementary teachers: attitudes toward STEM education and mobile devices
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines Moroccan pre-service elementary teachers’ attitudes toward integrated STEM education and toward using mobile devices to support STEM projects in elementary school. The study is motivated by Morocco’s recent curriculum revisions, which introduced integrated STEM education and encouraged ICT/mobile device use in elementary teaching, but require teachers to be prepared and willing to implement these changes.

The authors surveyed 226 Bachelor of Education Elementary Specialty (BEES) students from two Moroccan universities using an online questionnaire. The study focused on second- and third-year pre-service teachers, since first-year students had not yet received the full pedagogy training. The questionnaire measured attitudes toward integrated STEM education and toward mobile devices in that context, and the authors also tested whether attitudes differed by gender, grade level, or pre-university background (scientific vs literary baccalaureate).

Findings showed that participants generally believed integrated STEM education is important, but they lacked confidence in their ability to implement it and were uncertain about how much they would enjoy doing so. In contrast, attitudes toward mobile devices were positive overall, with participants expressing willingness to use them in STEM teaching. Gender and grade level were not associated with attitudes for either topic, but pre-university background mattered for STEM attitudes: students with a scientific baccalaureate were more positive and more confident than those with a literary background. The study concludes that BEES programs should strengthen theoretical and practical preparation for integrated STEM teaching and help future teachers connect content knowledge, pedagogy, and technology.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-site correlational survey study using a convenience sample and self-report questionnaire, with Mann-Whitney comparisons but no experimental manipulation. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically transparent, but it does not meet causal-design standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports attitudes and readiness rather than observed learning or implementation outcomes, so the practical effect on schooling is indirect and uncertain. Its implications are institutionally relevant for teacher preparation, but the measured impact is modest and not demonstrated empirically.

interventions.use_case: Survey of Moroccan pre-service elementary teachers’ attitudes toward integrated STEM education and the use of mobile devices in STEM teaching; the paper evaluates readiness and perceptions rather than a functioning AI tool.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds generally positive attitudes toward using mobile devices in integrated STEM education (overall M=3.91/5, n=226). Respondents especially endorsed willingness to use tablets/smartphones to mentor STEM projects and to recommend their use in schools, suggesting perceived usefulness and adoption readiness rather than measured performance gains.
finding.measure: Attitudes toward the use of mobile devices in integrated STEM education (Likert questionnaire; perceived usefulness, ease of use, enjoyment, intention to use)

finding.finding_summary: Attitudes toward integrated STEM education were neutral overall (M=2.92/5, n=226), with teachers agreeing on its importance (M=4.15) but disagreeing on self-confidence to implement it (M=2.08). This suggests positive value beliefs but low readiness and confidence for classroom implementation.
finding.measure: Attitudes toward integrated STEM education; dimensions of importance, enjoyment, and self-confidence (Likert questionnaire)
finding.effect_size: r=0.39 for scientific vs literary baccalaureate difference on overall STEM attitude; other reported comparisons non-significant

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies a training and curriculum gap in Moroccan elementary teacher preparation: second- and third-year BEES students had no significant differences by grade level in STEM or mobile-device attitudes, implying the program had not yet shifted readiness. The authors recommend adding theoretical courses and practical workshops, and adapting the curriculum to reduce inequities tied to pre-university pathways.
finding.measure: Differences in attitudes by gender, grade level, and pre-university studies; implications for teacher preparation and curriculum design

paper_profiles.title: Pre-service Teachers’ Perception of using Mobile Devices in Teaching Climate Change in Primary Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines pre-service teachers’ perceptions of using mobile devices to teach climate change in primary schools. The authors motivate the study by arguing that climate change education and disaster awareness are increasingly important, especially for children in erosion- and flood-affected areas of Nigeria, and that mobile technologies could help make climate change learning more active, contextual, and participatory.

The study surveyed 150 second-year pre-service teachers from two Colleges of Education in southeastern Nigeria. The paper asks whether mobile devices can create climate-change awareness, help reduce climate-change devastations, and whether the pre-service teachers themselves are competent in using mobile devices. Data were collected with a questionnaire and analyzed descriptively using mean scores.

The findings suggest that participants believed mobile devices could enhance awareness, support information sharing, and help children respond during emergencies, thereby contributing to climate-change risk reduction. However, the pre-service teachers reported limited competence in using mobile devices for teaching, and the study concludes that teacher education programs should incorporate mobile technology training and strengthen ICT implementation in the curriculum.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive survey study using self-reported perceptions from a purposive sample of pre-service teachers, not an experimental or quasi-experimental design. It provides useful context but limited causal credibility and limited generalizability beyond the sampled colleges.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for climate-change awareness and emergency preparedness, but it reports perceptions rather than demonstrated learning gains or behavioral outcomes. No effect sizes are reported, so the practical impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: Use of mobile devices (phones, smart phones, cameras, PDAs) by pre-service teachers and primary pupils to teach climate change awareness, collect and share photos, store/retrieve information, and support emergency alerting and collaboration in primary school lessons.

finding.finding_summary: This survey study reports that pre-service teachers believed mobile devices would support climate change teaching in primary schools, with a grand mean of 3.27 on awareness/learning items. Respondents agreed the devices could create deeper awareness (mean=3.6), enable knowledge building (mean=3.5), help pupils share information (mean=3.14), and support active participation in climate change interventions.
finding.measure: Likert-scale perception survey on climate change awareness, knowledge construction, information sharing, and participation

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames mobile-device use as supporting collaboration, observation, conversation, reflection, and knowledge construction, which are treated as durable learning skills. Pre-service teachers also agreed that mobile devices would change patterns of learning/work activities (mean=2.92) and enable anytime/anywhere learning (mean=3.2).
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey items on collaboration, reflection, knowledge building, and learning patterns

finding.finding_summary: The study found strong perceived value for mobile devices in climate-change teaching, but also a clear institutional readiness gap: pre-service teachers lacked competence in using mobile devices, with a grand mean of 2.19 on competence items. They owned devices (mean=3.86) but reported that colleges did not provide devices, teach with them, or train them to design lessons using them, suggesting implementation barriers rather than immediate impact.
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey items on pre-service teacher competence, device provision, and training access

paper_profiles.title: Virtual Reality in Teacher Education: Insights from Pre-Service Teachers in Resource-limited Regions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how pre-service teachers in a resource-limited context perceive virtual reality (VR) as a tool in teacher education. It asks whether participation in a VR-facilitated lesson changes their perceptions of VR in education and what challenges and opportunities they identify for using VR in educational settings.

The intervention was a facilitated guest lecture on technology in education delivered through a VR environment, with participants viewing the session on a portal screen rather than using headsets themselves. The study used a qualitative case study approach with focus group discussions and reflective journal entries to gather participants’ reactions, experiences, and concerns.

The sample consisted of 36 Ghanaian pre-service teachers from two colleges of education, specifically early childhood and visual arts trainees. The broader setting is a resource-limited educational context in Ghana, where unreliable internet connectivity, limited infrastructure, and lack of access to VR equipment were salient constraints.

Findings suggest that first exposure to VR produced generally positive attitudes. Participants saw VR as engaging, interactive, and potentially useful for experiential learning, teaching preparation, and simulating in-person presentations or field trips. At the same time, they emphasized barriers to adoption, especially weak internet access, insufficient equipment, and limited foundational training. The paper concludes that VR could support teacher education in similar low-resource settings, but only if institutions and policymakers address infrastructure and access challenges first.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative case study based on focus groups and reflective journals, so it provides credible descriptive evidence but not causal estimates. The methodology is clear, but it does not meet experimental or quasi-experimental standards for stronger causal confidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests potentially meaningful institutional and teacher-preparation benefits for a priority population in a resource-limited setting, but the evidence is self-reported and non-quantitative. No effect sizes are reported, so the observed impact is suggestive rather than demonstrably large.

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative case study found that 36 Ghanaian pre-service early childhood and visual arts teachers generally perceived VR positively after a first facilitated exposure. Participants described VR as engaging, interactive, and enjoyable, and many believed it could enhance learner engagement and support experiential learning in teacher preparation.
finding.measure: Focus group discussions and reflective journals on perceptions of VR usefulness, engagement, and enjoyment

finding.finding_summary: Participants saw VR as promising for teacher education in resource-limited regions, but they also identified major implementation barriers, including limited infrastructure, unreliable internet connectivity, and insufficient access to VR equipment. The study therefore suggests institutional potential alongside substantial adoption constraints in Ghanaian colleges of education.
finding.measure: Thematic analysis of focus group discussions and reflective journals on implementation challenges and opportunities

finding.finding_summary: Participants believed VR could support learning of educational content and simulate experiences such as in-person presentations and expensive field trips. The paper does not report quantitative achievement outcomes, but it documents strong perceived value for teacher preparation and content understanding in early childhood and visual arts contexts.
finding.measure: Perceived knowledge enhancement and instructional usefulness from qualitative reflections

finding.finding_summary: VR was viewed as potentially useful as an alternative to synchronous online learning platforms, especially for simulating presentations and supporting teacher training. However, participants also reported that VR could be time-consuming and practically difficult to use because of connectivity and equipment constraints, limiting efficiency gains.
finding.measure: Participant comparisons of VR with synchronous online learning and comments on practicality/time demands

paper_profiles.title: Preparing pre-service physics teachers to diagnose students’ conceptions not covered by physics education textbooks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need to prepare pre-service physics teachers to diagnose students’ conceptions that are not covered in physics education textbooks (“off-textbook” conceptions). The authors argue that although textbook-based misconceptions are commonly discussed in physics teacher education, teachers also need to recognize novel or uncommon student ideas encountered in everyday classroom practice.

To address this, the authors developed a learning environment added to an existing diagnostic competence intervention. The new unit focused on diagnosing off-textbook conceptions about the viscous behaviour of fluids. Pre-service physics teachers first completed preparatory homework comparing their own explanations of a spoon sinking in honey with scientific literature, then discussed their ideas in groups, completed a multiple-choice activation task, and practiced diagnosing authentic student statements from video vignettes in small groups. The unit was originally intended as face-to-face but was implemented online because of COVID-19.

The study was piloted twice with pre-service physics teachers at the University College of Teacher Education Styria in Austria (May 2021: N=11; December 2021: N=16). The accompanying research combined questionnaires with videotaped and transcribed group discussions to identify learning barriers and facilitating elements. The main conclusion is that participants could often spot that a student statement was incorrect, but they struggled to connect those statements to underlying conceptions and to integrate physics content knowledge with pedagogical content knowledge. The authors conclude that the learning environment likely needs stronger supports to help pre-service teachers interlink content and pedagogical reasoning when diagnosing unfamiliar student thinking.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative exploratory pilot within a design-based research approach, not an RCT or QED. The paper provides useful process evidence from videotaped sessions and questionnaires, but credibility is limited by small samples and the absence of causal testing.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper addresses an important teacher-education problem for a priority population (pre-service physics teachers), but it reports no measurable student-learning effect and no effect size. Its practical impact is suggestive rather than demonstrated, so it fits a yellow tier.

finding.finding_summary: This exploratory design-based study piloted a learning environment for pre-service physics teachers to diagnose off-textbook student conceptions about the viscous behavior of fluids (May 2021: n=11; Dec 2021: n=16). The main finding was that participants could often identify that a student statement was scientifically incorrect, but they struggled to infer the underlying conception and to connect their physics content knowledge with pedagogical content knowledge. No effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of videotaped group work, discussion/reflection transcripts, and end-of-session questionnaire responses about diagnosing student conceptions

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT as a tool for honing teachers’ Socratic dialogue skills
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper explores whether ChatGPT can be used as a training tool for teachers to practice Socratic dialogue, especially in physics education. The authors argue that modern versions of ChatGPT are better able to participate in back-and-forth questioning than earlier versions and may therefore be useful for helping teachers learn how to guide students through reasoning rather than simply giving answers.

The study combines illustrative examples of Socratic exchanges with ChatGPT-4 and a pilot classroom-style activity using ChatGPT-3.5. In the pilot, 17 pre-service physics and mathematics teachers from one Swedish and one Slovenian university interacted with ChatGPT as part of their coursework. Participants were asked to find correct and incorrect answers, use guiding questions to improve flawed responses, and reflect on the interaction.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT, particularly the newer versions, can simulate a student-like dialogue partner that is useful for teacher training. The chatbot was better than earlier versions at revising incorrect answers and responding to prompts, which made the dialogue more productive. The pilot participants reported positive engagement and saw value in the activity, although they also experienced frustration when trying to correct the model. The authors conclude that ChatGPT has potential as a safe, controlled environment for practicing specific teaching skills, but it is not a replacement for real student interaction.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a proof-of-concept paper with a small pilot study and descriptive analysis, not a controlled experiment. The evidence is qualitative and observational, so it meets limited credibility criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests a potentially useful training application, but it reports no formal effect sizes and only a small pilot with 17 pre-service teachers. Impact is therefore promising but unclear and modest at present.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a Socratic dialogue partner and simulated student for teacher training, specifically to help pre- and in-service physics teachers practice questioning, probing, and responding to student reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT-4 and ChatGPT-3.5 can be used to practice teachers’ Socratic dialogue skills, supporting critical questioning, active listening, and the ability to detect and reconcile inconsistencies in responses. In the pilot with 17 pre-service physics and mathematics teachers, all participants were positive about the activity, and 16 of 21 dialogues initiated by wrong answers were considered successful, though 5 participants reported frustration.
finding.measure: Pre-service teacher reflections and dialogue success counts from ChatGPT interactions

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT offers a controlled, private, safe, and readily available environment for teacher practice, potentially reducing the need for access to human students during rehearsal of Socratic dialogue. The pilot suggests the tool can support teacher training coursework with repeated practice opportunities, though the paper does not report formal efficiency metrics.
finding.measure: Feasibility and usability observations from teacher-training pilot

paper_profiles.title: Teacher training in the age of AI: Impact on AI Literacy and Teachers' Attitudes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a structured professional development course can improve teachers’ AI literacy and their attitudes toward using generative AI in educational practice. The study is motivated by the rapid spread of generative AI in schools and the need for teachers to understand both the opportunities and risks of AI, including lesson planning, feedback, differentiated materials, and assessment support.

The intervention was a four-week online certificate course, “Artificial Intelligence in Everyday School and Classroom Practice,” delivered by fobizz. It combined synchronous webinars, self-paced modules, optional enrichment units on machine learning, AI ethics, inclusive education, and data protection, and a project in which participants created an AI-supported lesson plan. The course was designed mainly for in-service primary and secondary teachers, though some participants from adult education, higher education, and school administration also joined. The study used a pre-post design with German in-service teachers of all subjects and school forms; outcome measures included a validated AI literacy test and a self-report attitude questionnaire administered before and after the training.

Results showed significant gains in overall AI literacy and in most competency domains, with small effect sizes. Teachers also reported greater use of AI in daily life, lesson preparation, and assessment/grading, as well as increased willingness and perceived preparedness to integrate AI into teaching. The authors conclude that systematic teacher training can strengthen both competency and confidence for AI adoption, though some knowledge gaps remained and the study highlights the need for more education-specific AI literacy tools and longer-term follow-up.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed pre-post intervention study, but it lacks a control group and uses self-reported outcomes, so causal claims are limited. It provides useful descriptive evidence of change but does not meet stronger experimental credibility criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention showed substantial gains in perceived preparedness and lesson-planning use, with several medium-to-large effect sizes (e.g., d=1.65, d=1.32). Because the sample is in-service teachers and effects are reported on self-reported practice/readiness rather than direct student outcomes, the overall impact is best characterized as modest-to-strong but not definitive.

interventions.use_case: teacher professional development on using generative AI/ChatGPT and the fobizz AI assistant for lesson planning, creating materials, grading support, and classroom integration

finding.finding_summary: The training improved teachers' reported AI use for work-related tasks, including creating lessons/materials and supporting assessments or grading. After the program, agreement increased substantially for daily AI use (I1: mean 1.37 to 2.28, d=1.07), lesson/material creation (I2: 1.27 to 2.35, d=1.32), and grading support (I3: 0.41 to 1.04, d=0.67) in a sample of n=436 for attitudes.
finding.measure: Self-reported AI use in daily life, lesson/material creation, and assessment/grading support (4-point Likert items)

finding.finding_summary: The program increased teachers' willingness and perceived preparedness to integrate AI, indicating gains in confidence and readiness for technology adoption. The strongest effect was for feeling well-prepared to integrate AI into teaching (I8: 1.03 to 2.28, d=1.65), alongside increased intention to integrate AI into daily teaching practice (I5: 2.45 to 2.72, d=0.49) in the attitude subsample (n=436).
finding.measure: Self-reported intention to integrate AI and perceived preparedness for teaching with AI (4-point Likert items)

finding.finding_summary: The training produced clearer, more critical views of AI's role in schools while also increasing optimism about AI supporting students. Concern that AI is more of a threat than an opportunity rose modestly (I4: 0.98 to 1.37, d=0.42) and fear of replacement also increased slightly (I7: 0.45 to 0.67, d=0.25), but belief that AI offers an opportunity to support students also increased (I6: 2.39 to 2.67, d=0.50).
finding.measure: Self-reported beliefs about AI's opportunities and risks in education (4-point Likert items)

paper_profiles.title: Dual-Role Dynamics in Prompting: Elementary Pre-service Teachers’ AI Prompting Strategies for Representational Choices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how pre-service elementary teachers prompt generative AI when asked to produce representations for explaining science concepts. The study is motivated by a gap in the literature on how teacher candidates use AI differently when acting in a teacher role versus a student role, especially in physics education and when generating representations rather than lesson plans or tasks.

The intervention/approach involved elementary education majors in a physical science course using Microsoft Co-Pilot Pro to generate representations for two tasks: explaining wave velocity to elementary students as if they were teachers, and explaining the Ideal Gas Law to an English teacher as if they were students. Participants first produced representations without AI and then repeated the task with AI assistance. The study analyzed the participants’ prompts and AI responses across these two role-based contexts.

The population was 20 pre-service elementary teachers enrolled in a required physical science course at a large midwestern U.S. university. The context was a lab-based teacher education setting with participants also engaged in field experiences shadowing in-service teachers, though those field experiences were not the focus of the study. The paper reports that prompts in the teacher role were more explicit about the audience, more prescriptive about the desired representation, and led to a wider variety of representations than prompts in the student role. The authors interpret this as evidence of greater agency and representational flexibility when participants conceptualize themselves as teachers, and they suggest implications for teacher education and AI literacy development.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, emergent-coding study of prompts and AI responses with a small sample (n=20), not an experiment or quasi-experiment. It is peer-reviewed-like scholarly work, but credibility is limited by the descriptive design and narrow task context.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper offers useful but modest insights into how pre-service teachers frame prompts when using generative AI, rather than demonstrating direct outcome gains. Its implications are mainly conceptual and practice-oriented, with no measured effect on learning or teaching performance.

interventions.use_case: Using Microsoft Copilot Pro / ChatGPT-style generative AI to help pre-service elementary teachers generate and compare representations for explaining wave velocity to elementary students and the Ideal Gas Law to an English teacher.

paper_profiles.title: Can NotebookLM Support English Language Learners? A Theoretical Perspective on AI Tools in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether Google’s NotebookLM could meaningfully support English language learners (ELLs) and, more broadly, how an emerging generative AI note-taking/research assistant might fit into language education. The author emphasizes that NotebookLM is very new and that there are currently no published empirical studies evaluating its effects on learning outcomes or specific learner populations. Rather than reporting a direct experiment, the paper offers a conceptual analysis grounded in prior research on AI tools in language learning and on learning strategies such as summarization and annotation.

The paper positions NotebookLM as a tool that can ingest user-provided documents and then generate summaries, answer questions, and simplify content. It argues that these functions may help ELLs with vocabulary acquisition, reading comprehension, academic writing, and self-regulated learning. The discussion links these features to established theories including Vygotsky’s Zone of Proximal Development, self-regulated learning theory, cognitive load theory, and Computer-Assisted Language Learning. In the author’s view, NotebookLM could act as a scaffold, a metacognitive aid, and an external memory support that reduces the burden of reading difficult English texts.

The population discussed is broad and mostly theoretical rather than an empirically sampled cohort. The paper refers to ELLs in general, including children in bilingual elementary programs, K-12 students in U.S. public schools, university students, and adults in EFL contexts. The main conclusion is cautiously optimistic: NotebookLM appears conceptually aligned with effective learning principles and may be useful for English language teaching and learning, but its actual benefits, risks, and limits still need empirical testing through future research and pilot studies.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical perspective paper with no empirical design, no comparison group, and no reported primary data. It is peer-reviewed journal content, but it provides conceptual analysis rather than evaluative evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no measured impact on learning or teacher outcomes. It is explicitly speculative and calls for future empirical research rather than demonstrating effect.

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers in low-resource schools collaborate with a generative AI lesson-planning system called Shiksha Copilot. The motivating problem is that teachers in constrained, multilingual public-school settings face heavy workloads, administrative documentation demands, and limited access to high-quality, locally relevant lesson plans. The authors ask how teachers work with LLM-generated lesson plans, what challenges arise when deploying such tools in non-English-medium classrooms, and how the system reshapes teachers’ everyday practices.

Shiksha Copilot was deployed in government schools across Karnataka, India. It used a human-in-the-loop workflow: LLMs generated draft learning objectives and lesson plans grounded in textbooks via retrieval-augmented generation; expert curators reviewed and revised these drafts; and teachers then customized the curated plans for their own classrooms. The system supported both English and Kannada lesson plans, included optional lesson-specific and general educational chat features for power users, and was explicitly designed for low-resource, multilingual contexts. The study involved 1,043 field teachers, 23 curators, and four mentors, with data from interviews, pre/post surveys, and usage logs.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods field deployment with surveys, logs, and interviews, but it is not a randomized or quasi-experimental causal design. The evidence is strong descriptively and context-rich, yet credibility for causal inference is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports practically meaningful workload and stress reductions for a priority population of teachers in low-resource, multilingual government schools. However, effects are mostly descriptive and qualitative in the provided text, so the impact is promising but not quantified as medium or large.

interventions.use_case: Human-in-the-loop LLM system for teacher lesson-plan generation, curriculum-grounded lesson customization, bilingual English-Kannada lesson planning, and lesson-specific/general pedagogical chat support for teachers in low-resource schools

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that Shiksha Copilot reduced bureaucratic workload and lesson-planning time for teachers in low-resource government schools. In the survey data, the authors measured weekly time spent on lesson planning and administrative tasks, and qualitatively found that teachers used the tool to meet documentation requirements while lowering teaching-related stress; the paper does not report a standardized effect size in the provided text.
finding.measure: Weekly time spent on lesson planning and administrative tasks; teacher reports of workload and record-keeping burden
finding.study_size: n=406 matched survey respondents; interviews n=22 teachers (plus 17 curators and 4 mentors)

finding.finding_summary: The study reports reduced teaching-related stress after deployment of Shiksha Copilot. Stress was measured with the Teacher Stress Scale (TSS), including teaching demands and school-based support subscales, but the provided text does not report a numeric pre-post effect size or confidence interval.
finding.measure: Teacher Stress Scale (teaching demands and school-based support subscales)

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that the tool supported curriculum-aligned lesson planning across Science, Mathematics, Social Science, and English, and that teachers often rated English lesson plans as highly usable. However, Kannada translations required extensive linguistic revision, and pedagogical change was constrained by staffing shortages and administrative demands, so the academic support effects were uneven across contexts and languages.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of lesson-plan quality/usability; curator ratings of content blocks; qualitative assessment of curriculum alignment and pedagogical fit
finding.study_size: n=1,043 teachers; 23 curators; 991 curated lesson plans; 5,544 teacher-created lesson plans

finding.finding_summary: The intervention altered teacher work practices and administrative routines in government schools by making lesson plans serve both instructional and bureaucratic functions. The paper also reports broader organizational constraints—staff shortages, administrative demands, and low-resource infrastructure—that limited the extent of pedagogical change, indicating institutional impact but not full transformation.
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of workflow change; deployment/log analysis of lesson-plan creation and customization; teacher and mentor interviews

paper_profiles.title: Dual-Role Dynamics in Prompting: Elementary Pre-service Teachers’ AI Prompting Strategies for Representational Choices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how pre-service elementary teachers prompt generative AI when asked to choose representations for explaining physics ideas in two different roles: as teachers and as students. The authors focus on whether the role a participant adopts changes the way they interact with AI, especially in how explicitly they specify the audience, whether they prescribe a representation type, and how diverse the resulting representations are.

The intervention consisted of two lab-based activities in a physical science course for elementary education majors. In the teacher-role task, participants explained wave velocity to elementary students and used Microsoft Co-Pilot Pro to help generate representations such as pictures, cartoons, analogies, graphs, or activities. In the student-role task, participants explained the Ideal Gas Law to an English teacher and again used AI after first reasoning through the topic. Data came from prompts and AI responses from 20 pre-service elementary teachers at one U.S. university.

The study found that participants were more explicit about the target audience, more prescriptive about the representation, and more likely to generate a wider variety of representations when acting as teachers than when acting as students. When acting as students, prompts were more exploratory and participants more often let AI decide the representation. The authors conclude that role-based prompting patterns may reflect greater agency in teacher mode and suggest that teacher education programs could use AI-supported representation tasks to strengthen science learning and representational competence.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, single-course study with emergent coding and a small sample size (n=20). It is peer-reviewed/academic but does not use a randomized or quasi-experimental design, so evidence strength is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful implications for teacher prompting and representational competence, but it does not measure student achievement or other direct impact outcomes. The observed effects are descriptive and context-specific, so broader impact is unclear.

interventions.use_case: Pre-service elementary teachers used Microsoft Co-Pilot Pro / ChatGPT-style generative AI to help generate representations for explaining wave velocity to elementary students and the Ideal Gas Law to an English teacher.

finding.finding_summary: In a qualitative study of 20 pre-service elementary teachers, AI prompting behavior showed more explicit audience specification, more prescriptive representation requests, and greater representational diversity when participants acted as teachers than when they acted as students. The paper interprets these patterns as evidence of stronger agency and representational competence in the teacher role, but it reports no effect sizes because the analysis was emergent coding rather than a quantitative outcome comparison.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of AI prompts for audience specification, prescriptive vs exploratory wording, and diversity of representations

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teachers should remain “in the loop” when using generative AI to personalize mathematics tasks. The central question is how teachers use ChatGPT to adapt existing curriculum problems, what kinds of prompts they use, and whether the resulting personalized tasks are perceived as interesting and relevant by students.

The intervention involved 7 middle school mathematics teachers using GPT-4o/ChatGPT to modify problems from the Illustrative Mathematics curriculum. Teachers personalized problems around students’ interests, mostly in popular culture, during training-supported sessions. The resulting assignments were delivered through ASSISTments to 521 7th-grade students across 6 U.S. schools. Data sources included ChatGPT interaction logs, video/audio of teacher sessions, teacher reflections, and student closed-ended and open-ended feedback.

The paper finds that teachers typically used broad popular-culture categories at first, then refined problems through multiple prompts to improve realism, numerical appropriateness, and fit with students’ age, location, or names. Students tended to prefer more specific, fine-grained references, while teachers spent substantial time correcting shallow or unrealistic AI outputs. The authors conclude that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can support professional learning and help monitor quality, but it is time-consuming and may not easily scale to the finer-grained personalization many students prefer.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed exploratory observational study with mixed-effects regression and qualitative coding, but not a randomized or controlled efficacy trial. It provides useful empirical detail on teacher use of GenAI, yet credibility is limited by the small teacher sample, lack of control group, and context-specific design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows modest-to-mixed benefits for perceived task relevance and clear costs in teacher time, but it does not demonstrate learning gains. Overall impact on K-12 practice is suggestive and context-specific rather than broadly transformative.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-in-the-loop use of ChatGPT/GPT-4o to rewrite and personalize middle school mathematics problems by adding or swapping popular-culture contexts, adjusting realism and quantities, and tailoring tasks to students' interests.

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on personalized middle school mathematics task creation rather than student achievement. Student-rated closeness/interestingness improved when teachers used 3-5 prompts, with ratings about 0.24 points higher on a 5-point scale (B=0.240, SE=0.085, p=0.0073), and Unit 6 problems were rated more favorably than Unit 4 (B=0.33, SE=0.095, p=0.0012). However, the study did not measure math test performance or learning outcomes, so the evidence is about task quality and perceived relevance rather than achievement.
finding.measure: Student 1-5 ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to interests; teacher time/prompts while creating math problems
finding.study_size: n=7 teachers; n=521 students; 143 personalized problems

finding.finding_summary: Students often found personalized problems more interesting when the context matched their interests, but many responses were negative or neutral, and preference depended strongly on specific popular-culture references. The paper reports 163 responses implying interest and 243 implying disinterest for the first feedback question, indicating that personalization increased engagement for some students but not others.
finding.measure: Open-ended student interest feedback and 1-5 interestingness ratings
finding.study_size: n=521 students; 454 open-ended responses to Q1

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-facing personalization with ChatGPT was time-consuming. Teachers spent an average of 246 seconds per problem (SD=165.7), and the authors estimate about 40 minutes for a 10-item assignment, with no clear evidence that efficiency improved as teachers gained experience; in fact, Unit 6 took longer than Unit 4 by about 70 seconds per problem (B=70.4, SE=29.6, p=0.0189).
finding.measure: Time spent creating each personalized problem; number of prompts per problem

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint examines how pre-service elementary science teachers envisioned using ChatGPT in lesson planning, and how they evaluated the tool's usefulness and concerns for science teaching and learning. The paper addresses a gap in the empirical literature on generative AI by moving beyond general claims about ChatGPT to analyze actual lesson plans and teacher perceptions.

The intervention/approach was a short professional learning experience in which 29 pre-service elementary teachers at a Korean university learned about ChatGPT, science teaching methods, and lesson-plan design, then created lesson plans that incorporated ChatGPT. Their plans were analyzed with a modified TPACK-based rubric, and their written survey responses were coded qualitatively. The lesson plans were built for a typical 45-minute elementary science class and often integrated ChatGPT with methods such as cooperative learning, POE, the learning cycle, analogy generation, experimentation, and concept mapping.

The participants were pre-service elementary teachers in South Korea, most of whom were sophomores and had recently completed a 3-week school practicum. The paper reports that they saw ChatGPT as useful for questioning, individualized support, formative feedback, and extending textbook content across several science domains, especially biology, chemistry, and earth science. At the same time, they raised concerns about accuracy, bias, and student over-dependence. Overall, the authors conclude that pre-service teachers showed moderate competence in integrating ChatGPT, and they argue for more professional development and empirical classroom research on generative AI in science education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/descriptive preprint study of lesson plans and survey responses from 29 pre-service teachers. It has a clear methodology, but it does not test student outcomes experimentally, so it fits a lower-credibility evidence tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful applications of ChatGPT in science lesson planning, but the evidence is indirect and based on perceptions rather than measured learning effects. Its generalizable impact is therefore unclear and modest at best.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used by pre-service elementary science teachers to support lesson planning and envisioned student-facing questioning, adaptive explanations, role-play scripting, and formative feedback in science lessons.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is primarily a descriptive study of how 29 pre-service elementary teachers integrated ChatGPT into science lesson plans, not a student outcome trial. Teachers anticipated ChatGPT could support scientific inquiry, prediction/explanation in POE, and concept development across biology, chemistry, earth science, physics, and environmental science, but no experimental learning gains were measured.
finding.measure: Lesson plan analysis; TPACK-based rubric; qualitative survey responses about anticipated science learning uses
finding.std_deviation: SD = .91 on overall TIAR score; SD = .87, .99, .93, .83 on subscales

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers expected ChatGPT to foster critical thinking through consecutive questioning, comparison of sources, and structured discussion, and to support collaboration through cooperative learning and role-play. These are perceived/anticipated benefits rather than measured learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses and lesson plan coding for intended uses related to critical thinking, self-directed learning, and collaboration

finding.finding_summary: Participants commonly anticipated that ChatGPT would increase motivation and interest by enabling individualized and self-directed learning, and by making science activities more engaging. The study reports perceptions and planned uses only; it does not measure motivation or engagement outcomes directly.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses about anticipated usefulness and lesson-plan intent

finding.finding_summary: Teachers viewed ChatGPT as useful for saving time in lesson planning, summarizing role-play scenarios, generating additional information beyond textbooks, and providing quick feedback. The paper does not quantify time savings or workload reduction, but it does report that lesson plans scored highly on the TIAR rubric (M=3.29, SD=.91), with especially high scores for instructional strategies & ChatGPT (M=3.48, SD=.99).
finding.measure: Lesson plan quality rubric; qualitative reports of anticipated planning support and feedback support
finding.std_deviation: SD = .91 overall TIAR; SD = .99 instructional strategies subscale

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VLM@school, a benchmark dataset for evaluating vision-language models on German-language, middle school-level tasks that require combining image understanding with subject-specific background knowledge. The authors argue that existing benchmarks are often English-only, overly reliant on multiple-choice formats, and too decontextualized to reflect real-world multimodal reasoning. Their dataset was constructed from German school textbooks and related materials for grades 8–10 and covers nine subject domains, including arts, biology, geography, history, math, music, physics, religion, and sports.

The intervention/approach is not a classroom intervention but a benchmark and evaluation protocol. The dataset includes 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions, including intentionally adversarial questions that cannot be answered from the image alone. The authors evaluate 13 open-weight vision-language models using an LLM-as-a-judge setup with multiple judges to score free-text answers against ground truth. They also examine performance by domain and compare results to public benchmark scores such as MMMU.

The paper’s main conclusion is that middle school-level tasks are surprisingly challenging for current VLMs, especially when answers require visual reasoning plus contextual knowledge in German. Best overall accuracy remains below 45%, with strong variation by subject; performance is notably weaker on music, math, and adversarial questions. The authors conclude that benchmark performance on popular datasets does not necessarily translate to this German educational context and that better evaluation data are needed for non-English, school-based multimodal reasoning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark/evaluation paper for vision-language models, not a study of an educational intervention with learner or teacher outcomes. It is peer-reviewed, but it does not use a causal or comparative design relevant to K-12 intervention evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no measured educational impact on students or teachers; it reports model benchmark accuracy on middle-school curriculum questions. Any implications are indirect and methodological rather than evidence of educational effectiveness.

paper_profiles.title: Learning beyond Teacher: Generalized On-Policy Distillation with Reward Extrapolation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies on-policy distillation (OPD) for large language models, asking how the standard objective can be generalized to better control distillation behavior.
