The authors first show theoretically that OPD can be viewed as a special case of dense KL-constrained reinforcement learning, then introduce a Generalized On-Policy Distillation (G-OPD) framework with two added degrees of freedom: a flexible reference model and a reward-scaling factor.

The proposed method is evaluated in math reasoning and code generation tasks using Qwen3 models. In same-size teacher-student settings, the paper examines reward interpolation and reward extrapolation; in the latter regime (ExOPD), the student can outperform the teacher and, in multi-teacher settings, merge multiple domain-specific RL teachers into a single student that surpasses all domain teachers. In strong-to-weak distillation, ExOPD also improves over standard OPD, and an optional reward-correction variant further boosts performance when the teacher’s pre-RL model is available.

The study is entirely about model distillation for LLMs, not classroom-based educational use. It uses math and code benchmarks and focuses on the behavior of student and teacher language models under different distillation objectives. The main conclusion is that reward extrapolation and reference-model choice materially improve OPD performance, but they can increase computation and, in some cases, response length.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a methodological/theoretical machine learning paper on generalized on-policy distillation, not a study of teacher-facing generative AI in education. It does not evaluate an educational intervention, teacher population, or school context.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational outcomes, teacher outcomes, or school-level impacts are measured. The paper has no direct relevance to the requested K-12 evidence framework for teacher-facing generative AI coaching or lesson-plan feedback.

paper_profiles.title: LearnLens: An AI-Enhanced Dashboard to Support Teachers in Open-Ended Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge teachers face in understanding students’ open-ended responses in exploratory learning environments, where conceptual understanding and misconceptions can be difficult to detect in real time. The authors present LearnLens, a generative AI-enhanced teacher-facing dashboard intended to help teachers interpret student work from digital assessments and adjust instruction accordingly.

LearnLens aggregates student responses and provides multiple views, including tables of responses, filtering by class section, sample-response viewing, word clouds, bar charts, and AI-generated summaries of collective understanding and misconceptions. The GenAI component uses GPT-4o and was developed through iterative prompt engineering with human validation, informed by professional development interactions with teachers.

The system was implemented as a high-fidelity prototype in a 15-lesson middle school Earth science curriculum in an urban public school. The evaluation involved semi-structured interviews with two 6th-grade science teachers who had previously taught the curriculum. Teachers valued the visualizations and especially the AI-generated summaries for identifying gaps and misconceptions, and they said the tool could support instructional adjustment. They trusted summaries grounded in student data but were cautious about AI-generated prescriptive recommendations that went beyond the evidence in the responses.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative prototype evaluation based on a small interview study with two teachers and no experimental comparison. It provides useful design evidence but not strong causal evidence of effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful classroom impact for middle school science teachers, but the evidence is limited to perceived usefulness in a very small sample. There are no measured learning gains or workload reductions with quantified effect sizes.

interventions.use_case: GenAI-enhanced teacher-facing dashboard that uses GPT-4o to summarize open-ended student responses and identify common misconceptions in a middle school Earth science classroom.

Teacher dashboard that aggregates classroom assessment data (exit tickets, check-ins, formative assessments) to surface patterns in understanding and potential misconceptions for instructional decision-making.

finding.finding_summary: Two 6th-grade science teachers (n=2) reported that LearnLens made it easier to review open-ended responses and obtain quick summaries that their existing tools did not provide. They valued the dashboard’s modular visualizations, filtering, and AI-generated insights for reducing the effort needed to interpret student work and prepare instructional responses; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher interview feedback on usability, sense-making, and instructional decision support

finding.finding_summary: In a middle school Earth science curriculum, teachers said the AI-generated summaries and misconception detection helped them identify gaps in students’ understanding of concepts such as absorption, runoff, and rainfall. The evidence is qualitative from a structured walkthrough and interview with two teachers (n=2), and no quantitative achievement effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of student conceptual understanding from open-ended science assessment responses

paper_profiles.title: Distance Teaching Experience of Campus-based Teachers at Times of Pandemic Confinement
paper_profiles.venue: ACM 5th International Conference on Education Technology Management (ICETM 2022)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how campus-based university teachers adapted to emergency remote teaching during the COVID-19 pandemic, with a focus on student engagement, interaction, and the practical challenges of shifting traditionally in-person courses online. The authors ask how teachers adjusted their instruction, what they perceived as effective for keeping learning engaging, and whether the experience would influence future campus teaching.

The study was conducted through online semi-structured interviews with six teachers in the Department of Computer Science at Blekinge Institute of Technology in Sweden. The participants came from different computer science teaching areas, including computer security, data science, digital scheduling, software engineering, game technology, and telecommunication. The paper is not about generative AI; rather, it is about emergency distance teaching practices during the pandemic, including live lectures, recorded sessions, Zoom chats, polls, Mentimeter, Padlet, Kahoot, and related digital tools.

The authors found that interaction was harder to maintain online, especially when students kept webcams off and verbal/non-verbal cues were missing. At the same time, asynchronous tools such as chat and polls sometimes increased participation and reduced shyness barriers. Teachers valued lecture recordings for flexibility and review, but worried about reduced live interaction and procrastination. The paper concludes that teachers want better technical readiness, more use of digital tools, and a blended/flipped approach after the pandemic, while noting that remote teaching increased workload and fatigue and that VR-based solutions were seen as impractical in this context.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative interview study with six teachers, using inductive thematic analysis. It provides contextual insight but does not meet experimental or quasi-experimental credibility standards for causal inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports perceptions of mixed-to-positive pedagogical changes during emergency remote teaching, but no quantified intervention effect sizes or student outcome data are provided. Impact is therefore modest and unclear rather than demonstrably large.

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative interview study (n=6 teachers) found that distance teaching during pandemic confinement both increased and hindered student engagement. Teachers reported improved interaction in some cases through chat, polls, and asynchronous communication, but also noted reduced verbal participation, loss of non-verbal cues, and 'Zoom fatigue' affecting engagement.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on student engagement, interactivity, and Zoom fatigue

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that teachers perceived gains in communication, adaptability, and digital-tool use during the emergency shift to online teaching, and believed these practices could carry over into future campus-based teaching. However, the evidence is anecdotal and based on reflections from 6 Computer Science faculty members rather than direct student skill measures.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported reflections on adaptation, communication practices, and future pedagogical transfer

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described online recordings, quizzes, polls, and chat as useful for reaching students and enabling later review, but also emphasized increased workload from recording/editing videos, adapting assessments, ensuring legal correctness of home exams, and monitoring chat. The overall operational effect was therefore mixed: some processes became easier, while others became more time-consuming.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on workload, recording, assessment preparation, and digital tool use

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that the pandemic prompted lasting institutional changes in higher education practice, including interest in hybrid/flipped classrooms and broader adoption of digital tools in campus-based teaching. The finding is based on thematic analysis of 6 teachers and reflects perceived longer-term institutional influence rather than measured organizational outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher recommendations and perceptions about post-pandemic teaching models and institutional practice

paper_profiles.title: FACET: Teacher-Centred LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems—Towards Personalized Educational Worksheets
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of supporting teachers in heterogeneous classrooms with AI systems that do more than performance-based personalization. The authors argue that existing generative AI tools for education are often student-facing and narrowly focused on quiz performance, while teachers need support that also accounts for motivation, prior knowledge, and didactical structure. The paper proposes FACET, a teacher-centered large-language-model multi-agent framework intended to generate individualized classroom worksheets.

FACET uses three specialized agents: a learner agent that simulates student profiles, a teacher agent that generates differentiated instructional materials, and an evaluator agent that scores the resulting worksheet on didactical structure, clarity, creativity, and suitability. The implementation is tested with authentic grade 8 mathematics curriculum content from German secondary education. The learner profiles vary along mathematical proficiency and intrinsic motivation, and the system is designed to produce personalized one-page worksheets with scaffolds, hints, and motivational support.

The study evaluates feasibility through automated agent-based assessment and exploratory feedback from five K-12 in-service mathematics teachers. The teachers generally rated the worksheets positively and highlighted the value of differentiated task difficulty, clearer scaffolding for lower-knowledge learners, and motivational framing for less engaged learners. The authors conclude that multi-agent LLM systems can support scalable teacher-facing personalization in mathematics classrooms, while noting that the current prototype remains preliminary and should be extended with richer learner profiles and authentic in-class trials.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/feasibility study with exploratory teacher feedback and internal agent-based evaluation, not a controlled effectiveness trial. It provides useful early evidence but lacks randomization, a student outcome measure, and a clear causal design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potential practical value for math worksheet personalization, but it reports no student learning effect sizes and no real classroom implementation outcomes. The demonstrated impact is therefore modest and preliminary.

interventions.use_case: teacher-facing LLM-based multi-agent system for generating individualized mathematics worksheets with learner simulation, didactical adaptation, and automated quality evaluation
evaluator agent that scores worksheet didactical structure, clarity, creativity, and suitability for learner needs

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that FACET generated math worksheets tailored to grade 8 mathematics curriculum content and aligned to learner profiles. In agent-based evaluation across 10 iterations for 4 learner profiles, suitability for the task was rated high (M=4.78/6, SD=0.06) and clarity was also high (M=4.76/6, SD=0.12), suggesting strong math-task adaptation.
finding.measure: Agent-based and teacher expert ratings of worksheet quality for grade 8 mathematics tasks
finding.study_size: n=4 learner profiles, 10 iterations each; n=5 teacher experts

finding.finding_summary: The framework explicitly models intrinsic motivation and motivational support, and teacher feedback highlighted benefits for engagement, especially for low-motivation learners. Teachers noted that the personalized worksheets could prevent boredom and better sustain motivation by adjusting difficulty and adding narrative or everyday-life relevance.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings and qualitative think-aloud feedback on motivation/engagement suitability

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the teacher-facing multi-agent system reduces prompting overhead and supports scalable generation of individualized worksheets, which teachers viewed as useful for heterogeneous classrooms. This is a feasibility/acceptability finding rather than a direct workload experiment, but the teacher comments indicate perceived time-saving potential.
finding.measure: Teacher qualitative feedback on usability and perceived utility for worksheet preparation

paper_profiles.title: Do Inquiring Minds Have Positive Attitudes? The Science Education of Preservice Elementary Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether inquiry-based science content courses can improve preservice elementary teachers’ attitudes toward science. The authors focus on four attitude dimensions: confidence, enjoyment, anxiety, and perceived relevance. The motivating problem is that many elementary teachers report low confidence and negative affect toward science, which may in turn reduce science instruction quality and shape students’ attitudes.

The intervention studied is the Hands on Science (HoS) undergraduate program at the University of Texas at Austin. HoS is a guided-inquiry sequence of science content courses required for preservice elementary education majors, spanning multiple semesters and covering physics, chemistry, geology, biology, astronomy, and earth science. Students engage in hands-on investigations, small-group work, prediction, data collection, explanation building, and whole-class discussion rather than lecture-based instruction. A comparison group of noneducation, nonscience majors took traditional lecture-style undergraduate science courses.

The sample includes 238 preservice elementary teachers in HoS and 263 comparison students. The study is situated in a single U.S. university context and uses pre/post surveys with multilevel models to compare change over time. Results show that HoS students increased in confidence, enjoyment, and perceived relevance, and decreased in anxiety, while the comparison group generally declined in favorable attitudes. The authors conclude that inquiry-based content courses may help prepare future elementary teachers to enter classrooms with more positive dispositions toward science, with possible downstream benefits for their own students.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quantitative quasi-experimental study with a comparison group, pre/post measures, and multilevel models controlling for background covariates. It is not an RCT and the comparison groups differ in important ways, so credibility is strong but not definitive.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports modest-to-moderate positive attitudinal shifts in a priority population of preservice elementary teachers, with large relative gains in anxiety reduction and meaningful gains in confidence and enjoyment. Because outcomes are attitudinal rather than direct achievement measures, the overall impact is best characterized as green rather than blue.

finding.finding_summary: This quasi-experimental study found that preservice elementary teachers in the Hands on Science (HoS) inquiry-based sequence improved on multiple attitudinal outcomes relative to peers in traditional lecture-based science courses. In adjusted multilevel models (n=501 observations; HoS n=238, comparison n=263), the HoS × time interaction was positive for confidence (b=.500***), enjoyment (b=.391***), and relevance (b=.200***), and negative for anxiety (b=-.553***), indicating improved affect and confidence toward science over time.
finding.measure: Science attitude scales measuring confidence, enjoyment, anxiety, and perceived relevance

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was an inquiry-based science content sequence centered on scientific questions, experimentation, data analysis, explanation building, and evidence-based discussion. Although the paper did not measure scientific reasoning directly with a performance test, it substantively argues that the HoS curriculum developed students' engagement in scientific inquiry practices and their understanding of science as a process of discovery.
finding.measure: Participation in inquiry-based science content instruction; attitudinal proxies related to science learning

paper_profiles.title: FACET: Multi-Agent AI Supporting Teachers in Scaling Differentiated Learning for Diverse Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of helping teachers create differentiated instructional materials for heterogeneous classrooms, where learners vary in prior knowledge, motivation, language proficiency, and learning differences such as dyslexia and ADHD. The authors argue that existing AI educational tools are mostly student-facing and tend to optimize only for performance, leaving teachers without support for inclusive, curriculum-aligned differentiation.

To address this, the paper presents FACET, a teacher-facing multi-agent framework with four agents: learner simulation, diagnostic assessment, material generation, and evaluation. FACET is designed for teacher-in-the-loop use, allowing educators to define learner profiles, upload or select tasks, and review AI-generated worksheets before use. The system embeds curriculum alignment, didactic guidance, and accessibility-oriented formatting intended to support diverse learners.

The evaluation combines exploratory workshops with German school principals and an online survey of 70 in-service K–12 teachers from the United Kingdom, United States, Canada, and Australia. The workshops identified strong practitioner demand for differentiation support, curriculum fit, accessibility, and teacher control. Survey results showed that teachers generally rated the generated worksheets positively, especially for didactic structure and clarity, while also indicating weaker performance for enrichment materials and some dyslexia-specific typography. Overall, the paper concludes that multi-agent AI can meaningfully support teacher-facing differentiation, but further refinement is needed for advanced learners and accessibility details.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods design with exploratory workshops and a descriptive teacher survey, not a controlled causal study. It provides useful formative evidence about feasibility and perceived quality, but it does not measure student learning outcomes or estimate intervention effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical promise for teacher workflow support and differentiated material generation, but the evidence is limited to perceptions and descriptive ratings. Impact on learning or adoption at scale remains unclear, so the demonstrated impact is modest and preliminary.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-facing multi-agent generative AI for differentiated worksheet generation, using simulated learner personas, diagnostic reasoning, and evaluator feedback to create curriculum-aligned lesson materials for heterogeneous K–12 classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: FACET was designed and evaluated as a workflow-support tool for teachers, with principals and in-service teachers reporting that it could reduce the burden of creating differentiated materials. In the workshops (n=30 principals), participants emphasized that differentiation is currently difficult to sustain due to workload and teacher shortages, and the system’s teacher-in-the-loop design was seen as supporting practical classroom use. No formal effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness, workflow integration, and teacher workload reduction in workshops and survey ratings

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluated motivational support and learner engagement indirectly through teacher ratings of generated worksheets for low- and high-motivation learner profiles. Teachers rated scaffolding-oriented worksheets for low-motivation learners relatively highly (didactic structure M=4.41-4.50; clarity M=4.23-4.46 on a 6-point scale), but worksheets for high-motivation learners received lower ratings across dimensions (e.g., structure M=3.87, clarity M=3.57), suggesting uneven support for motivation-related needs. No effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of worksheet quality for learner profiles differing in motivation
finding.std_deviation: SDs reported by worksheet dimension ranged roughly 1.02-1.46, with specific values in Table 2; not a single effect size

finding.finding_summary: The survey used a grade 7 mathematics task (area calculation) to assess the quality of FACET-generated worksheets for mathematical instruction. Teachers rated the math worksheets favorably overall for didactic structure and clarity, especially for low-performance/low-motivation and high-performance/low-motivation profiles (e.g., didactic structure M=4.41-4.50; clarity M=4.23-4.46), but the high-performance/high-motivation worksheet was weaker (structure M=3.87; clarity M=3.57). No direct student learning outcomes or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of generated grade-7 mathematics worksheets
finding.std_deviation: Worksheet-level SDs ranged about 1.02-1.46 across criteria

paper_profiles.title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can be used effectively as an automated writing evaluation tool in university English as a new language (ENL) instruction, and whether students prefer AI-generated feedback over feedback from a human tutor. The authors frame the study around broader concerns about the ethical and practical use of GenAI in education, especially for writing instruction where feedback quality, trust, and efficiency matter.

The paper reports two longitudinal studies conducted over six weeks at a small liberal arts university in the Asia-Pacific region. In Study 1, 48 ENL undergraduates were divided into a human-tutor control group and an experimental group that received GPT-4-generated feedback on weekly writing assignments; writing performance was measured with pre- and posttests scored by independent raters. In Study 2, a separate group of 43 ENL students received both human and AI feedback each week and completed weekly surveys plus open-ended responses about their preferences.

Study 1 found no significant difference in writing gains between students who received AI-generated feedback and those who received human tutor feedback. Study 2 found an approximately even split in preference between human and AI feedback, with students valuing human interaction, immediacy, and speaking practice on one hand, and AI’s clarity, specificity, and availability on the other. The authors conclude that GPT-4 feedback can likely be incorporated into ENL writing support without harming learning outcomes, but recommend a blended approach that combines AI efficiency with human pedagogical benefits.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental longitudinal study with a comparison group and repeated measures, plus a separate longitudinal preference survey. It is not randomized and has modest sample sizes, so it falls short of blue-tier rigor but provides reasonably credible evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The measured learning effect was null, with no significant advantage for AI feedback over human tutoring. Student perceptions were mixed rather than strongly favorable, indicating unclear overall impact despite practical promise for workload reduction.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4-generated corrective writing feedback for ENL students' weekly academic paragraphs and revisions, compared against human tutor feedback
Using ChatGPT/GPT-4 in a teacher-like prompting setup to provide explanatory, sentence-level guidance on student writing

finding.finding_summary: In Study 1 (n=48; EG n=23, CG n=25), students receiving GPT-4-generated writing feedback made similar gains to those receiving human tutor feedback over six weeks. Repeated-measures ANOVA found no significant group-by-time interaction (F=3.094, p=0.085, ηp2=0.063) and no significant between-group effect on posttest writing scores (F=0.241, p=0.626, ηp2=0.005).
finding.measure: Pre/post analytic rubric scores for writing (content, coherence, language use, sources and evidence; max score 40)

finding.finding_summary: In Study 2 (n=43; weekly survey responses varied from 32 to 41, average 37.7), ENL students were nearly evenly split in preference between AI-generated and human tutor feedback. Mean ratings slightly favored human tutor feedback across satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and preference items, but differences were nonsignificant and both feedback sources were rated highly (grand means mostly above 4 on a 5-point scale).
finding.measure: Weekly preference survey items on satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, overall preference, and forced-choice feedback preference

paper_profiles.title: The role of ChatGPT in higher education: Benefits, challenges, and future research directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the potential benefits and challenges of using ChatGPT in higher education, framing the discussion through constructivist theory of learning. Rather than reporting an empirical intervention study, the authors develop a perspective-based analysis of how generative AI could shape teaching, learning, assessment, research support, and administration in tertiary education. The paper is motivated by the rapid uptake of large language models and the need to understand their educational value and risks.

The article focuses on ChatGPT as a general-purpose AI tool that could support adaptive learning, individualized feedback, research and writing assistance, automated administrative support, and innovative assessment activities. It also discusses major risks, including academic integrity concerns, ethical and equity issues, unreliable or biased outputs, falsified information, inability to evaluate graduate skill sets, and the difficulty of assessing learning outcomes when AI is used in student work. The analysis is situated in higher education, with explicit attention to students, academics, and institutional administrators.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT has meaningful potential to enhance learning and streamline educational processes, but only if institutions use it cautiously and responsibly. The authors argue that institutions should promote AI literacy, maintain academic integrity, redesign assessments to be harder to replicate with AI, and ensure human oversight and equitable access. Overall, the paper positions ChatGPT as a tool that can support constructivist learning, but one that requires careful governance to avoid superficial learning, bias, and misuse.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective/theoretical paper with propositions, not an empirical study. It does not present a formal research design, comparison group, or original quantitative or qualitative data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No causal impact can be estimated because the paper reports conceptual claims only and provides no measured outcomes. Any effects discussed are speculative rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a higher-education conversational AI for adaptive learning, individualized formative feedback, research/writing support, administrative support, and generating innovative assessment materials.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can support academic writing by helping generate drafts, summarize sources, translate text, and provide individualized feedback on grammar and structure. However, it also emphasizes risks of hallucinated content, fabricated references, and academic misconduct, so the overall writing-related implication is beneficial but constrained by reliability concerns; no primary study effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Narrative claims about writing support, draft generation, and feedback quality; no empirical outcome measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly claims ChatGPT may support critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and metacognition through scaffolded prompts, authentic assessment design, and critique of generated outputs. It also warns that overreliance may weaken these same skills and reduce active construction of knowledge; this is a conceptual argument rather than a measured effect, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Narrative discussion of critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and metacognition

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can reduce workload and improve efficiency through automated administrative support, faster feedback generation, and assistance with research and data analysis. It cites prior claims that grading effort could be reduced by up to 85% in related LLM contexts, but this paper itself does not report a new empirical estimate or sample size.
finding.measure: Narrative claims about administrative workload, feedback automation, and research productivity

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes institutional implications for academic integrity policy, equitable access, assessment redesign, AI literacy, and governance of generative AI use in higher education. The direction is mixed because ChatGPT is framed as potentially transformative and efficient, but also as creating risks for bias, inequity, and misconduct; no empirical institutional effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Narrative discussion of policy, governance, equity, and assessment design implications

paper_profiles.title: How Generative AI Influences Students’ Self-Regulated Learning and Critical Thinking Skills? A Systematic Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how generative AI, especially ChatGPT and related tools, affects students’ self-regulated learning (SRL) and critical thinking (CT) in educational settings. The authors conduct a systematic review using the PRISMA framework to identify and synthesize recent studies published between 2022 and 2024, a period chosen because ChatGPT began widespread adoption in 2022.

The review searches Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect, initially retrieving 3,214 documents and ultimately including 38 studies for analysis. The included studies span multiple educational contexts and countries, with most evidence coming from higher education and language/education-related settings. The paper does not test a single intervention itself; rather, it synthesizes findings on how generative AI is used for personalized learning, metacognitive support, reflective feedback, and adaptive guidance.

Overall, the review concludes that generative AI is generally associated with positive effects on SRL and CT, especially when it supports feedback, reflection, personalization, and learner autonomy. At the same time, the authors caution that overreliance and dependence can weaken independent thinking and that effects vary by context, culture, and pedagogy. They recommend structured integration of AI within human-guided frameworks such as hybrid human-AI regulation, alongside educator training, equity-focused access, and future longitudinal research.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review using PRISMA with database searches, screening, and explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria. However, it synthesizes heterogeneous primary studies rather than reporting a single causal estimate, so the evidence is strong for mapping but not for experimental attribution.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests broad positive influence on self-regulated learning and critical thinking, but the evidence is descriptive and heterogeneous with no pooled effect sizes. Reported impacts are therefore promising but unclear in magnitude at the individual-student level.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of ChatGPT and related generative AI chatbots used as learning support tools that provide instant guidance, adaptive feedback, metacognitive prompts, and reflective questioning to support student self-regulated learning and critical thinking.

finding.finding_summary: Across 38 included studies, 71.4% reported a positive role for generative AI in self-regulated learning. Effects were described as coming through personalized learning, metacognitive support, and motivational support rather than a single pooled effect size; the review does not report a meta-analytic estimate. The synthesis indicates that students using ChatGPT-style tools were better supported in goal setting, monitoring, and self-management, though benefits varied by context.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning outcomes / SRL-related constructs reported in included studies
finding.study_size: n=38 studies (review-level); individual study sample sizes not reported in the review text

finding.finding_summary: The review found that 62.5% of studies reported positive effects on critical thinking, while 33.3% reported neutral effects and 4.2% reported negative effects due to dependency risks. The positive findings centered on reflective feedback, collaborative learning, analysis, evaluation, and problem-solving, but some studies cautioned that overreliance on AI can weaken independent thinking.
finding.measure: Critical thinking / higher-order thinking / problem-solving and reflective reasoning outcomes
finding.study_size: n=38 studies (review-level); individual study sample sizes not reported in the review text

paper_profiles.title: The Educational Affordances and Challenges of ChatGPT: State of the Field
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses an early question in the post-release period of ChatGPT: how can generative AI be used in education, and what are its limitations and risks? The authors conducted a configurative systematic review of peer-reviewed literature published from November 30, 2022 through August 1, 2023, following PRISMA principles and then used grounded coding to synthesize themes across the included studies.

The review is not an intervention study with participants; instead, it synthesizes 44 published papers about ChatGPT use in educational contexts. The analysis separated educator-facing uses from student-facing uses. For educators, the paper identifies teaching support, task automation, and professional development, including lesson planning, content creation, personalization, assessment support, communication, summarization, and writing support. For students, it identifies 24/7 support, explanation of difficult concepts, conversational practice, personalized feedback/materials, writing support, self-assessment, engagement, and self-determination.

The paper also synthesizes limitations and misuse concerns that recur across the literature, including inaccuracies and hallucinations, potential bias, tool constraints, plagiarism and cheating, privacy issues, and the spread of false information. The authors conclude that ChatGPT has substantial educational affordances but should be used cautiously because of reliability, transparency, and equity concerns. They call for further research on specific learner populations, subject areas, and other generative AI tools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review using PRISMA principles and grounded coding, but it synthesizes early qualitative/heterogeneous literature rather than conducting a quantitative meta-analysis. The evidence is therefore methodologically organized yet not high on causal credibility for outcome effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests broad potential benefits and risks for education, but it reports no pooled effect sizes or direct outcome trials. Its impact claims are therefore important and plausible, but still preliminary and mostly qualitative.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of ChatGPT use in education, including teacher support, task automation, professional development, student tutoring, conversational practice, and feedback generation.

finding.finding_summary: Across 44 peer-reviewed articles, the review found ChatGPT could automate teacher tasks such as drafting emails, summarizing documents, proofreading/editing, and generating lesson materials, suggesting clear productivity gains. No pooled effect size was reported because this was a configurative systematic review of early literature rather than a quantitative meta-analysis.
finding.measure: Qualitative synthesis of reported educator uses and task automation functions

finding.finding_summary: The review found strong literacy-related affordances, especially for writing support, language assistance, personalized feedback, and generating leveled texts and questions. At the same time, it also highlighted substantial risks for literacy tasks, including inaccuracies, hallucinations, plagiarism, and fabricated citations; no pooled effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative synthesis of writing support, feedback, text generation, and literacy-related misuse/limitations

finding.finding_summary: The review identified uses of ChatGPT for foreign-language conversation practice, dialogue generation, text leveling, translation, and language assistance for non-native speakers. These uses were described as beneficial for communication practice and accessibility, but the paper did not report quantitative effects.
finding.measure: Qualitative synthesis of language-learning and conversational use cases

finding.finding_summary: The review reported that ChatGPT can support higher-order skills by prompting critical thinking, problem solving, argumentation, self-assessment, and self-determination, and it can also facilitate student engagement. However, it also noted a limitation: ChatGPT is less competent on higher-order thinking tasks and conceptual reasoning, so the overall pattern is mixed.
finding.measure: Qualitative synthesis of reported learning affordances and limitations related to critical thinking, engagement, and self-determination

finding.finding_summary: The review found that ChatGPT may increase student engagement, accessibility, and feelings of autonomy and competence, which the authors linked to self-determination. These claims were synthesized from early peer-reviewed studies and conceptual papers rather than tested with a pooled quantitative estimate.
finding.measure: Qualitative synthesis of engagement, accessibility, autonomy, competence, and relatedness themes

finding.finding_summary: The review emphasized institutional concerns including academic integrity, privacy, bias, misinformation, and the need for guidance and assessment redesign. It also argued that ChatGPT may change teacher workload and assessment practices, but the paper did not estimate an aggregate effect size.
finding.measure: Qualitative synthesis of policy, governance, integrity, privacy, and assessment implications

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the impact of ChatGPT: conversational AI in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the educational impact of ChatGPT, with a particular focus on its benefits, challenges, ethical concerns, and effects on educators and students. The review was motivated by growing interest in conversational AI and the need to understand how generative AI tools can be used responsibly in educational settings, especially given concerns about bias, accuracy, privacy, and overreliance.

The authors conducted a systematic literature review following Kitchenham and Charters and PRISMA-style reporting. They searched multiple digital libraries, screened roughly 729 records, and retained 70 peer-reviewed papers published between 2022 and 2023. The review synthesized findings across studies about ChatGPT’s role in education, including personalized assistance, prompt feedback, improved access to information, and enhanced learning engagement.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT can support student-centered and differentiated learning, help educators shift from content delivery to facilitation, and improve access to information and learning support. At the same time, it emphasizes that responsible deployment requires human supervision, training, privacy protection, transparency, critical thinking, and ongoing monitoring to address bias, inaccuracy, and ethical risks. The paper is broad and conceptual rather than an evaluation of one classroom intervention, so its main contribution is a synthesized set of implications and recommendations for educational use.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic literature review, but it is not a primary empirical study and does not synthesize effect sizes through a formal meta-analysis. Its conclusions depend on the quality and heterogeneity of the included studies, so credibility is moderate rather than high.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful educational and institutional implications of ChatGPT, but it reports no direct measured impact or effect sizes from an intervention study. The impact is therefore plausible but unclear and largely descriptive.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of ChatGPT as a conversational AI tool in education, including uses as a virtual tutor/assistant, prompt-response support, and teacher-facing guidance for classroom use.

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that ChatGPT can increase student engagement by providing personalized responses, prompt feedback, and immediate access to information. These benefits are described as helping students participate more actively and stay engaged, but the paper does not report original quantitative effect sizes because it is a systematic review of prior studies.
finding.measure: Student engagement and perceived learning experience in the reviewed literature

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, ChatGPT is said to support critical thinking, inquiry, and question formulation by offering conversational practice and rapid feedback. The paper frames these as learning benefits, but provides no pooled numerical effect estimates because it synthesizes prior studies rather than testing an intervention itself.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, inquiry/questioning, and reflective learning as reported in the reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that ChatGPT can transform educators’ roles from content delivery to facilitation and guidance, but it also raises institutional needs around policies, monitoring, privacy, transparency, and bias mitigation. The paper emphasizes that responsible implementation depends on human supervision and clear guidelines rather than reporting a measurable causal effect.
finding.measure: Teacher role change, policy/guideline needs, ethical safeguards, and institutional implementation considerations

paper_profiles.title: Investigating the Effectiveness of ChatGPT for Providing Personalized Learning Experience: A Case Study
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can support personalized learning in data science education, specifically for a deep learning lesson. The authors ask whether ChatGPT can improve student engagement, participation, and learning outcomes compared with traditional instruction, and whether students perceive the ChatGPT-supported experience positively.

The intervention was a case study using the 5Es instructional model (engage, explore, explain, elaborate, evaluate) with ChatGPT acting as a virtual co-teacher. The study compared an experimental group that learned with ChatGPT against a control group that received standard teacher-led instruction. Data came from quiz scores and qualitative observations of student interaction and engagement.

The participants were 20 university students enrolled in an Internet of Things class at Qassim University in Saudi Arabia, with the lesson focused on deep learning concepts such as forward propagation, activation functions, convolutional neural networks, and network architecture. The authors report that the ChatGPT-supported group showed positive engagement and learning outcomes, and students generally perceived the experience favorably. However, they also note that ChatGPT sometimes produced incorrect evaluations or repeated/omitted steps, so teacher supervision remained necessary.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small mixed-methods case study with a 10/10 experimental-control comparison and qualitative observations, but it is not a randomized controlled trial and provides limited methodological detail and no effect sizes. The evidence is useful but has clear credibility and generalizability limitations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests modest positive impacts on student engagement and conceptual understanding, but the sample is very small and effects are not quantified. Without effect sizes or stronger design controls, the practical impact remains unclear beyond this pilot context.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a virtual co-teacher to deliver personalized deep-learning instruction, answer student questions, provide tailored explanations/examples, and guide learners through the 5E instructional model with an automated evaluation quiz.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students using ChatGPT within the 5E model showed improved understanding of deep learning concepts on a multiple-choice quiz, with several students answering all items correctly. The study is a small case study (n=20; 10 experimental, 10 control) and does not report effect sizes or confidence intervals, but the experimental group was described as performing better than the traditional-instruction control group on concept comprehension.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice quiz on deep learning concepts (forward propagation, activation functions, convolutional neural networks, network architecture)

finding.finding_summary: The authors report higher student engagement, participation, and a more positive perceived learning experience when ChatGPT was used as a personalized virtual co-teacher. Evidence is qualitative and based on observations plus learner perceptions rather than a validated engagement scale; no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative observations of engagement/participation and students' perceived personalized learning experience

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can function as a low-cost, automated teacher coach for classroom instruction. The authors focus on three coaching-oriented tasks: predicting classroom observation scores from transcript segments, identifying instructional highlights and missed opportunities, and generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

The study uses the NCTE transcript dataset of U.S. elementary mathematics classrooms. The data contain 1,660 classroom observations from 317 teachers across four school districts, with expert ratings from two established observation instruments: CLASS and MQI. The authors evaluate ChatGPT in a zero-shot setting using transcript segments and compare score predictions to human ratings, while also recruiting two experienced math teachers to judge the quality of generated feedback for the qualitative tasks.

Results show that ChatGPT has clear potential but performs inconsistently and often shallowly. Its score predictions correlate weakly with human ratings, and prompting with rubric descriptions or reasoning does not meaningfully improve performance. For the feedback tasks, teachers often judged responses as relevant only to a limited extent, with many outputs lacking insightfulness or faithfulness to the transcript. For the suggestion task, the model frequently repeated what the teacher already did rather than offering novel advice. Overall, the paper concludes that current generative AI is not yet a reliable teacher coach, but it may become useful with better training, calibration, and educator involvement in development.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/benchmarking study of an LLM on a sampled set of classroom transcripts with two expert raters, not an experimental impact study. It provides useful evidence about model limitations, but the design has limited sample size and no randomized comparison of educational outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report demonstrated positive effects on teaching or student outcomes; instead it shows mostly weak or mixed performance, with low correlations and high redundancy in suggestions. Any practical impact is therefore currently unclear and likely modest at best.

interventions.use_case: Zero-shot use of ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) as a teacher-facing coaching assistant to score classroom observation transcript segments, identify highlights and missed opportunities, and generate actionable suggestions for eliciting more student mathematical reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues ChatGPT could potentially provide scalable, cost-effective feedback for instructional coaching, but the empirical results show substantial limitations. On 100 transcript segments, Spearman correlations with human ratings were low across all items (e.g., CLASS CLBM 0.35 at best; MQI items mostly 0.00-0.17), and teachers judged many generated highlights/suggestions as low relevance or low novelty (e.g., 82% of suggestions repeated what teachers already did).
finding.measure: Spearman correlation with expert observation scores; teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty/redundancy
finding.study_size: n=100 transcript segments for scoring; n=216 CLASS examples; n=288 MQI examples; n=36 suggestion examples

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI Adoption in Postsecondary Education, AI Hype, and ChatGPT’s Launch
paper_profiles.venue: Open/Technology in Education, Society, and Scholarship Association Journal
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the early public and educational response to ChatGPT’s launch, focusing on how generative AI was framed in mainstream discourse and what those framings meant for postsecondary education. Rather than evaluating a classroom intervention or measuring student outcomes, the paper asks how AI hype influenced educators’ and institutions’ understanding of generative AI during the first six months after release.

The paper uses critical discourse analysis and interpretive reading of two news sources, The Globe and Mail and The Economist, along with related public and organizational texts, to analyze how ChatGPT was represented. The author argues that news and public discourse produced four dominant themes: overwhelming capability, impending job loss, anthropomorphism of AI, and vulnerability/fear/existential risk. These themes shaped how students, teachers, and administrators perceived ChatGPT and contributed to panicked rather than measured adoption.

The context is postsecondary education in Canada and broader international English-language media discourse, with ChatGPT as the focal generative AI tool. The paper concludes that hype can distort adoption practices, delegitimize educators’ expertise, and encourage fear-based responses. It recommends more deliberate, ethically grounded planning for generative AI in education, including attention to digital literacy, co-design, marginalized communities, and responsible policy development.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed article, but it is a critical discourse analysis and commentary on media narratives rather than an empirical evaluation of a learning intervention. It provides no experimental, quasi-experimental, or outcome-measure evidence for educational effects of generative AI use.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear relevance to education policy and teacher-facing generative AI adoption, but it reports no measured impact sizes on learners or teachers. Its impact is mainly conceptual and systemic, not empirically demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT as a generative AI chatbot discussed as an educator- and student-facing tool for drafting lesson plans, generating quiz questions, providing writing feedback, tutoring support, and critiquing AI-generated text in postsecondary education.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not test learning outcomes; it qualitatively analyzes how news discourse shaped postsecondary adoption of ChatGPT during the first six months after launch. Across 55 education-related news articles, it finds that hype, fear, and uncertainty influenced institutional thinking about policy, governance, and responsible adoption, with four dominant themes: overwhelming capabilities, impending job loss, anthropomorphism, and existential risk.
finding.measure: Critical discourse analysis of 55 education-related news articles (44 Globe and Mail, 11 The Economist) mentioning ChatGPT

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT was publicly framed as highly efficient for educators and students, especially for drafting, brainstorming, generating prose, and speeding up routine academic work. However, this is a discursive/interpretive finding rather than a measured productivity effect, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of claims about time-saving, drafting, and automation in mainstream discourse and OpenAI educator examples
finding.study_size: n=55 articles plus OpenAI educator-facing examples

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI Toolkit - A Framework for Increasing the Quality of LLM-Based Applications over Their Whole Life Cycle
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of developing, testing, deploying, and monitoring large language model (LLM)-based applications over their full life cycle. The authors argue that existing workflows for LLM applications are still largely manual and ad hoc, making it difficult to maintain quality, detect hallucinations, compare prompt or model variants, and monitor systems after deployment. Their goal is to provide a more systematic, automated DevOps-style approach for LLM applications.

The proposed intervention is the Generative AI Toolkit, an open-source framework that supports automated agent creation, custom evaluation metrics, repeatable test cases, model/prompt permutation testing, CI/CD integration, infrastructure-as-code deployment, a debugging GUI, and logging/monitoring via traces. The framework is demonstrated through several example use cases, including a text-to-SQL agent, a RAG-based restaurant menu agent, an in-vehicle voice assistant, and a comparison of different model sizes and prompts. These examples are used to illustrate how the toolkit can be applied to testing, evaluation, and monitoring of LLM-based agents.

The paper is not a study of students, teachers, or classrooms; it is a software engineering framework paper aimed at developers building LLM-based applications. The main conclusion is that the toolkit can reduce manual work, shorten development cycles, and improve quality by making evaluation and monitoring more standardized and automated. The authors emphasize that it can help teams identify optimization opportunities and quality issues more efficiently across the life cycle of LLM-based systems.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a preprint framework/tool paper rather than a peer-reviewed empirical study. It does not use a controlled design, and the evaluation is largely illustrative and descriptive with no rigorous causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for operational benefits and improved quality, but reports no quantitative effect sizes and no direct educational outcomes. Any impact is therefore plausible but unclear and limited to general software/LLM operations rather than demonstrated learner impact.

interventions.use_case: A DevOps/LLMOps toolkit for configuring, testing, monitoring, and optimizing LLM-based applications and agents over their full lifecycle, including prompt permutation, custom metrics, CI/CD integration, and tracing.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the toolkit significantly reduces cycle time and manual work in developing and operating LLM-based applications, but it does not provide a quantified effect size. Benefits are described across use cases as faster project initiation, easier test development, automated evaluation, and reduced manual testing/documentation effort.
finding.measure: Development cycle time, manual work, and workflow automation efficiency described across representative LLM agent use cases

finding.finding_summary: The framework is presented as an open-source lifecycle toolkit intended to improve production readiness, reliability, and governance of LLM applications at organizational scale. The paper emphasizes audit-proof logging, monitoring, CI/CD integration, and standardized evaluation as mechanisms for more robust operational practice, but provides no quantitative institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Adoption-oriented workflow capabilities such as audit-proof logging, monitoring, deployment automation, and repeatable evaluation

paper_profiles.title: Comparing Large Language Model AI and Human-Generated Coaching Messages for Behavioral Weight Loss
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Technology in Behavioral Science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language model (LLM) artificial intelligence, specifically ChatGPT, can generate behavioral weight loss coaching messages that are perceived as helpful as those written by a human coach. The authors address a practical problem in automated health coaching: existing rule-based or templated messages can feel repetitive, impersonal, and costly to scale, potentially limiting engagement and effectiveness.

The study used messages drawn from an ongoing year-long behavioral weight-loss trial (Project ReLearn) involving adults in the United States with overweight or obesity. Eighty-seven participants rated ten coaching messages across two phases: five human-written and five ChatGPT-generated messages. After Phase 1 feedback suggested the AI messages felt impersonal, overly negative, and overly data-driven, the prompt was revised to better convey empathy and encouragement, and a second set of messages was generated for Phase 2. Participants rated helpfulness, judged whether messages were AI- or human-written, and provided open-ended feedback.

Quantitatively, ChatGPT messages improved from Phase 1 to Phase 2 and were rated nearly as helpful as human-written messages by the end of the study, though human messages still held a small advantage. Participants often could not reliably distinguish AI from human messages, suggesting the model could mimic human-like coaching fairly well. Qualitatively, however, participants preferred messages that felt more authentic, personalized, autonomy-supportive, and context-aware, and they were wary of formulaic, overly prescriptive, or overly enthusiastic wording. The authors conclude that LLMs show promise for scalable weight-loss coaching, but further prompt refinement and future trials are needed to evaluate actual clinical effectiveness.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed, small-sample comparative study with mixed quantitative and qualitative methods, but it is not an RCT and does not evaluate real-world outcomes beyond subjective ratings. It provides useful early evidence but has notable concerns about ecological validity and generalizability.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests modest-to-moderate perceived helpfulness gains after prompt refinement (e.g., d=0.15 in Phase 2 human-vs-AI comparison), but the outcome is subjective and limited to a weight-loss coaching context. The practical impact is promising but still unclear for broader deployment or behavioral outcomes.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) generated behavioral weight-loss coaching messages from structured participant data and prompts, with prompt refinement across two phases to improve tone, empathy, and helpfulness.

finding.finding_summary: Participants rated ChatGPT-generated coaching messages as less helpful than human-written messages in Phase 1 (median 3 vs 4; t(234)=8.41, p<0.001, d=0.55), but after prompt revisions in Phase 2 the gap narrowed substantially (median 4 vs 4; t(199)=2.10, p=0.037, d=0.15). Qualitative feedback indicated the AI messages were more empathetic and personalized in Phase 2, yet still often felt formulaic, impersonal, and overly prescriptive.
finding.measure: Perceived helpfulness ratings of coaching messages on a 1–5 Likert scale; open-ended participant feedback
finding.effect_size: d=0.55 (Phase 1 human vs AI); d=0.15 (Phase 2 human vs AI); d=0.48 (AI improvement from Phase 1 to Phase 2)

paper_profiles.title: Making AI-Enhanced Videos: Analyzing Generative AI Use Cases in YouTube Content Creation
paper_profiles.venue: Extended Abstracts of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI EA '25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how generative AI tools are being used by YouTube creators during the process of making how-to videos. The authors note that, while GenAI tools such as ChatGPT, MidJourney, Leonardo.AI, and others are increasingly used in video production, there was limited understanding of the concrete tasks they support across the workflow.

To address this gap, the study analyzes 274 YouTube how-to videos about using GenAI in video creation. The authors first filtered a larger set of videos for relevance, then used thematic analysis to identify use cases across four phases of production: planning, production, editing, and uploading. They found that creators use GenAI to identify topics, generate scripts, refine prompts, create visuals and audio, animate images, create avatars, perform lip-syncing, upscale and restyle media, clip long videos, translate speech, add subtitles, and generate titles.

The paper concludes that GenAI is already embedded in creator workflows as a tool for reducing labor and streamlining creative tasks. It also argues that future HCI research should focus on the risks and design implications of over-reliance on AI, prompt creation as a new skill, the originality and authenticity of multimodal AI content, and transparency around AI-generated content in social media publishing.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative thematic analysis of publicly available YouTube videos, not a controlled intervention study. The methodology is systematic and peer-reviewed, but it provides descriptive evidence rather than causal estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful workflow efficiency gains for creators, but it reports no outcome effect sizes and no direct evaluation of educational impact. Its relevance to teacher-facing GenAI is indirect, so the practical impact for the retrieved topic is unclear.

interventions.use_case: Qualitative content analysis of YouTube how-to videos showing how creators use generative AI tools to support video creation tasks such as scriptwriting, prompt refinement, image/video generation, voiceover creation, editing, subtitle generation, and title generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that generative AI is used extensively to streamline YouTube content-creation workflows across planning, production, editing, and uploading. In the analyzed corpus of 274 how-to videos (2,829 clips), the most common uses included prompting for images/videos (n=167, 60.9%), creating AI voiceovers (n=93, 33.9%), and scripting/storytelling (n=85, 31%), indicating clear productivity and labor-saving benefits rather than measured learning gains.
finding.measure: Qualitative thematic analysis of GenAI use cases in YouTube how-to videos; frequency counts of use-case mentions

paper_profiles.title: Guardrails for avoiding harmful medical product recommendations and off-label promotion in generative AI models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the risk that general-purpose generative AI models may recommend medical products for unapproved or otherwise potentially harmful uses. The authors argue that because large language models are trained on broad internet-scale data with limited human oversight, they can learn off-label product-indication associations and surface them in responses, creating public-health and regulatory concerns.

To address this, the paper proposes a post-hoc detection method for identifying off-label promotion in multimodal large language model outputs. The method standardizes the user query, applies biomedical named entity recognition to the model response, matches detected products and indications to FDA labeling data, and then uses a zero-shot T5 model to decide whether an identified product-indication association constitutes a recommendation and thus off-label promotion.

The approach is demonstrated on Anthropic Claude 3 Sonnet in a shopping-style question-answering setting where a user uploads a product label image and asks about it. The authors generated 14,300 synthetic queries across 35 pharmaceuticals with known off-label uses, finding that 15.4% of responses contained off-label indications. They conclude that guardrails can be used to filter or modify responses so that generative AI systems adhere to approved labeling when discussing medical products, though the work is framed as a proof of concept rather than a comprehensive prevalence study.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical paper with a clear evaluation pipeline, but it is a proof-of-concept on synthetic queries rather than a field study or randomized design. Evidence is therefore informative but limited in causal relevance to educational deployment contexts.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not test educational outcomes directly; its main contribution is identifying a safety/regulatory failure mode and a detection method. The practical impact is important for governance, but effect on learner outcomes is indirect and unclear.

interventions.use_case: evaluating a multimodal generative AI model (Claude 3 Sonnet) in a medical product question-answering / recommendation setting where users ask about product labels and the model may recommend uses

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that a multimodal GenAI model can produce potentially harmful off-label medical product recommendations, with 15.4% of 14,300 synthetic customer queries yielding off-label indications. In a random sample of 2,000 responses, the proposed detector achieved precision 85.75%, recall 80.47%, and F1 83.02% for identifying off-label promotion, suggesting the issue is measurable and nontrivial.
finding.measure: Rate of off-label indications in model responses; detection performance against human annotations (precision, recall, F1)
finding.study_size: n=14300 synthetic queries; n=2000 annotated sample

paper_profiles.title: Foundations of GenIR
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter presents a conceptual overview of how modern generative AI changes information access systems. It argues that generative models create two major opportunities: information generation, where systems directly create content tailored to a user’s request, and information synthesis, where models integrate external information to produce grounded responses. The paper frames these as foundational directions for future IA systems, contrasting them with traditional retrieval systems that primarily surface existing content.

The chapter surveys the technical foundations needed for these directions, including model architecture, scaling laws, training stages, prompt optimization, and multimodal applications. It also discusses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) as the major paradigm for information synthesis, covering naive RAG, modular RAG, optimization issues, retrieval planning, and composite information needs. In parallel, it outlines alternatives such as generative retrieval and domain-specific modeling, positioning large language models as possible replacements for or collaborators with traditional retrieval systems.

The paper does not report any empirical study, participants, educational setting, or teacher-facing intervention. Its main conclusion is that generative AI can improve information access by either creating directly responsive outputs or synthesizing grounded answers from external sources, but that major challenges remain, especially hallucination, controllability, updateability, and the difficulty of integrating retrieval and generation effectively.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/chapter-style overview of generative AI and information retrieval, not an empirical study of teacher-facing AI coaching or lesson-plan feedback. It reports no original evaluation design, sample, or measured outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct evidence is presented on trust, calibration, error detection, bias, dependence, or longitudinal use in educational settings. The chapter is useful background, but it does not demonstrate measurable educational impact.

paper_profiles.title: Benchmarking Adversarial Robustness to Bias Elicitation in Large Language Models: Scalable Automated Assessment with LLM-as-a-Judge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to systematically and scalably evaluate large language models for susceptibility to biased, stereotypical, and unsafe outputs under adversarial prompting. The authors argue that existing bias benchmarks are limited by single-bias focus, manual annotation costs, and weak coverage of adversarial manipulations, making it difficult to compare models or assess robustness across multiple social dimensions.

To address this, they introduce CLEAR-Bias, a benchmark of 4,400 prompts covering seven isolated bias categories and three intersectional categories, with both multiple-choice and sentence-completion tasks. The benchmark is augmented with seven jailbreak-style attack methods, including machine translation into low-resource languages, obfuscation, prompt injection, refusal suppression, reward incentives, and role-playing. They also propose an LLM-as-a-Judge workflow to automatically classify model responses into stereotyped, counter-stereotyped, debiased, or refusal categories, and to filter misunderstandings during adversarial testing.

The empirical evaluation is conducted on a set of general-purpose and domain-specific language models, including smaller models such as Phi-4 and Gemma2 variants and larger models such as GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.1 405B, and DeepSeek V3. The study finds that bias resilience varies substantially by category and model, with intersectional categories and socioeconomic status, disability, and age being especially difficult. No model is fully robust to adversarial elicitation, and some models that appear safe on base prompts remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. The authors conclude that safety is not determined solely by parameter scale, that model family and training matter, and that automated judge-based benchmarking can support more comprehensive bias and safety evaluation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical benchmarking study with a defined protocol, but it is not an education outcome study and does not use an experimental design for student learning. The methodology is systematic and quantitative, yet it is primarily a technical evaluation rather than a causal study in an educational setting.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear relevance for institutional AI governance and safe deployment, but it does not report direct educational impact or learner outcomes. Its implications are important for risk assessment, though the measured effects are model-safety metrics rather than educational gains.

finding.finding_summary: This paper benchmarks the safety, fairness, and adversarial robustness of multiple large language models against bias elicitation, using CLEAR-Bias (4,400 prompts) and a judge model selected with Cohen’s κ=0.82. It does not measure student learning; instead it evaluates model behavior relevant to institutional AI governance, showing uneven robustness across bias categories and that no model is fully robust to jailbreak attacks.
finding.measure: LLM safety, fairness, robustness scores; judge agreement (Cohen’s κ); attack effectiveness across bias categories
finding.study_size: n=10 evaluated models; CLEAR-Bias=4,400 prompts; control set=800 prompt-response pairs

paper_profiles.title: Quite Good, but Not Enough: Nationality Bias in Large Language Models - A Case Study of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines nationality bias in large language models, focusing on ChatGPT (GPT-3.5). The authors ask whether ChatGPT’s open-ended generation about nationalities is uniformly positive and neutral, or whether it still reproduces subtle stereotypes and offensive associations across languages and prompt types.

The approach uses 195 countries, 3 prompt types in Chinese and English, and 4 temperature settings to generate 4,680 nationality descriptions. The study evaluates outputs with automated metrics for vocabulary richness, sentiment, offensiveness, hate speech, and regard, and also introduces a pairwise-comparison framework for judging bias as a continuum rather than a binary label. Human expert annotators and ChatGPT itself both participate in the comparison-based evaluation.

The paper finds that ChatGPT generally produces mostly positive, non-offensive text, and is substantially less toxic than GPT-2. However, negative prompts can still elicit offensive or stereotyped content, and pairwise comparison reveals persistent nationality bias that varies by language. Human and ChatGPT judgments align reasonably well, but the Chinese and English versions of ChatGPT show different bias patterns, suggesting cross-language cultural variation in the model’s outputs.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical study, but it is observational/benchmark-style rather than an experiment, randomized trial, or causal design. It relies on automated metrics, expert annotation, and model self-annotation, which are appropriate for bias analysis but do not meet higher-credibility intervention standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper identifies meaningful bias patterns and shows ChatGPT can act as an annotator, but it does not test an educational intervention or demonstrate learner outcomes. The practical impact is therefore indirect and mainly methodological for AI evaluation rather than instructional practice.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) is used as the generative model under evaluation to produce open-ended nationality descriptions in Chinese and English, then to self-annotate the offensiveness/bias of its own outputs using direct scoring and pairwise comparison prompts.
The paper evaluates a generative language model as a bias-detection and annotation tool, including self-annotation of bias and pairwise comparison judgments of generated text against other texts.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that ChatGPT-generated text is mostly positive and non-offensive, but still contains subtle nationality bias that varies by language and prompt. Human annotators and ChatGPT often agree on the relative offensiveness of texts (human annotation kappa=0.729; ChatGPT same-order kappa=0.748 in English and 0.850 in Chinese), suggesting the model can partially self-detect bias while still reproducing real-world stereotypes.
finding.measure: Bias/offensiveness in generated nationality descriptions measured with automated metrics (MATTR, sentiment, hate speech, regard/offensiveness) plus expert and ChatGPT pairwise bias annotations
finding.study_size: n=4680 generated discourses; pairwise comparison subset n=780 texts for Chinese human annotation and 11,700 pairwise comparisons

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT substantially outperformed supervised Chinese classifiers for pairwise bias evaluation, with macro F1=0.746 versus 0.485-0.520 for the trained BERT/RoBERTa baselines. This suggests the LLM can serve as a high-performing automated annotator for bias assessment tasks, reducing the need for human labeling labor in this specific evaluation setting.
finding.measure: Precision, recall, and macro F1 for pairwise bias annotation/classification

paper_profiles.title: Transforming Software Development with Generative AI: Empirical Insights on Collaboration and Workflow
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI tools, especially ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot, are changing day-to-day work and collaboration in software development. The authors ask how software engineers and related knowledge workers use GenAI, what effects it has on their workflow, and how it may alter teamwork dynamics such as communication, feedback, and knowledge sharing.
