The study is an exploratory multi-case qualitative study based on semi-structured interviews with 13 participants across software-related roles, including developers, data scientists, managers, designers, and technical leaders. The context is companies in Norway that had introduced GenAI into product development processes. Participants described uses such as getting unstuck, learning, creating boilerplate code, copywriting, working with existing code, and prompt engineering.

The main conclusion is that GenAI is perceived as increasing productivity, speed, motivation, and enjoyment by reducing repetitive work and supporting learning. At the same time, the paper argues that GenAI can reduce human-to-human knowledge sharing and pair programming, potentially disrupting the teamwork learning loop and weakening collaboration over time. The authors also note practical challenges such as confidentiality concerns, limited tool integration, outdated training data, and culturally biased outputs.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative exploratory multi-case interview study with 13 participants and no control group or quantitative causal design. It offers useful descriptive evidence about perceived effects, but credibility is limited by self-report and small sample size.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful productivity and learning benefits, but the impact is based on qualitative perceptions rather than measured effect sizes. Overall impact is plausible but unclear in magnitude for general or priority populations.

interventions.use_case: Teacher- or worker-facing conversational use of ChatGPT/GPT-style systems for task support, including getting unstuck, interactive learning, prompt-based roleplay, boilerplate generation, code assistance, and feedback on writing.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that 13 interviewees across developer, manager, designer, and data science roles used ChatGPT/Copilot daily or 'all the time' to speed up repetitive work, reduce interruptions, and complete tasks faster. Participants described substantial time savings on boilerplate writing and bids (e.g., one manager reported a bid that would normally take much longer was completed in 20 minutes), but this was qualitative rather than a controlled effect estimate.
finding.measure: Interview-reported productivity, time savings, and workflow efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests GenAI supported learning, problem solving, and metacognitive 'rubber-ducking' by helping users articulate problems, explore alternatives, and learn faster. At the same time, it may reduce human collaboration and pair programming, potentially weakening team learning loops and knowledge sharing.
finding.measure: Interview themes on learning, collaboration, and problem-solving practices

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported increased motivation, fun, engagement, and work satisfaction from using GenAI, partly because it reduced tedious tasks and provided immediate feedback. The study is qualitative and does not report standardized scales or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Interview-reported motivation, enjoyment, and work satisfaction

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can function as an automated teacher coach by producing classroom-observation scores and actionable instructional feedback from classroom transcripts. The authors focus on three teacher-coaching tasks: scoring transcript segments using established observation rubrics, identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and generating suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

The study uses the NCTE transcript dataset of U.S. elementary mathematics classrooms, which contains 45–60 minute transcripts from 4th and 5th grade lessons across four school districts. The transcripts were originally scored by expert raters using two observation systems: CLASS and MQI. The authors prompt gpt-3.5-turbo in a zero-shot setting and evaluate quantitative score predictions against human ratings as well as qualitative feedback with two experienced math teachers, one of whom had decades of instructional-coaching experience.

Overall, ChatGPT performs poorly on score prediction, showing low correlation with human ratings and tending to default to similar score patterns across items. For qualitative feedback, the model often produces responses that are relevant in a broad sense but are frequently not insightful or novel; in the suggestion task, 82% of suggestions restate what the teacher already does in the transcript. The paper concludes that current generative AI has promise as a scalable complement to human coaching, but substantial improvements are needed to reduce hallucination, improve insightfulness, and better tailor feedback to instructional context.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical qualitative/benchmarking study of a generative AI tool with small human-evaluation samples and no causal design. It provides useful evidence on model performance, but credibility is limited by the small evaluator pool and the absence of a randomized or quasi-experimental impact study.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper finds some promise for scalable coaching support, but the measured performance is mostly weak or mixed and no direct outcome improvement is demonstrated. Any real-world impact is therefore uncertain and currently modest at best.

interventions.use_case: Zero-shot use of ChatGPT as a teacher-facing instructional coach to score classroom transcript segments, identify instructional highlights and missed opportunities, and generate actionable suggestions for eliciting more student mathematical reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies whether ChatGPT can provide scalable teacher-coaching feedback more efficiently than human expert coaching, but it does not measure time savings directly. Results suggest potential utility for automation, but the model’s low correlation with human scores and frequent redundant or non-insightful feedback indicate limited current operational value.
finding.measure: Quality of automated coaching outputs, including score prediction correlation with human ratings and human judgments of relevance/faithfulness/insightfulness/actionability/novelty
finding.study_size: n=100 transcript segments for scoring; n=216 CLASS examples and n=288 MQI examples for highlights/missed opportunities; n=36 suggestion examples

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how pre-service elementary science teachers integrated ChatGPT into lesson planning and how they perceived its usefulness and risks for science teaching and learning. The authors were interested in the practical applicability of generative AI in education, particularly because prior work had been mostly speculative rather than based on classroom-oriented empirical evidence.

The intervention/approach consisted of a short instructional sequence in a science education course at a Korean teachers’ university. Twenty-nine pre-service elementary teachers received four 2-hour sessions introducing ChatGPT, discussing potential uses in science instruction, reviewing science teaching strategies, and learning how to craft lesson plans. Participants then created a lesson plan for a 45-minute elementary science class that had to incorporate ChatGPT and include a simulated teacher/student conversation with the system. Their lesson plans were evaluated with a modified TPACK-based rubric, and they also responded to open-ended survey questions about their choices, perceived benefits, and concerns.

The study found that participants imagined ChatGPT being used across multiple science domains and instructional approaches, especially cooperative learning, POE, learning cycle, analogy generation, experimentation, and concept mapping. Overall lesson-plan quality was fairly strong, but teachers were less proficient at selecting appropriate ChatGPT functions than at aligning ChatGPT with goals or instructional strategies. Pre-service teachers saw ChatGPT as useful for questioning, individualized support, and formative assessment, but they also worried about inaccurate or misleading output, bias, and student overdependence. Many proposed safeguards such as using multiple information sources, teacher guidance, peer interaction, and reflection to reduce overreliance on ChatGPT.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/descriptive preprint study of lesson plans and survey responses from 29 pre-service teachers, not an experimental or quasi-experimental impact evaluation. It provides useful early evidence about intended use, trust, and concerns, but does not establish causal effects on student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests plausible positive effects on instructional support, scientific inquiry, and student self-directed learning, but these are perceptions and planned uses rather than measured outcomes. Actual impact remains unclear because no student achievement or behavioral effect sizes were reported.

interventions.use_case: Using ChatGPT as a teacher-facing and student-facing conversational tool in elementary science lesson planning, including questioning, role-play support, individualized guidance, formative assessment, and feedback within pre-service teachers' lesson plans.

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers envisioned ChatGPT supporting scientific inquiry and conceptual understanding in science lesson plans, with an average TIAR score of M=3.29/4 (SD=.91) across 29 plans. However, the paper also documents inappropriate uses of ChatGPT (e.g., non-existent video links, visual content it cannot provide, and experiment design that could weaken hands-on inquiry), so the overall evidence is mixed rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: TPACK-based Technology Integration Assessment Rubric (TIAR) scores; qualitative analysis of lesson plans for science inquiry and conceptual learning

finding.finding_summary: Participants expected ChatGPT to increase student motivation, interest, and self-directed learning in science activities. The paper reports these as perceived benefits from 29 pre-service teachers, but no causal student outcome data were collected.
finding.measure: Pre-service teacher survey responses about anticipated motivation, interest, and self-directed learning

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers believed ChatGPT could support critical thinking, collaboration, and digital literacy, and some proposed structured classroom routines to reduce over-dependence on AI. At the same time, they explicitly worried that students might become overly dependent on ChatGPT and that inaccurate responses could create misconceptions, indicating both potential skill benefits and risks.
finding.measure: Pre-service teacher survey responses and lesson plan analyses for critical thinking, collaboration, digital literacy, and dependence concerns

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was perceived as a way to provide individualized support, feedback, and concise summaries during lesson planning and classroom activities, potentially helping teachers manage instruction more efficiently. The paper does not report a causal productivity measure, but it does document teacher candidates' expectations that ChatGPT could reduce workload and support real-time formative feedback.
finding.measure: Pre-service teacher perceptions of individualized support, feedback, and classroom management efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how an AI-assisted lesson planning system, Shiksha Copilot, was used to support teachers in low-resource public schools. The central problem is that teachers in such settings face heavy administrative burdens, limited instructional resources, and substantial time constraints, making it difficult to create high-quality lesson plans that are both pedagogically sound and aligned with mandated curricula. The authors ask how teachers collaborate with generative AI in lesson planning, what implementation challenges arise in multilingual classrooms, and how an LLM-based tool reshapes teachers’ work practices.

Shiksha Copilot was deployed in government schools across Karnataka, India, supporting English- and Kannada-medium lesson planning for Grades 5–10. The system used retrieval-augmented generation to draft curriculum-aligned lesson plans, a human-in-the-loop curation workflow in which expert curators reviewed and edited AI-generated lesson objectives and plans, and a translation module for Kannada. Teachers then accessed curated lesson plans through a distribution platform and customized them for their classrooms. A subset of teachers also received access to additional AI tools such as lesson-specific chat, general educational chat, and question generation. The study combined system logs, interviews, and pre/post surveys from 1,043 teachers and 23 curators, making it a large mixed-methods deployment study.

The findings suggest that the system was useful both for instructional planning and for bureaucratic documentation. English lesson plans were generally rated as high quality with relatively few edits, while Kannada translations required much more extensive linguistic correction. Teachers often made few recorded edits, but interviews showed they routinely adapted plans off-platform using their own expertise, peer networks, and classroom knowledge. Overall, the paper concludes that teacher-AI collaboration can reduce workload, lower stress, and support more activity-based pedagogy, but that meaningful change in low-resource settings depends on strong human oversight, localization, and attention to organizational constraints. The authors argue for human-in-the-loop, community-driven approaches to generative AI in education, especially for multilingual contexts in the Global South.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods field deployment with surveys, logs, and interviews, but it is not a randomized or quasi-experimental causal design. The study is strong descriptively, yet credibility for causal claims is limited by self-selection, no control group, and mostly qualitative/observational evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful workload relief and workflow integration, but the text provided does not give a quantitative effect size for the main benefits. Overall impact appears modest-to-clear for teachers in a priority population, but not large enough to justify a higher tier from the evidence shown.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-facing generative AI system for curriculum-aligned lesson-plan generation, curation, translation, and lesson-specific Q&A support in low-resource Kannada- and English-medium government schools.

Human-in-the-loop AI curation and validation of generated lesson plans, including review of learning objectives, content blocks, translations, and assessment items for pedagogical quality, accuracy, and contextual relevance.

finding.finding_summary: Shiksha Copilot reduced lesson-planning and record-keeping burden for teachers. The paper reports measurable reductions in lesson planning time and teacher stress, with teachers using the system both for classroom instruction and bureaucratic documentation; however, the excerpt does not provide a numeric effect size in the text shown. Teachers also used the system to generate plans in one sitting, indicating time-saving utility in a high-workload setting.
finding.measure: Survey measures of weekly time spent on lesson planning and administrative tasks; teacher stress scale (TSS); system logs and interviews on workflow use
finding.study_size: n=406 survey matched responses; n=22 teacher interviews; 1,043 total teachers deployed

finding.finding_summary: The tool supported administrative documentation and fit existing school workflows, but broader pedagogical change was constrained by staffing shortages and administrative demands. The paper describes organizational change in lesson-planning practices and workflow integration across 757 schools in 35 districts, but the impact on deeper instructional transformation was limited by institutional constraints.
finding.measure: Interview themes and deployment analysis of workflow change; descriptive use across schools/districts

paper_profiles.title: AI prediction leads people to forgo guaranteed rewards
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether merely framing a decision as being predicted by AI changes how people choose, even when the AI provides no recommendation and the prediction itself is never revealed at the moment of choice. The authors ask whether perceived predictive authority can alter decision-making in ways beyond standard persuasion or incentive effects. They frame this phenomenon as "predictive binding," in which people may treat an AI prediction as linked to their own anticipated action and therefore align their choice with what they believe the system expects.

Across four preregistered online experiments, participants completed Newcomb’s paradox-inspired choice tasks in which they could either take a guaranteed reward or choose an option that sometimes yielded a larger payoff depending on a prior prediction. Study 1 compared AI framing with a random mechanism; Study 2 tested robustness across interactive and non-interactive interfaces, including an LLM-based chatbot interaction using GPT-4.1; Study 3 generalized the paradigm to vignette scenarios involving job interviews, mobile data coupons, and freelancing tasks; and Study 4 examined repeated exposure across five rounds with fixed AI prediction policies. Participants were adults recruited online through Prolific in the United States. The studies found that AI framing substantially increased the likelihood of forgoing the guaranteed reward, that participants perceived AI predictions as more accurate than random chance, and that the effect persisted even after repeated predictive failures. The authors conclude that AI prediction can reshape how people decide, not just what they decide, and that this influence can emerge without direct recommendation, coercion, or verified predictive accuracy.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a set of preregistered controlled experiments with a fixed-effect meta-analysis across studies, which is strong causal evidence. However, it is not a field trial in an educational setting and the main task is a stylized behavioral paradigm rather than a direct educational intervention, so relevance/credibility for education-specific claims is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The observed behavioral shift is meaningful in magnitude for the experimental task, but it concerns a non-educational decision paradigm and does not demonstrate impact on learning outcomes or schooling systems. For education-facing generative AI, the implications are indirect and therefore the practical impact tier is modest/unclear.

interventions.use_case: experimental use of AI-prediction framing in a Newcomb's-paradox decision task, including an LLM-based chatbot interaction variant (GPT-4.1) to study perceived predictive authority rather than tutoring or feedback

finding.finding_summary: Across four preregistered online studies (total n=1,305), AI-prediction framing led participants to forgo a guaranteed reward more often, indicating that perceived predictive authority can constrain decision-making. In Studies 1-2, one-boxing rose from 26.0% in the random condition to 41.0%-45.0% in AI conditions, with a fixed-effect meta-analytic odds ratio of 3.39 (95% CI 2.45-4.70) for forgoing the guaranteed reward and earnings reduced by 10.7%-42.9%.
finding.measure: Choice to forgo guaranteed reward / one-boxing rate; realized earnings
finding.study_size: n=1,305 total; Study 1 n=200; Study 2 n=601; Study 3 n=303; Study 4 n=201

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that AI prediction can reduce objective payoffs by altering user choices, which is relevant to efficiency in decision processes. In the incentivized task, the shift toward one-boxing reduced earnings by 10.7%-42.9% relative to the two-box baseline, and the effect persisted even after repeated predictive failures in Study 4 (final one-boxing 30.6% vs 15.3% baseline random condition).
finding.measure: Realized earnings; proportion of one-boxing across repeated rounds

paper_profiles.title: Perception-Aware Bias Detection for Query Suggestions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of detecting systematic topical bias in search engine query suggestions, especially when the suggestions are sparse, contextless, and only briefly perceived by users. The authors argue that prior bias-detection methods for query suggestions did not adequately reflect how users actually see suggestions, because they ignored both the frequency of suggestions over time and their rank in the suggestion list.

To address this, the paper extends an existing bias-detection pipeline for person-related query suggestions by introducing perception-aware metrics based on Discounted Cumulative Gain (DCG) and normalized DCG (nDCG). The pipeline still uses data acquisition, preprocessing, topical clustering, and regression analysis, but now incorporates rank and frequency information so that bias is estimated more realistically from a user-perception perspective. The data come from German-language autocomplete suggestions collected from Google, DuckDuckGo, and Bing for person-related search terms, primarily names of German politicians and politically relevant people.

The authors report that the updated pipeline detects more meaningful and more numerous bias patterns than the earlier version. In particular, it identifies significant gender bias and age bias, and additional patterns associated with party affiliation and federal state. The paper concludes that perception-aware metrics better capture bias that users would actually notice in query suggestions, and argues that these metrics may be useful for other ranked-list bias detection settings as well.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed methodological/analytical paper rather than an intervention study in education. It uses a structured pipeline with regression analysis on observational search-query data, so it fits correlational/technical evidence rather than experimental causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports modest, domain-specific improvements in bias detection for query suggestions, but no educational outcomes or end-user learning effects. Its impact is indirect and primarily methodological, with relevance to search audit and fairness rather than classroom intervention effects.

paper_profiles.title: Towards Standardizing AI Bias Exploration
paper_profiles.venue: AIMMES 2024 Workshop on AI bias: Measurements, Mitigation, Explanation Strategies (co-located with EU Fairness Cluster Conference 2024)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to systematically explore and measure bias in AI systems across many fairness concerns, rather than relying on a small set of ad hoc metrics. The authors argue that existing fairness libraries and measures are narrow in scope, context-dependent, and difficult to extend to new settings, especially when fairness concerns involve multiple sensitive attributes, intersections of groups, ranking/recommendation settings, or individual fairness.

To address this, the paper proposes a mathematical framework that decomposes measures of bias into four building blocks: group/subgroup selection, base measures, comparison mechanisms, and reduction mechanisms. Using this framework, the authors show how many existing fairness metrics can be reconstructed and how new variants can be created by recombining components. They also present FairBench, an open-source Python library that implements the framework and provides reusable interfaces for computing and visualizing fairness reports.

The paper is not an empirical study of people, schools, or teachers; it is a framework and software contribution aimed at AI fairness auditing in general computing environments. The authors emphasize that the framework can support systematic bias exploration, backtracking to raw quantities, multidimensional fairness analysis, and interactive report inspection. They conclude that the approach can standardize fairness measurement and facilitate broader exploration of bias concerns, while leaving further taxonomy expansion and additional building blocks to future work.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/methods paper with no empirical study, no comparison group, and no educational intervention evaluation. It is peer-reviewed workshop/technical paper content, but it does not meet criteria for experimental or correlational evidence on the requested topic.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no measured effect on trust, calibration, error detection, bias, dependence, or longitudinal use in teacher-facing generative AI. Its contribution is infrastructural and conceptual rather than demonstrated impact on educational practice or outcomes.

interventions.use_case: A fairness auditing and measurement library (FairBench) that standardizes decomposition of bias metrics into reusable building blocks for evaluating AI systems across group, subgroup, intersectional, and individual fairness settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes a mathematical framework and open-source Python library (FairBench) to standardize and systematize fairness auditing across many bias concerns. However, it is a framework/concept paper and does not report empirical effects on educational or learner outcomes (no n, effect size, or confidence interval reported).
finding.measure: Framework utility / fairness-audit standardization; no empirical educational outcome measure reported

paper_profiles.title: To what extent is ChatGPT useful for language teacher lesson plan creation?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can be useful for foreign language teachers when generating lesson plans, and specifically how prompt specificity affects the quality, consistency, and pedagogical alignment of outputs. The authors are concerned with whether generative AI can support instructional design while also introducing variability or bias toward outdated teaching practices.

The study used ChatGPT-4.0 and a set of five zero-shot prompts that gradually increased in specificity. The prompts were designed around a 45-minute high school Level I Spanish lesson for 30 novice students, with objectives related to describing a Costa Rican restaurant, asking and answering price questions, and identifying foods on a menu. Each prompt was run 10 times in separate chats, producing 50 lesson plans total. Outputs were scored against a 25-item rubric based on language-teaching best practices and edTPA-related criteria, and the authors analyzed score trends, output variability, and missing components.

Results showed that ChatGPT could generate generally strong lesson plans, but more detailed prompting did not consistently improve quality. The most useful addition was a checklist of required criteria, which improved average scores more than adding a lesson template or standards references alone. However, outputs were highly variable even for identical prompts, with some replicates missing many rubric elements and others scoring very highly. The authors also found recurring weaknesses related to cultural connections and teacher-student interaction, and they argue that some outputs reflected historic or outdated pedagogical practices such as audiolingual-style activities. They conclude that teachers can use ChatGPT as a lesson-planning aid, but outputs require careful human review and revision because of variability and potential bias.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical study with a clear methods section and systematic analysis, but it is not an RCT or QED in an educational outcome sense. The evidence is based on generated outputs and rubric scoring rather than learner outcomes, so it fits a lower-causal-inference tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical utility for teacher lesson planning and flags meaningful concerns about variability and bias, but it reports no learner-effect sizes or direct educational gains. The impact is therefore plausible and operationally relevant, yet still modest and indirect.

interventions.use_case: Using ChatGPT-4.0 to generate foreign language teacher lesson plans via zero-shot prompting, then varying prompt specificity to assess output quality, variability, and rubric alignment.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was generally useful for lesson plan creation and could streamline teacher planning, but performance depended on prompt design. Across 50 generated lesson plans (5 prompts x 10 iterations), mean rubric scores ranged from 19.6/25 to 21.6/25, with the highest mean occurring when a checklist of required criteria was included; output also showed significant variability within identical prompts, with scores ranging from 16/25 to 25/25.
finding.measure: Rubric-based scoring of lesson plans for presence/absence of 25 required components; word count; prompt-output variability via Jaccard distance, NMDS, PERMANOVA, and ANOSIM
finding.study_size: n=50 outputs from ChatGPT across 5 prompts, 10 iterations each

finding.finding_summary: The lesson plans were often well aligned to foreign language teaching goals, but alignment did not increase linearly with added prompt specificity. Mean rubric scores did not consistently improve from P.1 to P.5 (e.g., 21.2/25 at P.2, 19.8/25 at P.3, 19.6/25 at P.4, 21.6/25 at P.5), indicating that more detailed prompts sometimes produced shorter or less aligned plans rather than better ones.
finding.measure: Foreign-language lesson plan quality rubric aligned to ACTFL and edTPA-style criteria

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests teachers cannot rely on prompt specificity alone and must critically evaluate AI output because identical prompts produced highly variable lesson plans. The authors explicitly argue for teacher AI literacy in evaluating, revising, and guarding against anachronistic or biased pedagogical recommendations.
finding.measure: Observed output variability and qualitative assessment of strengths/weaknesses in generated lesson plans

finding.finding_summary: The paper raises concerns about algorithmic/historic bias in teacher-facing generative AI, noting that some outputs reflected outdated 20th-century pedagogies and weak cultural integration. These biases could shape instructional materials at scale if teachers adopt outputs uncritically, but the paper does not quantify downstream institutional effects.
finding.measure: Presence/absence of rubric components related to culture, communicative practice, and standards alignment; qualitative identification of outdated pedagogical patterns

paper_profiles.title: Case Study of GAI for Generating Novel Images for Real-World Embroidery
paper_profiles.venue: GenAICHI: CHI 2024 Workshop on Generative AI and HCI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can support the creation of embroiderable artwork patterns that are accessible to disabled makers. The authors focus on a practical problem in embroidery design: producing novel images that preserve the cultural or aesthetic intent of a design while also meeting strict real-world constraints such as low detail, centered composition, clean outlines, and compatibility with embroidery digitization workflows.

The intervention studied was an auto-ethnographic, disabled-led case study using DALL-E 2, DALL-E 3, GPT-4, and custom GPTs (CU-GPTs). One researcher with cognitive and motor disabilities first documented an initial exploration with DALL-E 2, then a five-person team with varying disabled identities and access needs iteratively built and refined custom GPTs using few-shot examples, prompt engineering, and uploaded training files. The generated images were converted into SVGs and then into embroidery files using software such as Adobe tools, Embrilliance, and Inkscape, and were fabricated on embroidery machines.

The paper reports that GAI had mixed success. It sometimes enabled more accessible and satisfying design generation, reducing the burden of drawing and helping create successful embroidered outputs such as a lotus or monstera leaf. However, it also frequently produced problematic outputs with too much detail, unwanted textures, off-center layouts, excessive SVG paths, or persistent features such as dots in paisley designs, even after explicit instruction changes. The authors conclude that GAI can contribute creativity and inclusion for disabled makers, but current models remain difficult to control reliably for embroidery-specific requirements, motivating future work on more accessible, better-optimized embroidery generation tools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed auto-ethnographic case study with iterative qualitative evaluation, but it is not experimental and does not report controlled comparisons or quantitative causal evidence. The methodology is exploratory and context-specific, so it provides only lower-to-moderate credibility evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful accessibility benefits for a priority population of disabled makers, but the evidence is qualitative and based on a very small case study. The impact appears promising but uncertain, with no effect sizes or scalable outcome evaluation reported.

interventions.use_case: custom GPTs and DALL-E/GPT-4-style generative AI used to generate embroiderable images with prompt engineering and few-shot conditioning for accessible design and fabrication

finding.finding_summary: The team found that generative AI sometimes reduced burden by producing images that were easier to convert into embroidery files, with fewer off-center images, fewer excessive SVG paths, and fewer back-and-forth prompt iterations than the initial DALL-E 2 exploration. However, it also introduced substantial inefficiency through repeated prompt refinement, failed generations, and conversion issues when details such as dots, textures, or background elements were not suppressed.
finding.measure: qualitative auto-ethnographic logs of prompt iterations, SVG conversion issues, and embroidery file success/failure
finding.study_size: n=5 researchers in the case study; n=1 end-user evaluator in initial exploration

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can improve accessibility and inclusion in creative making for disabled makers by lowering barriers to creating embroiderable artwork. At the same time, it emphasizes that current tools remain unreliable and require further design and evaluation before they can support broader accessible creative participation.
finding.measure: qualitative assessment of accessibility and inclusion implications in an auto-ethnographic case study

finding.finding_summary: This paper studies creative/artistic image generation for embroidery rather than a conventional academic learning outcome. The findings are mixed: GAI enabled novel culturally relevant designs and successful embroidered outputs, but also frequently produced unusable or overly complex images that failed real-world fabrication constraints.
finding.measure: qualitative evaluation of generated imagery and successful/failed embroidery fabrication outcomes
finding.study_size: n=5 researchers; repeated iterative generations over 2 months

paper_profiles.title: Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope Coronagraph Instrument Observation Calibration Plan
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a detailed calibration plan for the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope Coronagraph Instrument, a technology demonstration intended to enable high-contrast imaging of exoplanets and other faint point sources near bright stars. The central problem is how to remove or control the many sources of error that affect the conversion from detector counts to the planet-to-star flux ratio Fp/Fs, which is the key metric for coronagraphic performance. The paper frames calibration as part of the instrument’s overall flux-ratio noise budget and focuses on observation-based calibration products rather than internal calibration hardware.

The approach is organized around six calibration areas: absolute flux, charge transfer inefficiency, core throughput, flat fields, image corrections, and related processing steps. For each area, the authors describe the purpose, error allocation, current best estimate, observing strategy, and processing concept. The plan relies on on-sky standards and solar-system targets, including HST CALSPEC standard stars for absolute flux, trap-pumping frames for CTI characterization, FSM raster scans for core throughput mapping, Uranus and Neptune for flat-field calibration, and detector calibration sequences for K gain, nonlinearity, EM gain, and cosmic-ray masking.

The context is the Roman Coronagraph’s Technology Demonstration phase, with calibrations designed for on-sky operations and ground-based processing. The paper does not report a participant population in the educational sense, but rather an engineering/instrument context for space-based astronomical observations. Its main conclusion is that the proposed calibration strategy is feasible within the stated error budget, though several elements remain future work and will require additional optimization, especially around sampling patterns, CTI correction for photon-counted data, and calibration cadence.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a technical calibration plan for the Roman Space Telescope coronagraph, not an empirical education study. It contains no peer-reviewed educational intervention evaluation, no participant-level methodology, and no instructional or learner outcomes relevant to the requested taxonomy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational impact is measured or implied. The paper is about instrument calibration and error budgeting for astronomy, so it has no demonstrable effect on teaching, learning, or school operations.

paper_profiles.title: Twenty-Four Years of Empirical Research on Trust in AI: A Bibliometric Review of Trends, Overlooked Issues, and Future Directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews over two decades of empirical research on trust in AI. The authors ask how trust in AI has been studied across disciplines, what publication and citation patterns characterize the field, and what conceptual or methodological gaps remain. Their motivation is to map a fragmented literature and identify overlooked issues in how trust is defined, measured, and interpreted.

The study uses a mixed-method review approach combining bibliometric analysis with qualitative content analysis. The corpus includes 1,156 core empirical articles and 36,306 cited articles published from 2000 to 2023, drawn from Scopus, Web of Science, ACM Library, PubMed, and IEEE Explorer. The paper does not study a single educational intervention or user population; instead, it surveys trust research across domains such as human-robot interaction, computer science, healthcare, transportation, and consumer AI. The analysis highlights publication trends, co-citation structures, keyword clusters, and the most influential theoretical works.

The main conclusions are that trust in AI research is dominated by Western/global-North and technical perspectives, with heavy reliance on exploratory methods and limited theoretical grounding. The literature heavily draws on foundational work in trust in automation, especially calibration, reliance, and appropriate use. The authors argue that more contextualized, inclusive, and theory-driven research is needed, along with stronger methodological rigor and attention to long-term, real-world human-AI interactions.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a bibliometric and qualitative review of prior trust-in-AI studies, not an empirical evaluation of an educational intervention. It does not present a clear experimental, quasi-experimental, or correlational study of outcomes in learners or teachers.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct measured educational impact; it synthesizes the research field on trust in AI and offers methodological recommendations. Any relevance to teacher-facing generative AI is indirect and conceptual rather than evidence of impact.

paper_profiles.title: User Trust on an Explainable AI-based Medical Diagnosis Support System
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Workshop on Trust and Reliance in AI-Human Teams at CHI 2022 (TRAIT at CHI 2022)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how medical professionals trust and rely on an explainable AI system for chest X-ray diagnosis. The authors focus on the gap between technical model performance and user trust, asking whether providing causal explanations for a diagnosis can improve agreement with the system and calibrate reliance.

The intervention is an explainable AI-based medical diagnosis support system that predicts three emergency-department prognosis classes from chest X-rays and also outputs 13 causal anomaly probabilities as explanations. Users could view the image, inspect the model’s prediction and explanation, and then adjust the explanation probabilities via a slider if they disagreed. Trust was measured in two ways: observed trust (agreement with predictions and alignment with explanations) and self-reported trust using a five-item Likert questionnaire.

The study was conducted online with five radiology/clinic professionals from institutions in Germany. Results showed a 46.4% agreement rate with the model’s final predictions, while self-reported trust was moderate (median score 3.2/5). Users tended to align with the model’s explanations more than with its final predictions, suggesting some over-reliance on explanations and mixed trust overall. The authors conclude that explanation-based XAI alone did not fully calibrate trust, and that better communication of model uncertainty and more user training may be needed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small, peer-reviewed user study with qualitative and correlational elements, not an RCT or QED. The methodology is clear, but the sample size is very small (n=5), limiting credibility for causal claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests an unclear-to-modest impact on decision support behavior, with 46.4% agreement and signs of over-reliance but no intervention effect size on educational outcomes. Because the study is in a medical setting and primarily measures trust/calibration, the practical impact is informative but limited.

interventions.use_case: An explainable AI-based medical diagnosis support system for chest X-ray interpretation, showing model predictions plus causal explanations that users can edit before final diagnosis output.

finding.finding_summary: This study focused on user trust, agreement, and reliance when professionals interacted with an explainable diagnosis support system rather than on patient or learning outcomes. The main observed-behavior metric was agreement with the model’s final prediction: radiologists agreed in 46.4% of cases (n=5, 6 images each), despite the model achieving 74.12% accuracy on the test set. Explanations were often aligned with users’ edited causal explanations, but the system also showed signs of over-reliance on some incorrect explanations, indicating mixed effects on decision support behavior.
finding.measure: Agreement rate with model prediction; alignment of user-edited causal explanations with model explanations; self-reported trust questionnaire

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities, challenges, and responsible-use considerations of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT, in education. Rather than reporting an empirical intervention study, it synthesizes early research and current use cases to discuss how LLMs may affect learning and teaching across educational levels. The paper asks what educational value LLMs can provide, what risks they introduce, and what conditions are needed for safe and effective adoption.

The authors describe potential applications for students, including support for reading, writing, problem solving, curiosity prompting, feedback, tutoring, and language learning. For teachers, they highlight uses in lesson planning, personalized feedback, assessment, research support, and professional development. The discussion spans elementary, secondary, tertiary, group/remote learning, disability support, and professional training contexts, but it does not present a single implemented intervention or participant sample.

The main conclusion is that LLMs have substantial promise for education but require careful integration with human oversight, critical thinking, fact-checking, and strong attention to bias, privacy, copyright, sustainability, and fair access. The paper argues that these systems should complement rather than replace teachers or learners’ independent reasoning, and it offers mitigation strategies and design recommendations for responsible educational deployment.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper rather than an empirical study, with no original design, comparison group, or outcome data. It synthesizes prior literature and offers recommendations, so it does not meet criteria for experimental or quasi-experimental evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially broad educational relevance, but it reports no measured impacts and no effect sizes. Its practical implications are important but remain theoretical and therefore the observable impact is unclear.

interventions.use_case: Position paper discussing ChatGPT and other large language models as educational chatbots, conversational tutors, pedagogical agents, and teacher assistants for feedback, lesson planning, and adaptive student support.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can save teachers substantial time by automating or semi-automating feedback, quiz generation, lesson planning, and assessment tasks. Examples cited include grading effort reductions of up to 85% in prior NLP-based feedback work, though this paper itself does not report new experimental estimates.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, and task efficiency in lesson planning/assessment workflows

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims LLM-mediated instructional support can increase student engagement, curiosity, and willingness to participate in discussions, especially through pedagogical agents and conversational practice. These are presented as anticipated benefits and supported by cited prior studies, but no new effect size is reported in this position paper.
finding.measure: Student engagement, curiosity, participation, and anxiety/willingness to communicate

finding.finding_summary: A major theme is that LLMs may support critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and fact-checking when used as a complementary tool rather than a replacement for human instruction. The paper is conceptual and forward-looking, so it does not provide a quantified estimate of skill gains.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and fact-checking capabilities

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes substantial institutional opportunities alongside substantial risks: responsible use could broaden access, improve personalization, and support innovation, but poor governance could increase bias, privacy risks, plagiarism, and inequity. Because this is a position paper, the evidence is argumentative rather than experimental and no numeric effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, privacy, fairness, access, and institutional adoption considerations

paper_profiles.title: Examining Science Education in ChatGPT: An Exploratory Study of Generative Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory paper examines the use of ChatGPT in science education and asks three broad questions: how ChatGPT responds to science-education prompts, how educators might use ChatGPT in science pedagogy, and how ChatGPT itself can function as a research tool. Rather than testing a formal intervention with participants, the paper uses a self-study approach in which the author interacts with ChatGPT and reflects on its outputs in relation to science education literature.

The approach is centered on prompt-based examples. The author asks ChatGPT to identify characteristics of effective science teaching, compare teacher-centred and student-centred approaches, respond to a hypothetical struggling student, and generate teaching resources such as a Year 7 unit using the 5Es model, a rubric, and a quiz on renewable and non-renewable energy sources. These outputs are then compared with existing research and discussed for their usefulness and limitations.

The paper is framed in the context of educators and researchers experimenting with generative AI, especially in science education. The author concludes that ChatGPT can be helpful as a starting point for lesson planning, resource generation, and writing support, but its responses often lack evidence, context sensitivity, and specificity. The paper emphasizes that teachers must critically evaluate AI-generated material, adapt it to their setting, and consider ethical issues such as bias, copyright, and transparency in research use.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed exploratory self-study with clearly described prompts and qualitative analysis, but it is not a controlled comparative design and provides no causal evidence. Credibility is limited to the author’s reflective analysis and alignment checks against literature.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests plausible practical benefits for teacher planning and research drafting, but it reports no measured learner outcomes or effect sizes. Its impact is therefore informative and timely, but still unclear and unquantified for K-12 practice.

interventions.use_case: Exploratory self-study of ChatGPT as a generative AI tool for answering science education questions and generating teacher-facing resources such as a 5Es unit plan, rubric, quiz, and draft text for research writing.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT’s responses to science-education prompts often aligned with established themes in the literature, including inquiry-based learning, real-world connections, and assessment for learning. The paper is qualitative and exploratory, so it does not report effect sizes; rather, it argues that ChatGPT can serve as a useful starting point for designing science units and prompts, while requiring teacher verification and contextual adaptation.
finding.measure: Qualitative comparison of ChatGPT-generated responses against science education literature; usefulness of generated unit plans, rubrics, and quizzes

finding.finding_summary: The author finds ChatGPT potentially helpful for supporting critical thinking, brainstorming, and overcoming writer’s block, but also warns that it can present unsupported claims as authoritative and may encourage uncritical acceptance of outputs. No numeric effect sizes are reported because this is an exploratory self-study rather than an outcome comparison study.
finding.measure: Qualitative reflections on critical thinking, evidence evaluation, and writing support

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was reported to be useful for teacher-facing productivity tasks, especially drafting a science unit, generating a rubric, producing a quiz with answer key, and editing/rephrasing manuscript text. The paper provides no quantitative efficiency metrics, but the practical finding is that ChatGPT can reduce blank-page time and accelerate initial resource creation.
finding.measure: Qualitative assessment of teacher/researcher task support and drafting efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI raises important institutional concerns, including evidence quality, hallucinated citations, authorship, transparency, bias, copyright, and environmental impact. At the same time, it suggests that schools and journals will need clearer guidance and disclosure rules, indicating a positive governance role if institutions respond appropriately.
finding.measure: Qualitative discussion of ethical, policy, and publication implications

paper_profiles.title: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can improve real-time instructional support in K-12 tutoring by providing novice tutors with expert-like guidance during live sessions. The central problem is that novice educators often lack the experience to respond effectively in the moment, while traditional professional development is costly, slow to scale, and poorly aligned with immediate classroom or tutoring needs.

The authors introduce Tutor CoPilot, a human-AI system that embeds a language model inside a virtual tutoring platform. When activated during a tutoring session, the tool uses the ongoing conversation, lesson topic, and a selected pedagogical strategy to generate suggestions such as hints, guiding questions, minor corrections, or worked examples. The system was designed using prior work on extracting expert reasoning from think-aloud protocols, and tutors could edit, regenerate, or switch strategies to customize suggestions.

The study was a randomized controlled trial in a live virtual tutoring program with FEV Tutor and a U.S. southern school district. Participants included 900 tutors and 1,800 students from Title I schools, with students in grades 3-8, mostly Hispanic and economically disadvantaged. Tutors were randomly assigned to receive access to Tutor CoPilot or serve as controls. The study lasted two months and focused on math tutoring. Quantitative analyses showed that access to Tutor CoPilot increased exit-ticket mastery, especially for students supported by lower-rated or less-experienced tutors, and improved the language tutors used toward more constructive, understanding-oriented strategies. Tutor interviews suggested the system was helpful but sometimes produced suggestions that were not well aligned to grade level.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a preregistered randomized controlled trial with tutor-level random assignment, a large real-world sample, balance checks, and clustered regression analyses. It also triangulates effects with behavioral message data and reports nulls for some secondary outcomes, which strengthens credibility.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main academic outcome is a statistically significant 4 percentage point increase in exit-ticket mastery, with larger gains for lower-rated tutors (9 points), which is a medium-sized practical impact for a priority K-12 population. The intervention is low-cost and directly embedded in authentic tutoring practice, increasing its potential real-world value.

interventions.use_case: Human-AI tutoring support tool that generates real-time, expert-like pedagogical suggestions for K-12 math tutors during live tutoring sessions, including hints, guiding questions, worked examples, and strategy options.

finding.finding_summary: Tutor CoPilot improved proximal math learning outcomes in a preregistered RCT with 782 tutors and 4,136 tutoring sessions. Students whose tutors had access to the system were 4 percentage points more likely to pass exit tickets (62% to 66%, p<0.01), and the conditional pass rate increased by 3 percentage points among students who attempted the ticket (p<0.01).
finding.measure: Math exit ticket pass rate (unconditional and conditional on attempt)
finding.study_size: n=4136 sessions; 782 tutors at launch; 1800 students mentioned in abstract

finding.finding_summary: The intervention had larger effects for lower-performing tutors, indicating greater gains for students taught by tutors who started less effective. Lower-rated tutors’ students were 9 percentage points more likely to pass exit tickets (56% to 65%), and lower-experience tutors’ students were 7 percentage points more likely to pass (61% to 68%).
finding.measure: Math exit ticket pass rate by tutor quality rating and tutoring experience

finding.finding_summary: Tutor CoPilot changed tutor instructional behavior in ways consistent with stronger pedagogical reasoning and student thinking. Treatment tutors were about 2 standard deviations more likely to use strategies such as prompting students to explain and asking questions to guide thinking, and less likely to give away answers or solution strategies.
finding.measure: NLP-classified pedagogical strategy use in tutor chat messages (high-quality vs low-quality strategies)
finding.effect_size: approximately 2 standard deviations on a log-odds scale for some strategy categories

finding.finding_summary: Student self-report survey outcomes did not show statistically significant improvements. Measures including perceived tutor care, confidence in learning math when it is hard, and rating the session or tutor were near zero and non-significant, with treatment effects ranging roughly from -0.004 to 0.03.
finding.measure: Student post-session survey items on tutor care, learning confidence, session rating, and tutor rating

paper_profiles.title: Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence: Early experiments with GPT-4
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the capabilities and limitations of an early, text-only version of GPT-4 and argues that it represents a meaningful step toward artificial general intelligence (AGI). The authors do not study an educational intervention, but instead use a series of exploratory prompts and qualitative demonstrations to probe whether the model can generalize across domains, reason, plan, and communicate in human-like ways.

The paper presents examples spanning language, coding, mathematics, vision-like tasks through text, tool use, theory of mind, explainability, and common-sense reasoning. The authors compare GPT-4 with ChatGPT on selected examples and show that GPT-4 often produces more coherent, creative, and instruction-following outputs. They emphasize that the model can combine skills across disciplines, such as writing Shakespearean proofs, generating code for graphics, and answering complex questions about the world and human behavior.

The context is a research exploration by Microsoft Research of an early development version of GPT-4, not a study with human participants. The main conclusion is that GPT-4 exhibits unusually broad capabilities for a language model and may be reasonably viewed as an incomplete early AGI system, while still retaining important limitations such as hallucinations, arithmetic mistakes, lack of true planning, and other biases typical of large language models.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive research/demo paper and opinionated capability analysis, not a controlled educational study. It provides no K-12 sample, no experimental design, and no causal evidence about instructional impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not evaluate student or teacher outcomes in K-12 settings, and it reports no measurable educational effect sizes. Its relevance is conceptual rather than impact-based for education.

interventions.use_case: Early-version GPT-4 used as a general-purpose conversational AI to generate, explain, compare, and critique outputs across tasks; the paper probes its capabilities via teacher-like comparison prompts, dialogue generation, and interactive natural-language instruction.

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence is changing education and argues that effective educational use of AI depends on three core competencies: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. The author frames the issue as a response to the rapid spread of tools such as ChatGPT in academic work and classroom practice, alongside concerns about hallucinations, overreliance, academic integrity, and uneven educator preparedness. The paper is positioned as a conceptual discussion rather than an evaluation of a specific intervention.

The article combines a case study of AI adoption at Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich, Switzerland, with a narrative literature review. In the case study, the institution responded to student use of generative AI by creating internal AI guidelines that permit use under strict transparency, documentation, and critical review requirements. The paper also describes ways AI is already being used in teaching, such as student AI experiments, case-study construction, curriculum support, gamification, and immersive technologies, while noting practical constraints such as teacher anxiety, lack of training, and limited institutional support.

The paper concludes that simple restrictions or permissive policies are insufficient on their own. Instead, it recommends building an AI culture in educational institutions through workshops, updated guidance, budgeted support, and dedicated roles, along with formal AI literacy courses and explicit instruction in prompt engineering. The author argues that these measures can help students and teachers use AI responsibly, critically evaluate outputs, and integrate AI productively into learning and teaching, especially in higher education, though the ideas are also suggested to be potentially useful in school contexts.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual discussion with a small case-study component and narrative literature review, not a controlled empirical study. The paper provides no randomized, quasi-experimental, or systematic qualitative methodology sufficient for higher-confidence evidence grading.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper likely has modest or unclear impact because it offers actionable institutional guidance and teacher-facing recommendations, but it does not measure student learning or organizational effects. Its value is mainly normative and practical rather than demonstrably outcome-changing.

interventions.use_case: Use of ChatGPT and comparable LLMs as an informed conversational partner for student academic work, classroom experimentation, brainstorming, and feedback during paper writing and lesson activities; also discussed as a tool for generating case studies and supporting teacher planning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking are essential skills for responsible AI use, but it does not report direct causal evidence from an experiment. It provides conceptual and case-based claims that prompt engineering and critical reflection can improve students' ability to evaluate AI outputs and avoid hallucinations, but no effect sizes or controlled outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion; no formal outcome measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that AI tools can improve efficiency for teachers in curriculum design, case study construction, and classroom preparation, but this is presented as a practical recommendation rather than measured evidence. No quantitative estimates, sample sizes, or effect sizes are reported; the claims are based on informal discussions and the author's institutional experience.
finding.measure: Perceived efficiency in curriculum creation, case study generation, and preparation

finding.finding_summary: The paper's central empirical content is a case study and narrative review describing an institutional AI policy framework at a Swiss university, including guidelines for disclosure, acceptable use, and critical reflection. It reports the adoption of internal AI guidelines effective July 1, 2023, but does not quantify institutional outcomes or provide controlled evidence of policy impact.
finding.measure: Institutional AI guidelines, governance procedures, and implementation practices

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a generative AI model, specifically ChatGPT, can serve as a useful automated coach for teachers. The authors focus on three teacher-coaching tasks: scoring classroom transcript segments using classroom observation rubrics, identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

The study uses the NCTE Transcript dataset, a collection of elementary mathematics classroom transcripts from 4th- and 5th-grade classrooms in the United States. These transcripts were originally scored by expert raters using two established observation systems: CLASS and MQI. The authors evaluate ChatGPT in a zero-shot setting, comparing its score predictions against human ratings for quantitative scoring tasks and recruiting experienced math teachers to judge the quality of generated qualitative feedback.

Overall, the paper finds that ChatGPT has some promise but is far from matching expert coaching. Its score predictions correlate weakly with human ratings, and its qualitative feedback is often relevant but not especially novel or insightful. For suggestions, the model frequently repeats actions the teacher already performed in the transcript, limiting its usefulness as coaching feedback. The authors conclude that generative AI may eventually complement human instructional coaching, but current models need substantial improvement in truthfulness, novelty, and pedagogical insight.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical evaluation, but it is a small-sample observational/benchmark study rather than an RCT or strong QED. It has useful direct evidence on model behavior, but limited human raters and no causal design reduce credibility for impact claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows mostly weak or mixed performance, with only limited signs of usefulness (e.g., some actionable suggestions) and no demonstrated educational gains. Effect sizes are generally small or near zero, so the practical impact is currently unclear to modest.

interventions.use_case: zero-shot evaluation of ChatGPT as an automated teacher coach for classroom observation scoring, identifying instructional highlights/missed opportunities, and generating actionable coaching suggestions from elementary math transcript segments

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies whether ChatGPT can reduce the labor of teacher coaching by automating classroom observation scoring and feedback generation. Across 100 scored segments for Task A, correlations with human ratings were low (e.g., CLASS: CLBM up to r=0.35, CLPC near 0; MQI: mostly r=0.00-0.17), and teachers judged many Task B/C outputs as non-novel or insufficiently insightful, indicating limited current utility despite some actionable feedback.
finding.measure: Spearman correlation with human rubric scores; teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty on 3-point scales
finding.study_size: n=100 for scoring task; n=216 CLASS examples; n=288 MQI examples; n=36 suggestion examples

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI Toolkit - A Framework for Increasing the Quality of LLM-Based Applications over Their Whole Life Cycle
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of developing, testing, deploying, and monitoring large language model (LLM)-based applications over their full life cycle. The authors argue that current workflows are still largely manual, slow, and fragmented, which makes it difficult to improve quality, track prompt/model changes, and manage hallucinations or other failures at scale.

To address this, they introduce the Generative AI Toolkit, an open-source framework that automates DevOps-style workflows for LLM applications. The toolkit supports agent bootstrapping, custom metrics, repeatable evaluation cases, permutation-based comparison of models and prompts, CI/CD integration, deployment automation, debugging through a GUI, and logging/monitoring with traces. The paper illustrates these features through several representative use cases, including text-to-SQL, a RAG-based restaurant menu assistant, an in-car voice assistant, and model-comparison experiments.

The work is framed as a software engineering contribution rather than an educational intervention. It does not study students, teachers, or schools; instead, it targets developers building and operating LLM-based agents. The authors conclude that the toolkit can reduce cycle time, improve test coverage, and make quality monitoring more scalable, though they note that detailed quantitative benefits are difficult to generalize from the showcased examples.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a preprint framework/tool paper with illustrative use cases, not a peer-reviewed empirical study. It contains no randomized, quasi-experimental, or correlational evidence tied to K-12 education, and no rigorous causal evaluation of outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not evaluate any K-12 learner or teacher outcome, and it reports no measurable educational effect sizes. Its relevance is indirect, focusing on software engineering workflows for LLM applications rather than educational impact.

interventions.use_case: framework for building, testing, monitoring, and deploying LLM-based agents and conversational assistants, including text-to-SQL, restaurant menu RAG, and in-car voice assistant examples

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the Generative AI Toolkit reduces development cycle time and manual work across the LLM application lifecycle. It claims automation of evaluation, CI/CD integration, logging, and trace inspection can significantly shorten release cycles, but it does not provide controlled effect sizes or a formal experimental design.
finding.measure: Development cycle time; manual work reduction; qualitative efficiency gains in toolkit use cases

finding.finding_summary: The toolkit is positioned as infrastructure that standardizes development, deployment, and monitoring workflows for LLM systems, with open-source release intended to support broader adoption. The evidence is descriptive and implementation-oriented rather than causal, and no school- or K-12-specific institutional outcomes are measured.
finding.measure: Framework capability for lifecycle automation, CI/CD integration, and monitoring at scale

paper_profiles.title: AI for Proactive Mental Health: A Multi-Institutional, Longitudinal, Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether a generative AI system can provide proactive, strengths-based mental health support that improves well-being at scale for young adults, rather than waiting to treat symptoms after they emerge. The authors argue that most AI mental health tools are reactive and deficit-focused, and test whether a purpose-built app can instead promote resilience, belonging, mindfulness, and flourishing.

The intervention was the Flourish mobile app, which includes an AI chatbot (“Sunnie”), brief emotion check-ins, personalized science-based recommendations, gamification, weekly insight summaries, and safety monitoring. The app was designed around a closed-loop personalization framework and a STAR model (Science-based, Timely, Action-oriented, Real-life-focused) to encourage emotionally intelligent conversations and real-world well-being activities.

The study was a six-week randomized controlled trial conducted in Fall 2024 across three U.S. higher-education institutions: Chapman University, the University of Washington, and Foothill College. A total of 486 undergraduate students were randomized to receive app access or waitlist control, and outcomes were measured through repeated self-report surveys across four waves. The treatment group showed higher positive affect, greater resilience, belonging, and closeness to campus, as well as better mindfulness and flourishing over time, while negative affect, depression, anxiety, and stress did not significantly change. The authors conclude that generative AI can deliver scalable preventive well-being support, though the evidence is preliminary and the design cannot isolate which app components drove the effects.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a preregistered, longitudinal randomized controlled trial with multi-site recruitment, intent-to-treat analysis, validated measures, and appropriate mixed-effects modeling. There are some credibility caveats (waitlist rather than active control, self-reported app engagement, potential conflicts of interest), but the overall design is strong for causal inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced modest but statistically significant improvements in several well-being outcomes, with effect sizes mostly in the small range (e.g., d=0.33 for positive affect; β≈0.03-0.05 for other outcomes). This suggests meaningful but not large impact, especially for a general/college population rather than a clearly prioritized K-12 group.

interventions.use_case: generative AI-powered well-being mobile app (Flourish) delivering brief check-ins, conversational coaching, science-based activities, weekly insights, and gamified reinforcement for students
AI-powered well-being chatbot (Sunnie) that engages users in multi-turn conversations, offers emotionally intelligent feedback, and recommends coping and social-connection activities

finding.finding_summary: In a 6-week multi-institutional RCT with undergraduate students (n=486), access to the Flourish generative-AI app improved several well-being outcomes relative to waitlist control. Positive affect increased by Week 4 and Week 6 (e.g., Week 6 d=0.33; Condition × Time b=0.22, p=.020), and resilience, mindfulness, and flourishing also showed significant positive Condition × Time effects (b≈0.11-0.20, p<.05).
finding.measure: Positive/negative affect, loneliness, belonging, resilience, mindfulness, flourishing, depression, anxiety, stress, academic self-efficacy
finding.effect_size: d=0.33 for positive affect at Week 6; β≈0.03-0.05 across other significant outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved social well-being outcomes over time. Loneliness decreased more in the treatment group than in control (Condition × Time b=-0.05, p=.038, β=-0.03), while belonging increased (b=0.06, p=.030, β=0.04) and closeness to school showed a marginal positive trend (b=0.04, p=.070).
finding.measure: UCLA 3-item Loneliness Scale, campus belonging, closeness to school/university
finding.effect_size: β=-0.03 for loneliness; β=0.04 for belonging

finding.finding_summary: The study found no statistically significant effect on negative affect or its subcomponents. The Condition × Time interaction was non-significant for aggregated negative affect (b=0.0008, p=.933) and for depression, anxiety, and anger (all p>.516), suggesting the app’s benefits were concentrated on positive rather than deficit-oriented well-being.
finding.measure: Negative affect, depression, anxiety, anger

finding.finding_summary: Academic self-efficacy was assessed as an additional outcome, but the authors report no statistically significant change (p≥.462). The paper does not provide an effect size for this null finding, and the main discussion emphasizes that the short, light-touch intervention was not primarily designed to shift academic outcomes.
finding.measure: Academic self-efficacy

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Advanced Large Language Models with LLMSuite: A Free Comprehensive Recap of Techniques, Architectures, and Practical Applications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a tutorial-style overview of advanced large language model (LLM) techniques rather than an empirical study in education. It addresses the limitations of modern generative AI systems such as hallucinations, temporal knowledge cutoffs, and poor mathematical reasoning, and surveys methods intended to improve reliability and functionality. The central question is how LLMs can be made more accurate, useful, and scalable in real-world applications by combining them with external tools, retrieval systems, prompting strategies, and fine-tuning methods.

The paper reviews several approaches, including Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), chain-of-thought prompting, Program-Aided Language Models (PAL), ReAct, and LangChain for building tool-using applications. It also summarizes transformer architectures, multi-GPU training strategies such as DDP and FSDP/ZeRO, and efficient model variants like 1-bit LLMs. In addition, it explains fine-tuning approaches including instruction fine-tuning, multitask fine-tuning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA and prompt tuning), and alignment methods such as RLHF and ReST.

The paper does not study K-12 learners, teachers, or classrooms. Its audience is researchers and practitioners working on LLM development and deployment. The main conclusion is that modern generative AI systems are best understood as composite pipelines rather than standalone language models, and that combining retrieval, reasoning frameworks, and efficient fine-tuning can substantially improve performance, reliability, and efficiency across many application domains.

Because this is a conceptual/tutorial paper, it does not present participant-based educational intervention data, comparison groups, or outcome measures.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a tutorial/survey paper synthesizing LLM techniques and architectures rather than reporting an empirical study in K-12 education. It does not present a clear methodology, comparison design, or primary data collection.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper provides no direct evidence of educational impact in authentic K-12 teacher planning or coaching cycles, and no effect sizes or outcome data are reported. Its relevance is conceptual/background only for generative AI tooling.

paper_profiles.title: Testing for Reviewer Anchoring in Peer Review: A Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
