This paper investigates whether reviewers in academic peer review anchor to their original scores when they are later exposed to new information, such as an author rebuttal. The authors focus on a common peer-review workflow in which reviewers submit an initial review, receive additional evidence, and then revise their scores. They ask whether revised scores remain biased toward the original score, which could help explain why rebuttals often have limited impact on final decisions.

To test this, the authors ran a randomized controlled trial with 108 participants who were PhD students or PhDs in computer science-related fields. Participants acted as reviewers in a mock conference-review setting over Zoom and reviewed the same fabricated paper. The control group saw a paper with an animated GIF showing a strong result, while the experimental group initially saw a frozen frame of that GIF showing a weaker result. After submitting an initial review, the experimental group was told there had been a technical error and was shown the correct animated version, after which they could revise their scores and comments. The study measured overall scores and category scores, especially the Evaluation category, before and after the manipulation.

The manipulation successfully created a perceived quality difference between the initial experimental version and the control version, especially for the Evaluation category. However, when the revised scores from the experimental group were compared with the control scores, the study found no significant evidence of anchoring. The authors conclude that, in this simulated peer-review setting, reviewers did not systematically remain attached to their initial judgments after seeing corrected information. They note that real-world peer review may still differ in important ways, but this experiment provides no direct support for anchoring as an explanation for muted rebuttal effects.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed randomized controlled trial, but it does not study a K-12 educational intervention or an AI/technology intervention in education. The paper is methodologically strong for its own question, yet it has essentially no direct relevance to the requested education intervention taxonomy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study measures reviewer anchoring in academic peer review, not student, teacher, or school outcomes. It therefore provides no evidence of impact on K-12 educational outcomes or technology-mediated instruction.

paper_profiles.title: AI and the EU Digital Markets Act: Addressing the Risks of Bigness in Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the policy problem of how to regulate the emergence of large, entrenched actors in generative AI markets. The authors argue that the European Union’s Digital Markets Act (DMA), which targets platform gatekeepers, does not explicitly cover generative AI services even though such services may become important gateways for business users and end users.

Rather than presenting an empirical study or educational intervention, the paper proposes a legal and regulatory framework for extending the DMA to generative AI. It discusses how generative AI can be offered as a platform service, identifies possible gatekeeper characteristics in the sector, and explains why computing power, early-mover advantage, data resources, and integrated systems could produce durable market power among a small number of firms.

The paper’s context is the EU digital regulatory environment, including the DMA and related AI governance efforts such as the AI Act. The authors conclude that certain generative AI services should be treated as core platform services and that some developers should be designated as gatekeepers, so that DMA obligations can support contestability, fairness, diversity, and innovation in generative AI markets.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual policy/opinion paper, not an empirical evaluation of an educational intervention. It contains no study design, no sample, and no measured outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report any educational or student-level effects, so there is no measurable impact on K-12 outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Demystifying Instruction Mixing for Fine-tuning Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how different instruction dataset mixtures affect large language model (LLM) fine-tuning performance. The authors focus on a core question in instruction tuning: how to combine datasets so that a model gains broad capability without harming specific skills. They categorize instructions into three types: NLP downstream tasks, coding, and general chat.

The study fine-tunes LLaMA-2 7B and 13B models using representative datasets for each type: P3 for NLP tasks, CodeAlpaca for coding, and Alpaca for general instructions. They evaluate all eight combinations of these datasets on three outcome areas: NLP benchmark performance, code generation, and alignment/chat ability. The evaluation uses standard benchmarks such as ARC, MMLU, HumanEval, and the FLASK alignment framework with GPT-4 scoring.

Results show that specialized datasets improve performance in their own domains, but mixing all instruction types does not uniformly improve every capability. Alpaca is strongest for alignment and general NLP performance, CodeAlpaca improves coding and can also support chat quality, while P3 improves NLP task performance but tends to reduce alignment/chat ability when combined with other instruction types. The paper concludes that instruction mixing should be chosen carefully based on target use case and model size, since larger models appear better able to benefit from diverse instruction mixtures.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical benchmarking study with a clear experimental setup, but it is not a K-12 educational study and does not evaluate learner outcomes in authentic classrooms. It provides correlational/experimental evidence about LLM fine-tuning mixtures rather than a rigorous education intervention trial.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct impact on K-12 learners or educators and reports model benchmark changes rather than educational effects. Its findings are about LLM capability tradeoffs, not student or teacher outcomes.

interventions.use_case: instruction tuning and mixing for LLaMA-2 chat-style and task-following behavior using Alpaca, CodeAlpaca, and P3 datasets; the paper evaluates how fine-tuning mixtures affect model capabilities in chat/alignment and downstream task performance

finding.finding_summary: This paper evaluates efficiency-like model utility in terms of benchmark performance and alignment skill under different instruction mixtures, not human learner outcomes. Instruction mixing improves some capabilities but can also hurt others: for example, P3 hurts alignment by -2.8 points for LLaMA-2-7B and -3.6 for 13B, while Alpaca and CodeAlpaca improve alignment and task performance.
finding.measure: Zero-shot NLP benchmark averages, HumanEval pass@1/pass@10, FLASK alignment skill scores
finding.study_size: n=2 model sizes (LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-2-13B); 20K samples per dataset condition; alignment eval n=1,180 prompts

paper_profiles.title: Tinkering in Primary School: From Episode to Science Practice
paper_profiles.venue: The Primary School as a Playful Space
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how tinkering, understood as an open-ended constructionist practice, can be integrated into formal primary school science education without losing its exploratory character. The authors are interested in a central tension: tinkering can generate authentic student questions and deep engagement, but teachers often feel unprepared to connect those questions to disciplinary learning, especially in physics.

The study centers on the TIDE model (Tinkering, Ideas generation, Disciplinary connection, Exploration), which the authors developed as a way to bridge tinkering experiences with school curriculum. The implemented project, Oﬃcina della Luce (Light Workshop), ran in four primary schools in Bologna and involved 13 classrooms, 24 teachers, and approximately 300 students. Teachers received professional development in tinkering, access to a resource library of light-related activities, and a documentation protocol using fishbowl discussions; classrooms then carried out multiple light-tinkering workshops, though the original eight-month plan was compressed to four months because of pandemic-related disruption.

The analysis combines questionnaire responses from 20 teachers with qualitative examination of fishbowl documentation. Findings suggest that tinkering helped re-engage students, especially those who struggle in conventional school settings, while also revealing unexpected vulnerabilities among some high-performing, highly school-oriented students. At the same time, teachers reported uneasiness in handling emergent scientific questions and tended to choose humanities, storytelling, or expressive pathways more often than direct science follow-up. The authors conclude that tinkering can be a powerful entry point for student agency and scientific curiosity, but that effective integration into primary science teaching requires stronger disciplinary support for teachers and more sustained documentation of learning over time.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/action-research study with teacher questionnaires, coded open-ended responses, and one fishbowl protocol. It offers rich contextual evidence but no controlled design, randomization, or quantitative causal estimate.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful classroom-level benefits for engagement and inquiry, especially for students on the margins of school success, but it reports no effect sizes and provides only preliminary, context-specific evidence. The impact is therefore promising but unclear in magnitude.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that tinkering positively affected classroom dynamics, teacher engagement, and student access to knowledge, based on feedback from 20 teachers and fishbowl protocol analysis. Teachers also reported unexpectedly high engagement and participation among students often seen as disengaged, while some high-performing students experienced frustration or crisis during open-ended tasks.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire responses and qualitative fishbowl protocol analysis of classroom documentation
finding.study_size: n=20 teachers; approximately 300 students across 13 primary school classrooms

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that tinkering supported collaboration, self-reflection, mutual assistance, creativity, and student agency, especially in open-ended group work. The paper provides qualitative evidence that students developed persistence in managing frustration and working through failure, though no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher reports coded from open-ended questionnaire responses and classroom documentation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that tinkering surfaced relevant scientific questions, particularly around the physics of light, and prompted students to formulate and investigate research questions. In the fishbowl example, students generated a substantive question about producing white light with colored filters, but teachers were often unable to fully relaunch the inquiry because they felt underprepared scientifically.
finding.measure: Emergent student research questions, teacher documentation/reflection on physics inquiry, and disciplinary follow-up choices

finding.finding_summary: Although the project aimed to connect tinkering with disciplinary learning, teachers more often chose humanities, language, expression, and storytelling pathways than science-based follow-ups. The paper also notes that some classes did pursue physics experiments and hands-on activities, but this was less common and largely optional.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire on post-tinkering disciplinary integration choices

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Recommendations in EdTech: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether personalized content recommendations can increase engagement in an educational app, compared with a manually curated editorial recommendation system. The motivation is to provide direct causal evidence on whether personalization is useful in digital education, where evidence has been limited and often confounded by other interface changes.

The intervention was a personalized recommendation system built using matrix factorization on historical user-story interaction data. The authors first compared several candidate recommendation models offline, then deployed the selected model in a randomized experiment. Treatment users received personalized recommendations in the app’s “Recommended Story” section, while control users continued to see editorially curated stories. The study focused on children using Freadom, an English reading app developed by Stones2Milestones and used in India.

The experiment randomized 7,750 eligible users who each had at least 60 prior story interactions. The trial ran for two weeks, and outcomes were based on logged app behavior rather than self-report. The main findings are that personalized recommendations substantially increased engagement in the personalized section and also increased overall app usage, suggesting the gains were not merely shifting attention within the app. The benefits were larger for heavy users, users with niche preferences, and users with longer interaction histories. The paper concludes that personalization can meaningfully improve content consumption in digital education settings, at least for users with sufficient prior data for the model to work well.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled trial with a clear treatment/control comparison, pre-specified outcome measures, and multiple robustness checks. The main concern is that outcomes are engagement proxies rather than direct learning measures, but the causal design is strong.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced a modest-to-medium effect on a priority population’s app engagement, with a 60% increase in section engagement and 14% increase overall. However, the paper does not measure learning gains, so the educational impact is promising but not fully demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: personalized content recommendation for an educational reading app, ranking stories for children based on predicted engagement using matrix factorization rather than editorial curation
mobile and web educational app delivering short illustrated reading stories and quizzes to children, with a personalized Recommended Story section

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies reading-content engagement in an English literacy app for Indian children, using story completion and reading time as proxies for literacy-related learning use. Personalized recommendations increased engagement in the Recommended Story section by 60% (SE 17%; roughly n=3,023 app launchers, 7750 randomized) and increased total app usage by 14% (SE 7%), but the paper does not directly measure reading achievement or learning gains.
finding.measure: Story Engagement, completed stories, and reading time in a children’s reading app
finding.study_size: n=7750 randomized; n=3023 launched app during experiment
finding.effect_size: 60% increase in Recommended Story engagement; 14% increase in overall app usage

finding.finding_summary: The main demonstrated effect is higher user engagement with the educational app, which the authors frame as improved sustained use and willingness to spend more time reading. Total Story Engagement in the personalized section rose by 60% (SE 17%), and overall app engagement rose by 14% (SE 7%), indicating stronger interest and persistence in using the content rather than a direct skill outcome.
finding.measure: Engagement, session interactions, stories completed, and reading time
finding.study_size: n=7750 randomized; n=3023 launched app during experiment
finding.effect_size: 60% increase in section engagement; 14% increase in overall engagement

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) as the Reflective Partner: Empowering Teachers for Deep Learning Pedagogy
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Business (RIGGS)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emerging idea of artificial intelligence as a reflective partner for teachers, especially in relation to deep learning pedagogy. The authors argue that AI is increasingly capable of supporting teachers not only with technical tasks, but also with reflective teaching, lesson design, formative assessment, and instructional decision-making. They frame the problem as a gap between the acknowledged potential of AI and its limited, partial, and often non-systematic use in teacher professional development.

To address this question, the paper conducts a systematic literature review using PRISMA procedures. The review searched the SpringerLink database and selected 21 recent articles, which were then qualitatively analyzed with Atlas.ti to identify themes and conceptual relationships. The review does not study one cohort directly; rather, it synthesizes existing research on teachers, teacher education, and AI-enabled pedagogical tools across a range of educational contexts, with special attention to reflection and deep learning.

The synthesis produces five major themes: AI-supported deep learning lesson design, AI in orchestrating deep learning processes, AI-augmented deep learning assessment, AI-driven reflective teaching practices, and ethical/contextual AI integration. The authors conclude that AI can function as a co-designer, co-orchestrator, and reflective partner for teachers, but only when human judgment remains central and implementation is supported by practice-based training, ethical safeguards, contextual adaptation, and data protection. They also emphasize that further longitudinal and cross-cultural research is needed to test long-term effectiveness in real classrooms.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic literature review with qualitative synthesis, not a primary causal study. It provides structured evidence from 21 included articles, but the paper itself does not estimate effects from original data and includes mixed study types with varying rigor.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for teacher reflection and instructional quality, but most claims are synthesized from prior studies and the focal article reports no direct outcome data from its own sample. The impact is therefore plausible but still unclear in magnitude for K-12 practice.

interventions.use_case: AI-generated personalized feedback and teacher-facing analytics to support reflective teaching, questioning quality improvement, and classroom discourse analysis in teacher professional learning cycles
Generative AI and large language models used as reflective partners for teachers, including prompt generation, inquiry prompts, and reflective dialogue support
AI-powered teacher dashboard and analytics that adaptively summarize classroom video/discourse data and recommend instructional adjustments

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes evidence that AI-supported reflection and feedback can improve teachers’ instructional reasoning, questioning, and reflective practice. Across cited studies, automated feedback increased teachers’ use of focusing questions by about 20% in K-12 classrooms, indicating stronger support for higher-order thinking and reflective decision-making.
finding.measure: Teacher questioning quality, focusing-question use, reflective practice indicators from classroom discourse analytics

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that AI dashboards, automated summaries, and knowledge-curation functions reduce the burden of analyzing classroom video, identifying patterns, and translating evidence into action plans. These tools are described as helping teachers work more efficiently during planning, reflection, and professional development cycles, although the paper does not provide a pooled quantitative effect size.
finding.measure: Teacher dashboard utility, time/effort for reflection, instructional action planning support

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that successful AI integration in teacher professional development depends on policy, ethics, privacy, and local contextualization. It emphasizes human-in-the-loop governance, data protection, and curriculum alignment as necessary institutional conditions for sustainable adoption, but this is synthesized from literature rather than directly tested.
finding.measure: Policy/ethics/contextual readiness themes from systematic review

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how generative AI, especially large language models such as ChatGPT, can be aligned with the core pedagogical principles of formative assessment and feedback. The authors argue that much existing work on AI in education emphasizes technical performance or automation, but often misses the formative purpose of helping learners understand where they are, where they are going, and how to move forward.

Rather than reporting an empirical intervention study, the paper offers a narrative, practice-oriented framework. It organizes discussion around three formative assessment functions: clarifying learning goals, diagnosing where the learner is, and providing feedback that moves learning forward. Within each, it shows how generic LLMs, domain-specialized LLMs, and LLM-integrated educational technologies can be used through prompting to rewrite learning objectives in student-friendly language, co-construct success criteria, generate exemplars or sample work, create diagnostic questions and MCQs, and produce different levels of feedback.

The paper focuses on classroom educational practice, especially K-12 and higher-education teaching scenarios, but it does not present a participant sample, implementation trial, or direct comparative evaluation. Its main conclusion is that LLMs can augment formative assessment at scale, but only when used with teacher expertise, pedagogical judgment, and careful prompt design. The authors also emphasize that future research should develop better metrics for formative feedback quality and create pedagogically grounded prompt templates and evaluation frameworks.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative/practical review rather than an empirical study, and it does not report a systematic methodology, comparison design, or primary outcome data. It is peer-reviewed scholarly commentary, but not causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has potentially broad relevance for K-12 teacher planning and feedback workflows, but it reports no measured impact on student or teacher outcomes. Its contribution is conceptual and practice-oriented rather than demonstrably outcome-changing.

interventions.use_case: Narrative review and practical guidance on using generic LLMs like ChatGPT to support formative assessment tasks such as rewriting learning objectives, generating classroom discussion prompts, creating sample work, and producing feedback that helps students move forward.
Using LLMs to generate task-, process-, and self-regulation-level feedback on student work, including examples for code, essays, and methods sections, as part of formative assessment cycles.

paper_profiles.title: Reflecting in the Reflection: Integrating a Socratic Questioning Framework into Automated AI-Based Question Generation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint addresses the problem of generating high-quality reflection questions for learning environments, a task that is pedagogically important but time-consuming and inconsistent when done manually by teachers. The authors argue that existing automatic question generation systems mainly focus on factual recall and do not adequately support reflective, metacognitive prompts.

To address this gap, the paper proposes a "reflection-in-reflection" framework that uses two LLM-based agents: a Student–Teacher agent that drafts and revises reflection questions, and a Teacher–Educator agent that applies Socratic questioning to coach revisions. The system takes as input a teacher-specified topic, key concepts, optional instructional materials, and optionally student level. The agents iteratively refine a single question until the Teacher–Educator signals that it is satisfactory.

The empirical evaluation was conducted in an authentic lower-secondary ICT context in Czechia, using instructional materials for 8th–9th grade students about how the internet works. The backbone model was GPT-4o-mini, and a stronger GPT-4-class model served as an external evaluator in pairwise comparisons. The study varied whether student level and supporting materials were provided and compared dynamic stopping with fixed-length refinement, then also compared the two-agent protocol against a one-shot baseline.

The main conclusion is that dynamic, context-aware refinement generally produces better questions than fixed-length iteration, and that the two-agent Socratic protocol outperforms the one-shot baseline, especially for relevance and depth. The gains are strongest when contextual information is supplied, though the authors note that longer fixed dialogues can drift off topic and that the structured protocol trades a small amount of surface clarity for better pedagogical alignment and deeper reflection.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a preprint with an experimental comparison design and substantial quantitative evaluation, but it uses an LLM judge rather than human raters and does not report a randomized educational outcome study with learners. The evidence is informative but best treated as qualitative/engineering evidence rather than high-credibility causal evidence in K-12 classrooms.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful improvements in prompt quality, especially relevance and depth, but the study evaluates generated questions rather than downstream student learning or teacher productivity with measured effect sizes. The likely practical impact is promising but remains indirect and unquantified.

interventions.use_case: Two-agent LLM-based reflective question generation for teachers, using a Student–Teacher agent to draft and revise questions and a Teacher–Educator agent to provide Socratic coaching feedback in an iterative dialogue.

LLM-generated pedagogical feedback on candidate reflection questions, with the Teacher–Educator agent evaluating clarity, depth, relevance, engagement, and interconnections and returning targeted coaching questions rather than rewrites.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether AI-generated reflection questions are better aligned to an ICT topic (fundamentals of how the internet works) in an authentic lower-secondary setting. Compared with a one-shot baseline, the two-agent reflection-in-reflection protocol is judged substantially more relevant and deeper, with relevance preference indices ranging from 0.60 to 0.92 and depth commonly above 0.60 across context settings.
finding.measure: LLM pairwise judgments of relevance and depth for generated reflection questions

finding.finding_summary: The system is designed to reduce teacher authoring time by automating the iterative refinement of reflection questions. The paper reports that dynamic stopping with contextual information consistently outperforms fixed 5- and 10-step refinement, suggesting a more efficient generation process than longer fixed dialogues, though no direct time metric is reported.
finding.measure: Protocol behavior and comparative quality of generated questions under dynamic vs fixed iteration regimes

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main pedagogical target is reflective, metacognitive question quality rather than student achievement. The two-agent Socratic protocol is judged to produce questions that are deeper and more reflective than a one-shot prompt, indicating stronger support for critical thinking and metacognitive engagement, but the study does not measure learner outcomes directly.
finding.measure: LLM pairwise judgments of depth and overall quality of reflection prompts

paper_profiles.title: GenAI in the Classroom: The Interplay of Teachers’ Pedagogical Beliefs and Perceptions of the Technology
paper_profiles.venue: Shaping the Future of Education in the Age of AI: Empowering Inclusion, Innovation and Ethical Growth : EDEN 2025 Annual Conference Proceedings
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle-school teachers perceive generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and how those perceptions interact with their pedagogical beliefs. The central question is not whether GenAI can be used in classrooms, but how teachers’ views of teaching, learning, and assessment shape their willingness to adopt or restrict the technology.

The study used semi-structured interviews with 24 middle-school teachers in Israel, drawn from different subject areas. Interviews were conducted during the summer break of 2024 and focused on teachers’ views of GenAI, their sense of the education system’s readiness, and how they expected to adapt their teaching practices. The paper is therefore situated in an authentic K-12 context, but it is a qualitative study of teacher perspectives rather than an intervention study.

Findings show that teachers generally distinguish between using GenAI for their own lesson preparation and allowing students to use it. Most were more open to teacher-facing uses than student-facing uses. Their choices were strongly linked to pedagogical orientation: teachers focused on content transmission were more likely to distrust GenAI as an information source, while teachers emphasizing student thinking worried that GenAI could reduce cognitive effort. Assessment concerns were especially prominent, with teachers often preferring classroom work, tests, and homework controls to limit unethical student use. The authors conclude that GenAI adoption is shaped both by pedagogical beliefs and by teachers’ understanding of the technology’s capabilities and limitations.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative study based on semi-structured interviews with 24 teachers. It offers useful contextual evidence but no experimental design, no comparison group, and no quantitative effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially important implications for classroom GenAI adoption and assessment practice, but it reports perceptions rather than measured impacts on student outcomes. Its practical impact is therefore plausible but unclear and not demonstrated with effect sizes.

interventions.use_case: GenAI-enabled instructional chatbots and classroom AI use for lesson preparation and student learning support in middle-school settings

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative study of 24 middle-school teachers in Israel found that teachers differentiated between using GenAI for their own lesson preparation and allowing student use, with strong concerns about ethics, reliability, and assessment integrity. The paper does not report effect sizes; instead it shows that pedagogical beliefs and perceptions of GenAI’s affordances/limitations shaped whether teachers endorsed classroom adoption or restricted it.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on teachers' perceptions of GenAI, school readiness, and adaptation strategies

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed GenAI could support knowledge construction and autonomy, but many also felt it could undermine students’ thinking effort and critical engagement. The study highlights this tension qualitatively rather than with quantitative effect estimates, and reports that some teachers responded by preferring tests and classroom work over projects and term papers.
finding.measure: Interview-reported perceptions of critical thinking, cognitive effort, and learner autonomy

paper_profiles.title: Marketing Education in the Age of Generative AI: Preparing Graduates for Human–AI Collaboration
paper_profiles.venue: Academy of Marketing Marketing Education SIG white paper
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This white paper examines how generative AI is reshaping marketing education and what that means for curriculum, pedagogy, assessment, employability, ethics, and institutional policy. The central problem is not whether AI should be used, but how educators can integrate it in ways that preserve disciplinary learning, critical judgement, transparency, and ethical accountability. The paper argues that GenAI has become a normal condition of both student learning and marketing practice, and that education must shift from focusing on output production to evaluating, directing, and justifying AI-assisted work.

The paper draws on three sources of evidence: a review of contemporary literature, the experience and expert contributions of the Academy of Marketing Marketing Education Special Interest Group development team, and an online survey of 89 marketing educators conducted in September–October 2025. The survey sample was predominantly UK-based and included educators teaching undergraduate and postgraduate programmes. The paper uses these inputs to identify where GenAI is changing teaching most strongly, especially in branding and communications, customer insight and analytics, and strategic decision-making.

Across the paper, the authors recommend redesigning learning around process visibility and human-led reasoning. Suggested practices include AI-use disclosure, prompt and version logs, critique of AI outputs, verification checklists, reflective commentary, and oral defences. The paper concludes that effective marketing education should embed AI within core modules, strengthen staff capability in judgement-led pedagogy, support equitable access, and align policy with teaching design. It positions GenAI as a collaborator that can support creativity and efficiency, but only when human expertise remains responsible for interpretation, contextualisation, and ethical judgement.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a sector white paper and literature synthesis with a convenience survey of 89 educators, not a controlled empirical study. It provides useful descriptive insights but does not meet criteria for rigorous causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful but unquantified educational and institutional effects, especially for curriculum redesign and assessment practices. Because the evidence is descriptive and no effect sizes are reported, the observed impact is best classified as modest or unclear rather than clearly large.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI used as a co-creator and feedback partner in marketing education, including chat-based prompting for brainstorming, drafting, refinement, critique, and iterative comparison of AI-generated outputs against human-revised work.

AI-generated formative feedback and critique on student marketing outputs, especially through compare-and-improve tasks, prompt/version logs, verification checklists, and revision cycles that surface reasoning rather than only final products.

finding.finding_summary: This white paper reports survey findings from n=89 marketing educators and synthesizes literature on curriculum, pedagogy, assessment, employability, and governance. The evidence indicates broad perceived institutional disruption from GenAI, alongside calls for structural redesign of policy and assessment rather than simple prohibition or detection-based control. No causal effect sizes are reported because the paper is a sector white paper and not an intervention study.
finding.measure: Survey perceptions of institutional readiness, curriculum/assessment change, and governance needs; literature synthesis
finding.study_size: n=89 (survey); broader literature review not specified

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI can support critical thinking, reflection, and judgement when students are required to critique, refine, and justify outputs, but may also erode deep reasoning through cognitive offloading and over-reliance. Evidence is qualitative and conceptual, informed by survey responses (n=89) and cited classroom accounts rather than a controlled impact estimate.
finding.measure: Perceived development or erosion of critical thinking, metacognition, and judgement in marketing tasks

finding.finding_summary: Across marketing curriculum areas, educators report that GenAI can improve ideation, scenario testing, branding, analytics interpretation, and strategic comparison, but can also produce generic, stereotyped, or strategically flawed outputs that weaken disciplinary understanding if used uncritically. The paper provides no experimental effect size; it relies on survey perceptions (n=89) and examples of classroom use cases.
finding.measure: Perceived changes in marketing curriculum learning and disciplinary reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly notes that GenAI accelerates drafting, brainstorming, feedback cycles, and workflow orchestration in marketing education and practice. This is presented as a practical benefit rather than a quantified causal effect; no effect size or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: Perceived productivity, drafting speed, and workflow efficiency in AI-supported tasks

paper_profiles.title: School guidance support and growth in mathematics discourse feedback skills: a three-wave longitudinal mediation study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether perceived school guidance support is associated with growth in students’ mathematics discourse feedback skills, and whether that association operates through two time-ordered mediators: major decision-making self-efficacy and feedback literacy behavior. The authors frame the problem as a challenge of how contextual support helps students not only receive feedback, but also use it productively in classroom mathematical dialogue.

The study used a three-wave longitudinal design with Chinese senior high school students in Hebei, China. Students reported school guidance support at Time 1, major decision-making self-efficacy at Time 2, feedback literacy behavior at Time 3, and mathematics discourse feedback skills across all three waves. The sample included 2,120 adolescents from three senior high schools, with data collected at approximately three-month intervals. Analyses used longitudinal structural equation modeling with controls for prior skill levels and demographic covariates.

Results showed that higher perceived school guidance support predicted stronger later mathematics discourse feedback skills both directly and indirectly. The association was mediated by major decision-making self-efficacy and by feedback literacy behavior, and a sequential pathway from guidance support to self-efficacy to feedback literacy behavior to mathematics discourse feedback skills was also supported. The authors conclude that school guidance services may support disciplinary feedback skill development by strengthening students’ confidence in decision-making and by fostering habitual feedback-seeking and feedback-use behaviors.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed longitudinal correlational study with three waves, measurement invariance testing, and structural equation modeling. However, it is not an experimental or quasi-experimental intervention study, so causal credibility is limited despite strong statistical controls.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are positive and moderately sized in standardized terms, but they concern student self-report constructs rather than direct achievement or implementation outcomes. The study is informative for theory and school guidance practice, yet it does not test an education technology or AI intervention and has unclear direct operational impact.

finding.finding_summary: This three-wave longitudinal study found that higher T1 school guidance support predicted higher T3 mathematics discourse feedback skills, controlling for prior skills and demographics. In the fully adjusted sequential mediation model, the total standardized effect was β=0.371, with a remaining direct effect of β=0.112 and a significant indirect pathway via major decision-making self-efficacy and feedback literacy behavior (β=0.054).
finding.measure: High School Students’ Mathematics Discourse Feedback Skills Scale (MDFSS), measured at T1, T2, and T3
finding.effect_size: β=0.371 total; β=0.112 direct; β=0.054 sequential indirect

finding.finding_summary: School guidance support was strongly associated with greater major decision-making self-efficacy at T2, which then predicted later mathematics discourse feedback skills. In the single-mediator model, the path from guidance support to self-efficacy was β=0.476, and the indirect effect through self-efficacy was β=0.126 (95% CI [0.107, 0.142]).
finding.measure: Major Decision-Making Self-Efficacy Scale
finding.study_size: n=2120 at T1; longitudinal SEM on retained sample
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI [0.434, 0.512] for guidance→self-efficacy; [0.107, 0.142] for indirect effect

finding.finding_summary: Feedback literacy behavior was positively associated with later mathematics discourse feedback skills, and it partially explained the effect of school guidance support. In the sequential mediation model, guidance support predicted feedback literacy behavior (β=0.213), and the indirect pathway via feedback literacy behavior was significant (β=0.059, 95% CI [0.034, 0.088]); the full sequential chain through self-efficacy and feedback literacy was also significant (β=0.054).
finding.measure: Feedback Literacy Behavior Scale and MDFSS
finding.study_size: n=1938 at T3 in the final wave; structural model based on longitudinal sample
finding.effect_size: β=0.213 path; β=0.059 indirect; β=0.054 sequential indirect
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI [0.034, 0.088] for feedback-literacy indirect; [0.037, 0.076] for sequential indirect

paper_profiles.title: Fostering Interactional Competence through AI-Based Virtual Dialogue: Task Awareness Transformation in Japanese Pre-service Elementary School Teachers
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of English Language Teaching and Linguistics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study examines how repeated interaction with a generative AI-based virtual dialogue environment can change pre-service teachers’ understanding of interactional competence (IC). The paper starts from a teacher-education problem common in Japan: pre-service elementary teachers often focus on their own English accuracy rather than on how to facilitate interaction with children, even though classroom teaching requires them to manage incomplete, spontaneous, and learner-driven communication.

To address this, the researchers created a two-week AI dialogue activity using ChatGPT voice mode, in which two Japanese university students acted as elementary school teachers conversing with an AI programmed to behave like a child with intentionally incomplete, unpredictable, and sometimes off-topic responses. After the practice period, the participants completed semi-structured interviews, and the transcripts were analyzed using Grounded Theory Approach. The study did not use a comparison group; instead, it focused on how participants made sense of the experience and how their task awareness shifted over time.

The analysis produced a four-stage model: initial difficulty due to a mismatch between expectations and the AI’s behavior, a shift from self-focused English anxiety toward learner-focused pedagogy, a concretization of likely classroom conflicts, and an emerging desire for support such as feedback, teaching-method guidance, and customizable practice scenarios. The authors conclude that AI-mediated “friction” can productively destabilize pre-service teachers’ assumptions and help them reframe IC as co-constructing meaning with learners. They argue that AI for teacher training should not aim for perfect fluency alone, but should include intentional imperfection plus scaffolded feedback and reflection.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative exploratory pilot grounded in interviews with only two participants, so it provides limited credibility for causal claims. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically transparent, but it does not meet experimental or quasi-experimental standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests potentially meaningful professional learning for a priority population (pre-service teachers), but the evidence is conceptual and qualitative rather than outcome-based. Any impact is currently unclear and cannot be quantified from this pilot.

interventions.use_case: generative AI voice-mode virtual dialogue with ChatGPT acting as a Japanese elementary school child in repeated teacher-practice conversations designed to create intentional interactional friction

finding.finding_summary: In this two-participant pilot, repeated AI-based virtual dialogue was associated with a shift from self-focused English anxiety toward a more pedagogically grounded view of interactional competence. Participants reported greater awareness of how to adjust English for learner understanding, with one explicitly saying IC became 'the most important thing next to speaking English' after the intervention (n=2; no effect size reported).
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes about task awareness, interactional competence, and self-reported shifts in teacher talk orientation

finding.finding_summary: The intervention appeared to strengthen reflective judgment and pedagogical awareness rather than discrete language performance. Through AI-generated 'friction,' participants moved from viewing difficulties as personal English deficits to recognizing instructional problems, suggesting growth in metacognitive noticing and professional vision (n=2; no effect size reported).
finding.measure: Grounded-theory analysis of interview transcripts on awareness transformation and reflective interpretation of interactional trouble

finding.finding_summary: Participants initially felt overwhelmed and pushed by the AI, but this discomfort was interpreted as productive rather than discouraging, eventually prompting curiosity, a desire for more practice opportunities, and requests for supportive feedback. The paper does not report quantitative affect measures, but the qualitative evidence suggests improved tolerance for ambiguity and constructive engagement with challenge (n=2).
finding.measure: Interview-derived reports of overwhelm, frustration, desire for feedback, and willingness to continue practice

paper_profiles.title: THE ROLE OF SPEAKING CLUBS IN THE FORMATION OF COMMUNICATIVE COMPETENCE OF STUDENTS OF AGRICULTURAL UNIVERSITIES
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the role of language clubs as an innovative extracurricular format for developing foreign-language communicative competence among students in non-language majors, especially agricultural specialities. The central problem is that conventional foreign-language instruction does not always provide enough authentic speaking practice, motivation, or intercultural engagement for future agricultural professionals.

The paper argues for language clubs (Sprachklubs) as a flexible intervention that creates a low-anxiety, informal environment for communication. It describes common formats such as thematic meetings, role plays, free conversation, games, film clubs, book clubs, debates, tandems, and mini-lessons, and then adapts these to the agricultural university context through discipline-related discussion evenings, culinary workshops, film discussions, role-play simulations of agrarian forums, project work, and meetings with native speakers. The article also highlights CLIL (Content and Language Integrated Learning) as a useful framework for combining subject content with language practice.

The population discussed is undergraduate students at a Ukrainian agricultural university, with examples drawn from students at Sumy National Agrarian University and specifically a food technologies faculty scenario. The paper concludes that language clubs can strengthen motivation, reduce speaking anxiety, support intercultural communication, and build professional terminology and oral communication skills. It also notes that online/digital language clubs are increasingly important because of COVID-19 and wartime disruptions, although the paper remains primarily conceptual and practice-oriented rather than empirical.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/theoretical discussion paper rather than an empirical study. It does not report a controlled design, sample, or quantitative outcomes for AI use in writing instruction.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper identifies potentially meaningful pedagogical effects of AI writing tools, but it provides no measured effect sizes or direct evidence of impact. Its practical relevance is clear, but the magnitude of impact remains unclear from the evidence presented.

interventions.use_case: Use of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and other AI-based writing assistants to support university students’ English writing through idea generation, grammar/style correction, text refinement, and feedback on drafts.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-driven writing tools can improve the efficiency and polish of student writing by supporting idea generation, contextual prompting, grammar correction, and style refinement. At the same time, it warns that such tools may reduce authenticity, individuality, and creativity in written texts, especially when students over-rely on generated content. No original sample, effect size, or quantitative outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: Narrative assessment of writing quality, creativity, authenticity, and revision support in AI-assisted English writing

paper_profiles.title: CaseMaster: Designing and Evaluating a Probe for Oral Case Presentation Training with LLM Assistance
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of training medical students to deliver effective oral case presentations (OCPs), a core communication skill in clinical education. The authors argue that traditional OCP training methods—such as case discussion, case writing, and role-play—can be difficult to scale, may not provide enough structured guidance, and often fail to deliver timely, constructive feedback. They also identify an opportunity for large language models (LLMs) to support training, but note concerns about prompt burden, reliability, and integration into educational workflows.

To explore this space, the authors conducted a formative study with six medical educators to understand current OCP teaching practices, difficulties in student presentations, and attitudes toward LLM use. Based on these insights, they designed CaseMaster, a web-based system probe that supports OCP training through two stages: preparation and reflection. In preparation, students browse patient cases, draft presentations using the SOAP structure, and use preset LLM-assisted actions to search for key knowledge, evaluate logic, generate examples, and receive presentation advice. In reflection, they compare their responses against reference answers and receive rubric-based scoring and feedback generated with an LLM.

The evaluation involved two user studies in a hospital-linked medical education context in China. The first study compared CaseMaster with a baseline workflow among 12 university medical students completing OCP tasks; the second collected feedback from five experienced educators. Results suggested that CaseMaster improved presentation quality, confidence, and efficiency relative to the baseline workflow, while educators generally viewed the tool favorably but emphasized the need for careful use and critical review of LLM outputs. The paper concludes with design guidelines for creating adaptive, transparent, and user-centered LLM-based training tools for medical education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed design-and-evaluation study with formative qualitative work plus a small controlled user study, but it is not a well-powered randomized trial and reports limited quantitative outcome evidence. The methodology is credible for prototype evaluation, yet the evidence base is mainly qualitative and early-stage.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests promising positive effects on presentation quality, confidence, and workload, but the impacts are not quantified with effect sizes and come from a small n=12 study. That makes the likely impact plausible but still modest and unclear for broader educational settings.

interventions.use_case: LLM-assisted oral case presentation training probe that generates case-specific content, suggests presentation improvements, searches key knowledge points, and provides reflective feedback/scoring on student presentations.
LLM-based validation and rubric scoring of student oral case presentations, highlighting omissions, discrepancies, and rubric-based performance across history, labs, assessment, plan, and style.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that CaseMaster had the potential to improve presentation quality in oral case presentation training, with students and educators describing clearer, more coherent delivery. In the 12-student experiment, the authors state that the tool had positive impacts on confidence and presentation skills, but they do not report a standardized effect size for this outcome.
finding.measure: Oral case presentation quality / presentation skills, participant feedback on confidence and usability

finding.finding_summary: CaseMaster was designed to support structured reasoning, self-reflection, and error detection during case preparation and review. The paper reports that the reflection stage highlighted discrepancies and missing elements in student drafts, suggesting improved metacognitive review, but no quantitative effect size is provided for these learning-process outcomes.
finding.measure: Self-reflection, error identification, and structured reasoning during OCP preparation and review

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that CaseMaster can reduce workload compared with traditional methods by automating feedback and scoring, and educators reinforced this implication in qualitative feedback. However, the paper does not provide a quantified workload reduction estimate or time-on-task effect size.
finding.measure: Perceived workload / efficiency of feedback and evaluation workflow
finding.study_size: n=12 students; 5 educators in follow-up evaluation

paper_profiles.title: Generative artificial intelligence-driven adaptive learning for sustainable, personalized, and resilient education systems
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Applied Resilience and Sustainability
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of how generative artificial intelligence can be used to make education more personalized, scalable, resilient, and sustainable. The authors argue that traditional educational systems struggle to meet diverse learner needs, support individualized pacing, and remain effective under disruption, while also raising concerns about equity, privacy, and pedagogical fit. To examine this problem, they conduct a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review of recent work on generative AI in education, with emphasis on developments from 2023 onward.

The paper synthesizes literature on generative AI tools such as large language models, multimodal systems, intelligent tutoring agents, and adaptive learning platforms. It discusses applications including personalized content generation, real-time feedback, automated assessment, curriculum sequencing, pedagogical agents, and simulation-based learning. The review also considers implementation methods such as prompt engineering, fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation, learner modeling, real-time adaptation, and explainability features, alongside pedagogical frameworks like constructivism, sociocultural learning, cognitive load management, and universal design for learning.

The context spans K-12 education as well as higher education, professional development, and lifelong learning, but the paper is not an empirical intervention study with a specific participant sample. Its main conclusion is that generative AI offers substantial promise for personalized and resilient learning systems, while also creating important risks related to algorithmic bias, privacy, digital inequity, hallucinations, and weak pedagogical integration. The authors emphasize hybrid human-AI models, continuous monitoring, and careful governance as the most promising directions for future educational implementation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative/systematic literature review rather than an empirical evaluation, and it does not report original study design, effect estimation, or K-12 authentic teacher planning/coaching cycle evidence. Although it cites PRISMA, the paper is primarily conceptual synthesis and grey-literature style discussion of generative AI applications.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for potentially broad educational benefits, but it provides no direct causal evidence or effect sizes from K-12 settings. The likely impact is therefore unclear and only modestly informative for the target research question about authentic teacher planning and coaching cycles.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI tutoring and conversational educational agents used for personalized explanations, open-ended dialogue, misconception remediation, and adaptive feedback in K-12 and other learning contexts.
AI-driven adaptive learning systems that personalize content, difficulty, pacing, curriculum sequencing, and learning pathways based on learner models and performance signals.
Generative AI systems providing real-time personalized feedback on student work, including essay feedback, math misconception feedback, and formative assessment responses.
Language-learning and writing-support applications using generative AI for grammar correction, pronunciation feedback, conversational practice, and multilingual content generation.
Generative AI-created scenario-based simulations and role-play environments for business, medical, and history learning, enabling practice in dynamic risk-free contexts.

paper_profiles.title: On Cyber-social Learning: How to Value the Human in Computational Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues for a “cyber-social learning” perspective that brings together cybernetic principles and the social nature of learning. The central question is how educational technology can preserve and value human agency while also taking advantage of computational systems, feedback loops, and learning analytics.

The paper is primarily conceptual rather than empirical. It draws on historical discussion of cybernetics and on examples from the Cyber-Social Learning Laboratory to illustrate how decentralized, heterarchical systems can inform educational design. It also presents a learning analytics system as an example of recursive feedback mechanisms that support and augment human feedback in formal education.

The paper positions this approach as a way to rethink education in the digital age. It claims that cyber-social environments can encourage self-regulation and collaboration while supporting individual learning pathways within community contexts. Overall, the paper concludes that cybernetic principles offer a promising avenue for designing more adaptive and effective learning experiences, and it calls for a reimagination of traditional education models.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conference proceedings/front matter and mostly descriptive conference information plus abstracts. No clear empirical study design, comparison, or measurable intervention effects are presented in the provided text.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report outcome data or any measurable impact on learners, teachers, or institutions in the text provided. It is not evidence of an intervention effect in K-12 planning/coaching cycles for generative AI feedback.

paper_profiles.title: AI-Generated Rubric Interfaces: K–12 Teachers’ Perceptions and Practices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K–12 teachers perceive and use AI-generated rubrics for assessing block-based programming work, with a focus on whether such tools can support rubric creation, grading, and feedback while preserving teacher control. The authors are motivated by the fact that rubric design is time-consuming and often difficult for teachers, especially when defining clear performance levels and aligning criteria with instructional goals.

The intervention studied was a professional development workshop in which teachers used MagicSchool.ai to generate rubrics, refined prompts to tailor criteria, created a manual rubric for comparison, and then applied the AI-generated rubric to a sample block-based programming task. Teachers also used a chatbot feature to produce rubric-based feedback on the same work. The study collected pre- and post-workshop surveys, open-ended responses, exit tickets, and discussion data from 25 teachers.

Participants were middle- and high-school teachers in North Carolina, USA, with varied experience in computer science and block-based programming. The study found that teachers generally viewed AI-generated rubrics as useful starting points that improved structure, clarity, and speed, but they consistently stressed the need for human oversight, editing, and alignment with grade level and instructional priorities. Teachers were most positive about clarity and transparency, while usability—especially editing criteria—was the main weakness. Overall, hands-on exposure increased willingness to adopt AI rubric tools, but only conditionally: teachers wanted flexible, teacher-directed workflows that preserve assessment control and support equitable use across learners.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative mixed-methods professional development study with surveys and thematic analysis, not a controlled impact evaluation. It provides useful evidence about teacher perceptions and adoption intentions, but it does not meet stronger causal credibility criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceived usefulness and increased willingness to adopt, but no student outcome effects or causal impact estimates are provided. Its practical impact is promising yet unclear, based on a small sample of teachers in a workshop setting.

interventions.use_case: AI-supported rubric generation and rubric-based feedback for K-12 block-based programming assignments, using MagicSchool.ai to draft/edit rubrics and a chatbot to generate rubric-aligned feedback on student work

finding.finding_summary: Teachers consistently reported that AI-generated rubrics reduced the time and cognitive effort required to create assessment tools from scratch. In this PD workshop with n=25 K-12 teachers, AI rubrics were viewed as strong starting drafts that improved structure and clarity, though they still required editing; the post-survey showed especially low usability for adding/removing/revising criteria (M=2.75, SD=1.23).
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of rubric creation efficiency, usability, and workload reduction from surveys, exit tickets, and thematic analysis

finding.finding_summary: The study found that hands-on exposure in professional development increased teachers' willingness to adopt AI rubric tools in future classroom practice, but only conditionally and with teacher control preserved. Teachers valued the potential for clearer expectations, consistency, and transparency, while also emphasizing policy, privacy, and equity constraints that shape school-level adoption.
finding.measure: Pre/post workshop surveys and open-ended reflections on future adoption intentions, transparency, fairness, and workflow fit

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can serve as an automated teacher coach for classroom observation and feedback. The authors frame three coaching tasks relevant to teacher professional development: scoring classroom transcript segments using observation rubrics, identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

The study evaluates ChatGPT in a zero-shot setup on transcript data from the National Center for Teacher Effectiveness (NCTE) dataset. The data consists of elementary mathematics classroom observations from fourth- and fifth-grade classrooms in the United States, scored by expert raters using two observation systems: CLASS and MQI. For the quantitative scoring task, the model predicts rubric scores for selected CLASS and MQI dimensions. For the qualitative tasks, experienced math teachers rate the model’s responses for relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT can produce responses that are often contextually relevant and sometimes actionable, but it performs poorly as a teacher coach overall. Its score predictions correlate weakly with human ratings, its qualitative feedback is frequently not insightful, and many suggestions are redundant or merely restate what the teacher already did. The paper concludes that current generative AI is not yet reliable for high-quality instructional coaching, though it may become useful with further development and teacher-informed tuning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical evaluation with human ratings and quantitative correlation analyses, but it is primarily a small-sample, single-model observational/benchmarking study rather than a causal design. It does not meet RCT or strong QED standards, and the human evaluation sample is limited to two teachers.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows mostly low correlations and high redundancy, indicating limited current practical impact of the evaluated ChatGPT coaching approach. Any positive signal is modest and indirect, so overall impact on educational practice is unclear and likely modest at best.

interventions.use_case: zero-shot use of ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) as an automated teacher coach to score classroom transcript segments, identify instructional highlights/missed opportunities, and generate actionable coaching suggestions for eliciting student mathematical reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether ChatGPT can provide scalable automated teacher feedback, but finds substantial limitations in coaching quality. On 100 transcript segments for scoring tasks, Spearman correlations with human ratings were low across CLASS and MQI items (e.g., CLBM up to 0.35; most others near 0 or negative), while qualitative feedback was often non-novel (82% redundant in Task C) and not consistently relevant or insightful.
finding.measure: Spearman correlation with human rubric scores; human ratings of relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty on teacher-evaluated outputs
finding.study_size: n=100 scoring segments; n=216 CLASS examples; n=288 MQI examples; n=36 suggestions; 2 human teachers
finding.effect_size: Spearman rho range: CLASS -0.06 to 0.35; MQI -0.11 to 0.17

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how pre-service elementary science teachers integrated ChatGPT into lesson planning and what they believed the tool could contribute to science teaching and learning. The authors address a gap in empirical research on generative AI in education by moving beyond purely speculative discussion and analyzing actual lesson plans plus teacher perceptions.

The study involved 29 pre-service elementary teachers at a Korean university. Participants completed a short instructional sequence over four weekly 2-hour sessions introducing ChatGPT, discussing possible uses in science education, reviewing science teaching methods, and learning how to write lesson plans. They then created a 45-minute elementary science lesson plan that had to incorporate ChatGPT and included a simulated chat transcript. The plans were evaluated with a modified TPACK-based technology integration rubric, and open-ended survey responses were analyzed qualitatively.

Findings showed that participants envisioned ChatGPT being useful across multiple elementary science domains, especially biology, chemistry, and earth science, and across a wide range of instructional strategies such as cooperative learning, POE, learning cycles, analogy generation, experimentation, and concept mapping. Overall lesson-plan quality was moderately high, but participants were weaker at selecting ChatGPT functions appropriately than at aligning ChatGPT with curriculum goals or instructional strategies. They viewed ChatGPT as useful for questioning, individualized support, and formative feedback, but also expressed concerns about inaccuracy and overdependence. The paper concludes that pre-service teachers see strong potential for ChatGPT in science education, while also needing more preparation to use it critically and appropriately.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/descriptive preprint analyzing lesson plans and survey responses from a small convenience sample of pre-service teachers. It has a clear methodology but no control group, randomization, or direct classroom outcome measurement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper indicates promising but indirect benefits of ChatGPT for lesson design and anticipated student support, without demonstrating measurable learning impact. Its findings are modest and exploratory, centered on planning rather than observed K-12 achievement effects.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used in pre-service elementary science teachers' lesson plans as a conversational AI tool for questioning, generating explanations, supporting role-play activities, providing individualized support, and giving formative feedback within science lessons.

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests ChatGPT may support scientific inquiry and reasoning in lesson planning, but also shows inconsistent appropriateness in function selection. Pre-service teachers envisioned ChatGPT aiding questioning, prediction, explanation, and formative assessment, yet some plans misused it for visually oriented tasks or unverified content; no student learning effect size was reported because the paper evaluated lesson plans rather than classroom outcomes.
finding.measure: TPACK-based lesson plan rubric plus qualitative analysis of lesson plans and survey responses related to scientific inquiry and lesson design

finding.finding_summary: Participants expected ChatGPT to support critical thinking, self-directed learning, and collaboration when used in structured lesson plans. In the rubric results, lesson plans scored relatively well for integrating ChatGPT with instructional strategies (M=3.48/4), though function selection was weaker (M=3.0/4), indicating partial strength in designing durable-skill-supporting pedagogy.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses and TIAR rubric scores for instructional design

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers believed ChatGPT could increase students' motivation, interest, and engagement by enabling self-paced, individualized support and interactive questioning. These are perceived benefits rather than measured student outcomes, and the paper reports no experimental estimate of impact.
finding.measure: Qualitative survey responses on anticipated outcomes of ChatGPT-integrated lessons

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that pre-service teachers viewed ChatGPT as useful for lesson-planning efficiency and formative feedback, including summarizing lengthy student scenarios, supporting role-play preparation, and helping teachers manage large classes. The TIAR results were moderately high overall (M=3.29/4, SD=.91), suggesting perceived usefulness for organizing instructional tasks rather than measured efficiency gains.
finding.measure: Lesson plan quality rubric and qualitative descriptions of planning/support functions

paper_profiles.title: Understanding Teacher Revisions of Large Language Model-Generated Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers revise feedback generated by large language models (LLMs) before it is delivered to students. The central question is not whether the model can produce plausible feedback, but how educators actually mediate, edit, and sometimes accept that feedback in authentic instructional workflows. The authors frame teacher revision as a key part of evaluating AI feedback systems because it determines what learners ultimately receive.

The study analyzes 1,349 instances of AI-generated formative feedback paired with final teacher-edited versions from 117 teachers. The data came from Tutoria, an AI-supported feedback platform integrated with Moodle and Google Classroom, used in a mix of controlled studies and classroom deployments. Participants included Brazilian educators and students from multiple contexts, especially Brazilian high school chemistry and higher-education introductory computer science tasks involving short open-ended responses. Teachers could accept, edit, or rewrite LLM-generated drafts after tagging student responses for correctness.

The paper finds that teachers accepted the AI feedback unchanged in about 78% of cases, and when they did edit, they usually shortened the text while largely preserving its meaning. Editing varied greatly by teacher: over half never revised any feedback, while a small minority revised a large share. Text-only models could predict revision with above-chance accuracy, but only modestly. Qualitative coding showed that revisions often shifted feedback away from highly explanatory, high-information forms toward shorter corrective forms, suggesting that teachers frequently simplify overly verbose or pedagogically misaligned AI output. The authors conclude that default AI behavior is instructionally consequential because most feedback is delivered unchanged, and that future systems should better align with teacher preferences while reducing unnecessary editing burden.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical observational/quantitative study with descriptive, predictive, and coding analyses of real classroom logs, but it is not an experimental design and does not estimate causal effects on student learning. The evidence is informative for behavior in authentic use, yet credibility is limited by retrospective data and lack of outcome randomization.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests a potentially meaningful operational effect on teacher workload because 77.8% of AI feedback was accepted unchanged and revisions were usually brief, but it does not demonstrate learning gains or other direct educational impacts. Overall impact is therefore modest and somewhat unclear for general K-12 outcomes.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated formative feedback for short open-ended student responses, with teachers able to accept, edit, or rewrite the draft before delivery

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that most AI-generated feedback was delivered unchanged, with teachers accepting drafts without modification in 77.8% of cases (1050/1349). Editing was limited and heterogeneous across teachers, suggesting the system may reduce teacher editing effort even though revised feedback was sometimes shortened by a mean of 6.4 words relative to the original draft.
finding.measure: Teacher revision rate; word counts of AI feedback vs final teacher feedback; semantic similarity between drafts and final messages
finding.std_deviation: AI feedback length SD=19.60; final feedback length SD=19.81

finding.finding_summary: The study focuses on formative feedback for student writing/open-ended responses, but it does not measure learner writing outcomes directly. It does show that when teachers revised AI feedback, they often simplified high-information explanations into more concise corrective feedback, with revised messages shifting from 59.9% high-information at draft stage to 48.0% after editing (chi-square shift, Cramér’s V=0.12).
finding.measure: Feedback type coding of AI-generated and teacher-edited messages (corrective vs high-information vs reinforcement/punishment)
finding.study_size: n=834 deduplicated feedback messages coded; n=1349 logs overall
finding.effect_size: Cramér’s V=0.12; Cohen’s w=0.16-0.20 for distributional tests

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers in low-resource schools collaborate with generative AI to create and adapt lesson plans. The core question is how an LLM-based lesson-planning system can support teachers’ work while remaining aligned with curriculum requirements, local classroom realities, and bilingual instruction needs. The paper is motivated by the difficulty teachers face in producing high-quality lesson plans under heavy administrative load, limited resources, and multilingual teaching conditions.

The intervention studied is Shiksha Copilot, a human-in-the-loop lesson planning platform deployed in government schools in Karnataka, India. The system used retrieval-augmented generation to draft lesson plans from state curriculum textbooks, after which expert curators reviewed and refined the outputs before teachers customized the curated plans for their own classrooms. It also included optional AI features such as lesson-specific chat, general educational chat, and question generation. The deployment involved 1,043 teachers across Kannada- and English-medium public schools, plus 23 curators and 4 mentors supporting rollout and training. Data came from system logs, surveys, and semi-structured interviews.

The study finds that the tool reduced lesson-planning time, lowered stress, and helped teachers satisfy bureaucratic documentation requirements while also supporting classroom instruction.
