English lesson plans were generally high quality with few edits, whereas Kannada translations often required extensive linguistic revision to fit textbook language and local usage. Teachers used the tool in flexible ways, often adapting plans mentally and supplementing them with peer networks and prior experience. Overall, the paper concludes that teacher-AI collaboration can be effective when AI is embedded in a structured workflow with human review, but that multilingual and low-resource contexts still require substantial human oversight and community-based adaptation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods field deployment with substantial qualitative and descriptive quantitative evidence, but not an experimental or quasi-experimental causal design. The paper provides credible evidence on usage, perceptions, and workflow change, yet lacks a clear counterfactual for attributing outcomes to the intervention.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported impacts are meaningful for a priority population of teachers in low-resource K-12 schools, especially for workload reduction and documentation efficiency. However, the paper does not report clear effect sizes for the main outcomes, so the magnitude of impact is difficult to judge and appears modest/qualitative rather than large.

interventions.use_case: Human-in-the-loop LLM system for teacher lesson planning and classroom support, generating curriculum-aligned lesson plans, lesson-specific chat, general educational chat, and question-paper generation for K-12 teachers in low-resource schools.
AI-assisted lesson planning and content customization platform that helps teachers curate, modify, and distribute lesson plans aligned to the 5E instructional model and state curriculum.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that Shiksha Copilot reduced bureaucratic workload, lesson-planning time, and teacher stress in a large mixed-method deployment with 1,043 teachers and 23 curators. Survey and log evidence indicate the tool made record-keeping easier and supported faster planning, with teachers using it to generate and customize plans in ways that reduced effort relative to manual planning, though exact pre-post effect sizes for time and stress are not reported in the excerpt.
finding.measure: Teacher stress scale (TSS), self-reported weekly time spent on lesson planning and administrative tasks, system logs of lesson-plan creation and editing
finding.study_size: n=1043 teachers; survey analyses on n=406 matched responses; logs on 991 curated LPs and 5,544 teacher-created LPs

finding.finding_summary: The intervention helped teachers satisfy administrative documentation needs in addition to supporting instruction, indicating institutional value beyond classroom use. The paper describes a shift in work practices around lesson-plan record keeping and documentation compliance, but also notes that staffing shortages and administrative demands constrained broader pedagogical change.
finding.measure: Interview themes on bureaucratic documentation and workflow change; teacher-reported use of lesson plans for record-keeping

finding.finding_summary: The system appears to support teacher adaptation, contextualization, and collaboration by requiring teachers to evaluate and customize AI-generated lesson plans, but the paper does not quantify gains in these skills. Qualitative evidence suggests teachers drew on professional judgment and peer networks to refine AI outputs, while systemic constraints limited deeper changes in practice.
finding.measure: Interview themes on teacher-AI collaboration, adaptation, and use of professional networks

paper_profiles.title: The TalkMoves Dataset: K-12 Mathematics Lesson Transcripts Annotated for Teacher and Student Discursive Moves
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces the TalkMoves dataset, a curated corpus of 567 K-12 mathematics lesson transcripts drawn from classroom video recordings. The central problem addressed is the lack of publicly available, richly annotated classroom discourse data for studying teacher-student interaction and for developing AI/NLP tools that can analyze instructional talk. The authors position the dataset as a resource for both educational research and machine learning, grounded in accountable talk theory.

The approach is not an intervention study in the traditional sense, but a dataset release and annotation framework. Each transcript is human-transcribed, segmented by speaker, and annotated at the sentence level for ten discursive moves for teachers and students, plus utterance-level dialogue act labels. The dataset combines publicly available transcripts, TIMSS video-study transcripts, Video Mosaic materials, Inside Mathematics resources, and additional anonymized transcripts from the TalkMoves project. The paper also describes the TalkMoves application, which uses these annotations and transformer-based models to provide teachers with automated, immediate feedback about their mathematics discourse.

The population consists of K-12 mathematics classrooms, primarily in-person lessons with whole-class discussion and small-group work, along with some online lessons. The dataset is skewed toward U.S. middle school classrooms and female-taught lessons, though the exact participant breakdown varies and some descriptive details are not available. The main conclusion is that TalkMoves offers a large, theory-grounded, publicly accessible resource for analyzing classroom discourse and supporting future AI systems that can coach teachers and potentially students in authentic instructional settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a dataset and system description with benchmarked model performance, not a controlled evaluation of educational impact. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically clear, but the evidence is descriptive/technical rather than experimental or quasi-experimental.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potential for scalable teacher feedback and reports strong model accuracy, but it does not demonstrate measured downstream educational gains or workload reduction in authentic teacher planning/coaching cycles. Impact on education practice is therefore plausible but currently unclear.

interventions.use_case: automated, immediate, and actionable feedback to K-12 mathematics teachers about classroom discourse and talk moves based on lesson transcript analysis
teacher-facing NLP/ML dashboard that supports classroom discourse analysis and provides instructional analytics rather than direct student tutoring

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main applied contribution is a teacher-facing system that automates detection and classification of teacher and student talk moves from classroom transcripts, aiming to scale feedback that would otherwise require highly trained observers. The benchmarked models achieved macro-F1 scores of 76.32 for the teacher model (RoBERTa-base) and 73.12 for the student model (BERT-base), indicating strong classification performance for automating feedback generation, but the paper does not report a causal improvement in teacher workload or time savings.
finding.measure: Macro-F1 and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) for talk-move classification; system functionality for feedback generation
finding.study_size: n=567 transcripts; test set size not_reported

paper_profiles.title: LLMs to Support K–12 Teachers in Culturally Relevant Pedagogy: An AI Literacy Example
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the difficulty K–12 teachers face when trying to implement culturally relevant pedagogy (CRP), especially in fast-changing areas such as AI literacy where culturally tailored instructional resources are limited. The authors ask whether large language models (LLMs) can help teachers adapt AI literacy activities so they better reflect students’ cultural backgrounds and lived experiences.

To explore this, the paper presents CulturAIEd, an LLM-powered tool that combines student demographic information, a CRT checklist, rubric-based feedback, and a chatbot for just-in-time pedagogical support. The system is designed to help teachers revise AI literacy lessons through progressively more structured culturally responsive modifications, including basic and advanced adaptation suggestions. The paper describes the tool’s design and evaluates it through an exploratory pilot study.

The study involved four K–12 teachers from North America and East Asia in 90–120 minute online Zoom sessions. Participants completed adaptation tasks for AI literacy activities, first without guidance, then with a CRT checklist, and finally with CulturAIEd. The teachers represented secondary-grade teaching contexts and included science, music, and information technology educators. Survey responses and interview transcripts were analyzed to understand perceived usefulness, confidence, and implementation challenges.

Findings suggest that CulturAIEd improved teachers’ confidence in identifying culturally responsive opportunities and making meaningful lesson modifications, while also reducing time and planning burden. Participants valued the tool’s demographic integration, structured rubric feedback, and actionable suggestions. The authors conclude that LLMs may support efficient CRP integration in AI literacy planning, but they also emphasize that the results are preliminary and that larger, controlled, and longer-term studies are needed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small exploratory qualitative-dominant mixed-methods pilot (n=4) without a control group, randomization, or inferential testing. It is peer-reviewed research, but credibility is limited by the very small sample and descriptive analysis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports promising but unquantified improvements in perceived efficiency and confidence, with no effect size or student outcome evidence. The observed impact is modest and preliminary, so it cannot yet be judged as strong evidence of broad effectiveness.

interventions.use_case: LLM-powered teacher support tool (CulturAIEd) that helps K-12 teachers adapt AI literacy activities to students' cultural contexts using demographic information, rubric-based feedback, and just-in-time coaching

finding.finding_summary: In an exploratory pilot with n=4 K-12 teachers, CulturAIEd was perceived to reduce lesson-planning burden by streamlining access to student demographics, culturally responsive modifications, and rubric-based feedback. Teachers reported that the tool saved time and reduced the research needed for culturally relevant pedagogy; however, the study was qualitative/descriptive and did not report an effect size.
finding.measure: Teacher survey ratings and semi-structured interview themes on time savings, workflow efficiency, and perceived ease of CRP lesson adaptation

paper_profiles.title: To what extent is ChatGPT useful for language teacher lesson plan creation?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can support foreign language teachers in creating lesson plans, and more specifically whether increasing prompt specificity improves the quality and consistency of AI-generated plans. The authors frame the problem as a practical one for language education: teachers often must design their own materials, while generative AI may help streamline that work but may also reproduce outdated or weak pedagogical practices.

The study used ChatGPT 4.0 with five zero-shot prompts of increasing specificity. The prompts were designed around a 45-minute high school Level I Spanish lesson for novice learners, with objectives tied to Costa Rican restaurant vocabulary and communicative tasks. The authors generated 10 lesson plans per prompt, producing 50 outputs total, and scored each output against 25 rubric criteria adapted from best-practice lesson design and edTPA-related expectations used in a teacher preparation context at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. They then analyzed scores, word counts, and output dissimilarity using ANOVA, Jaccard distances, NMDS, PERMANOVA, ANOSIM, and hierarchical clustering.

The main finding was that greater prompt specificity did not produce a simple linear improvement in lesson quality. Adding a lesson plan template sometimes reduced scores, while adding an explicit checklist of required criteria produced the highest average scores. The outputs were highly variable even when the same prompt was repeated, showing that ChatGPT was not deterministic and could produce both strong and weak lesson plans from identical inputs. The authors also found that some generated plans reflected outdated or anachronistic language-teaching approaches, including behaviorist or audio-lingual elements and weak treatment of cultural connections. They conclude that ChatGPT can be useful for lesson planning, but only if teachers critically evaluate outputs and are trained to refine prompts and revise AI-generated materials.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical observational/comparative prompt-engineering study with systematic scoring, but it is not a randomized educational impact evaluation and has no human learner outcomes. It provides useful evidence about model behavior and output quality, but credibility is limited to a descriptive lab-style design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical value for teacher planning efficiency and flags institutional risks in lesson design, but it does not demonstrate measured student learning gains or large-scale implementation effects. Its impact is therefore plausible but indirect and modest/unclear at the population level.

interventions.use_case: Using ChatGPT 4.0 via zero-shot prompting to generate foreign language teacher lesson plans, then evaluating how prompt specificity and templates affect output quality and variability.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that ChatGPT can substantially streamline foreign language lesson-plan creation, with generally high-quality outputs and an overall mean score up to 21.6/25 when a checklist of criteria was provided (P.5). However, increased prompt specificity did not improve quality linearly, and repeated runs of the same prompt varied widely, ranging from 16/25 to 25/25 across 10 iterations for a given prompt.
finding.measure: Rubric-based lesson plan quality scores, word count, and presence/absence of 25 lesson-plan criteria across 50 generated plans
finding.study_size: n=50 generated lesson plans (5 prompts x 10 iterations)

finding.finding_summary: The study highlights that ChatGPT outputs can reproduce anachronistic or research-rejected pedagogical practices, including weak cultural integration and occasional audio-lingual style activities, which raises concerns for teacher preparation and curriculum quality. The authors argue that teacher AI literacy and critical review are necessary because generative AI may subtly bias instructional materials toward outdated practices.
finding.measure: Presence/absence of rubric components aligned to ACTFL standards and edTPA-style lesson plan criteria; qualitative inspection of generated lesson plan features

paper_profiles.title: Foundations of GenIR
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how modern generative AI models reshape information access systems. It argues that the major contribution of generative AI is not simply better document retrieval, but two new paradigms: information generation, where models directly create tailored content in response to user needs, and information synthesis, where models combine externally retrieved information into grounded responses.

The paper is conceptual rather than empirical. It reviews foundational aspects of generative models, including Transformer architectures, scaling laws, training stages such as pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and RLHF, as well as prompt optimization and multimodal applications. It then connects these foundations to information access, discussing retrieval-augmented generation, modular RAG, retrieval planning, generative retrieval, and domain-specific modeling.

The chapter does not study a specific school, classroom, teacher, or learner population, and it does not present an educational intervention. Its main conclusion is that generative AI can both augment retrieval systems and potentially transform them into more capable information agents, but important challenges remain, especially hallucination, external knowledge integration, controllability, and the high cost of scaling large models.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/chapter-style survey of generative AI and information retrieval foundations, not an empirical study of a K-12 educational intervention. It does not report a study design, comparison groups, or causal evidence relevant to the requested topic.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational outcomes are tested and no K-12 teacher planning/coaching cycle intervention is evaluated. The paper is theoretically informative for AI infrastructure but provides no direct impact evidence in education.

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines a central question in AI-for-education research: how K-12 educators evaluate lesson plans generated by generative AI models compared with those authored by human curriculum designers. The authors argue that, despite rapid adoption of GenAI tools for planning, there is still limited direct comparative evidence about whether AI-generated lesson plans meet educators’ pedagogical expectations in authentic K-12 settings.

The study compares lesson plans produced by a customized GPT-4 model, a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model, and human curriculum designer-created plans. The materials were mathematics lesson plans aligned to Common Core standards and structured into warm-up, main tasks, and cool-down sections. Twenty experienced K-12 math educators participated in a blinded pairwise preference study delivered through a web-based interface. Participants reviewed multiple plan pairs, gave binary preferences across several instructional dimensions, and wrote comments explaining their choices. The analysis combined quantitative preference comparisons with qualitative thematic analysis and LDA topic modeling.

The participants were elementary, middle, and high school math educators in the United States. The study ran over several weeks in 2024, with each educator completing practice trials and then evaluating 20 pairs. The authors report that human-authored plans were generally preferred overall, especially for elementary instruction and for warm-up and main-task sections. However, GenAI plans were competitive in certain areas, especially cool-down activities, and in some cases in higher-grade contexts. The results suggest that GenAI is most useful as a planning assistant for structured lesson components, but human expertise remains important for engagement, differentiation, discourse, and inclusive supports.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed comparative user study with direct pairwise evaluation, but it is qualitative/mixed-method and not a randomized controlled trial. Internal validity is limited by subjective preferences, small educator sample size, and some dataset imbalance across pair types and grade bands.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests potentially meaningful benefits for AI-assisted lesson planning in certain contexts, but the evidence is preference-based rather than outcome-based. Any impact on instruction or learning is unclear because the paper does not measure student achievement, workload reduction, or implementation effects directly.

interventions.use_case: comparative evaluation of GenAI-generated K-12 math lesson plans versus human curriculum designer lesson plans, using customized GPT-4 and fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b as lesson-plan generators

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily suggests operational benefits for lesson planning, indicating that GenAI can reduce educator workload by generating structured lesson plans that some teachers found competitive with human-authored plans. However, this is based on educator preference data rather than measured time savings or workload reduction outcomes, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Educator preferences for lesson-plan usefulness and overall quality; qualitative comments about planning workload and usefulness

finding.finding_summary: In K-12 mathematics lesson-plan comparisons, educators generally preferred human-created plans overall, especially for elementary-level warm-up, main task, and overall quality. GenAI plans were competitive in specific components, especially cool-downs, and in some contexts the fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b outperformed human plans at high school level (59.2% vs. 40.8% preference), but the study reports no standardized effect size.
finding.measure: Binary educator preference for math lesson-plan sections and overall quality across grade bands

paper_profiles.title: From Teacher to Colleague: How Coding Experience Shapes Developer Perceptions of AI Tools
paper_profiles.venue: GenAICHI: CHI 2025 Workshop on Generative AI and HCI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how coding experience relates to developers’ awareness of, experience with, and mental models of AI-assisted development tools. The authors ask whether more experienced developers are more likely to adopt AI tools and what roles they assign to AI in their workflow. The study is motivated by prior work suggesting that expertise shapes technology acceptance, but the role of expertise in perceptions of AI tools in software development remains unclear.

The paper analyzes survey data from JetBrains’ State of Developer Ecosystem Report 2024. From the broader survey, the authors focus on respondents who indicated coding/programming as part of their work, yielding a developer sample of 19,820 for the cleaned dataset, with 8,073 answering AI-awareness/experience questions and 3,380 selecting at least one AI role. The study is based on self-reported coding experience, AI awareness, AI experience, and selected AI roles such as teacher, junior colleague, content generator, and others.

Using Spearman correlations and logistic regression, the authors find that coding experience is not meaningfully associated with AI experience and is only negligibly related to AI awareness. However, coding experience does shape the roles developers assign to AI: less experienced developers more often view AI as a teacher, while more experienced developers are more likely to see it as a junior colleague, a content generator, or as having no role. The authors conclude that expertise has little relationship to adoption itself but does influence how developers conceptualize AI tools, suggesting that AI tools should be designed to align with differing user mental models across experience levels.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational survey analysis with logistic regression and Spearman correlations, but it is not an experimental or causal design. The evidence is descriptive and based on self-reported perceptions rather than direct intervention effects, so it meets only limited credibility criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not test educational outcomes or demonstrate measurable improvement in productivity beyond perceptions of AI roles. Its practical impact is unclear for K-12 education because it studies professional developers, not teachers or students, and reports no intervention effect sizes on learning-related outcomes.

interventions.use_case: survey-based examination of developers' perceptions and adoption of AI-assisted coding tools, including how they assign roles such as teacher, junior colleague, content generator, and collaborator to AI

finding.finding_summary: This survey study found no meaningful relationship between coding experience and AI tool adoption/experience (Spearman's rho = -0.005, p = 0.652; n=8073), but coding experience did shape how developers interpreted AI's role in their workflow. More experienced developers were more likely to view AI as a junior colleague or content generator, while less experienced developers more often saw AI as a teacher; however, this is perceptual rather than performance evidence.
finding.measure: AI awareness, AI experience, and self-reported role assignments for AI tools in coding workflows
finding.study_size: n=3380 for role analysis; n=8073 for AI awareness/experience analysis
finding.effect_size: rho=0.031 for coding experience vs AI awareness; rho=-0.005 for coding experience vs AI experience; OR=1.170 for 'junior colleague', OR=1.087 for 'content generator', OR=0.883 for 'teacher'
finding.confidence_interval: teacher OR 0.814-0.958; junior colleague OR 1.053-1.299; content generator OR 1.025-1.152

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging Peer, Self, and Teacher Assessments for Generative AI-Enhanced Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teacher, peer, and self-assessments relate to one another in a GenAI-enhanced feedback workflow, with the broader goal of improving the design of AI-supported feedback systems. The core question is whether different human evaluative sources provide consistent, reliable, and sufficiently informative inputs for generating pedagogically meaningful feedback, and whether those inputs should be weighted differently rather than treated as equivalent.

The study was conducted inside the AICoFe collaborative feedback system, which combines rubric-based teacher, peer, and self-assessments with a generative AI model (GePeTo) that produces personalized feedback. The authors analyzed 46 evaluation sets from undergraduate engineering students delivering oral presentations. Students completed peer and self-assessments using the same validated rubric as the teacher, and the teacher also provided an independent overall grade. The analysis focused on agreement, correlations, and systematic scoring differences across evaluator types.

Results showed moderate to substantial agreement overall, with peer ratings aligning reasonably well with teacher ratings and self-ratings showing the weakest alignment. The teacher’s rubric scores were stricter than peer and self scores, while peers and students tended to score slightly higher. Based on these findings, the paper proposes an enhanced GenAI feedback design that gives greater weight to teacher assessments, incorporates self-assessments as an additional signal, and includes bias/divergence detection before generating feedback. The study concludes that human judgments are complementary but not interchangeable, and that GenAI systems for feedback should explicitly model those differences.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a correlational observational study with paired comparisons and agreement analysis, not an experimental design. It provides useful empirical evidence, but causal claims about the GenAI feedback system improving outcomes are not directly tested.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are mostly on agreement, validity, and score alignment rather than learner gains, and no direct learning effect size is established. The practical implications for feedback design are meaningful, but the demonstrated impact on students is still indirect and modest.

interventions.use_case: GenAI-enhanced collaborative feedback in the AICoFe system, using rubric-based teacher, peer, and self-assessments to generate personalized feedback for student oral presentations
GePeTo generative model that produces context-aware feedback messages from aggregated evaluator inputs within learning analytics dashboards

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies oral presentation performance feedback in engineering education, using rubric scores and teacher grades for 46 presentations (n=46). While it does not test learning gains directly, it finds substantial alignment among evaluators and strong correlations between rubric-based scores and the teacher’s overall oral presentation grade (teacher rubric vs grade r=0.88; peers vs grade r=0.69; self vs grade r=0.59), suggesting the feedback process validly captures speaking performance.
finding.measure: Oral presentation rubric scores and teacher's overall grade for presentations

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines evaluative judgment, self-assessment, and peer assessment consistency in a rubric-based feedback cycle for 46 undergraduate oral presentations. Agreement was moderate to substantial depending on the statistic used (Gwet’s AC2=0.58-0.63 pairwise; Kendall’s W=0.46-0.51 overall), indicating the system supports structured comparison and reflective judgment across students and teachers.
finding.measure: Inter-rater agreement (weighted Cohen’s kappa, Gwet’s AC2, Kendall’s W) across teacher, peer, and self-assessments

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure motivation or engagement directly, but it discusses self-assessment and reflective use of video-rubric review as part of the feedback cycle. Self-assessments showed moderate alignment with the teacher grade (r=0.59) but also a small positive bias relative to teacher rubric scores (+0.36, p=0.037), implying reflective benefits alongside calibration limits.
finding.measure: Self-assessment rubric scores and their correlation/difference relative to teacher scores

finding.finding_summary: A central aim of the paper is to improve scalable feedback generation by combining human assessments with GenAI in AICoFe. The study argues that weighted aggregation and bias detection could make feedback generation more efficient and pedagogically valid, but it does not report a direct workload or time-saving effect.
finding.measure: Proposed efficiency of GenAI-enhanced feedback workflow; no direct workload metric reported

paper_profiles.title: LessonPlanner: Assisting Novice Teachers to Prepare Pedagogy-Driven Lesson Plans with Large Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: UIST '24 (ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how novice teachers can efficiently prepare high-quality lesson plans, especially when they lack teaching experience and struggle to find suitable teaching materials and effective instructional strategies. The authors focus on whether large language models (LLMs) can support lesson planning in a structured, pedagogy-driven way rather than through an unstructured chat interface.

The paper presents LessonPlanner, a web-based system that guides users through lesson-goal setting and lesson-plan drafting using LLM-generated content. The system is structured around Bloom’s Taxonomy and Gagne’s Nine Events of Instruction, and it provides preset prompts, editable outline blocks, contextual LLM actions, and a markdown editor so users can refine or regenerate content. The design was informed by a formative study with six novice teachers and teaching assistants, and then evaluated in a within-subjects comparison against a baseline ChatGPT web interface.

The main evaluation involved 12 university students acting as teachers, preparing lesson plans for familiar data structures topics, followed by expert interviews with six teachers across university, primary, and high school contexts. Results showed that LessonPlanner improved the quality of the resulting lesson plans and reduced workload relative to the baseline. Participants especially valued the structured outline and pedagogy-aligned prompts, while also raising concerns about content accuracy and the need for human judgment. The study concludes that LLMs are more useful for lesson planning when embedded in an interactive, theory-informed workflow with flexible user control.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed HCI system paper with a within-subjects comparative study and expert interviews, but the evidence is primarily qualitative/UX-oriented with a small convenience sample and no reported effect sizes in the provided text. It is not a randomized K-12 efficacy trial.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows a useful improvement in teacher planning quality and reduced workload, but the measured effect is on planning artifacts and perceived effort rather than direct student learning outcomes. The impact appears modest and mostly on a specific novice-teacher population.

interventions.use_case: Interactive lesson-planning assistant powered by GPT-4 that generates lesson goals, outlines, pedagogically structured content, teaching activities, and refinements for novice K-12/university teachers.

finding.finding_summary: In a within-subjects study (n=12), LessonPlanner significantly improved the quality of outcome lesson plans versus the baseline ChatGPT interface and reduced users' workload during lesson preparation. The paper also reports expert interviews (n=6) indicating the system was useful for making lesson planning more efficient by organizing content and suggesting relevant materials/strategies, but no numeric effect sizes or confidence intervals are provided in the text excerpt.
finding.measure: Lesson plan quality ratings by an expert teacher; NASA-TLX workload measures; SUS and trust questionnaires

finding.finding_summary: LessonPlanner significantly improved the quality of the resulting lesson plans compared with the baseline ChatGPT interface in a within-subjects study with 12 participants. Quality was judged by an experienced teacher using CIPP-inspired criteria covering alignment with learning objectives, useful materials, balance of theory/practice, effective strategies, and sufficient detail; the excerpt does not report the exact statistic or effect size.
finding.measure: Expert-rated lesson plan quality using CIPP-inspired criteria

paper_profiles.title: AI-Based Feedback in Counselling Competence Training of Prospective Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-based feedback can support the development of counselling competence in prospective teachers, specifically in simulated teacher-parent conversations. The authors focus on communicative skills in three dimensions: verbal, paraverbal, and nonverbal communication. They ask whether measurable communication features correlate with expert-rated conversation quality, how students perceive AI-generated feedback, and whether models can be trained to identify conversation phases and communication techniques.

The intervention was an iterative four-day block seminar for university students in elementary school pedagogy in Germany. Students learned counselling theory, practiced role-play, recorded simulated teacher-parent conversations, received expert and AI-based feedback, and then participated in guideline-based interviews about the feedback and seminar design. The AI system used NOVA and related tools to extract and visualize features from speech, text, gaze, smiling, and facial expressions, and it also supported annotation of verbal categories such as conversational phases and communication techniques.

The study combined quantitative analyses of feature–rating relationships and annotation agreement with qualitative interview analysis of student perceptions. The sample was small, but the results suggested that some paraverbal and nonverbal features had predictive value for expert ratings, students generally perceived the AI feedback positively, and the verbal annotation task showed promising but imperfect inter-rater agreement. The authors conclude that AI-based feedback has potential to enrich teacher training for parent-teacher communication, while also noting that stronger annotation guidelines and larger datasets are needed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative + correlational exploratory study with a small sample (n=29) and no randomized comparison or causal design. It provides useful early evidence, but credibility is limited by the small dataset, iterative design changes, and reliance on interviews and cross-validation rather than a controlled evaluation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests modest benefits for teacher-training feedback and workflow efficiency, but the measured predictive performance is only slightly above chance and the outcomes are based on a small pilot sample. Impact on broader K-12 practice remains unclear pending stronger validation and larger-scale deployment.

interventions.use_case: AI-based multimodal feedback for prospective teachers’ simulated teacher-parent counselling conversations, using speech, transcript, gaze, facial expression, smile, sentiment, pitch, and loudness features to visualize and comment on communication quality.
NOVA/DISCOVER-supported instructional workflow for teacher training seminars, where recordings are annotated, visualized, and replayed to support reflection and coaching in counselling competence.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that integrating WhisperX into the interview transcription workflow reduced transcription time by two-thirds, indicating substantial efficiency gains for qualitative analysis and feedback preparation. The AI tools also enabled automated extraction, synchronization, and visualization of multimodal features for feedback generation, reducing manual analysis burden in teacher training sessions.
finding.measure: Transcription time reduction; workflow efficiency for preparing qualitative interview and AI-based feedback materials

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived the AI feedback as helpful for self-reflection on counselling competence, and the authors report that the feedback could support identification of areas to work on. In the classification experiment for predicting expert ratings from paraverbal/nonverbal features, the best model reached 56.0% accuracy (SD=16.0%) versus a 50% dummy baseline, showing weak but above-chance predictive signal from the extracted features.
finding.measure: Student interview responses; five-fold stratified cross-validation accuracy for predicting expert counselling ratings

finding.finding_summary: The study found that students positively perceived AI-based feedback and preferred the combined visualizations and playback for reflecting on their performance. The feedback was seen as functional and motivating, with students expressing interest in additional cues and data-driven insights, suggesting improved self-awareness and reflective regulation during training.
finding.measure: Qualitative interview perceptions of AI-based feedback usefulness, clarity, and motivation for improvement

paper_profiles.title: Teacher training in the age of AI: Impact on AI Literacy and Teachers' Attitudes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an online teacher professional development program can improve in-service teachers’ AI literacy, their current and intended use of AI, and their attitudes toward AI in educational settings. The authors frame the study around a practical problem: teachers are increasingly expected to understand and use generative AI, yet many lack systematic preparation and confidence.

The intervention was a four-week certificate course, “Artificial Intelligence in Everyday School and Classroom Practice,” delivered by the digital professional development platform fobizz. The course combined synchronous and asynchronous components, including kickoff webinars, self-paced modules, optional topical units on machine learning, ethics, inclusion, and data protection, live webinars/workshops, and a project phase in which participants created an AI-supported lesson plan. The study used a pre-post design with German in-service teachers from different school types, and measured AI literacy with a validated test and attitudes with a custom questionnaire.

Results showed significant gains in overall AI literacy and in most competency domains, along with stronger reported use of AI in daily life, lesson preparation, and assessment/grading. Teachers also reported feeling better prepared to integrate AI and expressed more positive views about AI’s educational potential, although some critical risk awareness also increased. The authors conclude that structured, hands-on professional development can support teachers’ AI readiness, but they also note that more specialized, longitudinal, and education-specific AI training and assessment tools are needed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed pre-post intervention study, but it lacks a control group and relies on self-report for the attitude outcomes. Credibility is limited to a single-group design despite reasonable sample sizes and validated AI literacy measurement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention shows modest-to-large pre-post gains, especially in AI-use confidence and reported instructional use, with several effect sizes above 0.20. The impact is promising for a priority K-12 population, but the design limits causal strength and generalizability.

interventions.use_case: Online teacher professional development course on artificial intelligence and generative AI for in-service K-12 teachers, including webinars, self-paced modules, and an AI-supported lesson-planning project using a classroom AI assistant.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers' AI literacy improved significantly after the training program. Overall AI literacy increased from pre-test M=13.15 (SD=5.46) to post-test M=15.13 (SD=5.14) for n=291, with a small effect size (d=0.37, p<0.001). Ten of 14 competency domains also showed significant gains, including recognizing AI, AI's strengths and weaknesses, decision-making, ML steps, human role in AI, and ethics.
finding.measure: Validated AI literacy test (29 multiple-choice items + 1 sorting item) based on 14 AI literacy competencies

finding.finding_summary: The training was associated with greater reported use of AI for teacher workflow tasks and preparation. Teachers reported significantly higher agreement that they regularly use AI in daily life, use AI to create lessons and teaching materials, and use AI to support assessments/grading, with effects ranging from d=0.67 to d=1.32 across these items (n=436 for attitude assessment).
finding.measure: Self-reported AI use items for daily life, lesson/material creation, and assessment/grading

finding.finding_summary: Teachers' confidence and willingness to integrate AI increased substantially after the program. Agreement rose for imagining AI use in daily teaching practice (d=0.49) and for feeling well-prepared to integrate AI technologies into teaching (d=1.65), indicating stronger readiness and self-efficacy for adoption.
finding.measure: Self-reported readiness, imagined use, and preparedness to integrate AI into teaching

finding.finding_summary: Teachers became more positive about AI's educational potential, but critical concern also increased slightly. Agreement that AI in schools is more of a threat than an opportunity and that AI will replace teachers both rose modestly (d=0.42 and d=0.25), while belief that AI offers an opportunity to support students also increased (d=0.50), suggesting more nuanced risk-awareness alongside optimism.
finding.measure: Self-reported beliefs about AI's opportunities and risks in schools

paper_profiles.title: Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence: Early experiments with GPT-4
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an early, text-only version of GPT-4 exhibits capabilities that could be interpreted as signs of broader or more general intelligence. The authors frame the work as an exploration rather than a conventional benchmark study, arguing that standard evaluation methods are insufficient because GPT-4 may have seen similar benchmark data during training and because many of its most interesting abilities involve open-ended generation and interaction rather than single correct answers.

The paper presents a series of prompt-based demonstrations across multiple domains, including language, code generation, mathematics, vision-related tasks represented through text-to-code outputs, tool use, commonsense reasoning, and social understanding. The authors compare GPT-4 with ChatGPT on selected tasks such as rhymed proofs, Shakespeare-style dialogue, and interdisciplinary writing prompts, as well as tasks involving code repair, math reasoning, and plausibility judgments. They interpret GPT-4’s outputs as showing strong cross-domain composition and flexible adaptation to prompts.

The paper concludes that GPT-4 represents a major step toward artificial general intelligence, while also emphasizing important limitations such as hallucination, arithmetic errors, lack of robust planning, and biases. The study is presented as an informal, exploratory assessment rather than a controlled empirical evaluation, and the authors repeatedly note that results reflect an early version of the model whose behavior may differ from later released systems.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/position-style paper demonstrating GPT-4 capabilities through illustrative prompts and outputs, not a study of an educational intervention in K-12 settings. It does not use a rigorous experimental, quasi-experimental, or qualitative design relevant to the requested evidence framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no K-12 educational impact, no teacher planning/coaching intervention, and no student or teacher outcome data. Its relevance is indirect and theoretical only, so there is no measurable educational effect to rate.

paper_profiles.title: The Potential of AI Chatbots in Enhancing Lesson Planning in K-12 Education - Insights from Practicum-Experienced Teaching Graduate Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This thesis examines how generative AI chatbots are being used to support lesson planning in K-12 education, focusing on preservice teachers during their practicum experiences. The study asks three questions: how teacher candidates use AI chatbots to prepare lessons, what benefits and challenges they encounter, and how they perceive school-age students’ use of these tools. The paper is motivated by a gap in the emerging literature on ChatGPT and related tools from the perspective of new teachers.

The study used a mixed-methods design combining an anonymous online survey with semi-structured interviews. The participants were teaching graduate students and practicum-experienced teacher candidates, primarily from a University of Toronto Master of Teaching context, with 103 valid survey responses and 4 interviewees. The tools discussed included ChatGPT, Magic School AI, Eduaide.AI, Auto Classmate, and others, used for generating lesson ideas, classroom discussion prompts, feedback on student work, homework support, rubrics, slides, and other planning tasks.

Findings suggest that AI chatbots were widely adopted by respondents, with most using them occasionally or about half the time. Participants generally viewed them as helpful for efficiency, creativity, and instructional quality, while also raising concerns about technical issues, poor output quality, over-reliance, privacy, intellectual theft, bias, and academic integrity. The thesis concludes that AI chatbots can function as useful instructional supports for preservice teachers, but their use requires ethical oversight, training, and careful alignment with educational goals.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods thesis with a survey and four interviews, which provides useful descriptive and qualitative evidence but not a controlled causal design. It is rigorous for a graduate thesis, yet credibility is limited by self-selection, self-report, and the absence of a comparison condition or pre-post measurement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests modest practical value for teacher planning efficiency and highlights important governance concerns, but it does not report causal effect sizes or student outcome gains. Its impact is therefore informative but unclear beyond the surveyed preservice-teacher population.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI chatbots used by K-12 preservice teachers during practicum to support lesson planning, generate lesson content ideas, create interactive activities, draft rubrics and questions, provide feedback on student work, and retrieve quick instructional information. The paper focuses mainly on ChatGPT, with smaller use of education-specific chatbots such as Magic School AI and Eduaide.AI.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that 78% of the 103 valid survey respondents used AI chatbots for lesson planning during practicum, and most reported that the tools improved efficiency and reduced preparation time. In the survey, 50.67% used chatbots occasionally and 25.33% about half the time, suggesting routine but not universal adoption; the paper reports perceptions rather than a controlled effect size.
finding.measure: Self-reported use of AI chatbots for lesson planning; perceived efficiency and usefulness from survey and interviews
finding.study_size: n=103 survey respondents; n=4 interview participants

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that AI chatbots supported idea generation, lesson design, and feedback drafting, which may help planning and reflective practice. However, some teachers expressed concerns about over-reliance on AI and diminished critical thinking, so the net effect on higher-order teaching skills was mixed rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Survey and interview reports of perceived support for planning, creativity, and critical thinking concerns
finding.study_size: n=103 survey respondents; n=4 interview participants

finding.finding_summary: The thesis highlights institutional concerns around privacy, intellectual property, academic integrity, bias, and the need for professional development and oversight when integrating AI chatbots in K-12 teaching. It does not estimate a policy effect size, but it documents that these governance issues materially shaped participants' acceptance and use of the tools.
finding.measure: Survey items and interview themes about ethical concerns, privacy, training, and acceptable use
finding.study_size: n=103 survey respondents; n=4 interview participants

paper_profiles.title: Rankings and Reactivity: How Public Measures Recreate Social Worlds
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines how public rankings and other quantitative performance measures change the behavior and perceptions of the people and institutions they evaluate. The central question is not whether rankings accurately measure quality, but how measurement itself produces effects through reactivity. The authors develop a conceptual framework for analyzing reactivity in public measures, focusing on two mechanisms: self-fulfilling prophecy and commensuration.

The empirical case is U.S. News and World Report law school rankings and their effects on legal education. The study draws primarily on 136 open-ended interviews with law school deans, administrators, faculty, and other staff across roughly 70 U.S. law schools, supplemented by observations, public documents, admissions data, and additional interviews with students and business school administrators. The context is graduate/professional education in the United States, specifically law schools competing for applicants, faculty, funding, and reputation.

The paper concludes that rankings do more than describe institutions: they reshape them. Rankings influence student applications and yield, affect reputational surveys, alter internal resource allocation, encourage schools to conform to ranking criteria, and intensify attention to small differences between schools. More broadly, the authors argue that commensurative measures simplify complex realities, create new hierarchies, and can become self-reinforcing social forces that reorganize institutions and status systems.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative/theoretical case study, not an experiment or quasi-experiment. It offers a strong analytic framework and triangulated evidence, but it does not meet higher-credibility causal criteria for an intervention effect estimate.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has important institutional relevance and documents substantial reactivity in law school rankings, but it does not estimate a measurable effect size for a K-12 intervention. Its implications are broad and conceptual rather than demonstrating direct educational impact on student outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: This is a theoretical/qualitative case study of U.S. News law school rankings and their reactivity, based primarily on 136 open-ended interviews plus triangulating documents and observations. The paper argues that rankings reshape institutional behavior through self-fulfilling prophecy and commensuration, producing resource shifts, changed admissions and recruitment practices, altered organizational identities, and gaming strategies; it does not report a single causal effect size.
finding.measure: Interviews, organizational documents, observed admissions fair interactions, public application/yield data, and comparative evidence on law school ranking effects
finding.study_size: n=136 interviews; plus 17 admissions staff interviews, 92 short student interviews, 30 business school administrator interviews

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how K-12 educators evaluate lesson plans created by generative AI compared with lesson plans created by human curriculum designers. The authors focus on educator preferences rather than student outcomes, aiming to understand which kinds of lesson-plan components are seen as stronger or weaker when produced by AI models versus humans.

The intervention/approach is a controlled comparison of three lesson-plan sources: a customized GPT-4 model, a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model trained on K-12 lesson plans, and human curriculum designer-created plans retrieved from open educational repositories. Educators judged paired lesson plans on warm-up activities, main tasks, cool-down activities, and overall quality. The study combined quantitative pairwise preference analysis with qualitative comments, using thematic analysis and topic modeling to interpret why educators preferred one plan over another.

The population was 20 experienced K-12 mathematics educators in the United States, spanning elementary, middle, and high school levels. They completed a web-based blind comparison task over several weeks and evaluated 529 lesson-plan pairs, yielding 2,116 ratings and 2,979 comments. The context was K-12 mathematics lesson planning, with lesson plans aligned to Common Core standards and standardized lesson-plan structures.

The main conclusion is that human-authored lesson plans were generally preferred overall, especially for elementary grades and for components such as warm-ups, main tasks, student discourse, and supports for diverse learners. However, GenAI plans were competitive in specific areas, particularly cool-down activities and, in some cases, higher-grade or more structured content. The authors conclude that GenAI is better viewed as an assistive planning tool than a replacement for human expertise, and that human-AI collaboration may be the most promising direction for lesson planning support.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a comparative mixed-method study with blinded pairwise judgments and bootstrapped summaries, but it is not an RCT and does not evaluate student learning outcomes. The evidence is informative for educator preference and feasibility, yet remains observational and subject to sampling/selection limits.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical promise for GenAI as a lesson-planning assistant, but the impact is indirect and based on preferences rather than measured changes in teacher productivity or student outcomes. Reported differences are meaningful for design guidance, but not large or outcome-validated enough for a higher impact tier.

interventions.use_case: Comparative evaluation of GenAI-assisted lesson planning for K-12 math, using a customized prompt-based GPT-4 model and a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model to generate lesson plans (warm-up, main task, cool-down, overall structure) for educators to judge against human-authored plans.

finding.finding_summary: This paper directly assesses whether GenAI can support teacher planning efficiency by producing usable lesson plans comparable to human curriculum designer output. Educators still preferred human-authored plans overall (e.g., HCD vs. CGPT-4: 58.7% vs. 41.3%; HCD vs. LLaMA-2-13b FT: 53.6% vs. 46.4%), but the authors argue GenAI could function as an assistive planning tool that reduces educator workload, especially for structured components like cool-downs.
finding.measure: Educator pairwise preference judgments of lesson plan usefulness/overall quality across warm-up, main task, cool-down, and overall plan quality
finding.study_size: n=16 educators; 529 lesson-plan pairs; 2,116 total evaluations
finding.confidence_interval: 95% bootstrap CIs reported for aggregated preferences, but no single effect size reported

paper_profiles.title: How K-12 Educators Use AI: LLM-Assisted Qualitative Analysis at Scale
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 educators use generative AI in authentic professional contexts and, methodologically, how large language models (LLMs) can be used to scale qualitative analysis of those interactions. The core research question is not an intervention trial but an empirical description of educator-AI use, alongside a demonstration of an LLM-assisted analytic workflow for qualitative coding.

The study analyzes more than 13,000 unscripted educator-AI conversations from an open-access platform used by K-12 teachers, administrators, paraprofessionals, and instructional specialists. The authors use a multi-stage human-in-the-loop pipeline with grounded-theory-inspired open coding, axial coding, selective coding, and large-scale deductive annotation. LLMs (Claude 3 Sonnet and Claude 3.5 Haiku) support theme discovery, codebook development, and structured labeling, while human researchers retain conceptual control and validate outputs.

Findings show that educators primarily use AI for instructional planning and content design, differentiation and accessibility, assessment and feedback, and professional responsibilities such as communication and professional development. The most common uses include lesson planning, activity design, assessment creation, and adapting materials for multilingual learners or students with different ability levels. The paper concludes that generative AI is functioning as a pedagogical planning partner in real-world K-12 practice, and that LLM-assisted qualitative analysis can be feasible at scale when paired with human oversight.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, descriptive study of authentic educator-AI conversations using LLM-assisted coding and human validation. It is methodologically substantial, but it is not an experimental or causal impact study, so it meets the lower evidence bar for qualitative/correlational work.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful practical value for teacher productivity and instructional design, especially for K-12 educators using generative AI, but it does not estimate causal effects or report outcome improvements. Impact is therefore promising but unclear in magnitude.

interventions.use_case: A generative AI platform used by K-12 educators in unscripted, real-world conversations for lesson planning, differentiation, assessment design, and pedagogical reflection; the paper analyzes how educators prompt and revise LLM outputs rather than evaluating student learning directly.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that K-12 educators use generative AI to streamline instructional planning, differentiation, assessment creation, and professional communication across 13,071 conversations (104,529 messages). Planning appeared in 63.8% of educator requests, assessment and feedback in 47.2%, and professional responsibilities in 34.4%, indicating that AI is widely used to reduce workload and accelerate teacher task completion, though the study does not report effect sizes because it is descriptive/qualitative.
finding.measure: Descriptive frequency of coded educator-AI conversations and qualitative thematic analysis of instructional/professional tasks

finding.finding_summary: The analysis shows educators using AI to support planning-related reasoning, instructional design, and reflective revision, including iterative refinement of lesson structures, differentiation choices, and evaluation of AI-generated suggestions. These are presented as patterns of pedagogical reasoning and critical evaluation in authentic teacher-AI interactions, but no inferential effect estimates are reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of educator prompts and follow-up revisions, including instructional strategy and reflection-related codes

paper_profiles.title: FACET: Teacher-Centred LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems—Towards Personalized Educational Worksheets
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of helping teachers personalize instructional materials for highly heterogeneous K-12 classrooms, especially in mathematics. The authors argue that existing AI personalization tools are often student-facing and focused mainly on performance, while teachers need support that also accounts for motivational and pedagogical factors.

To address this, the paper introduces FACET, a teacher-facing large-language-model-based multi-agent framework. FACET uses three agents: learner agents that simulate student profiles, a teacher agent that generates differentiated worksheets based on curriculum and didactical principles, and an evaluator agent that provides rubric-based quality feedback. The system is demonstrated with authentic grade 8 mathematics curriculum content from German secondary education and is designed to produce one-page personalized worksheets with scaffolding, hints, motivational comments, and Bloom-aligned task sequencing.

The study evaluates feasibility through automated agent-based assessment and exploratory feedback from five K-12 in-service teachers. Across ten iterations per learner profile, the generated worksheets were rated as stable and well aligned to learner needs, and teacher feedback highlighted strong structure, clarity, and suitability. The authors conclude that multi-agent LLM systems can support scalable teacher-facing personalization, but note that richer learner profiles and real classroom trials are needed before broader claims about effectiveness can be made.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed-style prototype/feasibility study using exploratory teacher feedback and automated rubric evaluation, not a controlled experiment. The methodology is clear, but it lacks randomization, a true comparison group with outcome testing, and direct learner outcome measures.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests promising medium-scale potential for teacher planning and worksheet personalization, but it reports no measured student learning gains and no effect sizes on educational outcomes. Impact is therefore plausible but currently unclear beyond feasibility and perceived usefulness.

interventions.use_case: teacher-facing LLM-based multi-agent system that simulates learner profiles and generates personalized grade 8 mathematics worksheets with scaffolding, motivational comments, and Bloom-aligned tasks
evaluator-agent layer that automatically scores generated worksheets on didactical structure, clarity, creativity, and suitability for learner needs

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that FACET-generated worksheets were judged to be suitable for grade 8 mathematics personalization across four learner profiles. Internal agent-based evaluation over 10 iterations per profile showed high scores for suitability (M=4.78, SD=0.06) and clarity (M=4.76, SD=0.12), with didactical structure also favorable (M=4.12, SD=0.22).
finding.measure: Agent-based rubric ratings of worksheet quality and suitability for mathematics tasks
finding.study_size: n=4 learner profiles x 10 iterations each (internal evaluation)

finding.finding_summary: Five K-12 in-service teachers gave the personalized mathematics worksheets favorable ratings, especially for didactical structure (M=4.95) and suitability for learners (M=5.05). Qualitative feedback suggested the outputs aligned well with heterogeneous learner needs, though teachers also recommended additional scaffolding and richer contextualization.
finding.measure: Teacher expert ratings and think-aloud feedback on mathematics worksheets
finding.std_deviation: SD=6.6 years teaching experience; worksheet ratings reported as means and ranges rather than inferential effect sizes

finding.finding_summary: The framework is presented as reducing prompting overhead for teachers by using reusable learner and teacher agents, and teachers explicitly valued the ability to personalize tasks more efficiently. However, this was not measured with a direct time-on-task outcome, so the evidence is feasibility-based rather than causal.
finding.measure: Exploratory teacher feedback on usability and perceived workload reduction

paper_profiles.title: Enabling Multi-Agent Systems as Learning Designers: Applying Learning Sciences to AI Instructional Design
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems, when guided by a learning-sciences framework, can generate higher-quality K–12 instructional materials than a simple single-agent prompting baseline. The authors focus on the common challenge that teachers use LLMs for lesson and activity planning but often lack the time or expertise to craft prompts that reliably produce pedagogically strong outputs.

To address this, the study embeds the Knowledge–Learning–Instruction (KLI) framework into three generation systems: a single-agent baseline representing typical teacher prompting, a sequential role-based multi-agent system, and a collaborative multi-agent system using a conquer-and-merge discussion process. The systems generated secondary math and science learning activities from 10 curriculum-aligned objectives taken from the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education lesson library. Outputs were evaluated by practicing teachers using the Quality Matters K–12 rubric, and also by an LLM-as-a-judge using both the QM rubric and a custom learning-sciences rubric.

The population consisted of 20 U.S.-based secondary math and science teachers who rated the generated activities, making the context clearly K–12 and specifically grades 7–12. Quantitative rubric results showed only small and often non-significant differences among systems, but the qualitative teacher feedback consistently favored the collaborative multi-agent system, MAS-CMD, for creativity, contextual relevance, completeness, and classroom readiness. The authors conclude that embedding pedagogical theory directly into AI architectures can improve the usefulness of generated instructional materials, though this comes with higher computational cost and rubric-based quantitative measures may miss important qualities valued by teachers.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods comparative study with practicing teachers, repeated-measures ANOVAs, and qualitative thematic analysis, but it is not an RCT and relies on a small sample (n=20) with low inter-rater reliability. The evidence is useful and theory-informed, but credibility is limited by the absence of classroom implementation and by mostly non-significant quantitative effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests a modest practical benefit for teacher planning quality, especially for collaborative MAS-CMD outputs, but the measurable effects are small or inconsistent and do not demonstrate student learning gains. Because the study evaluates generated materials rather than classroom outcomes, the broader educational impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: Comparing multi-agent LLM systems for generating K-12 secondary math and science learning activities and instructional plans, including a baseline single-agent prompt, a role-based sequential multi-agent pipeline, and a collaborative conquer-and-merge multi-agent design guided by the KLI framework.

finding.finding_summary: The study found a clear quality–efficiency trade-off across LLM-based activity-generation systems. SAS was fastest and lightest (25±16 sec; ~3,376±1,601 tokens; 1 request), MAS-Roles required about 3× the time and ~7× the tokens, and MAS-CMD took the longest and most compute-intensive route (272±168 sec; ~71,638±25,222 tokens; 13 requests).
finding.measure: Generation time, tokens used, and number of requests per generated learning activity
finding.study_size: n=30 human-evaluated activities plus n=120 LLM-evaluated activities; efficiency stats reported across 10 objectives per system/model
finding.std_deviation: SAS 25±16 sec; MAS-Roles 77±45 sec; MAS-CMD 272±168 sec; tokens and requests also reported

finding.finding_summary: For secondary math activities, teachers rated MAS-CMD highest overall, but most quantitative differences across systems were not statistically significant except on QM criterion 5.2 (active learning). On the human-rated total score, MAS-CMD averaged 10.05 versus 9.55 for SAS and 9.05 for MAS-Roles, but the omnibus ANOVA was not significant (F(2,38)=2.66, p=.083); only criterion 5.2 showed a significant system effect, F(2,38)=4.75, p=.014, ηp²=.20, with MAS-CMD rated higher than MAS-Roles (p=.050).
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of math learning activity quality using QM rubric criteria and total score
finding.study_size: n=20 teachers (11 math, 9 science), with 10 math/science objectives total
finding.effect_size: ηp²=.20 for QM criterion 5.2; total-score ANOVA not significant

finding.finding_summary: For secondary science learning activities, the same pattern held: experts qualitatively preferred the collaborative MAS-CMD outputs, but rubric-based quantitative differences were mostly small and often non-significant. The only statistically significant human-rater finding was again on active learning (QM 5.2), F(2,38)=4.75, p=.014, ηp²=.20, while the overall total score difference did not reach conventional significance.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of science learning activity quality using QM rubric criteria and total score
finding.study_size: n=20 teachers (11 math, 9 science), with 10 math/science objectives total
finding.effect_size: ηp²=.20 for QM criterion 5.2; total-score ANOVA not significant

paper_profiles.title: Partnering with AI: A Pedagogical Feedback System for LLM Integration into Programming Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how large language models (LLMs) can be used to generate pedagogically sound feedback for programming education, with a particular focus on whether LLM feedback can better align with teacher feedback strategies than typical one-size-fits-all prompting approaches. The authors argue that prior automated feedback systems often optimize technical correctness but neglect pedagogical principles such as mastery level and task progress.

To study this, the authors first conducted a preliminary semi-structured interview with one secondary-school computer science teacher to derive adaptation criteria for feedback. They then developed a web-based feedback system for Python programming that used multi-agent LLM prompts, validation agents, and pedagogically informed response policies. The system was evaluated with eight secondary-school computer science teachers in Germany through mixed-method semi-structured interviews, where teachers reviewed synthetic student requests, judged LLM-generated feedback on several quantitative scales, and discussed similarities and differences relative to their own feedback practices.

The study population consisted of in-service secondary-school computer science teachers teaching Python in German schools, with the evaluated scenarios framed around student programming tasks and help requests at secondary-school grade levels. The main conclusions are that teachers generally judged the LLM feedback to be pedagogically sound, comprehensive, and effective, especially for supporting high-performing students and detecting small code errors quickly. However, teachers also emphasized important limitations: the system could not adapt well to classroom context, could not observe real-time student work, and lacked interactive and visual teaching strategies. The paper concludes that LLMs can complement but not replace human teachers, and that pedagogically grounded prompting is preferable to generic prompting.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods teacher evaluation with a very small sample (n=8) and no randomized comparison or student learning outcome measure. It provides useful design evidence but limited causal credibility.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for feedback efficiency and instructional support, but the evidence is indirect and based on teacher judgments rather than measured student gains. The likely impact is therefore modest and still uncertain.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated pedagogical feedback for secondary-school Python programming tasks, including adaptive hints, motivational prompts, and explanations tailored to student mastery level, task progress, and student input
multi-agent LLM system used as a conversational teacher/feedback partner to generate and validate student-facing responses in programming education

finding.finding_summary: In a mixed-method evaluation with eight secondary-school computer science teachers, the LLM feedback system was judged to be technically correct in 91.7% of reviewed cases (55/60 correct; 5/60 partially correct) and was rated as pedagogically sound, comprehensive, and effective. Mean ratings were 3.84/5 for pedagogical soundness (SD=1.10), 4.04/5 for comprehensiveness (SD=1.01), and 3.89/5 for effectiveness (SD=1.14).
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of correctness, pedagogical soundness, comprehensiveness, and effectiveness for programming feedback responses
finding.study_size: n=8 teachers; 60 sampled student requests/responses rated

finding.finding_summary: Teachers repeatedly reported that the system could provide instant, precise feedback and help identify small code errors faster than human teachers, suggesting workload and time-saving benefits. The study did not report a formal task-time effect size, but the qualitative evidence strongly favored faster feedback generation and parallel support for routine queries.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of speed, precision, and workload reduction in feedback provision

paper_profiles.title: Comparative Analysis of STEM and non-STEM Teachers’ Needs for Integrating AI into Educational Environments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines what K-12 teachers need from AI-enhanced educational platforms, especially those used for block-based programming (BBP) and related classroom tasks. The authors focus on three areas: student assessment, course development and resource expansion, and student monitoring/support. The study was motivated by the claim that common BBP platforms such as Code.org, Scratch, and Snap lack AI features that could better support teachers across both STEM and non-STEM subjects.

The study used semi-structured interviews with 8 K-12 teachers from North and South Carolina in the United States, split evenly between STEM and non-STEM disciplines. Participants had prior experience using coding activities in their classrooms, and interviews lasted 40 to 60 minutes. The researchers applied thematic analysis to identify recurring needs and differences between groups. Reported needs included customizable rubrics, more detailed feedback, authenticity/originality checks, AI-supported resource generation, individualized materials, peer-collaboration support, and monitoring tools such as screen control, reminders, and progress tracking.

The main conclusion is that both STEM and non-STEM teachers want AI features that make educational platforms more adaptive, more informative for assessment, and better integrated with classroom workflows. Non-STEM teachers especially emphasized creative and qualitative assessment needs, while STEM teachers more often stressed workflow efficiency and authenticity of student work. The paper argues that future educational platforms should incorporate AI-supported personalization, analytics, and feedback features, while also addressing privacy and school-policy constraints.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative semi-structured interview study with thematic analysis of 8 teachers, so it offers descriptive evidence about needs and perceptions rather than causal effects. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically coherent, but it does not test an intervention or measure outcomes experimentally.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct impact estimate on student or teacher outcomes; it surfaces requirements for future AI-enabled tools. Any impact is indirect and currently unclear, so the evidence supports only a yellow tier.

interventions.use_case: Semi-structured interview study of K-12 teachers' needs for AI-enhanced educational platforms in block-based programming contexts, including assessment, course development, and student monitoring features.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports teacher demand for AI features that would streamline assessment, course development, and monitoring tasks, suggesting perceived gains in teacher workflow efficiency rather than measured learning gains. Across 8 interviewed K-12 teachers (n=8), participants emphasized AI support for rubric customization, detailed feedback, automated content generation, progress tracking, and reducing time spent switching between systems.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes about teacher workload, grading, resource creation, and student monitoring needs

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified institutional needs around LMS integration, single sign-on, privacy controls, and cross-platform data management for school use of AI-enabled educational tools. In this qualitative sample of 8 K-12 teachers (n=8), the findings indicate that adoption depends on compatibility with school systems and compliance with privacy/security expectations.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes about integration, access control, and privacy/security requirements

finding.finding_summary: A recurring theme was the desire for AI to support collaboration, peer matching, conflict resolution, and creative problem solving in coding and interdisciplinary projects.
