The study does not quantify effects, but the 8 teacher interviews (n=8) suggest AI-enabled platforms were viewed as potentially helpful for collaboration and creativity in classroom workflows.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes about collaboration, peer feedback, and creativity support

finding.finding_summary: Teachers wanted monitoring and support features such as reminders, pop-up tips, progress alerts, and motivational tools to help students stay on task and persist during assignments. This is a qualitative perception finding from 8 K-12 teacher interviews (n=8), not a measured student outcome, but it indicates expected benefits for engagement and self-regulation.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes about motivation, distraction prevention, reminders, and help prompts

paper_profiles.title: Unlocking Scientific Concepts: How Effective Are LLM-Generated Analogies for Student Understanding and Classroom Practice?
paper_profiles.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language model (LLM)-generated analogies can support understanding of scientific concepts in K-12 education and how teachers can use and adapt such analogies in real classroom practice. The authors focus on two related questions: first, whether analogies generated by GPT-4o improve student problem solving when students use them without teacher intervention; and second, what teachers need from such analogies and how effective they are when teachers integrate them into instruction.

The study uses a two-stage design in a Chinese high school. In Study I, 49 ninth-grade students completed an in-class test on unfamiliar physics and biology concepts, comparing a textbook-only condition with a textbook-plus-LLM-analogy condition. The researchers measured answer accuracy and self-confidence and also interviewed a subset of students. In Study II, the authors interviewed two teachers and two senior students to derive requirements for classroom use, then conducted a one-week field study in two first-year high school classes where two teachers used LLM-generated analogies in one class and regular instruction in the other.

The paper finds that LLM-generated analogies can help with some biology concepts, but their effectiveness is inconsistent across subjects and can also produce overconfidence and occasional misunderstanding when students rely on incomplete or erroneous analogies. In the classroom study, teachers were able to refine analogies, discard unnecessary ones, and use them in ways that matched their instructional goals; the analogies were most useful when they were vivid, aligned with subject needs, and focused on key parts of a concept rather than trying to explain everything. The authors conclude that current LLM-generated analogies are not well suited for unsupervised student self-learning, but can be useful as teacher-facing preparation tools when combined with teacher judgment and modification.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical study using a controlled in-class comparison plus a qualitative field study, but it is not a full randomized controlled trial with strong causal controls across settings. The evidence base is mixed-method and locally bounded to one high school, so credibility is moderate rather than high.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The findings suggest some positive effects on biology concept understanding and student confidence, but effects were inconsistent across subjects and sometimes negative due to over-reliance and missing information. Overall impact is modest and unclear for general K-12 use rather than clearly large or broadly transferable.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated analogies for science concept explanation and teacher lesson preparation/refinement in high school biology and physics; GPT-4o was used to generate, revise, and select analogies for classroom use.

finding.finding_summary: In a controlled in-class test with valid data from 44 students (n=22 per group), LLM-generated analogies improved understanding for some biology concepts but not physics overall. The paper reports a significant association between group and accuracy for biology (exact Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney p=0.042), while physics showed no significant benefit; confidence ratings also increased significantly for both subjects, indicating stronger subjective understanding without consistent accuracy gains.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice concept question accuracy and 5-point self-confidence ratings on four unfamiliar science concepts
finding.study_size: n=44 valid test papers (22 textbook-only, 22 textbook+LLM analogy)

finding.finding_summary: In the one-week classroom field study, teachers reported that LLM-generated analogies were useful for teaching key points, stimulating interest, and supporting classroom understanding when they were selectively edited to fit lesson goals. The evidence is qualitative rather than effect-size based, but teachers observed better classroom feedback and homework performance in the analogy condition relative to usual practice.
finding.measure: Teacher observations, student feedback, and reported homework/classroom performance during 12 lessons

finding.finding_summary: Student self-confidence was higher when LLM-generated analogies were provided, but this did not reliably translate into better accuracy. The paper also notes overconfidence and over-reliance on analogies, suggesting the tool can increase perceived understanding while sometimes weakening calibration.
finding.measure: 5-point self-confidence ratings; interview evidence of overconfidence/over-reliance
finding.study_size: n=44 valid test papers; 8 interviewed students

paper_profiles.title: Learning About Algorithm Auditing in Five Steps: Scaffolding How High School Youth Can Systematically and Critically Evaluate Machine Learning Applications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to support high school students in critically evaluating machine learning systems through algorithm auditing. The authors argue that while AI education often introduces students to AI/ML concepts, there is little guidance on how to help them systematically investigate how such systems work, what biases they may contain, and what their broader implications are. To fill this gap, the paper proposes a five-step auditing process for learning activities: developing a hypothesis, generating systematic inputs, running tests, analyzing results, and reporting findings.

The approach is presented through a case study from a two-week summer workshop in an after-school science program in the northeastern United States. Fourteen rising high school sophomores worked in pairs to design and audit peer-created generative AI TikTok filters using TikTok Effect House. The workshop included scaffolds such as hypothesis examples, a two-axis input organizer, input-output tables, and guidance for reporting findings to peers. The paper focuses on one pair of students, Ishmael and Ziyi, to show how they engaged with each step of the audit process.

The main conclusion is that high school youth can meaningfully engage in a structured auditing workflow when given appropriate scaffolds and time. The authors found that the five-step model helped students move beyond ad hoc observations toward more systematic critique of AI behavior, including noticing gendered and racialized effects in a filter’s outputs. They also conclude that learner-centered scaffolding should blend expert auditing structure with youth-relevant, user-driven observations. The paper emphasizes that future classroom implementations will need further support for input generation, analysis, reporting, and teacher facilitation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative design-based case study with rich artifact and video analysis, but no comparison group, randomization, or quantitative estimate of learning impact. The methodology is credible for exploratory insight, yet it does not meet stronger causal-evidence criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests a promising instructional approach for supporting critical AI evaluation, but it provides no measurable effect size and only a small workshop case study. Its impact is therefore informative but still unclear at the population level.

interventions.use_case: Scaffolded algorithm-auditing learning activity for high school students using peer-designed generative AI TikTok filters in TikTok Effect House, with five steps (hypothesis, input generation, testing, analysis, reporting) to evaluate model behavior and bias.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the five-step algorithm-auditing scaffold enabled 14 high school students to engage in systematic, critical evaluation of machine learning applications. In the focal case study, two students (Ishmael and Ziyi) were able to generate a hypothesis, build a 33-image test set, analyze outputs, and report findings about gendered and racialized filter behavior.
finding.measure: Qualitative case study of youth engagement with auditing steps; artifact analysis, screen/video recordings, and audit report content
finding.study_size: n=14 overall workshop; focal case study n=2

paper_profiles.title: An Experience Report on a Pedagogically Controlled, Curriculum-Constrained AI Tutor for SE Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the design and early evaluation of an AI tutor intended to support learners in a digital programming and computational thinking course. The authors are concerned with how to constrain a large language model so that it provides curriculum-aligned, age-appropriate help rather than generic or incorrect answers, and how such a system is perceived by both learners and educators.

The intervention, RockStartIT Tutor, is a GPT-4/GPT-4o-based assistant built with OpenAI’s Assistant API, a threaded chat interface, prompt engineering, and a modular Markdown knowledge base with pedagogically tagged content such as tasks, hints, explanations, motivations, and hidden solutions. The system is designed to scaffold learner inquiry, avoid direct solution giving, and remain strictly within the course content. The paper frames the tutor as a complementary support tool rather than a replacement for teachers.

The study was conducted in a RockStartIT course context with 13 participants total: 7 learners and 6 teachers/prospective teachers. Participants used the tutor for a short session on their own devices and then completed a TAM-based questionnaire plus open-ended questions. Quantitative ratings were generally positive for usefulness, ease of use, and intention to use, and qualitative feedback highlighted value for low-pressure question asking, explanations, and support for independent learning.

Overall, the paper concludes that carefully constrained generative AI can provide practical, pedagogically coherent support in secondary computing education and can be accepted by both learners and teachers. However, the authors emphasize that the evidence is preliminary and that stronger validation with the intended school-age population, longer deployments, and richer behavioral data is still needed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-method experience report with a very small convenience sample and no control group, randomization, or pre-post learning measures. It provides useful early-stage qualitative and descriptive evidence, but credibility is limited by prototype status and weak internal validity.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful but unquantified benefits for support, confidence, and teacher workload in a niche secondary computing context. Because outcomes are based on perceptions rather than observed learning gains or efficiency metrics, the impact is best characterized as modest and unclear.

interventions.use_case: pedagogically controlled GPT-4o tutor for a curriculum-constrained secondary school software engineering and computational thinking course, using prompt engineering, threaded chat memory, and tagged knowledge-base retrieval to provide scaffolded hints and explanations without revealing solutions

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and learners perceived the AI tutor as potentially helpful for reducing teacher workload and providing on-demand support during independent work. On the TAM items, teachers rated usefulness highly for classroom use (PU8 M=4.50, SD=0.55, n=6), and open-ended responses emphasized that it could relieve teachers while enriching students, though this was based on perceptions rather than measured time savings.
finding.measure: Technology Acceptance Model usefulness items; open-ended teacher and learner feedback on workload/support

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that the tutor supported inquiry, reflection, and metacognitive problem solving by giving hints, paraphrasing concepts, and prompting learners to trace errors. Qualitative comments noted that the tutor helped students understand why they answered questions incorrectly and encouraged deeper engagement with the content, but no objective learning-gain measure was reported.
finding.measure: Open-ended qualitative feedback; TAM usefulness perceptions related to understanding and reflection

finding.finding_summary: The tutor was perceived as a low-stakes, nonjudgmental environment that made learners more comfortable asking questions, suggesting improved confidence and reduced hesitation. TAM ratings for ease of use were high (PEOU2 M=4.62, SD=0.51, n=13), and qualitative feedback highlighted emotional safety and encouragement, but the study did not directly measure motivation or anxiety.
finding.measure: TAM ease-of-use items; qualitative comments on emotional safety and willingness to ask questions

paper_profiles.title: Free-text Rationale Generation under Readability Level Control
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can be prompted to generate free-text rationales at different readability levels, and whether those readability instructions change both the content and perceived quality of the explanations. The authors frame the work as a perturbation test of natural language explanations: if rationales can be steered by readability prompts, they may behave more like general text generation than like fixed internal explanations of model decisions.

The approach uses instruction prompting to request explanations targeted at four readability levels (college, high school, middle school, and sixth grade), mapped to Flesch Reading Ease ranges. The study evaluates generated rationales with automatic readability metrics, reference-free TIGERScore, BERTScore, and human annotations. Experiments are run on four NLP tasks with explanatory annotations: fact-checking (HealthFC), hate speech classification (HateXplain), hate speech detection (CAD), and natural language inference (SpanEx), using four open-weight LLMs (Mistral-0.2, Mixtral-0.1, OpenChat-3.5, and Llama-3). Human validation is conducted on HateXplain with five annotators who rated readability, coherence, informativeness, and label agreement.

The main findings are that LLMs do respond to readability instructions, but the resulting text complexity only partially matches the intended levels. Rationales tend to cluster around medium complexity, and both metric-based and human judgments often favor high-school-level explanations. The authors conclude that rationale generation is sensitive to prompting and shares characteristics with controllable text generation, but current readability control is imperfect and evaluation remains challenging because of hallucination, metric limitations, and weak alignment between metric scores and human perceptions.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical NLP study, but it is not a K-12 intervention trial. The evidence is observational/benchmark-based with human judgment components rather than a controlled educational design, so it fits a lower-certainty qualitative/correlational tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows modest, indirect impact: readability prompting can alter explanation style and perceived usefulness, but it does not test student learning gains or classroom outcomes. The relevance to education is secondary and the measured effects are not tied to K-12 achievement or behavior outcomes.

interventions.use_case: LLM-based free-text rationale generation under prompted readability-level control, using instruction prompting to make explanations target sixth-grade, middle-school, high-school, or college readers.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether readability-controlled LLM rationales preserve task accuracy across fact-checking, hate speech detection, and NLI. Task accuracy varies substantially by model and dataset (e.g., OpenChat-3.5 reaches 82.1% on SpanEx, while performance is much lower on HateXplain and HealthFC), but readability prompting itself does not systematically improve or degrade accuracy; the main finding is that task predictions remain broadly consistent while rationale text complexity changes.
finding.measure: Task accuracy on classification/fact-checking benchmarks (HateXplain, CAD, SpanEx, HealthFC)
finding.study_size: multiple datasets; test sizes reported as n=1,924 (HateXplain), n=5,307 (CAD), n=3,865 (SpanEx), n=750 (HealthFC)

finding.finding_summary: The core substantive outcome is explanation quality/readability as a form of clarity and communicative usefulness. Human annotators generally found the rationales satisfactory across all readability levels, but agreement on the intended readability levels was low (Krippendorff’s α = 3.67%, Fleiss’ κ = 13.92%), and annotators only recognized the prompted readability level correctly 23.7% of the time. High-school-level rationales were most commonly perceived and favored, indicating that the intervention changes expression but only imperfectly achieves the targeted audience adaptation.
finding.measure: Human ratings of readability, coherence, informativeness, and accuracy; readability metrics (FRE, GFI, CLI)

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that LLMs can be steered to generate rationale text at different readability levels via prompting, which may help automate explanation tailoring without additional fine-tuning. However, the generated complexity only loosely matches the target levels, so the efficiency gain is in controllability rather than precise compliance.
finding.measure: Readability metrics on generated rationales and model-following of instructed output format
finding.study_size: multiple model-dataset runs; exact total n not reported

paper_profiles.title: AI tutoring can safely and effectively support students: An exploratory RCT in UK classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates whether a generative AI tutoring system, LearnLM, can safely and effectively support students in real classroom settings. The central question is whether an AI model fine-tuned for pedagogical dialogue can provide tutoring that matches or exceeds human tutoring, while still being safe for student use.

The study deployed LearnLM in the Eedi mathematics platform used by UK secondary schools. In the intervention, LearnLM generated draft tutoring messages in chat-based sessions, and expert human tutors supervised each message, approving, editing, or rewriting it before students saw it. The comparison conditions were static, pre-written hints and human tutor–only sessions. The trial involved 165 students in Years 9 and 10 across five UK secondary schools, with 17 expert teachers acting as tutors.

Results showed that interactive tutoring improved immediate remediation and misconception resolution relative to static hints, and LearnLM performed about as well as human tutors on those short-term outcomes. On the transfer outcome, students supported by LearnLM did somewhat better than those tutored by humans alone. Tutor interviews suggested that LearnLM was especially strong at generating Socratic questions, while human supervision remained important for pacing, tone, and social-emotional nuance. The paper concludes that responsibly supervised genAI tutoring may help scale individualized support in mathematics classrooms.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a well-designed exploratory randomized controlled trial with within-session randomization and Bayesian estimation, providing relatively strong causal evidence. However, it is exploratory, short-term, and partially reliant on platform-based outcomes rather than longer-term standardized assessments, so it falls short of blue-tier certainty.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The effect on durable learning transfer is modest in magnitude (+5.5 percentage points) but appears practically meaningful for a priority K-12 population in mathematics. The intervention also shows promise for scaling individualized tutoring, though the evidence is still preliminary and context-specific.

interventions.use_case: generative AI tutoring integrated into a K-12 mathematics platform, where LearnLM drafts Socratic chat responses to students' incorrect answers and a human tutor supervises, edits, or approves each message before sending

finding.finding_summary: In an exploratory RCT with n=165 students across five UK secondary schools, supervised LearnLM tutoring performed at least as well as human tutoring on immediate math learning outcomes and better on transfer. Students receiving LearnLM were more likely to solve the next-unit novel problem correctly than those with human tutors alone (66.2% vs 60.7%), a +5.5 percentage point difference with a 95% credible interval of [-1.4, +12.4].
finding.measure: performance on Eedi mathematics study-unit outcomes: second-attempt correctness, misconception resolution within unit, and correct response to the first question in the next unit (knowledge transfer)
finding.effect_size: +5.5 percentage points on next-unit transfer vs human tutors; effect size not otherwise reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper treats next-unit problem solving as a measure of knowledge transfer, a durable skill proxy for applying learning to a new context. LearnLM outperformed human tutors on this transfer outcome: 66.2% of students solved the novel next-topic item correctly versus 60.7% with human tutoring alone, corresponding to a +5.5 percentage point advantage.
finding.measure: knowledge transfer to a new topic, operationalized as correctness on the first question of the next study unit

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that supervising tutors found LearnLM made tutoring feel more fluid and efficient, especially because it helped them support multiple students at the same time. This was based on qualitative interviews and surveys (e.g., 82.4% of tutors selected 'supporting multiple students at the same time' as the most useful feature), but the authors note the RCT design did not rigorously measure throughput or efficiency.
finding.measure: tutor interviews, post-trial tutor survey item on most useful feature, and informal scalability observations

paper_profiles.title: TUTORBENCH: A Benchmark to Assess Tutoring Capabilities of Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces TUTORBENCH, a benchmark for evaluating the tutoring capabilities of large language models (LLMs). The work addresses the gap between general-purpose LLM benchmarks and the more nuanced human-centered skills needed for tutoring, such as adaptive explanation, feedback on student work, and active learning support. The authors argue that existing benchmarks are too narrow and often fail to capture multimodal tutoring interactions or the need for rubric-based evaluation of open-ended responses.

TUTORBENCH contains 1,490 human-expert-curated tutoring conversations centered on high-school and AP-level STEM content across biology, physics, chemistry, statistics, calculus, and computer science. Each sample includes sample-specific rubrics, and model outputs are scored using an LLM-judge with rubric-based pass/fail criteria. The benchmark includes both text-only and image-based student work, reflecting realistic tutoring interactions where learners upload handwritten or printed work.

The paper evaluates 16 frontier LLMs on TUTORBENCH and finds that even the best models score only about 56% overall, with particular weakness in adaptive explanation generation and in providing fully effective tutoring behaviors. The authors also validate their automated judge against human expert ratings and conclude that rubric-based benchmarking can provide scalable, fine-grained evidence about model strengths and limitations for AI tutoring.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark and evaluation paper rather than an intervention study with learner outcomes. It uses a comparatively rigorous rubric-based methodology and human-expert validation, but it does not test causal effects on students or classrooms.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper’s impact is methodological and diagnostic: it provides a benchmark that may improve future tutor models, but it reports no direct learner outcome gains. The practical contribution is substantial for model development, yet the measured impact on education is indirect and unclear.

interventions.use_case: benchmarking large language models on tutoring-style interactions for high-school/AP STEM questions, including adaptive explanation generation, assessment and feedback, and active learning hint generation with text and image inputs
evaluating LLM-generated feedback on student work by detecting mistakes, classifying errors, and providing corrective comments against sample-specific rubrics

paper_profiles.title: MathScale: Scaling Instruction Tuning for Mathematical Reasoning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of limited high-quality training data for mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs), especially data that spans a wide range of difficulty levels. The authors argue that existing math instruction-tuning datasets are too small and often generated by augmentation methods that stay too close to the original examples. They also note that current benchmarks are fragmented, making it hard to compare models fairly across elementary, secondary, college, and competition-level mathematics.

To address this, the paper proposes MathScale, a scalable synthetic data generation pipeline that uses GPT-3.5 to extract topics and knowledge points from seed math questions, build a concept graph over those concepts, and then sample new concept combinations to generate novel math question-answer pairs. The resulting dataset, MathScaleQA, contains about two million generated examples. The paper also introduces MWPBENCH, a benchmark combining ten math datasets spanning K-12, college, and competition-level problems, with unified evaluation procedures. The authors fine-tune open-source LLMs such as LLaMA-2 and Mistral on MathScaleQA and show improved mathematical reasoning performance compared with prior open-source math-tuned models.

The work is evaluated on benchmark datasets rather than human learners, so the relevant populations are the math problem levels represented in the benchmark: elementary, middle school, high school, and undergraduate/college. No educator, student intervention, or classroom deployment is studied. The main conclusion is that concept-based synthetic data generation is a more scalable and effective way to improve math reasoning in LLMs than earlier augmentation-heavy approaches, and that the benchmark better supports fair comparison across difficulty levels.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a preprint methods/benchmark paper with model-training and evaluation experiments, but not a K-12 field study, RCT, or QED involving learners or teachers. It provides useful comparative evidence on LLM math capability, yet does not meet higher-evidence criteria for educational intervention impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains in benchmark accuracy are large for mathematical reasoning models, but the paper evaluates model performance rather than direct effects on K-12 learners or classrooms. Educational impact is therefore indirect and unclear for the requested teacher-planning/coaching context.

interventions.use_case: Frontier LLMs (GPT-3.5/GPT-4) are used to extract math concepts, generate synthetic math question-answer pairs, and fine-tune open-source LLMs for mathematical reasoning; the paper also evaluates these models as math-solving systems on benchmark problems.

finding.finding_summary: MathScaleQA fine-tuning substantially improved mathematical reasoning performance for open-source LLMs. On MWPBENCH, MathScale-7B reached 35.0% micro-average accuracy and 37.5% macro-average accuracy, outperforming the best same-size peers by 42.9% and 43.7%, respectively. The paper reports similar gains for MathScale-13B and MathScale-Mistral across K-12, college, and competition-level math word problems.
finding.measure: Accuracy on MWPBENCH math word-problem benchmark (micro-average and macro-average accuracy across 10 datasets)

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents MathScale as a scalable pipeline for generating large-scale synthetic math instruction data using GPT-3.5, reducing dependence on manual authoring of math QA pairs. The authors report producing 2 million unique concept compositions and a 2 million-example MathScaleQA dataset, suggesting substantial gains in data-generation throughput for model training workflows.
finding.measure: Dataset generation scale / number of synthetic math QA pairs produced

paper_profiles.title: Assessment Design in the AI Era: A Method for Identifying Items Functioning Differentially for Humans and Chatbots
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a measurement and assessment-design problem created by the rapid adoption of generative AI in education: how to identify assessment items on which large language models (LLMs) and human learners behave differently, in ways that matter for validity, reliability, and fairness. The authors argue that standard benchmark-style comparisons of chatbot performance are insufficient because they mostly report overall scores rather than item-level differences conditioned on ability.

To address this, the paper proposes a psychometrically grounded method that combines Differential Item Functioning (DIF) analysis with negative control testing and item-total correlation diagnostics. Humans are treated as the reference group and chatbots as the focal group. The approach is evaluated on response data from two instruments: a high school chemistry diagnostic test and a university entrance exam quantitative section. Six chatbots were tested, including multiple versions of GPT, Gemini, and Claude, with repeated runs to simulate artificial students.

The study finds that LR-DIF is more stable and useful than MH-DIF for this purpose, especially when combined with an ITC threshold to filter unstable items. Domain experts reviewing chemistry items concluded that chatbots tended to outperform humans on items requiring rule-governed conceptual reasoning, but underperformed on items requiring visual interpretation, linguistic nuance, and multi-step quantitative reasoning. The main conclusion is that DIF-based analysis can provide a reliable framework for detecting human–GenAI differences and informing better assessment design in AI-rich contexts.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a method-development and comparative psychometric study, not an intervention trial. It uses a clear analytic design with human and chatbot response data plus negative controls, but it is observational and primarily diagnostic rather than causal.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear relevance for assessment design in AI-rich K-12 and higher-education contexts, but it reports no learning effect size or direct educational impact. Its contribution is methodological and likely important for validity/fairness, yet the demonstrated impact on student outcomes is indirect and unclear.

interventions.use_case: Evaluating six leading chatbots (GPT-4o, GPT-5.2, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 4.5 Sonnet) as respondents on multiple-choice assessment items to characterize where generative AI answers differ from human learners.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test student learning gains; instead, it evaluates how well chatbots and humans respond to chemistry assessment items. Subject-matter experts found chatbot advantages on items requiring rule-governed chemistry reasoning (e.g., NaCl ionic structure, conservation of matter, oxidation states) and disadvantages on items requiring visual interpretation and multi-step quantitative problem solving.
finding.measure: Item-level correct responses on a 22-item high school chemistry diagnostic test; DIF flags validated by expert content analysis
finding.study_size: n=931 students; chatbot responses from 6 LLMs, 20 runs each per model

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can function as an automated teacher coach. The authors focus on a longstanding problem in teacher professional development: classroom observation and coaching are valuable but difficult to provide consistently because of time, cost, and limited expert access. Rather than training or deploying a classroom intervention, the study evaluates ChatGPT’s zero-shot ability to perform coaching-related tasks on existing classroom transcript data.

The paper proposes three tasks for AI-based coaching: (A) scoring transcript segments using classroom observation rubrics, (B) identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and (C) generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student reasoning. The evaluation uses the NCTE transcript dataset of U.S. elementary mathematics classrooms, containing 4th- and 5th-grade observations from 317 teachers across four school districts. The authors compare ChatGPT’s rubric scores with expert annotations and recruit experienced math teachers to judge the quality of the model’s qualitative feedback.

The main finding is that ChatGPT shows promise but is not yet reliable enough to replace expert coaching. Its score predictions correlate weakly with human ratings, and its qualitative feedback is often relevant but frequently not novel or insightful. For suggestions on eliciting reasoning, most outputs were actionable, but 82% repeated something already present in the transcript. The paper concludes that generative AI could eventually complement human coaching, but substantial improvements in faithfulness, novelty, and pedagogical insight are needed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed-style empirical evaluation with human ratings and quantitative comparisons, but it is not an intervention trial and lacks causal assignment or student outcome measurement. It is best characterized as a qualitative/benchmarking study of model capability with a small human evaluation sample.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows limited practical promise for automated coaching, but no demonstrated impact on teacher practice or student outcomes. The observed performance is mixed and often weak, so the real-world impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: Zero-shot use of ChatGPT/gpt-3.5-turbo as an automated teacher coach to score classroom transcript segments, identify highlights and missed opportunities, and generate actionable suggestions for eliciting student mathematical reasoning.
Automated feedback on teacher instructional practice from classroom transcript segments using rubric-based scoring and qualitative coaching suggestions for CLASS and MQI observation items.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether ChatGPT can serve as a scalable, cost-effective complement to expert coaching for classroom observation and feedback. It finds the system can produce relevant and sometimes actionable feedback, but it is often not novel or insightful; for example, 82% of suggestions repeat what the teacher already does, and scoring correlations with human ratings are low across items.
finding.measure: Spearman correlation with human rubric scores; human teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty/redundancy
finding.study_size: n=100 transcript segments for scoring; n=216 CLASS items; n=288 MQI items; n=36 suggestion items; 2 human raters

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether K-12 educators prefer lesson plans created by human curriculum designers or by generative AI systems, and which parts of a lesson plan are perceived as stronger or weaker across author types. The study is motivated by the growing use of GenAI for lesson planning and the lack of direct comparative evidence on how educators evaluate AI-generated instructional materials.

The intervention/approach compared three sources of mathematics lesson plans: a human curriculum designer source, a customized prompt-based GPT-4 model, and a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model trained on expert-designed lesson plans. Educators completed blinded pairwise comparisons of lesson plans across four dimensions: warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall quality. The study also collected written comments explaining preferences and analyzed them with both quantitative preference counts and qualitative thematic analysis/topic modeling.

The participants were 20 experienced K-12 mathematics educators spanning elementary, middle, and high school levels in the United States. Over several weeks, participants evaluated 20 lesson-plan pairs each, producing 529 complete pairwise evaluations and 2,979 comments. The context was an online web-based user study focused on mathematics lesson planning aligned to grade-level standards.

The main conclusion is that human-authored lesson plans were generally preferred overall, especially for elementary grades and for instructional components requiring student engagement, scaffolding, discourse, and differentiated support. However, GenAI lesson plans performed comparatively well in cool-down activities and, in some higher-grade contexts, became more competitive; the fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b was especially strong in high school comparisons. The authors conclude that GenAI is better viewed as an assistive planning tool than a replacement for human curriculum expertise, and that human-AI collaboration is likely the most promising path for lesson planning support.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-method comparative preference study with blinded pairwise evaluations and bootstrapped descriptive analyses, but not a randomized impact study on student outcomes. The evidence is useful and reasonably structured, yet it primarily captures educator judgments rather than causal effects on learning.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study indicates a potentially useful, moderate practical contribution of GenAI for teacher planning, especially for structured lesson components, but it does not demonstrate measurable student-learning gains or large-scale workflow effects. Impact is therefore promising but still unclear and mostly indirect.

interventions.use_case: comparative evaluation of AI-generated K-12 mathematics lesson plans for teacher lesson planning, comparing customized GPT-4 and fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b against human-authored curriculum designer lesson plans
generative AI lesson plan generation using customized GPT-4 and fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b for K-12 math instruction, including warm-up, main task, and cool-down sections

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests GenAI can reduce teacher lesson-planning burden by generating structured lesson plans, positioning it as an assistive tool rather than a replacement for educator expertise. However, this study measured educator preferences for plan quality rather than actual time savings, so the efficiency benefit is inferred rather than directly estimated.
finding.measure: Educator preference judgments of lesson plan usefulness/quality; qualitative comments about planning support
finding.study_size: n=16 educators (529 lesson plan pairs; 2,116 evaluations)

finding.finding_summary: In K-12 mathematics lesson planning, human-authored lesson plans were preferred overall in warm-up, main task, and overall quality, while GenAI plans were comparatively stronger for cool-down tasks and became more competitive in middle and high school settings. For example, educators preferred human-authored plans 58.7% vs. CGPT-4 and 53.6% vs. LLaMA-2-13b FT overall, but preferred CGPT-4 over human plans for cool-down activities (59.7%) and LLaMA-2-13b FT also over human plans (57.9%) in that section.
finding.measure: Pairwise educator preference for lesson plan sections and overall quality in K-12 mathematics
finding.study_size: n=16 educators; 529 lesson plan pairs; 2,116 evaluations
finding.confidence_interval: bootstrapped 95% CIs reported but not numerically specified in text

paper_profiles.title: Predicted Composite Signed-Distance Fields for Real-Time Motion Planning in Dynamic Environments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of real-time motion planning for robots operating in dynamic environments with moving obstacles. The authors argue that conventional signed-distance field (SDF) approaches are too slow to recompute online, and that planners which ignore obstacle motion or use only binary collision costs can produce inefficient or unsafe trajectories.

To solve this, the paper introduces predicted signed-distance fields and a composite SDF method that updates the environment representation by combining precomputed SDFs for static and moving objects. The approach uses a constant-velocity model to predict obstacle motion and integrates the resulting predicted SDFs with the GPMP2 motion planner, allowing obstacle factors in the factor graph to be updated in real time.

The work is evaluated in simulation and hardware with 7-DoF robotic arms, including a WAM arm and a Franka Emika Panda, navigating around moving obstacles such as a pillar or a mobile robot. Results show that composite SDF prediction is substantially faster than exact recomputation, and that including predicted obstacle trajectories improves the likelihood of collision-free planning and reduces trajectory jerk, producing smoother behavior than execute-and-update baselines.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a robotics motion-planning paper, not an education study, and it does not evaluate any K-12 instructional intervention. There is no relevant educational methodology or learner/teacher outcome evidence to rate under the requested framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports technical performance improvements in robot motion planning, not educational impact. No K-12 teaching, learning, coaching, or teacher-planning outcomes are studied.

paper_profiles.title: DeBiasMe: De-biasing Human-AI Interactions with Metacognitive AIED (AI in Education) Interventions
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Workshop: AI Augmented Reasoning (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper addresses a gap in AI literacy and human-AI interaction research: how to reduce human cognitive biases such as anchoring, confirmation bias, and automation bias when learners use generative AI tools. The author argues that current AI literacy approaches focus too heavily on technical prompting and on algorithmic/systemic bias, while paying too little attention to the human side of the interaction, especially metacognition and self-regulation.

The paper proposes DeBiasMe, a metacognitive AI in education intervention intended to support bias awareness and critical engagement with AI. The design is built around deliberate friction, bi-directional intervention across both prompt formulation and output interpretation, and adaptive scaffolding for different user needs. Two illustrative components are described: a prompt refinement tool that flags potentially biased prompts before submission, and a bias visualization map that helps users inspect AI outputs for different kinds of bias and their relationships.

The context discussed is higher education, based on a mixed-methods user study with university students using surveys and interviews to identify metacognitive support needs. However, the paper is primarily a conceptual and design-oriented position paper rather than a full evaluation study. Its main conclusion is that bias-aware AI literacy should move beyond operational prompt skills toward metacognitive support that helps students monitor their own reasoning, recognize bias interactions, and use AI more critically and intentionally.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper with conceptual framing and design proposals, not a controlled empirical study. It includes references to prior and ongoing work, but the paper itself does not report a clear experimental or quasi-experimental methodology or outcome estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The proposed intervention has plausible educational value for metacognition and responsible AI use, but the paper provides no measured effect sizes or demonstrated population-level impact. As a result, impact remains promising but unclear based on this paper alone.

interventions.use_case: Metacognitive AI literacy intervention (DeBiasMe) that adds deliberate friction to human-AI workflows via prompt refinement feedback and post-response bias visualization to help students detect and mitigate cognitive biases when using GenAI/LLMs.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the DeBiasMe prototype and its prior user research support improvements in metacognitive knowledge and regulation, helping students become more aware of their own reasoning and bias patterns during AI use. The paper reports that earlier prototype evaluation using usability heuristics, think-aloud studies, and expert reviews suggested the tool made implicit human and AI biases explicit and actionable, but it does not provide controlled effect sizes or inferential statistics.
finding.measure: Metacognitive awareness/regulation, critical thinking during AI interaction; usability heuristics, think-aloud studies, expert reviews, and mixed-method user research

finding.finding_summary: The paper positions DeBiasMe as a bridge between academic integrity policies and students’ everyday GenAI use, with the goal of supporting responsible AI governance in educational settings. This is a conceptual and design-oriented claim rather than an outcome evaluation, so no effect size or sample-based impact estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Policy and governance relevance for academic integrity and responsible AI use

paper_profiles.title: RLHF-Blender: A Configurable Interactive Interface for Learning from Diverse Human Feedback
paper_profiles.venue: Interactive Learning with Implicit Human Feedback Workshop at ICML 2023
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a tooling gap in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF): researchers lack standardized, configurable software for systematically studying how different kinds of human feedback affect reward learning. The authors argue that current approaches are held back by ad hoc interfaces and simplified assumptions about human feedback quality, which makes it difficult to compare feedback types or study human factors such as irrationality, bias, and cognitive demand.

To address this, the paper proposes RLHF-Blender, a modular interactive interface and experimentation framework for collecting and learning from diverse feedback types. The system supports evaluative feedback (ratings), comparative feedback (rankings and pairwise comparisons), corrective feedback (action advice/corrections), demonstrative feedback (demonstrations), and descriptive feedback (feature-level annotations or goal-state descriptions). It also includes a standardized encoding scheme, feedback translation and sampling modules, and reward-model integration to support offline or online experimentation.

The paper is primarily a framework and system design contribution rather than an empirical study. It is positioned for use in RL environments such as BabyAI, Safety-Gym, and HighwayEnv, and the authors outline research opportunities such as multi-type feedback comparison, calibration of human irrationality estimates, continuous calibration, and the effect of explainability on feedback quality. The main conclusion is that RLHF-Blender can enable more systematic and reproducible human-subject studies of diverse feedback in RLHF, though the system itself has not yet been fully evaluated in a large-scale user study.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a framework and interface proposal, not an empirical K-12 study. It does not report a controlled evaluation with student, teacher, or classroom outcomes, and the paper explicitly notes that the system has not yet been fully evaluated in a realistic environment.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational impact is demonstrated because the paper reports no outcome data in K-12 settings. The contribution is methodological and infrastructural, with potential future relevance but no measured effect size or observed impact.

interventions.use_case: A configurable RLHF experimentation framework and interface for collecting diverse human feedback (ratings, comparisons, corrections, demonstrations, descriptions) to train reward models; this is a tooling/framework paper rather than a K-12 instructional intervention.

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Plan by Updating Natural Language
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of helping large language models solve complex tasks by providing them with a usable natural-language task plan. The authors argue that direct zero-shot or few-shot prompting is often insufficient for reasoning-intensive tasks because models may need not just step-by-step answers, but also general behavioral instructions that cover different cases and avoid common errors.

To address this, they propose Learning to Plan, a two-phase method in which the model first iteratively updates a natural-language task plan using error feedback from training examples, and then uses the learned plan to guide test-time inference. The method generates candidate plan updates from wrong examples, validates them on a held-out set, compresses them to remove redundancy, and appends the best updates to the plan. The approach is evaluated on eight reasoning datasets spanning mathematics, causal reasoning, logical reasoning, symbolic reasoning, and combinatorial reasoning, using ChatGPT and also open-source models such as Vicuna.

The paper reports that the learned plans improve performance over zero-shot/few-shot chain-of-thought prompting, self-plan baselines, APE, and kNN selection in most settings. It also finds that plans learned from one LLM can transfer to another LLM, suggesting that natural-language task plans can serve as portable reasoning knowledge. The work is presented as a general prompting and planning framework rather than a human-subject educational intervention.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a computer science method paper using benchmark evaluations, not a K-12 educational intervention study. There is no randomized or quasi-experimental design in schools, no learner sample from K-12 classrooms, and no direct educational implementation evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports benchmark accuracy improvements in reasoning tasks rather than educational impact in K-12 settings. Because it does not evaluate teacher planning or instructional coaching in classrooms, there is no demonstrated K-12 impact to rate.

interventions.use_case: Prompt-based planning and self-refinement for large language models, where an LLM learns a reusable natural-language task plan from error feedback to improve step-by-step reasoning on benchmark tasks.

finding.finding_summary: The method improved performance on mathematical reasoning tasks, including the AMPS benchmark average from 48.3% to 66.6% in zero-shot CoT and from 64.0% to 73.9% in few-shot CoT. On the Math dataset, average accuracy increased from 27.4% to 29.8% in zero-shot CoT and from 30.6% to 31.3% in few-shot CoT, indicating modest but consistent gains across math task types.
finding.measure: Accuracy on math reasoning benchmarks (AMPS and Math datasets)
finding.study_size: n=10 AMPS tasks; n=7 Math tasks

finding.finding_summary: The method improved performance on non-mathematical reasoning tasks, including causal, counterfactual, logical, symbolic, and combinatorial tasks. Average accuracy on the non-math set rose from 54.0% to 66.0% in zero-shot CoT and from 63.5% to 67.1% in few-shot CoT, with the largest single gain on last-letter concatenation (44.6% to 75.2%).
finding.measure: Accuracy on reasoning benchmarks (Causal Judgment, CRASS, LSAT, Date Understanding, Last Letter Concatenation, SayCan)

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates an automatic planning/update procedure that reduces reliance on manual task-plan writing by iteratively generating, validating, and compressing plan candidates. Although no teacher workload measure is reported, the method is explicitly designed to automate plan creation and updating, improving inference performance without human expert-authored plans.
finding.measure: Algorithmic plan-update automation and inference-time use of learned natural-language plans

paper_profiles.title: PresentCoach: Dual-Agent Presentation Coaching through Exemplars and Interactive Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that existing AI presentation coaching tools usually provide either exemplar generation or performance feedback, but not both in an integrated, pedagogically coherent workflow. The authors argue that effective presentation learning requires a cycle of observing a good model, practicing, and receiving targeted reflection-oriented feedback, rather than isolated scoring or script generation.

To address this, they introduce PresentCoach, a dual-agent system with an Ideal Presentation Agent and a Coach Agent. The Ideal Presentation Agent converts a user’s slides and voice sample into a personalized exemplar presentation video, while the Coach Agent evaluates the user’s practice recording against that exemplar and provides structured Observation–Impact–Suggestion feedback, plus conversational follow-up. The system also includes an Audience Agent intended to simulate listener reactions and make feedback feel more human-centered and context-aware.

The study evaluated the system in a controlled between-subjects user study with 24 Mandarin-speaking university students in China who were practicing short English presentations. Participants used either PresentCoach with slides or slide-only self-practice. Quantitative results showed higher post-test speaking confidence in the PresentCoach condition, moderate cognitive workload, and strong usability ratings. Qualitative interviews suggested that the exemplar video and feedback were perceived as complementary, with the exemplar serving as a motivating reference and the coach providing clear, actionable guidance. Overall, the paper concludes that combining personalized demonstration with interactive coaching can reduce anxiety and improve learners’ confidence in presentation rehearsal.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a controlled between-subjects user study with quantitative and qualitative components, but it is small (n=24) and focuses on short-term self-report outcomes rather than objective learning gains. It is stronger than a purely qualitative report, but it does not meet blue/green evidence standards for robust causal evidence in K-12 settings.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows a statistically significant improvement in self-reported presentation confidence, but the sample is small and the outcome is affective rather than a direct academic achievement measure. The impact is therefore promising but still modest and uncertain for broader K-12 educational use.

interventions.use_case: dual-agent presentation coaching system that generates slide-aware exemplar presentations and provides conversational, multimodal feedback on user practice recordings
multimodal evaluation of presentation delivery against an ideal benchmark with structured Observation–Impact–Suggestion feedback
guided presentation rehearsal environment that scaffolds observe-practice-reflect cycles using AI-generated exemplars and feedback

finding.finding_summary: In a controlled between-subjects user study (n=24), PresentCoach+PPT improved self-reported speaking confidence on the PRCS from 3.69±0.81 pre-test to 5.03±0.63 post-test, a +36.3% increase; the within-group change was significant (p=.016). The PPT-only group increased from 3.18±0.65 to 3.69±1.17 (+16.1%) but was not significant (p=.219), and post-test confidence was higher for PresentCoach+PPT than PPT-only, t(22)=2.83, p=.014.
finding.measure: Personal Report of Confidence as a Speaker (PRCS) pre/post scores

finding.finding_summary: The system was usable and cognitively manageable during rehearsal, with moderate NASA-TLX workload (M=2.9, SD=0.8 on a 7-point scale) and high SUS subset usability (M=4.1, SD=0.5 on a 5-point scale). These are descriptive results rather than an effect estimate, but they indicate that the AI coaching workflow did not impose excessive burden while remaining easy to use.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX workload and 5-item SUS usability ratings

finding.finding_summary: Participants rated the dual-agent experience positively, reporting clear role differentiation, complementary guidance, and motivational balance. Quantitatively, items such as role distinguishability (M=6.3, SD=0.6) and complementarity (M=6.1, SD=0.7) were high, suggesting the system supported motivation and confidence during practice.
finding.measure: Custom 7-point dual-agent collaboration questionnaire and interview feedback

paper_profiles.title: Distilling Feedback into Memory-as-a-Tool
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of repeatedly paying the full inference-time cost of self-correction and critique in large language models. The authors argue that iterative refinement methods such as self-critique are effective but ephemeral: the model improves only within a single interaction, and the learning signal is lost when the context resets.

To address this, the paper proposes a Memory-as-a-Tool framework that converts transient evaluator feedback into persistent, file-based memory entries. Instead of storing raw interaction logs, the model abstracts feedback into generalizable guidelines, saves them to a /memories/ directory, and later retrieves relevant notes before answering similar tasks. The system is evaluated on the new Rubric Feedback Bench, which includes rubric-based writing, behavioral, and ethical reasoning tasks, and is compared against zero-shot and inference-time self-critique baselines.

The empirical setting is not a K-12 educational intervention but an LLM benchmark using frontier models such as Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5.1, and Gemini 3 Pro. Across short continual-learning sequences and a longer mixed-task horizon, the memory-augmented approach is reported to match or exceed self-critique performance while substantially reducing cost. The main conclusion is that distilling feedback into persistent memory can amortize reasoning costs and support continual adaptation across tasks.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conference paper with a clearly described evaluation protocol, but it is not a K-12 study and does not use a randomized or quasi-experimental educational design. The evidence is primarily benchmark-based and computational, so it fits a lower internal-validity category for the education evidence framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are meaningful for model performance and cost efficiency, including a clear advantage in rubric-score trajectories and a lower-cost Pareto frontier. However, the impact is indirect for K-12 education because the study is on synthetic/open-ended writing tasks rather than teachers, students, or classroom implementation.

interventions.use_case: memory-augmented large language model agents that use rubric-based feedback, file-based read/write memory, and self-critique to improve generated responses across sequential tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates rubric-based writing tasks and finds that the memory-augmented LLM improves writing quality over time. In continual-learning experiments across 15 examples per model (H=3 per category), the Memory + Feedback approach rapidly matched or exceeded the self-critique baseline after about two feedback rounds; in a long-horizon mixed-task setting (H=12), the memory agent achieved 0.78 ± 0.10 versus 0.52 ± 0.25 without memory on final task scores.
finding.measure: Judge scores on rubric-based writing tasks / open-ended text generation quality
finding.study_size: n=15 per model in continual-learning evaluation; n=12 in long-horizon mixed-task experiment

finding.finding_summary: A central result is that distilling feedback into persistent memory substantially reduces inference-time cost relative to repeated self-critique. The paper reports that Memory + Feedback achieves performance comparable to iterative self-correction while keeping the cost profile much closer to zero-shot generation, because critique is paid for once and retrieval is cheap thereafter.
finding.measure: Average cost per task and cost-score Pareto frontier

paper_profiles.title: AI-Generated Rubric Interfaces: K–12 Teachers’ Perceptions and Practices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K–12 teachers perceive and use AI-supported rubric generation for assessment and feedback in block-based programming contexts. The central question is whether generative AI can help teachers create rubrics more efficiently while still preserving teacher judgment, alignment with instructional goals, and fairness for students.

The intervention studied was a professional development workshop in which teachers used MagicSchool.ai to generate rubrics, compared AI-generated rubrics with manually created ones, and then used the rubrics to assess a sample block-based programming task. Teachers also used the AI chatbot Reina to generate rubric-based feedback on the same work. The workshop included pre- and post-surveys, open-ended reflections, and group discussions, combining quantitative Likert-scale ratings with thematic analysis of qualitative data.

Participants were 25 middle- and high-school teachers in the United States, with most teaching grades 6–8 and a smaller group teaching grades 9–12. The study found that teachers generally viewed AI-generated rubrics as useful starting drafts that improved structure, clarity, and speed, but not as final products. Teachers emphasized that substantial editing and teacher oversight were necessary to address generic wording, grade-level misalignment, and mismatches with instructional priorities. They also saw AI feedback as potentially more detailed and scalable than their own comments, but sometimes too strict. Overall, hands-on exposure increased teachers’ willingness to adopt AI rubric tools, provided the tools support easy customization, transparency, and teacher control.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-method professional development study with survey and thematic analysis, not a causal impact evaluation. It provides credible descriptive evidence about teacher perceptions and intended adoption, but lacks experimental comparison and student outcome data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but indirect benefits mainly for teacher workflow and perceived assessment clarity, with no measured student achievement gains. Reported effects are modest, perception-based, and context-specific to a small sample of K–12 CS teachers.

interventions.use_case: AI-generated rubric creation and rubric-based feedback for K-12 block-based programming assignments, using MagicSchool.ai to draft rubrics and Reina chatbot to generate feedback from the rubric.
Chatbot-mediated rubric-based feedback generation for student coding work during teacher professional development, used as a companion to AI-generated rubric creation.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers consistently viewed AI-generated rubrics as time-saving starting points that reduced the burden of drafting rubrics from scratch. In the workshop sample (n=25), teachers rated the rubric as a flexible starting point (M=3.56, SD=1.31) and reported that AI improved structure and clarity, though editing remained a bottleneck.
finding.measure: Teacher survey ratings and qualitative reflections on rubric creation workload, editability, and usefulness

finding.finding_summary: Teachers expressed conditional willingness to adopt AI rubric tools, but adoption depended on teacher control, LMS integration, district policy fit, and equity safeguards. In the post-survey, perceived confidence in using AI rubrics was moderately positive (M=3.87, SD=1.024), yet usability for adding/removing criteria was notably weak (M=2.75, SD=1.23), indicating institutional barriers to implementation.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of confidence, transparency, bias, and workflow fit; qualitative adoption intentions

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI-generated rubrics clarified criteria and performance-level distinctions, which they believed could help students understand expectations and improve self-regulation in approaching assignments. The strongest positive item was whether the rubric could help students understand how work would be evaluated (M=4.12, SD=0.95), but this was based on perception rather than student outcome measurement.
finding.measure: Perceived student understanding of evaluation expectations and clarity of performance criteria

paper_profiles.title: Data-Efficient Learning of High-Quality Controls for Kinodynamic Planning used in Vehicular Navigation
paper_profiles.venue: Machine Learning for Motion Planning (MLMP) Workshop at ICRA 2021
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of improving the practical performance of kinodynamic motion planning for vehicular robotic systems. The authors focus on the difficulty of obtaining high-quality trajectories when planners rely on random controls for expansion, which often leads to slow convergence and higher-cost paths.

They propose a supervised learning framework that learns a controller offline. The model takes a difference vector between the current state and a local goal state as input and returns a control and propagation duration that should move the system closer to that local target. The training data are generated efficiently using discretization, propagation, pruning, and additional random sampling to ensure target dispersion and retain only higher-quality controls. The paper also introduces two planner-side waypoint-generation strategies: an exploratory sample-based expansion and an exploitative medial-axis-based expansion.

The approach is evaluated in simulation on first-order and second-order differential drive systems in city benchmark environments derived from real-world maps, including Berlin, London, and Boston. The learned controller is integrated into the DIRT kinodynamic planner and compared against random-control baselines and blossom-expansion variants. The paper reports that the learned-controller methods produce lower-cost paths in fewer iterations and less time than traditional random propagation, and that medial-axis expansion further improves path quality and convergence speed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a robotics motion-planning paper, not an education study, and it does not evaluate any K-12 teaching or learning intervention. No education-relevant empirical design is present for the requested taxonomy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports performance improvements for vehicular navigation planning, with no demonstrated impact on K-12 educational outcomes, teacher planning, or instructional coaching.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models, especially ChatGPT, for education. Rather than evaluating a specific intervention, the authors synthesize early research and propose a conceptual overview of how LLMs may support learning and teaching. The paper focuses on uses such as content generation, personalized feedback, assessment support, language learning, tutoring, and teacher assistance, while also discussing major concerns including bias, privacy, copyright, overreliance, misinformation, sustainability, and unequal access.

The paper considers educational contexts across primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional learning, with specific examples for elementary, middle, and high school learners, university students, and teachers. For teachers, it highlights possible uses in lesson planning, differentiated instruction, feedback generation, grading support, and professional development. For students, it discusses LLMs as tools for quizzes, explanations, writing support, and conversational practice, including support for learners with disabilities and multilingual needs.

The authors conclude that LLMs hold substantial promise for education but require cautious, responsible adoption with human oversight, ethical safeguards, and clear pedagogical framing. They argue that future work should focus on evidence-based integration, mitigation of bias and misuse, privacy-preserving deployment, and equitable access so that LLMs enhance rather than distort educational practice.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper, not an empirical study, and it reports no primary research design, sample, or causal identification strategy. Its claims are conceptual and literature-synthesizing rather than experimentally tested.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has potentially broad relevance for K-12 generative AI adoption, but it does not estimate observed impacts or effect sizes. Its practical influence is mainly advisory and interpretive rather than demonstrated through measured outcomes.

interventions.use_case: position paper on ChatGPT and other large language models as educational assistants for tutoring, personalized feedback, lesson planning, and conversational support across K-12 and higher education
LLM/NLP-based automated scoring and adaptive feedback for student writing and other responses, including semi-automated grading and feedback generation
LLM-supported writing, grammar, translation, summarization, and language-learning assistance for students and teachers

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that large language models can support reading and writing through grammar correction, summaries, outlines, translation, and personalized feedback, but it is a position paper rather than a test of literacy outcomes. It does not report effect sizes or study-level literacy gains; the evidence is descriptive and based on cited prior work and examples.
finding.measure: Proposed support for reading comprehension, writing quality, grammar/style correction, summaries, and translation

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests LLMs can support language learning and conversation practice, including oral/written dialogue and vocabulary support, especially for multilingual and language-class contexts. However, no primary empirical evaluation or effect estimate is reported in this paper.
finding.measure: Proposed language practice, conversation support, vocabulary and grammar assistance

finding.finding_summary: A major theme is that LLM use may help prompt critical thinking, problem-solving, curiosity, and fact-checking, while also risking overreliance that could weaken these skills. The paper is conceptual and does not provide measured effects, only arguments and mitigation recommendations.
finding.measure: Proposed critical thinking, problem-solving, curiosity, and fact-checking support/risks

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by generating lesson plans, quizzes, feedback, and summaries, and by semi-automating grading and assessment. It cites prior work suggesting grading effort could be reduced by up to 85% with high precision in large courses, but this paper itself does not present a new evaluation.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, and content-generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses heavily on institutional risks and governance issues such as bias, fairness, privacy, copyright, sustainability, access, and the need for human oversight and policy frameworks. No quantitative institutional outcome is evaluated; the contribution is a conceptual analysis with recommendations for responsible adoption.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, fairness, privacy/security, access, and responsible deployment considerations

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the emerging role of artificial intelligence in education, with a particular emphasis on chatbots and ChatGPT. Rather than testing a specific intervention, the authors synthesize existing literature to explain how AI tools may affect teaching, learning, feedback, assessment, engagement, and educational administration, while also highlighting ethical, privacy, bias, and academic integrity concerns.

The article is a review and conceptual discussion of AI technologies such as chatbots, intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment systems, and personalized learning platforms. It discusses how these tools can provide individualized feedback, support self-directed learning, reduce teacher workload, and assist with administrative tasks. The paper also notes potential benefits for special education, language learning, and student motivation, but frames these as possibilities drawn from prior studies rather than findings from a new empirical sample.

The context is broad K-12 and higher education, though the paper does not report a primary participant sample or a single implementation site. Its main conclusion is that AI, including ChatGPT, has substantial promise for personalized instruction and feedback, but responsible adoption requires attention to fairness, privacy, accuracy, teacher preparation, and human oversight. The paper argues for further research and careful policy and pedagogical integration before wide-scale use.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review/opinion-style article rather than an empirical study. It does not report a systematic search, comparison groups, or original outcome data, so it provides no direct causal evidence on subgroup or school-context differences.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No original measured impact is reported. The paper discusses potential benefits and risks of ChatGPT in education, but it does not estimate effect sizes or demonstrate outcomes in K-12 settings.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual overview of ChatGPT as a generative AI chatbot for educational use, including tutoring, question answering, feedback provision, and teacher support such as lesson planning and student assistance.

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses how artificial intelligence is reshaping education and argues that three capabilities are especially important in AI-adopted classrooms: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. The paper is framed as a conceptual discussion rather than an empirical evaluation, and it uses a case study from Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich, Switzerland, together with a narrative literature review, to motivate its recommendations.

The first part of the paper describes challenges that arose at the Swiss university after the rapid adoption of ChatGPT and other large language models by students and staff. In response, the institution developed internal AI guidelines for academic writing that require transparency about model use, how AI was used, where it was used, and how outputs were critically evaluated. The paper argues that guidelines alone are insufficient and that schools need a broader AI culture supported by workshops, regular updates, financial support, and dedicated expertise.

The paper then broadens to theoretical discussion of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in education. It proposes components of AI literacy courses, describes several prompting methods such as zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, expert prompting, self-consistency, automatic prompt engineering, generated knowledge prompting, and tree-of-thought prompting, and suggests that these approaches can make students more thoughtful users of AI. Overall, the paper concludes that AI should be treated as a sparring partner rather than a tutor or ghostwriter, and that responsible classroom use depends on transparency, critical evaluation, and explicit instruction.

Although the paper mainly focuses on higher education, it notes that the ideas may also be useful for children. It is not an intervention study and does not report subgroup effects, teacher effectiveness outcomes, or K-12 implementation data relevant to specific teacher or school contexts such as middle school, high school, special education, multilingual classrooms, or low-resource schools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual discussion with a narrative literature review and a single institutional case description, not a controlled empirical study. It reports no original quantitative evaluation, effect sizes, or rigorous causal design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has potentially meaningful implications for AI policy and classroom practice, but it does not demonstrate measured impact. Its conclusions are plausible and relevant, yet the evidence base is theoretical and descriptive rather than empirical.

interventions.use_case: Use of ChatGPT and similar large language models as classroom and academic-work support, including as a 'sparring partner' for brainstorming, case-study generation, curriculum suggestions, and student experimentation with prompting in higher education.
