Generative AI used to assist with written academic papers, including drafting, rewriting, and documenting AI-assisted text production in student manuscripts.
AI-driven games and immersive/virtual reality environments used to create interactive classroom learning experiences and practice content in engaging settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking are necessary skills for students and teachers to use generative AI responsibly. It does not report a new quantitative estimate, but it repeatedly frames prompt engineering and critical evaluation of AI outputs as ways to strengthen critical thinking and reduce uncritical dependence on AI.
finding.measure: Conceptual emphasis on AI literacy, prompt engineering competence, and critical thinking development

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that AI tools can help teachers create curricula, case studies, and classroom materials more efficiently, and can support students in drafting and organizing academic work. No empirical effect sizes are reported; the claim is based on a conceptual discussion and case observations from a Swiss university.
finding.measure: Perceived teacher and student productivity, reduced time for curriculum/case-study preparation

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on institutional AI guidelines, training, transparency requirements, and the need for a broader AI culture in schools and universities. It argues that these policy and governance changes are necessary to manage AI use, but provides no empirical evaluation of outcomes.
finding.measure: Institutional policy/guideline development and governance practices

paper_profiles.title: The effect of ChatGPT on students’ learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking: insights from a meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT improves student learning outcomes and under what conditions its effects are strongest. The authors note that prior studies reported mixed findings about ChatGPT’s value in education, so they conducted a meta-analysis to estimate its overall effects on learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking, and to test whether those effects vary by grade level, course type, learning model, duration, role of ChatGPT, and application area.

The study synthesized 51 experimental and quasi-experimental studies published between November 2022 and February 2025, yielding 72 independent effect sizes. The included studies covered primary, secondary, and college settings, but the final moderator analyses for higher-order thinking were based only on college-level studies. ChatGPT was used in a variety of instructional roles, including intelligent tutor, intelligent partner, and intelligent learning tool, across STEM, language/writing, and skills/competencies courses, often in personalized, problem-based, project-based, contextual, or reflective learning arrangements.

Overall, the meta-analysis found that ChatGPT had a large positive effect on learning performance and moderate positive effects on learning perception and higher-order thinking. For learning performance, the strongest effects appeared in skills-and-competencies courses, problem-based learning, and interventions lasting 4–8 weeks. For learning perception, duration was the only significant moderator, with longer interventions producing larger effects. For higher-order thinking, effects varied by course type and were strongest when ChatGPT functioned as an intelligent tutor. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can support learning when used in well-structured ways, but they also emphasize the need for appropriate scaffolds and more evidence from broader contexts.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis of 51 experimental/quasi-experimental studies with explicit inclusion criteria, effect-size computation, heterogeneity tests, publication-bias checks, and sensitivity analyses. The design is high credibility for causal synthesis, though most primary studies are varied in context and the paper does not focus on K-12 subgroup differences.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The synthesized effects are medium-to-large and consistently positive for learning performance (g=0.867), perception (g=0.456), and higher-order thinking (g=0.457). However, the evidence is not specifically K-12 subgroup-focused and much of the sample is college-based, so the impact for the user’s target K-12 subgroups is only indirectly supported.

interventions.use_case: Meta-analysis of ChatGPT use as an intelligent tutor, intelligent partner, and intelligent learning tool for student learning tasks, including tutoring, assessment/feedback, and personalized recommendations across K-12 and college contexts.

finding.finding_summary: Across 44 independent effects, ChatGPT had a large positive effect on learning performance (Hedges g=0.867, 95% CI 0.683 to 1.052). The meta-analysis included 51 studies and found the strongest performance gains in skills/competencies development and problem-based learning contexts, with effects moderated by course type, learning model, and duration.
finding.measure: Learning performance tests/exams; post-test standardized mean differences
finding.study_size: n=varied across 44 independent effects from 51 studies

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT showed a moderately positive effect on learning perception across 19 independent effects (g=0.456, 95% CI 0.287 to 0.625). The paper reports that longer interventions were associated with larger gains in perception, with the >8 week subgroup showing the strongest effect (g=1.054).
finding.measure: Learning perception scales/questionnaires

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT had a moderately positive effect on higher-order thinking across 9 independent effects (g=0.457, 95% CI 0.255 to 0.650). The strongest effects were reported when ChatGPT acted as an intelligent tutor (g=0.945), and effects varied by course type, with STEM-related courses showing the largest gains.
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking scales/questionnaires (e.g., critical/creative thinking dimensions)

paper_profiles.title: What if the devil is my guardian angel: ChatGPT as a case study of using chatbots in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates the concerns and opportunities of using chatbots in education, focusing on ChatGPT as a representative case of generative AI. The authors ask what concerns arise when chatbots are used in educational contexts and examine the topic through a three-stage instrumental case study.

The study combines social network analysis of tweets about ChatGPT and education, content analysis of 19 publicly posted interviews from early users, and hands-on user experience testing by three experienced educators over one week. The population is not a K-12 sample; instead, it is made up of early adopters and educators/students who discussed or used ChatGPT, including participants from the United States, China, the United Kingdom, and other locations. The paper therefore addresses higher-education and general education use rather than school-specific implementation.

The main conclusions are that ChatGPT is viewed as highly promising for educational transformation, lesson design, feedback, and learning support, but it also raises substantial concerns about cheating, inaccurate or misleading responses, fairness, privacy, manipulation, and weak emotional/personality modeling. The authors argue against simple bans and instead recommend new teaching philosophies, stronger guidelines, upskilling in prompt/critical-thinking competencies, and the development of responsible, transparent, and human-centered chatbots for education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative instrumental case study using sentiment analysis, interviews, and educator scenarios rather than an experimental or quasi-experimental design. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically structured, but it does not provide causal evidence of learning effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful institutional and instructional implications, but it reports no quantitative impact estimates on student outcomes or teacher performance. Its contribution is mainly conceptual and cautionary, so the observed impact is unclear and modest at best.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a conversational AI case study for education, including lesson-planning support, instructional design assistance, quiz and assessment generation, answer generation, and student/teacher question answering in early-adopter educational scenarios.

finding.finding_summary: Participants generally viewed ChatGPT as useful for saving teacher time, generating outlines, quizzes, and immediate feedback, and helping with instructional design (n=19 interviewees plus 3 educators in user testing). However, the study also found that outputs were sometimes inaccurate, inconsistent, or poorly structured, which could increase rather than reduce teacher workload when results required verification or revision.
finding.measure: Qualitative interview themes and educator user-experience scenarios on lesson/material creation and feedback support

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly raises concerns that ChatGPT can weaken critical thinking, encourage cheating, and reduce independent problem solving, while also noting that effective use requires prompt skill, question formulation, and critical evaluation. Evidence is qualitative and descriptive rather than quantitative, drawn from interviews, tweets, and 10 user-experience scenarios.
finding.measure: Qualitative judgments about critical thinking, cheating, prompt skill, and user competencies
finding.study_size: n=22 (plus 2330 tweets and 10 scenarios, all analyzed qualitatively)

finding.finding_summary: Users reported ChatGPT as exciting, fun, and sometimes emotionally engaging, but also noted disappointment because it lacks genuine empathy, emotions, and human-like reflection. The paper presents these as qualitative experience findings rather than measured emotional outcomes.
finding.measure: User experience and interview reports on enjoyment, emotional attachment, empathy, and human-like interaction

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that ChatGPT is generating policy, ethics, and governance concerns in schools, including cheating bans, privacy, fairness, misinformation, and responsible-use guidelines. Evidence comes from social media discourse (2330 tweets), interviews, and scenario analysis, showing both enthusiasm for adoption and caution about regulation and school-level controls.
finding.measure: Sentiment analysis of tweets, qualitative interview themes, and scenario-based institutional concerns

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT in higher education: Considerations for academic integrity and student learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines how ChatGPT was being discussed in mainstream news coverage about higher education in early 2023. Rather than testing an educational intervention directly, the paper asks what themes dominated public and institutional discussion of generative AI, especially around academic integrity, learning opportunities, assessment redesign, and policy responses.

The study uses qualitative content analysis of 100 English-language news articles from Australia, New Zealand, the United States, and the United Kingdom. The articles were selected because they discussed ChatGPT in relation to academic integrity, teaching responses, or institutional policy in tertiary education. The coded material emphasized university responses, cheating concerns, AI detection, assessment adaptation, and the potential for ChatGPT to support learning through feedback, drafting, plain-language explanations, and other pedagogical uses.

The paper concludes that public discussion was dominated by concerns about cheating and avoidance, while more constructive uses of ChatGPT for learning and equity were less visible. It also found that university voices were much more prominent than student voices, and that discussion of accessibility, multilingual support, and other equity benefits was limited. The authors argue that universities should move beyond bans and instead develop clearer policies, redesigned assessments, and more intentional strategies for helping students use AI ethically and productively.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed content analysis of news coverage, not an intervention study and not a causal evaluation of student or teacher outcomes. It provides useful descriptive context but lacks experimental design, comparison groups, or direct measures of educational impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The article suggests potentially important institutional and pedagogical implications for generative AI in education, especially around assessment and equity, but it reports no direct outcome effects. Its relevance is high, yet the empirical impact is unclear because the study analyzes discourse rather than measured educational change.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT as a generative AI tool for student support in higher education, including brainstorming, drafting, grammatical feedback, plain-language explanations, and potential feedback on student work.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can support writing through drafting, grammatical feedback, generating citations, and simplifying complex concepts, which may help students produce text more effectively. At the same time, it emphasizes risks to writing development because students may bypass the learning process and rely on AI-generated text; this article does not report original effect sizes or experimental learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Content analysis of news articles discussing writing support, feedback, and learning implications

finding.finding_summary: A major theme in the discussion is that ChatGPT may either support or undermine critical thinking and independent learning. The article repeatedly notes that AI could help students brainstorm and understand complex ideas, but also warns that overreliance may reduce critical thinking by letting students bypass the struggle that supports learning; no quantitative effect estimates are reported.
finding.measure: Content analysis of references to critical thinking, learning process, and assessment design

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes ChatGPT as potentially improving efficiency for teachers and students by generating first drafts, rubrics, practice quiz questions, and feedback, and by saving time on routine writing tasks. However, it also notes that the main public discourse framed the tool as a cheating risk, and no empirical productivity measures are reported.
finding.measure: Content analysis of reported uses for task completion and feedback generation

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that public and institutional responses to ChatGPT were dominated by academic integrity concerns, policy uncertainty, bans, and assessment redesign. Across 100 articles, mentions of banned policies (n=18), allowed use (n=10), and undecided policy positions (n=22) show that institutions were still adapting rather than converging on a clear approach.
finding.measure: Content analysis of media coverage of university policies and responses

paper_profiles.title: The Manifesto for Teaching and Learning in a Time of Generative AI: A Critical Collective Stance to Better Navigate the Future
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a manifesto-style, critical collective position paper examining the growing role of generative AI (GenAI), chatbots, and algorithms in teaching and learning. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it asks how educational systems should respond to GenAI’s promises and risks, especially around personalization, efficiency, assessment, creativity, equity, human agency, and ethics. The authors frame GenAI as non-neutral and argue that it can both support and undermine educational values depending on how it is designed, governed, and used.

The paper is based on collective writing using a modified Delphi process with a panel of educators and researchers from higher education institutions worldwide. The population is therefore not K-12 students or teachers but higher education experts contributing reflections from their own practice and scholarship. The context is higher education and broader educational systems, with discussion of potential uses such as tutoring, lesson planning, formative feedback, multilingual support, and collaborative learning, alongside risks such as bias, misinformation, academic integrity issues, and digital inequality.

The main conclusions are normative rather than empirical: GenAI should be adopted cautiously, with human oversight, ethical safeguards, and evidence-based research guiding use. The authors call for institutions to develop policies, infrastructure, and professional development, while preserving human relationships, critical thinking, and equity. They emphasize that GenAI may enhance education only if it complements rather than replaces human judgment, and they warn that uncritical adoption could deepen inequality and reduce authentic learning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an editorial/manifesto using collective writing and Delphi-informed reflection, not an empirical evaluation of an intervention. It does not present a testable study design, comparison group, or outcome data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No measurable intervention effect is reported, and the paper offers conceptual arguments rather than evidence of impact on learners, teachers, or institutions.

interventions.use_case: Critical manifesto about generative AI, chatbots, and large language models in teaching and learning, including AI-assisted feedback, tutoring, lesson planning, and classroom interaction in higher education contexts.

paper_profiles.title: Investigating High School and Pre-High School Teachers’ Perceptions and Experiences Introducing Quantum Concepts: A Survey of QuanTime and other Quantum-related Activities
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers perceive and experience the use of QuanTime and other quantum-related activities for introducing foundational quantum concepts. The central question is whether these packaged, ready-to-use activities are feasible, engaging, and curriculum-compatible for pre-high school and high school classrooms, and whether teachers see them as useful for building early quantum literacy and student interest in quantum science and technology.

The intervention/approach studied is a set of QuanTime quantum-learning activities and related quantum resources, which include hands-on, interactive lessons on topics such as wave-particle duality, electron transitions, art and polarization, entanglement, and quantum games. The study used a survey with 12 Likert-scale items and open-ended questions. Teachers were grouped into pre-high school (grades 4-8) and high school (grades 9-12) categories, and were recruited through the National Q-12 Education Partnership. Of 132 teachers contacted, 36 completed more than 60% of the survey; 12 were pre-high school teachers and 23 were high school teachers, with one additional outreach coordinator/informal educator.

Findings suggest generally positive teacher perceptions across both grade bands. Most teachers reported that the activities fit their curriculum, were manageable to implement, and engaged students without requiring substantial extra preparation or support. High school teachers tended to report slightly stronger agreement than pre-high school teachers on many items, including curriculum fit, student enjoyment, and classroom engagement. Teachers also expressed strong interest in using the activities again. Open-ended responses emphasized that the activities were easy to integrate, visually engaging, and useful for sparking curiosity, though some teachers noted that more support would help with more advanced questions and that younger students sometimes needed more time and scaffolding. Overall, the study concludes that QuanTime is a promising teacher-friendly resource for early quantum education in K-12 settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/descriptive survey study with self-selected respondents and no experimental comparison, so causal inference is limited. The paper provides useful implementation evidence, but it relies on teacher self-report rather than direct student outcome measures.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests modestly positive implementation and engagement effects, but the impact is unclear because outcomes are based on perceptions rather than measured learning gains. The study is relevant to K-12 quantum education, yet it does not demonstrate medium or large effects on student achievement or broader system outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-facing packaged quantum science classroom activities (e.g., Wave-Particle Duality, Electron Transitions, Art & Polarization) used to introduce foundational quantum concepts in middle and high school lessons

finding.finding_summary: This survey study found that teachers viewed QuanTime and related quantum activities as supporting students' learning of foundational quantum concepts and their ability to discuss quantum phenomena. Across 36 respondents (12 pre-high school, 23 high school, plus 1 outreach coordinator), most teachers agreed that the activities fit their curriculum, were manageable to implement, and helped students engage with concepts such as wave-particle duality and electron transitions; average Likert ratings for perceived student learning/engagement were generally above 5.0 on a 7-point scale.
finding.measure: Teacher Likert-scale ratings and open-ended feedback on student learning, engagement, and interest in quantum concepts

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that students enjoyed and were engaged by the quantum activities, with particularly strong endorsement from high school teachers. On average, teachers rated student enjoyment at 5.8/7 and engagement at 5.7/7 overall, and 87% of high school teachers and 82% of pre-high school teachers said they would like to do the activities again next year.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported student enjoyment, engagement, and willingness to repeat activities

finding.finding_summary: Open-ended responses suggested that the activities prompted curiosity, discussion, and collaborative work, especially around visually rich concepts like wave-particle duality and entanglement. Teachers noted students asking deeper questions and working in groups to collect results and plot graphs, indicating some support for critical thinking and collaboration, though these outcomes were not directly measured with standardized instruments.
finding.measure: Qualitative teacher feedback on student questioning, group work, and sense-making

finding.finding_summary: Teachers generally reported that the activities were easy to integrate and did not require substantial extra preparation or support. Mean ratings were 4.0/7 for needing more preparation time and 3.6/7 for wanting more support, suggesting low implementation burden; open-ended comments repeatedly described the materials as ready-to-use and simple to implement.
finding.measure: Teacher survey ratings on preparation time and implementation support; qualitative implementation feedback

paper_profiles.title: Experience gravity in the classroom using the rubber sheet: an educational proposal from the collaboration between University and School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of teaching General Relativity and related modern physics topics in high school in a way that is accessible, playful, and usable by teachers. The authors argue that while GR is important for helping students understand contemporary scientific discoveries, it is difficult to teach rigorously at the secondary level because of its mathematical demands.

The paper presents an educational proposal built around the rubber sheet analogy, including a low-cost DIY spacetime simulator and eight step-by-step educational cards. The materials were co-developed through collaboration between university researchers and Italian high school teachers, with iterative feedback used to refine the activity so it could be implemented autonomously in classrooms. The cards cover topics from Newtonian gravity and Kepler’s laws to gravity assist, binary systems, gravitational lensing, black holes, and gravitational waves.

The population targeted is high school students, especially those around the age at which Kepler’s laws are typically taught in the Italian system, along with the teachers who would implement the activity. The context is Italian high school outreach and teacher professional development connected to Roma Tre University. The paper concludes that the rubber sheet approach can help teachers introduce GR in a structured, low-cost, and engaging way, and it reports positive initial feedback from teachers and students, though the work is primarily descriptive and developmental rather than a controlled effectiveness study.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed educational proposal with some empirical classroom feedback, but the reported evidence is descriptive and qualitative rather than a rigorous controlled study. The paper references pre/post questionnaires and teacher feedback, yet does not provide full methodological details or statistical results in the article itself.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The proposed activity appears potentially useful for high school science learning, especially for conceptual understanding of general relativity. However, the impact is only qualitatively described and no effect size is reported, so the demonstrated impact remains unclear.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that a rubber-sheet analogy activity for teaching general relativity in high school improved students’ understanding of gravity-related concepts. In a pre/post questionnaire study with more than 200 high school students, the authors state there was a "remarkable improvement" in knowledge, especially for topics like Kepler’s laws, black holes, and gravitational lensing; however, no effect sizes, CIs, or SDs are reported.
finding.measure: Pre- and post-questionnaires assessing comprehension/knowledge of general relativity and gravity-related concepts

paper_profiles.title: Need of AI in Modern Education: in the Eyes of Explainable AI (xAI)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book chapter examines the role of explainable AI (xAI) in modern education, with a focus on transparency, interpretability, and fairness in high-stakes educational decision-making. Rather than studying a classroom intervention, it argues conceptually that AI systems used in education can reproduce or amplify social bias, especially when decisions are tied to socioeconomic variables such as parental income.

The chapter uses the Adult Census Income dataset and an XGBoost classifier as a worked example to demonstrate several post-hoc explanation and fairness methods, including permutation importance, SHAP, LIME, surrogate decision trees, and FairML. The central question is not about student outcomes, but about how different explanation methods reveal model behavior and whether they are sufficient to detect unfairness.

The population and context are not K-12 teachers or students; the empirical example is an adult census dataset, used to proxy parental income and its relationship to educational opportunity. The chapter concludes that common feature-importance methods may miss important bias signals, while FairML surfaces dependence on sensitive attributes such as race, nationality, and sex. The authors argue that educational AI should prioritize transparency, equal opportunity, and accessibility, and that bias mitigation remains an important unresolved challenge.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/book-chapter-style discussion with a single illustrative modeling exercise rather than a rigorous educational intervention study. It is not an RCT or QED, and the paper does not evaluate K-12 outcomes or subgroup effects with a clear causal design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not provide measurable K-12 impact estimates or evidence of improved student or teacher outcomes. Its main contribution is methodological and normative, focusing on explainability and fairness concerns rather than demonstrated educational effects.

interventions.use_case: Explainable AI / model interpretability and fairness auditing for educational decision-making, using XGBoost, decision trees, LIME, SHAP, and FairML on the Adult Census Income dataset to illustrate bias and transparency issues in education-related access contexts

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that AI in education can improve transparency and policy-making in principle, but its own empirical example shows persistent bias and fairness problems in model-based educational decision contexts. Using the Adult Census Income dataset (n=not_reported), the authors show that fairness auditing via FairML reveals dependence on sensitive attributes such as race, nationality, and sex, even when other explanation methods (e.g. SHAP) do not surface these biases clearly.
finding.measure: Model fairness / bias audit using explanation methods (FairML, SHAP, LIME) on income-prediction models as a proxy for educational opportunity access

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents AI and XAI as tools that can speed up decision-making, improve transparency, and support data-driven educational policy and performance monitoring. However, these claims are conceptual rather than experimentally evaluated, and no direct effect sizes on teacher workload or administrative efficiency are reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of AI-assisted transparency, explainability, and decision support

paper_profiles.title: Perspectives on astronomy: probing Norwegian pre-service teachers and middle school students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines astronomy knowledge, beliefs, and pedagogical perspectives among two Norwegian groups: pre-service science teachers and middle school students. The authors ask whether an adapted astronomy questionnaire can reveal how these groups understand astronomy concepts, how they reason about science-related questions, and whether their responses change before and after astronomy instruction.

To study this, the authors translated and adapted the Introductory Astronomy Questionnaire into Norwegian (the NIAQ) and administered it to pre-service teachers enrolled in Science II at Norway’s largest teacher education institution, as well as to students from eight middle schools in and around Oslo. The teacher sample completed the questionnaire before and after astronomy instruction; the middle school sample was split into a year 8 pre-test group and year 10 post-test group, reflecting their exposure to the standardized astronomy module.

The study reports that pre-service teachers improved on several astronomy explanation tasks after instruction, but also showed an unexpected decline in pedagogical responses when asked how they would answer hypothetical students. Middle school students showed little or no improvement on key astronomy knowledge items between year 8 and year 10, and their scores on distance/size tasks were strongly stratified by gender. The authors conclude that the NIAQ can surface useful insights into astronomy understanding and teaching perspectives, and that some misconceptions persist even after instruction, especially among middle school students.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/observational instrument study with pre/post comparisons, not a randomized controlled trial. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically careful, but evidence credibility is limited by nonrandom samples, descriptive analysis, and ongoing/incomplete reporting of results.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports some meaningful conceptual gains for pre-service teachers, but the observed effects are largely descriptive and no effect sizes are reported. The most policy-relevant finding is the decrease in pedagogical responses, which is important but not quantified as a generalizable intervention effect.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports substantial pre/post changes in astronomy conceptual understanding for pre-service teachers, including significant gains in explaining astronomical objects and more complex concepts such as why Earth remains in stable orbit. For middle school students (n=535 year 8 pre-test; n=387 year 10 post-test), however, there was little to no improvement on size/distance reasoning tasks; year 10 scores were statistically identical to or slightly lower than year 8 scores, and many misconceptions remained above 40%-60% prevalence.
finding.measure: Free-response explanations of astronomical objects; ranking tasks on sizes and distances in the universe; multiple-choice astronomy concept responses
finding.study_size: n=41 pre-service teachers; n=535 year 8 students; n=387 year 10 students

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that pre-service teachers’ positive views of physics and astronomy started high and did not change significantly pre- to post-instruction. For middle school students, similarly high baseline opinions about how interesting and important physics/astronomy are also showed no significant change after instruction.
finding.measure: Likert-style ratings of interest in physics/astronomy, perceived importance to society, and belief that there is more to discover
finding.study_size: n=41 pre-service teachers; n=535 year 8 students; n=387 year 10 students

finding.finding_summary: On prompts asking pre-service teachers what they would say to hypothetical year 10 students, pedagogical responses dropped sharply after instruction: more than one-third were pedagogical pre-instruction, but fewer than 10% were pedagogical post-instruction, with the remainder mostly authoritative. This suggests a deterioration in student-centered explanatory stance after the course rather than improvement.
finding.measure: Categorization of free-response explanations as pedagogical vs authoritative

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teacher-in-the-loop use of generative AI can support personalized mathematics task design in middle school, and how that process affects both teacher workflow and student perceptions. The central question is whether teachers should remain involved when using large language models to adapt tasks to students’ interests, and whether such involvement leads to useful personalization or simply adds time and complexity.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers used ChatGPT (with GPT-4o) to modify existing Illustrative Mathematics problems so they were more aligned with their students’ interests, especially popular culture references. The teachers participated in training on personalization, bias, readability, and cultural relevance, then worked through two curriculum units while prompting ChatGPT in Zoom sessions that were recorded and logged. Their 521 students completed the personalized assignments in ASSISTments and provided closed-ended ratings and open-ended feedback.

The study found that teachers used a wide range of prompts to adjust grain size, realism, age appropriateness, location, names, readability, and mathematical clarity. Students generally preferred finer-grained, specific references, while teachers often worked at broader interest categories and spent substantial effort correcting realism issues. Personalization took about 4 minutes per problem on average, and it did not become clearly faster over time; in fact, teachers used more prompts and more time in the second unit, although student ratings improved. The authors conclude that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can support professional learning and oversight, but it is time-intensive and may not achieve the small-grain personalization many students prefer.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory qualitative/mixed-methods study with descriptive and correlational analyses, not a randomized controlled trial. It provides useful evidence about teacher prompting and student reactions, but credibility is limited by the absence of a control group and reliance on observational data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows modest positive effects on student interest ratings under certain prompting conditions, but the primary efficiency finding is negative and direct learning outcomes were not measured. Overall impact is unclear-to-modest for K-12 practice, especially beyond the specific middle school math context.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-in-the-loop use of ChatGPT/GPT-4o to personalize middle school mathematics word problems to students’ interests, including prompting, revising, and checking realism, readability, and mathematical clarity.

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily evaluates personalized middle school math problem creation, not direct achievement. Students’ ratings of the personalized problems’ interestingness and closeness to their interests were significantly higher when teachers used 3-5 prompts, by about 0.24 points on a 5-point scale (B=0.240, SE=0.085, t=2.84, p=0.0073). However, the study did not measure standardized math performance or learning gains, so evidence on numerical achievement remains indirect.
finding.measure: Student ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to interests on 1-5 scales
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.24 interestingness; SD=1.28 closeness for rating items; problem creation SD=2.6 prompts

finding.finding_summary: Students generally responded favorably to personalized math tasks when the popular-culture reference matched their interests, but disliked tasks when the reference did not match. Across 454 responses to the interestingness question, 163 implied the problem was interesting versus 243 implying it was not, and the paper reports slightly higher average ratings in Unit 6 than Unit 4 for interestingness (2.56 vs 2.27) and closeness (2.66 vs 2.28), with the increase statistically significant (B=0.33, SE=0.095, t=3.49, p=0.0012).
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests; open-ended feedback on interest
finding.study_size: n=521 students; 454 open-ended responses for interest question
finding.std_deviation: Unit 4 interestingness SD=1.17; Unit 6 interestingness SD=1.26; Unit 4 closeness SD=1.20; Unit 6 closeness SD=1.29

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-facing personalization with ChatGPT was time-intensive rather than time-saving. Teachers used an average of 3.2 prompts per problem and spent about 246 seconds (roughly 4 minutes) per problem overall; in the second unit, time increased to 286 seconds per problem and prompts increased to 4.6 per problem, indicating no efficiency gains with iteration and a statistically significant increase in time (B=70.4 seconds, SE=29.6, t=2.38, p=0.0189).
finding.measure: Teacher time to create each personalized problem and number of prompts used
finding.std_deviation: SD=165.7 seconds per problem; SD=2.6 prompts per problem

paper_profiles.title: Cosmic rays studied with a hybrid high school detector array
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes a hybrid detector setup for cosmic ray research that also serves education and outreach purposes in Dutch high schools. The authors present the LORUN/NAHSA system, which combines radio antennae and particle detectors to detect air showers from very high energy cosmic rays in coincidence. The project is framed as a pathfinder to extend cosmic ray detector arrays on high school buildings while giving students hands-on experience with scientific instrumentation.

The intervention/approach is not an instructional study in the usual sense, but a technology-and-outreach implementation in which high school students helped set up particle detectors on school buildings and the system was linked to university-based radio antennas. The setting is the Netherlands, primarily Nijmegen, where the NAHSA high school array triggered LORUN observations. The paper explains the hardware, triggering, data acquisition, and offline analysis pipeline used to match radio and particle signals.

The main results are engineering/observational rather than educational outcomes. The authors report three candidate cosmic ray events detected between January and August 2005, showing that the hybrid system worked as intended. They conclude that the setup demonstrates the feasibility and educational potential of combining radio and particle detection at high schools, and argue that additional development could eventually make such hybrid arrays more broadly available to high school students.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a physics/astronomy pathfinder report on cosmic ray detector hardware and student participation, not an education intervention study. It contains no evaluative methodology relevant to K-12 instructional technology, teacher feedback/coaching, or subgroup comparisons.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no measured educational impact, teacher outcome, or school-context effect reported. The paper only notes outreach and student involvement in building detectors, without evidence of learning or coaching outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Quadratic Forms and Automorphic Forms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a set of revised lecture notes on quadratic forms and automorphic forms, originally prepared for a graduate-level Arizona Winter School course. It surveys foundational theory rather than reporting an empirical study. The text develops basic definitions and classification results for quadratic forms over fields and rings, including equivalence, direct sums, orthogonal decomposition, local invariants, lattice duals, Jordan decomposition, and local-global principles such as the Hasse-Minkowski theorem.

A major second theme is the connection between quadratic forms and modular/automorphic forms through theta functions. The paper explains how theta series encode representation numbers of quadratic forms, why they converge, and how Poisson summation leads to modular transformation laws. It then situates these theta series inside the theory of modular forms, including weight, level, character, cusp forms, and Eisenstein series, and uses these ideas to discuss asymptotic representation results such as Tartakowski's theorem.

The intended audience is graduate students in mathematics, and the context is a theoretical lecture-note setting rather than a classroom intervention or education study. No educational population, teacher subgroup, school context, or generative-AI-related intervention is studied. The conclusions are mathematical: they summarize classical results and methods and provide a pathway from quadratic forms to automorphic forms and related arithmetic applications.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mathematics lecture note / survey on quadratic forms and automorphic forms, not an empirical education or AI intervention study. It contains no K-12 design, participants, outcomes, or evaluation methodology relevant to the research topic.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention or student/teacher outcome is evaluated, so there is no impact evidence to code for K-12 settings, teacher subgroup differences, or school context effects.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT, for education. Rather than evaluating a specific classroom intervention, it surveys potential uses of LLMs for learning, teaching, assessment, feedback, content generation, and educational technology design, while emphasizing risks such as bias, plagiarism, overreliance, privacy, and the difficulty of distinguishing machine-generated from human-generated text.

The paper discusses applications across educational levels and roles, including primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional learning, with particular attention to teachers’ uses of LLMs for lesson planning, personalized feedback, assessment support, and professional development. It also considers broader human-AI interaction issues such as transparency, fact checking, continuous human oversight, and the need for critical thinking and digital literacy when integrating LLMs into education.

The main conclusion is that LLMs have substantial promise for enhancing educational experiences and supporting teachers, but their adoption should be cautious, ethical, and human-centered. The authors argue for strong governance, verification practices, bias mitigation, privacy protections, and ongoing human monitoring, and they recommend that education systems develop competencies and curricula that help learners and educators use these tools responsibly.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper and grey literature-style conceptual review rather than an empirical study. It provides recommendations and cites prior work, but does not present a controlled methodology or original outcome evaluation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has broad relevance for education practice and policy, especially around human oversight and verification of LLM output, but it reports no original effect estimates. Its impact is therefore important conceptually, yet empirically unclear.

interventions.use_case: position paper on educational uses of large language models and ChatGPT for student support, teacher assistance, lesson planning, feedback generation, and instructional workflows in education

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can support reading and writing through summaries, explanations, grammar/style suggestions, and feedback, but also warns that generated text may be inaccurate, biased, or plagiarized. These claims are conceptual rather than based on a new empirical study, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of reading and writing support, grammar/style correction, summaries, and feedback quality

finding.finding_summary: A major theme is that LLMs may help build critical thinking, problem-solving, curiosity, and fact-checking skills when used as a supplement, but may also weaken them if learners rely on model output uncritically. The paper offers mitigation strategies such as verification, human review, and curriculum design, but does not report empirical estimates.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of critical thinking, problem-solving, fact-checking, and curiosity

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly claims that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by automating or semi-automating lesson planning, personalized feedback, assessment, quiz generation, and text revision. It cites prior work suggesting grading effort could be reduced by up to 85% in large courses, but this position paper itself does not run a new evaluation.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, and efficiency of feedback/lesson-material generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s core contribution is a policy and governance argument: LLMs in education require human oversight, transparency, privacy protections, bias mitigation, and guidance on verification and integrity. It frames adoption as promising but contingent on institutional controls and responsible deployment rather than presenting empirical effects.
finding.measure: Governance, privacy, bias mitigation, oversight, and responsible deployment considerations

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how artificial intelligence is changing educational practice and argues that effective use of AI in classrooms depends on three core competencies: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. The author frames current concerns around large language models such as ChatGPT, including hallucinations, overreliance by students, unclear academic integrity boundaries, and educator uncertainty about how to use AI responsibly. Rather than testing a specific AI product or intervention, the article develops a conceptual argument for how schools and universities should respond.

The paper is grounded in a case study of Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich, Switzerland, where informal discussions with students and staff informed the creation of internal AI guidelines. These guidelines emphasize transparency about AI use, critical evaluation of outputs, and limits on direct copying from generative systems. The paper then extends the case with a narrative literature review on AI literacy and prompting methods, and it proposes practical educational strategies such as AI literacy courses, workshops, regular updates for staff, and integrating AI across curricula.

The paper’s main conclusion is that banning AI entirely or allowing it without restrictions are both inadequate. Instead, institutions should create an AI culture that prepares students and educators to use generative systems as sparring partners rather than authoritative sources. The author argues that teaching prompt engineering and critical evaluation can improve both responsible use of AI and the quality of human-AI interaction in education, while reducing risks such as hallucinations and passive dependence on machine-generated outputs.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual discussion and narrative literature review with an illustrative case study, not an empirical evaluation of an intervention. There is no controlled design, no outcome measurement, and no quantitative evidence to assess causal credibility.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper offers potentially useful institutional guidance and practical recommendations, but it does not report measurable impact. Any influence on K-12 practice is therefore indirect and currently unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Use of ChatGPT and other large language models as classroom and academic-work sparring partners for brainstorming, case-study creation, curriculum suggestions, and student experimentation with prompting in K-12-relevant AI literacy instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI literacy and prompt engineering can strengthen students’ critical thinking, problem-solving, and metacognitive checking of AI outputs. No quantitative effect sizes are reported; the support is conceptual and based on narrative review plus a case study from a Swiss university context (n not reported).
finding.measure: Conceptual claims about critical thinking, critical evaluation of AI outputs, and responsible prompting; no standardized outcome measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper recommends institutional AI guidelines, workshops, dedicated budgets, paid AI-support roles, and ongoing staff/student training to improve human-AI interaction and governance in schools and universities. These are proposed solutions rather than tested interventions, and no effect sizes or sample sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Institutional policy and governance practices for AI use; transparency/documentation requirements; staff development structures

paper_profiles.title: The role of ChatGPT in higher education: Benefits, challenges, and future research directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the potential benefits and challenges of ChatGPT in higher education, using constructivist learning theory as the main conceptual lens. Rather than reporting an empirical intervention, it synthesizes existing literature and offers a perspective on how generative AI may reshape teaching, learning, assessment, administration, and research support in tertiary education.

The paper organizes ChatGPT’s potential into five benefits: adaptive learning, individualized feedback, support for research and data analytics, automated administrative services, and innovative assessment design. It also identifies five major challenges: ethical and equity concerns, maintaining academic integrity, potential bias and falsified information, inability to adequately evaluate graduate skill sets, and difficulty assessing learning outcomes. The discussion emphasizes that ChatGPT can be useful when it supports active, constructivist learning and human judgment.

The context is higher education, with intended users including students, academics, and administrative staff. The authors argue that institutions should promote AI literacy, responsible use, equitable access, and assessment designs that focus on learning processes rather than easily reproduced outputs. They conclude that ChatGPT should augment rather than replace human instruction, and that effective use depends on balancing innovation with caution, oversight, and ethical safeguards.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective/theoretical article rather than an empirical study. It offers conceptual arguments and propositions about ChatGPT in higher education, but no original data, design, or causal identification strategy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper describes potentially broad institutional and pedagogical implications, but provides no empirical evidence of effect magnitude. Its impact is therefore conceptually important yet empirically unverified.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a conversational AI for higher education support, including adaptive learning interactions, individualized feedback, research and writing assistance, automated administrative help, and assessment generation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can support writing tasks, language translation, drafting, and feedback for academic writing, but it also warns that outputs may contain hallucinations, fabricated references, and biased or falsified information. No original empirical effect estimate is reported; the claims are theoretical and literature-based rather than experimentally tested.
finding.measure: Writing and research support; quality/accuracy of AI-generated text and references

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests ChatGPT may increase engagement and support personalized, self-regulated learning through immediate feedback and adaptive interaction, but it also cautions that overreliance can reduce active learning and human interaction. No empirical effect sizes are reported because this is a perspective paper.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, self-regulated learning, interaction quality

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is ChatGPT’s implications for critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and graduate skill development. The authors argue it may scaffold these skills when used appropriately, but may also weaken them if students use it for superficial, shortcut-based learning. No empirical estimate is provided.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and related graduate skills

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims ChatGPT can reduce workload by automating administrative support and some elements of feedback and assessment, potentially saving time and costs for educators and institutions. At the same time, it warns that accuracy checking and human oversight are still necessary, so efficiency gains may be offset by verification demands.
finding.measure: Administrative support efficiency, feedback/assessment workload, time and cost savings

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes institutional-level implications such as academic integrity, equity of access, copyright, policy development, AI literacy, and assessment redesign. It does not report empirical outcomes, but argues that institutions must create governance and training structures to use ChatGPT responsibly.
finding.measure: Academic integrity, equity, policy, assessment design, AI literacy

paper_profiles.title: Speculative Futures on ChatGPT and Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Collective Reflection from the Educational Landscape
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what promising and problematic futures may emerge as ChatGPT and other generative AI tools become more visible in education. Rather than evaluating a specific intervention with participants, the authors use speculative methodology and collective writing to generate fictional future narratives that explore how conversational AI might reshape educational practices, roles, ethics, and institutional norms.

The paper focuses on imagined educational contexts rather than a single empirical sample. The narratives span higher education, school settings, language learning, and broader instructional uses, and they are written by a globally diverse group of education scholars. These vignettes consider uses such as personalized learning, automated assessment, translation, feedback, collaboration, and accessibility support, alongside risks such as bias, privacy loss, surveillance, over-reliance, academic integrity problems, and teacher replacement.

The main conclusion is that generative AI in education is neither uniformly beneficial nor inherently harmful; its effects depend on how it is positioned, governed, and integrated. The authors argue for critical AI literacy, human-centered educational practice, and careful attention to ethics, equity, and the continued role of educators. They conclude that AI should support, not displace, human agency in education, and that future educational change will require rethinking assessment, pedagogy, and the value of human versus AI-generated contributions.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a speculative, collective reflection paper using fictional narratives rather than an empirical design. It does not report a systematic methodology, measured outcomes, or inferential evidence relevant to intervention effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear conceptual relevance to K-12 and education policy, especially around human oversight, trust, and AI use norms, but it offers no measurable intervention impact. Its contribution is primarily agenda-setting and interpretive rather than demonstrably effective.

interventions.use_case: Speculative discussion of ChatGPT and similar generative AI chatbots as educational assistants for tutoring, feedback, translation, lesson support, and conversational interaction in schooling and higher education.
Speculative use of ChatGPT-like systems for automated grading, immediate feedback on assignments, and generating quiz/test questions.
Speculative use of conversational AI for writing support, language learning, translation, and improving grammar/vocabulary/pronunciation through text and voice interaction.
Speculative mobile AI applications used for on-device language practice, conversational coaching, and accessible learning support in low-resource contexts.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI may support writing, translation, grammar checking, and language learning, but also warns that it may reduce originality, creativity, and authentic writing development. These claims are speculative rather than empirical, with no sample size, effect size, or quantitative literacy outcome reported.
finding.measure: Speculative discussion of writing, translation, grammar, and creative writing outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents generative AI as potentially improving language skills through instant feedback, translation, pronunciation practice, and conversational interaction. Examples include a mobile AI used for oral and written English practice and a chat-based coach for language tasks, but no quantitative outcomes are reported.
finding.measure: Speculative language practice, pronunciation, oral/written conversation support

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly frames AI as both supporting and potentially undermining durable skills such as critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, and learner agency. It argues that AI may help with idea generation and collaborative learning, but over-reliance could weaken critical thinking and problem-solving; no empirical effects are reported.
finding.measure: Speculative discussion of critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, and learner agency

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests generative AI can save teachers time by handling routine work such as lesson planning, grading, summarizing, writing emails, and generating assessments. These are argued benefits of ChatGPT-like tools, but the paper provides no empirical estimate, sample size, or effect size.
finding.measure: Speculative teacher workload reduction and productivity gains

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI could broaden access, inclusion, and multilingual participation, but it also raises concerns about equity gaps, privacy, ethics, bias, surveillance, and institutional dependence on commercial platforms. The discussion is conceptual and speculative, with no empirical system-level effect size reported.
finding.measure: Speculative institutional access, equity, governance, privacy, and policy implications

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a review article that explores the transformative potential of artificial intelligence in education, with particular attention to chatbots and ChatGPT. Rather than evaluating a specific intervention, the authors synthesize prior literature to explain what AI is, how chatbots work, and how generative AI systems such as ChatGPT might be used across educational settings. The paper frames AI as a set of technologies that can support personalized learning, instant feedback, assessment, administrative efficiency, and student engagement.

The article discusses both benefits and risks. On the benefit side, it highlights AI-supported feedback, tutoring, grading, language learning, and support for teachers and administrators. On the risk side, it emphasizes ethical issues such as bias, privacy, deception, over-reliance, limited human interaction, and threats to academic integrity. The authors argue that effective adoption requires pedagogical alignment, teacher preparation, and responsible use policies.

Because the paper is conceptual and literature-based, it does not report a primary sample, intervention duration, or outcome evaluation in a specific school setting. Its main conclusion is that ChatGPT and related AI tools may substantially change education, but only if educators, researchers, and policymakers address ethical concerns and ensure appropriate support and oversight.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review/opinion-style article with no original empirical design, no comparison groups, and no statistical testing of outcomes. It synthesizes prior literature and discusses implications, so it does not meet the credibility standards for causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper describes potentially meaningful impacts of generative AI on teaching efficiency and learner experience, but it provides no direct effect estimates or new outcome data. The practical implications are plausible but remain unclear and unquantified in this study.

interventions.use_case: A narrative review of ChatGPT and related generative chatbot systems for educational use, including conversational support, question answering, feedback, and instructional assistance in teaching and learning contexts.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT and related AI tools can reduce teacher workload by automating repetitive tasks such as grading, assignment evaluation, and providing feedback, thereby freeing time for lesson planning and student support. This is a conceptual synthesis rather than a measured intervention study, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: teacher workload, grading/feedback automation, administrative efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The review claims AI-supported learning can increase motivation, engagement, confidence, and reduce anxiety, citing prior studies on chatbot and AI tutoring applications. However, these claims are aggregated from prior literature and not newly tested in this paper; no single effect size is reported here.
finding.measure: motivation, engagement, confidence, anxiety

finding.finding_summary: The article suggests AI tools may support higher-order skills such as critical thinking, creativity, self-reflection, and self-regulation by providing personalized feedback and step-by-step guidance. These are theoretical claims grounded in cited literature rather than direct empirical results from the paper itself.
finding.measure: critical thinking, creativity, self-regulation, self-reflection

finding.finding_summary: The paper highlights both the transformative potential of AI in education and substantial institutional risks, including privacy, bias, academic integrity, accountability, and the need for teacher training and governance. Because the article is a narrative review and policy discussion, it does not provide quantitative estimates of institutional impact.
finding.measure: ethics, privacy, bias, academic integrity, teacher preparedness, governance

paper_profiles.title: A large-scale comparison of human-written versus ChatGPT-generated essays
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how well ChatGPT-3 and ChatGPT-4 can write argumentative student essays, how these AI-generated essays compare with human-written essays, and which linguistic features distinguish them. The authors frame the study as important for education because generative AI may change how homework and writing are assessed, and because educators need evidence about the quality and structure of AI-generated text.

The study used 90 argumentative essay topics from an existing essay corpus. For each topic, the authors compared one human-written essay from an online forum used by German high-school students with essays generated by ChatGPT-3 and ChatGPT-4 using a simple zero-shot prompt. The essays were evaluated by 111 secondary-school teachers who had participated in an online training session about ChatGPT and NLG systems. Teachers rated six essays each on seven criteria covering topic relevance, logic, expressiveness, language mastery, complexity, vocabulary and text linking, and language constructs; they also reported confidence and English self-assessment. The authors additionally computed linguistic measures such as lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, nominalization, modals, epistemic markers, and discourse markers.

The main finding is that both ChatGPT models produced essays rated significantly higher than the human-written student essays across all assessment criteria, with ChatGPT-4 outperforming ChatGPT-3 on several dimensions. The paper also finds systematic linguistic differences: AI essays were more structured, used more nominalizations, and showed different patterns in discourse markers and modality. The authors conclude that generative AI is already strong enough to affect school writing tasks and that educators should rethink homework and writing instruction, emphasizing critical evaluation, reasoning, and appropriate use of AI tools rather than simple essay production.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed observational comparative study with a strong multi-rater design, but it is not randomized and does not evaluate an educational intervention in K-12 classrooms. The evidence is rigorous for benchmarking generated writing quality, yet it is still a correlational/assessment study rather than a causal impact study.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests that generative AI can produce high-quality argumentative writing and may affect homework and writing instruction, but it does not test student learning gains or classroom outcomes. Its practical impact is potentially meaningful, but the direct educational effect is unclear and not measured in K-12 implementation.

interventions.use_case: zero-shot ChatGPT-generated argumentative essay writing for high-school-style essay prompts, compared against human-written student essays
human teacher evaluation of AI-generated versus human-written essays using an essay-rating rubric

finding.finding_summary: Teachers rated ChatGPT essays higher than human-written student essays on all rubric criteria for argumentative writing. Mean overall scores were 3.69 for humans, 4.36 for ChatGPT-3, and 4.68 for ChatGPT-4; differences between humans and ChatGPT were significant with medium-to-very-large effects (human vs ChatGPT-3 d=0.52 to 1.15; human vs ChatGPT-4 d=0.88 to 1.43).
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of argumentative essay quality across topic/completeness, logic/composition, expressiveness, language mastery, complexity, vocabulary/text linking, and language constructs
finding.std_deviation: Human overall SD=1.26; ChatGPT-3 overall SD=1.14; ChatGPT-4 overall SD=1.11

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT-4 outperformed ChatGPT-3 on several writing-quality dimensions, including logic/composition, vocabulary/text linking, and complexity. The reported effects were small-to-medium (d=0.45 to 0.50), with mean overall scores rising from 4.36 for ChatGPT-3 to 4.68 for ChatGPT-4.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of essay quality comparing ChatGPT-3 and ChatGPT-4 outputs
finding.study_size: n=180 AI-generated essays (90 topics per model)
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT-3 overall SD=1.14; ChatGPT-4 overall SD=1.11

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the potential of artificial intelligence tools in educational measurement and assessment
paper_profiles.venue: EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review article examines how artificial intelligence, especially large language models, can be used across the educational measurement and assessment process. The paper addresses the promise of AI for improving efficiency, personalization, and feedback while also acknowledging risks such as bias, privacy concerns, plagiarism, and overreliance on automation. It is framed as a conceptual discussion rather than an empirical study.

The article surveys a broad set of AI tools and applications in education, with particular emphasis on large language models such as ChatGPT, BARD, and related NLP-based systems. It walks through potential uses in test purpose specification, blueprint development, item generation, instruction writing, item selection, administration, scoring, interpretation, appraisal, and reporting. The paper also discusses the role of teachers in AI-based assessment, arguing that educators remain essential for designing assessments, interpreting results, providing contextual judgment, and ensuring ethical use.

The context is general education and classroom assessment, with examples drawn from educational measurement rather than a specific intervention, school level, or participant sample. The paper concludes that AI can improve educational assessment when used alongside human oversight, but that its implementation requires stakeholder participation, transparency, training, and safeguards against bias and misuse. It recommends collaborative strategies for maximizing AI’s benefits while mitigating its limitations.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review/opinion-style article with no original empirical design, no comparison group, and no quantitative evaluation of outcomes. It is peer-reviewed, but the evidence strength for causal claims is low because the paper is primarily conceptual and descriptive.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for potentially meaningful improvements in assessment efficiency and quality, but it provides no measured effect sizes or outcome data. Its likely impact is therefore unclear and mostly theoretical rather than demonstrated in K-12 settings.

interventions.use_case: Use of large language models such as ChatGPT, Bing, and Bard to support classroom assessment tasks including test purpose/specification, blueprinting, item generation, instructions, assembly/selection, administration, scoring, interpretation, analysis, and reporting.
AI-generated feedback and scoring for student written responses, essays, and test results, including automated essay scoring and interpretive feedback on strengths, weaknesses, and next steps.
Use of AI to analyze student performance, attendance, engagement, and assessment data to flag at-risk students and support targeted intervention decisions.
Computer-based testing, digital assessment, learning management, and formative assessment tools used to deliver assessments and collect responses in educational settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI and LLMs can substantially reduce teacher workload by automating test item generation, scoring, reporting, and other assessment tasks. It describes these tools as enabling faster assessment workflows and immediate feedback, but it does not report original quantitative effects.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, assessment processing time, and efficiency of assessment tasks

finding.finding_summary: The review claims AI-supported assessment can improve the accuracy, validity, and reliability of educational measurement, including better alignment of items to objectives and more consistent scoring. These are conceptual claims rather than empirically estimated effects, and no sample size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Validity, reliability, assessment accuracy, and alignment of test items to learning objectives

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests AI-based assessment can support critical thinking by prompting students to reflect on automated feedback and by helping teachers foster higher-order thinking through better assessment design. This is presented as a theoretical benefit with no quantitative evaluation.
finding.measure: Critical thinking and reflective thinking in assessment contexts

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that AI in educational assessment could transform assessment systems, but it also highlights concerns about transparency, bias, privacy, cost, and stakeholder participation. The overall institutional implication is mixed: potentially transformative, but contingent on governance, ethics, and implementation quality.
finding.measure: Assessment system transformation, governance, transparency, and stakeholder acceptability

paper_profiles.title: Curriculum Engineering: Organisation, Orientation, and Management
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a curriculum engineering and assessment framework focused on the organisation, orientation, and management of educational programmes. It emphasizes curriculum mapping, competency alignment, career assessment, compliance, traceability, audit readiness, and the use of logical modelling tools such as logigrams and algorigram structures. The stated purpose is to equip educators, curriculum developers, and organisational managers with a structured approach to designing, implementing, and evaluating curriculum frameworks.

Rather than reporting an empirical study, the text functions as a descriptive and instructional framework document. It outlines inputs, processes, and outputs for curriculum development; discusses advantages and disadvantages of the proposed system; and describes principles of management-system information investigation, research methodology, and audit. It also references lesson-plan development, assessment preparation, and quality assurance procedures, suggesting how the framework can be operationalised in educational settings.

No participant sample, intervention study, or evaluation data are reported. The document appears to be a conceptual or training-oriented resource intended for educators and curriculum professionals, with examples drawn from qualification development, assessment systems, and engineering-related curriculum design. Its main conclusion is that structured, traceable, and auditable curriculum engineering processes can support compliance, innovation, and alignment with career pathways.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a grey-literature style curriculum/assessment document with no clear empirical study design, sample, comparison group, or statistical analysis. It does not present peer-reviewed evidence evaluating an AI or educational intervention.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report measurable outcomes, effect sizes, or impact on learners, teachers, or institutions. It is primarily descriptive and speculative, so no evidence of impact can be inferred.

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT as a Lesson Planning Assistant with Preservice Secondary Mathematics Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how preservice secondary mathematics teachers used ChatGPT as a lesson-planning assistant in a methods-course microteaching assignment. The authors were interested in two related questions: how the preservice teachers reacted to ChatGPT’s mathematical output, and what they found useful or not useful when using ChatGPT during lesson planning. The study is positioned against the broader problem that preservice teachers often struggle with lesson planning and that generative AI may provide both support and misleading output.

The intervention consisted of a structured, course-based activity in which each preservice teacher first solved a mathematics task independently, then asked ChatGPT to solve the same task and to generate an aim and objectives for a mini-lesson. Students reflected on the chatbot’s answers, revised their lesson-planning materials, and continued using ChatGPT informally over several weeks while developing a microteaching lesson. Data came from reflective written responses and lesson-planning artifacts, and analysis focused on qualitative coding of those reflections and outputs.

The participants were 22 preservice secondary mathematics teachers in two sections of a methods course at a public urban university in the northeastern United States. Most were undergraduate students, with a smaller group of graduate career changers. The findings suggest that preservice teachers were generally selective and critical users: they often improved their aim/objectives using ChatGPT, but none used its output unchanged. However, many students failed to recognize mathematical inaccuracies in ChatGPT’s problem solutions, even when their own solutions were correct. Overall, the paper concludes that ChatGPT can be a helpful starting point for lesson planning, but effective use requires reflective evaluation, especially for mathematical correctness and pedagogical quality.
